title: Exercise: Linear systems in R and solution spaces
text:
Background
A bulk expression sample is a mixture of cell types. With known signatures (columns of \(A\)) and a measured bulk profile \(\mathbf{b}\), the cell-type amounts \(\mathbf{x}\) satisfy \[
A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.
\]
The shape of \(A\) tells you a lot. Let \(A\) have \(m\) rows (genes / equations) and \(n\) columns (cell types / unknowns):

\(m = n\), \(A\) non-singular \(\to\) exactly one solution (well-determined).
\(m > n\), equations conflict \(\to\) no exact solution (over-determined). Use least squares for the closest fit.
\(m < n\), or \(A\) singular \(\to\) infinitely many solutions (under-determined).

Two key facts:

\(A\) (square) is singular when one equation is a combination of the others — it carries no new information. Its columns are then not independent, and solve() stops with an error. (Bonus, not for exam: then \(\det A = 0\).)
The rank of \(A\) is the number of genuinely independent equations. Full rank (\(=n\)) with a square \(A\) is exactly the unique-solution case.

title: Exercise: Linear systems in R and solution spaces
text:
By hand
Decide the solution space before running any R. For a \(2\times 2\) system, each equation is a line in the \((x_1, x_2)\) plane; the solutions are where the lines meet.

Problem 1 — classify three systems
For each, state whether it has one, none, or infinitely many solutions, and explain in one sentence (lines crossing / parallel / identical).

\(\;x_1 + x_2 = 4,\quad x_1 - x_2 = 0\)
\(\;x_1 + x_2 = 4,\quad 2x_1 + 2x_2 = 7\)
\(\;x_1 + x_2 = 4,\quad 3x_1 + 3x_2 = 12\)



Problem 2 — which deconvolution scenario?
Match each situation to one solution / no solution / infinitely many, and to well- / over- / under-determined:

You measure 5 marker genes to resolve 3 cell types, data is exact and consistent.
You measure 2 marker genes to resolve 3 cell types.
You measure 3 marker genes to resolve 3 cell types, signatures all distinct and independent.

title: Exercise: Linear systems in R and solution spaces
text:
In R

Step 1 — solve a well-determined system
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(8, 9)

x <- solve(A, b)
x
# expected: 3 2

A %*% x          # should reproduce b = c(8, 9)


Step 2 — confirm your by-hand classifications
Run each system from Problem 1 through solve and read the result or the error message.
# (a) one solution
solve(matrix(c(1, 1, 1, -1), 2, byrow = TRUE), c(4, 0))

# (b) no solution (inconsistent, singular A)
solve(matrix(c(1, 1, 2, 2), 2, byrow = TRUE), c(4, 7))
# Error: ... system is exactly singular ...

# (c) infinitely many (consistent, singular A)
solve(matrix(c(1, 1, 3, 3), 2, byrow = TRUE), c(4, 12))
# Error: ... system is exactly singular ...
Note that solve gives the same “singular” error for (b) and (c): it cannot tell “no solution” from “infinitely many”. Use the diagnostics below to distinguish them.


Step 3 — diagnose without solving
A_bc <- matrix(c(1, 1, 2, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
qr(A_bc)$rank    # 1   -> only one independent equation (of 2 unknowns)
det(A_bc)        # 0   -> bonus: the same verdict from the determinant
Use qr$rank and dim to characterise a system before trying to solve it.


Step 4 — an over-determined system and least squares
Five genes, two cell types, noisy data: no exact solution, so find the best fit.
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 3,
              1, 1,
              3, 2,
              0, 2), nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE)   # 5 genes, 2 cell types
b <- c(8.1, 8.9, 5.2, 10.8, 4.1)               # noisy measurements

# solve(A, b) would error: A is not square. Use least squares:
xhat <- qr.solve(A, b)
xhat

# Same answer via linear regression (no intercept):
coef(lm(b ~ A - 1))

# How far off is each equation? (the residuals)
A %*% xhat - b
We return to least squares and why it is the right notion of “closest” when we cover projection (Vectors, dot product & projection) and regression later.

title: Exercise: Linear systems in R and solution spaces
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — building the matrix





Use matrix with byrow = TRUE so the numbers read in the same row order as the equations. Print the matrix and check it against the equations before solving.









Hint 2 — reading the lines (Problem 1)





Two lines either cross once (one solution), are parallel and distinct (no solution), or are the same line (infinitely many). Compare the coefficient ratios to the right-hand-side ratio: e.g. in (b) the left sides differ by a factor 2 but the right sides (\(4\) vs \(7\)) do not.









Hint 3 — matching scenarios (Problem 2)





Count \(m\) = number of marker genes (equations / rows) and \(n\) = number of cell types (unknowns / columns). Then use the shape rule: \(m > n\) is over-determined, \(m < n\) is under-determined, \(m = n\) with independent signatures is well-determined. “Exact and consistent” data means the extra equations agree, so an over-determined-by-shape system can still land on one exact solution; with noise it would have none and need least squares.









Hint 4 — what solve’s error means





solve errors with “system is exactly singular” for both no-solution and infinitely-many cases, and with “‘a’ must be a square matrix” for any non-square \(A\). The error tells you the system is not well-determined, but not which of the two singular cases it is.









Hint 5 — distinguishing none vs infinitely many





Both have singular \(A\). Check consistency: does \(\mathbf{b}\) lie in the column space? A practical check for these small cases is whether the proportionality of the rows of \(A\) is also matched by \(\mathbf{b}\). In Problem 1, (b) breaks it (\(4 \to 7\) is not \(\times 2\)) so no solution; (c) preserves it (\(4 \to 12\) is \(\times 3\)) so infinitely many.









Hint 6 — least squares functions





For an over-determined (tall, non-square) \(A\), use qr.solve(A, b) or fit a no-intercept regression with lm(b ~ A - 1) and read coef. The - 1 drops the intercept so the model is purely \(A\mathbf{x}\).

title: Exercise: Linear systems in R and solution spaces
text:
Solutions






Solution






Problem 1

One solution. Adding the equations: \(2x_1 = 4 \Rightarrow x_1 = 2\), then \(x_2 = 2\). The two lines cross once. (Solution \(x_1 = x_2 = 2\).)
No solution. Left sides are proportional (\(2\times\)) but right sides are not (\(4 \times 2 = 8 \ne 7\)). The lines are parallel and distinct — they never meet.
Infinitely many. The second equation is exactly \(3\times\) the first (including the right side: \(3 \times 4 = 12\)). It is the same line; every point on \(x_1 + x_2 = 4\) is a solution.



Problem 2

5 genes, 3 cell types, consistent \(\to\) over-determined by shape but consistent, so it happens to have one solution here (with exact data the extra equations agree). With noise it would have no exact solution and need least squares.
2 genes, 3 cell types \(\to\) under-determined, infinitely many solutions — too few markers to resolve the cell types.
3 genes, 3 cell types, independent \(\to\) well-determined, one solution.



R, step by step
Step 1 — the well-determined system. First confirm the answer by hand so you know what to expect. The system is \(2x_1 + x_2 = 8\) and \(x_1 + 3x_2 = 9\). From equation 1, \(x_2 = 8 - 2x_1\); substitute into equation 2: \[
x_1 + 3(8 - 2x_1) = 9 \;\Rightarrow\; x_1 + 24 - 6x_1 = 9
\;\Rightarrow\; -5x_1 = -15 \;\Rightarrow\; x_1 = 3,
\] then \(x_2 = 8 - 2(3) = 2\). So \(\mathbf{x} = (3, 2)\), which is what solve returns.
A <- matrix(c(2, 1, 1, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
solve(A, c(8, 9))           # 3 2
A %*% c(3, 2)               # 8 9  (check: reproduces b)
Step 2 — confirm the classifications. (a) is the one-solution system; adding the two equations gives \(2x_1 = 4\), so \(x_1 = 2\) and \(x_2 = 2\) — solve returns 2 2. (b) and (c) both have a singular \(A\), so solve throws the same “system is exactly singular” error for both and cannot tell them apart.
solve(matrix(c(1, 1, 1, -1), 2, byrow = TRUE), c(4, 0))   # 2 2
# (b) and (c) both throw "system is exactly singular"
Step 3 — diagnostics. For the (b)/(c) matrix, row 2 is \(2\times\) row 1, so only one of the two rows is independent (rank 1). (Bonus: the determinant is \(1\cdot2 - 1\cdot2 = 0\).) Rank \(1 < 2\) unknowns confirms the system is not unique without even attempting to solve it.
A_bc <- matrix(c(1, 1, 2, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
qr(A_bc)$rank    # 1   (< 2 unknowns -> not unique)
det(A_bc)        # 0   (bonus)
Step 4 — over-determined system, least squares. \(A\) is \(5\times 2\) (tall), so solve(A, b) would error (“‘a’ must be a square matrix”). qr.solve returns the least-squares estimate — the \(\mathbf{x}\) minimising \(\|A\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}\|^2\) — and lm(b ~ A - 1) gives the same numbers (the - 1 removes the intercept). The residual vector \(A\hat{\mathbf{x}}-
\mathbf{b}\) is not all zeros: that is the signature of an over-determined system — no exact fit exists, and least squares returns the closest compromise.
A5 <- matrix(c(2,1, 1,3, 1,1, 3,2, 0,2), nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE)
b5 <- c(8.1, 8.9, 5.2, 10.8, 4.1)

qr.solve(A5, b5)            # 2.508511 2.089362
coef(lm(b5 ~ A5 - 1))       # A51 2.508511   A52 2.089362  (same values)

A5 %*% qr.solve(A5, b5) - b5
# row residuals, not zero:
# -0.9936170 -0.1234043 -0.6021277  0.9042553  0.0787234

title: Exercise: Linear systems in R and solution spaces
text:
Where this leads

Vectors, dot product & projection explains why least squares is the right “closest” answer, through the geometry of vectors, dot products, and projection.
The full treatment of regression and constrained (non-negative) deconvolution comes later in the course; today’s unconstrained solve/lm is the stepping-stone, not the production tool.

title: Exercise: dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
In R
Read the standard pipeline as a recipe (no packages are installed here — nothing runs), then reproduce the neighbour step yourself in base R.

The standard Seurat pipeline
library(Seurat)
# `seu` is the QC-ed, normalized object from the preprocessing unit

seu <- ScaleData(seu)
seu <- RunPCA(seu, npcs = 50)
ElbowPlot(seu)                       # how many PCs to keep? (scree/elbow)

seu <- FindNeighbors(seu, dims = 1:30, k.param = 15)  # kNN graph in PC space
seu <- FindClusters(seu, resolution = 0.5)            # Leiden/Louvain communities
seu <- RunUMAP(seu, dims = 1:30)                      # 2D layout, display only

DimPlot(seu, reduction = "umap", label = TRUE)        # UMAP coloured by cluster
Note the two calls that share dims = 1:30: FindNeighbors and RunUMAP both start from the same top-30 PCs, and FindClusters works on the graph that FindNeighbors built — not on the UMAP.


Reproduce the kNN step in base R
# the six toy cells, already reduced to 2 PCs
Z <- rbind(
  A = c(0, 0), B = c(1, 0), C = c(0, 1),
  D = c(5, 5), E = c(6, 5), F = c(5, 6))

D2 <- as.matrix(dist(Z))     # all pairwise Euclidean distances
round(D2, 2)

# two nearest neighbours of each cell (column 1 of each sort is the cell itself)
apply(D2, 1, function(col) names(sort(col))[2:3])


Tasks
R1. Type in the Z matrix and run as.matrix(dist(Z)). Confirm the distances match your hand answers from B1.
R2. Run the apply(...) line. Confirm the two-nearest-neighbour lists match your B2 answers, and that each cell’s neighbours are its own group-mates.
R3. Change \(k\) from 2 to 3 conceptually: with only three cells per group, what happens when a cell must pick a third neighbour? Predict whether the two groups stay separate, then reason about it (you may modify the [2:3] index to [2:4] to check).
R4. In the Seurat block, which single line would you edit to (a) keep more principal components, (b) get more clusters, (c) change how many neighbours each cell connects to? Name the argument in each case.

title: Exercise: dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — Euclidean distance (B1)





The distance between points \(\mathbf{a}=(a_1,a_2)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(b_1,b_2)\) is \(\sqrt{(a_1-b_1)^2 + (a_2-b_2)^2}\) — the Pythagorean length of the difference vector. For A\((0,0)\) and B\((1,0)\) that is \(\sqrt{1^2+0^2}=1\). In R this is one call to dist.









Hint 2 — nearest neighbours (B2)





For each cell, compute its distance to the other five and keep the two smallest. The three “origin” cells (A, B, C) are all within distance \(\le \sqrt{2}\approx1.41\) of each other, while any origin-to-far distance is \(\ge\sqrt{50}\approx7.07\) — so a cell’s nearest neighbours are always in its own group.









Hint 3 — communities (B3)





A connected group is a set of nodes you can reach from one another by following edges. If no edge ever links an origin cell to a far cell, the graph falls into two separate pieces. Graph-based clustering (Leiden / Louvain) returns one cluster per such densely connected community.









Hint 4 — why PCA first (B4)





Think about (i) noise: single-cell counts are noisy, and distances in 2000 noisy dimensions are dominated by scatter, whereas the top PCs concentrate the real signal; (ii) speed/stability: computing neighbours in 30 dimensions for thousands of cells is far cheaper and more stable than in 2000. This is the denoising role of PCA from Choosing components & pitfalls.









Hint 5 — reading a UMAP (B5)





The rule from the lecture: local grouping is trustworthy; axes, inter-cluster distances, and island sizes are not. Same island ⇒ similar (OK). Anything that reads a number off the axes, or treats the gap between islands or the area of an island as quantitative, is not legitimate.









Hint 6 — resolution (B6)





Higher resolution ⇒ more, smaller clusters; lower resolution ⇒ fewer, larger clusters (monotone). There is no true number of clusters — the right granularity depends on the biological question. Validate a cluster against known marker genes, not against which picture looks tidiest (previewing cell-type annotation).









Hint 7 — the R neighbour step (R1–R3)





dist(Z) returns pairwise Euclidean distances; wrap it in as.matrix to get a full labelled matrix. For each row, sort puts the cell itself first (distance 0), so its nearest neighbours are entries 2:3. To take three neighbours instead of two, index 2:4.

title: Exercise: dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. Using \(\sqrt{(\Delta \text{PC}_1)^2 + (\Delta \text{PC}_2)^2}\):


A\((0,0)\)–B\((1,0)\): \(\sqrt{1^2+0^2} = 1\).


A\((0,0)\)–C\((0,1)\): \(\sqrt{0^2+1^2} = 1\).


B\((1,0)\)–C\((0,1)\): \(\sqrt{(1)^2+(1)^2} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\).


A\((0,0)\)–D\((5,5)\): \(\sqrt{5^2+5^2} = \sqrt{50} \approx 7.07\).


D\((5,5)\)–E\((6,5)\): \(\sqrt{1^2+0^2} = 1\).


The within-group distances (\(1\) and \(\sqrt2\)) are tiny next to the between-group distance (\(\sqrt{50}\)).
B2. By symmetry the far group (D, E, F) mirrors the near group (A, B, C). Distances: within each group the two “axis” cells are at distance \(1\) from the corner and \(\sqrt2\) from each other. Two nearest neighbours (\(k=2\)):

A → B \((1)\), C \((1)\) → \(\{B, C\}\)
B → A \((1)\), C \((\sqrt2)\) → \(\{A, C\}\)
C → A \((1)\), B \((\sqrt2)\) → \(\{A, B\}\)
D → E \((1)\), F \((1)\) → \(\{E, F\}\)
E → D \((1)\), F \((\sqrt2)\) → \(\{D, F\}\)
F → D \((1)\), E \((\sqrt2)\) → \(\{D, E\}\)

The graph: A–B, A–C, B–C form a triangle; D–E, D–F, E–F form a second triangle. No edge ever crosses between the two triangles.
B3. The graph splits into two connected groups: \(\{A, B, C\}\) and \(\{D, E, F\}\). No path of edges links one triangle to the other. A graph-based clustering algorithm (Leiden/Louvain) would return 2 clusters, because each triangle is a community densely connected within itself and disconnected from the other — exactly the “two cell populations” answer we wanted.
B4. Any two of:

Denoising. Single-cell counts are noisy; in 2000 gene-dimensions the Euclidean distance is dominated by random scatter, so neighbours computed there are unreliable. The top ~30 PCs concentrate the coordinated (biological) variation and discard per-gene noise, so distances — and hence neighbours — are more meaningful.
Speed and stability. Finding nearest neighbours for thousands of cells is far cheaper and numerically more stable in ~30 dimensions than in 2000; the whole downstream pipeline (kNN, UMAP, clustering) runs faster and more reproducibly.
(Also acceptable: PCA removes redundancy — co-regulated genes are highly correlated, so 2000 genes carry far fewer than 2000 independent directions.)

B5.


Legitimate. Same tight island = neighbours in the graph = similar expression. Local structure is what UMAP preserves.


Not legitimate. Inter-cluster distances in a UMAP are not quantitative — a bigger gap does not mean “more different”. You cannot compare gaps.


Not legitimate. Island size / spread reflects the layout algorithm’s crowding control, not biological variability or cell count. To compare abundance, count the cells; to compare variability, look in PC or expression space.


Legitimate. Several clearly separated islands is reasonable evidence of several populations — a qualitative, local reading. (It still needs confirmation by marker genes.)


Not legitimate. The UMAP axes have no interpretation; never report or reason from an axis value.


B6. Fewest to most clusters: resolution \(0.2\) < \(0.8\) < \(2.0\). Resolution and cluster count move together (monotone): raising it lets the community-detection algorithm split groups more finely, lowering it merges them. There is no correct number of clusters — the right granularity depends on the biological question (broad lineages vs fine subtypes), and pushing resolution too high eventually splits noise into fake “types”. Before believing a cluster, check it against known marker genes (does it express a coherent, recognisable programme?), not against which resolution produced the tidiest picture. This is the handoff to cell-type annotation.
R1. as.matrix(dist(Z)) gives (rounded):
     A    B    C    D    E    F
A 0.00 1.00 1.00 7.07 7.81 7.81
B 1.00 0.00 1.41 6.40 7.07 7.81
C 1.00 1.41 0.00 6.40 7.81 7.07
D 7.07 6.40 6.40 0.00 1.00 1.00
E 7.81 7.07 7.81 1.00 0.00 1.41
F 7.81 7.81 7.07 1.00 1.41 0.00
The A–B, A–C entries are \(1\), B–C is \(1.41=\sqrt2\), A–D is \(7.07=\sqrt{50}\), D–E is \(1\) — matching B1 exactly.
R2. apply(D2, 1, function(col) names(sort(col))[2:3]) returns, for each column (cell), its two nearest neighbours:
     A   B   C   D   E   F
[1,] "B" "A" "A" "E" "D" "D"
[2,] "C" "C" "B" "F" "F" "E"
Every cell’s two neighbours are its own group-mates — identical to the hand answer in B2. (sort puts the cell itself, distance 0, first, so we take entries 2:3.)
R3. With \(k=3\) each cell must add a third neighbour, but there are only two other cells in its own group. The third-nearest cell is therefore in the other group — so an edge now crosses between the triangles, and the graph becomes connected. Taking [2:4] shows, e.g., A’s third neighbour is a D/E/F cell. Lesson: with tiny groups, a large \(k\) forces cross-group edges and can merge genuinely separate clusters — \(k\) (like resolution) is a parameter that trades off how finely you resolve structure. (On real data with thousands of cells this is rarely a problem, since each group has far more than \(k\) members.)
R4.


keep more PCs → change npcs in RunPCA (and widen dims = 1:30 in FindNeighbors/RunUMAP to use them).


more clusters → raise resolution in FindClusters.


more/fewer neighbours per cell → change k.param in FindNeighbors.

title: Exercise: dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
Where this leads

Cell-type annotation: the anonymous clusters (0, 1, 2, …) become named cell types by checking marker genes — the biological validation that today’s caveats keep pointing to.
Cell-cycle analysis: proliferating cells vary strongly along the cell cycle, which can dominate a UMAP and split a real cell type by phase. That unit returns to PCA to identify and regress out the cell-cycle signal — a direct reuse of the eigen-decomposition machinery.
Trajectory / pseudotime methods (beyond this course) build on the same kNN graph to order cells along differentiation paths, rather than cutting it into discrete clusters.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
text:
About this lecture
In Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC the last preprocessing step was one line: log1p. This unit is about that line: why we transform counts at all, what the log does to the numbers, and what the “+1” quietly changes.

Why transform: expression spans orders of magnitude, changes are fold changes, and the variance of a count grows with its mean.
Log: turns fold changes into differences. It is nonlinear, which has consequences.
Pseudolog \(\log(1 + x)\): the log with a pseudocount, so that zeros survive. The pseudocount is a choice.
Plotting: a log axis is not the same as plotting log values.

All data today are simulated counts: 400 cells (200 T cells, 200 B cells), 300 genes.

This unit zooms in on one step of the standard pipeline from the previous unit (normalize, then log1p). It is short on new maths: logs are school maths. The new content is what the log does to data, and why the pseudocount is not an innocent detail. The simulated data: negative-binomial counts with cell-to-cell differences in capture, 280 background genes with means from 0.01 to 30, 5 very highly expressed genes (like ribosomal or mitochondrial genes), and 15 marker genes that are on (mean 4) in one cell type and nearly off (0.3) in the other. The figure script is make-log-figs.R in the unit folder.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
text:
Expression spans orders of magnitude


One point per gene: its mean UMI count per cell. The means run from 0.003 to 410 UMIs per cell, a ratio of about 160,000.
On a linear axis almost every gene sits at “0”, and 5 genes (ribosomal-like) carry 54% of all UMIs.
On a log axis each factor of 10 gets the same space, and the genes spread out.

Biology works in ratios too: a transcription factor at 0.5 UMIs per cell going to 1 is as much a doubling as a ribosomal gene going from 200 to 400.

This is the first reason for the log. Real data look the same: in a 10x dataset a few ribosomal protein genes, MALAT1 and mitochondrial genes have hundreds of UMIs per cell, most transcription factors fewer than one. On a linear scale any summary (sum, variance, distance) is decided by the few big genes. The log axis gives every order of magnitude equal room. Ask: which change matters more biologically, +1 UMI in a ribosomal gene at 300, or +1 in a transcription factor at 0.5? The log answers that question the same way biologists do: by ratio.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
section: Count variance grows with the mean
text:
Count variance grows with the mean


Left: for counts, variance ≥ mean (Poisson: variance = mean; negative binomial: more). The 5 very high genes have variances of 6,900–50,000; the cell-type markers only 7.5–10.
Right: after log1p, the markers (green) have the largest variance (1.75–1.95); the very high genes drop to 0.17–0.20.

The log does not make variance perfectly constant (genes near 0 stay low), but it stops size from deciding what looks variable.

Second reason: heteroskedasticity. For count data the variance is tied to the mean (overdispersion from the distributions block: the negative binomial has variance mu + mu^2 / theta). So a highly expressed gene is “variable” just because it is big. After log1p, the genes that vary because of biology (the markers, on in one cell type and off in the other) rise to the top. This is exactly what highly variable gene selection needs. Be honest about the right panel: very lowly expressed genes have small log variance, and the curve is a hump, not flat. Variance-stabilising transforms are approximate; that is fine for PCA.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
section: Raw counts: PCA sees a few genes
text:
Raw counts: PCA sees a few genes


Normalized counts: the 5 very high genes contribute 92% of the total variance. PC1 is their noise; T and B cells overlap.
After log1p: they contribute 0.5%. PC1 is made of the 15 marker genes and splits the two cell types.

Same cells, same genes, same PCA. Only the transform changed.

Payoff for the PCA block: PCA finds directions of largest variance, so it inherits whatever scale the data are on. On normalized counts the top loadings on PC1 are the very high genes, whose Poisson-plus-overdispersion noise is in the hundreds. On log1p data the top loadings are marker genes. The separation of the cell-type means along PC1, in units of the PC1 standard deviation, goes from 0.09 to 1.96. This is why every scRNA-seq pipeline logs (or uses another variance-stabilising transform) before PCA. Scaling each gene to variance 1 (ScaleData in Seurat) also helps, but it is done after the log, not instead of it.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
section: Log turns fold changes into differences
text:
Log turns fold changes into differences
The one rule that makes logs useful:
\[\log(a \cdot b) = \log a + \log b, \qquad \log\frac{a}{b} = \log a - \log b\]
So a fold change (a ratio) becomes a difference of logs. With base 2:



Control
Treated
Fold change
\(\log_2\) fold change




50
200
4
\(\log_2 200 - \log_2 50 = 2\)


40

\(-2\)

0.58



\(\log_2\) FC = 1 means doubling, \(-1\) halving, 0 no change. Up and down are now symmetric: 4× up is \(+2\), 4× down is \(-2\).
The base only rescales: \(\log_{10} x = \log_2 x / \log_2 10\). R’s log() is natural log; log1p() too.

This is why differential expression results are reported as log2 fold changes: a 4-fold increase and a 4-fold decrease are +2 and -2, equal and opposite, instead of 4 and 0.25. It also means that a multiplicative effect (a cell captures twice as much RNA, so every gene is doubled) becomes an additive shift of log 2 on every gene, which is easy to remove. Natural log versus log2 versus log10 only changes the units, like centimetres and inches. Seurat and scanpy use natural log for log1p; fold changes are usually reported in log2.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
text:
Log is not linear
The linear test from Polar coordinates: \(f\) is linear if \(f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b)\) and \(f(c\,a) = c\,f(a)\). The log fails both:
\[\log_{10}(10 + 1000) = 3.004 \quad\text{but}\quad \log_{10} 10 + \log_{10} 1000 = 1 + 3 = 4\]
\[\log_{10}(2 \cdot 1000) = 3.30 \quad\text{but}\quad 2 \cdot \log_{10} 1000 = 6\]

The log turns products into sums, not sums into sums. Scaling by \(c\) becomes adding \(\log c\).
So there is no matrix for it, and the order of operations matters: anything linear (summing counts, averaging, library-size scaling, compensation in flow cytometry) must be done before the log, on the original scale.


Same test as for polar coordinates in the Applications block: a matrix map always passes it, so the log is not a matrix. Most of single-cell preprocessing is linear: adding up UMIs, dividing by the library size, averaging cells into a pseudobulk sample. These are meaningful on counts. After the log, a sum of logs is the log of a product, which usually means nothing biologically. The next slide shows the most common case: averaging.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
section: Average, then log ≠ log, then average
text:
Average, then log ≠ log, then average
Four cells of one cluster, counts for one gene: \(0, 1, 3, 15\).




\(\log_2(1 + x)\) per cell
Average




Log, then average
\(0, 1, 2, 4\)
1.75


Average, then log
mean count \(= 4.75\)
\(\log_2(5.75) =\) 2.52




The mean of logs is always ≤ the log of the mean (equal only if all values are the same). Big values count less after the log.
Pseudobulk: add up the raw counts of all cells in a cluster per sample, then normalize and log. Do not average the log1p values and call that the expression of the cluster.
A fold change of mean log values is not the log of the fold change of means. Know which one a tool reports.


Concrete version of “not linear”. The mean of log values is the log of the geometric mean, which is pulled down by small values; for 1, 10, 100 the arithmetic mean is 37 but the geometric mean is 10 (exercise B3). Pseudobulk is the standard way to do differential expression between conditions with replicates: sum counts over cells within each sample and cell type, then use bulk tools on the summed counts. Summing is linear, so it must happen on counts. Several tools report a log fold change computed from mean log-normalized values; that is a different number from the log of the ratio of mean expression, and the two can disagree a lot for lowly expressed genes.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
section: The zero problem, and the pseudolog
text:
The zero problem, and the pseudolog
Half the entries in our matrix are 0 (real datasets: 90% or more), and \(\log 0 = -\infty\).
The fix: add a pseudocount \(c\) before taking the log. With \(c = 1\) this is the pseudolog:
\[\text{pseudolog}(x) = \log(1 + x)\]
In R: log1p(x).

\(0 \mapsto 0\): zeros stay zeros, so the matrix stays sparse.
For large \(x\), \(\log(1 + x) \approx \log x\): the +1 does not matter.
For small \(x\) it matters a lot: \(\log(1 + x) \approx x\), the transform is almost linear near 0.

In general, \(\log(x + c)\) with any pseudocount \(c > 0\). Our 0, 1, 3, 15 example used \(c = 1\) in base 2.

Pseudolog is our name for log(1 + x), the log with a pseudocount of 1. The pseudocount is not a correction derived from a model; it is a practical choice to make the log defined at zero. Two properties make c = 1 popular: zero maps to zero (so sparse storage still works), and near zero log(1+x) is approximately x, so tiny values are not blown up to large negative numbers. log1p in R also computes log(1 + x) accurately when x is very small, which is where the name comes from. For x = 1000, log(1001) and log(1000) differ by 0.001.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
section: The pseudocount is a choice that matters
text:
The pseudocount is a choice that matters




\(\log_2\) fold change \(\log_2\frac{b + c}{a + c}\) for counts \(a \to b\):

True fold change for the last three rows: 3, i.e. \(\log_2 3 = 1.58\).


Small \(c\): the gap between 0 and 1 count is huge; noise at low counts is blown up.
Large \(c\): low counts are squashed together; fold changes between small values shrink towards 0.
Values well above \(c\) are hardly affected.


Read the figure first: with c = 0.1, the step from 0 to 1 count is 3.5 log2 units, larger than the step from 1 to 10. With c = 10 everything below about 10 counts is squashed into a narrow band. Then the table: the same true 3-fold change gives anything from 0.24 to 1.58 depending on c and on how many counts the gene has. A difference of 0 versus 1 UMI, which is mostly sampling noise, gets log2 FC 3.46 with c = 0.1. So the pseudocount sets the count level below which differences are treated as noise. There is no single right value; c = 1 is a convention.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
text:
Try it: choose the pseudocount




Simulated counts in the same spirit as our data: 200 cells (100 T, 100 B) with sequencing depths from about 1,300 to 12,600 UMIs, 60 background genes, 4 very high genes and 10 cell-type markers. Panel (a) is the curve from the previous slide, with the 0 and 1 UMI points and the size of the step between them. Panel (b) shows every cell for a gene with mean 0.35 (73% zeros) and one with mean 30. Panel (c) is the variance after the log for every gene, against its mean; the dashed line marks the 10 most variable genes, which is what highly variable gene selection would pick. Start at c = 1: all 10 top genes are markers. Click c = 0.01: the zeros of the low gene drop to log 0.01 = -4.6, the step from 0 to 1 UMI becomes 4.6, and background genes with many zeros climb into the top 10 (5 of 10). Click c = 10 and 100: everything below about c counts is squashed, the low gene’s variance goes to 0, and the very high genes take over the top 10, as on raw counts. Switching to base 2 only rescales the axis (variances by about 2.1), the ranking does not change. Finally tick “normalize first”: the step from 0 to 1 UMI now depends on the depth of the cell, which is the next slide.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
section: The pseudocount meets the scale factor
text:
The pseudocount meets the scale factor
Seurat’s NormalizeData computes \(\log\!\big(1 + \tfrac{x}{n} \cdot 10{,}000\big)\) for a cell with \(n\) UMIs. Rewrite it:
\[\log\!\Big(1 + \tfrac{10{,}000}{n}\, x\Big) = \log\tfrac{10{,}000}{n} + \log\!\Big(x + \tfrac{n}{10{,}000}\Big)\]
So in raw counts, the pseudocount is \(n / 10{,}000\), and it differs per cell:



UMIs in the cell, \(n\)
1,000
5,000
20,000




effective pseudocount
0.1
0.5
2


log1p value of 1 UMI
2.40
1.10
0.41



Changing the scale factor (10,000 vs \(10^6\) for CPM) changes the pseudocount. Ahlmann-Eltze & Huber (2023, Nature Methods 20:665) show the pseudocount acts like an assumed overdispersion \(\alpha\), with \(c \approx 1/(4\alpha)\): 10,000 is a reasonable choice for typical droplet data; CPM (\(10^6\)) is not.

The first term, log(10000 / n), is a per-cell shift that is the same for every gene; the second is a log with pseudocount n / 10000 in raw counts. So a single UMI in a small cell becomes a large value (2.40), and in a big cell a small one (0.41). Ahlmann-Eltze and Huber, “Comparison of transformations for single-cell RNA-seq data”, Nature Methods 20, 665-672 (2023): they write the shifted logarithm log(y/s + y0) and show it approximates the variance-stabilising transform of the negative binomial when y0 = 1/(4 alpha). With the 10,000 scale factor and about 5,000 UMIs per cell the pseudocount is 0.5, i.e. alpha = 0.5, close to real data; CPM gives a pseudocount around 0.005, i.e. alpha = 50, far too large. They also found that this simple shifted log followed by PCA performed as well as or better than more sophisticated transforms in their benchmarks.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
text:
Log axis, or log values?


scale_y_log10() takes the log of 0, which is \(-\infty\): the boxplot drops the zeros, with only a console warning. 161 of 200 B cells are 0, so the true median is 0; the log-axis boxplot shows 3.82.
Plotting log1p(expr) keeps every cell; the axis can still be labelled in counts (code on the next slide).


A log axis is a display choice: the data are untouched, only the ruler is stretched. For data with zeros this silently changes the statistics: ggplot2 computes boxplots, densities and smoothers after transforming the scale, so zeros become -Inf and are removed, with a warning in the console that is easy to miss. For a gene that is off in most B cells, the log-axis boxplot shows the median of the few B cells that expressed it, the opposite of the biology. Base R’s plot(…, log = “y”) omits zero values with a warning too. Plotting log1p values is honest about the zeros. The breaks/labels trick on the next slide puts familiar numbers on the log1p axis.

title: Log and pseudolog transforms
text:
The whole transform in R
# X: cells x genes matrix of raw UMI counts
n <- rowSums(X)                     # library size per cell
N <- X / n * 10000                  # library-size normalize (linear: do it first)
L <- log1p(N)                       # pseudolog, natural log

pc <- prcomp(L)                     # PCA on log values (after selecting HVGs)

# pseudobulk: sum RAW counts per cluster, then normalize and log
pb <- rowsum(X, cluster)            # one row per cluster
log1p(pb / rowSums(pb) * 1e6)

# log2 fold change with an explicit pseudocount
lfc <- log2((mean_B + 1) / (mean_A + 1))

# plot log1p values, label the axis in counts
ggplot(d, aes(type, log1p(expr))) + geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = log1p(c(0, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100)), labels = c(0, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100))
Every number on the slides comes from this recipe applied to the simulated data (make-log-figs.R).

Point out the order: rowSums and division are linear and happen on counts; log1p comes once, at the end. rowsum (no capital S) sums the rows of a matrix by group, which is the pseudobulk step. For pseudobulk the summed library sizes are in the hundreds of thousands to millions, so the CPM pseudocount n / 10^6 is around one count, a sensible value; on single cells CPM would give about 0.005 (previous slides). For a formal differential expression test, give the summed counts to a bulk tool such as edgeR or DESeq2 instead. The fold change line shows that a pseudocount is always lurking in a log fold change of means; write it explicitly so you know what you chose. Seurat’s NormalizeData does lines 2 and 3 in one call.

The one-line takeaway: the log is the right scale for expression because biology works in fold changes, but it is nonlinear, so do everything linear first, and the pseudocount you need for the zeros is a modelling choice with visible consequences for low counts. Next unit runs PCA on exactly this log-normalized, HVG-selected matrix.

title: Quiz: single-cell RNA-seq data & QC
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of single-cell RNA-seq data and quality control. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. These are conceptual — the kind of understanding checked on the on-campus exam.

Q1. What does a single entry \(X_{cg}\) of a single-cell count matrix represent, and what shape is the matrix (what are the rows and columns)?






Hint





Think “sample × feature”, but the samples are now individual cells.









Answer





\(X_{cg}\) is the number of UMIs (mRNA molecules) of gene \(g\) detected in cell \(c\) — a non-negative integer count. The matrix has cells in rows and genes in columns (one row per cell, one column per gene). It is the single-cell analogue of a sample × feature omics table, with cells playing the role of samples.




Q2. Single-cell count matrices are typically 90%+ zeros. Give the two distinct reasons a zero can appear, and say why we store the matrix in a sparse format.






Hint





One reason is biology; one is a limitation of the measurement. And a dense 20,000 × 50,000 table of numbers is huge.









Answer





A zero can be biological (the gene is genuinely not expressed in that cell) or technical — a dropout, where the gene is expressed but its molecules were not captured/sequenced (a false zero from limited sensitivity). We usually cannot tell which from the count alone. We store the data sparsely (only the non-zero entries) because a dense matrix of, say, 20,000 genes × 50,000 cells would take tens of gigabytes, most of it storing zeros.




Q3. In the droplet workflow, what are the roles of the cell barcode and the UMI?






Hint





One identifies which cell; the other identifies which original molecule.









Answer





The cell barcode tags every molecule from a given droplet with the same code, so after pooled sequencing the reads can be sorted back into individual cells (which cell). The UMI (unique molecular identifier) tags each original mRNA molecule before amplification, so reads sharing a UMI came from one molecule and are counted once (which molecule) — this removes PCR amplification bias, giving true molecule counts.




Q4. A cell has 95% of its counts coming from mitochondrial genes. What does this suggest about the cell, and what is the biological mechanism?






Hint





Where is mitochondrial RNA physically located when the cell membrane breaks?









Answer





A very high mitochondrial fraction is a hallmark of a dying or damaged cell, so it would normally be filtered out. Mechanism: when the cell membrane is compromised, cytoplasmic mRNA leaks out of the cell, but mitochondrial mRNA stays trapped inside the mitochondria. The proportion of remaining counts that is mitochondrial therefore rises. (Thresholds are dataset-dependent — some healthy, metabolically active tissues are genuinely mito-rich.)




Q5. What is a doublet, and why is it more dangerous than simple random noise?






Hint





Two cells, one barcode. What would a T-cell + B-cell doublet appear to express?









Answer





A doublet is a single barcode that captured two cells, so its expression is a blend of two profiles. It is dangerous because it does not look like noise — it looks like a plausible cell. A T-cell + B-cell doublet expresses both T-cell and B-cell markers and can masquerade as a novel “hybrid” cell type or a fake transitional state, leading to false biological conclusions. Its signatures are unusually high total counts/genes and co-expression of markers that should be mutually exclusive.




Q6. What is an empty droplet, and what does a barcode-rank (“knee”) plot show about it?






Hint





Even a droplet with no cell captures a little floating RNA. Rank barcodes by total counts and look for a sudden drop.









Answer





An empty droplet contains no cell but still captures a little ambient RNA (mRNA released by lysed cells into the suspension), giving a low-count background profile. A barcode-rank plot sorts barcodes by total counts (descending, on log-log axes); real cells sit at high counts and there is a sharp “knee” where counts drop steeply to the empty-droplet background. The knee is used to separate true cells from empty droplets (dedicated tools like EmptyDrops model the ambient profile to do this more carefully).




Q7. After filtering, we library-size normalize and then apply log1p. What problem does each step solve?






Hint





One step makes cells with different total counts comparable; the other tames genes that span orders of magnitude.









Answer





Library-size normalization (divide each cell by its total counts, rescale to a common size) removes differences in total counts that come from technical capture/sequencing depth rather than biology, making cells comparable — it converts counts into relative expression per cell. log1p (\(\log(1+x)\)) compresses the huge dynamic range of expression so a few very-high genes do not dominate variance/distance calculations, and stabilizes variance; the \(+1\) keeps zeros at zero and avoids \(\log 0 = -\infty\).




Q8. We keep only the ~2,000 highly variable genes. Why not simply keep the genes with the highest variance?






Hint





In count data, how does a gene’s variance relate to its mean expression?









Answer





Because in count data variance grows with the mean: a highly expressed gene (e.g. a housekeeping gene like ACTB) has a large raw variance simply because it is big, not because it distinguishes cell types. Ranking by raw variance would just pick the highest-expressed genes. HVG selection instead ranks genes by variance relative to the mean–variance trend — keeping genes that vary more than expected for their mean, which are the ones carrying real biological signal (e.g. cell-type markers that are off in most cells and high in one type).

title: Exercise: single-cell RNA-seq data & QC
text:
Background
A single-cell experiment produces a count matrix \(X\) with cells in rows and genes in columns; entry \(X_{cg}\) is the number of UMIs (molecules) of gene \(g\) detected in cell \(c\). It is a non-negative integer, and most entries are 0.
For each cell \(c\) we compute:

total counts (library size): \(\;n_c = \sum_g X_{cg}\)
genes detected: \(\;\#\{g : X_{cg} > 0\}\)
mitochondrial fraction: \(\;\text{pct.mt}_c = 100 \times \dfrac{\sum_{g \in \text{MT}} X_{cg}}{\sum_g X_{cg}}\)

QC removes cells that are empty droplets (very low counts = ambient background), doublets (very high counts, blended profiles), or dying (high pct.mt).
Preprocessing then makes cells comparable and tames the dynamic range:

Library-size normalize: \(\;\tilde X_{cg} = \dfrac{X_{cg}}{n_c}\times s\;\) (scale factor \(s\), e.g. 10,000).
Log transform: \(\;Y_{cg} = \log(1 + \tilde X_{cg})\).

Finally we keep the highly variable genes (HVGs) — genes that vary more than expected for their mean — because in count data variance grows with the mean, so raw variance alone just picks the highest-expressed genes.
Throughout, use this tiny toy matrix of 4 cells × 5 genes. Genes MT-1 and MT-2 are mitochondrial; G1, G2, G3 are not.
\[
X=\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
& G1 & G2 & G3 & \text{MT-1} & \text{MT-2}\\\hline
\text{Cell A} & 4 & 0 & 6 & 0 & 0\\
\text{Cell B} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 & 2\\
\text{Cell C} & 10 & 8 & 0 & 1 & 1\\
\text{Cell D} & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0
\end{array}
\]

title: Exercise: single-cell RNA-seq data & QC
text:
By hand
B1. For each of the four cells, compute the total counts \(n_c\) and the number of genes detected.
B2. Compute the mitochondrial fraction pct.mt for each cell. Which cell has the highest, and what does that suggest about its quality?
B3. Suppose your QC rule is: keep a cell only if it has at least 2 genes detected, total counts \(\ge 5\), and pct.mt \(< 50\%\). Apply all three filters and list which cells survive. For each cell you drop, name the likely problem (empty droplet / dying cell / too little data).
B4. Take Cell C (the row 10, 8, 0, 1, 1). Library-size normalize it with scale factor \(s = 100\) (we use 100 instead of 10,000 so the numbers stay friendly): divide each entry by the cell’s total, then multiply by 100. Then apply the log1p transform \(\log(1+x)\) to the normalized values. (Use natural log; a calculator is fine.)
B5. The matrix has 20 entries. How many are zero? What fraction is that? Explain, in one sentence each, the two different reasons a zero might appear in a real dataset.
B6. Consider two hypothetical cells from a much larger experiment:

Cell X: total counts = 150, genes detected = 90.
Cell Y: total counts = 42,000, genes detected = 9,500, and it co-expresses the T-cell marker CD3E and the B-cell marker MS4A1 (CD20) strongly.

For each, say whether you would suspect an empty droplet, a doublet, or a healthy cell, and give your reason.
B7. (concept) You have two genes measured across many cells: ACTB (a housekeeping gene, very high mean, similar in all cells) and CD3E (a T-cell marker, zero in most cells but high in T cells). ACTB has the larger raw variance. Which gene is more useful for distinguishing cell types, and why is ranking genes by raw variance a poor way to select features?

title: Exercise: single-cell RNA-seq data & QC
text:
In R
You can run the small base-R snippets below. The Seurat block at the end is read-only — no single-cell packages are installed for this course, and you are not expected to run it.

Build the toy matrix
# cells in rows, genes in columns
X <- matrix(c(4, 0, 6, 0, 0,
              0, 0, 0, 3, 2,
             10, 8, 0, 1, 1,
              0, 0, 1, 0, 0),
            nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(X) <- c("A", "B", "C", "D")
colnames(X) <- c("G1", "G2", "G3", "MT-1", "MT-2")
X


Per-cell QC metrics
total_counts   <- rowSums(X)          # library size per cell
genes_detected <- rowSums(X > 0)      # count of non-zero genes per cell

mt <- grepl("^MT-", colnames(X))      # which columns are mitochondrial
pct_mt <- 100 * rowSums(X[, mt]) / total_counts

cbind(total_counts, genes_detected, round(pct_mt, 1))


Apply the QC filter (B3)
keep <- genes_detected >= 2 & total_counts >= 5 & pct_mt < 50
X[keep, , drop = FALSE]               # surviving cells


Normalize + log a single cell (B4)
cellC <- X["C", ]
norm  <- cellC / sum(cellC) * 100     # library-size normalize, scale = 100
log1p(norm)                           # log(1 + x), the standard transform


Read-only: the same steps in Seurat
library(Seurat)
obj <- CreateSeuratObject(counts, min.cells = 3, min.features = 200)
obj[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(obj, pattern = "^MT-")
obj <- subset(obj, subset = nFeature_RNA > 200 & percent.mt < 15)
obj <- NormalizeData(obj)                    # library-size + log1p
obj <- FindVariableFeatures(obj, nfeatures = 2000)   # highly variable genes


Tasks
R1. Run the QC-metrics block and confirm it matches your hand answers from B1 and B2.
R2. Run the filter block (B3) and check the surviving cells match your by-hand list. Change the pct_mt < 50 threshold to pct_mt < 100 and see which cell comes back.
R3. Run the normalize + log block for Cell C (B4) and confirm it matches your hand computation. Then confirm that a genuine zero stays zero after log1p (try log1p(0)).

title: Exercise: single-cell RNA-seq data & QC
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — total counts and genes detected





Total counts for a cell is just the sum of its row. Genes detected counts how many entries in the row are strictly greater than 0 (the number of non-zero genes, not their sum). In R, rowSums(X) gives totals and rowSums(X > 0) gives genes detected (because X > 0 is a TRUE/FALSE matrix and TRUE counts as 1).









Hint 2 — mitochondrial fraction





Add up only the mitochondrial columns (MT-1 and MT-2) for a cell, divide by that cell’s total counts, and multiply by 100. A cell whose counts are almost all mitochondrial has a compromised membrane — cytoplasmic RNA has leaked out, leaving mitochondrial RNA behind — a classic dying-cell signature.









Hint 3 — applying multiple filters





A cell must pass all three conditions to be kept. Evaluate each condition per cell (TRUE/FALSE), then keep a cell only where every condition is TRUE. In R, combine conditions with &. Very low counts / few genes suggest an empty droplet or near-empty capture; very high mito suggests a dying cell.









Hint 4 — normalize then log





Normalize first: divide each count by the cell’s total (\(n_c\)) so the row sums to 1, then multiply by the scale factor \(s\). Only after that do you apply log1p \(=\log(1+x)\). The \(+1\) is what keeps a zero at zero: \(\log(1+0)=\log 1 = 0\).









Hint 5 — empty droplets vs doublets





Empty droplet: very low total counts / few genes — it is mostly ambient background RNA. Doublet: unusually high counts / genes, and co-expression of markers that should be mutually exclusive (e.g. a T-cell marker and a B-cell marker together) — a sign two different cells landed in one droplet.









Hint 6 — why raw variance is a bad feature score





In count data, variance grows with the mean — a highly expressed gene has a large variance just because it is big, not because it carries cell-type information. A housekeeping gene like ACTB is high and roughly constant across cells (high variance, low information); a marker like CD3E is zero in most cells and high only in one type (lower raw variance, but exactly the signal you want). HVG selection ranks genes by variance relative to the mean–variance trend, not raw variance.
