Survivors: A and C. Reasons for the drops: Cell B fails on mitochondrial fraction → likely a dying cell. Cell D has just 1 count in 1 gene → empty droplet / too little data (almost no real RNA captured).
B4. Cell C is 10, 8, 0, 1, 1 with total \(n_C = 20\). Normalize (divide by 20, ×100 → i.e. ×5), then log1p.
Normalized values (\(X_{cg}/20 \times 100 = X_{cg}\times5\)):
\[10\to50,\quad 8\to40,\quad 0\to0,\quad 1\to5,\quad 1\to5.\]
Now \(\log(1+x)\) (natural log):

\(\log(1+50) = \log 51 \approx 3.932\)
\(\log(1+40) = \log 41 \approx 3.714\)
\(\log(1+0) = \log 1 = 0\)
\(\log(1+5) = \log 6 \approx 1.792\)
\(\log(1+5) = \log 6 \approx 1.792\)

So the transformed Cell C is approximately \((3.93,\ 3.71,\ 0,\ 1.79,\ 1.79)\). Note the zero stayed exactly 0, and the large 50 was pulled down close to the 40 — the log compresses the dynamic range.
B5. The 20 entries are: A (4,0,6,0,0), B (0,0,0,3,2), C (10,8,0,1,1), D (0,0,1,0,0). Zeros: A has 3, B has 3, C has 1, D has 4 → \(3+3+1+4 = 11\) zeros out of 20, i.e. 55% (real data is often 90%+).
The two reasons a zero appears: - Biological zero: the gene is genuinely not expressed in that cell. - Technical zero (dropout): the gene is expressed but its molecules were not captured/sequenced — a false zero from limited sensitivity.
B6. - Cell X (150 counts, 90 genes): very low counts and few genes → suspect an empty droplet (or a broken/near-empty cell) — mostly ambient background, little real RNA. - Cell Y (42,000 counts, 9,500 genes, co-expresses CD3E and MS4A1): unusually high counts/genes and simultaneous expression of two markers that should be mutually exclusive (T-cell and B-cell) → strong doublet signature: two cells captured in one droplet, giving a blended profile that could masquerade as a fake “hybrid” cell type.
B7. CD3E is far more useful: it is off in most cells and on only in T cells, so it separates a cell type — exactly the signal we want. ACTB is high everywhere and roughly constant, so despite its large raw variance it tells you almost nothing about which cell is which. Ranking by raw variance is poor because in count data variance scales with the mean: high-mean genes look variable just from their size. HVG selection instead scores each gene by how much its variance exceeds the mean–variance trend, catching genes like CD3E that vary more than their expression level alone would predict.
R1–R3. The R blocks reproduce the hand answers directly:
X <- matrix(c(4, 0, 6, 0, 0,
              0, 0, 0, 3, 2,
             10, 8, 0, 1, 1,
              0, 0, 1, 0, 0),
            nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(X) <- c("A", "B", "C", "D")
colnames(X) <- c("G1", "G2", "G3", "MT-1", "MT-2")

total_counts   <- rowSums(X)          # A 10, B 5, C 20, D 1
genes_detected <- rowSums(X > 0)      # A 2,  B 2, C 4,  D 1
mt     <- grepl("^MT-", colnames(X))
pct_mt <- 100 * rowSums(X[, mt]) / total_counts   # A 0, B 100, C 10, D 0

keep <- genes_detected >= 2 & total_counts >= 5 & pct_mt < 50
X[keep, , drop = FALSE]               # A and C survive

cellC <- X["C", ]
log1p(cellC / sum(cellC) * 100)       # 3.93 3.71 0 1.79 1.79
log1p(0)                              # 0  -> a true zero stays zero
Relaxing the mito threshold to pct_mt < 100 brings Cell B back (its 100% is not strictly < 100; use <= 100 to include it) — showing how sensitive the surviving set is to a threshold you must choose from the data.

title: Exercise: single-cell RNA-seq data & QC
text:
Where this leads

Log and pseudolog transforms (next unit): why the log1p step in B4 is there, why you average counts before logging, and how the pseudocount and scale factor change low counts.
Dimensionality reduction & clustering: the cleaned, normalized, log-transformed, HVG-selected matrix is fed to PCA (the eigen-decomposition of a covariance matrix you built in the linear algebra block) and then UMAP, to visualize and cluster cells by type.
Count models (distributions block): the noisy, overdispersed counts motivate Poisson and negative-binomial models and more principled normalization — the simple library-size + log1p here is a first-pass baseline.
Ambient-RNA correction and doublet removal have dedicated tools (EmptyDrops, scDblFinder, SoupX); today you learned the concepts and the QC metrics they build on.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
About this lecture
You cluster a single-cell dataset and two “cell types” appear — but on closer look they are the same cell type, split into a dividing half and a resting half. The cell cycle has leaked into your analysis.

The cell cycle is one of the strongest sources of cell-to-cell variation in expression, so it can dominate the data.
We score each cell for cell-cycle phase (G1 / S / G2M) from small marker gene sets.
Because it is a big axis of variation, the cycle often lines up with a principal component — closing the loop to Principal component analysis.
If the cycle is a nuisance here, we can regress it out; if proliferation is the biology, we keep it.
The broader lesson: PCA components are axes of variation — cell cycle, stress, batch, ambient RNA — so we must interpret them, not just use them.

This is an applied concept day. R is shown but not run; the goal is to understand what each step does and why.

The single mental image: the cell cycle is a smooth, strong program that turns on hundreds of genes as a cell prepares to divide. Because it is strong, it behaves like any other big axis of variation in the data — it can eat a whole principal component and pull apart a cluster. Everything today hangs off that: scoring the phase, seeing it in PCA, deciding whether to remove it. Emphasise the judgement call at the end — cell cycle is not always noise. This unit deliberately ties the Single-cell block back to the Applications block: PCA is not a black box; its components mean something biological or technical, and cell cycle is the cleanest example.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
A biology picture first
You sequence a tumour biopsy or a developing tissue. Many cells are actively dividing; others are quiescent.

A cell preparing to divide synthesises DNA, then builds the mitotic machinery — hundreds of genes switch on in a coordinated wave.
Two cells of the same type can therefore look very different in their expression profile — not because they are different, but because they are caught at different points in the cycle.
Plot the cells and the dividing ones drift off to one side, forming what looks like a separate population.

The question for today: how do we recognise this, measure it, and decide what to do about it?


Anchor everything in a real situation before any method: proliferating tissue (tumour, bone marrow, embryo, regenerating gut) is full of cycling cells. The key biological fact is that division is a coordinated transcriptional program, so cells of one identity fan out along a “how far through the cycle am I” direction. Stress that this within-type spread is genuine biological signal about proliferation, but it is often not the signal we came for (we usually want cell identity). That tension — real signal, wrong question — is the whole motivation.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
section: The cell cycle in one minute
text:
The cell cycle in one minute
The division cycle runs through ordered phases, each with a characteristic transcriptional signature:

G1 — cell grows; no strong division program yet (the “resting-looking” default).
S — DNA replication: histones and replication genes are high (e.g. PCNA, MCM family, TYMS).
G2/M — preparing for and executing mitosis: spindle and division genes are high (e.g. TOP2A, MKI67, CCNB1/2, CDK1).

We collapse this into three labels a single-cell tool can assign: G1, S, G2M.
Key point: these are sets of co-expressed genes that rise and fall together — exactly the kind of coordinated pattern that dimensionality reduction picks up.


Keep the biology light and correct: G1 growth, S is DNA synthesis, G2/M is mitosis. Name a few canonical markers so students recognise them in loadings later (PCNA/MCM/TYMS for S; TOP2A/MKI67/CCNB/CDK1 for G2M). The pedagogical hook for the maths: because these genes are co-regulated, they move together across cells, which is precisely a direction of high covariance — the thing PCA finds. Do not over-detail checkpoints or cyclin biochemistry; three labels is all the downstream method needs.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
section: Why this is a single-cell problem
text:
Why this is a single-cell problem
In bulk RNA-seq you average over millions of cells, so the cycle mostly washes out. In single-cell data every cell is caught at its own moment in the cycle.

Hundreds of genes vary together across cells purely because of cell-cycle position.
That coordinated variation is often larger than the difference between two related cell subtypes.
So a naive clustering or embedding can group cells by “how much are they dividing” instead of by “what are they”.

This is the classic confounder: a strong, unwanted axis of variation sitting on top of the biology you actually want.


Contrast bulk vs single-cell explicitly — this is why the problem is new here. In bulk, cell-cycle heterogeneity is averaged away; in single-cell it is front and centre because each cell has a definite phase. The magnitude point matters: cell-cycle variance can exceed subtype variance, so it wins in an unsupervised method that just chases the biggest variance. Frame it with the word confounder, which they know from the statistics course (covariates in lm): an axis correlated with the structure we see but not the structure we want.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
section: Idea: score a phase from a gene set
text:
Idea: score a phase from a gene set
We do not trust any single gene (dropouts, noise). Instead we use a set of phase markers and summarise them into one number per cell — a module score.
For cell \(c\) and an S-phase gene set \(\mathcal{S}\), a simple score is the average expression of those genes:
\[\text{Score}_S(c) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{g \in \mathcal{S}} x_{gc}\]
where \(x_{gc}\) is the (log-normalised) expression of gene \(g\) in cell \(c\).

A high \(\text{Score}_S\) means the S-phase program is switched on in that cell.
We compute an analogous \(\text{Score}_{G2M}\) from the G2/M gene set.



Motivate the set-based approach from noise: single-cell counts are sparse and any one marker is unreliable, so we pool a curated set and average. Present the plain mean as the intuition-level score. This connects to descriptive statistics they already have — it is just a mean over a chosen list of features. The next slide refines it with a background correction, but the core idea (one number per cell summarising a program) is the takeaway. Note the expression is log-normalised, not raw counts, so averaging is reasonable.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
section: Making the score fair: a background control
text:
Making the score fair: a background control
A problem: some cells simply have more counts or more genes detected, inflating any average. We want a score that reflects the program, not sequencing depth.
The standard fix (the AddModuleScore idea): subtract the average expression of a matched set of control genes picked to have similar overall expression levels:
\[\text{Score}_S(c) = \underbrace{\overline{x}_{\mathcal{S}}(c)}_{\text{marker average}} \;-\; \underbrace{\overline{x}_{\text{ctrl}}(c)}_{\text{control average}}\]

The control genes track the background a cell would show anyway, so the difference isolates the cell-cycle signal.
A score near 0 means “no more than background”; a clearly positive score means the program is active.



This is the one non-obvious refinement and it is worth a slide because it explains the negative/positive scores students will see. Depth and complexity differences would make richer cells score high on everything; subtracting a background of expression-matched control genes cancels that. The genes are binned by average expression and controls are drawn from the same bins — no need to detail the binning, just the logic: compare markers against a fair background. Emphasise the interpretation of the sign: positive = above background = program on.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
Assigning the phase
Each cell now has two numbers, \(\text{Score}_S\) and \(\text{Score}_{G2M}\). Assign a label by which program is on:

If both scores are low (near or below 0) → G1 (not obviously cycling).
If \(\text{Score}_S\) is the highest positive → S.
If \(\text{Score}_{G2M}\) is the highest positive → G2M.

This is the logic behind Seurat’s CellCycleScoring: it returns S.Score, G2M.Score, and a discrete Phase.
Now we have both a continuous readout (the scores) and a categorical one (the phase) for every cell.


Keep the decision rule simple and correct: take the larger of the two positive scores; if neither program is on, call it G1. Stress that we get two representations — continuous scores (good for regression and for correlating with PCs) and a discrete phase label (good for colouring plots and cross-tabs). Both matter downstream. Mention that “G1” here really means “no strong S or G2M signal”, which includes truly resting/G0 cells; the method cannot cleanly separate G0 from G1.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
section: In R: score and assign phase
text:
In R: score and assign phase
Using the marker sets shipped with Seurat (from Tirosh et al. 2016) — shown, not run:
library(Seurat)

# Built-in curated gene sets
s.genes   <- cc.genes.updated.2019$s.genes     # S-phase markers
g2m.genes <- cc.genes.updated.2019$g2m.genes   # G2/M markers

# obj is a Seurat object that has been normalised (LogNormalize)
obj <- CellCycleScoring(
  obj,
  s.features   = s.genes,
  g2m.features = g2m.genes,
  set.ident    = FALSE
)

head(obj[[]][, c("S.Score", "G2M.Score", "Phase")])
#>                    S.Score  G2M.Score Phase
#> cell_1           -0.0421     0.6215   G2M
#> cell_2            0.5130    -0.1002   S
#> cell_3           -0.0880    -0.1131   G1
Each cell gets two continuous scores and one phase label, stored in the metadata.

This is the canonical call and the students should recognise it. Point out the prerequisites: the object must be normalised first (LogNormalize), because the scores average log-normalised expression. cc.genes.updated.2019 is the built-in human set from the Tirosh melanoma paper; for other species you map orthologues. set.ident = FALSE keeps their original cell identities as the active identity. The printed metadata is the deliverable — two scores plus Phase per cell — and everything downstream uses these columns. Remind them this is static code; nothing runs at render time.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
The link to PCA
Recall from Principal component analysis: PCA finds the directions of greatest variance in the data (eigenvectors of the covariance matrix). It does not know or care what those directions mean.

The cell-cycle genes are strongly co-expressed → they contribute a large chunk of variance.
So one of the top principal components frequently aligns with the cell-cycle axis.
Cells then spread along that PC by phase: G1 at one end, S and G2M at the other.

PCA is doing exactly its job — capturing the biggest variation. It just happens that here the biggest variation is dividing vs. resting, not the identity we were after.


This is the conceptual centre of the lecture and the payoff of the whole Applications block. Restate what PCA guarantees: it returns the top-variance orthogonal directions, agnostic to meaning. Because cell-cycle genes move together, they form a high-covariance bundle, so their shared direction is a leading eigenvector — a top PC. Hence colouring the PCA scatter by Phase reveals a gradient. Be careful and honest: say “one of the top PCs” or “often a leading PC”, not “always PC1” — where it lands depends on how much other structure there is. The lesson: a PC is a direction, and its meaning is an empirical question.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
Diagnosing what a PC means
Because a PC is just a direction, we interpret it by looking at two things:

Loadings — which genes define the axis. If the top-loading genes of a PC are MKI67, TOP2A, PCNA, TYMS…, that PC is the cell cycle.
Correlation with a covariate — relate the PC scores to something we measured, e.g. the cell-cycle score.

# Correlate each cell's PC1 score with its cell-cycle scores
pc1 <- Embeddings(obj, "pca")[, 1]
cor(pc1, obj$S.Score)     # e.g. 0.71  -> PC1 tracks the S program
cor(pc1, obj$G2M.Score)   # e.g. 0.66  -> ... and the G2M program
A high correlation says: this principal component is (largely) the cell cycle.


Give them a concrete, reusable diagnostic recipe, because “interpret your components” is otherwise vague. Two complementary tools: read the loadings (top genes on the eigenvector — they met loadings in the PCA units) and correlate PC scores against a known covariate. High correlation between PC1 and the cell-cycle scores is direct evidence the axis is the cycle. Generalise: the same trick diagnoses batch (correlate PC with batch label), depth (with total counts), mitochondrial stress (with percent.mt). This is the transferable skill.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
Cell cycle confounds clustering
Clustering and neighbour graphs are built on top of the PCA embedding. So if a top PC is the cell cycle:

cells of one type can be split into a “G1 cluster” and a “cycling cluster”,
or two genuinely different types can be merged because both are dividing.

Either way the clusters answer “how much is this cell dividing?” instead of “what is this cell?”.
A quick check — cross-tabulate clusters against phase:
table(Cluster = Idents(obj), Phase = obj$Phase)
#>          Phase
#> Cluster    G1   S  G2M
#>       0   410  12    8    <- almost all G1
#>       3    18 205  190    <- almost all cycling: a cell-cycle artefact?
A cluster that is almost entirely one phase is a red flag.


Make the downstream damage concrete: clustering uses the PCA neighbour graph, so a cell-cycle PC propagates straight into the clusters. Two failure modes: one identity torn into resting vs cycling sub-clusters, or two identities fused because they share a proliferative signature. The cross-tab against Phase is a cheap, powerful diagnostic — a cluster that is ~100% G2M is probably a cell-cycle artefact, not a cell type. Caveat for honesty: sometimes a real cell type genuinely is highly proliferative (e.g. transit-amplifying cells), so the cross-tab is a flag to investigate, not an automatic verdict.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
section: Removing the effect: regress it out
text:
Removing the effect: regress it out
If the cell cycle is a nuisance here, we remove its contribution before PCA. The tool is one they already know: a linear model per gene.
For each gene \(g\), fit its expression across cells on the cell-cycle scores and keep the residuals:
\[x_{gc} = \beta_{0g} + \beta_{1g}\,\text{Score}_S(c) + \beta_{2g}\,\text{Score}_{G2M}(c) + \varepsilon_{gc}\]

The fitted part is the variation explained by the cell cycle.
The residual \(\varepsilon_{gc}\) is what is left after removing it — this is what we feed to PCA.

The cell-cycle axis is now flattened, so it no longer claims a top PC.


This is the reassuring “you already own this tool” slide. Regressing out a covariate is exactly the lm they used in the statistics course, applied one gene at a time with the cell-cycle scores as predictors. The residual is the gene’s expression with the cell-cycle-explained part subtracted. Do it before PCA/clustering so the axis is gone when variance is computed. Emphasise it is a per-gene regression across cells; the scores are continuous predictors. This also explains why the continuous scores (not just the phase label) were worth keeping.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
section: In R: regress and re-run PCA
text:
In R: regress and re-run PCA
In Seurat this happens inside ScaleData via vars.to.regress — shown, not run:
obj <- ScaleData(
  obj,
  vars.to.regress = c("S.Score", "G2M.Score"),
  features = rownames(obj)
)

obj <- RunPCA(obj)                 # PCA on the corrected (residual) data
Check it worked — the cell-cycle correlation with the top PCs should now be weak:
pc1 <- Embeddings(obj, "pca")[, 1]
cor(pc1, obj$S.Score)     # e.g. 0.05  -> cycle no longer drives PC1

Connect the earlier lm slide to the actual API: vars.to.regress inside ScaleData does the per-gene regression and passes residuals forward; RunPCA then operates on the corrected matrix. The verification is the same diagnostic as before, now expected to be near zero — always check that a correction did what you intended rather than assuming. Mention the common alternate recipe (regress the single difference S.Score - G2M.Score) on the next slide, which preserves cycling-vs-noncycling while removing phase-within-cycling.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
section: When NOT to regress it out
text:
When NOT to regress it out
Correcting the cell cycle is a choice, not a default. Ask: is proliferation part of the answer?

Tumour, immune activation, development, stem/progenitor cells — here dividing vs. resting is real biology. Remove the cycle and you may erase your result.
Resolving fine cell subtypes in a proliferating tissue — here the cycle is a nuisance hiding identity; removing it helps.

A common middle path: regress the difference \(\text{Score}_S - \text{Score}_{G2M}\) instead of both. This removes phase differences among cycling cells but keeps cycling vs. non-cycling — useful when you still care that a cell divides, just not where in the cycle it is.


This is the judgement slide and arguably the most important message. Regression is destructive: it removes a real signal, so only remove it when it is genuinely a nuisance for the current question. Give the two contrasting scenarios. Then the nuanced Seurat “alternate workflow”: regressing S.Score minus G2M.Score collapses the within-cycle phase gradient but retains the cycling/non-cycling contrast — the right tool when proliferation status matters but exact phase does not. The meta-lesson: correction decisions must be driven by the biological question, not applied reflexively.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
section: The broader point: PCs are axes of variation
text:
The broader point: PCs are axes of variation
Cell cycle is the cleanest example of a general truth from the Applications block: a principal component is whatever varies most — and that can be anything.







A top PC might actually be…
Diagnose by correlating PC scores with…




Cell cycle
S.Score, G2M.Score


Sequencing depth
total counts per cell (nCount_RNA)


Mitochondrial / stress
percent.mt


Batch / donor
batch or donor label


Ambient / background RNA
empty-droplet profile


Real cell identity
marker genes of the cell type



PCA is unsupervised: it hands you directions, not labels. Interpreting each component — biological signal vs. technical artefact — is the analyst’s job.

Zoom out to the transferable principle and make it a checklist. The exact same reasoning that catches cell cycle catches depth, mitochondrial stress, batch, and ambient RNA: each is a coordinated source of variance that can seize a top PC, and each is diagnosed by correlating PC scores against the relevant covariate. This is the antidote to treating PCA as a magic black box, which the whole Applications block was building toward. End the block’s arc here: eigenvectors of covariance -> PCA -> components have meaning -> you must interpret them.

title: Cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
Summary







Idea
Key point




Cell cycle
a strong, coordinated transcriptional program (G1 / S / G2M)


Why it matters
in single-cell data it is a major axis of variation


Scoring
average phase-marker expression minus a background control → S.Score, G2M.Score, Phase


Link to PCA
co-expressed cycle genes → high variance → often a top PC


Diagnose a PC
read loadings; correlate PC scores with the covariate


Confounding
clustering runs on PCA, so the cycle can split or merge clusters


Regress out
per-gene lm on the scores, keep residuals, then re-run PCA


Judgement
remove only if proliferation is a nuisance, not the biology


Big lesson
PCA components are axes of variation — interpret them



This closes the loop from Principal component analysis: a PC is a direction, and its meaning is an empirical, biological question.

The summary is the takeaway sheet. Drill the pipeline once verbally: normalise, score the phases, look at whether a top PC is the cycle (loadings + correlation), decide whether the cycle is nuisance or signal, regress out only if nuisance, re-run and verify. Land the final message hard: this unit was the concrete demonstration that principal components mean something, tying the Single-cell block back to the Applications block. Cell cycle is the exemplar; batch, depth, and stress follow the identical diagnostic logic.

title: Quiz: cell-type annotation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of annotating single-cell clusters. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Several are written in the style of the on-campus exam (no computer).

Q1. What is the difference between a cluster and a cell type?






Hint





One is produced by an algorithm; the other is a biological label.









Answer





A cluster is a group of similar cells found by an unsupervised algorithm — it is just an anonymous label (“cluster 3”). A cell type is the biological identity (T cell, macrophage). Annotation is the step that attaches a cell-type name to a cluster, using marker genes or a reference.




Q2. In a one-vs-rest marker search, a gene has avg_log2FC = 3. How many-fold higher is its mean expression in the cluster than in the rest?






Hint





The value is a \(\log_2\); invert it.









Answer





\(2^3 = 8\)-fold higher. avg_log2FC is the \(\log_2\) of the ratio of mean expression (cluster / rest), so exponentiate base 2 to get the fold change.




Q3. In a FindMarkers table, a gene for cluster 3 shows pct.1 = 0.95 and pct.2 = 0.08. What do these two numbers tell you, and is this a good marker?






Hint





pct.1 is inside the cluster, pct.2 is outside. Think sensitivity vs specificity.









Answer





pct.1 = 0.95: the gene is detected in 95% of the cluster cells (sensitive — on in almost all of them). pct.2 = 0.08: detected in only 8% of the rest (specific — off elsewhere). High pct.1 with low pct.2 is exactly the profile of a good marker.




Q4. Why is the default differential-expression test for markers the Wilcoxon rank-sum test rather than a t-test?






Hint





Think about the distribution of single-cell counts — are they Gaussian?









Answer





Single-cell expression is sparse, skewed, and overdispersed (count data, not Gaussian — recall the negative-binomial story). The Wilcoxon rank-sum test is non-parametric: it only asks whether one group ranks systematically higher, so it does not assume normality and is robust to the many zeros and the long tail.




Q5. A cluster’s p_val_adj for its top gene is essentially \(0\), yet you are told a tiny p-value alone does not confirm a marker. Why not?






Hint





How many cells are in the test, and what does that do to p-values?









Answer





With thousands of cells per group, even a biologically trivial difference becomes statistically significant, so almost every gene gets a tiny p-value. Significance must be paired with effect size (avg_log2FC) and detection (pct.1 high, pct.2 low). The p-value says the difference is real; the fold change and pct columns say whether it is useful as a marker. (The p-value is also adjusted for multiple testing because ~20 000 genes are tested per cluster.)




Q6. You find a small cluster that expresses both CD3D (a T-cell marker) and MS4A1 (a B-cell marker) at high level. What is the most likely explanation, and what should you do?






Hint





Two exclusive lineages in “one cell.” What could put two cells’ RNA together?









Answer





Most likely a doublet cluster — droplets that captured two cells (a T cell and a B cell), whose profile is the sum of both types. Do not call a new “T/B hybrid” type. Run a doublet detector (scDblFinder, DoubletFinder), remove flagged cells, and re-check. Co-expression of two lineages’ exclusive markers is a doublet until proven otherwise.




Q7. Contrast manual (marker-based) and reference-based annotation. Give one strength of each and the main weakness of reference-based annotation.






Hint





Where does each get its knowledge — a curated marker list, or a labelled dataset?









Answer





Manual: match a cluster’s markers to curated signatures — transparent and encodes expert knowledge, good for novel or unusual tissue, but slow and subjective. Reference-based (e.g. SingleR, Azimuth, CellTypist): copy labels from a labelled atlas by similarity (correlation) to reference profiles — fast, consistent, per-cell. Its main weakness: it is only as good as the reference — a cell type absent from the reference cannot be labelled correctly and will be forced onto the nearest wrong label. In practice the two are combined.




Q8. In a developing tissue, cells lie on a smooth gradient from progenitor to mature. What is the danger of forcing them into discrete cluster labels, and what alternative better matches the biology?






Hint





Is identity here a set of boxes or a continuum?









Answer





Clustering discretises what is really a continuum, so the boundaries — and therefore the “types” — are partly arbitrary and can be artefacts of where the algorithm cut the gradient. A trajectory / pseudotime analysis, which orders cells along the continuous developmental axis instead of boxing them, is truer to the biology. (Activation states and the cell cycle are other continuous states that resist discrete labels.)

title: Exercise: cell-type annotation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain the difference between a cluster (found by the algorithm) and a cell type (a biological label),
compute a cluster centroid (mean expression profile) from a small expression matrix by hand,
compute a log\(_2\) fold change and the detection fractions pct.1 / pct.2 for a gene, one-vs-rest,
read a FindMarkers-style table and decide which gene is a marker and which is housekeeping,
assign a cell-type label to a cluster by matching its markers to a signature table,
recognise the classic traps: doublets and continuous states.

The by-hand parts are the exam-relevant skill: they are just group means and a difference of logs, applied per gene. The R section confirms the same numbers at scale (full workflow fluency continues in Cell-cycle analysis and the single-cell practical).

title: Exercise: cell-type annotation
text:
Background
Each cell is a vector of gene expression. A cluster is a set of these vectors; its centroid is the mean vector — the typical profile of that group. A marker gene for a cluster is a gene whose expression is much higher inside the cluster than outside it (the “rest”).
For a gene, the one-vs-rest comparison produces:

the log fold change (effect size), \[\log_2\text{FC} = \log_2\frac{\text{mean expression in the cluster}}{\text{mean expression in the rest}},\]
the detection fractions pct.1 (fraction of cluster cells with the gene detected, i.e. count \(>0\)) and pct.2 (fraction of the rest with it detected),
and a p-value from a two-group test (default: the non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test), reported after multiple-testing correction because thousands of genes are tested.

A good marker has a large positive \(\log_2\)FC, high pct.1, low pct.2, and a small adjusted p-value.
We use this toy dataset throughout (rows = genes, columns = cells — the single-cell convention). Values are already-normalised expression.

text:
By hand

B2. For the one-vs-rest comparison cluster 1 vs the rest (here “the rest” = cluster 2), compute \(\log_2\)FC for each of the three genes. Which gene is up in cluster 1, which is down, and which is flat? (You may leave \(\log_2\) of a nice ratio as-is, e.g. \(\log_2 8 = 3\).)
B3. Still for cluster 1 vs the rest, compute pct.1 and pct.2 for CD3D (fraction of cells with count \(>0\) in the cluster, and in the rest).
B4. Using your B2 and B3 numbers, which gene is the marker for cluster 1? Justify it against all three criteria (fold change, pct.1, pct.2). What role does ACTB play, and why is it not a marker?
B5. Here is a signature table. Assign a cell-type label to cluster 1 and to cluster 2.



Cell type

B6. (doublet) A seventh cell arrives with expression CD3D = 8, MS4A1 = 8, ACTB = 11. It co-expresses the exclusive T-cell and B-cell markers at high level. Should you call it a new “T/B hybrid” cell type? What is the more likely explanation, and how would you check?
B7. (continuous state) In a bone-marrow dataset the cells form a smooth gradient from stem cells to mature cells, with no gaps. You still run clustering and get 5 clusters. In one sentence, what is the risk of labelling these 5 clusters as 5 discrete “types”, and what representation might be truer to the biology?

title: Exercise: cell-type annotation
text:
In R
Use R to reproduce the by-hand numbers. Nothing here needs a single-cell package — it is rowMeans and comparisons. (The production tool, Seurat::FindAllMarkers, does exactly this across all genes and adds the statistical test.)

Build the toy matrix
expr <- matrix(
  c( 9,  7,  8,  0,  0,  3,   # CD3D
     0,  1,  0,  7,  8,  9,   # MS4A1
    10, 12, 11, 11, 10, 12),  # ACTB
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("CD3D", "MS4A1", "ACTB"),
                  c("c1","c2","c3","c4","c5","c6")))

cluster1 <- c("c1","c2","c3")   # T cells (to be confirmed)
cluster2 <- c("c4","c5","c6")


Centroids (mean expression per gene)
m1 <- rowMeans(expr[, cluster1])   # cluster-1 centroid
m2 <- rowMeans(expr[, cluster2])   # cluster-2 centroid ("the rest")
m1                                 # CD3D 8.00  MS4A1 0.33  ACTB 11
m2                                 # CD3D 1.00  MS4A1 8.00  ACTB 11


Log2 fold change, cluster 1 vs the rest
log2fc <- log2(m1 / m2)
log2fc          # CD3D  3.00   MS4A1 -4.58   ACTB 0.00
# CD3D up 8-fold in cluster 1; MS4A1 down; ACTB flat.
# NOTE: real tools add a small pseudocount, log2((m1+eps)/(m2+eps)),
#       so a gene absent in one group does not divide by zero.


Detection fractions for CD3D
pct <- function(x) mean(x > 0)         # fraction of cells with count > 0
pct(expr["CD3D", cluster1])            # pct.1 = 1.00  (3/3)
pct(expr["CD3D", cluster2])            # pct.2 = 0.33  (1/3)


What the real call looks like (static — do not run)
# after clustering, with cluster labels set as identities:
markers <- FindAllMarkers(seurat_obj, only.pos = TRUE,
                          min.pct = 0.25, logfc.threshold = 0.25)
# one row per (gene, cluster) with columns:
#   p_val  avg_log2FC  pct.1  pct.2  p_val_adj  cluster  gene
head(markers[markers$cluster == 1, ], 5)


Tasks
R1. Reproduce B1 and B2 with the code above. Confirm log2fc["CD3D"] is \(3\) and log2fc["MS4A1"] is negative.
R2. Reproduce B3: confirm pct.1 = 1.0 and pct.2 = 0.33 for CD3D. Then compute pct.1/pct.2 for MS4A1 with respect to cluster 1 — do the values make sense for a non-marker of cluster 1?
R3. Add the doublet cell from B6 as a new column c7 = c(8, 8, 11) and confirm it is high in both CD3D and MS4A1. Explain in a comment why a naive marker match would mislabel it.

title: Exercise: cell-type annotation
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — the centroid is just a mean





The centroid of a cluster is the mean expression of each gene over the cells in that cluster — one number per gene. For cluster 1, average across columns c1, c2, c3. In R this is rowMeans(expr[, cluster1]).









Hint 2 — log fold change





\(\log_2\)FC compares the two centroids you just computed: \(\log_2(\text{mean}_{\text{cluster}} / \text{mean}_{\text{rest}})\). Recall \(\log_2\) of a ratio is a difference of logs, and \(\log_2 8 = 3\), \(\log_2 1 = 0\), \(\log_2(\text{small}) < 0\). A gene with \(\log_2\)FC \(\approx 0\) is expressed equally in both groups — not a marker.









Hint 3 — detection fractions





pct.1 = fraction of cluster cells where the gene is detected (count \(>0\)); pct.2 = the same for the rest. Count the non-zero entries and divide by the group size (3 here). A specific marker has pct.1 high and pct.2 low.









Hint 4 — what makes a marker





A marker must satisfy all of: large positive \(\log_2\)FC (higher in the cluster), high pct.1 (on in most cluster cells), low pct.2 (off elsewhere). A housekeeping gene like ACTB is high everywhere, so its \(\log_2\)FC is \(\approx 0\) and both pct values are high — high expression is not the same as being a marker.









Hint 5 — assigning the label





Match the cluster’s up markers to the signature table: whichever cell type’s canonical genes appear as the cluster’s markers gives the label. CD3D up in cluster 1 → look it up in the table.









Hint 6 — the doublet





CD3D and MS4A1 mark different, exclusive lineages (T vs B). A single real cell almost never expresses both strongly. When it does, suspect a doublet — two cells in one droplet, whose profile is the sum of two types. Check with a doublet detector (scDblFinder) and remove flagged cells before annotating.

title: Exercise: cell-type annotation
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. Average each gene over the cluster’s cells.
Cluster 1 = {c1, c2, c3}:

CD3D: \((9+7+8)/3 = 24/3 = 8\)
MS4A1: \((0+1+0)/3 = 1/3 \approx 0.33\)
ACTB: \((10+12+11)/3 = 33/3 = 11\)

so the cluster-1 centroid is \((\text{CD3D}, \text{MS4A1}, \text{ACTB}) = (8,\ 0.33,\ 11)\).
Cluster 2 = {c4, c5, c6}:

CD3D: \((0+0+3)/3 = 1\)
MS4A1: \((7+8+9)/3 = 8\)
ACTB: \((11+10+12)/3 = 11\)

so the cluster-2 centroid is \((1,\ 8,\ 11)\).
B2. \(\log_2\)FC = \(\log_2(\text{cluster-1 mean} / \text{cluster-2 mean})\):

CD3D: \(\log_2(8/1) = \log_2 8 = 3\) → up (about \(8\times\) higher in cluster 1).
MS4A1: \(\log_2(0.33/8) = \log_2(0.0417) \approx -4.58\) → down (much lower in cluster 1; it is instead a cluster-2 gene).
ACTB: \(\log_2(11/11) = \log_2 1 = 0\) → flat (equal in both groups).

B3. Detection = fraction of cells with count \(>0\).

pct.1 (CD3D in cluster 1): all of 9, 7, 8 are \(>0\) → \(3/3 = 1.0\).
pct.2 (CD3D in cluster 2): of 0, 0, 3 only one is \(>0\) → \(1/3 \approx 0.33\).

B4. CD3D is the marker for cluster 1: it has a large positive \(\log_2\)FC (\(=3\)), high pct.1 (\(=1.0\), on in every cluster-1 cell), and low pct.2 (\(=0.33\), mostly off elsewhere) — it satisfies all three criteria. MS4A1 fails (its \(\log_2\)FC for cluster 1 is negative — it marks cluster 2, not cluster 1). ACTB is a housekeeping gene: it is highly expressed in both clusters, so its \(\log_2\)FC is \(0\) and it carries no information about which type a cell is. High expression alone does not make a marker; differential expression does.
B5. Cluster 1’s up-marker is CD3D, which the table lists under T cell → cluster 1 = T cells. Cluster 2’s up-marker is MS4A1 (high in cluster 2, low in cluster 1), listed under B cell → cluster 2 = B cells.
B6. Do not call it a new hybrid type. CD3D (T cell) and MS4A1 (B cell) mark exclusive lineages that a single cell essentially never co-expresses at high level. The profile (8, 8, 11) looks like the sum of a T-cell profile and a B-cell profile — the signature of a doublet: two cells captured in one droplet and sequenced as one. Check by running a doublet detector (e.g. scDblFinder or DoubletFinder); if flagged, remove the cell before finalising annotation. Co-expression of two lineages’ exclusive markers is a doublet until proven otherwise.
B7. If identity is really a smooth continuum (stem → mature), cutting it into 5 clusters draws boundaries that are partly arbitrary, so the 5 “types” may be artefacts of where the algorithm split a gradient rather than genuine discrete populations. A trajectory / pseudotime representation, which orders cells along the continuous axis instead of boxing them, is truer to this biology.
R1. Running the centroid and log-fold-change blocks gives log2fc["CD3D"] = 3 and log2fc["MS4A1"] ≈ -4.58, matching B2.
m1 <- rowMeans(expr[, cluster1])
m2 <- rowMeans(expr[, cluster2])
log2(m1 / m2)     # CD3D 3.00  MS4A1 -4.58  ACTB 0.00
R2. For CD3D, pct(expr["CD3D", cluster1]) = 1.0 and pct(expr["CD3D", cluster2]) = 0.33, as in B3. For MS4A1 vs cluster 1:
pct(expr["MS4A1", cluster1])   # 0.33  (only c2 is > 0)  -> pct.1
pct(expr["MS4A1", cluster2])   # 1.00  (all of c4,c5,c6) -> pct.2
For a cluster-1 marker we want pct.1 high and pct.2 low; MS4A1 shows the opposite (pct.1 = 0.33, pct.2 = 1.0), confirming it is not a marker of cluster 1 — it marks cluster 2.
R3.
expr2 <- cbind(expr, c7 = c(8, 8, 11))
expr2[, "c7"]      # CD3D 8  MS4A1 8  ACTB 11  -> high in BOTH lineage markers
# A naive match would see CD3D -> T cell AND MS4A1 -> B cell and might invent a
# "T/B" type. The profile is really the sum of a T cell and a B cell: a doublet.

title: Exercise: cell-type annotation
text:
Where this leads

Cell-cycle analysis: a continuous state (the cell cycle) that can create spurious clusters and confound annotation — you will score it per cell and, if needed, regress it out. The same signature-scoring idea from this unit reappears.
Reference-based annotation at scale: tools such as SingleR, Azimuth, and CellTypist transfer labels from a curated atlas by correlation to reference profiles — the vector-similarity idea from Vectors, dot product & projection, applied per cell.
Differential expression proper: the one-vs-rest test here is the entry point to comparing conditions (treated vs control) within a cell type — where the count-data distributions (Poisson / negative binomial) matter for choosing the right test.
