title: Exercise: introduction to R-STAN
text:
Background
A Bayesian model combines a prior with a likelihood to give a posterior:
\[p(\theta \mid y) \;\propto\; p(y \mid \theta)\,p(\theta).\]
Stan describes such models in three blocks and then samples the posterior:

data — the knowns you pass in from R (counts, sample sizes, predictors), each with a type (int, real) and optional constraints (<lower=0>).
parameters — the unknowns you want to learn; the posterior is a distribution over these.
model — ~ (“distributed as”) statements giving the prior on each parameter and the likelihood of the data.

The running example from the lecture — 13 of 20 cells express a marker — is:
// gene_marker.stan
data {
  int<lower=0> N;                 // cells assayed
  int<lower=0> y;                 // cells expressing the marker
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;   // fraction expressing
}
model {
  theta ~ beta(2, 2);             // prior
  y ~ binomial(N, theta);         // likelihood
}
You run it from R by passing a named list whose keys match the data block, then summarise the returned draws:
library(rstan)
stan_data <- list(N = 20, y = 13)
fit <- stan(file = "gene_marker.stan", data = stan_data,
            chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 1)
print(fit, pars = "theta")
The output is thousands of samples of theta. The posterior mean is mean(draws); a 95% credible interval is the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the draws. Always check Rhat (\(\approx 1\), want \(< 1.01\)) and n_eff (bigger is better) before reading the means.

title: Exercise: introduction to R-STAN
text:
By hand
B1. For each scenario, state what goes in the data block and what goes in the parameters block. (Types and names, not full code.)

You count reads mapping to a gene in one RNA-seq sample and want the underlying expression rate \(\lambda\).
You measure a continuous phenotype in \(n\) mice and want its mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\).

B2. In the gene_marker.stan model above, point to the exact line that is the prior and the exact line that is the likelihood. In one sentence each, say what they encode.
B3. A colleague passes this data list to the gene_marker.stan model:
stan_data <- list(n = 20, successes = 13)
Stan errors. Why? Give the corrected list.
B4. Fill in the three blanks so this becomes a valid model for a single Poisson count \(y\) with rate \(\lambda\) (a gene’s read count with an unknown expression rate):
data {
  int<lower=0> y;        // observed read count
}
parameters {
  real<______> lambda;   // (1) constraint: a rate cannot be negative
}
model {
  lambda ~ ______;       // (2) a prior on lambda (name any reasonable one)
  y ~ ______;            // (3) the likelihood for a Poisson count
}
B5. You fit a model and print(fit) shows:
        mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   50% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
lambda  8.10    0.02 0.55  7.05  8.08  9.22   980 1.00

What is the posterior mean of \(\lambda\)?
Write down a 95% credible interval and state, in words, what it means.
Is this fit trustworthy? Which two numbers did you check?

B6. A different fit reports Rhat = 1.18 and n_eff = 32 for its key parameter, even though the posterior mean “looks reasonable”. Should you report the posterior mean? What would you do instead?
B7. (concept) The lecture said MCMC returns draws rather than a formula for the posterior. If you have 4000 draws of \(\theta\) stored in a vector draws, write (in words or R) how you would obtain: (a) the posterior mean, (b) the 95% credible interval, (c) the posterior probability that \(\theta > 0.5\).

title: Exercise: introduction to R-STAN
text:
Explore
Stan’s sampler is a black box; this demo opens a simple version of it. The posterior here has two parameters: intercept \(a\) (expression at age 50) and slope \(b\) (change per 10 years) of a small regression of gene expression on age, the example of the next Bayesian unit. The orange ellipses and curves show the true posterior, which you would not know in a real problem. The sampler is random-walk Metropolis: from the current point, propose a random jump of about “step size”; if the posterior is higher there, move; if it is lower, move only with probability (new posterior / old posterior); otherwise stay and record the current point again. Stan uses a smarter sampler (HMC/NUTS), but its output is read the same way: chains, warm-up, trace plots, Rhat.



E1. Press Step about ten times and watch the four chains. What happens when a jump is rejected (red cross)? Why must the sampler record the old point again instead of simply trying another jump?
E2. Load “tiny steps (0.02)” and press Run. What is the acceptance rate? Do the four chains meet before the warm-up ends? Read R-hat and compare the histograms with the orange curves. Why is a very high acceptance rate not a good sign?
E3. Load “huge steps (3)” and run it. What is the acceptance rate now, and what do the trace plots look like? Relate this to a low n_eff.
E4. Load “good steps (0.4)” and run it. Describe the traces after warm-up, the acceptance rate and R-hat. Then drag one start point (big circle) to the edge of the plot, even farther from the posterior, and run again: which part of the run absorbs the long walk in, and why is it discarded?






Solutions





E1. A rejected chain does not move: the trace stays flat for that iteration and the same \((a, b)\) is stored again. Repeating the point is what makes the draws proportional to the posterior: high-posterior points are hard to leave, so they are recorded many times, while low-posterior points are left quickly. If rejected jumps were simply retried, every visited point would count once and the histogram would no longer match the posterior.
E2. About 90% of the jumps are accepted, but each is tiny, so the chains crawl. After 1000 iterations they are still on their way in from the corners and have not met; R-hat for \(a\) is about 3.6 (far above 1.01, “chains disagree”), and the histograms are lumpy and too wide compared with the orange curves. Nearly every jump is accepted because nearly every jump is too small to change the posterior much; the chain explores very slowly.
E3. Only about 1% of the jumps are accepted: almost every proposal lands far out in the tails, where the posterior is tiny. The traces are flat staircases, each chain often sitting on the same value for a hundred iterations or more, and the post-warm-up draws contain only about a dozen distinct values. Thousands of draws carry the information of a handful of independent ones, which is exactly what a low n_eff reports; R-hat (about 1.4) also flags the problem.
E4. About 30% of the jumps are accepted. After warm-up the traces of the four chains overlap like “fuzzy caterpillars” around the same level, the histograms follow the orange curves, and R-hat is about 1.00–1.01 (“chains agree”). A start far away just makes the walk in longer; that walk happens during the warm-up, drawn faint on the left and shaded on the traces. Those iterations reflect where the chain started, not the posterior, which is why they are thrown away. (If a chain still has not arrived by the end of warm-up, R-hat will show it.)

title: Exercise: introduction to R-STAN
text:
In R
All code below is illustrative — treat it as something you reason about, not something that must execute here (no Stan is installed at render time). In a real session you would run it.

Run the marker model and summarise the draws
library(rstan)

stan_data <- list(N = 20, y = 13)          # keys match the data block
fit <- stan(file = "gene_marker.stan", data = stan_data,
            chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 1)

print(fit, pars = "theta")                 # mean, quantiles, n_eff, Rhat


Pull the draws out and compute summaries yourself
draws <- as.data.frame(fit)$theta          # a vector of ~4000 posterior draws

mean(draws)                                # posterior mean
quantile(draws, c(0.025, 0.975))           # 95% credible interval
mean(draws > 0.5)                          # posterior P(theta > 0.5)
The point: once you hold the draws, every posterior summary is ordinary descriptive statistics.


A Poisson count model (the B4 answer, assembled)
// gene_count.stan
data {
  int<lower=0> y;                 // observed read count
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> lambda;           // expression rate (non-negative)
}
model {
  lambda ~ normal(10, 5);         // a weakly-informative prior
  y ~ poisson(lambda);            // likelihood for a count
}
fit2 <- stan(file = "gene_count.stan", data = list(y = 8),
             chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 1)
print(fit2, pars = "lambda")


The brms shortcut (for a regression)
library(brms)

# cells: a data frame with a 0/1 column `expressed` and a `treatment` column
fit3 <- brm(expressed ~ treatment, data = cells,
            family = bernoulli(),                    # 0/1 -> logistic regression
            prior  = prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
            chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 1)
summary(fit3)                                        # same Rhat / credible-interval output


Tasks
R1. Using the “pull the draws out” block, explain what each of the three summary lines returns for the marker model, and why mean(draws > 0.5) is a probability.
R2. Modify the gene_marker.stan model to use a flat prior theta ~ beta(1, 1) instead of beta(2, 2). Would you expect the posterior mean to move toward or away from the raw ratio \(13/20 = 0.65\)? Explain in one sentence. (You do not need to run it.)
R3. For the Poisson model, write the R call that fits it to an observed count of y = 15, then the two lines that extract the draws of lambda and report a 95% credible interval.

title: Exercise: introduction to R-STAN
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — data vs parameters





Ask: is this number something I measured and will type into R? If yes it is data. Is it something I do not know and want the posterior over? If yes it is a parameter. Counts and sample sizes are data; rates, means, fractions, and standard deviations are usually parameters.









Hint 2 — spotting prior vs likelihood





The prior is the ~ statement whose left side is a parameter (it constrains the unknown before seeing data). The likelihood is the ~ statement whose left side is the data (it says how the observed numbers arise from the parameter).









Hint 3 — matching the data list





The keys of the R list must be character-for-character the identifiers in the data block. The model declares N and y; anything else (n, successes) is a different name and Stan will not find it. See stan().









Hint 4 — the Poisson block





A rate is continuous and non-negative, so real<lower=0>. Any sensible prior works, e.g. normal(10, 5) (weakly informative) — Stan respects the <lower=0> constraint. The likelihood for a single count is poisson(lambda). The Poisson is the natural first distribution for counts (from the distributions block).









Hint 5 — reading the printout





The mean column is the posterior mean. The 2.5% and 97.5% columns bracket the central 95% of the draws — that is the credible interval, and it is a direct probability statement about the parameter. Judge trust from Rhat (want \(\approx 1\), definitely \(< 1.01\)) and n_eff (want at least a few hundred).









Hint 6 — summaries are just statistics on the draws





Posterior mean = mean(draws). A 95% credible interval = quantile(draws, c(0.025, 0.975)). A posterior probability like \(P(\theta>0.5)\) = the fraction of draws above 0.5 = mean(draws > 0.5) (an average of TRUE/FALSE, which R treats as 1/0).

title: Exercise: introduction to R-STAN
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. (a) RNA-seq rate. Data: the observed read count, int<lower=0> y; (and, if you had several observations, an int<lower=0> N; for how many). Parameters: the rate, real<lower=0> lambda;. The count is measured; the rate is unknown. (b) Mouse phenotype. Data: the sample size and the measurements, int<lower=0> n; and vector[n] y;. Parameters: the mean and spread, real mu; and real<lower=0> sigma; (a standard deviation is non-negative). The measurements are known; \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) are what we infer.
B2. - Prior: theta ~ beta(2, 2); — it encodes the belief, before seeing the data, that \(\theta\) is probably near 0.5 (a gentle hump on \([0,1]\)). - Likelihood: y ~ binomial(N, theta); — it says the observed count \(y\) out of \(N\) arises as a Binomial draw with success probability \(\theta\), linking the data to the unknown.
The tell: the prior’s left side (theta) is a parameter; the likelihood’s left side (y) is data.
B3. The data block declares the identifiers N and y, but the list supplies n and successes. Stan looks for N and y, cannot find them, and errors (and it also receives two variables it does not recognise). Names must match exactly. Corrected:
stan_data <- list(N = 20, y = 13)
B4. The three blanks:
parameters {
  real<lower=0> lambda;   // (1) a rate is non-negative
}
model {
  lambda ~ normal(10, 5); // (2) any reasonable prior; normal(10,5) is weakly informative
  y ~ poisson(lambda);    // (3) Poisson likelihood for a count
}

<lower=0>, (2) any sensible prior such as normal(10, 5) — Stan keeps lambda non-negative because of the constraint, so a normal prior is fine here — and (3) poisson(lambda).

B5. (a) The posterior mean of \(\lambda\) is 8.10. (b) A 95% credible interval is \([7.05,\ 9.22]\) (the 2.5% and 97.5% columns). In words: given the data and prior, there is a 95% posterior probability that \(\lambda\) lies between 7.05 and 9.22. (c) Yes — Rhat = 1.00 (the chains agree, so the sampler converged) and n_eff = 980 (comfortably large, so the summaries are not noisy). These are the two numbers to check before reading the mean.
B6. No — do not report the posterior mean. Rhat = 1.18 is far above 1, meaning the chains did not converge to the same distribution, so the draws are not a reliable sample of the posterior; a “reasonable-looking” mean from an unconverged sampler is meaningless. n_eff = 32 is very low, confirming poor mixing. What to do: run longer (increase iter/warmup), run more chains, reconsider the priors or the model parameterisation, and only report results once Rhat < 1.01 and n_eff is adequate.
B7. With draws holding the 4000 posterior samples of \(\theta\): (a) Posterior mean: mean(draws). (b) 95% credible interval: quantile(draws, c(0.025, 0.975)) — the 2.5% and 97.5% empirical quantiles. (c) Posterior probability \(\theta > 0.5\): the fraction of draws exceeding 0.5, mean(draws > 0.5) (the mean of a TRUE/FALSE vector is the proportion of TRUEs).
R1. mean(draws) is the posterior mean of \(\theta\) (a point summary of the cloud of draws). quantile(draws, c(0.025, 0.975)) returns the values below which 2.5% and 97.5% of the draws fall — the 95% credible interval. mean(draws > 0.5) compares every draw to 0.5, giving a vector of TRUE/FALSE; averaging that vector (TRUE = 1, FALSE = 0) gives the proportion of draws above 0.5, which estimates the posterior probability \(P(\theta > 0.5)\) — a probability precisely because the draws are distributed as the posterior.
R2. With beta(1, 1) (the flat/uniform prior) the prior no longer pulls toward 0.5, so the posterior is driven by the data alone and its mean moves toward the raw ratio \(13/20 = 0.65\). (Under beta(2, 2) the mean was pulled slightly below 0.65 toward 0.5; removing that pull lets it sit closer to 0.65.)
R3.
fit_pois <- stan(file = "gene_count.stan", data = list(y = 15),
                 chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 1)

lambda_draws <- as.data.frame(fit_pois)$lambda
quantile(lambda_draws, c(0.025, 0.975))     # 95% credible interval for lambda
The first call fits the Poisson model to the observed count 15; the next two lines pull the lambda draws out and report the 2.5%/97.5% quantiles as a 95% credible interval.

title: Exercise: introduction to R-STAN
text:
Where this leads

Bayesian regression: the brms formula interface scales the three-block idea to real models — logistic regression for 0/1 outcomes, Poisson and negative binomial regression for (overdispersed) counts, and hierarchical models that share information across genes or samples.
Count models (distributions block): swapping the likelihood line for poisson or neg_binomial turns this same skeleton into a model for RNA-seq counts — the honest treatment of overdispersion you met when comparing Poisson and negative binomial.
Posterior predictive checks: beyond summarising parameters, the draws let you simulate new data from the fitted model and check it against the real data — the standard way to ask “does this model actually fit?” (a later Bayesian topic).

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
About this lecture
In Linear models we fit \(\mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol\beta\) by least squares — the best straight-line predictor. That works beautifully when we have many samples and few predictors. In genomics we usually have the opposite: thousands of genes, a few dozen samples. Ordinary least squares breaks. Today we fix it by penalizing large coefficients.

Ridge (L2): shrink all coefficients toward zero — tames collinearity, keeps every predictor.
Lasso (L1): shrink and set some coefficients exactly to zero — automatic feature selection (a sparse model).
Elastic net: a tunable mix of the two.
The geometry behind why lasso zeros coefficients but ridge does not (a diamond vs. a circle).
The tuning parameter \(\lambda\), and how to choose it by cross-validation.
In R: the glmnet package. Biology: selecting a handful of predictive genes from a whole transcriptome.


The single mental image for today: least squares chases the training data too hard when predictors outnumber samples, so we add a “leash” that pulls the coefficients back toward zero. Ridge shortens every leash a bit; lasso can pull some coefficients all the way to zero and drop those predictors entirely. Everything else — the geometry, lambda, cross-validation, glmnet — hangs off that one picture. Emphasise that this is the first time the course meets a genuinely high-dimensional problem (p much greater than n), which is the normal situation in omics. Keep an R session open but do not depend on live output; the code is illustrative.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
section: A note on where this sits
text:
A note on where this sits






Important


This Penalized linear models block is provisional. It may move to a later dedicated statistics / machine-learning course (Statistics and machine learning in bioinformatics), which is not a prerequisite here. We include it now because penalized regression is the most direct answer to a problem biologists hit immediately — too many genes, too few samples — and it needs nothing beyond the linear-algebra and linear-model machinery we have already built. Treat the cross-validation and model-selection parts as a first look, not the full treatment.




Be transparent with students and with reviewers: this unit is a candidate for relocation. It is included because it is a natural, self-contained payoff of the linear-models material and it solves a problem they will recognise from their own data. Nothing here requires the ML course. If a colleague reviewing the syllabus decides penalized regression belongs with cross-validation, resampling, and train/test splits in the ML course, this block moves wholesale. Say this out loud so nobody assumes it is load-bearing for later units.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
section: Biology first: too many genes, too few samples
text:
Biology first: too many genes, too few samples
You measure expression of 20 000 genes in 40 patients and want to predict a phenotype (drug response, tumour subtype, survival). You would like a model
\[\text{phenotype} \approx \beta_1\,\text{gene}_1 + \beta_2\,\text{gene}_2 + \dots + \beta_p\,\text{gene}_p.\]

Predictors \(p = 20\,000\) hugely exceeds samples \(n = 40\). This is the \(p \gg n\) regime — the normal situation in omics.
Ordinary least squares has infinitely many perfect fits and picks nonsense: huge, unstable coefficients that memorise noise.
Many genes are co-regulated (collinear), so their coefficients trade off wildly.

We want a model that is stable and, ideally, short — built on a few genes we could take to the bench. That is exactly what penalties deliver.


Ground the whole lecture in the wide-matrix picture. In omics the data matrix is short and very wide: far more features than samples. Two concrete failures of ordinary least squares here: (1) with more unknowns than equations there is no unique solution — the fit is underdetermined; (2) co-regulated genes are near-duplicates, so the design matrix is nearly collinear and coefficients become huge and sign-unstable. Both are cured by shrinkage. Also plant the biological wish: a sparse predictor built from a handful of genes is testable and interpretable, unlike a dense 20 000-gene formula. That wish is what lasso answers.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
section: Recall: least squares and where it breaks
text:
Recall: least squares and where it breaks
Ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses \(\boldsymbol\beta\) to make the residual sum of squares as small as possible:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{OLS}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta\big)^2}_{\text{RSS} \,=\, \lVert \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2}, \qquad \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{OLS}} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top \mathbf{y}.\]

The formula needs \(X^\top X\) to be invertible. When \(p > n\), or when predictors are collinear, \(X^\top X\) is singular (or nearly so) — no stable inverse.
OLS has only one goal: fit the training data. With enough predictors it fits it perfectly, including the noise — overfitting.

We need a second goal that competes with “fit the data”: keep the coefficients small.

Reconnect to Linear models and to the singular-matrix idea from Linear systems by hand: OLS relies on inverting X-transpose-X, and that inverse fails to exist (or explodes) exactly when p exceeds n or predictors are collinear — the same “no unique solution / columns (nearly) parallel” situation they met with linear systems. The conceptual pivot of the whole lecture is here: OLS optimises a single objective (fit). Penalized regression adds a second, competing objective (small coefficients). The tug-of-war between the two is regularisation. Do not write the ridge formula yet; just set up the need.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
section: The idea: add a penalty for big coefficients
text:
The idea: add a penalty for big coefficients
Keep the fit term, but add a cost that grows with the size of the coefficients:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \Big\{\ \underbrace{\lVert \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2}_{\text{fit the data}} \ +\ \underbrace{\lambda \cdot \text{penalty}(\boldsymbol\beta)}_{\text{keep }\boldsymbol\beta\text{ small}}\ \Big\}\]

\(\lambda \ge 0\) sets the exchange rate between the two goals. \(\lambda = 0\) gives plain OLS; larger \(\lambda\) buys smaller coefficients at the price of some fit.
The shape of the penalty is what distinguishes the three methods:




Method
penalty\((\boldsymbol\beta)\)
name




Ridge
\(\sum_j \beta_j^2\)
L2 (squared)


Lasso
\(\sum_j \lvert\beta_j\rvert\)
L1 (absolute)


Elastic net
mix of both
L1 + L2





This is the master equation of the lecture: minimise fit plus lambda times penalty. Read it aloud as a compromise — we deliberately fit the data slightly worse in exchange for smaller, more stable coefficients. Lambda is the dial controlling that compromise. Stress that only the shape of the penalty differs between ridge, lasso, and elastic net; the fit term and the role of lambda are identical. Everything that follows is “what does each penalty shape do?” A small but crucial technical point coming up: the penalty is applied to standardised predictors and never to the intercept.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
section: First: put predictors on a common scale
text:
First: put predictors on a common scale
The penalty \(\sum_j \beta_j^2\) (or \(\sum_j |\beta_j|\)) adds up coefficients across all predictors. That only makes sense if the predictors are comparable in scale.

A gene measured in large units gets an artificially small coefficient and is under-penalized; a gene in small units is over-penalized. The penalty would depend on your units, which is unacceptable.
Fix: standardize each predictor to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 before fitting. Then a coefficient’s size reflects importance, not units.
The intercept is never penalized — it just anchors the overall level of \(\mathbf{y}\).

glmnet does this standardization for you (standardize = TRUE by default) and reports coefficients back on the original scale.

Standardisation is easy to forget and it matters a lot. Because the penalty sums coefficients across predictors, predictors must be on the same footing or the penalty silently favours whichever ones happen to be in big units. The cure is to centre and scale each column before penalising. Reassure students that glmnet handles this automatically and, helpfully, back-transforms the coefficients to the original units so the output is interpretable. Also note the intercept is excluded from the penalty: we never want to shrink the baseline level of the response toward zero. This is a good place to connect to standardisation they saw in the statistics course.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
Ridge regression (L2 penalty)
Penalize the sum of squared coefficients:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \lVert \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2\]
This has a clean closed form — just add \(\lambda\) to the diagonal of \(X^\top X\):
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{ridge}} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}\]

Adding \(\lambda I\) makes the matrix invertible again, even when \(X^\top X\) alone is singular (\(p>n\) or collinear). This is why ridge tames collinearity.
Every coefficient is shrunk toward zero, but essentially none becomes exactly zero — ridge keeps all predictors.



Ridge is the gentle one. Two things to land. First, the closed form: it is OLS with lambda added to the diagonal of X-transpose-X. That single change guarantees an invertible matrix — connect straight back to the eigenvalue idea: adding lambda*I shifts every eigenvalue up by lambda, so a zero eigenvalue (singular, non-invertible) becomes lambda (invertible). That is the exact mechanism by which ridge rescues the p greater than n case and stabilises collinear predictors, which otherwise fight over a shared signal. Second: ridge shrinks everything smoothly but sets nothing exactly to zero, so the model still uses all p genes. If you want selection, ridge alone will not give it — that is lasso’s job.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
When collinear predictors fight
Two co-regulated genes \(g_1, g_2\) carry almost the same signal. OLS is free to write
\[100\,g_1 - 98\,g_2, \quad\text{or}\quad -50\,g_1 + 52\,g_2, \quad\text{or}\dots\]
— wildly different coefficients that predict almost identically. The coefficients are unstable: a tiny change in the data flips them.

Ridge dislikes large coefficients (they cost \(\beta^2\)), so it spreads the weight smoothly and roughly equally between \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) — small, stable, sensible values.
This “sharing” behaviour is a hallmark of the L2 penalty and is often desirable in biology, where truly co-regulated genes should share credit.



Make collinearity concrete with the near-duplicate-gene example: because the two genes carry the same information, OLS can trade one off against the other without hurting the fit, producing gigantic and sign-flipping coefficients. Ridge, penalising squared size, prefers to split the weight evenly between them — two moderate coefficients cost less than one huge one. Frame this as a feature, not just a fix: in biology, co-regulated genes arguably should receive shared, comparable weights. Contrast with what lasso will do next (arbitrarily pick one of the pair and zero the other), which is sometimes what you want and sometimes not.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
Lasso regression (L1 penalty)
Penalize the sum of absolute values instead:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \lVert \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p}\lvert\beta_j\rvert\]

One small change — squares become absolute values — has a dramatic effect: as \(\lambda\) grows, coefficients are driven exactly to zero, one after another.
A coefficient of exactly zero means the predictor is dropped. Lasso therefore performs automatic feature selection: it returns a sparse model using only a subset of the genes.
No closed form (the \(|\beta|\) kink is not differentiable at \(0\)); solved numerically — which is what glmnet does.



Lasso is the selector. The headline: switching the penalty from squared to absolute values changes the behaviour qualitatively, not just quantitatively. Instead of shrinking everything a little, the L1 penalty sends coefficients to exactly zero as lambda increases, and a zero coefficient means that gene is out of the model. So lasso does variable selection and estimation in one step, returning a sparse, interpretable model — exactly the “few genes we can take to the bench” wish from the motivation slide. Flag that there is no tidy formula because the absolute value has a corner at zero; the solver handles it. The next two slides explain why the corner produces zeros.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
section: Why lasso zeros coefficients: the geometry
text:
Why lasso zeros coefficients: the geometry
Equivalent view: minimize RSS subject to a budget on the coefficients.
\[\text{Ridge: } \sum_j \beta_j^2 \le t \qquad\qquad \text{Lasso: } \sum_j \lvert\beta_j\rvert \le t\]
In two dimensions (\(\beta_1,\beta_2\)) the budget region is:

Ridge → a circle (disk): \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2 \le t\) — smooth, round, no special points.
Lasso → a diamond (square on its corner): \(\lvert\beta_1\rvert + \lvert\beta_2\rvert \le t\) — with sharp corners sitting on the axes.

The RSS forms elliptical contours around the OLS solution. The penalized estimate is where the smallest ellipse first touches the budget region.


This is the money slide and worth going slowly. Recast the penalty as a hard budget: minimise the fit error while keeping the coefficients inside a region of a fixed size. The shape of that region is set by the penalty. L2 gives a round disk; L1 gives a diamond with corners poking out along the axes. Now overlay the RSS contours — concentric ellipses centred on the unconstrained OLS solution — and grow them until they first touch the budget region. The touch point is the solution. On the circle the touch happens at a generic point with both coordinates nonzero. On the diamond it tends to happen at a corner. A corner lies on an axis, meaning one coordinate is exactly zero. That is the geometric origin of sparsity. Draw it live if you can.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
section: The corner is on the axis = a zero coefficient
text:
The corner is on the axis = a zero coefficient

A corner of the diamond sits on an axis: at that point one of the coordinates is exactly zero (e.g. \(\beta_2 = 0\)).
Expanding ellipses are very likely to first touch a pointy corner rather than a flat edge — so the lasso solution often lands with some coefficients exactly zero.
The circle has no corners, so the touch point almost never sits exactly on an axis — ridge coefficients get small but stay nonzero.

One sentence: the corners of the L1 diamond are what create sparsity; the roundness of the L2 circle is what prevents it.
In higher dimensions the diamond becomes a many-cornered shape whose edges and faces lie in coordinate subspaces — touching one zeros several coefficients at once.


Reinforce the punchline in words: corners equal zeros. Because the diamond’s corners are the parts that stick out furthest toward the ellipses, the growing RSS contour usually meets a corner first, and a corner has one (or in high dimensions, many) coordinates exactly zero. The circle, being smooth, offers no such preferred points, so ridge never sets things exactly to zero. Students remember this as “diamond selects, circle shrinks.” Then generalise: in p dimensions the L1 ball is a cross-polytope with low-dimensional faces lying in coordinate subspaces, and contact with those faces zeros many coefficients simultaneously — which is why lasso can prune thousands of genes down to a handful.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
section: Elastic net: the best of both
text:
Elastic net: the best of both
Combine both penalties, with a mixing parameter \(\alpha \in [0,1]\):
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{enet}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \lVert \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol\beta \rVert^2 + \lambda\Big[\, \alpha\sum_j \lvert\beta_j\rvert \;+\; (1-\alpha)\sum_j \beta_j^2 \,\Big]\]

\(\alpha = 1\) → pure lasso; \(\alpha = 0\) → pure ridge; in between → a blend.
Fixes a real lasso weakness: among a group of correlated genes, lasso tends to pick one arbitrarily and zero the rest. Elastic net’s L2 part encourages grouping — correlated genes are selected (or dropped) together.
Also lets lasso select more than \(n\) predictors (pure lasso caps at \(n\) when \(p>n\)).

A common recipe: keep some sparsity (\(\alpha\) around \(0.5\)) so you still get a short gene list, but with stabler, group-aware selection.


Elastic net is the pragmatic default for genomics. It literally adds the two penalties with a knob alpha that dials from pure ridge (0) to pure lasso (1). The reason it matters biologically: pure lasso, faced with a cluster of co-regulated genes, arbitrarily keeps one and discards its neighbours, which is unstable and biologically misleading — the whole pathway is relevant, not one gene. The ridge component makes elastic net keep or drop such correlated groups together (the grouping effect). It also lifts lasso’s technical ceiling of at most n selected variables when p exceeds n. Note glmnet uses exactly this alpha parameterisation, so the code will feel natural. Suggest alpha around 0.5 as a sensible starting point, to be tuned.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
The tuning parameter \(\lambda\)
\(\lambda\) controls how hard we shrink — it trades bias against variance.

\(\lambda \to 0\): back to OLS — low bias, high variance, overfits.
\(\lambda \to \infty\): all coefficients \(\to 0\) — the model becomes a flat line at \(\bar y\): high bias, low variance, underfits.
Somewhere in between is the \(\lambda\) that predicts new data best.

We cannot read the best \(\lambda\) off the training fit — training error just keeps dropping as \(\lambda\to0\). We must estimate performance on data the model did not see.


Lambda is the single most important knob and it embodies the bias-variance trade-off, which for many students is the first time they meet that idea explicitly. Too small: essentially OLS, fits noise, great on training data and poor on new data. Too large: crushes all signal, predicts the mean. The sweet spot minimises error on unseen data. Crucial pedagogical warning: you cannot choose lambda by minimising training error, because training error falls monotonically as lambda shrinks toward zero — it would always pick the overfit model. You need an honest estimate of out-of-sample error, which is what cross-validation provides on the next slide. This is a first look at the idea; the full ML treatment lives elsewhere.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
Choosing \(\lambda\) by cross-validation
\(k\)-fold cross-validation estimates out-of-sample error honestly:

Split the samples into \(k\) groups (folds), e.g. \(k = 10\).
For each fold: train on the other \(k-1\) folds, predict the held-out fold, record the error.
Average the errors across folds → a cross-validated error for that \(\lambda\).
Repeat over a grid of \(\lambda\) values; pick the \(\lambda\) with the lowest CV error.

Two standard choices glmnet reports:

lambda.min — the \(\lambda\) with minimum CV error.
lambda.1se — the largest \(\lambda\) within one standard error of that minimum: a simpler, sparser model that performs about as well. Often preferred for a short gene list.



Cross-validation is the engine that turns lambda from a mystery into a data-driven choice. Walk the k-fold loop slowly: hold out a fold, train on the rest, predict the fold, and rotate so every sample is held out exactly once; average to get a fair error estimate for each candidate lambda. Then scan the lambda grid and pick the best. Introduce the two conventions glmnet gives: lambda.min is the raw minimiser; lambda.1se deliberately errs toward more shrinkage, taking the simplest model statistically indistinguishable from the best. For a biologist wanting a short, robust gene list, lambda.1se is usually the better pick because it is sparser and less likely to be a fluke of one CV split. Mention that with tiny n, CV estimates are themselves noisy — honesty about a stepping stone.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
In R: glmnet
The glmnet package fits ridge, lasso, and elastic net over a whole grid of \(\lambda\) efficiently.
library(glmnet)

# x: samples x genes matrix (n rows, p columns); y: the phenotype vector
x <- as.matrix(expr)      # e.g. 40 patients x 20000 genes
y <- response            # numeric outcome (e.g. drug IC50)

# alpha = 1 -> lasso, alpha = 0 -> ridge, 0 < alpha < 1 -> elastic net
fit <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1)     # fits a path of lambda values

plot(fit, xvar = "lambda")          # coefficient paths vs log(lambda)
print(fit)                          # Df (# nonzero), %Dev, Lambda per step

glmnet standardizes predictors internally (standardize = TRUE) and returns coefficients on the original scale.
It does not fit a single \(\lambda\) — it returns the whole path, so you see how coefficients enter and leave as \(\lambda\) changes.


Keep this practical and reassuring: one function, one alpha argument, and you have all three methods. glmnet is fast because it solves the entire lambda path at once using warm starts, so the coefficient-path plot comes essentially for free — and that plot is the best way to see shrinkage and selection happening. Remind them the code here is illustrative and not executed at render time; they will run it in the exercise. Point out the Df column in print(fit) is the number of nonzero coefficients, i.e. how many genes the model currently uses — the sparsity, made visible. Reiterate the internal standardisation so they do not double-scale.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
section: In R: cross-validated fit and the gene list
text:
In R: cross-validated fit and the gene list
set.seed(1)                              # CV is random; fix the seed for reproducibility
cvfit <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)

plot(cvfit)                              # CV error vs log(lambda), with lambda.min / .1se
cvfit$lambda.min                         # lambda with lowest CV error
cvfit$lambda.1se                         # sparser model within 1 SE

# coefficients at the chosen lambda
beta <- coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.1se")    # a sparse vector; most entries are 0
selected <- rownames(beta)[which(beta != 0)]
selected                                 # the genes the model kept  <- the biology

# predict the phenotype for new samples
predict(cvfit, newx = x_new, s = "lambda.1se")

For a binary phenotype (responder vs. not) use family = "binomial" — penalized logistic regression, same machinery.


This slide is the payoff: from a 20 000-gene matrix to a named short list of genes in a few lines. cv.glmnet runs the k-fold loop across the lambda grid and stores lambda.min and lambda.1se. Extract the coefficients at the chosen lambda, drop the zeros, and the surviving row names are your selected genes — that vector is the biological result, a candidate signature to validate experimentally. Show predict() so they see the model is also usable for new patients. Finally note the family argument: swap to binomial and the identical framework does penalized logistic regression for a yes/no outcome, which is extremely common (responder vs non-responder, tumour vs normal). Remind them to set a seed because the fold assignment is random.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
section: Biology: from transcriptome to a testable signature
text:
Biology: from transcriptome to a testable signature

Predictive gene signatures. Lasso / elastic net on expression + drug response returns a small panel of genes that predict response — a candidate biomarker you can take to a targeted assay.
Interpretability & cost. A 20-gene panel can be run cheaply in the clinic; a 20 000-gene model cannot. Sparsity is not just statistics — it is assay design.
Stability matters. With \(n \approx 40\), different CV splits can select somewhat different genes. Report a stable core, prefer lambda.1se, and consider elastic net so correlated pathway members are kept together.
Not causal. A selected gene is predictive, not proven causal — collinearity means a dropped gene may be just as relevant as the one kept. Validate on the bench.


Bring it back to biology and to honesty. The realistic use case is building a compact predictive signature from omics data — the sort of thing behind commercial expression-based diagnostic panels. Emphasise three caveats that separate a naive from a careful analysis. First, sparsity has a practical payoff beyond parsimony: a short panel is assayable and affordable in a clinical setting. Second, selection is unstable at small n — do not over-interpret the exact membership of the list; look for genes that recur across resamples, and lean on lambda.1se and elastic net for robustness. Third, and most important scientifically: penalized regression finds predictive, not causal, genes; because of collinearity the specific gene kept may be a stand-in for a co-regulated neighbour. The model proposes; the bench disposes.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
Which penalty when?







Situation
Reach for




Many collinear predictors, want to keep them all
Ridge


Want a short, interpretable subset (feature selection)
Lasso


\(p \gg n\) and correlated groups of predictors
Elastic net


Purely predictive, interpretability not needed
Ridge (often lowest error)


Need a testable gene panel
Lasso / elastic net




All three reduce variance / overfitting relative to OLS; they differ in whether and how they zero coefficients.
Always standardize (glmnet does it), never penalize the intercept, and choose \(\lambda\) by cross-validation.


A decision table to consolidate. The one-line summary: ridge shrinks and keeps everything and is often the best pure predictor; lasso shrinks and selects, giving interpretability; elastic net blends them and is the safe default for wide, correlated omics matrices. All three beat OLS on new data whenever p is large or predictors collinear, because they trade a little bias for a lot less variance. End on the three non-negotiables: standardise predictors, leave the intercept unpenalised, and pick lambda by cross-validation rather than by eye or by training error. These are the habits that keep the analysis honest.

title: Ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Problem
\(p \gg n\) or collinearity → OLS unstable / overfits


General form
minimize \(\lVert \mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2 + \lambda\,\text{penalty}(\boldsymbol\beta)\)


Ridge (L2)
penalty \(\sum\beta_j^2\); shrinks all, keeps all; \((X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}\)


Lasso (L1)
penalty \(\sum\lvert\beta_j\rvert\); sets some \(\beta_j = 0\) → feature selection


Geometry
circle (ridge) vs diamond (lasso); corners on axes → zeros


Elastic net
\(\alpha\sum\lvert\beta_j\rvert + (1-\alpha)\sum\beta_j^2\); grouped selection


\(\lambda\)
shrinkage dial; bias–variance trade-off; choose by cross-validation


R
glmnet(x, y, alpha=…), cv.glmnet(…), coef(cvfit, s="lambda.1se")


Biology
short, testable gene signatures; predictive \(\neq\) causal



Next: apply this to a real wide expression matrix in the exercise, then test yourself with the quiz.

The summary is the revision sheet. Drill the storyline once more: OLS breaks when predictors outnumber samples or are collinear; adding a penalty times lambda fixes it; the penalty shape decides behaviour — squared (ridge) shrinks and keeps all, absolute (lasso) shrinks and selects, and the mix (elastic net) does grouped selection; the geometry (round circle vs cornered diamond) explains why only lasso zeros coefficients; lambda is chosen by cross-validation, not by training error; and glmnet does all of it in a few lines. Close on the biological through-line and the caveat that a predictive gene is not a proven causal one. Remind them this block is provisional and may migrate to the ML course.

title: Polar coordinates: measuring a ring
text:
About this lecture
Many things in biology grow or spread outwards from a centre: a drop of antibiotic, a colony, a tumour spheroid, a cell nucleus. For those, \((x, y)\) is the wrong way to describe a position. Distance from the centre and direction fit much better.

Polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\): how far from the centre, and in which direction.
A very useful transformation, but a nonlinear one: unlike rotation or shear, it is not a matrix.
Unwrapping an image around a centre turns rings into straight lines.
Biology: measuring the zone of inhibition of an antibiotic, from a photo of a real plate.

You need the jpeg package from Transforming images with matrices.

This unit comes after Fourier in the Applications block and reuses the setup from Transforming images with matrices (image as img[x, y], pixel coordinates as a 2 x N matrix). The new idea is a coordinate change that is not linear, and the payoff is a real measurement that clinical microbiology labs make every day. The plate photo is from the CDC Public Health Image Library (PHIL #10785, Gilda L. Jones, 1972), public domain.

title: Polar coordinates: measuring a ring
text:
Biology: the disk diffusion test




Is this bacterium resistant to an antibiotic? The disk diffusion (Kirby–Bauer) test answers it in one plate:

Spread bacteria evenly on agar; place 6 mm paper disks, each soaked in a different antibiotic.
The drug diffuses outwards. Where it is strong enough, nothing grows: a clear zone of inhibition.
Next day, measure each zone’s diameter in mm. A lab compares it with a breakpoint table (EUCAST or CLSI) for that drug and species: susceptible or resistant.

Diffusion spreads equally in all directions, so the zones are (nearly) circles. Circles are easy in polar coordinates.
Image: CDC / Gilda L. Jones, Public Health Image Library #10785, public domain.


This is the standard antimicrobial susceptibility test in clinical microbiology, and its result decides which antibiotic a patient gets. A bigger zone means the drug stops growth further from the disk, so the bacterium is more sensitive. In the lab the zone is usually read by eye with a ruler or calliper; automated plate readers do exactly what we do today: find each disk, then measure the zone around it. The disk numbers are ours; the photo does not say which drugs these are, so today we measure diameters, not S/R calls.

title: Polar coordinates: measuring a ring
text:
Polar coordinates


A point \((x, y)\), seen from a centre \((x_0, y_0)\):

\(r\) = distance from the centre
\(\theta\) = angle, counter-clockwise from the \(x\) direction

\[r = \sqrt{(x - x_0)^2 + (y - y_0)^2}, \qquad \theta = \operatorname{atan2}(y - y_0,\ x - x_0)\]
and back again:
\[x = x_0 + r\cos\theta, \qquad y = y_0 + r\sin\theta\]
dx <- 3; dy <- 4
sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2)          # r = 5
atan2(dy, dx) * 180 / pi   # theta = 53.1 degrees



Image: CDC / Gilda L. Jones, PHIL #10785, public domain.

r is Pythagoras, and the “back again” formulas are the same cos and sin that appear in the rotation matrix. Use atan2, not atan: atan(dy / dx) cannot tell (1, 1) from (-1, -1) because the ratio is the same, so it only covers half the circle. atan2(dy, dx) looks at both signs and returns an angle between -180 and 180 degrees. Note the argument order: y first. Angles in R are in radians; multiply by 180/pi to get degrees.

title: Polar coordinates: measuring a ring
section: Polar coordinates are not a matrix
text:
Polar coordinates are not a matrix


Every transformation in Transforming images with matrices kept straight lines straight: that is what a matrix does.
Polar coordinates turn circles into straight lines and straight lines into curves. No 2 × 2 matrix can do that.
Check with one point: doubling \((1, 1)\) doubles \(r\) but keeps \(\theta\). A linear map would double both outputs.


This is the conceptual point of the unit. A linear map satisfies f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b) and f(c a) = c f(a). For polar coordinates, f(2 p) = (2r, theta): theta does not scale. Also (1, 0) has theta = 0 and (0, 1) has theta = 90, but their sum (1, 1) has theta = 45, not 90. So there is no matrix for it, and we compute r and theta with sqrt and atan2 instead of %*%. The upside is the right panel: around the right centre, a circle is the simplest possible shape, a horizontal line.

title: Polar coordinates: measuring a ring
text:
Every pixel gets a distance
Load the plate as in Transforming images with matrices, then compute \(r\) for every pixel around disk 5:
img <- jpeg::readJPEG("plate.jpg")                # 600 x 600 grey levels, 0..1
img <- t(img[nrow(img):1, ])                      # flip so up is up; now img[x, y]
xy  <- t(expand.grid(1:nrow(img), 1:ncol(img)))   # 2 x N pixel coordinates
x0 <- 353; y0 <- 356                              # centre of disk 5
r  <- sqrt((xy[1, ] - x0)^2 + (xy[2, ] - y0)^2)   # one distance per pixel
near <- r <= 80
plot(r[near], img[near], pch = 16, cex = 0.3)     # grey level against distance

Download plate.jpg. Image: CDC / Gilda L. Jones, PHIL #10785, public domain.

No loop: r is computed for all 360 000 pixels in one vectorised line, just like A %*% xy moved every pixel at once. img[near] works because as.vector(img) has the same pixel order as the columns of xy. Reading the scatter: the dark disk (r < 13), the bright clear zone, a sharp drop at the zone edge near r = 53, then the darker lawn. Beyond r = 60 the cloud splits in two: towards the upper right the 80-pixel circle reaches into the next zone (disk 4). Ask students to find that in the left panel.

title: Polar coordinates: measuring a ring
section: The radial profile: average over the angle
text:
The radial profile: average over the angle
Group the pixels by distance and average: one number per radius.
prof <- tapply(img[near], round(r[near]), mean)   # mean grey level at r = 0, 1, ..., 80
rr   <- as.numeric(names(prof))
edge <- min(rr[rr >= 16 & prof < 0.55])           # first radius past the disk that is dark
edge                                              # 53 pixels
2 * edge / (26.8 / 6)                             # diameter: 24 mm (a 6 mm disk is 26.8 px)

Image: CDC / Gilda L. Jones, PHIL #10785, public domain.

Averaging over theta throws away direction and keeps distance: 360 000 pixels become 81 numbers, and the noise from scratches and streaks averages out. The edge is where the profile crosses a threshold halfway between the zone (about 0.9) and the lawn (about 0.3); rr >= 16 skips the dark disk itself. The disk gives us a free ruler: it is 6 mm across and about 26.8 pixels in this photo, so 1 mm is about 4.5 pixels. Zone diameter = 2 * edge, converted to mm.

title: Polar coordinates: measuring a ring
text:
Unwrapping: work backwards from (r, θ)
To turn the ring into a picture in \((\theta, r)\), go backwards: for each \((r, \theta)\) on a grid, compute \(x, y\) and look up the nearest pixel.
unwrap <- function(x0, y0, rmax = 80) {
  r     <- 0:rmax
  theta <- (0:359) * pi / 180                     # one column per degree
  x <- x0 + outer(r, cos(theta))                  # (rmax + 1) x 360 grid of positions
  y <- y0 + outer(r, sin(theta))
  matrix(img[cbind(round(as.vector(x)), round(as.vector(y)))], nrow = length(r))
}
u <- unwrap(353, 356)                             # rows = r, columns = theta

Image: CDC / Gilda L. Jones, PHIL #10785, public domain.

This is the “work backwards” trick mentioned at the end of Transforming images with matrices: instead of pushing input pixels forward (which leaves holes), we ask, for every output position, where it comes from in the input. Here that is easy, because x = x0 + r cos(theta) is an explicit formula. round() picks the nearest pixel; image software interpolates between neighbours instead. img[cbind(i, j)] looks up many pixels at once by their (x, y) indices. In the strip the zone edge is a straight horizontal line at r = 53, and rowMeans(u) gives the same radial profile as tapply on the previous slide.

title: Polar coordinates: measuring a ring
text:
Try it: move the centre




The same unwrapping as on the previous slide, live, with bilinear interpolation instead of round(). The demo starts with the centre about 11 pixels off disk 5. Point out the result first: in the strip (theta across, r up) the zone edge is a wave, not a line, and in the profile the drop is smeared out over many radii. Ask the class which way to move the centre: where the wave is highest, the edge is furthest away, so move towards that angle (0 degrees is to the right, 90 degrees is up). Drag the red cross, or press anywhere on the photo. When the centre is right the edge in the strip is flat, the profile drop is steep and it lies on the grey curve (the best centre). “Snap to best centre” first finds the dark paper disk, then nudges the centre until the edge is flattest. Then change the threshold: the yellow pixels are those brighter than the threshold, and the red line is the edge per angle, as in apply(u, 2, …). Disk 4 stays wavy even at the best centre: the zone itself is not round (next slide). Disk 11 has a fuzzy edge: watch how far the edge moves with the threshold. Disk 7 is the smallest zone.

title: Polar coordinates: measuring a ring
section: A zone that is not round
text:
A zone that is not round
Disk 4 sits near the plate edge, between two other zones. Find the edge separately for every angle, one column of the strip at a time:
u4 <- unwrap(478, 413, rmax = 100)
edge_at <- apply(u4, 2, function(v) min(which(0:100 >= 16 & v < 0.55)) - 1)   # row 1 is r = 0
range(edge_at)                                    # 69 to 83 pixels: not a circle


The edge \(r(\theta)\) is a curve in the strip, not a line. Averaging over \(\theta\) would hide that.
Lab rule of thumb: an irregular or merging zone is unreliable; repeat the test or read the undisturbed side.

Image: CDC / Gilda L. Jones, PHIL #10785, public domain.

apply(u4, 2, …) runs the edge rule down each column, i.e. each direction. The edge lies between 69 and 83 pixels (31 to 37 mm as a diameter). The shortest radius points up and to the right, towards the plate rim, where only a thin strip of lawn is left; the longest points down and to the left, towards disk 5, where the two zones almost touch. In polar coordinates, “is it a circle?” becomes “is r(theta) flat?”, a question about one curve. Large r also reaches into neighbouring zones (the bright bumps at the top of the strip), which is why rmax matters.

title: Polar coordinates: measuring a ring
text:
Measuring the whole plate
The same three lines for every disk: centre → unwrap → profile → edge.
disks <- data.frame(x = c(218, 386, 111, 478, 353, 226, 506, 101, 322, 436, 148, 298),
                    y = c(508, 511, 403, 413, 356, 306, 275, 247, 220, 147, 113,  82))
edge_of <- function(p) min(which(0:80 >= 16 & p < 0.55)) - 1   # row 1 is r = 0
edges <- sapply(1:12, function(i) edge_of(rowMeans(unwrap(disks$x[i], disks$y[i]))))
diam_mm <- 2 * edges / (26.8 / 6)


Each diameter is then compared with the breakpoint for its drug and species.
Disk 11 has a fuzzy edge: its diameter depends strongly on the threshold (exercise R5).

Image: CDC / Gilda L. Jones, PHIL #10785, public domain.

Zones range from 15 mm (disk 7) to 35 mm (disk 4). Measurements are only as good as the scale (the disk is 6 mm; the 26.8-pixel width was measured once) and the threshold. Sharp edges barely move when the threshold changes (1 to 2 mm between thresholds 0.5 and 0.6); the fuzzy zone of disk 11 (partial inhibition at its rim) shifts by about 8 mm, which is exactly the situation where human readers also disagree. The disk centres were found once from the dark disks; finding them automatically is another image analysis step.

title: Polar coordinates: measuring a ring
text:
Polar coordinates elsewhere
The same move, “pick a centre, then use distance and angle”, appears all over biology:







Where
What \(r\) or \(\theta\) tells you




Tumour spheroids, organoids
radial profile of a stain: living rim, oxygen-starved necrotic core


Cell nucleus
how chromatin or a protein is spread from the centre to the nuclear envelope


Centrosome, mitotic spindle
microtubules radiate outwards: in \((\theta, r)\) they become vertical lines


Cell migration
\(\theta\) alone: do cells move towards a chemoattractant? (circular statistics)


Fourier transform (later)
a complex coefficient is stored in polar form: size Mod() and phase Arg()




Pick one or two to mention depending on the audience. The spheroid case is the closest analogue to today: the same radial profile code, with a fluorescence image instead of a plate. Cell migration uses only the angle, which needs special statistics because 359 degrees and 1 degree are close. The Fourier link comes back in Fourier transform & basis functions: every complex number a + bi is a point in the plane, and Mod and Arg are its r and theta.

title: Penalties as priors
text:
About this lecture







Provisional placement


This block sits at the seam between the penalized-regression and Bayesian parts of the course. It may be moved to a later statistics / machine-learning course as the syllabus settles. Treat it as a bridge unit: it assumes you have already met ridge and lasso as optimisation, and Bayes’ theorem as inference.




In Ridge and lasso regression we added a penalty to least squares to tame wobbly coefficients. In the Bayesian inference block we learned to combine a prior with a likelihood. Today we show these are the same move seen from two sides.

A penalty on the coefficients is a prior belief about the coefficients.
Minimising penalised loss = finding the most probable coefficients given the data (the MAP estimate).
Ridge ⇔ a Gaussian prior; lasso ⇔ a Laplace (double-exponential) prior.
The penalty strength \(\lambda\) encodes how sure you were before seeing data — the prior precision.

This is a concept day: light math, one master equation, and a change of viewpoint that makes both blocks click together.

The single idea for today: a penalty and a prior are two languages for the same statement. The engineer says “I penalise large coefficients to stop overfitting”; the Bayesian says “I believe a priori that coefficients are small.” They write down the same objective and get the same answer. Everything else — ridge = Gaussian, lasso = Laplace, lambda = prior precision — is detail hanging off that equivalence. Stress that this reframes material students already own from Ridge and lasso regression and from Bayesian inference; nothing here is a brand-new technique, it is a unifying view. Flag the provisional-placement callout out loud: this bridge may migrate to a dedicated stats/ML course.

title: Penalties as priors
text:
A biology picture first
You want to predict a phenotype — say drug response — from a gene-expression profile.

You measure 20 000 genes in 80 patients. Far more predictors than samples (\(p \gg n\)).
Plain least squares is hopeless here: it has infinitely many perfect fits and memorises noise.
But you know things before you look: most genes are irrelevant to this drug, and the few that matter probably have modest effects, not wild ones.

That prior knowledge is exactly what a penalty quietly injects. Today we make the belief explicit: what does ridge assume about your genes? What does lasso assume?


Ground the abstraction in the canonical omics predicament: wide matrices, p far bigger than n, where ordinary least squares cannot even be computed uniquely. Biologists already carry strong priors into such problems — sparsity (few driver genes) and modest effect sizes (biology is buffered, single genes rarely swing a phenotype enormously). The penalty they used in Ridge and lasso regression was silently encoding one of these beliefs. The lecture’s promise: name the belief. By the end they should be able to say which biological assumption ridge makes and which lasso makes, and choose accordingly.

title: Penalties as priors
text:
Recap: the penalised objective
From Ridge and lasso regression, we fit coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta\) by minimising fit error + penalty:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta\big)^2}_{\text{residual sum of squares (RSS)}} \;+\; \lambda\, \underbrace{\mathcal{P}(\boldsymbol\beta)}_{\text{penalty}}\]

Ridge: \(\mathcal{P}(\boldsymbol\beta) = \sum_j \beta_j^2 = \lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2\) (sum of squares).
Lasso: \(\mathcal{P}(\boldsymbol\beta) = \sum_j |\beta_j| = \lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1\) (sum of absolute values).

\(\lambda \ge 0\) dials the penalty: \(\lambda = 0\) is plain least squares; large \(\lambda\) shrinks coefficients hard toward \(0\).

Pure recap, no new content — just re-establish the objective and notation so the Bayesian side has something to map onto. Remind them ridge shrinks all coefficients smoothly toward zero but keeps them nonzero, while lasso can set some exactly to zero (variable selection). Keep lambda’s role vivid: it is the single knob trading fit against simplicity. We are about to reinterpret every symbol here in probability language.

title: Penalties as priors
text:
Recap: Bayes in one line
From Bayesian inference: to learn parameters \(\boldsymbol\beta\) from data, combine what you believed before with what the data say.
\[\underbrace{p(\boldsymbol\beta \mid \text{data})}_{\text{posterior}} \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(\text{data} \mid \boldsymbol\beta)}_{\text{likelihood}} \;\times\; \underbrace{p(\boldsymbol\beta)}_{\text{prior}}\]

Likelihood — how well a given \(\boldsymbol\beta\) explains the observed data.
Prior — how plausible that \(\boldsymbol\beta\) was before seeing any data.
Posterior — the updated belief, combining both.

A quick summary of the posterior is its peak — the single most probable \(\boldsymbol\beta\). That is the MAP estimate (maximum a posteriori), and it is where the bridge to penalties is built.


Second recap slide. Reinstate the prior/likelihood/posterior trinity from the Bayesian block. Emphasise proportionality: we drop the normalising constant p(data) because it does not depend on beta and so does not move the location of the peak. Introduce MAP gently as “the top of the posterior hill” — a point summary, in contrast to the full posterior distribution a Bayesian would ideally report. Foreshadow the caveat slide: MAP throws away the width of the posterior, which matters, but it is exactly the quantity that equals penalised regression.

title: Penalties as priors
section: The one trick: turn products into sums
text:
The one trick: turn products into sums
Maximising a product of probabilities is awkward; maximising its logarithm is easy and gives the same peak (log is increasing). Taking \(-\log\) turns “maximise” into “minimise”:
\[\arg\max_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ p(\boldsymbol\beta\mid\text{data}) \;=\; \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \Big[\,-\log p(\text{data}\mid\boldsymbol\beta) \;-\; \log p(\boldsymbol\beta)\,\Big]\]
\[\underbrace{\ \ \text{MAP estimate}\ \ }_{\text{find the posterior peak}} \;=\; \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \big[\ \underbrace{\text{(negative log-likelihood)}}_{\text{fit term}} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{(negative log-prior)}}_{\text{penalty term}}\ \big]\]
This already looks like fit + penalty. The rest of the lecture is just plugging in specific likelihoods and priors and reading off the terms.

This is the mechanical heart of the equivalence and worth doing slowly. Two facts: (1) argmax is unchanged by a monotonically increasing transform, so we may take logs; (2) log turns products into sums and the minus sign flips max to min. The result is structurally already “fit term plus penalty term.” Point at the two braces and say: the negative log-likelihood will become the RSS, and the negative log-prior will become the ridge or lasso penalty. Nothing subtle remains — only substitution. Reassure the less mathematical students that they do not need to reproduce this derivation, only to recognise the shape.

title: Penalties as priors
text:
The likelihood of linear regression
The standard linear model assumes the noise is Gaussian:
\[y_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \sigma^2)\]
So each residual is Gaussian, and the negative log-likelihood is (dropping constants that do not involve \(\boldsymbol\beta\)):
\[-\log p(\text{data}\mid\boldsymbol\beta) \;=\; \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta\big)^2 \;+\; \text{const} \;=\; \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\,\text{RSS} \;+\; \text{const}\]
The fit term is just the residual sum of squares, scaled by \(1/(2\sigma^2)\). This is why ordinary least squares is maximum-likelihood under Gaussian noise — a fact from the Linear regression block, now in probability language.


Connect back to a result they have already been told, perhaps without proof: least squares equals maximum likelihood when errors are Gaussian. Here is the reason in one line — the Gaussian density has exp(-residual^2 / 2 sigma^2), so its negative log is residual^2 / 2 sigma^2, and summing over independent samples gives RSS / 2 sigma^2. The 1/(2 sigma^2) prefactor will matter on the next slides because it sets the exchange rate between the fit term and the penalty term, which is where lambda comes from. Keep sigma^2 in view; do not absorb it yet.

title: Penalties as priors
section: Adding a prior on the coefficients
text:
Adding a prior on the coefficients
Now assert a prior on each coefficient \(\beta_j\). Take them independent and centred at \(0\) — encoding “before seeing data, I expect effects to be small, and I have no reason to prefer positive over negative.”
\[p(\boldsymbol\beta) = \prod_{j=1}^p p(\beta_j)\]
The shape of \(p(\beta_j)\) is the modelling choice. Two natural bell-ish curves centred at \(0\):

a Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2)\) — smoothly peaked, light-ish tails;
a Laplace (double-exponential) — a sharp spike at \(0\) with heavier tails.

Each choice, pushed through \(-\log\), produces a different penalty. That is the whole story.


The prior is a statement about coefficients before data. Centring at zero encodes shrinkage-toward-zero and symmetry encodes no directional preference. The variance/scale of the prior encodes how small we think effects are. Preview the punchline visually: Gaussian is a smooth hump, Laplace has a pointed cusp at zero. Tell them to hold that cusp in mind — it is the geometric reason lasso produces exact zeros while ridge does not. The next two slides do the two substitutions explicitly.

title: Penalties as priors
text:
Ridge = a Gaussian prior
Put a Gaussian prior on each coefficient: \(\beta_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \tau^2)\). Its density is \(\propto \exp\!\big(-\beta_j^2 / 2\tau^2\big)\), so
\[-\log p(\boldsymbol\beta) \;=\; \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2 \;+\; \text{const} \;=\; \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\,\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2 \;+\; \text{const}\]
Add this to the fit term from the previous slide and minimise:
\[\arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\,\text{RSS} \;+\; \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\,\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2 \;\;\equiv\;\; \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \text{RSS} \;+\; \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}\,\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2\]
That second form (multiply through by \(2\sigma^2\)) is exactly ridge regression, with
\[\boxed{\ \lambda_{\text{ridge}} = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}\ }\]

First concrete substitution. Gaussian prior gives a squared penalty because the log of exp(-beta^2/…) is -beta^2/… . Adding to RSS/2sigma^2 and clearing the constant 2sigma^2 lands precisely on the ridge objective. The eye-opener is the boxed identity: the ridge penalty strength is the ratio of noise variance to prior variance. Walk through both extremes verbally (next slide formalises them). Emphasise this is an identity, not an analogy — the ridge estimator and the Gaussian-prior MAP estimator are the same vector of numbers.

title: Penalties as priors
text:
Penalty strength = prior precision
Read the identity \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\) as a statement about confidence. The precision of the prior is \(1/\tau^2\) — how tightly it is concentrated at \(0\).










Prior variance \(\tau^2\)
Prior belief
Precision \(1/\tau^2\)
\(\lambda\)
Effect




small
“effects are surely tiny”
high
large
strong shrinkage


large
“effects could be anything”
low
small
weak shrinkage


\(\tau^2 \to \infty\)
flat / no prior
\(0\)
\(0\)
plain least squares



So choosing \(\lambda\) is choosing how sure you were before the data. A big penalty is not an arbitrary knob — it is a strong, confident prior that the genes have small effects.


This slide converts the algebra into intuition and is the conceptual payoff. Large lambda equals small prior variance equals high prior precision equals strong conviction that coefficients are near zero. Small lambda equals diffuse prior equals letting the data speak. The limit tau^2 to infinity is a “flat” (improper) prior, under which MAP collapses to maximum likelihood, i.e. ordinary least squares. This reframes cross-validation for lambda (from Ridge and lasso regression) as data-driven tuning of how strong a prior to adopt. Biologically: setting lambda large is asserting you already believe most genes barely matter.

title: Penalties as priors
text:
Lasso = a Laplace prior
Now swap the Gaussian for a Laplace (double-exponential) prior: \(p(\beta_j) \propto \exp\!\big(-|\beta_j| / b\big)\). Its negative log is linear in \(|\beta_j|\):
\[-\log p(\boldsymbol\beta) \;=\; \frac{1}{b}\sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j| \;+\; \text{const} \;=\; \frac{1}{b}\,\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1 \;+\; \text{const}\]
Add the Gaussian-noise fit term and minimise:
\[\arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\,\text{RSS} \;+\; \frac{1}{b}\,\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1 \;\;\equiv\;\; \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \text{RSS} \;+\; \frac{2\sigma^2}{b}\,\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1\]
which is exactly the lasso, with \(\lambda_{\text{lasso}} = 2\sigma^2/b\). Same recipe, different prior: the absolute-value penalty comes from the Laplace’s \(|\beta|\) in the exponent.

Second substitution, mechanically identical to ridge but with a Laplace prior. The key structural difference: the Laplace density has exp(-|beta|/b), so its negative log is linear in |beta|, giving the L1 penalty rather than L2. Everything else — clearing 2sigma^2, reading off lambda — is the same. Stress the parallel so students see one unified derivation with a swappable prior, not two unrelated tricks. Next slide explains why this seemingly small change (|beta| vs beta^2) produces the qualitatively different behaviour of exact zeros.

title: Penalties as priors
text:
Why the shape matters: sparsity
The two priors differ most right at \(\boldsymbol\beta = 0\):

Gaussian (\(\propto e^{-\beta^2}\)) is smooth and flat at \(0\) — its slope there is zero, so it never insists a coefficient be exactly \(0\). Ridge shrinks everything but keeps all \(\beta_j \ne 0\).
Laplace (\(\propto e^{-|\beta|}\)) has a sharp cusp at \(0\) — a kink that puts a lot of prior mass on “exactly zero.” Lasso therefore sets weak coefficients exactly to \(0\) (variable selection).


So the biological reading is direct:

Ridge / Gaussian prior: “every gene contributes a little” — a polygenic, dense belief.
Lasso / Laplace prior: “a few genes contribute, most contribute nothing” — a sparse belief.


This is the intuition students should leave with. The cusp of the Laplace at zero is what makes lasso select variables: the kink means there is a genuine “corner” the optimiser can land on with a coefficient at exactly zero. The Gaussian’s rounded top has zero slope at the origin, so it gently discourages large values but never pins anything to zero. Translate to biology, which is the whole point of the pairing: choosing ridge vs lasso is choosing between a polygenic model (many small effects, e.g. height, complex traits) and a sparse model (a handful of drivers, e.g. a few oncogenes). The right choice is a biological hypothesis, now made explicit as a prior.

title: Penalties as priors
section: Try it: prior × likelihood → posterior peak
text:
Try it: prior × likelihood → posterior peak




Live version of the last few slides, for two coefficients. Green shading is the prior (darker = more prior belief), grey ellipses are the likelihood centred on the OLS / maximum-likelihood point, purple contours are the posterior, and the purple dot is the posterior peak (MAP), which is exactly the penalized estimate; the path panel on the right is the same ridge/lasso path as in Ridge and lasso regression. The demo fixes sigma squared at 1, so the readout shows tau squared = 1/lambda for the Gaussian and b = 2/lambda for the Laplace. Start with the Gaussian prior (ridge): the MAP sits between the prior centre and the OLS point, with both coefficients nonzero. Raise lambda: the prior tightens (a more confident prior) and pulls the MAP toward zero; lower it and the MAP slides back to OLS. Now click the Laplace prior at lambda = 2: the shading becomes diamonds, and the MAP jumps onto the beta-1 axis, so beta-2 is exactly zero (red mark) — the cusp at work. Drag the OLS point a little: the MAP stays on the axis over a whole range, while the Gaussian MAP never does. Close with the caveat slide in mind: the purple contours show a whole posterior, and MAP reports only its peak.

title: Penalties as priors
section: Choosing a prior is a biological statement
text:
Choosing a prior is a biological statement
Because the penalty is a prior, picking a penalty is picking a hypothesis about your system — state it out loud:









Biological belief
Prior
Penalty
Behaviour




“Many genes, each a small effect” (polygenic trait)
Gaussian
ridge (\(\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2\))
shrink all, keep all


“A few driver genes, rest irrelevant”
Laplace
lasso (\(\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1\))
select a sparse set


“Effects are small and mostly zero”
Gaussian + Laplace mix
elastic net
shrink + select


“I truly know nothing”
flat
none
least squares (fails if \(p\gg n\))



The elastic net (from Ridge and lasso regression) is the MAP under a blend of the two priors — which is why it both shrinks and selects.


Bring it together as a decision table the student can actually use. The framing to hammer: you are not tuning a machine, you are declaring what you believe about the biology, and different beliefs are different priors that happen to have familiar penalty names. Elastic net slots in naturally as a mixed prior (a combination of Gaussian and Laplace), explaining its hybrid behaviour without new machinery. The last row is a warning: a genuinely flat prior in the p>>n regime gives you nothing to lean on and least squares breaks — which is exactly why some prior/penalty is not optional in genomics.

title: Penalties as priors
text:
A glimpse in R
Nothing new to run — the same glmnet fit you used in Ridge and lasso regression is a MAP estimate under a prior. The point is only to read it that way:
library(glmnet)

# X: 80 patients x 20000 genes ; y: drug response
fit <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0)   # alpha = 0  -> ridge   (Gaussian prior)
fit <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)   # alpha = 1  -> lasso   (Laplace prior)
fit <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0.5) # 0<alpha<1  -> elastic net (mixed prior)

# lambda picked by cross-validation = data-driven choice of prior strength
cvfit  <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)
lambda <- cvfit$lambda.min       # small lambda = weak prior; large = strong prior
Reading each line as a prior:

alpha selects the prior shape (Gaussian, Laplace, or a blend).
lambda sets the prior precision — how strongly you assert small effects before the data.
cross-validating lambda = letting the data choose how confident a prior to hold.


Deliberately no new code — this is the code they already met, relabelled. glmnet’s alpha mixes L2 and L1 penalties, i.e. mixes Gaussian and Laplace priors, so alpha is literally a prior-shape dial and lambda a prior-strength dial. Reinforce that cross-validating lambda is an empirical way to set prior confidence, a pragmatic hybrid of Bayesian and frequentist thinking. Since no packages run at render time, this is a static illustration; students run it in the exercise. Do not overclaim: glmnet reports the MAP point, not a full posterior — segue to the caveat.

title: Penalties as priors
section: Caveat: MAP is only the peak
text:
Caveat: MAP is only the peak
The equivalence is exact, but it identifies penalised regression with the peak of the posterior — not the whole thing.

A full Bayesian analysis reports the entire posterior: the peak and its width (uncertainty), so you get credible intervals on each \(\beta_j\). MAP throws the width away.
The prior “variance” \(\tau^2\) (or scale \(b\)) is usually not known in advance. Cross-validating \(\lambda\) is a practical stand-in for a fully Bayesian treatment of that unknown.
Subtlety: under the Laplace prior, the MAP is sparse (exact zeros) but the posterior mean is not — so “lasso = Bayesian sparsity” holds for the peak, not for the averaged estimate.

The bridge is genuine and useful, but “penalised regression is secretly Bayesian” is a statement about the MAP point, with the honesty a real Bayesian analysis adds on top.


Intellectual honesty slide, in the spirit of the course’s “be honest about what we defer” principle. The penalty-equals-prior identity is real but partial: it matches the posterior mode, discarding the uncertainty that is arguably the whole benefit of going Bayesian. Two caveats worth stating: (1) treating tau^2/b as fixed and known is a simplification; a full hierarchical Bayesian model would put a prior on it too, and cross-validation is the frequentist workaround. (2) The Laplace-MAP is sparse but the Laplace-posterior-mean is not, so one must be careful about which “Bayesian lasso” is meant. Do not overstate the unification; present it as a clarifying viewpoint, not a replacement for either method.
