Take-home: a penalty is a prior in disguise. Choosing ridge vs lasso is choosing a biological hypothesis — polygenic vs sparse — and \(\lambda\) is how strongly you hold it. Next / related: full posteriors and uncertainty in the Bayesian inference block; the penalties themselves in Ridge and lasso regression.

The summary table is the one thing to photograph. Recite the mapping once more as a two-column dictionary: fit-plus-penalty on the left, MAP-of-a-posterior on the right, row by row. Land on the two headline messages: (1) penalty = prior, so (2) model choice is a biological hypothesis, and lambda is your confidence in it. Point forward to the Bayesian inference block for the full-posterior treatment this MAP view abbreviates, and back to Ridge and lasso regression for the mechanics of the penalties. Remind them of the provisional-placement note: this bridge may relocate to a later stats/ML course.

title: Quiz: why penalize?
text:
Short conceptual questions to test your grasp of why penalized regression exists. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. This block is provisional and may move to a later statistics / machine-learning course, so treat these as intuition checks rather than exam drills.

Q1. What does “p ≫ n” mean for a gene-expression dataset, and why is that shape a problem for ordinary least squares?






Hint





Count the predictors versus the samples. What does the model need in order to have a unique solution?









Answer





\(p\) is the number of predictors (genes) and \(n\) is the number of samples (patients/cells); \(p \gg n\) means far more genes than samples. Ordinary least squares needs \(X^\top X\) to be invertible, but with \(p > n\) that matrix is singular, so there is no unique solution — the model is unidentifiable.




Q2. In the OLS solution \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}\), which single matrix must be invertible, and what is its size?






Hint





Look for the inverse in the formula. \(X\) is \(n \times p\).









Answer





\(X^\top X\) must be invertible. It is a \(p \times p\) matrix (one row and column per predictor), even though it is built from only \(n\) samples.




Q3. Why exactly does \(p > n\) make \(X^\top X\) non-invertible? Use the word rank.






Hint





The rank of \(X^\top X\) cannot exceed the number of samples. When is a \(p\times p\) matrix invertible?









Answer





\(\text{rank}(X^\top X) \le n\). A \(p \times p\) matrix is invertible only if its rank equals \(p\). When \(p > n\), the rank is at most \(n < p\), so the matrix is rank-deficient (singular) and has no inverse.




Q4. Suppose \(p < n\), so \(X^\top X\) is invertible. Name a common biological situation that still makes OLS coefficients huge and unstable, and say what happens to \(X^\top X\).






Hint





Think about genes in the same pathway. What does that do to the columns of \(X\)?









Answer





Correlated predictors — co-regulated genes move together, so their columns in \(X\) are nearly the same. This makes \(X^\top X\) nearly singular (columns nearly parallel, an eigenvalue close to 0). Inverting a near-singular matrix amplifies noise, so the coefficients become large and unstable (multicollinearity).




Q5. True or false: the model that fits the training data best is the best model. Explain.






Hint





What do we actually want the model to do — describe this data, or predict new data?









Answer





False. A model flexible enough to fit the training data perfectly usually has learned the noise, not the signal, and predicts new data badly — it overfits. We care about generalisation to the next patient, not a perfect fit to the samples we already have.




Q6. Define bias and variance in one sentence each, and say which one OLS with many predictors suffers from.






Hint





One comes from a model that is too rigid, the other from a model that is too flexible.









Answer





Bias is error from a model too rigid to capture the true pattern (underfitting). Variance is error from a model so flexible it chases noise and changes wildly between samples (overfitting). OLS with many predictors is low bias, high variance — it overfits.




Q7. In words, what does adding a penalty term \(\lambda\cdot(\text{coefficient size})\) to the least-squares objective do, and what is the role of \(\lambda\)?






Hint





The objective now has two competing parts. What does the second part discourage, and what does \(\lambda\) set?









Answer





It charges for large coefficients, so the fit must justify every unit of coefficient it uses; this shrinks coefficients toward zero and stabilises them. \(\lambda \ge 0\) sets how strong the penalty is — the bias–variance dial: \(\lambda = 0\) is OLS (low bias, high variance), large \(\lambda\) heavily shrinks (high bias, low variance).




Q8. The ridge penalty changes the normal equations to use \(X^\top X + \lambda I\) instead of \(X^\top X\). Why does this matrix have an inverse even when \(p > n\)?






Hint





What does adding \(\lambda I\) do to the eigenvalues? When is a matrix invertible?









Answer





Adding \(\lambda I\) lifts every eigenvalue of \(X^\top X\) by \(\lambda\). A matrix is invertible exactly when none of its eigenvalues is zero, so any zero eigenvalue (which is what made the \(p > n\) case singular) becomes \(\lambda > 0\). Hence \(X^\top X + \lambda I\) is always invertible for \(\lambda > 0\), and there is again a unique solution.




Q9. Name one bonus a biologist gets from penalization beyond “the model is now computable,” and one price paid for it.






Hint





Think about reproducibility of gene signatures and prediction on new patients — and what shrinkage does to the estimates.









Answer





Bonus (any one): more stable, reproducible coefficients that don’t flip when you swap a few patients; better prediction on held-out patients; and with some penalties (lasso), most coefficients go exactly to zero, giving a short interpretable gene list. Price: shrinkage introduces bias — the estimates are systematically pulled toward zero, so choosing \(\lambda\) well (later, by cross-validation) matters.

title: Exercise: why penalize?
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

recognise the p ≫ n shape of omics data and say why it breaks ordinary least squares,
explain, using rank, why \(X^\top X\) has no inverse when there are more predictors than samples,
describe how correlated predictors make \(X^\top X\) nearly singular and coefficients unstable,
explain the bias–variance tradeoff in plain words and say which end OLS sits at,
do a one-parameter ridge calculation by hand and see the coefficient shrink as \(\lambda\) grows,
explain why adding \(\lambda I\) to \(X^\top X\) restores invertibility (eigenvalue shift).

This is a concept day. Most questions are reasoning, not arithmetic; the point is to internalise why penalization is needed before we meet the specific penalties (ridge and lasso) in later units.






Provisional block



This block is provisional and may move to a later statistics / machine-learning course. Nothing here is guaranteed exam material — do it to build intuition, not to memorise.

title: Exercise: why penalize?
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

recognise the p ≫ n shape of omics data and say why it breaks ordinary least squares,
explain, using rank, why \(X^\top X\) has no inverse when there are more predictors than samples,
describe how correlated predictors make \(X^\top X\) nearly singular and coefficients unstable,
explain the bias–variance tradeoff in plain words and say which end OLS sits at,
do a one-parameter ridge calculation by hand and see the coefficient shrink as \(\lambda\) grows,
explain why adding \(\lambda I\) to \(X^\top X\) restores invertibility (eigenvalue shift).

This is a concept day. Most questions are reasoning, not arithmetic; the point is to internalise why penalization is needed before we meet the specific penalties (ridge and lasso) in later units.






Provisional block



This block is provisional and may move to a later statistics / machine-learning course. Nothing here is guaranteed exam material — do it to build intuition, not to memorise.

title: Exercise: why penalize?
text:
Background
For a linear model \(\mathbf{y} \approx X\boldsymbol{\beta}\) with an \(n \times p\) design matrix \(X\) (\(n\) samples, \(p\) predictors), ordinary least squares (OLS) minimises the squared error and solves the normal equations:
\[X^\top X\,\boldsymbol{\beta} = X^\top \mathbf{y} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}.\]
This only works if the \(p \times p\) matrix \(X^\top X\) is invertible. Two things go wrong in biology:

\(p > n\) (more genes than samples). Then \(\text{rank}(X^\top X) \le n < p\), so \(X^\top X\) is singular — no inverse, no unique solution.
Correlated predictors (co-regulated genes). Then \(X^\top X\) is nearly singular — it has an eigenvalue close to 0, the inverse blows up, and coefficients become huge and unstable.

Penalized regression adds a price for coefficient size:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \ \|\mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2 + \lambda\,(\text{size of }\boldsymbol{\beta}),\qquad \lambda \ge 0.\]
Using the squared size \(\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2\) (ridge) changes the normal equations to
\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}.\]
Adding \(\lambda I\) lifts every eigenvalue of \(X^\top X\) by \(\lambda\), so \(X^\top X + \lambda I\) is always invertible for \(\lambda > 0\). The price is bias: coefficients are shrunk toward zero. \(\lambda\) is the bias–variance dial.

title: Exercise: why penalize?
text:
By hand
B1. For each experiment, write the shape of \(X\) as \(n \times p\) and state whether \(X^\top X\) (which is \(p \times p\)) can possibly be inverted for an OLS fit. Give the one-line reason.

200 patients, 5 clinical variables.
30 patients, 20,000 genes.
50 cells, 50 genes, all measurements distinct and uncorrelated.

B2. You have \(n = 2\) samples and \(p = 3\) predictors, so \(\mathbf{y} \approx X\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is 2 equations in 3 unknowns. Without computing anything, explain how many \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) vectors fit the data exactly, and connect this to “the model is unidentifiable.” (Recall the solution-space language from the Linear systems units.)
B3. Two genes are almost perfectly correlated, giving
\[X^\top X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1.01 \end{pmatrix}.\]

Compare the two columns of \(X^\top X\). Is the matrix close to singular? (b) Find \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) by row-reducing \([\,X^\top X \mid I\,]\) (as in the warm-up on the \(2\times2\) inverse). How large are its entries? (c) What does that do to \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}\)?

B4. (one-parameter ridge — the key calculation). Take the simplest possible model: one predictor, no intercept, so \(y \approx \beta x\) over the samples. The ridge objective is
\[f(\beta) = \sum_i (y_i - \beta x_i)^2 + \lambda \beta^2.\]

Differentiate with respect to \(\beta\), set to zero, and show \[\hat{\beta} = \frac{\sum_i x_i y_i}{\sum_i x_i^2 + \lambda}.\]
With \(\sum x_i y_i = 10\) and \(\sum x_i^2 = 5\), compute \(\hat{\beta}\) for \(\lambda = 0,\ 5,\ 20\).
What happens to \(\hat{\beta}\) as \(\lambda \to \infty\)? What is \(\hat{\beta}\) at \(\lambda = 0\), and what is that estimator called?

B5. (eigenvalue shift). Let \(X^\top X = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) (a rank-1 matrix — the second direction carries no information, as if \(p > n\)).

What are its eigenvalues? Is it invertible?
Form \(X^\top X + \lambda I\) with \(\lambda = 2\). What are its eigenvalues now?
Is it invertible? Explain in one sentence why adding \(\lambda I\) always fixes the singular case.

B6. (bias–variance in words). For each description, say whether it is mainly a bias problem or a variance problem, and whether the model is under- or over-fitting:

A model fits the 30 training patients perfectly but predicts new patients terribly.
A model predicts a constant (the overall mean) for everyone, ignoring gene expression.
Refitting the model after swapping 3 patients flips several coefficients from large positive to large negative.

title: Exercise: why penalize?
text:
In R
Use R to see the failures and the fix. These are static illustrations — the point is what the output would show, not to run them now.

OLS breaks when p > n
set.seed(1)
n <- 5; p <- 8                       # more predictors than samples
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
XtX <- t(X) %*% X                    # 8 x 8, but built from only 5 samples

qr(XtX)$rank                         # 5, not 8  -> rank-deficient
solve(XtX)                           # ERROR: system is computationally singular


A near-singular X^T X blows up the inverse
XtX <- matrix(c(1, 1,
                1, 1.01), 2, byrow = TRUE)
solve(XtX)                           # entries around 100 -> huge, unstable


The ridge fix: add lambda to the diagonal
XtX <- matrix(c(4, 0,
                0, 0), 2, byrow = TRUE)   # singular (rank 1)
lambda <- 2
XtX_ridge <- XtX + lambda * diag(2)       # add lambda to the diagonal
XtX_ridge                                  # 6 0 / 0 2
solve(XtX_ridge)                           # now invertible: diag(1/6, 1/2)


One-parameter ridge shrinks the coefficient
sxy <- 10; sxx <- 5                  # sum(x*y) and sum(x^2)
for (lambda in c(0, 5, 20)) {
  beta <- sxy / (sxx + lambda)
  cat("lambda =", lambda, "  beta =", beta, "\n")
}
# lambda = 0  -> 2.0 (this is OLS)
# lambda = 5  -> 1.0
# lambda = 20 -> 0.4  (shrinking toward 0)


Tasks
R1. Using the ridge-shift block, change \(\lambda\) to \(0.001\) and to \(100\). Confirm that a tiny \(\lambda\) barely changes \(X^\top X\) (close to OLS) while a large \(\lambda\) dominates the diagonal (heavy shrinkage). Relate this to the bias–variance dial.
R2. For the one-parameter ridge loop, add \(\lambda = 100\) and \(\lambda = 1000\). Describe in one sentence the trajectory of \(\hat{\beta}\) as \(\lambda\) grows, and name the value it approaches.
R3. In the near-singular block, change the 1.01 to 1.0001. Predict what happens to the size of solve(XtX) before reading it off, then check your prediction.

title: Exercise: why penalize?
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — rank and invertibility (B1, B2)





\(X^\top X\) is \(p \times p\) but its rank cannot exceed the number of samples \(n\): \(\text{rank}(X^\top X) \le \min(n, p)\). A \(p \times p\) matrix is invertible only if its rank equals \(p\). So if \(p > n\), the rank is at most \(n < p\) and the matrix is singular. In R the rank is qr(XtX)$rank.









Hint 2 — infinitely many solutions (B2)





Fewer independent equations than unknowns means the solution set is not a single point but a whole space of vectors, all fitting equally well. This is the same “infinitely many solutions” case you met when solving \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) with a rank-deficient \(A\) in the Linear systems units. “Unidentifiable” just means the data cannot single out one \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\).









Hint 3 — a nearly singular matrix and its inverse (B3)





Two columns that are almost parallel make a matrix nearly singular: row reduction leaves an almost-zero row on the left. Here R2 \(-\) R1 gives the row \((0,\ 0.01)\), and turning that \(0.01\) into a \(1\) means multiplying the row by \(100\) — which makes the inverse’s entries huge. Those large numbers multiply through to \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\), giving huge, unstable coefficients. Check with solve. (Bonus, not for exam: the determinant \(ad - bc\) is the number that sits in the denominator of the inverse; here it is \(0.01\).)









Hint 4 — differentiating the ridge objective (B4)





\(f(\beta) = \sum_i (y_i - \beta x_i)^2 + \lambda\beta^2\). Use the chain rule term by term: \(\frac{d}{d\beta}(y_i-\beta x_i)^2 = 2(y_i-\beta x_i)(-x_i)\), and \(\frac{d}{d\beta}(\lambda\beta^2)=2\lambda\beta\). Set the total to zero, divide by 2, and collect the \(\beta\) terms: \(\beta(\sum x_i^2 + \lambda) = \sum x_i y_i\). Notice that at \(\lambda = 0\) this is exactly the OLS slope \(\sum x_i y_i / \sum x_i^2\).









Hint 5 — eigenvalue shift (B5)





A diagonal matrix wears its eigenvalues on the diagonal. Adding \(\lambda I\) adds \(\lambda\) to every diagonal entry, hence lifts every eigenvalue by \(\lambda\) (this is the fact you proved with the identity shift in the eigenvalue unit). A matrix is invertible exactly when none of its eigenvalues is zero, so lifting a zero eigenvalue to \(\lambda > 0\) makes an otherwise-singular matrix invertible.









Hint 6 — bias vs variance (B6)





Bias = error from a model too rigid to capture the real pattern (predicts the same simple thing regardless of data → underfitting). Variance = error from a model so flexible it chases noise and changes wildly between samples (fits training data perfectly but generalises badly, coefficients lurch when data changes → overfitting).

title: Exercise: why penalize?
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. (a) \(X\) is \(200 \times 5\), so \(n = 200 > p = 5\). \(X^\top X\) is \(5\times5\) and can reach full rank 5 — invertible (assuming the variables are not exactly redundant). OLS is fine. (b) \(X\) is \(30 \times 20000\), so \(p \gg n\). \(\text{rank}(X^\top X) \le 30 \ll 20000\), so the \(20000\times20000\) matrix is singular — not invertible. OLS has no unique solution. (c) \(X\) is \(50\times50\), so \(n = p\). If all measurements are genuinely distinct and uncorrelated, \(X\) has full rank 50 and \(X^\top X\) is invertible — but this is the knife-edge case, and any correlation among genes would push it toward singularity.
B2. Two equations in three unknowns: there are more free parameters (3) than constraints (2), so the exactly-fitting \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) form a whole line (a one-dimensional solution space) — infinitely many vectors fit perfectly. The data cannot pick one out, so the model is unidentifiable. This is the same rank-deficient “infinitely many solutions” case from the Linear systems units, and it is exactly what \(p > n\) produces in general.
B3. (a) The columns \((1, 1)\) and \((1, 1.01)\) are almost identical — almost parallel — mirroring two almost-perfectly-correlated genes. With exactly parallel columns the matrix would be singular (no inverse); this one is nearly singular. (b) Row reduction: \[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1.01 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.01 & -1 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;100\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -100 & 100 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 101 & -100 \\ 0 & 1 & -100 & 100 \end{array}\right],
\] so \((X^\top X)^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}101 & -100\\ -100 & 100\end{pmatrix}\): entries around 100 — huge. The almost-zero row \((0,\ 0.01)\) had to be multiplied by 100. (c) Those large numbers multiply \(X^\top\mathbf{y}\), so \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) becomes enormous and unstable: a tiny change in the data (or the 1.01) swings the coefficients wildly. This is multicollinearity. (Bonus, not for exam: \(\det(X^\top X) = 1.01 - 1 = 0.01\), and the inverse is \(\frac{1}{0.01}\begin{pmatrix}1.01 & -1\\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\).)
B4. (a) Differentiate: \[f'(\beta) = \sum_i 2(y_i - \beta x_i)(-x_i) + 2\lambda\beta = -2\sum_i x_i y_i + 2\beta\sum_i x_i^2 + 2\lambda\beta.\] Set \(f'(\beta) = 0\) and divide by 2: \[-\sum_i x_i y_i + \beta\Big(\sum_i x_i^2 + \lambda\Big) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat{\beta} = \frac{\sum_i x_i y_i}{\sum_i x_i^2 + \lambda}.\] (b) With \(\sum x_i y_i = 10\), \(\sum x_i^2 = 5\):



\(\lambda\)
\(\hat{\beta} = 10/(5+\lambda)\)




0
\(10/5 = 2.0\)


5
\(10/10 = 1.0\)


20
\(10/25 = 0.4\)




As \(\lambda \to \infty\) the denominator grows without bound, so \(\hat{\beta} \to 0\) — heavy penalty shrinks the coefficient to nothing. At \(\lambda = 0\), \(\hat{\beta} = \sum x_i y_i / \sum x_i^2 = 2.0\), which is the ordinary least squares slope. So ridge is a family of estimators indexed by \(\lambda\), with OLS at one end and zero at the other.

B5. (a) \(X^\top X = \begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) is diagonal, so its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries 4 and 0. Because one eigenvalue is 0, the matrix is singular — not invertible (the second direction carries no information, like a \(p>n\) dead direction). (b) \(X^\top X + 2I = \begin{pmatrix}6&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\), with eigenvalues 6 and 2 — every eigenvalue lifted by \(\lambda = 2\). (c) Now no eigenvalue is zero, so the matrix is invertible. Adding \(\lambda I\) raises every eigenvalue by \(\lambda\); any zero eigenvalue becomes \(\lambda > 0\), so the singular case is always cured. This is exactly why the ridge normal equations \(X^\top X + \lambda I\) are solvable even when \(p > n\).
B6. (a) Variance problem — the model is flexible enough to fit the training data perfectly but the fit does not generalise. Overfitting. (b) Bias problem — the model is too rigid (predicts a constant) to capture any real signal. Underfitting. (c) Variance problem — coefficients swinging violently when the data changes slightly is the signature of high variance (here driven by multicollinearity). Overfitting / instability. Shrinkage would calm this.
R1. With \(\lambda = 0.001\), \(X^\top X + \lambda I \approx \begin{pmatrix}4.001&0\\0&0.001\end{pmatrix}\) — almost unchanged from the singular original, so we are essentially back at OLS (low bias, high variance; the tiny second eigenvalue still makes the inverse large). With \(\lambda = 100\), the matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}104&0\\0&100\end{pmatrix}\) — dominated by the penalty, so coefficients are heavily shrunk (high bias, low variance). Sliding \(\lambda\) from small to large moves you across the bias–variance dial.
R2. Extending the loop:



\(\lambda\)
\(\hat{\beta}=10/(5+\lambda)\)




0
2.0


5
1.0


20
0.4


100
≈ 0.095


1000
≈ 0.00995



\(\hat{\beta}\) decreases monotonically toward 0 as \(\lambda\) grows — the coefficient is shrunk ever harder and approaches zero in the limit.
R3. With 1.0001, the columns are even closer to parallel: row reduction now leaves the row \((0,\ 0.0001)\), which must be multiplied by 10,000. So solve(XtX) has entries around 10,000 (exactly \(\begin{pmatrix}10001 & -10000\\ -10000 & 10000\end{pmatrix}\)), 100 times larger than before. Prediction: closer to singular, larger and more unstable inverse — confirmed by running it. (Bonus, not for exam: the determinant drops from \(0.01\) to \(0.0001\).) This is why highly correlated genes are so damaging without a penalty.

title: Exercise: why penalize?
text:
Where this leads

Ridge and lasso (this block): the two standard penalties. Ridge uses \(\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2\) (the calculation you did in B4, generalised); lasso uses \(\sum|\beta_j|\) and drives coefficients exactly to zero, performing gene selection.
Choosing \(\lambda\) (this block): cross-validation picks the penalty strength that minimises prediction error on held-out data, rather than guessing.
PCA / dimensional reduction (Applications block): another route through the \(p \gg n\) problem — reduce the number of predictors instead of penalizing them.

contrast how lasso, ridge, and elastic net treat a correlated group,

title: Exercise: penalized models — case analysis & pitfalls
text:
Background
We fit a penalized linear model to a samples × features matrix \(X\) and a response \(y\). For the lasso,
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \tfrac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - \beta_0 - \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta\big)^2 \;+\; \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|,\]
with \(\lambda\) chosen by cross-validation. The penalty is scale-dependent, so predictors are standardized first (glmnet does this internally).
The recurring problem. Biological features are correlated — genes in a pathway or co-expression module rise and fall together, so \(X\) has blocks of near-duplicate columns. When two columns are near-identical:

the lasso puts essentially all the weight on one of them and zeros the rest; which one it picks is decided by a sliver of sample-specific noise, so it flips under tiny data changes,
the ridge penalty (\(\sum \beta_j^2\)) instead spreads the weight across the group, and
the elastic net (\(0<\alpha<1\)) keeps correlated members together (the grouping effect).

Stability selection tames the instability: subsample the data many times, refit the lasso each time, and record each feature’s selection frequency \(\pi_j\) = fraction of subsamples in which it was chosen. Keep features above a stated threshold.
Two interpretation rules to carry throughout:

Selected ≠ causal. A chosen feature may be a proxy, a downstream consequence, or a confounder marker. A penalized fit yields hypotheses, not mechanisms.
Coefficients are shrunk (biased toward zero) and you may not compute naive p-values for selected features on the same data (post-selection inference).

title: Exercise: penalized models — case analysis & pitfalls
text:
By hand
B1. (identifiability — the core mechanism). Two features are identical across three samples: column \(x_1 = x_2 = (1, 2, 3)^\top\). Suppose the fit wants the combined contribution \(\beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2\) to equal \(2\,x_1\) — i.e. any split with \(\beta_1 + \beta_2 = 2\) (and both \(\ge 0\)) fits the data equally well. Consider three splits: \((\beta_1,\beta_2) = (2,0)\), \((1,1)\), \((0,2)\). (a) Compute the lasso penalty \(|\beta_1| + |\beta_2|\) for each split. Which split does the lasso prefer? (b) Compute the ridge penalty \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2\) for each split. Which split does the ridge prefer? title: Exercise: penalized models — case analysis & pitfalls
section: Explore: which gene does the lasso keep?
text:
Explore: which gene does the lasso keep?
The demo shows B1–B2 for two standardized genes. The grey ellipses are RSS contours around the OLS point (drag it), the green region is the penalty region at the current \(\lambda\), and the purple dot is the penalized estimate where the smallest contour touches the region. “corr” is the correlation between the two genes; at \(0.9\) the ellipses become a long valley along which many splits of the weight fit almost equally well. The right panel shows the coefficient path against \(\lambda\). (The demo uses the objective \(\lVert\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2 + \lambda\,\text{penalty}\), so its \(\lambda\) is on a different scale from the \(\tfrac{1}{2n}\) version above.)



E1. After Reset (lasso, corr \(0.9\), OLS \(= (1.5, 0.5)\), \(\lambda = 2.5\)), which gene does the lasso keep? Drag the OLS point along the valley to about \((0.5, 1.5)\). Which gene is kept now? Relate this to B2.
E2. Repeat E1 with Ridge and with Elastic net (\(\alpha = 0.5\)). How are the two coefficients split at the two OLS positions?
E3. Back to the lasso at OLS \((1.5, 0.5)\): lower \(\lambda\) to \(0.5\). How many genes are in the model? Use the path panel to read off roughly the \(\lambda\) at which gene 2 drops out.






Solutions





E1. At OLS \((1.5, 0.5)\) the lasso gives \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} \approx (0.70, 0)\): gene 1 is kept and gene 2 is exactly zero (the solution is on a corner of the diamond). At \((0.5, 1.5)\) it gives \(\approx (0, 0.70)\): the choice flips to gene 2. With strongly correlated genes the OLS point is poorly determined along the valley, so a small change in the data (one sample dropped) can move it from one side of the diagonal to the other, and the lasso’s pick flips with it, as argued in B2.
E2. Ridge gives about \((0.45, 0.41)\) and \((0.41, 0.45)\); elastic net about \((0.44, 0.37)\) and \((0.37, 0.44)\). Both keep both genes with similar weights, and moving the OLS point only shifts the weights a little: the weight is spread across the group (ridge, B1(b)) and correlated genes stay in together (the elastic-net grouping effect).
E3. At \(\lambda = 0.5\) both genes are in the model, about \((1.37, 0.37)\). On the path, \(\hat\beta_2\) reaches zero at about \(\lambda \approx 1.9\), and \(\hat\beta_1\) at about \(\lambda \approx 3.9\). Which gene survives longest is decided by which side of the valley the OLS point fell on.

title: Exercise: penalized models — case analysis & pitfalls
text:
In R
Use these as static references — read them, predict the output, then run them in your own session. Assume x is a standardized samples × genes matrix and y a numeric response.

Fit the lasso and read the sparse signature
library(glmnet)

fit <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1, standardize = TRUE, nfolds = 10)
sel <- function(cvfit) which(as.vector(coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.1se"))[-1] != 0)
colnames(x)[sel(fit)]      # the (unstable) one-shot shortlist


See the instability: refit after a tiny change
set.seed(1)
fit_all  <- cv.glmnet(x,       y,      alpha = 1)
fit_drop <- cv.glmnet(x[-1, ], y[-1],  alpha = 1)   # drop one sample

setdiff(colnames(x)[sel(fit_all)],  colnames(x)[sel(fit_drop)])  # genes lost
setdiff(colnames(x)[sel(fit_drop)], colnames(x)[sel(fit_all)])   # genes gained


Lasso vs ridge on a correlated pair
# a and b are near-duplicate columns; compare how each penalty splits the weight
las   <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1, lambda = 0.05)
rdg   <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0, lambda = 0.05)
coef(las)[c("GENE_a", "GENE_b"), ]   # lasso: weight piles on one, other ~ 0
coef(rdg)[c("GENE_a", "GENE_b"), ]   # ridge: weight split across both


Stability selection
set.seed(1)
B <- 100
n <- nrow(x); p <- ncol(x)
counts <- integer(p)

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  idx    <- sample(n, floor(n / 2))            # a random half of the samples
  fb     <- cv.glmnet(x[idx, ], y[idx], alpha = 1)
  beta   <- as.vector(coef(fb, s = "lambda.1se"))[-1]   # drop intercept
  counts <- counts + as.integer(beta != 0)
}

freq        <- counts / B
names(freq) <- colnames(x)
stable      <- sort(freq[freq >= 0.6], decreasing = TRUE)
stable


Read the frequency profile
barplot(sort(freq, decreasing = TRUE)[1:30],
        las = 2, ylab = "selection frequency")
abline(h = 0.6, col = "red", lty = 2)         # your reporting threshold


Tasks
R1. Run the instability block with three different seeds (set.seed(1), set.seed(2), set.seed(3)), each time comparing the one-shot lasso shortlist across the full data vs one dropped sample. Do the gained/lost genes tend to be co-expressed with the ones they replace? (Inspect a small gene–gene correlation on the affected genes.)
R2. Compare the lasso and ridge coefficients for a known correlated gene pair (the “lasso vs ridge” block). Confirm that the lasso concentrates the weight on one member while the ridge spreads it. Then fit an elastic net (alpha = 0.5) and describe where it sits between the two.
R3. Run stability selection with B = 100. Produce the sorted selection-frequency bar plot with the threshold line. Is there a clear gap between a stable head and a noisy tail, or is the distribution smeared? State, in one sentence, what your plot licenses you to report.
R4. Take your stable shortlist from R3 and, for the top gene, write one sentence that reports it correctly — i.e. as a stably selected predictor and a hypothesis, not as a causal effect with a p-value.

title: Exercise: penalized models — case analysis & pitfalls
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — B1, comparing the two penalties





For identical columns, every split with \(\beta_1 + \beta_2 = 2\) (both \(\ge 0\)) gives the same fitted values, so only the penalty decides. The lasso penalty is \(|\beta_1| + |\beta_2|\); the ridge penalty is \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2\). Plug in \((2,0)\), \((1,1)\), \((0,2)\) and compare. One penalty gives a tie; the other has a unique minimum.









Hint 2 — B1(c), why a tie means instability





If several solutions are tied, the choice among them is decided by whatever breaks the tie — here, tiny sample-specific noise. A method with a unique minimum (ridge) is stable; a method with a tie (lasso on identical columns) is not. See Ridge, lasso & elastic net for the diamond-vs-circle geometry behind this.









Hint 3 — B3, selection frequency





Selection frequency for a gene is simply (number of subsamples in which it was selected) / (total subsamples). Count the × marks down each column and divide by 5. A threshold of \(\pi \ge 0.6\) means “selected in at least 3 of the 5 subsamples”.









Hint 4 — B3(c), reporting a split module





When two co-expressed genes each sit at a moderate frequency, the resamples are splitting their votes between interchangeable members. The stable finding is not “gene C” or “gene D” but the module they belong to.









Hint 5 — B4, three ways to be non-causal





Proxy: rides on a correlated true driver, no function of its own. Reverse causation: the phenotype changes the gene, not vice versa. Confounder marker: tracks a third variable (batch, tumour purity) that independently drives the response. Match each scenario to the phrase that fits.









Hint 6 — B5, what a methods paragraph must state





Think reproducibility: standardization, how \(\lambda\) (and \(\alpha\)) were chosen and by what CV, whether stability selection was used and with what \(B\) and threshold, and the random seed. The over-statement to watch for is treating a selected gene as a causal one. See the reporting slide in the lecture.









Hint 7 — the R workflow





Build the matrix with as.matrix; fit with cv.glmnet (alpha = 1 lasso, 0 ridge, between = elastic net); pull coefficients at s = "lambda.1se" with coef. Resample rows with sample and always set.seed so results are reproducible. colMeans of a 0/1 selection matrix (or counts / B) gives the selection frequency.

title: Exercise: penalized models — case analysis & pitfalls
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. (a) Lasso penalty \(|\beta_1| + |\beta_2|\): \((2,0) \to 2+0 = 2\); \((1,1) \to 1+1 = 2\); \((0,2) \to 0+2 = 2\). All equal 2 — the lasso is indifferent among these splits (a tie). It does not prefer any one; the solution is non-unique. (b) Ridge penalty \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2\): \((2,0) \to 4+0 = 4\); \((1,1) \to 1+1 = 2\); \((0,2) \to 0+4 = 4\). The even split \((1,1)\) is the unique minimum (2 < 4) — the ridge spreads the weight across the group. (c) Because the lasso penalty is tied across all same-sign splits summing to 2, the choice among the interchangeable features is decided by whatever tiny difference breaks the tie — i.e. sample-specific noise. Perturb the data slightly and the “winning” feature flips: the selection is unstable. The ridge, having a strict unique minimum at the even split, is stable and keeps both features (but never gives you an exact zero, so it is not sparse).
B2. The lasso keeps the feature with the marginally stronger correlation with \(y\) — here \(x_1\) — and drives \(x_2\) to zero, because concentrating the weight on the slightly-better predictor gives a marginally lower loss for the same penalty. This margin is tiny and noise-driven: if dropping one sample makes \(x_2\) the marginally stronger predictor, the lasso will switch to keeping \(x_2\) and zero \(x_1\). The two are near-interchangeable, so the predictions barely change while the selected gene flips — the identifiability problem in action.
B3. (a) Count × down each column, divide by 5: GENE_A: 5/5 = 1.0; GENE_B: 3/5 = 0.6; GENE_C: 2/5 = 0.4; GENE_D: 3/5 = 0.6; GENE_E: 1/5 = 0.2. (b) Threshold \(\pi \ge 0.6\): GENE_A (1.0), GENE_B (0.6), GENE_D (0.6) make the shortlist. GENE_C (0.4) and GENE_E (0.2) do not. (c) GENE_C and GENE_D are co-expressed and each has only moderate frequency (0.4 and 0.6) — the resamples are splitting their votes between two interchangeable members. The honest report is that the co-expression module (containing C and D) is associated with the response, rather than singling out D and discarding C as if they were independent findings. (Note GENE_D clears the threshold and C does not, but their difference of one subsample is within resampling noise.)
B4. (a) Confounder marker — the gene tracks tumour purity, and purity independently drives drug response, so the gene predicts \(y\) without acting on it. (b) Proxy — it is correlated with the true driver but has no function of its own; it predicts by association. (c) Reverse causation — the phenotype (proliferation) drives the gene up, so the causal arrow points from response to gene, not gene to response.
B5. Three things a reader needs (any three): (i) that predictors were standardized (and any supervised preprocessing was inside the CV, not before it); (ii) how \(\lambda\) — and \(\alpha\) if elastic net — was chosen and by what cross-validation scheme (e.g. 10-fold, lambda.1se); (iii) whether stability selection was used, with what number of resamples \(B\) and what threshold, and the random seed for reproducibility. Also acceptable: held-out performance on data untouched by tuning. The over-statement: calling the selected genes “the signature” implies they are the important / causal genes, when a lasso selection is an unstable, predictive list — a set of hypotheses, not established drivers.
R1. Across seeds you should see the one-shot shortlist wobble: genes drop out and near-duplicates take their place. Inspecting the correlation of a lost gene against its replacement typically shows a high correlation — they are members of the same co-expression module, so the lasso is swapping interchangeable columns. Example skeleton:
sel <- function(cvfit) which(as.vector(coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.1se"))[-1] != 0)

for (s in 1:3) {
  set.seed(s)
  fa <- cv.glmnet(x,       y,     alpha = 1)
  fd <- cv.glmnet(x[-1, ], y[-1], alpha = 1)
  cat("seed", s,
      "| lost:",   setdiff(colnames(x)[sel(fa)], colnames(x)[sel(fd)]),
      "| gained:", setdiff(colnames(x)[sel(fd)], colnames(x)[sel(fa)]), "\n")
}
# then, for a lost/gained pair g1, g2:
cor(x[, "g1"], x[, "g2"])     # typically high -> same module
R2. The lasso puts (almost) all the weight on one member of the correlated pair and leaves the other near zero; the ridge gives both a similar, smaller coefficient (weight spread). The elastic net (alpha = 0.5) sits between: it keeps both members (like ridge’s grouping) but shrinks small ones toward zero (like the lasso), so a correlated pair tends to enter or leave together with modest coefficients.
las  <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1,   lambda = 0.05)
rdg  <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0,   lambda = 0.05)
enet <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0.5, lambda = 0.05)
coef(las )[c("GENE_a", "GENE_b"), ]   # one big, one ~0
coef(rdg )[c("GENE_a", "GENE_b"), ]   # two similar, smaller
coef(enet)[c("GENE_a", "GENE_b"), ]   # both kept, shrunk
R3. Running the stability-selection loop and plotting the sorted frequencies, a clear gap between a handful of high-frequency genes and a long low tail means the data support a defensible signature (report the genes above the threshold). A smeared distribution with everything around 0.3–0.5 means no gene is reliably selected — the honest conclusion is that the data cannot support a stable signature at this sample size, and you should say so rather than lower the threshold until a story appears. What the plot licenses you to report is exactly the set of genes clearing the stated threshold, plus any module whose members split moderate votes.
R4. A correct one-sentence report, e.g.: “TYMS was selected in 94% of subsampled lasso fits, marking it as a stable transcriptomic predictor of drug response and a candidate for functional validation” — note it reports a selection frequency and frames the gene as a predictive hypothesis to be tested, with no effect-size p-value and no causal claim.

title: Exercise: penalized models — case analysis & pitfalls
text:
Where this leads

Cross-validation & model selection: the \(\lambda\) (and \(\alpha\)) tuning used here relies on the CV machinery from that unit; remember that the CV used to tune cannot also certify performance — that needs a held-out set or nested CV.
Penalties as Bayesian priors: the lasso penalty is a Laplace prior and the ridge penalty a Gaussian prior (the MAP view). Shrinkage bias is the prior pulling estimates toward zero — which is why coefficients are not unbiased effect sizes.
Beyond this course: valid inference after selection (selective / post-selection inference) and formal stability-selection error control are topics for a later statistics / machine-learning course, in line with this block’s provisional status.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
About this lecture
You have measured thousands of genes across hundreds of samples. You cannot plot a cloud of points in 20,000 dimensions. PCA finds a handful of new axes that capture most of the variation, so you can see the structure in two dimensions.

The covariance matrix of the data is symmetric, so (from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors) its eigenvectors are orthogonal and its eigenvalues are real and non-negative.
The leading eigenvector points along the direction of maximum variance — the first principal component (PC).
Scores = where each sample lands when we project it onto a PC. Loadings = the eigenvector entries = how much each gene contributes.
We centre (and sometimes scale) the data first, then rotate the axes to line up with the data cloud.

This is a concept day. We build PCA from the eigen-decomposition of a covariance matrix. The R function prcomp that does it all in one call comes in the next unit (PCA in R).

The one mental image: a high-dimensional data cloud is stretched more along some directions than others; PCA rotates our coordinate axes so the first new axis lies along the longest stretch, the second along the next longest, and so on. Everything else — scores, loadings, variance explained — hangs off that picture. Stress continuity with the eigen units: we already proved that a symmetric matrix has orthogonal eigenvectors and real eigenvalues, and that the covariance matrix is symmetric. PCA is just eigen-decomposition of that matrix, read in a biological way. Keep the maths light today; the mechanics of prcomp are the next unit.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
The biology problem
A typical RNA-seq experiment gives an expression matrix: samples (rows) × genes (columns).



sample
GENE1
GENE2
GENE3
…
GENE20000

Each sample is a point in 20,000-dimensional space. We cannot look at it.
But the genes are not independent — they are co-regulated in programmes (cell-cycle genes rise together, immune genes rise together…).
So the real structure lives in far fewer dimensions than 20,000. PCA finds them.



Ground the abstraction in the data format they actually meet: a wide expression matrix, samples as rows, genes as columns, tens of thousands of columns. The key biological fact that makes dimension reduction possible is co-regulation: genes move together in programmes, so the effective number of independent directions is small. PCA is the tool that discovers those directions from the data alone, without being told the sample labels. Emphasise “unsupervised”: we do not tell PCA which are tumours; we ask whether structure falls out on its own. That is exactly what makes a PCA plot a good first look at any omics dataset.

title: Principal component analysis
section: Why not just look at genes one at a time?
text:
Why not just look at genes one at a time?
You could plot GENE1 against GENE2, then GENE1 against GENE3, …

With 20,000 genes there are about 200 million pairwise scatter plots. Hopeless.
Any single gene is noisy and captures only a sliver of the biology.
The interesting signal — “these samples separate into two groups” — is usually spread across many genes at once, not visible in any single pair.

PCA builds new composite variables (mixtures of many genes) chosen so that the first few show the most variation. We look at those instead.


Motivate why marginal, one-gene-at-a-time thinking fails: too many pairs, each gene noisy, and the signal is distributed. This is the conceptual jump — from “measured variables” (genes) to “derived variables” (principal components) that are weighted combinations of all genes. Reassure them a PC is not mysterious: it is just a weighted sum of the genes, with weights (the loadings) chosen by the eigenvector. The choice criterion is “maximise variance”, which is where the covariance matrix and its leading eigenvector enter.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Recall: the covariance matrix
Variance measures spread of one variable; covariance measures how two vary together.
For \(p\) genes, the covariance matrix \(C\) is \(p \times p\):
\[C_{ij} = \text{cov}(\text{gene}_i, \text{gene}_j), \qquad C_{ii} = \text{var}(\text{gene}_i)\]

Diagonal = each gene’s own variance. Off-diagonal = co-variation between gene pairs.
\(C\) is symmetric because \(\text{cov}(g_i, g_j) = \text{cov}(g_j, g_i)\).

From Eigenvalues & eigenvectors, a symmetric matrix has:

real, non-negative eigenvalues (they are variances — they cannot be negative), and
orthogonal eigenvectors — a clean set of perpendicular axes.

Those eigenvectors are the principal components.


This is the load-bearing recall slide. Covariance generalises variance to pairs; stacking all pairwise covariances gives the symmetric p-by-p covariance matrix, diagonal = variances, off-diagonal = covariances. The symmetry is not a lucky accident — it is guaranteed because cov is symmetric in its two arguments. Then invoke the spectral theorem result they already proved: symmetric implies real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors. Add the biological reason eigenvalues are non-negative here: they equal variances along the eigen-directions, and variance cannot be negative. Land the punchline plainly: the eigenvectors of C are the principal components. The rest of the lecture unpacks that sentence on a tiny example.

title: Principal component analysis
section: A tiny worked example: two genes
text:
A tiny worked example: two genes
Keep it to 2 genes and 5 samples so we can see everything by hand.



sample
GENE_A
GENE_B




s1

5

Plot the 5 points with GENE_A on the x-axis, GENE_B on the y-axis.
The cloud is a tilted, elongated sausage — the two genes rise together (positive covariance).
PCA will find the long axis of that sausage.



Deliberately choose tiny round-ish numbers so every step is doable on the board. Two genes means the data cloud lives in the plane and the “long axis” is literally visible. Have students sketch the five points; they will see a diagonal, elongated cloud because gene A and gene B increase together. That visible long axis is PC1; the perpendicular short axis is PC2. Everything from here — centring, covariance, eigenvectors, scores — is making that visual intuition precise and numerical.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Step 1: centre the data
PCA describes variation around the mean, so we first subtract each gene’s mean (centring).
Means: \(\bar{A} = (1+3+4+5+7)/5 = 4\), \(\quad \bar{B} = (5+3+6+7+9)/5 = 6\).
Centred data (subtract the column mean from each column):



sample
\(A - \bar A\)
\(B - \bar B\)




s1
\(-3\)
\(-1\)


s2
\(-1\)
\(-3\)


s3
\(0\)
\(0\)


s4
\(1\)
\(1\)


s5
\(3\)
\(3\)



Now the cloud is centred on the origin. Each column sums to 0.


Centring is non-negotiable and a classic source of confusion, so do it explicitly. PCA is about the shape of the cloud around its centre, not where the centre sits, so we move the centre to the origin by subtracting each gene’s mean from that gene’s column. After centring, every column has mean zero. Warn them: if you forget to centre, the “first PC” tends to just point from the origin to the data centroid, capturing the mean rather than the variation — a common bug. Note that prcomp centres by default; today we do it by hand so they see why.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Step 2: the covariance matrix
With centred columns, the covariance uses \(\dfrac{1}{n-1}\sum (\text{centred}_i)(\text{centred}_j)\) (here \(n-1 = 4\)).
\[\text{var}(A) = \tfrac{1}{4}\big[(-3)^2 + (-1)^2 + 0^2 + 1^2 + 3^2\big] = \tfrac{1}{4}(9+1+0+1+9) = \tfrac{20}{4} = 5\] \[\text{var}(B) = \tfrac{1}{4}\big[(-1)^2+(-3)^2+0^2+1^2+3^2\big] = \tfrac{1}{4}(1+9+0+1+9) = \tfrac{20}{4} = 5\] \[\text{cov}(A,B) = \tfrac{1}{4}\big[(-3)(-1)+(-1)(-3)+0+1\cdot1+3\cdot3\big] = \tfrac{1}{4}(3+3+0+1+9) = \tfrac{16}{4} = 4\]
\[C = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\]
Symmetric, as promised. The large positive off-diagonal says the two genes strongly co-vary.

Walk the arithmetic slowly; the numbers are small on purpose. Emphasise the divide-by-(n-1) convention (sample covariance) matches what R’s var and cov use, so their hand answer will match prcomp later. The resulting 2x2 covariance matrix is symmetric with a big positive off-diagonal, quantifying the co-regulation they saw as a tilted cloud. This is exactly the kind of symmetric matrix they diagonalised in the eigen exercises (compare with the covariance-flavour problem there). The next step is to find its eigenvectors — the principal component directions.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Step 3: eigenvectors = principal components
Diagonalise \(C\) (by hand: the symmetric pattern from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors).
\(C = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\) has the form \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}\), so \(C(1,1) = 9\,(1,1)\) and \(C(1,-1) = 1\,(1,-1)\):
\[\lambda_1 = 9, \qquad \lambda_2 = 1,\]
with eigenvectors \(\mathbf{u}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)\) (for \(\lambda_1\)) and \(\mathbf{u}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1)\) (for \(\lambda_2\)). (This is exactly the covariance-flavour problem from the Eigenvalues & eigenvectors exercise.)

\(\mathbf{u}_1\) points along the \(45^\circ\) long axis of the cloud — this is PC1.
\(\mathbf{u}_2\) is perpendicular to it — PC2 — along the thin direction.
Each eigenvalue is the variance captured along its PC: \(9 \gg 1\), so most of the spread is along PC1.



Connect straight back to the by-hand toolbox: C has the symmetric [[a, b], [b, a]] pattern, so the eigenvectors are (1,1) and (1,-1) with eigenvalues a + b = 9 and a - b = 1; verify by multiplying. (Bonus, not for exam: the characteristic equation (5 - lambda)^2 - 16 = 0 gives the same.) Because this is the same matrix as the covariance-flavour problem in the eigen exercise, the answers are clean: eigenvalues 9 and 1, eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,-1), guaranteed perpendicular because C is symmetric. Stress the interpretation of the eigenvalue as variance along that direction: 9 vs 1 means PC1 captures most of the variation, so a 1-D summary would already be very good. Sanity check with trace: 5 + 5 = 10 = 9 + 1, which also equals the total variance — a fact we use for variance explained.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Principal components are new axes
The two eigenvectors form a new, rotated coordinate system:

PC1: the direction of greatest variance (biggest eigenvalue).
PC2: orthogonal to PC1, the direction of the next greatest variance.
In general, PC\(k\) is orthogonal to all earlier PCs and captures the largest remaining variance.

We have not thrown anything away yet — we have only rotated the axes to line up with the data cloud. Same points, new description.
\[\text{PCs are orthonormal: } \mathbf{u}_i \cdot \mathbf{u}_j = 0 \ (i \neq j), \quad \|\mathbf{u}_i\| = 1.\]


Emphasise that rotating to the PC axes is loss-less: no information is discarded, we have merely re-expressed each sample in a coordinate system aligned with the cloud instead of aligned with the genes. The PCs are orthonormal — mutually perpendicular and unit length — because they are eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix, normalised. Dimension reduction (the payoff) comes when we choose to keep only the first few PCs and drop the rest; that is a later choice, not part of the rotation itself. Keep the two ideas separate in their minds: rotate (exact), then optionally truncate (approximate). Callback: this is the same rotation matrix that turned the cell image in Transforming images with matrices, now applied to a cloud of samples instead of pixels — and, as with the image, rotating it back recovers everything.

title: Principal component analysis
section: Scores: projecting samples onto a PC
text:
Scores: projecting samples onto a PC
A score is the coordinate of a sample along a PC — its projection onto that PC direction (dot product with the unit eigenvector).
For a centred sample \(\mathbf{x}\) and unit PC direction \(\mathbf{u}\):
\[\text{score} = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{u} = x_1 u_1 + x_2 u_2\]

The PC1 score tells you where the sample sits along the long axis.
Samples with similar biology get similar scores; different groups spread apart along PC1.
Plotting PC1 score vs PC2 score for all samples is the PCA plot you see in papers.



This reuses projection intuition directly from the vector-geometry unit: the score is the dot product of the centred sample with the unit PC vector, i.e. the length of the sample’s shadow on the PC axis. Make the biology vivid: the PC1 score is a single number summarising each sample along the main axis of variation, and plotting PC1 vs PC2 scores is exactly the ubiquitous PCA scatter in omics papers. Samples close together in that plot are similar across many genes at once. Emphasise projection = dot product so this does not feel like new machinery; it is the same operation they already know, applied to the eigenvectors.

title: Principal component analysis
section: Loadings: how much each gene contributes
text:
Loadings: how much each gene contributes
The loadings of a PC are just the entries of its eigenvector — one weight per gene.
If PC1 \(= \mathbf{u} = (u_A, u_B)\), then
\[\text{PC1 score} = u_A \cdot (\text{gene A}) + u_B \cdot (\text{gene B}).\]

A gene with a large loading (positive or negative) drives that PC.
A gene with a loading near zero barely matters for that PC.
Loadings tell the biological story: “PC1 is high in the immune-gene programme”, read off from which genes load heavily.

Scores describe samples; loadings describe genes. Two sides of the same eigenvector.


The single most useful distinction to nail: scores are per-sample (where samples land), loadings are per-gene (how genes combine to build the PC). They are the two readings of the same eigen-decomposition — the eigenvector entries are the loadings, and dotting a sample with the eigenvector gives its score. Biologically, loadings are how you interpret a PC: sort genes by loading and the top ones tell you what biological programme that axis represents (cell cycle, immune response, batch, etc.). Warn that sign is arbitrary (eigenvectors are defined up to sign, from the eigen unit), so “positive vs negative loading” only matters relative to other genes on the same PC.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Variance explained
Each eigenvalue is the variance along its PC. The fraction of total variance captured by PC\(k\) is
\[\text{variance explained by PC}_k = \frac{\lambda_k}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \cdots + \lambda_p}.\]
For our example (\(\lambda_1 = 9\), \(\lambda_2 = 1\), total \(= 10\)):
\[\text{PC1}: \frac{9}{10} = 90\%, \qquad \text{PC2}: \frac{1}{10} = 10\%.\]

PC1 alone captures 90% of the variation — a 1-D summary keeps most of the signal.
The sum of all eigenvalues equals the total variance (the trace of \(C\): \(5+5=10\)) — so the fractions add to 100%.



Variance explained turns eigenvalues into an interpretable percentage: each PC’s eigenvalue over the sum of all eigenvalues. Tie the denominator back to the trace fact from the eigen unit — sum of eigenvalues equals the trace equals the total variance across all genes — which is why the fractions sum to one. In the toy example PC1 explains 90 percent, so summarising each sample by a single PC1 score keeps most of the signal. Introduce the word scree plot for the bar chart of eigenvalues; in real data you look for an elbow to decide how many PCs to keep. Do not over-formalise how many PCs to keep today; the concept (a ranked, exhaustive variance budget) is enough.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Try it: rotate the axis




Live version of the last few slides, on the same five samples (already centred). The green line is a candidate axis; the dashed lines drop each sample perpendicularly onto it, and the orange dots are the projections, i.e. the scores. The big percentage is the variance of those scores out of the total variance of 10. Start at 20 degrees and drag a handle round slowly: ask the room to call out when they think the percentage is largest. At 0 and 90 degrees it reads 50% (the variance of gene A alone, then gene B alone). It peaks at 45 degrees with 9 out of 10, 90%, which is lambda 1; at 135 degrees it bottoms out at 1, 10%, which is lambda 2. Tick “Show PC1 and PC2” to confirm the peak is the eigenvector we found by hand, with PC2 perpendicular. Point out that “along” plus “perpendicular” always adds to the total of 10: rotating moves variance between the two directions but never creates or destroys it. At 45 degrees the score readout matches the B5 table. If time: drag s3 away from the diagonal and watch PC1 and the percentage move.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Optional Step 0: scaling
Centring is always done. Scaling (dividing each gene by its standard deviation) is a choice.

Without scaling, a gene measured on a large numeric range dominates the variance — and therefore PC1 — just because of its units, not its biology.
With scaling, every gene has variance 1, so all genes get an equal say. (This uses the correlation matrix instead of the covariance matrix.)

When to scale:

Variables on different units (gene expression + a pH + a temperature)? Scale.
All variables already comparable (all log-expression)? Often leave unscaled.



Scaling is the one genuine judgement call in basic PCA. Make the failure mode concrete: if one gene ranges 0 to 10000 and another 0 to 2, the first swamps the covariance and hijacks PC1 purely because of its scale, not its importance. Dividing each variable by its standard deviation puts everything on equal footing, which is equivalent to running PCA on the correlation matrix rather than the covariance matrix. The rule of thumb: scale when variables have different units or wildly different ranges; you may skip it when they are already on one comparable scale such as log-transformed expression. prcomp exposes this as scale. = TRUE/FALSE, previewed for the next unit.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Reading a PCA plot biologically
A PCA plot is a scatter of samples: PC1 score on x, PC2 score on y.

Clusters of points = groups of samples with similar overall expression (e.g. tumour vs normal).
Separation along PC1 = the biggest source of variation splits those groups.
Outliers = possible failed libraries, contamination, or a genuinely unusual sample — worth checking.
A PC that separates by processing date, not biology, reveals a batch effect.

PCA is unsupervised: it never saw the labels. If the biology falls out anyway, the signal is strong.


This is the everyday payoff and the reason PCA is the first plot everyone makes on a new omics dataset. Walk through how to read it: clusters are similar samples, separation along PC1 is the dominant biological (or technical) split, outliers flag QC problems, and a PC aligned with batch/date rather than condition is the classic way PCA exposes batch effects. Reinforce unsupervised: labels were never used, so clustering by condition is real evidence of structure, not circular. Caution that a PCA plot is exploratory — it suggests hypotheses (groups, outliers, batches) that you then confirm with proper statistics, not a formal test in itself.

title: Principal component analysis
section: What PCA does and does not do
text:
What PCA does and does not do
Does:

Find orthogonal axes of decreasing variance — a compact, ranked summary.
Give an honest first look at structure, outliers, and batch effects.
Reduce thousands of genes to a few interpretable components.

Does not:

Use sample labels (it is unsupervised — it optimises variance, not class separation).
Guarantee PC1 is the biologically interesting axis — the largest variance might be a batch effect.
Capture non-linear structure — PCs are straight-line combinations of genes.



Set expectations honestly. PCA maximises variance, which is not the same as maximising anything biologically meaningful; the dominant axis can be a technical artefact, so always colour the PCA plot by known covariates (condition, batch, sex) to interpret what each PC is. Because PCA is linear, curved or manifold structure is not captured — name that non-linear methods (t-SNE, UMAP) exist and come later or in the ML course, without teaching them. And because it is unsupervised, it is a discovery tool, not a classifier. This slide inoculates against the two most common misreadings: “PC1 must be my biology” and “PCA proves my groups”.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Goal
rotate axes to line up with the data cloud; keep the high-variance ones


Covariance matrix \(C\)
symmetric \(p\times p\); diagonal = variances, off-diagonal = covariances


Principal components
eigenvectors of \(C\) — orthogonal, ranked by variance


Eigenvalue \(\lambda_k\)
variance captured along PC\(k\)


Centre first
subtract each gene’s mean (always)


Scale?
divide by SD when units differ (correlation vs covariance matrix)


Score
sample projected onto a PC: \(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{u}\) (describes samples)


Loading
eigenvector entry = gene’s weight in the PC (describes genes)


Variance explained
\(\lambda_k / \sum_j \lambda_j\); sums to 100% (denominator = trace)


Unsupervised
never uses labels; PC1 = most variance, not necessarily the biology



Next (PCA in R): prcomp does centring, scaling, and the eigen-decomposition in one call — you will read its scores, loadings, and variance explained.

The summary is the revision sheet. Recite the pipeline once: centre (and maybe scale), form the symmetric covariance matrix, take its eigenvectors as the PCs and eigenvalues as the variances, project samples for scores, read eigenvector entries as loadings, and divide eigenvalues by their sum for variance explained. Reinforce the two hardest distinctions: scores (samples) vs loadings (genes), and rotation (exact) vs truncation (the actual dimension reduction). Preview PCA in R: prcomp packages all of this, but its output only makes sense if today’s concepts are solid — they must map values, vectors, and rotation onto scores, variance explained, and loadings.

title: Quiz: choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of how many principal components to keep, and how PCA can mislead. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Several are written in the style of the on-campus exam (no computer).

Q1. A prcomp object reports sdev = c(3, 2, 1). What is the proportion of variance explained by PC1?






Hint





sdev is a standard deviation — the eigenvalue (variance) is its square. PVE is one eigenvalue divided by the sum of all of them.









Answer





Eigenvalues are \(3^2, 2^2, 1^2 = 9, 4, 1\), summing to 14. So PVE\(_1 = 9/14 \approx 0.64\), i.e. about 64%. (A common slip is to use sdev directly, \(3/6=0.5\) — wrong, because you must square first.)




Q2. In one sentence, what is the difference between the scree/elbow rule and the cumulative-variance threshold rule for choosing the number of PCs?






Hint





One is read by eye off a plot; the other is a fixed cut-off on a running total.









Answer





The elbow rule keeps the PCs before the scree plot flattens (an eyeballed, sometimes ambiguous judgement), while the threshold rule keeps the smallest number of PCs whose cumulative PVE reaches a chosen target (e.g. 90%) — reproducible, but with an arbitrary threshold. Both are heuristics.




Q3. The Kaiser criterion keeps PCs with eigenvalue \(> 1\). Why does this cut-off only make sense for a PCA of standardised data (scale. = TRUE)?






Hint





After standardising, what is the variance of each original feature, and what do the eigenvalues therefore average to?









Answer





Standardising sets every feature’s variance to 1, so the eigenvalues (which sum to the number of features \(p\)) average to exactly 1. Then “\(\lambda>1\)” means “this PC captures more than an average single feature’s worth of variance,” a meaningful bar. On raw covariance eigenvalues, whose scale depends on the data’s units, the number 1 has no special meaning. (Note Kaiser also tends to over-retain components.)




Q4. PCA of a dataset with two known tumour subtypes separates the subtypes cleanly, but only on PC6 (3% of variance), not on PC1–PC2. Did the PCA fail? What does this illustrate?






Hint





Does PCA ever look at your group labels? What does it actually maximise?









Answer





No, the PCA did exactly its job. PCA is unsupervised: it ranks directions by variance and never sees the labels. So the largest-variance axis need not be the biologically interesting one — here the subtype contrast is real but small, buried under larger nuisance variation. To find the axis that best separates known groups, use a supervised method such as the OPLS model (this block) or LDA.




Q5. You colour a PCA score plot by biological group and see no structure; colouring the same plot by sequencing run splits the samples perfectly along PC1. What is PC1 capturing, and why did it end up first?






Hint





Technical variation can be larger than biological variation. What does PCA sort components by?









Answer





PC1 is capturing a batch effect (the technical difference between sequencing runs), not biology. It lands on PC1 because the batch effect is large — often larger than the biological signal — and PCA orders components by variance, so the biggest source of variation comes first. Fixes: randomise samples across batches by design, apply batch correction (single-cell block), and always colour scores by technical variables before interpreting.




Q6. True or false: running prcomp(X, scale. = TRUE) versus prcomp(X, scale. = FALSE) can give you different principal components and a different scree plot. Briefly justify.






Hint





scale. = FALSE decomposes the covariance matrix; scale. = TRUE decomposes the correlation matrix. Are those the same matrix?









Answer





True. With scale. = FALSE PCA decomposes the covariance matrix (high-variance features dominate); with scale. = TRUE it decomposes the correlation matrix (every feature standardised to variance 1, all weighted equally). These are different matrices, so the eigenvectors, eigenvalues, and hence the scree plot differ. Scaling is a real modelling choice — standardise when features are on different scales/units, and always report which you used.




Q7. In a score plot, one sample sits far from a tight cluster of all the others along PC1, which “explains 50% of the variance.” What is the likely explanation, and what should you check?






Hint





Variance is dominated by large deviations. What is the largest deviation in this plot?









Answer





Almost certainly an outlier — a technical failure, mislabel, or contamination — that is single-handedly defining PC1 (its large deviation dominates the variance). Before interpreting PC1, investigate that sample (QC metrics, metadata), decide whether it is a genuine biological extreme or an artefact, and re-run the PCA without it to see how much PC1 changes. A “PC1” that is really one point’s variance is not describing your population.




Q8. PCA struggles to summarise data lying on a curved manifold (e.g. a developmental trajectory). Why, and what kind of method is designed for such structure?






Hint





What shape is a principal component — a straight line or a curve?









Answer





Every principal component is a linear combination of the features — a straight axis — so PCA can only capture linear structure. A curved trajectory has no good straight axis, so PCA flattens it or spreads it across many PCs. Non-linear embeddings such as UMAP (or t-SNE), which preserve local neighbourhoods, are built for this; you meet UMAP in the single-cell block (usually run on the top PCs, so today’s “how many PCs” choice still matters). Note UMAP is for seeing structure, not measuring it — inter-cluster distances on a UMAP are not meaningful.




Q9. In one sentence: what does ICA seek that ordinary PCA does not, and when does that difference actually matter?






Hint





PCA components are uncorrelated. Is “uncorrelated” the same as “independent”?









Answer





ICA seeks components that are statistically independent (a stronger condition than PCA’s mere lack of correlation), which matters for non-Gaussian signals — for Gaussian data, uncorrelated already implies independent, so ICA adds nothing there. In biology this can, for example, separate overlapping transcriptional programmes that PCA would blend.

title: Exercise: choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Background
PCA (from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors and Computing PCA) diagonalises the centred data’s covariance matrix. Each principal component is an eigenvector, and its eigenvalue \(\lambda_k\) is the variance along that PC. The eigenvalues are sorted \(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_p\ge 0\) and sum to the total variance.
Proportion of variance explained: \[\text{PVE}_k = \frac{\lambda_k}{\sum_{j=1}^p \lambda_j}, \qquad \text{cumulative PVE}_k = \sum_{j\le k}\text{PVE}_j.\]
In R, prcomp reports standard deviations in sdev, so the eigenvalue is sdev^2.
Choosing how many PCs (all heuristics, none authoritative):

Scree / elbow — plot PVE (or \(\lambda\)) vs PC index; keep the PCs before the flat tail begins.
Cumulative threshold — keep the smallest \(k\) reaching a target cumulative PVE (commonly 80/90/95%).
Kaiser — on standardised data (correlation matrix, so the eigenvalues average to 1), keep PCs with \(\lambda>1\). Tends to over-retain.
Permutation / parallel analysis — keep PCs whose eigenvalue exceeds what shuffled (noise) data produces.

Pitfalls. PCA is unsupervised (maximises variance, ignores labels) and linear (each PC is a straight axis). So the top PC can be a nuisance gradient, a batch effect, or an outlier; the components change with scaling (scale. = TRUE/FALSE); and curved structure is not captured. Supervised separation is the job of OPLS (this block) or LDA; curved structure calls for ICA (independence, not just decorrelation) or non-linear maps like UMAP (single-cell block).

title: Exercise: choosing components & pitfalls
text:
By hand
For B1–B4 use this set of eigenvalues from a PCA of a small dataset with \(p=6\) features:
\[\lambda = (6.0,\; 2.4,\; 0.9,\; 0.4,\; 0.2,\; 0.1).\]
B1. Compute the total variance \(\sum_j\lambda_j\), then the PVE of each of the six PCs (as a fraction and roughly as a percentage).
B2. Compute the cumulative PVE after 1, 2, 3, and 4 PCs. How many PCs do you need to explain at least 90% of the variance?
B3. Sketch the scree plot (PVE vs PC index) by hand. Where is the elbow, and how many PCs does the elbow rule suggest keeping? Does this agree with your 90% threshold answer from B2? Comment on any disagreement.
B4. These are raw (covariance) eigenvalues. Suppose instead the PCA had been run on standardised data with the same 6 features. Explain why the Kaiser rule (\(\lambda>1\)) would be applied to that PCA and not directly to the numbers above. (You are not asked to recompute — just explain the condition.)
B5. (scaling). A metabolomics dataset has two features: metabolite A with variance \(\approx 10{,}000\) (measured in large raw intensities) and metabolite B with variance \(\approx 2\) (a ratio). Without any standardisation, which feature will dominate PC1, and why? What does setting scale. = TRUE change, and when is that the sensible choice?
B6. (unsupervised). You have samples from two tumour subtypes. On the PCA, subtypes are not separated on PC1 or PC2, but they are cleanly separated on PC5, which explains only 3% of the variance. (a) Is anything wrong with the PCA? (b) What does this tell you about the relationship between “variance” and “biological interest”? (c) Name a method designed to find the axis that best separates the two known groups.
B7. (batch effect). You colour a PCA score plot by tumour subtype and see no pattern. You then colour the same plot by sequencing run and the two runs split perfectly along PC1. (a) What is PC1 most likely capturing? (b) Why did PCA place this on PC1 rather than a later component? (c) Give one design step and one analysis step that address this.
B8. (outlier). In a score plot, 39 of 40 samples sit in a tight cluster while 1 sample sits far away along PC1, which “explains 55% of the variance.” What is the most likely story, and what should you do before interpreting PC1?
B9. (beyond PCA). In one sentence each: (a) what does ICA look for that PCA does not, and when does that extra condition actually matter; (b) why would you run PCA before UMAP rather than UMAP on the raw features, and what must you not read off a UMAP plot?

title: Exercise: choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Explore
This demo shows three of the pitfalls on small 2D datasets. The solid red line is PC1, the dashed red line PC2; the two strips underneath show each sample’s score on PC1 and on PC2 (same scale as the scatter). Use it after B5–B8.



E1. (scaling, compare B5). Preset 1 · Units. How much variance does PC1 explain, and what are its loadings on A and B? Now tick “Scale variables”. What happens to the PC1 direction, its loadings, and its percentage? Why does PC1 end up at exactly \(45^\circ\)?
E2. (outlier, compare B8). Preset 2 · Outlier. Read the PC1 direction and percentage with and without the red sample. Then drag the red sample into the middle of the cloud, and finally far out to one side. What happens to PC1, and to the PC1 score strip?
E3. (unsupervised, compare B6). Preset 3 · Two groups. How much variance does PC1 explain? On which score strip are the blue and orange groups separated? What does this say about using PC1 to look for the group difference?






Solutions





E1. Unscaled, PC1 explains 99.99% and is \(\approx 1.00\cdot A + 0.01\cdot B\): it is simply metabolite A, because A’s variance (SD \(\approx 99\)) dwarfs B’s (SD \(\approx 1.6\)). After scaling, both variables have variance 1, PC1 turns to \(45^\circ\) with loadings \(0.71, 0.71\) (A and B count equally) and explains about 87%. The scaled covariance matrix is the correlation matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}1 & r\\ r & 1\end{pmatrix}\), which has the symmetric \(\begin{pmatrix}a & b\\ b & a\end{pmatrix}\) pattern, so its eigenvectors are \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\) whatever \(r\) is.
E2. Without the outlier, PC1 lies along the cloud at about \(18^\circ\) and explains about 77%. With it, PC1 swings to about \(100^\circ\) (explaining about 65%), pointing at the one sample. Dragged into the cloud, PC1 returns close to the grey dashed line; dragged far out, PC1 follows the outlier wherever it goes and the PC1 strip shows the typical symptom: one point far away, everyone else bunched together.
E3. PC1 explains about 89% of the variance, but the two colours overlap completely on the PC1 strip; they separate only on the PC2 strip (about 11%). PCA ranks directions by variance and never sees the colours, so the group difference can sit on a small PC. To find the separating direction from known labels you would use a supervised method (OPLS or LDA).

title: Exercise: choosing components & pitfalls
text:
In R
Use R to confirm the hand answers. Nothing here needs a real dataset except the last block.

PVE and cumulative PVE from eigenvalues (B1–B3)
lambda <- c(6.0, 2.4, 0.9, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1)

total <- sum(lambda)         # 10
pve   <- lambda / total      # 0.60 0.24 0.09 0.04 0.02 0.01
cumsum(pve)                  # 0.60 0.84 0.93 0.97 0.99 1.00

# smallest number of PCs reaching 90% cumulative variance
which(cumsum(pve) >= 0.90)[1]   # 3


A scree plot (B3)
plot(pve, type = "b",
     xlab = "PC", ylab = "Proportion of variance explained",
     main = "Scree plot")


From a real PCA object
# X: samples x features. scale. = TRUE standardises features first.
pca <- prcomp(X, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

eig <- pca$sdev^2            # eigenvalues (variance per PC)
pve <- eig / sum(eig)        # proportion of variance explained
cumsum(pve)                  # cumulative PVE

summary(pca)                 # prints PVE and cumulative proportion rows

# colour scores by a technical variable to check for a batch effect (B7)
plot(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2],
     col = batch,            # a factor: sequencing run / lot / site
     xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2")


Tasks
R1. Reproduce B1–B2: build lambda, compute pve and cumsum(pve), and confirm the 90% answer with which(cumsum(pve) >= 0.90)[1].
R2. Change the threshold to 95% with which(cumsum(pve) >= 0.95)[1]. How many PCs now? Relate the jump to the shape of the scree tail.
R3. For any prcomp object you have (or make a toy X <- matrix(rnorm(200), 20, 10)), compute pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2) and check it matches the “Proportion of Variance” row of summary(pca).

title: Exercise: choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — eigenvalue to PVE





The eigenvalue is the variance along a PC. Divide each eigenvalue by the sum of all eigenvalues to get the proportion. In R the eigenvalue is pca$sdev^2 (square it — sdev is a standard deviation). See prcomp.









Hint 2 — cumulative and the threshold rule





Cumulative PVE is a running total: cumsum(pve). “Reach 90%” means the smallest \(k\) with cumulative PVE \(\ge 0.90\); which(cumsum(pve) >= 0.90)[1] returns that \(k\).









Hint 3 — reading the elbow





Plot PVE against PC index. The elbow is where the steep drop turns into the shallow flat tail; keep the PCs before it. It is read by eye and is often ambiguous — there may be no single right answer, and it need not match the threshold rule.









Hint 4 — when Kaiser applies





The \(\lambda>1\) rule only makes sense on standardised data (a correlation-matrix PCA, scale. = TRUE), because standardising makes every feature contribute variance 1, so the eigenvalues average to exactly 1. On raw covariance eigenvalues the “1” is not a meaningful cut-off.









Hint 5 — scaling and who dominates PC1





PCA maximises variance, and variance depends on units. A feature with numerically huge variance dominates unless you standardise. scale. = TRUE gives every feature variance 1 so all count equally — the right choice when features are on different scales/units.









Hint 6 — unsupervised means label-blind





PCA never sees your group labels; it only ranks directions by variance. So the group-separating direction can be a small PC. If separating known groups is the goal, you want a supervised method — the OPLS model (this block) or LDA — that does use the labels.









Hint 7 — spotting a batch effect or an outlier





Colour the score plot by every technical variable you have (run, lot, date, library size). If a technical variable lines up with a PC, that PC is suspect. An outlier shows up as one lonely point far out with everyone else squashed together — a PC that “explains variance” but really only that one point’s.

B1. Total variance \(= 6.0+2.4+0.9+0.4+0.2+0.1 = 10.0\). Dividing each eigenvalue by 10:
