(The PVEs sum to 1.00, a useful check.)
B2. Cumulative PVE: after PC1 \(=0.60\); after PC2 \(=0.60+0.24=0.84\); after PC3 \(=0.84+0.09=0.93\); after PC4 \(=0.93+0.04=0.97\). The smallest number of PCs reaching \(\ge 0.90\) is 3 (0.84 at two PCs is short of 90%, 0.93 at three clears it).
B3. The scree plot drops steeply from 0.60 to 0.24 to 0.09, then flattens (0.04, 0.02, 0.01). The elbow sits at PC3: the big drops are over PC1→PC2→PC3 and the tail from PC4 on is flat and small. So the elbow rule suggests keeping about 2–3 PCs — one could argue the flat tail starts after PC2 (keep 2) or after PC3 (keep 3). The 90% threshold said 3. They roughly agree here; any disagreement comes from the elbow being an eyeball judgement while the threshold is a fixed rule. On this dataset the structure is clear (two dominant PCs, small tail), so the rules nearly coincide — which is not always the case.
B4. The Kaiser rule keeps PCs with \(\lambda>1\), and the “1” cut-off is only meaningful when each original feature has variance 1 — i.e. after standardising the data (a correlation-matrix PCA). Then the eigenvalues average to exactly 1 (they still sum to \(p\), the number of features), so “\(\lambda>1\)” means “this PC captures more than an average single feature’s worth of variance.” Applied to the raw covariance eigenvalues above (which sum to 10, not 6), the number 1 has no special status, so Kaiser should not be read off them directly. (Also worth knowing: Kaiser tends to over-retain components.)
B5. Without standardisation, metabolite A dominates PC1: its variance (\(\approx 10{,}000\)) dwarfs B’s (\(\approx 2\)), and PCA maximises variance, so PC1 will essentially align with A regardless of whether A is biologically more informative. This is an artefact of units/scale, not of biology. Setting scale. = TRUE standardises each feature to variance 1, so A and B contribute equally; the components then reflect correlation structure rather than raw magnitude. Standardising is the sensible default when features are on different scales or units (as here) — otherwise you are just ranking features by how big their numbers happen to be.
B6. (a) Nothing is wrong with the PCA — it did exactly its job, ranking directions by variance. (b) It shows that variance and biological interest are different things. The subtype contrast is real but small (3% of variance), sitting under larger, biologically uninteresting sources of variation (which occupy PC1–PC4). PCA, being unsupervised, cannot know that the 3% axis is the one you care about. (c) A supervised method that uses the labels — OPLS (this block) or LDA — is designed to find the direction that best separates the two known groups.
B7. (a) PC1 is most likely capturing the batch / technical effect (the difference between the two sequencing runs), not biology. (b) PCA puts it on PC1 because batch effects are often large — larger than the biological signal — and PCA ranks purely by variance, so the biggest source of variation lands first. (c) Design step: randomise samples across batches (don’t confound subtype with run) so the technical and biological variation are not aligned. Analysis step: apply a batch-correction / integration method (introduced in the single-cell block) and/or always colour the score plot by technical variables before interpreting.
B8. The single far-off sample is almost certainly an outlier — a technical failure (degraded sample, failed library), a mislabel, or contamination — and it is single-handedly defining PC1 (variance is dominated by large deviations, and this point is the largest deviation by far). Before interpreting PC1 you should investigate that sample: check its QC metrics and metadata, decide deliberately whether it is a genuine biological extreme or an artefact, and re-run the PCA with it excluded to see how much PC1 changes. A “PC1 explaining 55%” that is really one point’s variance is not describing your population.
B9. (a) ICA looks for components that are statistically independent, a stronger condition than PCA’s mere lack of correlation; the extra condition matters for non-Gaussian signals (for Gaussian data, uncorrelated already implies independent, so ICA adds nothing). (b) You run PCA before UMAP to denoise and reduce dimensionality (feed UMAP the top PCs rather than thousands of noisy raw features), which is faster and more stable; and you must not read distances between clusters (or the axis directions/units) off a UMAP plot — UMAP preserves local neighbourhoods, not global distances, and is stochastic.
R1–R3. The code blocks above reproduce these directly: pve gives \(0.60, 0.24, 0.09, 0.04, 0.02, 0.01\); cumsum(pve) gives \(0.60, 0.84, 0.93, 0.97, 0.99, 1.00\); which(cumsum(pve) >= 0.90)[1] returns 3. For R2, which(cumsum(pve) >= 0.95)[1] returns 4 (0.93 at three PCs is short of 95%, 0.97 at four clears it) — one extra PC buys only the small PC4, illustrating how a flat tail makes the last few percent expensive. For R3, pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2) reproduces the “Proportion of Variance” row of summary(pca) exactly.

title: Exercise: choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Where this leads

The OPLS model (Extra material): when you have group labels and want the axis that separates them (the B6/B7 situation), a supervised method is the right tool — OPLS is built for exactly that, and contrasts cleanly with today’s unsupervised PCA.
Multiome data integration (Extra material): choosing components and watching for batch effects recur when combining modalities (e.g. RNA-seq counts vs proteomics).
Single-cell analysis: the standard pipeline runs PCA first (using today’s “how many PCs” decision) and then a non-linear UMAP on the top PCs, plus explicit batch correction — the practical home of several pitfalls above.

title: Exercise: PCA in R
text:
Background
PCA re-expresses a samples × features table in a new coordinate system whose axes (principal components) are ordered by how much variation they capture. PC1 is the direction of greatest variance, PC2 the next-greatest and perpendicular to PC1, and so on.
The principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and the variance along each PC is its eigenvalue. So a full PCA by hand is:

Center the data: subtract each feature’s (column) mean. (Optionally scale: divide each column by its standard deviation.)
Form the covariance matrix \(C\) of the (centered) features.
Eigen-decompose \(C\): eigenvalues \(\lambda_k\) = variance along PC\(k\); eigenvectors = loadings (the PC directions).
Variance explained by PC\(k\) is \(\lambda_k / \sum_j \lambda_j\).
Scores = project each centered sample onto each PC (a dot product with the unit eigenvector).

In R, prcomp(X, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE) does all of this and returns $sdev (where \(\text{sdev}_k^2 = \lambda_k\)), $rotation (loadings), and $x (scores).
Convention: samples are rows, features are columns. If your omics table is genes × samples, transpose it with t first.
For the by-hand part, recall the symmetric pattern from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors: \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}\) has eigenvectors \((1,1)\) with \(\lambda = a+b\) and \((1,-1)\) with \(\lambda = a-b\), and \(\sum\lambda = \text{trace}\) is a handy check.

title: Exercise: PCA in R
text:
By hand
Use this tiny dataset throughout the by-hand section — 3 samples, 2 genes:
\[X = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\quad\text{(rows: s1, s2, s3; columns: gene1, gene2)}\]
B1. Compute each gene’s mean and center the data (subtract the column mean from every entry). Write out the centered matrix.
B2. Using the centered data, compute the \(2\times2\) covariance matrix \(C = \begin{pmatrix} \text{var}(g_1) & \text{cov}(g_1,g_2) \\ \text{cov}(g_1,g_2) & \text{var}(g_2) \end{pmatrix}\). Use the \(n-1\) denominator (here \(n-1 = 2\)).
B3. Find the eigenvalues of \(C\) (use the symmetric pattern and verify by multiplying). Confirm with the trace check.
B4. Find a unit-length eigenvector for each eigenvalue. These are the loadings — the directions of PC1 and PC2. Verify the two are orthogonal.
B5. Compute the proportion of variance explained by PC1 and by PC2.
B6. Compute the PC1 score of each sample: project each centered sample onto the PC1 unit eigenvector (a dot product). Which two samples end up closest together on PC1?
B7. (interpretation) Look at your PC1 loading. Do gene1 and gene2 contribute equally, or does one dominate? What would that tell a biologist about how these two genes vary across the samples?

title: Exercise: PCA in R
text:
In R
The same PCA, run with prcomp. (Here we center but do not scale, so the result matches the covariance eigen-decomposition you did by hand; the scaling task comes at the end.)

Run it and read the three outputs
X <- matrix(c(2, 2,
              4, 6,
              6, 4), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(X) <- c("s1", "s2", "s3")
colnames(X) <- c("gene1", "gene2")

pca <- prcomp(X, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)

pca$sdev            # [1] 2.449 1.414   -> sd along each PC
pca$sdev^2          # [1] 6 2           -> variance along each PC = eigenvalues

pca$rotation        # loadings (columns are PCs, rows are genes)
#          PC1     PC2
# gene1  0.707   0.707
# gene2  0.707  -0.707

pca$x               # scores (one row per sample)
#          PC1     PC2
# s1  -2.828   0.000
# s2   1.414  -1.414
# s3   1.414   1.414


Variance explained
prop <- pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
round(prop, 3)      # [1] 0.75 0.25   -> PC1 explains 75%, PC2 explains 25%
cumsum(prop)        # [1] 0.75 1.00


Show prcomp == eigen of the covariance matrix
C <- cov(X)         # covariance matrix (center is built into cov)
C
#        gene1 gene2
# gene1     4     2
# gene2     2     4

e <- eigen(C)
e$values            # [1] 6 2          -> same as pca$sdev^2
e$vectors           # same as pca$rotation (columns), up to sign


Plot PC1 vs PC2
plot(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2],
     xlab = "PC1 (75%)", ylab = "PC2 (25%)", pch = 19)
text(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], labels = rownames(X), pos = 3)


Tasks
R1. Reproduce the by-hand result in R: build X, run prcomp(X, scale. = FALSE), and confirm pca$sdev^2 matches your B3 eigenvalues and pca$rotation matches your B4 eigenvectors (allowing for a possible sign flip).
R2. Confirm the equivalence directly: compute eigen(cov(X)) and check that $values equals pca$sdev^2 and $vectors equals pca$rotation (up to sign).
R3. Confirm your B6 scores: check that pca$x[, 1] equals the PC1 scores you computed by hand.
R4. (why scaling matters) Two genes on very different scales:
Y <- matrix(c(100, 1,
              110, 5,
              120, 2,
              130, 6,
              140, 3,
              150, 7), nrow = 6, byrow = TRUE)
colnames(Y) <- c("geneHi", "geneLo")

pca_noscale <- prcomp(Y, scale. = FALSE)
pca_scale   <- prcomp(Y, scale. = TRUE)

round(pca_noscale$rotation[, 1], 3)   # PC1 loadings, unscaled
round(pca_scale$rotation[, 1],   3)   # PC1 loadings, scaled
Compare the two PC1 loadings. Without scaling, which gene dominates PC1, and why? What changes when you set scale. = TRUE? Which analysis would you trust if the two genes are measured in different units?

title: Exercise: PCA in R
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — centering (B1)





The mean of a column is the sum of its entries divided by the number of samples. Subtract that mean from every entry in the column. gene1 is \(2,4,6\) and gene2 is \(2,6,4\) — both have mean \(4\), so centering just subtracts \(4\) everywhere.









Hint 2 — covariance by hand (B2)





With centered columns \(u\) and \(v\) and \(n\) samples, \(\text{var}(u) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum u_i^2\) and \(\text{cov}(u,v) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum u_i v_i\). Here \(n-1 = 2\). The matrix is symmetric, so \(\text{cov}(g_1,g_2) = \text{cov}(g_2,g_1)\). In R this is cov(X).









Hint 3 — eigenvalues (B3)





\(C\) has the form \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}\), so multiply it by \((1,1)\) and by \((1,-1)\): the eigenvalues are \(a+b\) and \(a-b\). Check with $_1 + _2 = $ trace. In R: eigen(C)$values. (Bonus, not for exam: the characteristic equation \(\det(C-\lambda I) = 0\) gives the same.)









Hint 4 — unit eigenvectors (B4)





Solve \((C-\lambda I)\mathbf v = \mathbf 0\) for each \(\lambda\) to get a direction (e.g. \((1,1)\)), then make it length 1 by dividing by its norm \(\sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2}\). For \((1,1)\) the norm is \(\sqrt 2\), so the unit vector is \((1/\sqrt2,\ 1/\sqrt2) \approx (0.707, 0.707)\). Orthogonal means the dot product is 0.









Hint 5 — variance explained (B5)





Proportion for PC\(k\) is \(\lambda_k / (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)\). The denominator is the total variance, which also equals the trace of \(C\). In R: pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2).









Hint 6 — scores as projections (B6)





A score is a dot product: PC1 score of a sample \(=\) (centered sample) \(\cdot\) (PC1 unit eigenvector). For centered sample \((u_1, u_2)\) and unit vector \((0.707, 0.707)\) the score is \(0.707\,u_1 + 0.707\,u_2\). In R the whole score matrix is pca$x, or equivalently scale(X, scale = FALSE) %*% pca$rotation (see %*%).









Hint 7 — reading loadings (B7)





A loading is the weight of a gene in a PC. Equal loadings mean the two genes contribute equally to that axis — i.e. they vary together. A loading near zero means the gene is irrelevant to that PC. Compare the magnitudes within the PC1 column of pca$rotation.









Hint 8 — scaling (R4)





Variance has units. A gene measured in the hundreds has a large variance for trivial reasons and will dominate PC1 unless you scale. scale. = TRUE divides each gene by its standard deviation first, putting them on equal footing. See the scale. argument in prcomp (note the dot in the name) and the standalone scale.

title: Exercise: PCA in R
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1 — centering. Column means: gene1 \(=(2+4+6)/3 = 4\); gene2 \(=(2+6+4)/3 = 4\). Subtract 4 from each column:
\[X_c = \begin{pmatrix} 2-4 & 2-4 \\ 4-4 & 6-4 \\ 6-4 & 4-4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\]
B2 — covariance matrix. With \(n-1 = 2\) and the centered columns \(u = (-2, 0, 2)\), \(v = (-2, 2, 0)\):

\(\text{var}(g_1) = \frac{(-2)^2 + 0^2 + 2^2}{2} = \frac{8}{2} = 4\),
\(\text{var}(g_2) = \frac{(-2)^2 + 2^2 + 0^2}{2} = \frac{8}{2} = 4\),
\(\text{cov}(g_1,g_2) = \frac{(-2)(-2) + (0)(2) + (2)(0)}{2} = \frac{4}{2} = 2\).

\[C = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}.\]
B3 — eigenvalues. \(C\) has the symmetric pattern with \(a = 4\), \(b = 2\): \(C(1,1) = (6,6) = 6\,(1,1)\) and \(C(1,-1) = (2,-2) = 2\,(1,-1)\), so \(\lambda_1 = 6\), \(\lambda_2 = 2\). Check: trace \(= 4 + 4 = 8 = 6 + 2\) ✓. (Bonus, not for exam: \(\det(C-\lambda I) = (4-\lambda)^2 - 4 = \lambda^2 - 8\lambda + 12 = (\lambda-6)(\lambda-2) = 0\) gives the same, and \(\det C = 12 = 6\cdot2\).)
B4 — unit eigenvectors (loadings). For \(\lambda = 6\): \(C - 6I = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}\); row 1 gives \(-2v_1 + 2v_2 = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 = v_1\), so the direction is \((1,1)\). Normalise: \((1,1)/\sqrt2 = (0.707, 0.707)\) — this is PC1. For \(\lambda = 2\): \(C - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\); row 1 gives \(v_1 + v_2 = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 = -v_1\), so the direction is \((1,-1)\). Normalise: \((0.707, -0.707)\) — this is PC2. Orthogonal: \((1)(1) + (1)(-1) = 0\) ✓ (guaranteed, since \(C\) is symmetric).
B5 — variance explained. Total variance \(= 6 + 2 = 8\). PC1: \(6/8 = 0.75\) (75%); PC2: \(2/8 = 0.25\) (25%).
B6 — PC1 scores. Project each centered sample onto the PC1 unit vector \((0.707, 0.707)\), i.e. score \(= 0.707\,(u_1 + u_2)\):

s1: centered \((-2,-2)\) → \(0.707(-2-2) = 0.707(-4) = -2.83\),
s2: centered \((0,2)\) → \(0.707(0+2) = 0.707(2) = 1.41\),
s3: centered \((2,0)\) → \(0.707(2+0) = 1.41\).

So PC1 scores are \((-2.83,\ 1.41,\ 1.41)\). s2 and s3 land at the same PC1 score — they are the closest pair along PC1 (they differ only along PC2). These match pca$x[, 1] exactly.
B7 — interpretation. The PC1 loading is \((0.707, 0.707)\): gene1 and gene2 contribute equally. Biologically, the dominant source of variation across these samples is the two genes moving together — they are co-varying (here, perfectly correlated). PC1 is essentially “overall level of the gene1–gene2 program”, and a sample’s PC1 score says how high that joint program is.
R1. prcomp(X, scale. = FALSE) returns sdev^2 = c(6, 2) (matching the eigenvalues) and rotation with columns \((0.707, 0.707)\) and \((0.707, -0.707)\) (matching the eigenvectors; R may report either sign). The scores in pca$x[, 1] are \((-2.83, 1.41, 1.41)\), matching B6.
R2.
C <- cov(X)
e <- eigen(C)
e$values          # 6 2
pca$sdev^2        # 6 2   -> identical
e$vectors         # columns equal pca$rotation up to sign
The eigenvalues of the covariance matrix are exactly pca$sdev^2, and the eigenvectors are the columns of pca$rotation (possibly sign-flipped). This is the point of the lecture: PCA is the eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix.
R3. pca$x[, 1] is c(-2.828, 1.414, 1.414), identical to the hand-computed PC1 scores in B6 (up to the same overall sign as the PC1 eigenvector).
R4 — why scaling matters.
round(pca_noscale$rotation[, 1], 3)
# geneHi geneLo
#  0.997  0.081     -> PC1 is almost entirely geneHi

round(pca_scale$rotation[, 1], 3)
# geneHi geneLo
#  0.707  0.707     -> both genes contribute equally
Without scaling, geneHi (values in the hundreds) has a far larger variance than geneLo purely because of its magnitude, so PC1 loads almost entirely on geneHi (loading 0.997) and captures ~99% of the “variance” — a result driven by units, not biology. With scale. = TRUE, each gene is divided by its standard deviation first, so PC1 responds to the correlation pattern and both genes contribute equally (0.707 each). If the two genes are measured in different units, trust the scaled analysis; otherwise the PCA just reports which gene has the bigger numbers.

title: Exercise: PCA in R
text:
Where this leads

Real omics data: the same prcomp call scales to thousands of genes. You will transpose genes × samples tables to samples × genes, plot PC1 vs PC2 coloured by a metadata label, and pull the top-loading genes with sort(abs(pca$rotation[, 1]), decreasing = TRUE).
Production tools: Bioconductor workflows and DESeq2::plotPCA wrap exactly these steps with sensible defaults — the base-R prcomp you learned here is the transparent engine inside them.
Latent-variable methods (Applications block): PCA is the first and simplest dimension-reduction method; PC scores feed naturally into clustering, and the same “find low-dimensional structure” idea recurs in later methods.

title: The OPLS model
text:
About this lecture
In PCA we found the directions of greatest variation in a data matrix \(X\) — a purely unsupervised view that never looks at any outcome. Today we bring the outcome back in.

Why PCA can miss the biology: its biggest axis may be a batch effect, not your disease.
PLS: find directions in \(X\) that covary with an outcome \(Y\) (supervised latent variables).
OPLS: split \(X\)-variation into a predictive part (correlated with \(Y\)) and an orthogonal part (structured noise — batch, instrument, physiology).
Why this split makes a model easier to interpret, and where it is standard (metabolomics).
The catch: supervised models can fit noise, so we must validate honestly.

This is a concept day. The goal is to know what OPLS does, when to reach for it, and how not to fool yourself. Light math, heavy intuition.

This is an optional unit under Extra material, built on PCA, so lean on PCA hard: students already know that PCA diagonalises a covariance matrix and returns orthogonal axes ordered by variance. The one new idea today is supervision — letting a response Y steer which directions we care about — and then OPLS’s particular trick of separating Y-related variation from everything else. Emphasise up front that this is conceptual: the vocabulary (scores, loadings, predictive vs orthogonal, R2/Q2, permutation test) and the overfitting message are what they should leave with.

title: The OPLS model
text:
A biology picture first
A metabolomics study: serum from 40 patients, 20 with a metabolic disease and 20 healthy controls. An LC–MS or NMR platform measures thousands of metabolite features per sample.
The question is simple: which metabolites separate cases from controls?
But the measured variation is dominated by things you did not ask about:

samples run on different days / different instrument batches,
age, sex, BMI, diet differing between individuals,
baseline physiological spread that has nothing to do with the disease.

The disease signal is real but not the loudest thing in the data. We need a method that listens for the outcome, not just the loudest source of variance.


Ground the whole lecture in this one metabolomics scenario and return to it repeatedly. The defining features of the data: very wide (features far outnumber samples), highly collinear (metabolites move in correlated groups), and dominated by nuisance structure (batch, demographics). This is exactly the regime where PCA underperforms as a discovery tool and where PLS/OPLS were developed. Keep the biological question concrete — “which metabolites differ between sick and healthy” — because every abstract idea today (supervision, predictive vs orthogonal) answers a piece of it.

title: The OPLS model
text:
Recap: what PCA gives us
PCA takes the (centred) data matrix \(X\) and returns latent axes ordered by variance:

Scores \(T\) — coordinates of each sample on the new axes,
Loadings \(P\) — how each feature contributes to each axis,
reconstruction \(X \approx T P^\top\), with the first axes capturing the most variance.

\[\text{PC 1 = direction of maximum variance in } X.\]
PCA is unsupervised: it never sees any outcome \(Y\). It answers “what varies most?” — a fine question, but not “what varies with the disease?”


A one-slide refresher tying to the PCA unit. Reuse their vocabulary exactly: scores are the samples’ new coordinates, loadings tell you which original features build each component, and X factorises approximately as scores times loadings transposed. The single sentence to burn in: PCA maximises variance and is blind to Y. Everything today is a reaction to that blindness. Do not re-derive PCA; just re-activate it.

title: The OPLS model
section: The problem: PCA can point the wrong way
text:
The problem: PCA can point the wrong way
In our serum study, suppose the batch (day 1 vs day 2) creates more spread than the disease does. Then:

PC1 aligns with batch, not case/control,
the disease difference hides in some later, smaller component — or is smeared across several.

You plot PC1 vs PC2, colour by disease, and see… no clean separation. Not because the biology is absent, but because PCA optimised for the wrong thing.

PCA finds the loudest variation. It has no reason to care that your loudest variation is a nuisance.



This is the motivating failure. Make it vivid: the student does the natural thing (PCA, colour by phenotype) and it “fails,” and the trap is to conclude there is no signal. The real issue is that variance and relevance are different criteria. Nuisance variance — batch, demographic — is often larger than the effect of interest, so an unsupervised method will rank it first. Note honestly that this is not always the case; sometimes PC1 IS your biology. But when it is not, you need supervision. This sets up PLS on the next slide.

title: The OPLS model
text:
Bring in the outcome: supervision
Attach the response we care about as a vector (or matrix) \(Y\):

regression flavour: \(Y\) is a quantity — e.g. a drug dose, a bioactivity value;
classification flavour: \(Y\) encodes a class — e.g. case \(=1\), control \(=0\) (this is OPLS-DA, discriminant analysis).

Now ask a supervised question:
\[\text{find directions in } X \text{ that are useful for } Y.\]
Instead of maximising variance in \(X\) alone, we bring \(X\) and \(Y\) into the objective. That single change turns PCA into PLS.

Introduce Y as the pivot. Two modes: continuous Y (PLS regression) and categorical Y coded as dummy 0/1 (the discriminant variant, OPLS-DA, which is the common one in metabolomics case/control work). Keep the phrasing “directions in X useful for Y” deliberately loose here; the precise objective (covariance) comes next. The conceptual leap is small but important: we are no longer describing X, we are relating X to Y. Students who have used lm() know supervision; frame PLS as “regression that also builds its own latent axes.”

title: The OPLS model
section: PLS: directions that covary with Y
text:
PLS: directions that covary with Y
Partial Least Squares. PLS builds latent components \(t = Xw\) as linear combinations of the features, choosing the weights \(w\) so the component has maximum covariance with \(Y\):
\[\max_{\|w\|=1}\ \operatorname{cov}(Xw,\ Y).\]
Contrast with PCA, which maximises \(\operatorname{var}(Xw)\) alone.

Covariance = variance and correlation-with-\(Y\) together, so a PLS component must both vary and track \(Y\).
After extracting one component, PLS removes it from \(X\) (deflation) and finds the next — giving several ordered components, like PCA but \(Y\)-aware.



The clean contrast: PCA maximises var(Xw), PLS maximises cov(Xw, Y). Because covariance factors as std(Xw) times cor(Xw, Y) times std(Y), a PLS direction is pulled toward variation that also correlates with the outcome — a compromise between “big” and “relevant.” Mention deflation lightly: extract a component, subtract its contribution from X, repeat, so you again get an ordered set of components. Don’t derive the NIPALS algorithm. The takeaway is the objective swap. This is the parent method; OPLS is a re-parameterisation of it.

title: The OPLS model
text:
Scores and loadings, again
PLS keeps the same two-part vocabulary as PCA, now \(Y\)-aware:








Object
Meaning
Lives in




Scores \(t\)
each sample’s coordinate on a latent component
sample space


Loadings / weights
how each feature contributes to that component
feature space




Score plot → do the samples (cases vs controls) separate?
Loading plot → which metabolites drive that separation?

A latent component is still just a weighted combination of the original features — a new “meta-feature” — only now the weights are chosen with \(Y\) in view.

Reassure students that no new machinery is needed to read PLS output: scores and loadings mean what they meant in PCA. The score plot answers “do my groups separate,” the loading plot answers “which features are responsible.” The phrase “latent variable” simply means a constructed axis that is a linear combination of measured features; it is latent because it is not directly measured. This slide is the bridge that lets them interpret OPLS output later without new vocabulary.

title: The OPLS model
section: The OPLS idea: split the variation
text:
The OPLS idea: split the variation
PLS mixes two kinds of \(X\)-variation inside its components: variation that relates to \(Y\), and variation that is large but irrelevant (batch, physiology). That makes components hard to read.
OPLS (Orthogonal PLS) adds one idea: separate them.
\[\underbrace{\text{variation in } X}_{\text{systematic part}} = \underbrace{\text{predictive}}_{\text{correlated with } Y} \ +\ \underbrace{\text{orthogonal}}_{\text{uncorrelated with } Y} \ +\ \text{residual noise}\]

Predictive variation → put it in one component (for a single \(Y\)) that carries the \(Y\)-related signal.
Orthogonal variation → structured, but uncorrelated with \(Y\); parked in separate orthogonal components.



Here is the one genuinely new concept of the day. OPLS (Trygg and Wold, 2002) does not predict Y any better than PLS — it rearranges the same information so that all the Y-correlated variation is concentrated into a single predictive component and everything else systematic-but-irrelevant is pushed into orthogonal components. “Orthogonal” here means orthogonal (uncorrelated) to Y. For a single response there is exactly one predictive component; there can be several orthogonal ones. The payoff is entirely interpretational, which is why it caught on in metabolomics where interpretation is the goal.

title: The OPLS model
text:
What is “orthogonal variation”?
Orthogonal variation is real, structured signal in \(X\) that has nothing to do with \(Y\). In the serum study it might be:

instrument / batch drift between run days,
age, sex, BMI, diet differences between individuals,
baseline physiological differences unrelated to the disease.

It is not random measurement error — that lands in the residual. It is systematic nuisance that PCA would happily rank first.
OPLS says: keep it, but keep it separate — do not let it contaminate the axis you use to interpret the disease.

Clarify the three-way split that trips people up: predictive (correlated with Y), orthogonal (structured but uncorrelated with Y), and residual (unstructured noise). Orthogonal variation is the star of OPLS’s marketing because it is exactly the batch/physiology structure that plagues omics. The method does not discard it — discarding would be dangerous — it isolates it so the predictive component is clean. Connect to the multiome/integration and chemometrics units where nuisance structure recurs. A good analogy: OPLS is like adjusting for covariates, but the covariates are discovered from the data rather than measured.

title: The OPLS model
text:
The OPLS decomposition
For a single response \(Y\), OPLS factorises \(X\) as
\[X = \underbrace{t_p\, p_p^\top}_{\text{predictive}} \;+\; \underbrace{T_o\, P_o^\top}_{\text{orthogonal}} \;+\; E,\]
and predicts \(Y\) from the predictive score only:
\[\hat Y = t_p\, c + \text{(intercept)}.\]

\(t_p\) — the predictive scores (one per sample): the samples’ position along the \(Y\)-related axis.
\(T_o, P_o\) — orthogonal scores and loadings: the nuisance structure, set aside.
\(E\) — residual.

So a single number per sample, \(t_p\), carries the disease signal; everything Y-irrelevant is elsewhere.


Show the equation but do not derive it — flag it as “light math, for orientation.” The structure to read: X is a sum of a rank-one predictive piece (score vector times loading vector), a multi-component orthogonal piece, and residual. The prediction of Y uses only the predictive score t_p times a scalar c. The pedagogical point is that OPLS collapses “how diseased is this sample” into one coordinate t_p, which is what makes the score plot so readable. Symbols: subscript p = predictive, o = orthogonal. Reassure them the software computes all of this; they need to interpret it.

title: The OPLS model
text:
Reading an OPLS-DA model
The standard plot: predictive score \(t_p\) on the x-axis vs the first orthogonal score \(t_o\) on the y-axis.

Left–right (predictive axis): cases vs controls should separate horizontally.
Up–down (orthogonal axis): spread that is within the biology — batch, individual variation — but does not separate the groups.

To find which metabolites drive the separation, metabolomics often uses an S-plot: for each feature, plot its covariance with \(t_p\) against its correlation with \(t_p\). Features in the extreme corners are the strong, reliable discriminators.


This is how the model is actually consumed. The predictive axis is the interpretable one: group separation lives there, by construction. Orthogonal axes show you the nuisance spread you have quarantined. The S-plot (Wiklund et al., 2008) is a metabolomics staple for biomarker shortlisting: high covariance means the feature contributes a lot (magnitude), high correlation means it does so reliably (low relative noise); the corners have both. Caution students that S-plot “hits” are candidates requiring independent validation, not proven biomarkers — a recurring theme.

title: The OPLS model
text:
When to prefer OPLS



Situation
Reach for




Explore structure, no outcome in mind
PCA


Loudest variation is your biology
PCA is fine


Outcome known; nuisance variation large
PLS / OPLS


Many correlated features, wide matrix (\(p \gg n\))
PLS / OPLS


Want the \(Y\)-signal in one interpretable axis
OPLS




OPLS vs PLS: essentially the same predictive power — OPLS just rotates the solution so interpretation is cleaner (one predictive axis, nuisance set aside).
OPLS vs PCA: use OPLS when you have an outcome and PCA’s top axes are dominated by things you don’t care about.


Give an honest decision guide. Do not oversell OPLS: if you have no Y, it does not apply; if PC1 already captures your biology, PCA is simpler and safer. The key honesty point, and a common misconception to pre-empt: OPLS does NOT predict better than PLS. Same cross-validated performance. The entire benefit is interpretational — the predictive/orthogonal rotation. Wide, collinear omics matrices are the natural habitat for both PLS and OPLS because ordinary least squares regression breaks down when features outnumber samples.

title: The OPLS model
section: The catch: supervision can fit noise
text:
The catch: supervision can fit noise
The moment we let \(Y\) steer the axes, we gain a new danger PCA never had: with thousands of features and dozens of samples, a supervised model can separate the groups even when there is no real difference.

With \(p \gg n\), some linear combination of features will line up with any labelling — including a random one — by chance.
A beautiful case/control separation on the training data can be pure overfitting.


An OPLS-DA score plot that cleanly splits your groups is not, by itself, evidence of a real effect.



This is the single most important warning of the unit and worth dwelling on. Supervision is powerful precisely because it optimises to fit Y — which means it can fit Y even when Y is noise. In the p greater-than-n regime this is almost guaranteed: you can nearly always find a direction separating two arbitrary groups. Students must internalise that a pretty separation plot proves nothing on its own. This directly motivates validation on the next slides, and connects forward to the Cross-validation unit where the machinery is treated properly.

title: The OPLS model
text:
Validate honestly: R², Q²
Two numbers report the model’s fit and its generalisation:

\(R^2\) — variance explained on the data used to fit (\(R^2X\), \(R^2Y\)). Always looks good; rises as you add components.
\(Q^2\) — variance predicted under cross-validation (hold out samples, predict them). This is the honest number.

Healthy model: \(Q^2\) close to \(R^2Y\), both clearly above 0. Warning sign: high \(R^2Y\) but low or negative \(Q^2\) → the model fits the training data but does not generalise — overfitting.


Define the two metrics plainly. R2 is in-sample fit and is optimistic by construction — it never goes down as you add components, so it cannot tell you when to stop. Q2 is the cross-validated analogue: repeatedly leave samples out, predict them, measure how much variance you genuinely capture. The diagnostic gap between a high R2Y and a low or negative Q2 is the fingerprint of overfitting. This is students’ first close look at cross-validation as a guard; the Cross-validation unit builds it out. Rule of thumb only: there is no universal Q2 threshold, it depends on the field and problem.

title: The OPLS model
text:
Validate honestly: the permutation test
The strongest simple check: break the link between \(X\) and \(Y\) on purpose, many times.

Randomly shuffle the class labels \(Y\).
Refit OPLS-DA and record \(R^2Y\) and \(Q^2\).
Repeat hundreds of times to build a null distribution.
Compare your real model against that null.

If the real \(Q^2\) is not clearly better than what shuffled labels achieve, your separation is noise. If it sits far out in the tail, the signal is likely real.


The permutation test is the most intuitive safeguard and worth teaching as a habit. By shuffling Y you destroy any true X-Y relationship while preserving the shapes and sizes of both matrices, so the resulting R2/Q2 values show what this method can achieve on pure chance for data of exactly this dimensionality. Your real model must beat that null convincingly. This is a concrete instance of the general permutation-testing logic; frame it as the same reasoning students may meet elsewhere for significance. Emphasise: in the p greater-than-n regime, always permute — a good-looking plot is not enough.

title: The OPLS model
text:
OPLS in R (sketch)
The Bioconductor package ropls fits PCA, PLS(-DA) and OPLS(-DA) with built-in cross-validation and permutation testing.
library(ropls)

# X: samples x metabolite-features matrix   y: factor (case / control)
model <- opls(X, y,
              predI  = 1,      # 1 predictive component (single response)
              orthoI = NA,     # let CV choose the number of orthogonal comps
              permI  = 200)    # 200 permutations for the validation test

model                 # prints R2X, R2Y, Q2 and the permutation p-values
getScoreMN(model)     # predictive & orthogonal scores  (the score plot)
getLoadingMN(model)   # feature loadings                (which metabolites)
plot(model, typeVn = "x-score")   # the t_p vs t_o score plot
Read the printed \(Q^2\) and permutation p-values before you trust any score plot.

Static code only — nothing runs at render time. ropls is the de facto metabolomics tool (Thevenot et al., 2015) and conveniently bundles the validation we just described. Walk the arguments: predI = 1 because a single response has one predictive component; orthoI = NA lets cross-validation pick the orthogonal count (guarding against adding noise components); permI triggers the permutation test. The deliberate order of the punchline: look at Q2 and the permutation p-value first, plots second. Mention pls as the base-R-adjacent alternative for plain PLS regression, but ropls is the one to know here.

title: The OPLS model
text:
Summary







Idea
Key point




PCA
unsupervised; maximises variance, ignores \(Y\)


PCA pitfall
top axis may be batch/nuisance, not your biology


PLS
supervised; maximises covariance of \(Xw\) with \(Y\)


Scores / loadings
samples’ coordinates / features’ contributions (as in PCA)


OPLS
splits \(X\) into predictive (\(Y\)-correlated) + orthogonal (nuisance)


Predictive score \(t_p\)
one axis carrying the \(Y\)-signal — the interpretable one


OPLS vs PLS
same prediction, cleaner interpretation (a rotation)


Home field
metabolomics — wide, collinear, nuisance-heavy data


The danger
with \(p \gg n\), supervision can separate noise


Honesty
trust \(Q^2\) + permutation test, not a pretty plot



Next (Extra material): Chemometrics applies these latent-variable ideas to spectra.

The summary is the cheat-sheet for the concepts. Drill the arc: PCA maximises variance and is blind to Y; PLS maximises covariance with Y; OPLS re-parameterises PLS to separate predictive from orthogonal variation for interpretability, at no cost or gain in prediction; its home is metabolomics; and the overriding caution is overfitting in the wide-data regime, defended against by Q2 and permutation testing. If they remember only one sentence, make it: a clean supervised separation plot is a hypothesis, not a result. Forward pointers: Chemometrics and Multiome integration reuse these ideas; Cross-validation formalises the validation.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
About this lecture
Modern experiments often measure several kinds of molecule on the same cells or samples — RNA and protein, RNA and chromatin, and so on. Each measurement is a separate matrix, but they describe one biology. Today we learn how to put them into a shared picture.

Why integrate at all: the modalities share biology, and each one is separately noisy.
The setup: matched samples, one matrix per modality, wildly different scales and feature counts.
The key idea: a joint latent space — a few shared axes that all modalities are noisy views of.
Three families of methods, named without heavy math: concatenation-then-PCA, CCA, and MOFA-style shared factors.
Reading the result: which genes and proteins co-vary, and where mRNA and protein disagree.

This is an optional unit under Extra material. It builds directly on Principal component analysis: a latent space is still a small set of directions, found from covariance.

This lecture assumes students have already met PCA (covariance, eigenvectors as axes of variation, loadings and scores). The one new mental move today is: instead of one data matrix, we now have two or more matrices measured on the same samples, and we want a single low-dimensional summary that respects all of them. Keep the maths light — the learning objective is conceptual fluency (what each method tries to do, and what can go wrong), not the derivations of CCA or MOFA. Emphasise repeatedly that “same samples” is the whole premise: the rows of every matrix line up.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
A biology picture first
You run a CITE-seq experiment: for each single cell you measure

its transcriptome — counts for ~20,000 genes (RNA), and
a panel of surface proteins — say 100 antibody-tagged markers.

Two matrices, same cells in the same row order:
\[X_{\text{RNA}}:\ \text{cells} \times 20000, \qquad X_{\text{prot}}:\ \text{cells} \times 100.\]
A T cell is a T cell in both views. The cell types, the activation states, the biology — that shared structure lives in both matrices at once. We want to recover it jointly, not twice.


Anchor everything in one concrete paired assay before any method. CITE-seq (RNA + surface protein) or a true multiome kit (RNA + ATAC) are the canonical examples. The picture to plant: two matrices whose ROWS are the same cells, whose COLUMNS are completely different features. The biology (cell identity, state) is shared and is what we want; it shows up as correlated structure across the two views. Contrast with the wrong alternative: analysing each modality separately and trying to reconcile two independent clusterings afterwards. Integration means finding the shared structure once.

title: Multiome data integration
section: Why integrate: shared biology, separate noise
text:
Why integrate: shared biology, separate noise
Each modality on its own is an incomplete, noisy measurement of the same underlying state.

RNA is deep (thousands of genes) but very sparse and noisy per cell — dropouts, low counts.
Protein panels are shallow (a handful of markers) but often cleaner and closer to function.
The true cell state is not directly observed; each assay is a partial view of it.

Two payoffs from combining them:

Denoising / corroboration — a signal seen in both views is far more trustworthy than one seen in either alone.
Complementarity — protein resolves what RNA cannot (and vice versa); together they separate states neither could alone.



The core justification for integration is statistical: if two noisy measurements share an underlying signal, combining them averages down the independent noise and reinforces the common structure. Make the biology concrete — RNA dropout is severe in single cell, so a gene reading zero may just be unmeasured; a corroborating protein signal rescues it. Complementarity is the second, equally important reason: some distinctions are only visible in one modality (surface protein isotypes, chromatin priming). The goal is a representation richer than either modality alone, not just a tidier version of one.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
The premise: matched samples
Everything today rests on one condition:
\[\text{row } i \text{ of every matrix is the } \textbf{same physical sample}.\]

Same cells (a multiome droplet), or same tumour biopsy split for RNA-seq and proteomics, or same patient.
The columns differ completely: genes in one matrix, proteins in another, and different numbers of them.
This “same rows, different columns” layout is what lets us look for structure that is shared across modalities.

If the samples are not matched (different cells measured by each assay), this is a different problem — you would need anchor-based alignment, not the methods here.


Draw a hard line here. Today’s methods (concatenation-PCA, CCA, MOFA) all require paired observations: the same n samples measured by every modality. This is the “multiome” / “same-sample multi-omics” setting. Contrast explicitly with the un-paired case (two separate experiments on different cells, e.g. an RNA dataset and a separate ATAC dataset) which needs anchor/mutual-nearest-neighbour methods — mention it exists so students do not misapply CCA to unpaired data, but do not teach it. Reassure that bulk multi-omics (same patients, RNA + methylation + proteomics) fits the same paired template.

title: Multiome data integration
section: The obstacle: different scales and sizes
text:
The obstacle: different scales and sizes
The two matrices are not on speaking terms numerically:









RNA
Protein




# features
~20,000
~100


typical values
integer counts, 0–thousands
normalized intensities


total variance
huge (many features)
small (few features)



If we naively glue them together, the modality with more features and bigger numbers dominates everything — the small protein panel becomes invisible.
So before any integration we must put the modalities on a comparable footing: normalize within each modality, then scale each block so no one modality drowns out the others.


This is the practical crux and where naive integration fails silently. Total variance scales with the number of features, so a 20,000-gene block carries orders of magnitude more raw variance than a 100-protein block. Concatenate without scaling and PCA will essentially ignore the protein block. The fix has two stages: (1) modality-appropriate normalisation WITHIN each block (count transforms for RNA, whatever is standard for the protein intensities) — you cannot z-score raw counts meaningfully; (2) block-level scaling so each modality contributes comparably to the joint analysis. Preview that “how to scale a block” is the recurring theme of every method today.

title: Multiome data integration
section: The big idea: a joint latent space
text:
The big idea: a joint latent space
Recall from Principal component analysis: PCA replaces thousands of features with a few latent axes — directions along which samples vary.
For multiome, we want one shared set of latent axes that both modalities express:

each sample gets one set of coordinates (factor scores) in the joint space,
each modality contributes its own loadings — how its features read out along each shared axis.

\[\underbrace{\text{shared factors}}_{\text{same for all modalities}} \;\longrightarrow\; \underbrace{\text{RNA loadings}}_{\text{one per gene}} \;\;\text{and}\;\; \underbrace{\text{protein loadings}}_{\text{one per protein}}.\]
A factor is a piece of biology (a cell type, an activation programme) written in two languages at once.


This is the unifying abstraction that ties all three methods together. In single-modality PCA: scores (per sample) x loadings (per feature). In the joint version: ONE set of scores per sample, but a SEPARATE loading vector per modality — because a shared factor “cell is a T cell” manifests as particular genes AND particular proteins. This factor/loading language is exactly MOFA’s, and it is the cleanest way to think about all the methods. Stress that the factor is latent (unobserved biology) and the loadings are how we interpret it back in measurable features. This slide is the conceptual centre of the lecture.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
Approach 1: concatenate, then PCA
The simplest idea: paste the blocks side by side into one wide matrix, then run ordinary PCA.
\[X = [\,X_{\text{RNA}}\ \;|\;\ X_{\text{prot}}\,] \quad\text{(same rows, columns stacked)}\]

After per-modality normalization and block-scaling, this can work well.
The PCs are shared axes; loadings split naturally into a gene part and a protein part.

Danger: without block-scaling, the big modality dominates and the PCs are essentially just RNA PCs — the protein panel contributes nothing.
# static illustration — not executed
Xr <- scale(rna)                       # normalize/standardize RNA block
Xp <- scale(prot)                      # normalize/standardize protein block
Xr <- Xr / sqrt(sum(Xr^2))             # block-scale: equalize total variance
Xp <- Xp / sqrt(sum(Xp^2))
X  <- cbind(Xr, Xp)                    # concatenate: same cells, all features
pc <- prcomp(X)                        # joint latent space = the PCs


Start with the method they can already fully understand, since it is just PCA on a glued matrix. The entire subtlety is the pre-processing: normalise each block, then divide each block by its Frobenius norm (or its first singular value, as Multiple Factor Analysis does) so the blocks contribute equally. Point out that cbind is trivially valid ONLY because rows are matched. The honest limitation: concatenation-PCA treats all features as one pool and has no explicit notion of “shared vs modality-specific” variation — it cannot tell you a factor is protein-only. That motivates the next two methods. Keep the code static; nothing is installed at render time.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
Approach 2: canonical correlation (CCA)
Turn the question around: instead of maximizing variance, maximize agreement between the modalities.
CCA finds a direction in RNA space and a direction in protein space whose sample scores are maximally correlated:
\[\text{find } \mathbf a,\mathbf b \ \text{ maximizing } \ \operatorname{corr}\big(X_{\text{RNA}}\mathbf a,\ X_{\text{prot}}\mathbf b\big).\]

Each canonical pair is a shared axis defined by being consistent across modalities.
By construction it emphasizes the common signal and downweights modality-specific noise.

Caveat: with more features than samples (always, in omics) plain CCA overfits — practical versions are regularized / sparse (e.g. the PMA package’s sparse CCA).


CCA reframes integration as: find the linear combination of genes and the linear combination of proteins that move together across cells. The output is pairs of canonical variates with a canonical correlation each. Its philosophy differs from concatenation-PCA: PCA asks “where is the variance”, CCA asks “where do the modalities agree”. That makes CCA naturally robust to modality-specific noise but blind to modality-specific SIGNAL. The must-say caveat: with p >> n (thousands of features, hundreds of cells) the sample correlation can be driven to 1 spuriously, so real applications use sparse/regularised CCA. Note Seurat’s older integration used a CCA variant — good name-drop, but keep it a name.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
Approach 3: MOFA-style shared factors
The most general framing, and the one matching our “joint latent space” picture directly.
MOFA (Multi-Omics Factor Analysis) learns a small set of factors such that each modality is approximately
\[X_{\text{modality}} \approx \underbrace{Z}_{\text{shared factor scores}} \; \underbrace{W_{\text{modality}}}_{\text{modality loadings}} \;+\; \text{noise}.\]

One score matrix \(Z\) (samples × factors), shared by all modalities.
A separate loading matrix per modality — so a factor can be active in some modalities and silent in others.
Handles more than two modalities, missing data, and different noise models per block.

Think of it as PCA generalized to several matrices at once, with the honesty to say “this factor is protein-only.”


MOFA is the cleanest realisation of the factor/loading abstraction from the central slide, so present it as the natural destination. Key selling points over the first two methods: (1) explicit shared score matrix Z with per-modality loadings, so factors are directly interpretable; (2) a factor can load on one modality and not another, which neither concatenation-PCA nor two-block CCA expresses cleanly — this is how MOFA distinguishes shared biology from modality-specific biology; (3) it scales to many modalities and tolerates missing samples in some blocks. Frame it honestly as (approximately) group factor analysis / a probabilistic matrix factorisation — do not overclaim mechanism. It is a Bioconductor/Python tool (MOFA2); students call it, they do not implement it.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
The three at a glance









Method
Optimizes
Shared object
Sees modality-specific signal?




Concatenation + PCA
total variance of the glued matrix
principal components
no (one feature pool)


CCA
correlation between modalities
canonical variate pairs
no (only the agreement)


MOFA-style factors
reconstruction of each block
factor scores \(Z\) + per-block loadings
yes (per-factor activity)



All three produce a joint latent space — a few shared coordinates per sample — and all three require per-modality normalization and block-scaling first.

This is the summary table students should carry away. The distinguishing axis is what each method optimises and whether it can represent modality-specific structure. Reinforce the common denominator: every method reduces to “give each sample a handful of shared coordinates”, and every method breaks without the pre-processing from the scales/sizes slide. If a student remembers only one comparison, make it: PCA = variance, CCA = cross-modal correlation, MOFA = per-block reconstruction with shared factors.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
Reading the result: co-varying features
A joint factor is only useful once you interpret its loadings back into biology.
For a given factor, look at its top-loading features in each modality together:

genes with large loadings and proteins with large loadings on the same factor are co-varying — they rise and fall across samples in step.
Concordant example: the CD3 genes and the CD3 surface protein both load high on the “T-cell” factor — RNA and protein agree.

That agreement is the biological signal you trusted because it appears in both languages of the same factor.
# static illustration: features co-varying on factor 1
head( sort(loadings_rna[ , 1],  decreasing = TRUE) )   # top genes on factor 1
head( sort(loadings_prot[, 1],  decreasing = TRUE) )   # top proteins on factor 1


Interpretation is where the biology comes back. A factor is a direction; its meaning is read from which features load on it. The powerful move in multiome: line up the top RNA loadings and top protein loadings for the SAME factor. When a gene and its protein product both load strongly (CD3 mRNA and CD3 protein on a T-cell factor), you have cross-modal corroboration — the concordance case. Keep the R static and schematic; the point is the workflow (sort loadings per modality, compare across modalities on a shared factor), not a runnable pipeline.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
When mRNA and protein disagree
The more interesting cases are the discordant ones.

mRNA and protein levels correlate only modestly — post-transcriptional regulation, translation rate, and protein degradation all intervene.
A factor may load strongly on a protein but barely on its mRNA (or vice versa).

Biologically that discordance is a finding, not a nuisance:

surface protein present without high mRNA → protein is stable / long-lived, or already translated and the transcript has decayed,
high mRNA without protein → translational repression or rapid protein turnover.

Multiome integration makes these mismatches visible and quantifiable — something neither assay alone can do.


This slide is the biological payoff and a genuine research use of integration. The empirical fact: across genes, steady-state mRNA and protein abundance correlate only moderately (well documented across many systems) because protein level is set by translation and degradation as well as transcription. So a shared-factor model that puts mRNA and protein on the same axes lets you spot where they part ways. Give the two directions of discordance and their standard interpretations (protein stability / transcript decay vs translational repression / protein turnover). Frame discordance as signal — it is only detectable because the modalities are matched and jointly modelled.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
Caveats and failure modes

Normalize within each modality first. Counts, intensities, and peak accessibilities each need their own appropriate transform — you cannot treat them as one homogeneous table.
Block-scale so total variance is comparable; otherwise the biggest block dominates (the recurring trap).
Different dimensionalities (\(p\) differs wildly per modality) — a raw feature count is not a fair vote.
Batch effects live in each modality separately; integration does not automatically remove them.
Correlation is not mechanism — co-varying features share an axis; that is a hypothesis, not a proven regulatory link.


The consolidated warning list. The first two are the ones that actually bite in practice and have appeared throughout the lecture: modality-appropriate normalisation, then block-scaling. Add three more mature cautions: (1) unequal feature counts mean naive concatenation over-weights the large block even after per-feature standardisation, hence block-scaling; (2) batch/technical effects are per-modality and integration will happily carry them into the joint space unless corrected first; (3) the usual correlation-vs-causation discipline — a shared factor is a co-variation hypothesis. Tie back to the course’s habit of stating assumptions honestly.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
A minimal workflow in R
Putting the pieces together (schematic, base R for the simple route):
# 1. normalize WITHIN each modality (modality-appropriate transforms)
Xr <- scale(log1p(rna_counts))     # RNA: log-transform counts, then standardize
Xp <- scale(prot_intensity)        # protein: standardize its own values

# 2. block-scale so neither modality dominates the joint space
Xr <- Xr / sqrt(sum(Xr^2))
Xp <- Xp / sqrt(sum(Xp^2))

# 3a. simplest joint space: concatenate + PCA
joint <- prcomp(cbind(Xr, Xp))     # scores in joint$x, loadings in joint$rotation

# 3b. cross-modal agreement instead: canonical correlation
cc <- cancor(Xr, Xp)               # base-R CCA (use sparse CCA for real p >> n data)
For production multi-omics with many modalities, missing data, and interpretable per-block loadings, reach for MOFA2 (Bioconductor) rather than rolling your own.

One consolidated, static workflow so students see the pipeline end to end: normalise each block, block-scale each block, then either concatenate+PCA or CCA. Point out cancor exists in base R but overfits with p >> n, so it is a teaching tool not a production one — sparse CCA (PMA) or MOFA2 is the real route. The message: the easy route is a few lines they already understand from PCA; the hard parts are all in the pre-processing and interpretation, not the linear algebra. Nothing here runs at render time; it is illustrative.

title: Multiome data integration
text:
Summary







Idea
Key point




Premise
matched samples — same rows, different columns per modality


Why
shared biology, independent noise → corroborate and complement


Pre-processing
normalize within each modality, then block-scale


Joint latent space
one set of shared factor scores; per-modality loadings


Concatenation + PCA
glue blocks, run PCA — simplest; needs block-scaling


CCA
maximize cross-modal correlation; regularize when \(p \gg n\)


MOFA-style factors
shared \(Z\) + per-block loadings; factors can be modality-specific


Interpretation
co-varying genes/proteins = concordance; mismatch = discordance signal



Builds on Principal component analysis; the shared-factor view generalizes it to several matrices measured on the same samples.

The takeaway sheet. Drill the through-line one more time: matched samples make integration possible; normalisation + block-scaling make it fair; a joint latent space (shared scores, per-modality loadings) makes it interpretable; and the three method families trade off variance vs cross-modal correlation vs per-block reconstruction. End on the biology: concordance corroborates, discordance is a discovery. Reconnect to PCA as the foundation students already own — everything today is PCA-thinking extended to several matrices at once.

title: Matrices as transformations
text:
About this lecture
In Vectors, dot product & projection a vector was a point/arrow (a sample). Today we learn what a matrix does to vectors.

A matrix is a function that maps vectors to vectors.
The matrix–vector product \(A\mathbf{x}\) is a linear combination of the columns of \(A\) — and each output entry is a dot product (the tool from Vectors, dot product & projection).
Special transformations: identity, scaling, rotation.
Composing two transformations = multiplying their matrices.
All of it in R with %*%.

This is a hands-on R walkthrough day: follow along, run every block, and watch points move.

The mental shift today: stop seeing a matrix as a static grid of numbers and start seeing it as a verb — something that DOES things to vectors. Everything connects back to Vectors, dot product & projection: matrix-vector multiplication is just a stack of dot products. This day is deliberately R-heavy; tell students to keep an R session open and reproduce each transformation, ideally plotting the before/after points.

title: Matrices as transformations
section: A matrix is a function on vectors
text:
A matrix is a function on vectors
A function takes an input and returns an output. A matrix takes a vector in and gives a vector out:
\[\mathbf{x} \ \longrightarrow\ A\mathbf{x}\]
Example — take a 2-D point and transform it: \[A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \ \Rightarrow\ A\mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}\]

Here \(A\) stretches the x-axis by 2 and the y-axis by 3.
Think of \(A\) acting on every sample point at once — a uniform operation applied to a whole dataset.



Frame the matrix as a verb / machine from the very first slide. Input vector, output vector. The diagonal scaling example is the gentlest possible: each axis stretched independently. Stress “the same matrix is applied to every sample identically” — that is what makes it a transformation of the whole dataset, e.g. a normalisation or a coordinate change.

title: Matrices as transformations
text:
How to multiply \(A\mathbf{x}\) by hand
Each output entry is the dot product of a matrix row with \(\mathbf{x}\):
\[\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} ax + by \\ cx + dy \end{pmatrix}\]
Worked example: \[\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1\cdot3 + 2\cdot4 \\ 0\cdot3 + 1\cdot4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 11 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}\]

Row 1 of \(A\) dotted with \(\mathbf{x}\) → first output entry.
Row 2 of \(A\) dotted with \(\mathbf{x}\) → second output entry.



This connects directly to Vectors, dot product & projection: the matrix-vector product is literally a stack of dot products, one per row. Make students compute the (11, 4) example by hand on the spot. The “row dot vector” recipe is the single most important manual skill from this block for the written exam.

title: Matrices as transformations
text:
The same product, columns view
There is a second, equally important way to read \(A\mathbf{x}\): as a linear combination of the columns of \(A\), weighted by the entries of \(\mathbf{x}\).
\[\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = 3\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + 4\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 11 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}\]

“3 units of column 1, plus 4 units of column 2.”
This view explains why the output can only ever be a blend of the columns — the column space.



The columns view is conceptually deeper than the rows view and pays off later (column space, rank, PCA loadings). Same answer (11,4), different story: the input vector’s entries are mixing weights for the columns. Both views are worth memorising; rows are easier for hand computation, columns are better for understanding what outputs are reachable.

title: Matrices as transformations
text:
Matrix–vector product in R
A <- matrix(c(1, 2,
              0, 1), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
x <- c(3, 4)
A %*% x
#      [,1]
# [1,]   11
# [2,]    4

%*% is matrix multiplication. Plain * would be elementwise — wrong here.
byrow = TRUE fills the matrix row by row, so it matches how we write it on paper. (Default is column by column!)


The single most common beginner mistake: using * instead of %*%. Hammer this. Also flag the byrow trap: matrix() fills columns first by default, which silently transposes your matrix relative to what you wrote on paper. Recommend byrow = TRUE while learning, and always print the matrix to confirm.

title: Matrices as transformations
text:
The identity matrix — “do nothing”
\[I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad I\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x} \ \text{for every } \mathbf{x}\]
The identity leaves every vector unchanged — the matrix version of multiplying by 1.
I <- diag(2)      # 2x2 identity
I
#      [,1] [,2]
# [1,]    1    0
# [2,]    0    1
I %*% c(3, 4)     # 3 4  (unchanged)

The identity is the reference point for all transformations: it does nothing. diag(2) builds it in R. Later (eigenvalues, solving systems) the identity is everywhere, so introduce it now while it is trivial. Mention that diag() with a vector argument instead makes a scaling matrix — the next slide.

title: Matrices as transformations
text:
Scaling matrices
A diagonal matrix stretches each axis independently:
\[S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix} \ \Rightarrow\ \text{double the x-axis, halve the y-axis}\]
S <- diag(c(2, 0.5))
pts <- matrix(c(1, 1,
                2, 0,
                0, 3), nrow = 2)   # 3 points as COLUMNS
S %*% pts
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    2    4  0.0    # x doubled
# [2,]  0.5    0  1.5    # y halved

Putting samples in columns lets one %*% transform the whole dataset at once.
Biology: this is exactly a per-axis normalisation / rescaling of features.



Scaling is the most intuitive non-trivial transformation. The key practical pattern is on this slide: store your samples as columns, then a single S %*% data transforms every sample simultaneously. Connect to normalisation — rescaling each feature (gene) by a constant is a diagonal matrix multiply. Watch the dimensions: S is 2x2, data is 2x3, output is 2x3.

title: Matrices as transformations
text:
Rotation matrices
To rotate every point by angle \(\theta\) (counter-clockwise) about the origin:
\[R(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}\]
theta <- pi/2                       # 90 degrees
R <- matrix(c(cos(theta), -sin(theta),
              sin(theta),  cos(theta)), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
round(R %*% c(1, 0))                # 0 1  -> x-axis rotates onto y-axis

A rotation changes direction but never length (it is rigid).
The columns of \(R\) are where the old axes land — a recurring theme.



Rotation introduces a transformation that mixes the axes (off-diagonal entries). The check round(R %*% c(1,0)) == c(0,1) makes the geometry tangible: the x-axis swings up onto the y-axis under a 90-degree turn. Emphasise that rotations preserve length and angles — useful intuition for later when we talk about orthogonal matrices and PCA’s rotation of the data cloud.

title: Matrices as transformations
section: Reading the columns of a transformation
text:
Reading the columns of a transformation
The columns of any matrix \(A\) tell you where the standard axes go:
\[A = \begin{pmatrix} \color{red}{a} & \color{blue}{b} \\ \color{red}{c} & \color{blue}{d} \end{pmatrix}\]

\(A\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix} = \color{red}{(a,c)}\) → first column = image of the x-axis unit vector.
\(A\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix} = \color{blue}{(b,d)}\) → second column = image of the y-axis unit vector.

To design a transformation: decide where the axes should land, then write those as the columns.


This is a powerful shortcut and a frequent exam question: to understand or build a matrix, just ask where the unit axes go. Multiplying A by (1,0) selects column 1; by (0,1) selects column 2. This reframes “what does this matrix do?” as “look at its columns”, and reframes “build a matrix that does X” as “place the target axis images in the columns”.

title: Matrices as transformations
section: Bonus: the determinant is an area (not for exam)
text:
Bonus: the determinant is an area (not for exam)
The two columns of \(A\) span a parallelogram: the image of the unit square. Its area is the determinant \(\det A = ad - bc\).


\(\lvert \det A \rvert\): how much \(A\) scales areas (here 3 times).
Sign: negative means the picture is flipped (the turn from column 1 to column 2 goes clockwise).
Zero: the columns are parallel, so everything collapses onto a line, and \(A\) cannot be undone.

det(matrix(c(2, 1,
             1, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE))   # 3
Bonus material: you do not need to memorise determinants for the exam.

Bonus slide: not examined. It gives a picture for a number that otherwise looks like an arbitrary formula. Middle panel: the same columns as the left panel, swapped, so the same parallelogram, but the turn from red to blue is now clockwise, and the determinant changes sign. Right panel: column 2 is half of column 1, so the “parallelogram” is a line segment with area 0. This is the singular case from Linear systems: no inverse. It comes back in Transforming images with matrices (the gallery), and the formula ad - bc is used again in Eigenvalues & eigenvectors.

title: Matrices as transformations
text:
Composing transformations = multiplying matrices
Do \(B\), then \(A\). Applied to \(\mathbf{x}\): first \(B\mathbf{x}\), then \(A(B\mathbf{x}) = (AB)\mathbf{x}\).
So composition is matrix multiplication, and \(AB\) means “apply \(B\) first, then \(A\)” — right to left.
\[AB:\quad (AB)_{ij} = (\text{row } i \text{ of } A)\cdot(\text{column } j \text{ of } B)\]
A <- matrix(c(2,0, 0,1), 2, byrow = TRUE)   # scale x by 2
B <- matrix(c(0,-1, 1,0), 2, byrow = TRUE)  # rotate 90 deg
A %*% B          # rotate THEN scale
B %*% A          # scale THEN rotate -- NOT the same!

Order matters: \(AB \neq BA\) in general. (Try both above.)



Composition is the reason matrix multiplication is defined the way it is — each entry is a row-dot-column, the dot product from Vectors, dot product & projection again. The crucial cautionary point: matrix multiplication is NOT commutative, so the ORDER of operations matters, and AB applies the rightmost matrix first. Demonstrate A%%B vs B%%A giving different results live.

title: Matrices as transformations
text:
Try it: drag the columns




Live recap of the whole lecture in one picture. It starts at the first example, A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]] and x = (1, 1), so Ax = (2, 3). The red and blue handles are the columns of A: drag them and the grid, the unit square and the house follow, because every point is “x times column 1 plus y times column 2” (the dashed red and blue path to the green Ax). Click through the presets: Identity, Scale, Rotate 90°, Shear, Reflect (the door jumps to the other side: a mirror image), Project and Collapse (columns on one line: the plane flattens onto a line). Drag x to show the columns view of Ax. The area line is a bonus aside only. Then switch to “Order: AB vs BA”: A = scale x by 2, B = rotate 90°, the example from the previous slide. Left panel: B first, then A; right panel: A first, then B. Different houses, so AB ≠ BA. Try “Swap”, and try two rotations (Rotate 90° and Rotate 30°): rotations happen to commute.

title: Matrices as transformations
section: Putting it together: transform a small dataset
text:
Putting it together: transform a small dataset
# 4 sample points (2 features each) stored as COLUMNS
data <- matrix(c( 1, 0,
                  0, 1,
                 -1, 0,
                  0,-1), nrow = 2)

theta <- pi/4
R <- matrix(c(cos(theta), -sin(theta),
              sin(theta),  cos(theta)), 2, byrow = TRUE)
S <- diag(c(2, 1))

out <- S %*% (R %*% data)   # rotate 45 deg, then stretch x by 2
round(out, 2)

plot(t(data), xlim=c(-3,3), ylim=c(-3,3), pch=19)   # before (rows = points)
points(t(out), col = "red", pch = 19)               # after
One %*% chain applies the whole pipeline to every sample at once.


This capstone block is what students should reproduce and stare at: a rotation then a scaling applied to a little square of points, plotted before (black) and after (red). Note the transpose t() in plot() because plot expects points as ROWS but we stored them as columns for the math. This “columns for math, transpose for plotting” pattern recurs throughout the course.

title: Matrices as transformations
section: Design / contrast matrices: a biology aside
text:
Design / contrast matrices: a biology aside
In differential-expression analysis (e.g. limma, DESeq2) a design matrix \(X\) encodes which samples are control vs treated. The model is
\[\mathbf{y} \approx X\boldsymbol\beta\]

\(X\) is a matrix that maps coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta\) (e.g. baseline, treatment effect) to predicted expression \(\mathbf{y}\).
Same machinery as today: a matrix takes one vector and produces another, as a linear combination of its columns.

You will not build these by hand in this course — but recognise that the matrix-as-transformation idea is exactly what powers the statistics you already use.

This slide grounds the abstraction in tools the students likely already touch. A design matrix is just a transformation mapping effect sizes to expected measurements; fitting the model is “solving” that relationship (Linear systems by hand and Linear systems in R). The aim is recognition, not mastery: when they next see model.matrix() output, they should think “ah, a transformation, columns are the predictors”.
