title: Exercise: error models — exponential & Poisson
text:
Background
A measurement is signal plus noise. The error model is the probability distribution you assume the data came from given the truth; read as a function of the parameters, it is the likelihood (the same likelihood that feeds Bayes’ theorem in the prior, likelihood and posterior unit).
The four distributions of this unit:









Data type
Distribution
Mean
Variance




Continuous, symmetric
Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\)
\(\mu\)
\(\sigma^2\) (independent of \(\mu\))


Counts (idealised)
Poisson\((\lambda)\)
\(\lambda\)
\(\lambda\)


Waiting times / gaps
Exponential\((\lambda)\)
\(1/\lambda\)
\(1/\lambda^2\)


Overdispersed counts
Negative binomial\((\mu,\phi)\)
\(\mu\)
\(\mu + \phi\mu^2\)



Key formulas:
\[P_{\text{Pois}}(X=k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}, \qquad f_{\text{Exp}}(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}, \qquad P_{\text{Exp}}(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}.\]
Poisson process: one stream of random events at rate \(\lambda\). The number in a fixed window is Poisson\((\lambda)\); the waiting time to the next event is Exponential\((\lambda)\).
Overdispersion: real biological counts have variance > mean, because the true rate varies between replicates. The negative binomial adds a dispersion parameter to absorb this (\(\phi = 0\) recovers Poisson).

title: Exercise: error models — exponential & Poisson
text:
By hand
B1. For each dataset, name the error model you would use and give the one-line reason: (a) cell diameters in micrometres; (b) reads mapped to a gene across 5 technical replicates; (c) time between neuronal spikes; (d) reads per gene across 5 biological replicates (different mice).
B2. A gene has an average of \(\lambda = 2\) reads per sample under a Poisson model. Compute \(P(X=0)\), \(P(X=1)\), and \(P(X=2)\) by hand. What is \(P(X \ge 1)\)?
B3. For a Poisson\((\lambda)\), state the mean and the variance. A colleague reports count data with sample mean \(\approx 20\) and sample variance \(\approx 210\). Is Poisson an adequate error model? What does the discrepancy tell you, and which distribution should they use instead?
B4. Mutations occur along a genome at rate \(\lambda = 0.5\) per megabase, modelled as a Poisson process. (a) What is the expected waiting distance to the next mutation? (b) What is \(P(\text{no mutation in the next 2 Mb})\)? (Two equivalent routes: the exponential survival \(e^{-\lambda t}\), or the Poisson probability of zero events in a window of length 2.)
B5. A negative binomial has \(\text{Var}(X) = \mu + \phi\mu^2\). For \(\mu = 50\): (a) what is the variance when \(\phi = 0\), and what distribution is that? (b) what is the variance when \(\phi = 0.5\)? (c) A Poisson-based test analyses these \(\phi = 0.5\) data. Will its p-values be too large or too small, and does that inflate false positives or false negatives?
B6. True or false, with one line of reasoning each: (a) “A Gaussian is fine for counts as long as the mean is large.” (b) “If counts are Poisson, plotting sample variance against sample mean across many genes should fall near the line \(y = x\).” (c) “The exponential distribution can produce negative waiting times.”
B7. (waiting-time flavour) A DNA-binding protein has a dwell time on its site that is exponential with mean \(4\) seconds. (a) What is the rate \(\lambda\)? (b) What is \(P(\text{dwell} > 4\text{ s})\)? (c) Given it has already stayed 4 s, what is the probability it stays at least 4 s more — and what property does your answer illustrate?

title: Exercise: error models — exponential & Poisson
text:
Explore
Do B3 and B5 by hand first. The demo draws 1000 counts from a negative binomial with mean \(\mu\) and dispersion \(\phi\), in this unit’s convention \(\text{Var}(X) = \mu + \phi\mu^2\). The bars are the simulated counts, the red dots the NB probabilities, and the dashed blue outline the Poisson with the same mean.



E1. At \(\mu = 50\), read the theoretical variance for \(\phi = 0.5\), then click Poisson. Do the numbers match your B5 answers? What happens to the histogram and the dashed outline when \(\phi = 0\)?
E2. Back at \(\phi = 0.5\), click draw again a few times. Compare the sample mean and sample variance with theory. Which of the two jumps around more?
E3. Click low mean (\(\mu = 3\)), then step through Poisson, mild overdispersion and strong (many zeros). How many of the 1000 cells have a zero count in each case? What happens to the mean?
E4. Set \(\phi = 0.1\) and move \(\mu\) through 5, 50 and 500. Read var/mean each time (tick mean–variance plot to see it on log axes). Then find the \(\phi\) whose variance at \(\mu = 20\) is closest to the colleague’s 210 in B3.






Solutions





E1. \(\phi = 0.5\): \(50 + 0.5\cdot 50^2 = 1300\). \(\phi = 0\): variance \(= 50\), var/mean \(= 1\): the Poisson (B5a–b). At \(\phi = 0\) the histogram falls on the dashed Poisson outline.
E2. The first draw gives a sample mean of 50.0 and a sample variance of about 1390 (theory 50 and 1300); further draws (about 1280, 1200, 1250) move by a hundred or more, while the sample means stay within about 1 of 50. Variances are harder to estimate than means, especially for overdispersed counts, which is why tools like DESeq2 share dispersion information across genes.
E3. With \(\mu = 3\) (first draw): Poisson gives 49 zeros (theory \(1000\,e^{-3} \approx 50\)); mild overdispersion (\(\phi = 0.1\)) 69; strong (\(\phi = 2\)) 368, more than a third of all cells (theory \(1000\,(1+\phi\mu)^{-1/\phi} \approx 378\)). The theoretical mean stays at 3 throughout (the sample means stay close to it): the NB moves probability both to zero and to a long right tail.
E4. With \(\phi = 0.1\): var/mean \(= 1 + \phi\mu\) is 1.5 at \(\mu = 5\), 6 at \(\mu = 50\) and 51 at \(\mu = 500\); on log axes the NB curve peels away from the line var \(= \mu\) as \(\mu\) grows. At \(\mu = 20\), \(210 = 20 + 400\,\phi\) gives \(\phi \approx 0.48\); the slider’s \(\phi = 0.5\) (variance 220) is closest, so the data in B3 are clearly overdispersed.

title: Exercise: error models — exponential & Poisson
text:
In R
Use R to confirm your hand answers and to see the distributions. These are static illustrations; run them in your own session.

Poisson probabilities and the mean = variance identity
lambda <- 2
dpois(0:3, lambda)          # P(X=0..3);  P(0)=e^-2 ~ 0.135
1 - dpois(0, lambda)        # P(X>=1) = 1 - P(0)

x <- rpois(1e5, lambda)     # simulate
mean(x); var(x)             # both ~ 2  ->  mean = variance


Exponential waiting times
lambda <- 0.5               # events per Mb
pexp(2, rate = lambda, lower.tail = FALSE)  # P(T > 2) = e^{-1} ~ 0.368
mean(rexp(1e5, rate = lambda))  # ~ 2 = 1/lambda

# same process, counted per 2-Mb window: Poisson(lambda * 2) = Poisson(1)
dpois(0, lambda * 2)        # P(0 events in 2 Mb) = e^{-1}  -> matches


Poisson vs negative binomial: same mean, different spread
mu <- 50
mean(rpois(1e5, mu));            var(rpois(1e5, mu))            # ~50, ~50
# R uses 'size' = 1/phi;  Var = mu + mu^2/size
mean(rnbinom(1e5, mu = mu, size = 2)); var(rnbinom(1e5, mu = mu, size = 2))  # ~50, >>50


Tasks
R1. Confirm your B2 hand probabilities with dpois(0:2, 2), and check 1 - dpois(0, 2) against your \(P(X \ge 1)\).
R2. For B3, simulate x <- rpois(1e5, 20) and report mean(x) and var(x). Then simulate overdispersed counts with rnbinom(1e5, mu = 20, size = 4) and report its variance. Which one resembles the colleague’s data (mean \(\approx 20\), variance \(\approx 210\))? (Recall \(\text{Var} = \mu + \mu^2/\text{size}\).)
R3. For B4, verify both routes agree: pexp(2, rate = 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE) (exponential survival) and dpois(0, 0.5 * 2) (Poisson zero-count). They should give the same number.

title: Exercise: error models — exponential & Poisson
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — picking the distribution (B1, B6)





Ask two questions in order. First: continuous or a count? Continuous symmetric measurements \(\to\) Gaussian; continuous non-negative waiting times \(\to\) exponential; counts \(\to\) Poisson or negative binomial. Second, for counts: technical/idealised or biological replicates? Biological replicates are almost always overdispersed (variance > mean) \(\to\) negative binomial.









Hint 2 — Poisson probabilities (B2)





Use \(P(X=k) = \dfrac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}\) with \(\lambda = 2\). Note \(0! = 1! = 1\) and \(2! = 2\). For “at least one”, use the complement: \(P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - e^{-\lambda}\). See dpois.









Hint 3 — the mean = variance diagnostic (B3)





Poisson forces \(\text{Var} = \text{mean}\). If the sample variance is much bigger than the sample mean, the data are overdispersed and Poisson understates the noise. The fix is the negative binomial, whose variance \(\mu + \phi\mu^2\) can exceed the mean.









Hint 4 — exponential vs Poisson for the same process (B4)





For a Poisson process at rate \(\lambda\): the count in a window of length \(t\) is Poisson\((\lambda t)\), and the waiting distance to the next event is Exponential\((\lambda)\). “No event in length \(t\)” can be read either as the exponential survival \(P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}\) or as the Poisson zero-count \(P(X=0) = e^{-\lambda t}\) over that window — same number. See pexp and dpois.









Hint 5 — negative binomial variance (B5)





Plug into \(\text{Var} = \mu + \phi\mu^2\). In R the parameter is size \(= 1/\phi\), so \(\text{Var} = \mu + \mu^2/\text{size}\). A test that assumes less variance than the truth makes p-values too small (overconfident), which produces false positives. See rnbinom.









Hint 6 — memorylessness (B7)





Mean of an exponential is \(1/\lambda\), so \(\lambda = 1/\text{mean}\). The survival function is \(P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}\). Memorylessness means \(P(T > s + t \mid T > s) = P(T > t)\) — the past waiting does not matter, so the “already waited 4 s” answer equals the plain \(P(T > 4)\).

title: Exercise: error models — exponential & Poisson
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. (a) Gaussian — cell diameters are continuous and roughly symmetric; mean and variance are separate. (b) Poisson — reads are counts; across technical replicates the rate is essentially fixed, so variance \(\approx\) mean is plausible. (c) Exponential — a time between events in a stream (spikes), continuous and non-negative. (d) Negative binomial — reads are counts, but biological replicates (different mice) vary in their true rate, so the data are overdispersed (variance > mean).
B2. With \(\lambda = 2\): \[P(0) = \frac{2^0 e^{-2}}{0!} = e^{-2} \approx 0.135, \quad P(1) = \frac{2^1 e^{-2}}{1!} = 2e^{-2} \approx 0.271, \quad P(2) = \frac{2^2 e^{-2}}{2!} = 2e^{-2} \approx 0.271.\] \(P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(0) = 1 - e^{-2} \approx 0.865\).
B3. For Poisson\((\lambda)\) the mean and variance are both \(\lambda\). The colleague’s variance (\(\approx 210\)) is about ten times the mean (\(\approx 20\)), so \(\text{Var} \gg \text{mean}\): the data are overdispersed and Poisson is not adequate — it would badly understate the noise. The discrepancy signals extra variation in the rate between samples (biological variability). They should use the negative binomial. (Here \(\mu + \phi\mu^2 = 210\) with \(\mu = 20\) gives \(\phi \approx 0.475\), i.e. size \(= 1/\phi \approx 2.1\).)
B4. Rate \(\lambda = 0.5\) per Mb. (a) Expected waiting distance \(= 1/\lambda = 1/0.5 = **2\) Mb. (b) \(P(\text{no mutation in 2 Mb})\). Exponential route: \(P(T > 2) = e^{-\lambda \cdot 2} = e^{-0.5 \cdot 2} = e^{-1} \approx 0.368\). Poisson route: events in a 2-Mb window are Poisson\((\lambda \cdot 2) = \text{Poisson}(1)\), so \(P(0) = \frac{1^0 e^{-1}}{0!} = e^{-1} \approx 0.368\). Same answer**, as they must be for one Poisson process.
B5. \(\text{Var} = \mu + \phi\mu^2\), \(\mu = 50\). (a) \(\phi = 0\): \(\text{Var} = 50 + 0 = 50\); variance equals the mean, so this is the Poisson. (b) \(\phi = 0.5\): \(\text{Var} = 50 + 0.5 \cdot 50^2 = 50 + 0.5 \cdot 2500 = 50 + 1250 = **1300\)** — far above the mean. (c) The Poisson test assumes variance \(= 50\) but the truth is \(1300\); assuming too little noise makes the test overconfident, so p-values are too small. That inflates false positives (Type I errors) — you call noise as differential expression.
B6. (a) False. A Gaussian still allows negative and fractional values and, more importantly, assumes variance is independent of the mean; for counts the variance grows with the mean, and biological counts are overdispersed. (For very large means a Gaussian approximation can be workable after care with the variance, but “just use Gaussian” is not a fix.) (b) True. Poisson forces \(\text{Var} = \text{mean}\), so a mean-variance plot across genes should scatter around the line \(y = x\). Systematic points above \(y = x\) are the signature of overdispersion. (c) False. The exponential is defined only for \(t \ge 0\); waiting times cannot be negative.
B7. Exponential dwell time, mean \(4\) s. (a) \(\lambda = 1/\text{mean} = 1/4 = 0.25\text{ s}^{-1}\). (b) \(P(\text{dwell} > 4) = e^{-\lambda \cdot 4} = e^{-0.25 \cdot 4} = e^{-1} \approx 0.368\). (c) By memorylessness, \(P(T > 4 + 4 \mid T > 4) = P(T > 4) = e^{-1} \approx 0.368\) — the same as (b). The protein “does not age”: having already stayed 4 s tells you nothing about the remaining dwell time.
R1.
dpois(0:2, 2)        # 0.1353 0.2707 0.2707  -> matches B2
1 - dpois(0, 2)      # 0.8647               -> matches P(X>=1)
R2.
x <- rpois(1e5, 20)
mean(x); var(x)                       # ~20, ~20  (variance = mean)

y <- rnbinom(1e5, mu = 20, size = 4)  # Var = 20 + 20^2/4 = 20 + 100 = 120
mean(y); var(y)                       # ~20, ~120
The Poisson gives variance \(\approx 20\); the negative binomial with size = 4 gives variance \(\approx 120\). Neither exactly matches the colleague’s variance of \(210\) — that needs a smaller size (more dispersion): size \(= \mu^2/(\text{Var}-\mu) = 400/190 \approx 2.1\). Either way, the overdispersed NB, not the Poisson, is the family that can reproduce a variance far above the mean.
R3.
pexp(2, rate = 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE)   # 0.3679  (exponential survival, e^{-1})
dpois(0, 0.5 * 2)         # 0.3679  (Poisson zero-count over the 2-Mb window)
Both equal \(e^{-1} \approx 0.368\), confirming the two views of the same Poisson process agree.

title: Exercise: error models — exponential & Poisson
text:
Where this leads

Prior, likelihood and posterior: the error model is the likelihood — the term that multiplies the prior to give the Bayesian posterior. Today you chose it; there you use it in Bayes’ theorem.
Poisson and negative binomial distributions: a fuller treatment of count distributions and overdispersion, the statistical foundation of RNA-seq differential expression.
Genomics tools: DESeq2 and edgeR are negative-binomial models with shared dispersion estimation across genes — the production-grade version of the mean-variance reasoning practised here.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
About this lecture
In Matrices as transformations, a matrix is a function that moves vectors around — it stretches, rotates, mixes the axes. Today we hunt for the special directions a matrix leaves alone.

Most vectors get rotated by a matrix. A few special ones only get scaled — those are eigenvectors.
The amount of scaling is the eigenvalue \(\lambda\), and the whole idea is one equation: \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\).
How to find them by hand in the cases that matter: check a candidate, read a diagonal or triangular matrix, the symmetric \(2\times2\) pattern, and geometry. Everything else: eigen() in R.
Why symmetric matrices (like a covariance matrix) are special: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors.
Biology: the eigenvectors of a covariance matrix point along the main axes of variation in a dataset — the seed of PCA (in the Applications block).

This is a concept day. The exam asks you to check and find eigenvectors by hand in these simple cases, so practise them on paper. No determinants are needed (the classic determinant recipe is a bonus at the end).

The single mental image for today: a transformation grabs the plane and distorts it, but a couple of special directions don’t get knocked off their line — they only get longer or shorter. Those are eigenvectors. (Students have seen this literally in Transforming images with matrices: the gallery slide where 2 × 2 matrices stretch, shear and rotate a micrograph of a cell — e.g. under the shear, the x-axis is such a special direction.) Everything else (the by-hand checks, symmetric matrices, the PCA preview) hangs off that one picture. The examinable skills are deliberately determinant-free: multiply A by a candidate and see whether it only scales, read eigenvalues off diagonal and triangular matrices, use the symmetric [[a, b], [b, a]] pattern, and reason geometrically. The characteristic equation det(A - lambda I) = 0 is kept as bonus slides after the Summary, for those who want to see where eigenvalues come from in general. Keep an R session open for the demos but emphasise this is concept day, R fluency comes in Eigenvalues in R.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
A biology picture first
Measure two genes across many cells and plot each cell as a point (gene 1 on x, gene 2 on y).

The two genes are co-regulated, so the cloud is a tilted, elongated ellipse.
There is one direction along which the cells spread the most — the long axis of the cloud.
And a perpendicular direction with the least spread — the short axis.

These two axes are not the x- and y-axes. They are tilted. Where do they come from?
They are the eigenvectors of the data’s covariance matrix. Today we learn what that sentence means.


Anchor the whole abstraction in a concrete scatter before any algebra. Two co-regulated genes produce a diagonal sausage-shaped cloud. The intuitive “long axis” and “short axis” of that cloud are exactly the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and their lengths (how stretched the cloud is along each) are the eigenvalues. Don’t define covariance formally yet — just plant the idea that the interesting directions of a dataset are tilted, and matrices know how to find them. PCA comes in the Applications block; today is only the mathematical machinery.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Most vectors get rotated
Take a matrix \(A\) and feed it different input vectors. Watch the direction of the output.
\[A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\]

\(A\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}\) — pointed along x, came out tilted up. Direction changed.
\(A\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}\) — pointed along y, came out tilted. Direction changed.
\(A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\3\end{pmatrix}\) — pointed along the diagonal, came out on the same line, just longer!

That last one is special: \(A\) only scaled it (by 3), without rotating it.


This is the heart of the lecture. Pick a symmetric matrix so the special directions are clean. Show that generic inputs (the x-axis, the y-axis) get tilted, but the diagonal direction (1,1) comes out as (3,3) — exactly 3 times itself, no rotation. Make students feel the contrast: rotation is the rule, pure scaling is the exception, and the exceptional directions are what we care about. The number 3 here is the eigenvalue; (1,1) is the eigenvector. We will also find the other special direction, (1,-1).

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
The definition: \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\)
A nonzero vector \(\mathbf{v}\) is an eigenvector of \(A\) if \(A\) only scales it:
\[A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\]

\(\lambda\) (a scalar) is the eigenvalue — the stretch factor for that direction.
“Eigen” is German for own / characteristic: these are the matrix’s own special directions.

Reading the equation: transforming \(\mathbf{v}\) with \(A\) gives the same thing as just multiplying \(\mathbf{v}\) by the number \(\lambda\). The matrix acts like a plain number on that direction.
From the previous slide: \(A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\3\end{pmatrix} = 3\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}\), so \(\mathbf{v}=(1,1)\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(\lambda = 3\).

Write the defining equation and read it aloud in words several times: applying the matrix equals multiplying by a number, but only for these special vectors. Stress nonzero: the zero vector trivially satisfies it and is excluded by definition. Connect straight back to the (1,1) -> (3,3) example so the equation is not abstract. Mention the etymology — eigen = own — because it demystifies the intimidating word. Note that any nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is also an eigenvector with the same eigenvalue (the whole line is special).

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
The whole line is special
If \(\mathbf{v}\) is an eigenvector, so is \(2\mathbf{v}\), \(-\mathbf{v}\), \(0.5\mathbf{v}\) — any nonzero multiple:
\[A(2\mathbf{v}) = 2(A\mathbf{v}) = 2(\lambda\mathbf{v}) = \lambda(2\mathbf{v})\]

An eigenvector defines a direction (a line through the origin), not one specific arrow.
So we are free to pick a convenient representative — usually the simplest integers, or a unit vector (length 1).
R will hand you the unit version by default; on paper we keep nice whole numbers like \((1,1)\).



A frequent source of confusion: students compute (2,2) and panic because R reported (0.707, 0.707). They are the SAME eigenvector — the same direction, different length. Make this explicit now so it doesn’t bite in Eigenvalues in R. The takeaway: an eigenvector is really an eigen-line; we scale it to whatever length is convenient. By hand, pick small integers; R normalises to length 1. Both are correct.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Test a candidate: just multiply
To check whether a given \(\mathbf v\) is an eigenvector, compute \(A\mathbf v\) and ask: is the output a multiple of the input?
With \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\):

\(\mathbf v = (1, -1)\): \(\ A\mathbf v = (2-1,\ 1-2) = (1, -1) = 1\cdot\mathbf v\). Yes, eigenvector with \(\lambda = 1\).
\(\mathbf v = (1, 2)\): \(\ A\mathbf v = (2+2,\ 1+4) = (4, 5)\). Is \((4, 5) = \lambda(1, 2)\)? It would need \(\lambda = 4\) and \(\lambda = 2.5\). No.

The eigenvalue is read off by comparing entries: \(\lambda = (A\mathbf v)_1 / v_1 = (A\mathbf v)_2 / v_2\). Both ratios must agree.

This is the most basic and most useful by-hand skill: no formulas, only one matrix-vector product. The test is “same ratio in every entry”. Watch out for zero entries in v: if v_1 = 0, then (Av)_1 must also be 0. In R this is A %% v compared with lambda  v.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Eigenvalues you can read off
Diagonal matrix: each axis is only scaled, so the axes are the eigenvectors and the diagonal entries are the eigenvalues.
\[\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}: \quad \lambda = 4 \text{ for } (1,0), \qquad \lambda = 2 \text{ for } (0,1)\]
Triangular matrix (zeros below or above the diagonal): the eigenvalues are still the diagonal entries.
\[A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}: \quad \lambda = 3 \text{ and } \lambda = 2\]

One eigenvector comes for free: \(A(1, 0) = (3, 0) = 3\,(1, 0)\).
The other is found on the next slide.


Why the diagonal works for triangular matrices: A(1,0) is the first column, (3, 0), which is a multiple of (1,0), so the x-axis is an eigenvector with the top-left entry as eigenvalue. The other diagonal entry is also an eigenvalue (we take that as a rule here; the bonus slides show why). The shear from Transforming images with matrices, [[1, 0.5], [0, 1]], is triangular: its eigenvalue is 1 (twice), and the x-axis is its only eigen-direction.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
section: Finding the eigenvector for a known \(\lambda\)
text:
Finding the eigenvector for a known \(\lambda\)
Once you know \(\lambda\), the eigenvector is a small linear system. Start from \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\) and move everything to one side (write \(\lambda\mathbf{v} = \lambda I\mathbf{v}\) so the shapes match):
\[(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}, \qquad A - \lambda I = \text{$A$ with $\lambda$ subtracted from each diagonal entry.}\]
For \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\lambda = 2\):
\[A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\]
Row 1 says \(v_1 + v_2 = 0\), i.e. \(v_2 = -v_1\). Pick \(v_1 = 1\): \(\ \mathbf v = (1, -1)\).
Verify: \(A(1,-1) = (3-1,\ 0-2) = (2, -2) = 2\,(1,-1)\). ✓

Subtract lambda from the diagonal only, off-diagonals untouched. For an eigenvalue the two rows of A - lambda I always say the same thing (or one of them is all zeros), so one row gives the relation between v1 and v2. There is a free choice of scale (the whole line is special); pick the simplest integers. Always verify by multiplying: it is the cheapest check there is. This is the same row reasoning as in Linear systems by hand.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
The symmetric \(2\times2\) pattern
For a symmetric matrix with equal diagonal entries, the eigenvectors are always the two diagonals of the plane:
\[A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}: \qquad A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix} = (a+b)\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad A\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix} = (a-b)\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]
For our \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\): \(\lambda_1 = 2 + 1 = 3\) for \((1,1)\) and \(\lambda_2 = 2 - 1 = 1\) for \((1,-1)\).
Notice: \(\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_2 = (1)(1) + (1)(-1) = 0\) — the two eigenvectors are orthogonal!


Prove the pattern on the board by multiplying: A(1,1) = (a+b, b+a) and A(1,-1) = (a-b, b-a) = (a-b)(1,-1). Nothing to memorise beyond “the diagonals of the plane”. Many covariance matrices of two equally variable, correlated variables have exactly this form, so it covers a lot of exam-style examples. Then highlight the punchline: the dot product is zero, so the eigenvectors are perpendicular. This is not a coincidence; it happens because A is symmetric (next slides).

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Eigenvectors you can see
Think about what the matrix does; the directions it leaves on their own line are the eigenvectors.








Matrix
What it does
Eigenvectors and eigenvalues




\(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\)
projects onto the x-axis
\((1,0)\): \(\lambda = 1\) (kept); \(\ (0,1)\): \(\lambda = 0\) (squashed)


\(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\)
mirrors in the line \(y = x\)
\((1,1)\): \(\lambda = 1\) (on the mirror); \(\ (1,-1)\): \(\lambda = -1\) (flipped)


\(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\)
shear
\((1,0)\): \(\lambda = 1\); no other direction


\(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\)
rotates \(90^\circ\)
none: every direction is turned



Check your answer: the eigenvalues always add up to the trace (sum of the diagonal). For \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\): \(3 + 1 = 4 = 2 + 2\). ✓
For any other matrix: let R do it with eigen() (Eigenvalues in R).

Geometry first, algebra second: a projection keeps the line it projects onto (lambda 1) and kills the perpendicular direction (lambda 0); a mirror keeps the mirror line (1) and flips the perpendicular one (-1); a shear keeps only the x-axis; a rotation keeps nothing. Each can be verified by one multiplication. The trace check catches arithmetic slips for free: projection 1 + 0 = 1 = trace, mirror 1 + (-1) = 0 = trace. The examinable toolbox is now complete; general matrices are for eigen() in R. The determinant recipe is in the bonus slides at the end.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Try it: hunt for eigen-directions




Start with A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] from the start of the lecture. Drag the black handle (v, length 1) round the circle, or use the “direction of v” slider: Av (orange) is usually turned away from the dotted line through v. When v reaches (0.71, 0.71), Av lands on that line and turns green: Av = 3v, so lambda = 3 (it snaps there when you are close). Find the second direction, (0.71, -0.71), with lambda = 1. Then press “Sweep v around”: v turns once, the tip of Av traces an ellipse, and the demo pauses on each eigen-direction and marks it. Now repeat the table from the previous slide with the presets: Projection (lambda 1 and 0: Av shrinks to nothing), Mirror (lambda -1: Av points the opposite way, still on the line), Shear (only one direction), Rotate 90° (the sweep finds nothing), Scale ×2 (every direction). Ask before each sweep: how many directions will it find?

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Symmetric matrices are special
A matrix is symmetric if \(A = A^\top\) (it equals its own transpose — mirror across the diagonal). Our example \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) is symmetric (\(b = c = 1\)).
For symmetric matrices (a theorem — the spectral theorem):

All eigenvalues are real (no awkward complex numbers).
Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal (perpendicular).

This is exactly what we just saw: real eigenvalues \(3, 1\) and perpendicular eigenvectors \((1,1) \perp (1,-1)\).

This slide is the conceptual reward. Define symmetric (A = A transpose). State the spectral theorem in plain terms: symmetric matrices always have real eigenvalues and a full set of mutually perpendicular eigenvectors. No proof — just the fact and the reassurance that nothing weird (complex numbers, tilted non-orthogonal axes) can happen. Point back to the worked example as a live instance. The why-we-care comes next: covariance matrices are symmetric.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
section: Why biologists care: covariance is symmetric
text:
Why biologists care: covariance is symmetric
For a dataset (e.g. expression of 2 genes across many cells), the covariance matrix \(C\) summarises spread:
\[C = \begin{pmatrix} \text{var}(g_1) & \text{cov}(g_1,g_2) \\ \text{cov}(g_1,g_2) & \text{var}(g_2) \end{pmatrix}\]
\(C\) is symmetric (cov\((g_1,g_2)=\) cov\((g_2,g_1)\)), so by the spectral theorem:

its eigenvectors are orthogonal → they form clean perpendicular axes,
its eigenvalues are real and positive → the amount of variance along each axis.

The eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue points along the long axis of the data cloud — the direction of greatest variation. That is PCA (taught in the Applications block). Today you built its engine.


Close the loop opened on slide 2. The covariance matrix is symmetric by construction, so it inherits all the nice properties: orthogonal eigenvectors and real, non-negative eigenvalues. Interpret eigenvalue = variance captured along that eigen-direction; biggest eigenvalue = the long axis of the cloud = first principal component. Be disciplined: name PCA as the destination but do NOT teach it (centring, projection, scores) — that is week 2. Today’s deliverable is “eigen-decomposition of a covariance matrix finds the axes of variation.”

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Special cases & gotchas

Repeated eigenvalue: \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) has \(\lambda = 2\) twice. Every direction is an eigenvector (it scales everything equally).
Diagonal matrix: eigenvalues are just the diagonal entries; eigenvectors are the axes.
Complex eigenvalues: a pure rotation \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) has no real eigenvector — it rotates everything, leaving no direction fixed. (This can’t happen for symmetric matrices.)
Scale freedom: eigenvectors are only defined up to length and sign.



A short tour of the edge cases so they aren’t surprised: a scalar multiple of the identity makes every direction an eigenvector; a diagonal matrix wears its eigenvalues on its diagonal; a pure rotation has complex eigenvalues because no real direction survives unrotated. The last one beautifully reinforces today’s opening picture (rotation moves everything) and contrasts with symmetric matrices, which never go complex. Reiterate sign/scale freedom so R’s output (which may flip signs) doesn’t confuse them in Eigenvalues in R.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Eigenvector
direction \(A\) only scales, never rotates


Eigen relation
\(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\) (\(\mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}\))


Eigenvalue
the scaling factor \(\lambda\)


Test a candidate
compute \(A\mathbf{v}\): a multiple of \(\mathbf{v}\)?


Diagonal / triangular
eigenvalues = diagonal entries


Symmetric \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}\)
\((1,1)\): \(a+b\); \(\ (1,-1)\): \(a-b\)


Find \(\mathbf{v}\) for known \(\lambda\)
solve \((A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\), pick nice scale


Check
\(\sum\lambda\) = trace


Symmetric \(A\)

Biology
eigenvectors of covariance = axes of variation (PCA engine)



Next (Eigenvalues in R): compute all of this in R with eigen.

The summary is the exam cheat-sheet. Drill the by-hand toolbox one more time verbally: test a candidate by multiplying, read diagonal/triangular matrices, use the symmetric pattern, reason geometrically, find v for a known lambda from (A - lambda I) v = 0, and check with the trace. No determinants needed; the bonus slides after this one show the general determinant recipe for those who want it. Remind them symmetric = real + orthogonal, and that covariance matrices are the biological payoff. Preview Eigenvalues in R: eigen() does all the arithmetic instantly, but they must still understand the output, which only makes sense if today’s concepts are solid.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
section: Bonus: the characteristic equation (not for exam)
text:
Bonus: the characteristic equation (not for exam)
Where do eigenvalues come from in general? From \((A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\): we need a nonzero \(\mathbf{v}\) that \(A-\lambda I\) sends to zero. A matrix can only crush a nonzero vector to zero if it is singular — i.e. its determinant is zero:
\[\boxed{\ \det(A - \lambda I) = 0\ }\]
For a \(2\times2\), \(\det\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc\), so
\[\det(A - \lambda I) = (a-\lambda)(d-\lambda) - bc = 0,\]
a quadratic in \(\lambda\).

Bonus material: you do not need to memorise determinants for the exam.

Bonus slide: not examined. It explains where eigenvalues come from for any matrix. Key logical step: (A - lambda I) v = 0 with v nonzero means A - lambda I is not invertible, which means det = 0 (see the bonus determinant slide in Matrices as transformations: det 0 means the plane collapses onto a line). It also explains why the triangular rule works: for a triangular matrix bc = 0, so the quadratic is (a - lambda)(d - lambda) = 0.

title: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors
section: Bonus: a worked example (not for exam)
text:
Bonus: a worked example (not for exam)
\[A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(A - \lambda I) = (2-\lambda)(2-\lambda) - (1)(1) = \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda - 1) = 0\]
So \(\lambda_1 = 3,\ \lambda_2 = 1\) — the same as the symmetric pattern gave.
Two checks:

Sum of eigenvalues = trace: \(3 + 1 = 4 = 2 + 2\). ✓
Product of eigenvalues = determinant of \(A\): \(3 \times 1 = 3 = (2)(2) - (1)(1)\). ✓

The same method works for matrices without a pattern, e.g. \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) gives \(\lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 1 = 0\), so \(\lambda = 1 \pm \sqrt 2\). A rotation gives \(\lambda^2 + 1 = 0\): no real solution.
Bonus material: you do not need to memorise determinants for the exam.

Bonus slide: not examined. Expand (2 - lambda)^2 - 1, factor, and land on 3 and 1, matching the symmetric pattern from earlier. The product = det check is only available with determinants; the sum = trace check is the examinable one. The last line shows the method’s real strength: matrices with no pattern and the rotation’s missing real eigenvalues. In practice, eigen() in R does this for any size.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
About this lecture
In Eigenvalues & eigenvectors you found eigenvalues by hand in the simple cases: testing a candidate, diagonal and triangular matrices, the symmetric \(2\times2\) pattern. Those skills are examined — but most real matrices fit no pattern, and anything bigger than \(2\times2\) is out of reach by hand. Today R does the arithmetic.

eigen returns all eigenvalues and eigenvectors at once.
Read its output: $values and $vectors, and how eigenvectors sit in the columns.
R sorts eigenvalues from largest to smallest — and normalises eigenvectors to length 1.
Verify \(A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}\) in R, and reconstruct \(A = V\Lambda V^{-1}\) (and \(V\Lambda V^\top\) for symmetric \(A\)).
Biology payoff: eigen-decompose a small covariance matrix and watch the leading eigenvector point along the main axis of variation in a gene-expression scatter (the engine of PCA).

This is a hands-on R walkthrough: keep an R session open and run every block.

Frame the day as “Eigenvalues & eigenvectors was the concept and the by-hand recipe; today is the tool.” Reassure students the by-hand skills (test a candidate, read diagonal/triangular matrices, the symmetric pattern) still matter for the exam, but in practice any matrix without a pattern, and any 50x50 covariance matrix, goes to eigen(). The deliverables are: read eigen()’s output confidently, verify it, reconstruct the matrix, and apply it to a covariance matrix. Stress they should reproduce every block live; this is a walkthrough, not a slideshow to watch passively.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
The function: eigen()
Give it a square matrix; get back a list with two parts.
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
e <- eigen(A)
e
# eigen() decomposition
# $values
# [1] 3 1
#
# $vectors
#            [,1]       [,2]
# [1,] 0.7071068 -0.7071068
# [2,] 0.7071068  0.7071068

e$values — the eigenvalues, largest first: 3, 1.
e$vectors — the eigenvectors, one per column, each length 1.


Run eigen() on the worked example from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors so students recognise the answer (3 and 1). Two things to point out immediately: the result is a LIST with $values and $vectors, and the eigenvalues are returned largest-first (this ordering matters for PCA). The 0.707 = 1/sqrt(2) values are the normalised version of the (1,1) and (1,-1) from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors. The next slides unpack reading the vectors and reconciling with the hand answer.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Reading $vectors: columns, not rows
The eigenvectors are the columns of e$vectors. The \(i\)-th column matches the \(i\)-th eigenvalue.
e$values[1]        # 3
e$vectors[, 1]     # 0.7071068 0.7071068   <- eigenvector for lambda = 3
e$vectors[, 2]     # -0.7071068 0.7071068  <- eigenvector for lambda = 1

e$vectors[, 1] is the eigenvector paired with e$values[1].
This is \((1,1)\) from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors, scaled to length 1: \(1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707\).



The most common reading mistake is grabbing a row instead of a column. Drill the indexing: e\(vectors[, k] is the k-th eigenvector and pairs with e\)values[k]. Then reconcile with Eigenvalues & eigenvectors: (0.707, 0.707) is just (1,1) divided by its length sqrt(2). Same direction, unit length. Reassure them both are the “right” eigenvector — direction is what matters.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
section: Scale and sign are not unique
text:
Scale and sign are not unique
R returns unit-length eigenvectors, but the sign is arbitrary — R might give you \(\mathbf{v}\) or \(-\mathbf{v}\).
e$vectors[, 2]            # -0.707  0.707
-e$vectors[, 2]           #  0.707 -0.707   <- equally valid eigenvector

Both point along the same line (the eigen-direction); both satisfy \(A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}\).
So if your hand answer is \((1,-1)\) and R prints \((-0.707, 0.707)\), you are not wrong — same direction, opposite sign, unit length.



Pre-empt the panic: “R’s eigenvector has the opposite sign to mine!” Both are correct because eigenvectors are defined up to a nonzero scalar, including -1. Show v and -v side by side. This matters later in PCA, where the sign of a principal component is arbitrary and software may flip it between runs or versions. Teach them to compare DIRECTIONS, e.g. by ratio of components or by checking A v = lambda v, not raw numbers.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Verify the eigen relation
Never trust output you haven’t checked. Confirm \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\) directly:
lambda <- e$values[1]      # 3
v      <- e$vectors[, 1]   # unit eigenvector

A %*% v                    # 2.121320 2.121320
lambda * v                 # 2.121320 2.121320   <- identical

all.equal(as.vector(A %*% v), lambda * v)   # TRUE

Use all.equal, not ==: floating-point arithmetic gives tiny rounding differences.



This is the single most important habit of the day. A %% v should equal lambda  v. Note A %% v returns a column matrix, so wrap it in as.vector() to compare with the plain vector lambda  v. Crucially, use all.equal() not == : the two sides agree only to ~15 decimal places because of floating point, so == may return FALSE on values that are equal for all practical purposes. This floating-point lesson recurs all course.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Reconstruct \(A = V\Lambda V^{-1}\)
Stack eigenvectors as columns of \(V\) and eigenvalues on the diagonal of \(\Lambda\). Then
\[A = V\,\Lambda\,V^{-1}\]
V      <- e$vectors
Lambda <- diag(e$values)        # eigenvalues on the diagonal
V %*% Lambda %*% solve(V)       # rebuilds A
#      [,1] [,2]
# [1,]    2    1
# [2,]    1    2

diag turns the eigenvalue vector into a diagonal matrix \(\Lambda\).
solve(V) is the inverse \(V^{-1}\).
This eigendecomposition says: \(A\) = (change to eigen-coords) → (scale each axis by its \(\lambda\)) → (change back).



The reconstruction is the “aha” that eigenvectors fully describe the matrix: in the coordinate system of the eigenvectors, A is just a diagonal scaling. V changes into that coordinate system, Lambda scales, V-inverse changes back. Show it literally rebuilds the original A. Mention diag() does double duty (extracts a diagonal from a matrix, or builds a diagonal matrix from a vector). solve(V) is the inverse. Next slide: for symmetric A, the inverse is just the transpose.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Symmetric shortcut: \(A = V\Lambda V^\top\)
For a symmetric matrix, the eigenvectors are orthogonal and unit length (R gives them this way), so \(V^{-1} = V^\top\). No matrix inverse needed:
\[A = V\,\Lambda\,V^\top\]
isSymmetric(A)                  # TRUE
crossprod(V)                    # V^T V = identity (cols are orthonormal)
V %*% Lambda %*% t(V)           # rebuilds A, using transpose instead of inverse

t(V) is the transpose \(V^\top\); crossprod(V) computes \(V^\top V\).
eigen() automatically uses a faster, more accurate symmetric algorithm when it detects symmetry.



The orthonormal columns of V (for symmetric A) mean V is an orthogonal matrix, so its inverse equals its transpose — cheaper and numerically nicer. Show crossprod(V) is the identity to prove orthonormality, then rebuild A with t(V) instead of solve(V). Mention eigen() checks symmetry and switches to a specialised routine; you can force it with eigen(A, symmetric = TRUE). This symmetric case is exactly what covariance matrices are, leading into the biology demo.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Biology: covariance of two genes
Simulate expression of two co-regulated genes across cells, then look at the covariance.
set.seed(1)
n  <- 200
g1 <- rnorm(n)                       # gene 1
g2 <- 0.8 * g1 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.4)  # gene 2 tracks gene 1 (+ noise)
X  <- cbind(g1, g2)                  # n x 2: rows = cells, cols = genes

C <- cov(X)                          # 2 x 2 covariance matrix (symmetric)
round(C, 3)
#       g1    g2
# g1 0.863 0.683
# g2 0.683 0.703

cov computes the covariance matrix; it is symmetric by construction.
Diagonal = variance of each gene; off-diagonal = how they co-vary (positive → rise together).



Build the dataset live: gene 2 is mostly a scaled copy of gene 1 plus noise, so they are positively correlated — a tilted cloud. cov(X) gives the 2x2 covariance, symmetric, with variances on the diagonal and the (positive) covariance off-diagonal. Emphasise X is rows = cells (samples), columns = genes (features); cov() expects that orientation. This sets up the eigen-decomposition on the next slide.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
section: The leading eigenvector = main axis of variation
text:
The leading eigenvector = main axis of variation
ec <- eigen(C)
ec$values            # 1.470  0.096   (variance along each axis)
pc1 <- ec$vectors[, 1]   # leading eigenvector

plot(X, asp = 1, pch = 19, col = "grey40",
     xlab = "gene 1", ylab = "gene 2")
# draw the leading eigen-direction through the cloud's centre
m <- colMeans(X)
arrows(m[1], m[2], m[1] + 2*pc1[1], m[2] + 2*pc1[2], col = "red", lwd = 3)

The largest eigenvalue’s eigenvector (ec$vectors[, 1]) points along the long axis of the cloud.
Its eigenvalue is the variance captured along that direction.



This is the payoff slide. Eigen-decompose the covariance matrix; the leading eigenvalue is the variance along the cloud’s long axis, and the leading eigenvector is that axis’s direction. Plot the cloud with asp=1 (so it isn’t distorted) and draw a red arrow from the data centre along pc1 — it should lie right along the sausage. This is literally how PCA finds its first component. Be careful to say “this is the engine of PCA” and stop there.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Foreshadowing PCA (not today)
What you just did is the core computation of Principal Component Analysis:



Eigen concept (today)
PCA name (Applications block)




covariance matrix \(C\)
the thing PCA decomposes


leading eigenvector
first principal component (PC1)


its eigenvalue
variance explained by PC1


orthogonal eigenvectors
uncorrelated principal axes



PCA adds centring, projecting samples onto these axes (scores), and handling many genes at once. We are not doing that yet — today’s job was to see that eigenvectors of the covariance matrix are the axes of variation.

Make the boundary explicit so students don’t think they’ve already learned PCA. Today: eigen-decomposition of a covariance matrix yields the axes of variation. PCA (in the Applications block) wraps this with mean-centring, projecting the data onto the eigenvectors to get scores, ordering components by variance explained, and scaling to high-dimensional data. The mapping table is the takeaway. Resist any temptation to compute scores today.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Numerical notes & gotchas

Use all.equal, not ==, to compare floats — eigen results carry tiny rounding error.
Sign is arbitrary: R may return \(\mathbf{v}\) or \(-\mathbf{v}\). Compare directions, not raw numbers.
Ordering: eigen() sorts eigenvalues largest-first for symmetric matrices; for general matrices the order is by modulus (and values may be complex).
Complex output: a rotation gives 0+1i-style complex eigenvalues — expected, no real eigen-direction.
Symmetric flag: if you know \(A\) is symmetric, eigen(A, symmetric = TRUE) is faster and guarantees real output (avoids tiny imaginary parts from rounding).


A grab-bag of practical warnings. The float-comparison and sign points are the ones that bite beginners hardest, so repeat them. Ordering: for symmetric matrices (our case) eigen sorts descending by value, perfect for PCA; for general matrices it’s by modulus and can return complex numbers. Mention symmetric = TRUE as both a speed and a correctness safeguard — covariance matrices are symmetric, but floating point can introduce minuscule imaginary parts that the flag removes.

title: Eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Summary



Task
R




Decompose
e <- eigen(A)


Eigenvalues (largest first)
e$values


Eigenvectors (columns, unit length)
e$vectors


The \(k\)-th eigenvector
e$vectors[, k]


Verify
all.equal(as.vector(A %*% v), lambda * v)


Reconstruct (general)
V %*% diag(vals) %*% solve(V)


Reconstruct (symmetric)
V %*% diag(vals) %*% t(V)


Covariance matrix
cov(X) (rows = samples)


Main axis of variation
eigen(cov(X))$vectors[, 1]



Next (Markov chains): matrices applied repeatedly — where the eigenvalue \(\lambda = 1\) gives the long-run stationary distribution.

The summary is the working cheat-sheet for the exercises. Re-stress: read columns not rows, eigenvectors are unit length with arbitrary sign, verify with all.equal, and reconstruct with solve(V) generally or t(V) when symmetric. The biology one-liner eigen(cov(X))$vectors[,1] is the headline. Preview Markov chains: a transition matrix applied over and over drives a system to a steady state, which turns out to be the eigenvector with eigenvalue 1 — eigenvectors return with a new meaning.

title: Glossary
text: A running glossary of the mathematical, statistical, and R terms used in this course. Add terms here as the material is written; keep definitions short and link to a fuller treatment where one exists.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
About this lecture







Provisional block


This block (Penalized linear models) is provisional. It may move to a later statistics / machine-learning course. The material stands on its own, but treat the ordering as a working draft, not a contract.




In the penalty units (L1, L2 and elastic-net penalties) we met a knob \(\lambda\) that controls how hard a model is shrunk. This lecture answers two honest questions:

How do we choose \(\lambda\) without just eyeballing it?
How do we report a performance number we can actually trust on new samples?

The single tool for both is cross-validation (CV).

The whole point today is honesty. In the penalty units students learned that \(\lambda\) trades fit against simplicity, but we deliberately left “so what value do I use?” open. Today closes it. Frame CV as doing two distinct jobs — tuning (pick \(\lambda\)) and estimation (how good is the final model) — and stress that muddling these two jobs is the most common mistake in applied omics. This is a methods day: the exam-relevant skills are the by-hand fold arithmetic, computing MSE on held-out points, reading a CV curve, and spotting information leakage.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
Learning objectives
By the end you should be able to:

explain why training error is optimistic and what overfitting looks like,
describe k-fold cross-validation and what each fold is for,
use cv.glmnet to choose \(\lambda\), and read lambda.min vs lambda.1se,
separate the three roles train / validation / test,
recognise information leakage and know why feature selection must live inside the CV loop,
pick a sensible metric (MSE, deviance, AUC) for a given biological question.


Read these out; they map one-to-one onto the exercise and quiz. Emphasise the leakage objective — it is the one that most often bites real papers, and it is subtle enough that even experienced people get it wrong.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
section: A biology problem: a disease signature
text:
A biology problem: a disease signature
You have expression of 20,000 genes in 80 patients (40 disease, 40 healthy). You want a signature — a small set of genes that predicts disease — and a claim like “our classifier is 92% accurate.”

You fit a lasso logistic model. On your 80 patients it separates the groups almost perfectly.
A collaborator runs it on a new cohort. Accuracy collapses to barely better than a coin flip.

What went wrong? The model learned the noise of these 80 patients, not the biology. And the “92%” was measured on the very data used to fit it — so it was never a real prediction.
This lecture is the machinery that would have caught both problems before publication.


This \(p \gg n\) setting (20,000 features, 80 samples) is the canonical omics trap and exactly where penalties matter. With far more genes than patients you can always fit the training data perfectly, so a good-looking fit means nothing on its own. Two failures are bundled here: (1) \(\lambda\) chosen to look good on the training data, and (2) performance reported on training data. CV fixes the first; a held-out test set fixes the second. Keep coming back to this 80-patient example through the lecture.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
Training error always lies
Fit flexibility (here: less shrinkage, smaller \(\lambda\)) against error:

Training error keeps dropping as the model grows more flexible — it can memorise.
Error on new data drops, bottoms out, then rises again as the model starts fitting noise.

The gap between the two curves is overfitting. Training error is a biased, optimistic estimate of real performance, and the bias is worst exactly when \(p \gg n\).
\[\text{test error} \;=\; \underbrace{\text{bias}^2}_{\text{too rigid}} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{variance}}_{\text{too flexible}} \;+\; \text{irreducible noise}\]
We cannot see the “new data” curve directly — so we simulate having new data by holding some out. That is cross-validation.


The bias–variance decomposition is the theoretical backbone; keep it light — one line, one picture. The message students must leave with: a number computed on the data you fit on is not evidence. The U-shape of test error is why there is an optimal \(\lambda\) in the middle — too much shrinkage underfits (high bias), too little overfits (high variance). CV is literally a way to draw that U-shaped curve using only the data you have.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
section: The one honest idea: hold data out
text:
The one honest idea: hold data out
If you want to know how a model does on data it has never seen, then evaluate it on data it has never seen.

Split your samples into a part you fit on and a part you keep hidden.
Fit on the first part only.
Predict the hidden part and measure the error there.

The hidden part stands in for “future patients.” Everything today is a refinement of this one move.
The rule that is never broken: anything the model is scored on must have been invisible during fitting — including during any tuning, scaling, or feature selection.


State the golden rule now and repeat it every slide: the evaluation data must be untouched by fitting. Students nod at this and then violate it by scaling or gene-filtering on the full dataset first. Foreshadow that “fitting” is broader than calling glmnet — it includes every data-dependent choice, which is the crux of the leakage slide later.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
section: One split is wasteful and noisy
text:
One split is wasteful and noisy
A single train/test split has two problems:

Wasteful: with only 80 patients, setting aside 20 for testing means fitting on just 60. In omics, samples are precious.
Noisy: your performance estimate depends on which 20 landed in the test set. A lucky or unlucky split can move the number by a lot.

Fix: rotate the held-out part so every sample is tested exactly once, and average. That is k-fold cross-validation.


Motivate k-fold as the cure for the two weaknesses of a single split. The small-\(n\) point is deeply biological: recruiting 80 patients is expensive, so throwing away a quarter of them for one test is painful. Rotating the fold means every patient contributes to both training and testing (never simultaneously), so we use the data efficiently and average away the “unlucky split” noise.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
k-fold cross-validation
Split the samples into \(k\) equal folds (typically \(k = 5\) or \(10\)). Then, \(k\) times:

hold out one fold as the validation set,
fit the model on the other \(k-1\) folds,
record the error on the held-out fold.

Average the \(k\) errors → the cross-validated error. Every sample is held out exactly once; every model is trained on a fraction \(\frac{k-1}{k}\) of the data.
\[\text{CV error} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{f=1}^{k} \text{error on fold } f\]


Draw the classic k-fold grid on the board even though a figure is coming. Key numbers to make concrete with the 80-patient example: 10-fold means 10 folds of 8 patients; each model trains on 72, tests on 8; you fit 10 models and average 10 error estimates. Trade-off: larger \(k\) = more data per fit (less bias) but more computation and higher variance between folds; \(k=10\) is the standard compromise. \(k=n\) is a special case (next mention: LOOCV in the exercise).

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
Using CV to choose \(\lambda\)
CV turns “pick \(\lambda\)” into an experiment. Over a grid of candidate \(\lambda\) values:

run k-fold CV at each \(\lambda\),
plot CV error vs \(\lambda\) — it is the U-shaped curve, now measured.

Two standard choices come out:

lambda.min — the \(\lambda\) with the lowest CV error (best raw performance).
lambda.1se — the largest \(\lambda\) (simplest, most-shrunk model) whose CV error is within one standard error of the minimum.

lambda.1se deliberately trades a hair of accuracy for a simpler, more reproducible signature — often the better scientific choice.


This is where penalties and CV meet. The 1se rule is worth dwelling on: the CV error has uncertainty (the error bars = standard error across folds), so many \(\lambda\) values are statistically indistinguishable from the best. Among those, pick the simplest (largest \(\lambda\), fewest genes). Biologically this gives a shorter, more robust gene list that is likelier to replicate — which is usually what a biomarker paper actually wants. lambda.min is fine when raw predictive accuracy is the only goal.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
cv.glmnet in R
cv.glmnet does the whole loop for you: it builds the \(\lambda\) grid, runs k-fold CV, and stores both choices.
library(glmnet)

x <- as.matrix(expr)     # 80 patients x 20000 genes
y <- pheno$disease        # 0/1 label, length 80

set.seed(1)               # folds are random -> set a seed for reproducibility
cvfit <- cv.glmnet(
  x, y,
  family       = "binomial",  # logistic model for a 0/1 outcome
  alpha        = 1,           # 1 = lasso, 0 = ridge, in between = elastic net
  nfolds       = 10,          # 10-fold CV
  type.measure = "auc"        # score folds by AUC (see metrics slide)
)

cvfit$lambda.min   # best-CV lambda
cvfit$lambda.1se   # simplest lambda within 1 SE of the best
plot(cvfit)        # the CV curve with error bars

This is static code — nothing runs at render time. Walk the arguments: family selects the error model (gaussian / binomial / poisson), alpha selects the penalty type from the earlier units, nfolds sets \(k\), type.measure picks the scoring metric. Stress set.seed: the folds are assigned at random, so results shift run to run without a seed — a reproducibility gotcha. Note glmnet standardises the predictors internally on each training fold, so you do not standardise by hand (and standardising by hand on the full data would itself leak).

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
Extracting the chosen model
Once CV has picked a \(\lambda\), read off the coefficients and predict:
# sparse coefficient vector at the simpler lambda
coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.1se")     # most genes are exactly 0 (lasso)

# predicted probabilities for new patients
p_new <- predict(cvfit, newx = x_new,
                 s = "lambda.1se", type = "response")

The non-zero coefficients are your signature — the selected genes.
s = "lambda.1se" tells predict/coef which \(\lambda\) to use.
x_new must have the same genes, in the same order as the training x.


Tie back to the disease-signature story: the lasso zeroes out almost every gene, and the survivors are the candidate biomarkers. This is where penalized regression doubles as feature selection. Remind them that x_new must be matched columns — a silent reordering of genes is a common and disastrous bug. But note this predicted performance is still not an honest estimate if \(\lambda\) was tuned by CV on the same data — which motivates the next slide.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
Train / validation / test: three jobs
CV that chooses \(\lambda\) has already used up the held-out folds to make a decision. So its error is a mildly optimistic estimate of the final model. Three distinct roles:



Role
Job
Touched by tuning?




Training
fit coefficients for a given \(\lambda\)
yes


Validation (the CV folds)
choose \(\lambda\)
yes


Test
final, honest performance estimate
no — used once



The test set is locked away until the very end and used exactly once. If you peek at it to make any choice, it stops being a test set.


The subtlety: because CV picked \(\lambda\) to minimise the CV error, that minimum is slightly better than reality — you optimised against it. For a truly honest headline number you need data that took part in no decision. Practical recipe: hold out a test set first; do all CV/tuning on the rest; report the test-set number once. The gold-standard alternative is nested CV (outer loop for estimation, inner loop for tuning) — name it, and the exercise sketches it. With only 80 patients an external validation cohort is ideal but rarely available.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
Information leakage: the cardinal sin
Leakage = letting information from the held-out data influence the model. The result is a performance number that is too good and does not replicate.
The classic omics blunder:

Filter 20,000 genes down to the 50 most correlated with the outcome using all 80 patients, then cross-validate on those 50 genes.

The gene filter already looked at the outcome of every patient, including those later “held out.” The folds are no longer naive. Reported accuracy can look great and be completely spurious.
Rule: feature selection is part of the model. It must happen inside each CV fold, on the training portion only.


This is the most important slide of the day (Ambroise & McLachlan 2002 documented exactly this selection bias in microarray classifiers). The trap is seductive because prefiltering genes feels like harmless preprocessing, not modelling. But any step that uses \(y\) — supervised filtering, choosing a threshold, even scaling using the outcome — is part of fitting and must be redone inside every fold. Give the intuition: if the held-out fold helped choose the genes, it already “leaked” into the model and can no longer test it.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
Leakage: wrong vs right
## WRONG — filter uses y from ALL samples, then CV
gene_cor <- abs(cor(x, y))               # uses every patient's label
keep     <- order(gene_cor, decreasing = TRUE)[1:50]
cv.glmnet(x[, keep], y, family = "binomial")   # optimistic, leaked
## RIGHT — the WHOLE pipeline (filter + fit) sits inside CV
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(x)))
err   <- numeric(10)
for (f in 1:10) {
  tr <- folds != f;  te <- folds == f          # split first
  gc   <- abs(cor(x[tr, ], y[tr]))              # filter on TRAIN only
  keep <- order(gc, decreasing = TRUE)[1:50]
  fit  <- glmnet(x[tr, keep], y[tr], family = "binomial")
  p <- drop(predict(fit, newx = x[te, keep], type = "response"))
  err[f] <- mean((p - y[te])^2)                 # held-out Brier score
}
mean(err)                                        # honest mean CV Brier score

Contrast the two blocks line by line. The only real difference is where the split happens: in the wrong version the split comes after the filter; in the right version it comes first, and everything data-dependent is recomputed per fold. Note that cv.glmnet handles the glmnet fitting honestly per fold on its own, but it cannot know about a filtering step you did beforehand — so any supervised preprocessing you add must be wrapped in your own outer loop (or a pipeline tool). This is why leakage is an easy accident even for careful people.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
Choosing a metric
“Error” means different things for different outcomes. Match the metric to the biology and the model’s error family:








Outcome
Example
Metric




Continuous
predict age from methylation
MSE / RMSE, \(R^2\)


Count
predict read counts
deviance (Poisson)


Binary
disease vs healthy
AUC, deviance (log-loss), misclassification




MSE \(= \frac{1}{n}\sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\) — average squared error; RMSE \(= \sqrt{\text{MSE}}\) is back in the original units.
Deviance generalises MSE to GLMs — the natural loss when the error model is Poisson or binomial.
AUC measures ranking (does the model score sick patients above healthy ones?) and is robust to class imbalance and threshold choice.



The metric is a modelling decision, not an afterthought. For the disease classifier, plain accuracy is misleading when classes are imbalanced (95% healthy → predict “healthy” always scores 95%). AUC sidesteps this by scoring the ranking, and it needs no threshold. Deviance is the honest loss when you fit a GLM because it is the very quantity the model optimises — tie this back to the Poisson/negative-binomial error-model units. Set type.measure in cv.glmnet to whatever you will ultimately be judged on.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
Detecting overfitting in practice
Two cheap diagnostics:

Train vs CV gap. Near-perfect training error with much worse CV error = overfitting. A healthy model has a small gap.
Fold-to-fold spread. If CV error swings wildly between folds, the estimate is unstable — often too few samples, or correlated/grouped samples split across folds.

Responses: increase \(\lambda\) (shrink harder), reduce the feature set honestly, or get more samples.


Give them a reflex: always compare training error to CV error. A large gap is the fingerprint of overfitting and the direct signal to turn \(\lambda\) up. Unstable folds point to a data problem — most often that related samples (technical replicates, multiple cells from one patient, batches) are split across the train/test boundary, which leaks and inflates performance. That motivates the grouping pitfall next.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
Pitfalls in real omics data

Grouped samples. Cells from the same patient, technical replicates, or batches must stay together in one fold (grouped CV). Splitting them leaks and inflates performance.
Class imbalance. With few cases, use stratified folds so each fold has both classes; prefer AUC over accuracy.
Small \(n\). CV estimates are themselves noisy when \(n\) is small — report them with their spread, do not over-interpret the third decimal.
Batch effects. A model can “predict” disease by detecting the batch it was run in. CV will not catch this if batch is confounded with outcome.



These are the failure modes that turn a technically correct CV into a misleading one. The grouping point is the most common in single-cell and repeated-measures designs: thousands of cells from one patient are not independent samples, so splitting them across folds leaks patient identity. Stratification matters whenever cases are rare. And batch confounding is a study-design problem CV cannot rescue — the fix is upstream (randomised batches), connecting to the covariate-handling ideas in the regression units.

title: Cross-validation & model selection
text:
Summary







Idea
Key point




Training error
optimistic — never report it as performance


Hold-out
evaluate only on data unseen during fitting


k-fold CV
rotate folds; every sample tested once; average


Choosing \(\lambda\)
CV error vs \(\lambda\); lambda.min vs lambda.1se


cv.glmnet
family, alpha, nfolds, type.measure; set.seed


Train/val/test
three jobs; the test set is opened once


Leakage
any \(y\)-using step goes inside the CV loop


Metric
MSE/RMSE, deviance, AUC — match to the outcome



Where this leads: these same folds are how one compares lasso vs ridge vs elastic net, and how chemometrics models (PLS / OPLS) are validated. Cross-validation is the common ruler for every penalized and latent-variable model in the course.

The one-line exam summary: CV is how we choose \(\lambda\) honestly and estimate performance honestly, and the two jobs must not contaminate each other. Drill the leakage rule and the fold arithmetic — those are the examinable pieces. Preview that the same machinery generalises: comparing penalty types (the elastic-net unit) and validating chemometrics/PLS models all rest on exactly this cross-validation scaffolding.

title: Handling covariates
text:
About this lecture
Real experiments are never clean. Your samples differ in age, sex, BMI, batch, and treatment all at once. Today we learn how to put those extra variables — covariates — into a model, so the effect you care about is not corrupted by the ones you don’t.

What a covariate is, and the difference between a variable of interest and a nuisance variable.
How a model formula (y ~ treatment + age) becomes a design matrix \(X\) — the bridge back to Matrices as transformations.
Continuous vs categorical predictors, and what each coefficient means.
Confounding: why leaving a covariate out can flip your conclusion, and how adjustment fixes it.
Interactions: when a treatment works differently in different groups.







Provisional block


This Bayesian statistics block is provisional and may move to a later statistics / machine-learning course. The ideas here (design matrices, adjustment, interactions) are core to any linear model — Bayesian or frequentist — so they are worth your time regardless of where the block finally lands.




The single message of today: an effect estimate is only meaningful relative to what you did and did not account for. “Treatment raised expression by 2 units” is incomplete — raised it compared to what, holding what fixed? Covariates are how we make that precise. Emphasise that although this sits in the Bayesian block, everything today is identical machinery in a plain lm(); the Bayesian layer (priors on the coefficients) comes at the very end. Tell them the design-matrix idea is the same X they met in Matrices as transformations and in the linear-systems units — a formula is just a recipe for building X.

title: Handling covariates
text:
A biology picture first
You run an RNA-seq experiment: treated vs control mice, measuring one gene. Treated mice show higher expression. Success?

But the treated mice were, by accident, mostly old, and the controls mostly young.
This gene also rises naturally with age.
So is the difference due to the treatment, or due to age?

With the data as-is you cannot tell — treatment and age are tangled. The whole point of covariates is to untangle them: estimate the treatment effect as if the two groups had the same age distribution.


This is the confounding story that motivates everything. Keep it concrete: one gene, two groups, an accidental age imbalance. The naive comparison (mean treated minus mean control) mixes a treatment effect with an age effect because age differs between the groups. Do not yet say the word confounder or draw the DAG — just plant the tangle and the promise that a model with age in it can separate the two contributions. We return to this exact example on the confounding slide.

title: Handling covariates
text:
What is a covariate?
A covariate is any measured variable you put into the model alongside your predictor of interest.
Two roles, same machinery:

Variable of interest — the effect you actually want to estimate (e.g. treatment).
Nuisance / adjustment variable — something that also affects the outcome and that you want to control for so it doesn’t distort the effect of interest (e.g. age, sex, batch).

The model does not know which is which — you decide by how you interpret the coefficients. Mechanically, every covariate is just another column in the design matrix.

The interest-vs-nuisance distinction is conceptual, not mathematical: the fitting procedure treats all predictors symmetrically. What differs is which coefficient you report and which you treat as “just cleaning up”. Batch is the archetypal nuisance covariate in omics — students have all seen batch effects. Stress that “covariate” is an umbrella term; in some fields people reserve it for continuous nuisance variables, but here we use it for anything extra we add to the model.

title: Handling covariates
text:
The model formula
R (and Bayesian tools built on the same syntax) describes a model with a formula: outcome on the left, predictors on the right.
# outcome ~ predictor(s)
expr ~ treatment                 # effect of treatment only
expr ~ treatment + age           # treatment, adjusting for age
expr ~ treatment + age + sex     # adjust for age and sex
Behind every formula sits a linear predictor — a weighted sum of the predictors:
\[
\hat{y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \dots
\]
Each \(\beta\) is a coefficient: how much \(\hat y\) changes per unit of that predictor, holding the others fixed. Fitting the model = finding the \(\beta\)’s.

Formulas are the interface students will actually type, so anchor here. The + means “also include this term”, not arithmetic addition of the columns. Read each example aloud in words. The linear predictor is the same beta-dot-x you have seen throughout the course; a formula is a compact way to specify it. Note that lm(), glm(), and the Bayesian packages rstanarm/brms all accept this identical syntax — learn it once. Defer the meaning of “holding the others fixed” to the adjustment slide, but flag it now.

title: Handling covariates
text:
Continuous predictors: age, BMI
A continuous covariate enters as a single column of numbers. Its coefficient is a slope.
expr ~ age            #  y_hat = b0 + b1 * age

\(\beta_1\) = the change in expression for each additional year of age.
\(\beta_0\) (intercept) = predicted expression at age 0 — often meaningless, so we frequently centre the predictor.

expr ~ I(age - mean(age))   # now the intercept = expression at the MEAN age
Centring doesn’t change the slope; it just makes the intercept interpretable and helps the fit behave.


Continuous predictors are the easy case: one column, one slope, ordinary “rise over run”. The interpretation trap is the intercept — age 0 (a newborn, or worse, extrapolated nonsense) is rarely of interest, and for something like BMI, BMI 0 is impossible. Centring moves the intercept to the mean, which is both interpretable and numerically nicer. Mention that in Bayesian models centring/scaling predictors also makes default priors sensible, which we hit at the end. Do not overteach I(); just show it means “compute this expression as a literal predictor”.

title: Handling covariates
text:
Categorical predictors: sex, treatment
A categorical covariate (a factor) is not a number — it’s a label. R turns each factor into indicator (dummy) columns.
sex <- factor(c("F","M","F","M"))   # two levels: F, M
treatment <- factor(c("ctrl","treat","ctrl","treat"))
With the default treatment coding, one level is the reference (baseline), and each other level gets a 0/1 column:

sexM = 1 for males, 0 for females → its coefficient is the male − female difference.
The reference level (F) is absorbed into the intercept.

By default R picks the reference level alphabetically (F before M, ctrl before treat). Set it deliberately with relevel().


This is where most confusion lives. A factor with k levels becomes k-1 dummy columns plus the intercept; you never get a column for the reference level because it is the baseline the others are measured against. The coefficient sexM is not “the effect of being male in absolute terms” — it is the difference from the reference (female). The alphabetical default silently makes “ctrl” the reference for treatment, which is usually what you want, but warn them to check: if levels were “drug” and “placebo”, placebo would NOT be the reference. relevel() or factor(levels=…) fixes it. This dummy-coding scheme is exactly the contrast matrix, next.

title: Handling covariates
text:
From formula to design matrix \(X\)
A formula is a recipe for building a matrix. The outcome is \(\mathbf{y}\); the predictors become the columns of the design matrix \(X\), and the model is
\[
\mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
\]
model.matrix() shows you exactly what R built:
model.matrix(~ treatment + age)
#   (Intercept) treatmenttreat age
# 1           1              0  10
# 2           1              1  40
# 3           1              0  22
# 4           1              1  35
Column 1 is all 1’s (the intercept), column 2 is the 0/1 treatment dummy, column 3 is age. This is the same \(X\) from Matrices as transformations and the linear-systems units — the covariates just decide its columns.


This is the conceptual keystone and the tie-back the brief asks for. Everything abstract collapses here: fitting a model with covariates is solving y = X beta for beta, the same X they built columns for when we did linear systems and transformations. model.matrix() is the reveal — run it (statically here) so they SEE the intercept column of ones, the dummy column, and the raw continuous column side by side. Stress that choosing covariates literally means choosing columns of X. The least-squares / posterior machinery on top is unchanged; covariates are entirely about how X is constructed.

title: Handling covariates
text:
Contrasts: what the coefficients mean
The coding scheme for a factor is called its contrasts — it decides what each dummy column, and therefore each coefficient, compares.
Default treatment contrasts (contr.treatment) answer: “each level vs the reference.”
contrasts(treatment)
#       treat
# ctrl      0
# treat     1
So in expr ~ treatment:

Intercept = mean expression in the reference group (ctrl).
treatmenttreat = mean(treat) − mean(ctrl), the quantity you care about.

Other schemes exist (sum-to-zero contr.sum, etc.); they change what the numbers mean, not the model’s fit or predictions.

Contrasts are the same design/contrast-matrix idea used throughout omics differential-expression tools (limma, DESeq2 all revolve around a design and a contrast). Keep it light: the default treatment coding gives “difference from reference”, which is what people usually want and matches the categorical-predictor slide. The key insight is that the coefficient’s meaning is a CHOICE encoded in the contrast matrix, not a fact of nature — change the coding and the same data yields differently-defined coefficients with identical predictions. Don’t derive contr.sum; just name that alternatives exist so they aren’t thrown when they meet them.

title: Handling covariates
text:
Adjustment: adding a covariate
Return to the tangled experiment. Fit treatment alone, then adjusting for age:
lm(expr ~ treatment)          # unadjusted: treatment effect mixes in age
lm(expr ~ treatment + age)    # adjusted:  treatment effect "holding age fixed"
Adding + age gives age its own column in \(X\) and its own coefficient. The treatment coefficient now answers a different, cleaner question:

How much does treatment change expression among animals of the same age?

The model splits the observed variation into an age part and a treatment part, instead of blaming it all on treatment.

This is the operational heart. Emphasise that the unadjusted and adjusted treatment coefficients answer genuinely different questions, and only the second controls for age. “Holding age fixed” / “among animals of the same age” is the phrase to drill. Geometrically (optional): adjustment projects out the age direction before measuring the treatment effect — connects to projection/orthogonality from the vectors unit, but keep it a one-liner. The next slide shows how dramatic the difference can be.

title: Handling covariates
text:
Confounding: why it matters
