A confounder is a variable that influences both the predictor of interest and the outcome. Ignore it and the effect you report is biased.

In the extreme, adjusting can reverse an apparent effect (Simpson’s paradox): a treatment that looks harmful overall can be helpful within every age group, once age is accounted for.

Rule of thumb: adjust for variables that plausibly affect the outcome and differ between your groups (age, sex, batch, RIN, sequencing depth).
Not everything, though — see the pitfalls slide (adjusting for the wrong variable can add bias).


Define confounder precisely: associated with both exposure and outcome, and not on the causal path from exposure to outcome. The age->group and age->expression arrows are why the naive comparison fails. Mention Simpson’s paradox as the vivid extreme — the direction of an effect flips after adjustment — so they respect the stakes. Give the practical heuristic (adjust for plausible common causes that are imbalanced across groups) but immediately caveat that more covariates is not always better; colliders and over-adjustment come on the pitfalls slide. Batch, RIN, library size are the omics-flavoured confounders they will actually meet.

title: Handling covariates
text:
Interpreting adjusted effects
In expr ~ treatment + age with fitted coefficients
\[
\hat{y} = \underbrace{\beta_0}_{\text{ctrl, age }0} + \underbrace{\beta_1}_{\text{treat vs ctrl}}\cdot\text{treat} + \underbrace{\beta_2}_{\text{per year}}\cdot\text{age}
\]

\(\beta_1\) — treatment effect at any fixed age (the model assumes it’s the same at every age — that’s the no-interaction assumption).
\(\beta_2\) — age effect within each treatment group.

Every coefficient in a multi-predictor model is read “holding the other predictors constant.” That single phrase is the whole skill of interpreting adjusted models.

Hammer the “holding the others constant” reading — it is THE exam-worthy sentence. Point out the hidden assumption in the additive model: beta_1 is a single treatment effect assumed identical across ages, and beta_2 a single age slope assumed identical across treatment groups. That assumption is exactly what interactions relax, which is the natural cue for the next slide. Make sure they can state, for a given fitted equation, what each beta means in words — that is what we assess.

title: Handling covariates
section: Interactions: effects that depend on group
text:
Interactions: effects that depend on group
Sometimes a treatment works differently in different subgroups — the treatment effect depends on sex. That is an interaction.
expr ~ treatment + sex             # additive: same treatment effect in both sexes
expr ~ treatment * sex             # interaction: treatment effect may differ by sex
treatment * sex expands to treatment + sex + treatment:sex. The extra treatment:sex term lets the treatment effect be larger in one sex than the other.


Interaction = the effect of one predictor changes with the level of another. The picture is two lines: parallel lines mean no interaction (the additive model is fine); non-parallel lines mean an interaction (the gap between treated and control differs by sex). The star syntax is a shorthand that automatically includes both main effects and the product term — a very common student mistake is to write only treatment:sex and forget the main effects. Biologically, sex-specific or genotype-specific drug responses are everywhere, so this is not an edge case.

title: Handling covariates
text:
Reading interaction coefficients
For expr ~ treatment * sex with reference levels ctrl and F:
\[
\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{treat} + \beta_2\,\text{M} + \beta_3\,(\text{treat}\times\text{M})
\]







Coefficient
Meaning




\(\beta_0\)
mean of ctrl, F (both references)


\(\beta_1\)
treatment effect in females


\(\beta_2\)
female → male difference in controls


\(\beta_3\)
extra treatment effect in males (how much the treatment effect differs between sexes)



Treatment effect in males \(= \beta_1 + \beta_3\). If \(\beta_3 = 0\), the effect is the same in both sexes and you’re back to the additive model.


This table is the deliverable of the interaction pair. The trap: beta_1 is NOT “the treatment effect” — it is the treatment effect in the reference sex only. beta_3 is a difference-in-differences: how much the treatment effect changes when you switch sex. To get the male treatment effect you add beta_1 + beta_3. Testing beta_3 = 0 is the formal test of “does the treatment act differently by sex”. Have them practise reading each row aloud. This is directly examinable and directly what they will do with real differential-expression designs.

title: Handling covariates
text:
Covariates in a Bayesian model
The design matrix \(X\) is identical in a Bayesian fit. What changes is that we place priors on the coefficients and get a posterior distribution for each, rather than a single point estimate.
# same formula, Bayesian engine (rstanarm / brms, built on Stan)
rstanarm::stan_glm(expr ~ treatment + age, data = d,
                   prior = rstanarm::normal(0, 5)) # weakly informative betas

The linear predictor \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots\) and the design matrix are unchanged.
Each \(\beta\) now has a posterior — a full distribution, so “adjusted treatment effect” comes with an honest credible interval.
For count outcomes you swap the error model (Poisson/negative binomial via a log link) — see the error-models unit — but the covariates still enter through \(X\boldsymbol\beta\).



Bring it home to the block. The covariate machinery is completely orthogonal to the frequentist/Bayesian choice: same formula, same X, same “holding others constant” interpretation. The Bayesian additions are priors on the betas (weakly informative normals are a fine default, especially after centring/scaling predictors) and a posterior per coefficient instead of a point estimate plus a CI. Connect to the neighbouring units: the error-models unit supplies the Poisson/NB likelihood for counts, where covariates sit inside a log link (log mu = X beta); the hierarchical-models unit will let coefficients vary across biological/technical replicates. Keep the Stan code illustrative, not something they run today.

title: Handling covariates
text:
Pitfalls

Collinearity — two covariates that move together (e.g. weight and BMI) make their individual coefficients unstable and hard to interpret. The combined prediction is fine; the split between them is not.
Over-adjustment / colliders — adjusting for a variable that is a consequence of the treatment (or a common effect of treatment and outcome) can create bias, not remove it. More covariates is not always better.
Categorical with many levels — a factor with \(k\) levels costs \(k-1\) columns; with small \(n\) you run out of data.
Wrong reference level — check levels(); a silently-wrong baseline flips the sign of your comparison’s meaning.
Extrapolating the intercept — “expression at age 0”; centre instead.


A short defensive-driving tour. Collinearity: the model can’t tell apart two predictors that carry the same information, so their individual betas seesaw — mention this connects to identifiability, which the penalized-linear-models block addresses with regularization. Colliders/over-adjustment is the subtle one: adjusting is not free, and conditioning on a downstream variable opens a spurious path — so the rule is not “adjust for everything” but “adjust for confounders”. Many-level factors eat degrees of freedom. Reference-level and intercept traps recap earlier slides. Keep each to a sentence; this is a checklist to revisit, not new theory.

title: Handling covariates
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Covariate
any extra predictor; interest or nuisance — same machinery


Formula
y ~ a + b builds the design matrix \(X\); model is \(y = X\beta + \varepsilon\)


Continuous predictor
one column; coefficient = slope (per unit)


Categorical predictor
factor → \(k-1\) dummy columns; coefficient = difference from reference


Contrasts
the coding scheme; decides what each coefficient compares


Adjustment
+ covariate → effect “holding the others constant”


Confounding
a common cause of predictor & outcome; ignoring it biases the effect


Interaction
a * b → effect of a depends on b; product term \(\beta\)


Bayesian
same \(X\), plus priors on \(\beta\) and a posterior per coefficient



Next: the error-models unit (Poisson/NB likelihoods for counts) and hierarchical models (covariates that vary across biological vs technical replicates).

The summary is the revision sheet. Drill the pipeline once more: a formula builds X, continuous predictors give slopes, factors give differences-from-reference via dummy columns, adding a covariate changes the question the coefficient answers to “holding others constant”, confounders must be adjusted for, interactions let effects depend on subgroup, and the Bayesian layer only adds priors and posteriors on the same betas. Point forward to error models (counts) and hierarchical models (replicate structure) as the natural continuations in this block. Remind them the exam wants them to READ a fitted equation and say what each coefficient means.

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
About this lecture
A flow cytometer measures thousands of cells per second, each stained with several fluorescent dyes. The detectors do not see one dye each: the colours leak into each other’s detectors.

The leak is a 2 × 2 matrix \(S\): measured = \(S\) × true.
Compensation undoes it with the inverse, solve(S), just like undoing a misaligned image.
Spectral unmixing is the same equation, with \(S\) built from reference spectra.
When two dyes look too alike, \(\det(S)\) is close to 0, and unmixing amplifies noise.

All data today are simulated in base R; no packages needed.

This unit is a second biological use of “undo a known matrix with its inverse”, after the misalignment slide in Transforming images with matrices. It needs only matrix-vector products, solve(), and the idea that the columns of a matrix are where the axes land. Flow cytometry is used in immunology and haematology every day (immunophenotyping, sorting); compensation is a step every user meets.

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Biology: two dyes, two detectors


Cells are labelled with antibodies carrying dyes, e.g. FITC (green) and PE (orange). Each dye marks one protein.
Each detector collects one band of colours. But FITC’s emission has a long tail that reaches the PE detector.
A cell with only FITC therefore shows a false PE signal: this is spillover.


Emission spectra are broad, so filters cannot fully separate them. FITC into the PE detector is the classic case, typically around 10 to 30 percent depending on the instrument; PE leaks only slightly back into the FITC detector. The curves here are schematic shapes, not measured spectra. Without correction, FITC-positive cells look partly PE-positive, and a researcher would report a double-positive population that does not exist.

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
The spillover matrix
Each detector sees a mix of the two dyes:
\[\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \text{FITC detector} \\ \text{PE detector} \end{pmatrix}}_{\text{measured}} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.02 \\ 0.25 & 1 \end{pmatrix}}_{S} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \text{FITC} \\ \text{PE} \end{pmatrix}}_{\text{true}}\]

Column 1 = where FITC’s light lands: all in the FITC detector, plus 25 % of that in the PE detector.
Column 2 = where PE’s light lands: 2 % in the FITC detector.
By hand: a cell with FITC = 1000, PE = 0 is measured as \((1000,\ 250)\). A cell with PE = 1000 only: \((20,\ 1000)\).

S <- matrix(c(1,    0.02,                         # rows = detectors, columns = dyes
              0.25, 1   ), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
            dimnames = list(c("FITC det", "PE det"), c("FITC", "PE")))
S %*% c(1000, 0)                                  # 1000, 250

Same reading as in Matrices as transformations: the columns of a matrix are where the axes land. Here the “axes” are the pure dyes: one unit of pure FITC lands at column 1, one unit of pure PE at column 2. Each column is scaled so that the dye’s own (main) detector is 1. Each row is one detector, adding up its share of every dye. This is a linear model: double the dye, double every detector signal.

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Before: what the cytometer records
Four simulated populations, 1600 cells, one cell per column (like the pixels in Transforming images with matrices):
set.seed(1)
make_pop <- function(n, fitc, pe) {               # true dye amounts, one cell per COLUMN
  rbind(FITC = rlnorm(n, log(fitc), 0.3), PE = rlnorm(n, log(pe), 0.3))
}
true <- cbind(make_pop(600,  100,  100),          # unstained
              make_pop(400, 3000,  100),          # FITC+
              make_pop(400,  100, 2000),          # PE+
              make_pop(200, 3000, 2000))          # FITC+ PE+
group <- rep(c("unstained", "FITC+", "PE+", "FITC+ PE+"), c(600, 400, 400, 200))
noise <- function(n) matrix(rnorm(2 * n, 0, 30), nrow = 2)   # detector noise
measured <- S %*% true + noise(ncol(true))


One %*% applies the spillover to all 1600 cells. The FITC+ population (green) should lie flat along the x-axis, but in the measured data it is tilted: the brighter the FITC, the more false PE. That tilt has slope 0.25, column 1 of S. The PE+ population hardly moves, because PE leaks only 2 percent back. Real cytometry data are usually shown on log-like axes; we use linear axes so the matrix action is a straight-line tilt.

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
section: Estimating the spillover from a control
text:
Estimating the spillover from a control


How do we know the 0.25? Run a single-stained control: cells (or beads) carrying only FITC. Every PE-detector signal is then spillover.
ctrl <- S %*% rbind(FITC = rlnorm(500, log(3000), 0.5), PE = 0) +
        noise(500)
fit <- lm(ctrl[2, ] ~ ctrl[1, ])                  # PE detector vs FITC detector
coef(fit)[2]                                      # slope 0.249: about 0.25

The slope is the spillover coefficient: column 1 of \(S\), measured.
A PE-only control gives column 2 the same way.





This is how instruments and software build S in practice: one single-stained control per dye, and a regression (or a ratio of medians) between the dye’s own detector and every other detector. In real life we do not know the true S; the slope recovers 0.249, close to the 0.25 used in the simulation. A control that is too dim gives a poor estimate, which is why controls should be at least as bright as the samples.

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Compensation: undo the matrix
If measured \(= S\,\text{true}\), then true \(= S^{-1}\,\text{measured}\): the same solve() as in Linear systems in R.
solve(S)                          # [1.005 -0.020; -0.251 1.005]
comp <- solve(S) %*% measured     # compensated: one %*% for all cells

The FITC+ cells: median PE 850 before, 102 after (unstained cells: about 100).

Compensation literally means multiplying by the inverse of the spillover matrix. Its off-diagonal entries are negative: subtract 25 percent of the FITC detector from the PE detector (and a little the other way). After compensation every population is aligned with the axes, and the FITC+ population has the same PE level as unstained cells, as it should. The double-positive population (purple) moves down too: its true PE was 2000, but it was measured at about 2750 because of its FITC. Compare with the image misalignment in Transforming images with matrices: there solve(A) put every pixel back; here solve(S) puts every cell back.

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Try it: guess the spillover




Same simulated cells as on the previous slides (true spillover 0.25 and 0.02). Left: what the cytometer records. Right: the cells after multiplying by the inverse of the spillover we guess with the sliders. Start at “No compensation”: both plots are the same and the green FITC+ population tilts up, slope about 0.25. Drag s21 slowly up and ask the class when to stop: the dark green line through the FITC+ cells flattens, and its median PE comes down to that of the unstained cells (dashed line). Go past it, to “Over”: the line tilts down and FITC+ cells get negative PE, which no real cell can have. The orange PE+ population only tilts slightly, so s12 is small; set it the same way. Point out the readout: S has the guesses off the diagonal, and its inverse has negative entries of about the same size, the “subtract 25 percent” of the previous slide. “Reveal true S” shows the values used to simulate. In real data the truth is unknown; the flat single-positive population is the check.

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
section: Why it works: columns and the inverse
text:
Why it works: columns and the inverse

\(S^{-1}S = I\): undoing after doing changes nothing. Check: solve(S) %*% S is the identity.
In pictures: \(S\) tilts the FITC axis (column 1 points along \((1, 0.25)\)); \(S^{-1}\) tilts it back to \((1, 0)\).
For a 2 × 2 matrix the inverse has a formula:

\[\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det S = 1 \cdot 1 - 0.02 \cdot 0.25 = 0.995\]

Noise is not removed: compensated values still carry the detector noise, mixed through \(S^{-1}\). Here that costs little (unstained cells: sd 45 after compensation, 33 in the true amounts, the rest is detector noise). Next slide: when it costs a lot.


The 2 x 2 inverse formula is worth knowing by heart: swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant. With det close to 1 (dyes well separated) the inverse is close to the identity with small corrections. The last bullet sets up the problem slide: the inverse also acts on the noise. With det(S) near 1 the inverse barely changes the noise, so the compensated spread (sd 45) is just the true spread (33) plus detector noise (30).

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Spectral unmixing: the same equation
A spectral cytometer records each cell’s light in many detectors (often 30 or more). Each dye has a reference spectrum: how its light spreads over the detectors, measured from a single-stained control.

Put the reference spectra as columns of \(S\): measured = \(S\) × true, exactly as before.
With 2 dyes and 2 detectors, \(S\) is square, and unmixing is compensation: solve(S).
With more detectors than dyes, \(S\) is tall. No inverse exists, but least squares finds the best fit:

S4 <- cbind(FITC = c(1,    0.45, 0.10, 0.02),     # reference spectra over 4 detectors
            PE   = c(0.02, 0.30, 1,    0.40))
cell <- S4 %*% c(3000, 2000)                      # one FITC+ PE+ cell, no noise
qr.solve(S4, cell)                                # least squares: 3000, 2000

Preview only. Spectral unmixing is the modern version: instead of one filter per dye, the full emission spectrum is recorded, and every cell is written as a combination of the reference spectra (columns). Extra detectors give more equations than unknowns; qr.solve (or lm without intercept) finds the dye amounts that best explain the measured spectrum. This is the same least squares as regression in the Bayesian and penalized blocks. Autofluorescence can be added as one more column, an extra “dye”.

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
When unmixing fails: similar dyes
If two dyes have similar spectra, the columns of \(S\) point almost the same way and \(\det(S)\) is near 0:
S2 <- matrix(c(1,   0.9,
               0.9, 1  ), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)  # det(S2) = 0.19
solve(S2)                                          # [5.26 -4.74; -4.74 5.26]: large entries
comp2 <- solve(S2) %*% (S2 %*% true + noise(ncol(true)))

The inverse multiplies the noise by about 5: unstained cells spread from sd 45 to 209, and populations smear.
Bonus material: you do not need to memorise determinants for the exam.

This is the panel-design rule of thumb in flow cytometry, explained with linear algebra: avoid pairs of dyes with overlapping spectra on the same cells, or at least on markers that are co-expressed. Geometrically, the two columns of S2 are almost parallel, so the parallelogram they span is thin (small determinant), and the inverse has to stretch a lot to undo it. The singular case (det = 0, identical spectra) cannot be undone at all, as in the gallery of Transforming images with matrices. The true values are still recovered on average; it is the spread that grows.

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Real data in R (optional)
For those who want to try real cytometry files:

Bioconductor package flowCore: read.FCS() reads a measurement file, exprs() gives the cells × channels matrix.
spillover() estimates \(S\) from single-stained controls; compensate() applies \(S^{-1}\) to every cell, exactly our solve(S) %*% measured.
Example data: data(GvHD) in flowCore, an extract of a graft-versus-host disease monitoring experiment. Many public experiments are in FlowRepository.

# install.packages("BiocManager"); BiocManager::install("flowCore")   # optional
library(flowCore)
data(GvHD)
head(exprs(GvHD[[1]]))            # one sample: cells as ROWS, channels as columns

Not required for the exercises. Note that flowCore stores cells as rows (the usual data-frame layout), so in real code the multiplication is measured %*% solve(t(S)) or similar; compensate() handles that for you. FCS files usually carry the instrument’s own spillover matrix in their metadata (keyword SPILL or $SPILLOVER), which is what compensate() typically uses.

title: Compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Summary








Concept
Key fact
R




Spillover
measured = \(S\) × true; column \(j\) = where dye \(j\)’s light lands
S %*% true


Estimating \(S\)
single-stained control: slope of other detector vs own detector
lm(ctrl[2, ] ~ ctrl[1, ])


Compensation
true = \(S^{-1}\) × measured
solve(S) %*% measured


2 × 2 inverse
swap diagonal, negate off-diagonal, divide by \(\det\)
solve(S)


Spectral unmixing
reference spectra as columns; tall \(S\) → least squares
qr.solve(S4, cell)


Similar dyes
\(\det(S) \approx 0\) → large inverse → noise amplified
det(S2)



Next (Eigenvalues & eigenvectors): directions that a matrix only scales.

The one-line takeaway: if a measurement mixes signals linearly, and you know the mixing matrix, its inverse unmixes them; how well depends on how different the columns are (the determinant). The same idea returns in spectroscopy (Chemometrics), in mixed cell-type signals (deconvolution of bulk RNA-seq), and in Fourier and PCA, where a change of basis separates signals.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Draft skeleton — review before use







This unit is a DRAFT SKELETON


This lecture is a provisional outline written to hold the slot for Chemometrics II while a subject-matter contributor is recruited. It sketches the standard applications at a general level only.

Treat every claim as provisional and subject to expert review.
No specific instrument, dataset, threshold, or performance number here is authoritative — where a concrete value would normally appear, the text says so rather than inventing one.
Do not teach from this unit as-is. It must be reviewed, corrected, and fleshed out by someone with hands-on chemometrics experience before it is used in class.





Reviewer checklist appears in the speaker notes throughout, tagged [REVIEW].

[REVIEW] This whole deck is a placeholder. The goal of this first pass is to get the shape of the topic right — the applications a biologist should recognise and the validation discipline that makes them trustworthy — without committing to specifics that need an expert. Please verify terminology, add real datasets and figures, and replace every “typically / often / commonly” with a defensible statement or a citation.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
About this lecture
Chemometrics I introduced the setting: a spectrum is a high-dimensional vector, samples stack into a wide matrix, and PCA-style methods find structure in it. Today we turn to what we do with such data in practice.
By the end you should be able to:

frame a spectroscopy problem as either classification (which group?) or regression / calibration (how much?),
describe multivariate calibration and why spectra need it rather than plain lm,
explain what calibration transfer is and why a model can fail on a second instrument,
recognise multivariate process / quality control on scores and residuals,
state why variable selection helps and name a couple of standard approaches,
validate a model honestly with cross-validation and report RMSEP.

This is an applications and vocabulary day, built on the machinery from PCA, The OPLS model, and Chemometrics I.

[REVIEW] Confirm this list. Keep learning objectives at the level of “can explain and set up”, not “can derive”; the derivations live in PCA and the eigen units; this day is about applying and validating.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Why a biologist should care
Spectroscopy gives a fast, cheap, often non-destructive read-out that stands in for a slow wet-lab assay. Some recurring biological uses:

Near-infrared (NIR) / infrared (IR): composition of grain, feed, tissue, or fermentation broth — e.g. protein, moisture, or metabolite content without a full chemical assay.
Raman: label-free readout of cells and tissue; distinguishing cell states or identifying microbial isolates.
Mass spectrometry / NMR (metabolomics): hundreds to thousands of features per sample, used to separate phenotypes or detect a metabolic shift.

In every case the raw signal is many correlated numbers per sample, and the biological answer — a concentration or a class label — is hidden in their pattern, not any single channel.


[REVIEW] Replace these with the lab’s actual application areas and one real example spectrum. Keep the framing: the measured object is a curve/vector, the biological target is a scalar or a label. This is the method-biology pairing for the whole unit.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
section: The data shape: wide and collinear
text:
The data shape: wide and collinear
Stack \(n\) samples, each measured at \(p\) wavelengths, into a matrix \(X\) (\(n \times p\)), with a target \(\mathbf{y}\) (a property to predict, or a class):
\[X = \begin{pmatrix} x_{11} & \cdots & x_{1p} \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ x_{n1} & \cdots & x_{np} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{pmatrix}\]
Two features dominate spectral data:

Wide: often \(p \gg n\) (far more wavelengths than samples).
Collinear: neighbouring wavelengths are highly correlated — they carry nearly the same information.

Ordinary least squares (lm) breaks here: with \(p \gg n\) and collinear columns, \(X^\top X\) is not invertible and the fit is unstable. This is exactly the problem the latent-variable methods from PCA and The OPLS model were built to solve.


[REVIEW] Tie back explicitly to the singular / non-invertible discussion in the Linear systems and PCA units — students met “no unique solution” there. The punchline: chemometrics is largely the art of regressing/classifying when the classical assumptions (n > p, independent predictors) fail. Verify the p >> n framing matches the datasets you plan to use; for some metabolomics setups n and p are closer.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Preprocessing comes first
Raw spectra carry nuisance variation — scatter, baseline drift, path-length differences — that has nothing to do with the biology. Standard preprocessing steps (named here for recognition; details belong to Chemometrics I / an expert pass):

Baseline / scatter correction: e.g. Standard Normal Variate (SNV), Multiplicative Scatter Correction (MSC).
Derivatives (Savitzky–Golay): sharpen overlapping peaks, remove slow baselines.
Centering / scaling: mean-centre columns; sometimes autoscale (unit variance) so no channel dominates by magnitude alone.







Important


Preprocessing choices are part of the model. They must be decided on the training data and re-applied identically to new data — never fit using information from the test set.





[REVIEW] This slide is deliberately a checklist, not a tutorial. An expert should expand each item and, crucially, warn about the leakage trap: choosing preprocessing by peeking at validation performance inflates optimism. The centering/scaling point connects to mean-centering in PCA.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Two questions, two model families
Almost every spectral application is one of two supervised tasks:









Question
Target \(\mathbf{y}\)
“How much / which?”
Typical methods




Regression (calibration)
continuous
How much analyte?
PCR, PLS regression


Classification
categorical
Which group / is it OK?
PLS-DA, LDA, SIMCA, \(k\)-NN



Both share the same trick learned earlier: project the wide, collinear \(X\) onto a few latent components first, then model in that low-dimensional space.

Regression fits a line/plane in latent space (property vs components).
Classification separates groups in latent space.

We take them in turn.


[REVIEW] Confirm the method lists are the ones the course wants to name. PLS regression and PLS-DA are the workhorses; PCR, LDA, SIMCA, kNN are worth naming for recognition. Do not over-promise depth — these are named, not derived, in a draft. The shared idea (latent projection) is the throughline from PCA / OPLS.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Multivariate calibration (regression)
Goal: predict a continuous property \(y\) (e.g. concentration) from a spectrum \(\mathbf{x}\).
The physical motivation is roughly linear: by the Beer–Lambert idea, absorbance rises with concentration, so a linear model in the (preprocessed) spectrum is a sensible starting point:
\[\hat{y} = b_0 + \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{b}\]
But we cannot fit \(\mathbf{b}\) directly by OLS (\(p \gg p\), collinear). Instead:

PCR (Principal Component Regression): run PCA on \(X\), keep the top components, regress \(y\) on the scores.
PLS regression: like PCR, but the components are chosen to align with \(y\) — they explain variation in \(X\) that is relevant to \(y\), not just the largest variation in \(X\).

PLS is the standard chemometrics calibration tool for exactly this reason.


[REVIEW] Verify the Beer-Lambert framing is stated carefully enough — it is a motivation for linearity, with real caveats (scattering, non-linearities). The PCR-vs-PLS contrast is the key concept: PCR’s components are y-blind, PLS’s are y-aware. This builds directly on The OPLS model unit. An expert should decide how much of the PLS algorithm (if any) to show.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Calibration in R (sketch)
Static illustration only — no packages are installed at render time, so nothing here is executed. The pls package provides plsr().
library(pls)

# X: n x p spectra (preprocessed), y: property to predict, in one data frame
fit <- plsr(y ~ ., data = train,
            ncomp = 10,           # try up to 10 latent components
            validation = "CV")    # built-in cross-validation

# how many components? read the cross-validated error, pick the elbow
validationplot(fit, val.type = "RMSEP")
summary(fit)

# predict a held-out set with the chosen number of components
yhat <- predict(fit, newdata = test, ncomp = 4)
The single most important decision is how many components to keep — too few underfits, too many overfits. That decision is made by validation, which is the rest of this lecture.

[REVIEW] Keep this as a sketch; an expert should replace train/test with a real dataset and show a real RMSEP curve. Do not present the number 4 or 10 as meaningful — they are placeholders illustrating the workflow. Emphasise verbally that ncomp is the tuning knob everything hinges on.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Choosing model complexity
Every latent-variable model has a complexity dial: the number of components (latent variables) kept.


Too few components: the model misses real signal — underfitting (high error everywhere).
Too many components: the model starts fitting noise in the training spectra — overfitting (training error keeps dropping, but error on new samples rises).

The training-set error alone cannot tell you where to stop — it always improves with more components. You need an estimate of error on unseen data. That is what cross-validation provides.

[REVIEW] This is the conceptual core of the day and should survive expert review largely intact. The bias-variance trade-off framed as “components dial”. Students have seen overfitting informally; here it is tied to a concrete knob. The figure is the classic two-curve plot.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
section: Validation: why a test set is non-negotiable
text:
Validation: why a test set is non-negotiable
A model that has seen a sample can predict it well — that proves nothing about future samples.

Calibration (training) error, RMSEC: error on the samples used to fit. Optimistic — always looks better than reality.
Prediction error, RMSEP: error on an independent set the model never touched during fitting or tuning. This is the number you report and trust.







Important


Anything fit on the data — preprocessing, scaling, component count, variable selection — must be decided without the test set. Otherwise the test set is contaminated and RMSEP is optimistic.



The honest workflow: train to fit, validate to tune, test once to report.


[REVIEW] Hammer the leakage point; it is the most common real-world mistake. If the dataset is small, a single held-out test set is noisy — nested cross-validation is the rigorous answer, which an expert may want to add. Keep the three-way split language (train/validate/test) consistent with whatever the ML-adjacent units use.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Cross-validation
When data are scarce, holding out one fixed test set wastes samples. \(k\)-fold cross-validation reuses them:

Split the samples into \(k\) roughly equal folds.
For each fold: train on the other \(k-1\) folds, predict the held-out fold.
Every sample is predicted exactly once, by a model that did not see it.
Combine the held-out predictions into one error estimate.


Leave-one-out (LOO): \(k = n\) (each sample its own fold) — common for small spectral sets.
In spectroscopy, samples measured together can be correlated; folds should respect that (e.g. do not split replicate scans of the same specimen across folds).



[REVIEW] The correlated-samples warning matters a lot in practice (replicates, batches, time-adjacent scans) and an expert should sharpen it — naive random folds leak information and give too-rosy CV error. “Venetian blinds” and contiguous-block schemes are worth naming for someone who knows the field.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
RMSEP and friends
The standard regression error is the root-mean-square error of prediction:
\[\mathrm{RMSEP} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\hat{y}_i - y_i\right)^2}\]

Same units as \(y\) (e.g. mg/mL) — directly interpretable.
Computed on an independent set → RMSEP; from cross-validation → RMSECV; on the training set → RMSEC (optimistic).

Report alongside it:

Bias: mean of \((\hat{y}_i - y_i)\) — a systematic offset (ideally \(\approx 0\)).
\(R^2\) / explained variance: fraction of variation in \(y\) captured.

Pick the component count that minimises RMSECV (or the simplest model within noise of the minimum — the “one-standard-error” idea).


[REVIEW] Formula is standard; confirm the department’s preferred definition (some use n-1 or degrees-of-freedom corrections, some report SEP separately from bias). The “simplest model within one SE of the minimum” is a defensible default but an expert should confirm it is the convention taught elsewhere in the course. Units-of-y point is the intuition anchor.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Classification of spectra
Goal: assign each spectrum to a class — tissue type, disease vs control, species of a microbial isolate, pass/fail.
Same latent-projection idea, now separating groups:

PLS-DA: encode the class as a numeric target and run PLS regression toward it; assign by the predicted value. The default chemometrics classifier.
LDA: find the direction that best separates classes (often applied after PCA to tame \(p \gg n\)).
SIMCA: build a separate PCA model per class; a new sample joins the class whose model it fits best (can also say “none of them”).
\(k\)-NN: classify by the nearest training spectra in (latent) space.

Validate with the same discipline: cross-validated misclassification rate, sensitivity/specificity, or a confusion matrix on an independent test set — never the training accuracy.


[REVIEW] Method roster to confirm. SIMCA’s “none of the above” ability is genuinely useful for biology (novel/contaminant samples) and worth keeping. For imbalanced classes, plain accuracy misleads — an expert should add the caveat and preferred metrics. Cross-validation caveats from the previous slides apply identically.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Calibration transfer
A model calibrated on instrument A often fails on instrument B — different detector, different day, different temperature — because the same sample produces a slightly different spectrum.
Calibration transfer adapts a model so it works across instruments/conditions without rebuilding it from scratch:

Measure a small set of transfer / standardisation samples on both instruments.
Learn a mapping that makes B’s spectra look like A’s (or adjust the model coefficients).
Standard families (named for recognition): Direct Standardization (DS) and Piecewise Direct Standardization (PDS), and other spectral-space corrections.

For a biologist this is the difference between a model that lives only in the lab that built it and one that transfers to a collaborator, a clinic, or next year’s instrument.


[REVIEW] This is a genuine expert topic — DS/PDS details, robustness, and how many standardisation samples are needed all need a specialist. Keep the biological framing (portability of a model) as the motivation. Do not state specific sample counts or performance figures; none here are sourced.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Multivariate process / quality control
Once a good latent-variable model exists, use it to monitor a process or screen samples in real time — multivariate statistical process control (MSPC).
Two complementary alarms per new sample:

Hotelling’s \(T^2\): how far the sample sits from the centre inside the model’s latent space — unusual but of a known type of variation.
\(Q\) / SPE (squared prediction error): how far the sample lies off the model subspace — variation the model has never seen (a new, possibly out-of-spec state).

Plot these on control charts with limits; a point past a limit flags a sample or batch for attention.


[REVIEW] T^2-vs-Q is the standard MSPC pairing and maps cleanly onto “distance within the model” vs “distance to the model”. Control-limit derivations (distributional assumptions) need an expert; state them only qualitatively here. Biology hook: fermentation/bioprocess monitoring, or QC screening of incoming samples.

title: Chemometrics II: applications
text:
Variable selection
Spectra have hundreds of channels, but often only some carry the relevant signal. Selecting variables (wavelengths) can:

improve interpretability — which spectral regions drive the prediction (a chemically/biologically meaningful band),
sometimes improve robustness by dropping noisy, uninformative channels,
but risks overfitting the selection itself if not validated properly.

Standard approaches, named for recognition:

VIP (Variable Importance in Projection) scores from a PLS model,
selectivity ratio, interval methods (iPLS), or search-based selection.








Important


Variable selection is part of model fitting. Select inside the cross-validation loop, not before it — otherwise the reported error is optimistic.




[REVIEW] The leakage warning here is the subtle one that even practitioners get wrong: selecting variables on the full dataset before CV double-dips. An expert should decide how much detail (VIP threshold conventions, wrapper vs filter) to include. Keep it honest that selection is not free.

title: Quiz: Chemometrics I — spectra as data
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of spectra as data. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. They need no computer.

Q1. In what sense is a single spectrum a vector? What do its coordinates and its dimension correspond to?






Hint





The instrument records absorbance at a discrete grid of wavelengths.









Answer





A spectrum is the list of absorbances at each measured wavelength, \(\mathbf{x} = (A(\lambda_1),\dots,A(\lambda_p)) \in \mathbb{R}^p\). Each wavelength is a coordinate, and the dimension \(p\) is the number of wavelengths measured (often several hundred to a few thousand). It is one point in a high-dimensional space.




Q2. State the Beer–Lambert law and say, in one sentence, why it makes linear models natural for spectroscopy.






Hint





Which quantity is proportional to which?









Answer





\(A = \varepsilon\ell c\): absorbance equals molar absorptivity × path length × concentration. Because absorbance is proportional to concentration (and absorbances of a mixture add), a spectrum is a linear function of the concentrations — so linear models are the physically correct choice.




Q3. A pure compound with \(\varepsilon\ell = 1500\ \text{M}^{-1}\) (at \(\ell = 1\ \text{cm}\)) gives absorbance \(A = 0.45\). What is the concentration? If you double the concentration, what is the new absorbance?






Hint





Rearrange \(A = \varepsilon\ell c\); then use proportionality.









Answer





\(c = A/(\varepsilon\ell) = 0.45/1500 = 3\times10^{-4}\ \text{M}\). Doubling the concentration doubles the absorbance (proportionality): \(A = 0.90\).




Q4. A measured spectrum contains three absorbing substances with pure-component spectra \(\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_2, \mathbf{s}_3\). Write the mixture spectrum, and name the linear-algebra operation it represents.






Hint





At each wavelength the absorbances add, each weighted by a concentration.









Answer





\(\mathbf{x} = c_1\mathbf{s}_1 + c_2\mathbf{s}_2 + c_3\mathbf{s}_3\). It is a linear combination of the pure-component spectra, with the concentrations as coefficients.




Q5. Match each preprocessing step to the artefact it primarily removes: (i) baseline correction, (ii) normalization, (iii) smoothing, (iv) first derivative.






Hint





Additive vs multiplicative vs random vs constant-offset-and-overlap.









Answer






baseline correction → additive offset/drift; (ii) normalization → multiplicative scaling (path length, particle size); (iii) smoothing → random noise; (iv) first derivative → constant baseline offset (and it sharpens overlapping peaks). A second derivative additionally removes a linear (sloping) baseline.





Q6. Why does taking a derivative of a spectrum remove a constant baseline, and what is the price you pay for it?






Hint





What is the derivative of a constant? What happens to noise when you difference?









Answer





A constant baseline adds the same value at every wavelength; the derivative of a constant is zero, so it drops out (discretely, \((x_{i+1}+b)-(x_i+b) = x_{i+1}-x_i\)). The price is noise amplification — differencing makes noise worse — which is why derivatives are computed together with smoothing (e.g. Savitzky–Golay).




Q7. You have \(n = 10\) calibration spectra measured at \(p = 900\) wavelengths. Why can you not just fit an ordinary least-squares regression of concentration on all 900 wavelengths?






Hint





Compare the number of unknown coefficients to the number of samples; think about inverting \(X^\top X\).









Answer





OLS would estimate 900 coefficients from only 10 samples. It needs to invert \(X^\top X\) (a \(900\times900\) matrix), which is singular when \(p \gg n\) — no unique solution, and infinitely many coefficient vectors fit the 10 samples perfectly while predicting garbage on new ones (overfitting). Adjacent wavelengths are also highly collinear, which destabilises OLS even further.




Q8. In one or two sentences, what does PLS do that ordinary regression does not, and how does it differ from doing PCA first (PCR)?






Hint





PLS builds a few components; what quantity do those components pay attention to?









Answer





PLS compresses the many correlated wavelengths into a few latent components — combinations of wavelengths — and regresses on those, avoiding the singular/ill-conditioned inversion. Unlike PCA (which chooses components to capture variance in \(X\) only, as in PCR), PLS chooses components that also correlate with the response \(\mathbf{y}\), aiming them at the quantity being predicted. The number of components is chosen by cross-validation.

title: Exercise: spectra as data
text:
Background
A spectrum is a vector. The instrument records absorbance \(A\) on a discrete grid of wavelengths \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_p\), so one spectrum is
\[\mathbf{x} = (A(\lambda_1),\ \dots,\ A(\lambda_p)) \in \mathbb{R}^p,\]
and \(n\) samples stack as rows of an \(n\times p\) matrix \(X\) (samples × wavelengths).
Beer–Lambert law. For a single absorbing substance, \[A = \varepsilon\,\ell\,c,\] with \(c\) concentration, \(\ell\) path length, and \(\varepsilon\) the molar absorptivity at that wavelength. Absorbance is proportional to concentration.
Mixtures add. With \(k\) substances, the absorbances add at every wavelength, so the whole spectrum is a linear combination of pure-component spectra \(\mathbf{s}_i\) weighted by concentrations: \[\mathbf{x} = c_1\mathbf{s}_1 + \dots + c_k\mathbf{s}_k.\]
Preprocessing removes chemistry-free artefacts before modelling:



Step
Removes
One-line idea




Baseline correction
additive offset/drift
subtract a baseline


Normalization
multiplicative scaling
divide by length or SD


Smoothing
random noise
average neighbours (Savitzky–Golay)


Derivative
baseline + peak overlap
differentiate along \(\lambda\)



Calibration predicts concentration from a spectrum with a linear model \(\hat y = b_0 + \mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{x}\). Ordinary least squares fails because \(p \gg n\) and adjacent wavelengths are collinear; PLS compresses wavelengths into a few response-aware components instead.

title: Exercise: spectra as data
text:
By hand
B1. (Beer–Lambert, one substance). A purified compound has molar absorptivity \(\varepsilon = 2000\ \text{M}^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}\) at its peak wavelength, measured in a cuvette of path length \(\ell = 1\ \text{cm}\). (a) A solution of concentration \(c = 3\times10^{-4}\ \text{M}\) is measured. What absorbance do you expect? (b) A different solution reads \(A = 0.9\). What is its concentration? (c) You halve the path length to \(0.5\ \text{cm}\) and re-measure the solution from (b). What absorbance now?
B2. (a calibration line). You measure absorbance at one wavelength for standards of known concentration:



\(c\) (mM)
0
1
2
4




\(A\)
0.00
0.20
0.40
0.80




Do these obey Beer–Lambert? What is the slope \(\varepsilon\ell\) (in absorbance per mM)?
An unknown reads \(A = 0.50\). Estimate its concentration.

B3. (a spectrum is a vector). Two samples are measured at \(p = 4\) wavelengths: \[\mathbf{x}_A = (0.1,\ 0.4,\ 0.2,\ 0.1), \qquad \mathbf{x}_B = (0.2,\ 0.8,\ 0.4,\ 0.2).\] (a) Compute the Euclidean distance \(\lVert \mathbf{x}_A - \mathbf{x}_B\rVert\). (b) Show that \(\mathbf{x}_B = 2\,\mathbf{x}_A\). What physical effect (from the lecture) could make one sample’s spectrum an exact multiple of another’s? (c) After vector normalization (divide each by its own length), would \(\mathbf{x}_A\) and \(\mathbf{x}_B\) be equal, or different? Explain without full computation.
B4. (mixtures add). Two pure components have spectra over \(p = 3\) wavelengths: \[\mathbf{s}_1 = (1,\ 0,\ 2), \qquad \mathbf{s}_2 = (0,\ 3,\ 1).\] (a) Write the mixture spectrum for concentrations \(c_1 = 2\), \(c_2 = 1\). (b) You observe a mixture spectrum \(\mathbf{x} = (3,\ 3,\ 7)\). Assuming it is \(c_1\mathbf{s}_1 + c_2\mathbf{s}_2\), find \(c_1\) and \(c_2\). (Hint: each wavelength gives one equation.) (c) In one sentence, why is knowing the pure-component spectra enough to turn spectroscopy into solving a linear system?
B5. (baseline correction). A spectrum over 5 wavelengths reads \[\mathbf{x} = (0.3,\ 0.7,\ 0.5,\ 0.9,\ 0.4).\] A second measurement of the same sample is shifted up by a constant baseline of \(0.2\): \[\mathbf{x}' = (0.5,\ 0.9,\ 0.7,\ 1.1,\ 0.6).\] (a) Apply constant-offset baseline correction by subtracting each spectrum’s own minimum. Write both corrected spectra. (b) Are the corrected spectra identical? Why is that the point of baseline correction?
B6. (a first derivative removes an offset). Take \(\mathbf{x} = (0.3,\ 0.7,\ 0.5,\ 0.9,\ 0.4)\) from B5. (a) Compute the first differences \(\Delta_i = x_{i+1} - x_i\) (four numbers). (b) Now do the same for the baseline-shifted \(\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + 0.2\). What do you notice, and why does this show a first derivative is blind to a constant baseline?
B7. (smoothing). Apply a moving average of window 3 to \(\mathbf{x} = (0.2,\ 0.8,\ 0.2,\ 0.8,\ 0.2)\), i.e. replace each interior point by the mean of itself and its two neighbours (leave the two ends out). (a) Write the three smoothed interior values. (b) The original alternates sharply; describe what smoothing did to that oscillation, and name the risk if the oscillation had been a real narrow peak.
B8. (why not ordinary regression). You have \(n = 8\) calibration samples, each a spectrum at \(p = 700\) wavelengths, and you want a linear model for concentration. (a) Why can ordinary least squares not give a unique coefficient vector here? (Think about \(p\) vs \(n\).) (b) Even if you had \(n = 1000\) samples, adjacent wavelengths are nearly identical columns of \(X\). What word describes this, and why does it still destabilise the coefficients? (c) In one sentence, what does PLS do differently that sidesteps both problems?

title: Exercise: spectra as data
text:
In R
The R below is illustrative — run it if you like, but the point is to connect the maths to code you can read. No spectroscopy packages are assumed.

A spectrum as a vector, a dataset as a matrix
# a tiny "dataset": 3 samples, 4 wavelengths
X <- matrix(c(0.1, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1,
              0.2, 0.8, 0.4, 0.2,
              0.15, 0.5, 0.25, 0.12),
            nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
dim(X)            # 3 4  -> 3 samples (rows), 4 wavelengths (cols)
X[1, ]            # the first spectrum, as a length-4 vector

# distance between two spectra (B3a)
sqrt(sum((X[1, ] - X[2, ])^2))


Beer–Lambert both ways (B1)
eps <- 2000; l <- 1
A_from_c <- function(c) eps * l * c
c_from_A <- function(A) A / (eps * l)

A_from_c(3e-4)    # expected absorbance
c_from_A(0.9)     # concentration from a reading


Build and unmix a mixture (B4)
s1 <- c(1, 0, 2)
s2 <- c(0, 3, 1)
mix <- 2 * s1 + 1 * s2      # c1 = 2, c2 = 1
mix                          # the mixture spectrum

# recover concentrations by solving the linear system S %*% c = x
S <- cbind(s1, s2)           # 3x2 pure-component matrix
x <- mix                     # observed mixture spectrum
# more equations (3) than unknowns (2): least-squares solve
solve(t(S) %*% S, t(S) %*% x)


Preprocessing on a toy spectrum
x  <- c(0.3, 0.7, 0.5, 0.9, 0.4)
xs <- x + 0.2                        # same sample, +0.2 baseline

# baseline correction: subtract each spectrum's own minimum (B5)
x  - min(x)
xs - min(xs)                          # identical to the line above

# first difference ~ first derivative (B6)
diff(x)
diff(xs)                              # identical: derivative kills the offset

# vector (L2) normalization (B3c)
x / sqrt(sum(x^2))

title: Exercise: spectra as data
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — Beer–Lambert both directions





\(A = \varepsilon\ell c\) rearranges to \(c = A/(\varepsilon\ell)\). Keep units consistent. Halving \(\ell\) halves \(A\) for the same \(c\), because \(A\) is proportional to \(\ell\) as well as \(c\).









Hint 2 — a calibration line





“Obeys Beer–Lambert” means \(A\) is a straight line through the origin in \(c\): \(A = (\varepsilon\ell)\,c\). Read the slope off any point, e.g. \(0.20/1 = 0.20\) absorbance per mM, and invert to get concentration from a new reading.









Hint 3 — spectra as vectors





Euclidean distance is \(\lVert\mathbf a-\mathbf b\rVert = \sqrt{\sum_i (a_i-b_i)^2}\) (the norm from Vectors and dot products). If \(\mathbf{x}_B = 2\mathbf{x}_A\) they point the same way but differ in length — think which multiplicative effect scales an entire spectrum. Vector normalization sets every spectrum’s length to 1, so two spectra on the same line become the same point.









Hint 4 — unmixing





A mixture spectrum is \(c_1\mathbf s_1 + c_2\mathbf s_2\). Writing it out wavelength by wavelength gives one linear equation per wavelength — a linear system in the unknowns \(c_1, c_2\). With more wavelengths than components the system is overdetermined; solve it in the least-squares sense (this is exactly what a linear model does). See solve.









Hint 5 — baseline correction





A constant baseline adds the same number to every entry. Subtracting the spectrum’s minimum cancels a constant offset, so two measurements that differ only by a constant collapse onto each other. This is the whole idea: same chemistry → same corrected spectrum.









Hint 6 — first derivative vs a constant baseline





The first difference \(x_{i+1}-x_i\) of a shifted spectrum \((x+b)\) is \((x_{i+1}+b)-(x_i+b) = x_{i+1}-x_i\) — the constant \(b\) cancels. That is the discrete version of “the derivative of a constant is zero.” See diff.









Hint 7 — moving average





Each interior smoothed value is the mean of three numbers: the point and its two neighbours, e.g. the second point becomes \((x_1+x_2+x_3)/3\). Averaging cancels an up-down-up oscillation. The risk: if that oscillation were a real narrow peak, smoothing would flatten it too — the smoothing/noise trade-off.









Hint 8 — why OLS fails





Ordinary least squares must invert \(X^\top X\), a \(p\times p\) matrix. With \(p > n\) it is singular (no unique solution — recall singular matrices from the linear-systems unit). With correlated columns (adjacent wavelengths) it is near-singular even when \(n>p\): this is collinearity, and it makes the coefficients huge and unstable. PLS avoids both by regressing on a few combinations of wavelengths chosen to correlate with the response.

title: Exercise: spectra as data
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. (a) \(A = \varepsilon\ell c = 2000 \times 1 \times 3\times10^{-4} = 0.6\). (b) \(c = A/(\varepsilon\ell) = 0.9 / (2000\times1) = 4.5\times10^{-4}\ \text{M}\). (c) Absorbance is proportional to path length, so halving \(\ell\) halves \(A\): \(A = 0.9 \times 0.5 = 0.45\). (Concentration is unchanged; only the path shortened.)
B2. (a) Yes: \(A\) is exactly proportional to \(c\) (0, 0.20, 0.40, 0.80 for 0, 1, 2, 4 mM), a straight line through the origin. Slope \(\varepsilon\ell = 0.20/1 = 0.20\) absorbance per mM (every point gives the same ratio). (b) \(c = A/\text{slope} = 0.50 / 0.20 = 2.5\ \text{mM}\).
B3. (a) \(\mathbf{x}_A - \mathbf{x}_B = (0.1-0.2,\ 0.4-0.8,\ 0.2-0.4,\ 0.1-0.2) = (-0.1,-0.4,-0.2,-0.1)\). Distance \(=\sqrt{0.01+0.16+0.04+0.01} = \sqrt{0.22} \approx 0.469\). (b) Each entry of \(\mathbf{x}_B\) is twice the corresponding entry of \(\mathbf{x}_A\), so \(\mathbf{x}_B = 2\mathbf{x}_A\). A multiplicative effect — a longer path length (Beer–Lambert: \(A \propto \ell\)) or denser/thicker sample — scales the entire spectrum by a common factor. (c) They would be equal. Both lie on the same line through the origin (one is a scalar multiple of the other), so dividing each by its own length lands them on the same unit vector. Normalization removes exactly the multiplicative difference between them.
B4. (a) \(2\mathbf{s}_1 + 1\mathbf{s}_2 = 2(1,0,2) + (0,3,1) = (2,0,4) + (0,3,1) = (2,3,5)\). (b) Wavelength by wavelength, \(c_1\mathbf s_1 + c_2\mathbf s_2 = (c_1,\ 3c_2,\ 2c_1 + c_2)\). Matching to \((3,3,7)\): wavelength 1: \(c_1 = 3\); wavelength 2: \(3c_2 = 3 \Rightarrow c_2 = 1\); wavelength 3 checks: \(2(3)+1 = 7\) ✓. So \(c_1 = 3\), \(c_2 = 1\). (c) Because a mixture spectrum is a linear combination of the pure spectra, each wavelength contributes one linear equation in the unknown concentrations — so recovering concentrations is just solving a linear system.
B5. (a) \(\min(\mathbf{x}) = 0.3\), so \(\mathbf{x} - 0.3 = (0.0,\ 0.4,\ 0.2,\ 0.6,\ 0.1)\). For \(\mathbf{x}'\), \(\min = 0.5\), so \(\mathbf{x}' - 0.5 = (0.0,\ 0.4,\ 0.2,\ 0.6,\ 0.1)\). (b) They are identical. The two measurements differed only by a constant baseline, and subtracting each spectrum’s own minimum removes that constant — so the same chemistry yields the same corrected spectrum, which is exactly the goal of baseline correction.
B6. (a) \(\Delta = (0.7-0.3,\ 0.5-0.7,\ 0.9-0.5,\ 0.4-0.9) = (0.4,\ -0.2,\ 0.4,\ -0.5)\). (b) For \(\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + 0.2\), every difference is \((x_{i+1}+0.2)-(x_i+0.2) = x_{i+1}-x_i\) — the same four numbers \((0.4,-0.2,0.4,-0.5)\). The constant baseline cancels in the differencing, so a first derivative is blind to a constant offset (the discrete “derivative of a constant is zero”).
B7. (a) Interior means of window 3: point 2 \(\to (0.2+0.8+0.2)/3 = 0.4\); point 3 \(\to (0.8+0.2+0.8)/3 = 0.6\); point 4 \(\to (0.2+0.8+0.2)/3 = 0.4\). Smoothed interior \(= (0.4,\ 0.6,\ 0.4)\). (b) The sharp up-down-up oscillation was flattened toward its average — noise-like wiggles are suppressed. The risk: had that oscillation been a genuine narrow peak, the same averaging would have blunted or erased it. This is the smoothing/noise trade-off (a wider window smooths more but loses more real detail).
B8. (a) OLS requires inverting \(X^\top X\), a \(700\times700\) matrix, but with only \(n = 8\) samples \(X^\top X\) has rank at most 8 and is singular — there is no unique solution, and infinitely many coefficient vectors fit the 8 samples perfectly while predicting nonsense on new ones (overfitting). (b) Collinearity (multicollinearity): adjacent wavelengths are almost identical columns, so \(X^\top X\) is near-singular even when \(n > p\). Its near-zero eigenvalues blow up the inverse, making the coefficients enormous and wildly unstable to tiny changes in the data. (c) PLS builds a few latent components — combinations of wavelengths chosen to correlate with the response — and regresses on those, so it never inverts the ill-conditioned \(X^\top X\) and is untroubled by having many correlated wavelengths.

title: Exercise: spectra as data
text:
Where this leads

Chemometrics II: using spectra for classification (which class/species/grade is this sample?), honest model validation, and interpreting which wavelengths drive a prediction back to chemistry.
Principal component analysis: PLS is PCA’s response-aware cousin; the PCA unit builds the compression idea that both Principal Component Regression and PLS rely on.
Linear models: calibration \(\hat y = b_0 + \mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{x}\) is a linear model on a wide, collinear design — the reason regularised and latent-variable regressions exist.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
About this lecture
Your earlier statistics was almost certainly frequentist: fixed (but unknown) parameters, p-values, confidence intervals. Today we meet the other big framework — Bayesian reasoning — and see how they differ.

Probability as a degree of belief, updated by data — not just a long-run frequency.
Bayes’ rule in one line: \(\text{posterior} \propto \text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}\).
Frequentist vs Bayesian: fixed parameters + p-values vs distributions of belief + credible intervals.
One worked biology example: estimating a proportion (fraction of cells expressing a marker) with a prior.
Why a biologist might want this: honest uncertainty, using prior knowledge, and a natural fit for hierarchy.

This is a concept and intuition day. The maths stays light; the goal is to think in the Bayesian way and read a posterior.

The one message for today: there are two coherent ways to do statistics, and the students have only seen one of them. Frequentist statistics treats the parameter as a fixed unknown and asks “how surprising is my data?”; Bayesian statistics treats the parameter as uncertain and asks “what should I now believe about it?”. Everything else — Bayes’ rule, priors, posteriors, credible intervals — hangs off that shift in what “probability” means. Keep it conceptual; the algebra is deliberately kept to one conjugate example so nobody drowns in integrals. Tell them the exam-relevant skill is computing a small posterior by hand and reading a credible interval, not deriving anything.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
A note on this block







Provisional block


This Bayesian statistics block is provisional. It may be moved to a later, dedicated statistics / machine-learning course rather than staying in this linear-algebra-and-stats course. Treat it as a self-contained introduction: nothing later in this course hard-depends on it.




We still include it here because Bayesian thinking underlies a lot of modern omics analysis (differential expression, variant calling, hierarchical models), and the contrast with frequentist reasoning sharpens both.

Be upfront that this block might migrate to the ML course. It is not load-bearing for the rest of the linear-algebra material, so students who find it hard should not panic — it will not block later units. Still worth teaching because so many Bioconductor tools (limma/DESeq2 shrinkage, variant callers, phylogenetics) are quietly Bayesian, and understanding the vocabulary pays off when reading methods sections.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
A biology picture first
You stain a population of cells for a marker and count, under the microscope, how many are positive. Out of 20 cells, 6 are positive.

Your instinct (frequentist): the fraction is \(\hat p = 6/20 = 0.30\). Done.
But you have only 20 cells. How sure are you? Could the true fraction be 0.2? 0.45?
And you are not starting from nothing: in three previous experiments this marker sat around 20%. Should that count?

Frequentist analysis gives you a single number plus a confidence interval and ignores the earlier experiments. Bayesian analysis gives you a full distribution of belief over \(p\) and lets you fold in what you already knew.


Anchor everything in this one scene: counting positive cells. The frequentist reflex is p-hat = 6/20 = 0.3, full stop. Push on two discomforts a biologist actually feels: (1) 20 cells is a small sample, so how confident are we, and (2) we ran this before and have prior knowledge — throwing it away feels wasteful. Those two discomforts are exactly what the Bayesian machinery addresses: a whole posterior distribution instead of a point, and a principled way to include the prior. Do not write any formulas yet; just seed the motivation.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Two meanings of “probability”
The split between the two schools comes from what the word probability even means.









Frequentist
Bayesian




Probability is…
a long-run frequency
a degree of belief


The parameter \(p\) is…
fixed, just unknown
uncertain — described by a distribution


Data is…
random (repeatable)
the fixed thing you actually saw


A result is…
a point estimate + CI, a p-value
a posterior distribution



Frequentist question: “If \(p\) were really 0.2, how surprising is my data?” Bayesian question: “Given my data, what should I now believe about \(p\)?”


This is the philosophical fork, and it is worth stating slowly. Frequentists reserve “probability” for things that can be repeated — coin flips, cells sampled — so they will never write P(p = 0.3): the parameter is fixed, not random, so it has no probability distribution. Bayesians allow “probability” to describe uncertainty/belief about anything, including a fixed-but-unknown parameter, so P(p) is perfectly meaningful. That single move is what lets Bayesians put a distribution on the parameter and update it. Everything downstream (priors, posteriors, credible intervals) follows. Emphasise the two contrasting questions at the bottom — they are the cleanest one-line summary.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Bayes’ rule
Bayes’ rule is just the definition of conditional probability, rearranged. For a hypothesis \(H\) (a value of \(p\)) and observed data \(D\):
\[P(H \mid D) = \frac{P(D \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(D)}\]
Read left to right:

\(P(H)\) — the prior: what you believed about \(H\) before the data.
\(P(D \mid H)\) — the likelihood: how probable the data is if \(H\) were true.
\(P(H \mid D)\) — the posterior: your updated belief after seeing the data.
\(P(D)\) — the evidence: a normalising constant so the posterior sums to 1.


Reassure them this is not exotic: Bayes’ rule is a one-line consequence of P(A and B) = P(A|B)P(B) = P(B|A)P(A), which they have seen. The novelty is not the algebra, it is applying it with H = “a value of the parameter” and D = “the data” — that is the conceptual leap. Name each of the four pieces slowly and in plain English. The denominator P(D) is just whatever number makes the posterior a proper distribution (integrate the numerator over all H); for our purposes it is a normaliser we can often ignore, which is the next slide.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Posterior \(\propto\) prior \(\times\) likelihood
The denominator \(P(D)\) does not depend on \(H\) — it is the same for every hypothesis. So the shape of the posterior is fixed entirely by the numerator:
\[\underbrace{P(H \mid D)}_{\text{posterior}} \ \propto\ \underbrace{P(D \mid H)}_{\text{likelihood}} \times \underbrace{P(H)}_{\text{prior}}\]
(“\(\propto\)” means “proportional to” — equal up to a constant that we fix at the end so the total probability is 1.)
This is the sentence to memorise:

Posterior belief = prior belief, reweighted by how well each hypothesis explains the data.

Where the data is strong, the likelihood dominates and the prior barely matters. Where the data is weak (few cells!), the prior still has a say.


This is the single most useful line in the lecture — put it on a card. The proportionality trick matters because it lets you reason about the posterior’s shape without computing the ugly normalising integral P(D). Stress the interpretation at the bottom: the prior is your starting belief, the likelihood is the data’s verdict on each hypothesis, and multiplying them reweights the prior toward hypotheses that explain the data well. Then the crucial practical point for biologists: with lots of data the likelihood swamps the prior (Bayesian and frequentist answers converge), but with little data (our 20 cells) the prior genuinely influences the answer — which is a feature, not a bug, if the prior is honest.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Our example, set up
Estimate \(p\) = the true fraction of marker-positive cells. Data: \(k = 6\) positive out of \(n = 20\).
Likelihood — counting positives out of a fixed number of cells is a binomial experiment:
\[P(k \mid p) = \binom{n}{k}\, p^{k}\,(1-p)^{\,n-k} \ \propto\ p^{6}(1-p)^{14}\]
As a function of \(p\), this is peaked at the frequentist estimate \(\hat p = k/n = 0.30\).
Prior — we need a distribution over \(p \in [0,1]\). The natural choice is a Beta distribution:
\[p \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta), \qquad P(p) \propto p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}\]


Set up the two ingredients concretely. The likelihood is binomial because we count k positives in n independent cells with the same probability p — exactly the binomial story they met in earlier statistics. Drop the binomial coefficient when we write the proportionality, since it does not involve p. The prior needs to live on [0,1] because p is a proportion, and the Beta family is the standard flexible choice there. Show that alpha and beta act like “prior counts”: Beta(1,1) is flat/uniform (no prior opinion), Beta(2,8) leans toward small p (our previous ~20% experiments), Beta(8,4) leans large. Do not derive the Beta; treat it as the go-to distribution for a probability, analogous to how the Gaussian is the go-to for an unbounded quantity.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Why Beta? It multiplies cleanly
Look at the shapes: prior \(\propto p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}\) and likelihood \(\propto p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}\). Multiply them:
\[\text{posterior} \propto p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}\cdot p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k} = p^{(\alpha+k)-1}(1-p)^{(\beta+n-k)-1}\]
That is another Beta distribution:
\[p \mid \text{data} \ \sim\ \text{Beta}(\alpha + k,\ \beta + n - k)\]
The prior and posterior are the same family — the Beta is the conjugate prior for the binomial. The update rule is beautifully simple:
\[\alpha \to \alpha + (\text{successes}), \qquad \beta \to \beta + (\text{failures}).\]
You can read \(\alpha, \beta\) as pseudo-counts: prior “imagined” successes and failures, to which the real data adds.

This is the one piece of algebra worth doing on the board, because it is genuinely satisfying and requires only adding exponents. Multiplying prior by likelihood keeps the p(…)(1-p)(…) form, so the posterior is Beta with updated parameters. Define “conjugate prior”: a prior that yields a posterior in the same family, which makes the update pure arithmetic (no integrals). Then the intuition that makes it stick: alpha and beta are pseudo-counts of prior successes and failures; the data just adds its real successes and failures on top. Beta(1,1) = 1 pseudo-success + 1 pseudo-failure = barely any prior weight, so the data dominates. Conjugacy is special to nice pairings; in general the posterior has no closed form and we sample it (MCMC) — mention only as a pointer, do not teach it.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Turning the crank, two priors
Data: \(k = 6\), \(n - k = 14\).
Uniform prior Beta(1,1) — “no opinion”: \[\text{posterior} = \text{Beta}(1+6,\ 1+14) = \text{Beta}(7, 15), \quad \text{mean } \tfrac{7}{22} \approx 0.318\]
Informative prior Beta(2,8) — centred near the earlier \(\sim 20\%\): \[\text{posterior} = \text{Beta}(2+6,\ 8+14) = \text{Beta}(8, 22), \quad \text{mean } \tfrac{8}{30} \approx 0.267\]
(The mean of \(\text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\) is \(\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)\).)
The informative prior pulls the estimate down toward the earlier experiments — and with only 20 cells, that pull is real. Collect 200 cells and both posteriors would sit almost on top of the data.


Now make it numeric and concrete. Two priors, same data, worked in one line each thanks to conjugacy. The uniform-prior posterior mean 0.318 is basically the data estimate 0.30 (nudged slightly by the +1,+1 pseudo-counts). The informative-prior posterior mean 0.267 sits between the prior’s 0.2 and the data’s 0.3 — a compromise weighted by how much information each carries. Hammer the small-sample point: with n=20 the prior’s few pseudo-counts are a meaningful fraction of the total, so they move the answer; with n=200 the data’s 200 counts swamp the prior and both posteriors collapse onto ~0.30. This is the honest behaviour we want: priors matter exactly when data is scarce, and fade away when data is plentiful.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Credible interval vs confidence interval
Bayesian uncertainty comes straight from the posterior. A 95% credible interval is any interval holding 95% of the posterior probability:
\[P(\,0.14 \le p \le 0.52 \mid \text{data}\,) = 0.95 \quad (\text{for Beta}(7,15))\]
You are allowed to say the honest sentence: “there is a 95% probability that \(p\) lies in this interval.”
A frequentist 95% confidence interval does not mean that. It means: if you repeated the whole experiment many times, 95% of the intervals so constructed would contain the true fixed \(p\). Any single interval either contains \(p\) or does not — no probability attached.




Credible interval
Confidence interval




Statement about
the parameter
the procedure


“95% probability \(p\) is inside”
✓ allowed
✗ not allowed





This is the contrast students most often get wrong, so slow down. The credible interval is a direct probability statement about the parameter — legal for a Bayesian because p has a distribution. The confidence interval is a statement about the long-run behaviour of the interval-construction procedure, NOT about any single interval; strictly, a given 95% CI has already either caught p or missed it, with no probability. Most scientists secretly interpret their confidence intervals as credible intervals — the Bayesian version is the interpretation people actually want, made legitimate. Note the numbers here are illustrative (from qbeta on Beta(7,15)); the exact endpoints come from the R on the next slide.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
section: Try it: updating a prior with cells
text:
Try it: updating a prior with cells




Live version of the last three slides. Start on the preset “6/20 flat”: the posterior (solid red) sits almost on the scaled likelihood (dotted orange), and the Bayesian and frequentist bars below are close, matching the Beta(7,15) numbers from before. Click “6/20 Beta(2,8)”: the blue dashed prior appears near 0.2 and the posterior moves down to about 0.27, while the frequentist bar does not move at all, because it ignores the prior. Then “60/200 Beta(2,8)”: same fraction, ten times the cells, and the prior hardly matters any more; both bars are narrow and nearly agree. Show the danger case with “6/20 wrong prior” (Beta(40,10), 50 pseudo-counts centred at 0.8): the posterior lands between prior and data, far from 0.3; even “60/200 wrong prior” is still pulled visibly. Point at the readout line “prior share of counts” as the one-number summary of how much the prior weighs. If time allows, press “no data” and then “+10 random cells” a few times to watch the posterior narrow as cells accumulate (tick “show true p” to reveal the 0.3 used for the simulation).

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
p-value vs posterior probability
Suppose you care whether the true fraction exceeds 25%.

Frequentist: set up \(H_0: p = 0.25\), compute a p-value = probability of data at least this extreme if \(H_0\) were true. A small p-value means “the data would be surprising under \(H_0\).” It does not tell you \(P(H_0)\).
Bayesian: just read it off the posterior: \[P(p > 0.25 \mid \text{data}) = \int_{0.25}^{1} \text{Beta}(p;\,7,15)\, dp\] a direct probability that the hypothesis is true, given your data.

The Bayesian answers the question people think a p-value answers.


Reinforce the deepest and most common misreading in all of applied statistics: a p-value is P(data this extreme | H0), NOT P(H0 | data). It measures surprise under the null, not the probability the null is true. The Bayesian posterior gives you exactly P(hypothesis | data), the quantity everyone actually wants. Show that once you have the posterior Beta(7,15), a hypothesis like “p > 0.25” is just an area under the curve — one pbeta call. Do not turn this into a p-value-bashing rant; the point is that the two frameworks answer genuinely different questions, and the Bayesian question is often the scientifically natural one.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
The same computation in R
Everything above is a couple of built-in functions. (Static examples — nothing to install.)
k <- 6; n <- 20

# Frequentist point estimate
p_hat <- k / n                     # 0.30

# Bayesian update with a uniform prior Beta(1, 1)
a0 <- 1; b0 <- 1
a  <- a0 + k                       # 7   (prior successes + observed)
b  <- b0 + (n - k)                 # 15  (prior failures  + observed)

a / (a + b)                        # posterior mean            -> 0.318
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b)       # 95% credible interval     -> ~0.14 .. 0.52
1 - pbeta(0.25, a, b)              # P(p > 0.25 | data)        -> ~0.75
# An informative prior Beta(2, 8) (earlier experiments, ~20% positive)
a0 <- 2; b0 <- 8
a  <- a0 + k                       # 8
b  <- b0 + (n - k)                 # 22
a / (a + b)                        # posterior mean            -> 0.267

Show that the whole lecture reduces to arithmetic plus qbeta/pbeta — no special package, no MCMC, because conjugacy gives a closed form. Walk the first block: a and b are the updated Beta parameters, a/(a+b) is the posterior mean, qbeta gives credible-interval endpoints (the quantiles), and 1 - pbeta(0.25, a, b) is the posterior probability that p exceeds 0.25. The second block just swaps the prior and re-runs the same two lines. Emphasise these are static illustrations (no packages are installed at render time); students run them in their own session. The exercise has them reproduce these numbers and vary the prior.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
section: Why a biologist might go Bayesian
text:
Why a biologist might go Bayesian

Honest uncertainty. You get a full posterior, not a lone point estimate — and a credible interval you are actually allowed to interpret as “where the parameter probably is.”
Use what you already know. Prior experiments, known biology, or literature values enter formally through the prior instead of being ignored or hand-waved.
Small samples behave sensibly. With few cells the prior gently regularises the estimate; with many cells the data takes over automatically.
Natural hierarchy. Genes within pathways, cells within patients, patients within cohorts — Bayesian hierarchical models let lower levels “borrow strength” from the group, which is exactly how modern tools shrink noisy per-gene estimates in differential expression.


Sell the practical upside, tied to omics. Honest uncertainty: the posterior and credible interval say what scientists actually mean. Prior knowledge: biology is rarely a blank slate, and the prior is the formal slot for what you already know (used carefully). Small samples: the prior acts as principled regularisation, so a gene seen in three cells does not get a wild estimate. Hierarchy is the big one for genomics: hierarchical/partial-pooling models let a noisy per-gene estimate borrow strength from the distribution of all genes — this is exactly the empirical-Bayes shrinkage inside tools like limma and DESeq2, even if those are not taught here. Keep it as motivation, not a how-to.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Being fair to the frequentist
Bayesian is not automatically “better.” Trade-offs:

The prior is a choice, and a bad or overconfident prior biases the answer. You must be able to defend it — and check how much it matters (sensitivity analysis).
Frequentist methods are fast, standard, and prior-free — for a large, clean dataset the two usually agree, and a t-test is simpler than a model.
Computation. Only lucky (conjugate) cases give a formula; realistic models need MCMC sampling — more machinery, more that can go wrong.
Reproducibility. A frequentist pipeline has fewer subjective knobs, which some fields prefer.

Rule of thumb: lots of clean data → they agree; little data, strong prior knowledge, or nested structure → Bayesian earns its keep.

Guard against the common student overcorrection (“Bayesian is just correct and p-values are wrong”). Both frameworks are coherent and useful. The prior is a real responsibility: a sharp prior in the wrong place will drag the answer, so honesty demands reporting it and doing a sensitivity check (does the conclusion survive a weaker prior?).
