Frequentist tools are prior-free, fast, and standard, and with abundant data the posterior is dominated by the likelihood so both schools converge anyway. The cost of going Bayesian in realistic models is computational — MCMC and its diagnostics. Give them the practical rule of thumb at the bottom as the decision heuristic. This mirrors the course’s “honest about what we defer/assume” principle.

title: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Probability
frequentist = frequency; Bayesian = degree of belief


Parameter \(p\)
frequentist: fixed unknown; Bayesian: has a distribution


Bayes’ rule
\(P(H\mid D) = P(D\mid H)P(H)/P(D)\)


Working form
posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior


Prior/likelihood
Beta\((\alpha,\beta)\) prior, binomial likelihood


Update (conjugate)
Beta\((\alpha+k,\ \beta+n-k)\) — add successes/failures


Posterior mean
\(\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)\)


Credible interval
“95% probability \(p\) is inside” — allowed


Confidence interval
statement about the procedure, not the parameter


p-value
\(P(\text{data}\mid H_0)\), not \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\)


When it matters
small data / strong prior / hierarchy



Next: work the cell-counting posterior by hand and in R in the exercise, then the quiz.

The summary is the revision card. Drill the pipeline verbally one more time: pick a prior Beta(alpha,beta), count successes k and failures n-k, add them to get the posterior Beta(alpha+k, beta+n-k), read the mean alpha/(alpha+beta), and get intervals/tail probabilities from qbeta/pbeta. Re-state the two interpretation traps (credible vs confidence, p-value vs posterior) because those are the conceptual exam questions. Close on the decision rule: Bayesian pays off with little data, real prior knowledge, or hierarchical structure; otherwise the frameworks largely agree. Remind them this block is provisional and self-contained.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
text:
About this lecture
In the linear algebra block you fitted a straight line by least squares: one best line, one number per coefficient. Today we ask a different question — how sure are we? — and answer it by fitting the same line the Bayesian way.

The model is unchanged: \(y = a + b\,x + \text{noise}\). What changes is the answer: each coefficient becomes a distribution, not a single number.
Put priors on the intercept \(a\), slope \(b\), and noise scale \(\sigma\); combine with the data (likelihood) to get the posterior.
Read a slope as “there is a 96% chance it is positive” instead of a bare point estimate and a p-value.
Predict a new observation with uncertainty — a credible band, not just a line.
Biology: does a gene’s expression rise with donor age? With only a handful of samples, honest uncertainty matters more than a single best-fit slope.


The one-sentence pitch: same line, honest uncertainty. Students already know how to get the best-fit line (least squares, the normal equations from the linear algebra block). The new idea is that instead of one number per coefficient we carry a whole distribution, which lets us make probability statements about the slope and put error bars on predictions. Keep reassuring them that the model equation is identical to ordinary regression — only the machinery for answering “how confident?” is new. This is concept-plus-tooling day: understand prior/likelihood/posterior for a line, and read what brms hands back.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
section: A note on where this block sits
text:
A note on where this block sits







Provisional block


This Bayesian statistics block is provisional. It may be moved into a later statistics / machine-learning course rather than staying in this one. Treat the Bayesian machinery here as an enrichment of the least-squares fitting you already met — the core, examinable skill remains the by-hand linear fit from the linear algebra block. Nothing here is assumed by later units in this course.





Be upfront with students and reviewers: the placement of the whole Bayesian block is not settled. It builds on the frequentist regression they already have and could equally live in a dedicated stats/ML course. Say plainly that the examinable core is the least-squares fit; the Bayesian layer is enrichment. This keeps expectations calibrated and flags to any reviewer that dependencies must stay one-directional (this block leans on earlier blocks, nothing earlier leans on it).

title: Fitting equations (regression)
text:
A biology picture first
We measure expression of an ageing-associated gene (normalised RNA-seq, log scale) in blood from a small cohort of donors, and plot it against age.

The cloud slopes gently upward: older donors tend to have higher expression.
But there are only ~15 donors, and the points are scattered. Is the upward slope real, or could a flat line fit almost as well?
A single best-fit line cannot answer that. We need the range of slopes the data are compatible with.

The biological questions are really questions about uncertainty: Is the slope different from zero? By how much, plausibly? What expression should we expect for a new 70-year-old, and how tightly?


Anchor everything in a concrete, small-n biological problem before any formalism. Small n is deliberate: it is exactly where a single least-squares line is misleading and where honest uncertainty pays off. Emphasise that the interesting biological questions (is expression changing with age? how much? predict a new donor) are all uncertainty questions. Draw several plausible lines through the sparse cloud to make the point that many slopes are compatible with the data. This motivates wanting a distribution over slopes rather than one slope.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
section: The model: a line plus noise
text:
The model: a line plus noise
We assume each donor’s expression \(y_i\) is a straight-line function of age \(x_i\) plus random scatter:
\[y_i = a + b\,x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \sigma^2)\]
Three unknowns to learn from the data:

\(a\) — the intercept (expression at \(x=0\), or at a centred reference age),
\(b\) — the slope (change in expression per year of age); this is the biology we care about,
\(\sigma\) — the noise scale: how far points scatter around the line (donor-to-donor variability, measurement error).

This is the same model as ordinary linear regression. The Bayesian and least-squares approaches differ only in what they report about \(a\), \(b\), \(\sigma\).


Write the model and name all three parameters, stressing that sigma is a parameter too, not a nuisance to be swept away — its size controls how confident predictions can be. Interpret the slope in biological units (change in log-expression per year) because coefficients are only meaningful with units attached. Reiterate the through-line: identical model, different accounting of uncertainty. Mention centring age (subtracting the mean) so the intercept is interpretable as expression at the average age rather than at the biologically meaningless age zero.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
text:
Recap: the least-squares fit
From the linear algebra block, the least-squares line minimises the sum of squared residuals. Stacking the data into a design matrix \(X\) (a column of 1s for \(a\), a column of ages for \(b\)), the best-fit coefficients solve the normal equations:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}\]
In R this is one call:
fit_ls <- lm(expr ~ age, data = donors)
coef(fit_ls)      # (Intercept)  age   -> point estimates of a and b
confint(fit_ls)   # 95% confidence intervals
This gives one number for \(a\) and one for \(b\) (plus a confidence interval and a p-value). It is fast, familiar, and often enough.


Deliberately re-derive the connection to linear algebra: least squares is exactly the normal equations they solved by hand, beta_hat = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y. Show that lm() is the production tool for it. The point of this slide is continuity — the Bayesian fit is not a replacement or a rival, it is the same fit seen through a probabilistic lens. Note in passing that under Gaussian noise the least-squares estimate coincides with the maximum-likelihood estimate; this sets up the likelihood on a later slide. Keep it short; they know this material.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
section: What least squares does — and doesn’t — give
text:
What least squares does — and doesn’t — give
Least squares hands you a point estimate: the single most-consistent \(a\) and \(b\).

A confidence interval and p-value come with it, but their interpretation is subtle: the 95% refers to the procedure over hypothetical repeated experiments, not to this slope.
It gives no direct probability statement about the parameter, e.g. you cannot say “there is a 96% probability the slope is positive.”
Incorporating prior knowledge (we already know ageing genes change slowly) is awkward.
With few data points, the point estimate can look deceptively precise.

The Bayesian version fixes exactly these: it returns a full distribution for each parameter, so probability statements and honest prediction bands come for free.

This is the motivational hinge. Be careful and correct about the frequentist confidence interval: the 95% is a property of the long-run procedure, not a probability about the fixed-but-unknown parameter. Students almost always misread a CI as “95% probability the parameter is in here” — that misreading is actually the Bayesian credible interval, which is what they will get today. So the Bayesian output matches the intuition people already wrongly attach to CIs. Also flag prior knowledge and small-n as the practical wins. Do not disparage frequentism; frame Bayes as answering a directly probabilistic question.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
section: The Bayesian shift: parameters as distributions
text:
The Bayesian shift: parameters as distributions
Frequentist: \(a\), \(b\), \(\sigma\) are fixed unknown numbers; the data are random.
Bayesian: we describe our uncertainty about \(a\), \(b\), \(\sigma\) with probability distributions, and update them using data via Bayes’ theorem (from the prior/likelihood/posterior unit):
\[\underbrace{p(\theta \mid \text{data})}_{\text{posterior}} \ \propto\ \underbrace{p(\text{data} \mid \theta)}_{\text{likelihood}} \times \underbrace{p(\theta)}_{\text{prior}}\]
Here \(\theta = (a, b, \sigma)\). The output is the posterior: a distribution over all three parameters at once that says which combinations are plausible given the data.


State the philosophical switch cleanly, then immediately ground it in Bayes’ theorem, which they met in the prior/likelihood/posterior unit. The key mental move: uncertainty about a parameter is itself represented by a distribution. Read the theorem in words - posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. Stress that the posterior is joint over (a, b, sigma); we usually look at one coefficient at a time (a marginal), but the machinery handles their correlations. Keep the proportionality sign honest: the missing constant (the evidence) is what makes it a proper distribution, and is what MCMC lets us avoid computing directly.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
section: Priors: what we believe before the data
text:
Priors: what we believe before the data
A prior encodes what is plausible for each parameter before seeing this dataset. Weakly-informative priors are a good default — wide enough not to force a conclusion, tight enough to rule out the absurd.
\[a \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ 5), \qquad b \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ 0.1), \qquad \sigma \sim \text{Exponential}(1)\]

Intercept \(a\): centred, broad — expression at the mean age could be a range of values.
Slope \(b\): centred at 0 (no assumed direction) but on a biologically sane scale — ageing genes change slowly per year, so large slopes are implausible.
Noise \(\sigma\): must be positive, so an Exponential (or half-Normal) prior; mass on small-to-moderate scatter.

A centred prior on \(b\) is honest, not a thumb on the scale: it lets the data move the slope, but resists over-reacting to a few noisy points.


Priors are where students get nervous, so demystify them: a weakly-informative prior states the scale of plausible values, not the answer. Justify each choice biologically. The slope prior centred at zero is important to explain - it is the sceptical, conservative choice; it does not assume the gene is flat, it just requires evidence to move away from flat, which regularises small-n fits. Emphasise sigma must be positive so its prior lives on the positive line (Exponential or half-Normal). Mention prior predictive checks in passing as the principled way to sanity-check priors (simulate lines from the prior and see if they are biologically ridiculous). Numbers here are illustrative for a centred, standardised-ish response.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
section: The likelihood: how data pull on the parameters
text:
The likelihood: how data pull on the parameters
The likelihood measures how well a given \((a, b, \sigma)\) explains the observed points. Under the line-plus-Gaussian-noise model, each donor contributes a normal density:
\[p(y_i \mid a, b, \sigma) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(y_i \ \middle|\ a + b\,x_i,\ \sigma^2\right)\]
and, assuming donors are independent, the full likelihood is the product:
\[p(\text{data} \mid a,b,\sigma) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathcal{N}\!\left(y_i \ \middle|\ a + b\,x_i,\ \sigma\right)\]
Maximising this product alone (ignoring priors) gives back the least-squares line — the frequentist and Bayesian fits share the same likelihood, and differ only by the prior.


Define likelihood concretely: plug a candidate line into the model and ask how probable the observed points are. Each point is a Gaussian centred on the line’s prediction for that x; independence makes the joint likelihood a product. The punchline ties the whole lecture together: maximising the Gaussian likelihood on its own reproduces least squares (minimising squared residuals is the same as maximising a Gaussian likelihood). So least squares is the “no prior / flat prior, take the peak” special case. The Bayesian answer multiplies in the prior and keeps the whole distribution instead of only its peak.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
text:
The posterior: prior × likelihood
Multiply prior and likelihood and normalise — the result is the posterior over \((a, b, \sigma)\):
\[p(a, b, \sigma \mid \text{data}) \ \propto\ \left[\prod_{i} \mathcal{N}(y_i \mid a + b x_i,\ \sigma)\right]\ p(a)\,p(b)\,p(\sigma)\]

For a straight line with Gaussian noise there is no simple formula to write down for the full posterior, so we sample from it with MCMC (Markov-chain Monte Carlo).
MCMC returns thousands of draws \((a^{(k)}, b^{(k)}, \sigma^{(k)})\) — a cloud of plausible parameter sets.
The spread of the draws is the uncertainty. Summaries (mean, 95% interval) are just descriptions of that cloud.



Assemble the posterior explicitly as prior times likelihood, normalised. Be honest that for regression the posterior has no tidy closed form once you use general priors, which is why we sample. MCMC is the engine; you can name-drop that it is a Markov chain (link to the Markov chains block conceptually - it walks parameter space so its stationary distribution is the posterior) without teaching the algorithm. The crucial intuition: we get a big table of plausible (a, b, sigma) triples, and everything we report - coefficient distributions, prediction bands, probabilities - is computed by summarising that table. No integrals by hand.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
section: Fitting it in R with brms
text:
Fitting it in R with brms
brms writes and runs the MCMC for you from an lm-style formula.
library(brms)

fit <- brm(
  expr ~ age,                       # same formula as lm()
  data   = donors,
  family = gaussian(),              # line + Gaussian noise
  prior  = c(
    prior(normal(0, 5),    class = "Intercept"),
    prior(normal(0, 0.1),  class = "b"),        # slope
    prior(exponential(1),  class = "sigma")     # noise scale
  ),
  chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 1
)
The formula expr ~ age is identical to what you would pass to lm(). The extra arguments declare the priors and how much to sample.

Show that the Bayesian fit is a near drop-in for lm: same formula interface, plus explicit priors and sampling controls. Walk the prior() lines and match them to the previous slide’s choices - class Intercept, class b for the slope, class sigma for noise. Mention that family = gaussian() is exactly the line-plus-normal-noise assumption; swapping the family (e.g. to negative binomial for counts) is how this generalises to the count models from the distributions block, but today stays Gaussian. Note brms compiles a Stan model under the hood; chains and iter control the MCMC. This is static code - nothing runs at render time.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
text:
Always check the sampling
Before trusting anything, confirm the MCMC actually converged.
summary(fit)          # look at Rhat and ESS for every parameter
plot(fit)             # trace plots: chains should overlap like "fuzzy caterpillars"

Rhat should be \(\approx 1.00\) for every parameter (chains agree). Values \(\gtrsim 1.01\) signal trouble.
ESS (effective sample size) should be comfortably large (hundreds+).
Trace plots should look like stationary noise with the chains fully overlapping.

If these fail, the numbers are unreliable — re-run with more iterations or reconsider the model, don’t interpret.


Instil the discipline that sampling diagnostics come before interpretation, analogous to checking residuals before trusting an lm. Give the two headline numbers: Rhat near 1 means the independent chains have mixed to the same distribution; effective sample size tells you how many near-independent draws you effectively have. Trace plots that look like fuzzy caterpillars with overlapping chains are healthy; drifting or separated chains mean non-convergence. The rule: never read coefficients off a fit that failed diagnostics. This is a common exam-style “what would you check?” point.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
section: Reading the posterior: coefficients are distributions
text:
Reading the posterior: coefficients are distributions
posterior_summary(fit)     # mean, SE, and 95% credible interval per parameter



Parameter
Estimate
95% credible interval




Intercept \(a\)
4.20
[3.95, 4.45]


slope \(b\)
0.018
[0.001, 0.035]


\(\sigma\)
0.31
[0.22, 0.44]




Each row is a summary of that parameter’s marginal posterior — the shape of the whole distribution, boiled down.
The slope’s 95% credible interval \([0.001, 0.035]\) means: given the data and priors, there is a 95% probability the true per-year change lies in this range.
That is the plain-English reading people wrongly attach to a frequentist CI — here it is actually correct.



This table is illustrative, not computed. The teaching point: every coefficient now has a full distribution, summarised by a posterior mean and a credible interval. Hammer the interpretation contrast from earlier - the credible interval is a direct probability statement about the parameter, which is exactly the (incorrect) intuition students bring to confidence intervals. So Bayes legitimises the intuition. Point out the slope interval sits just above zero, foreshadowing the next slide’s probability-of-positive-slope computation. Note sigma also has a posterior; uncertainty about the noise scale feeds into prediction uncertainty.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
section: Interpreting a coefficient as a probability
text:
Interpreting a coefficient as a probability
Because the slope is a full distribution of draws, we can ask direct biological questions by counting draws:
draws <- as_draws_df(fit)

mean(draws$b_age > 0)          # P(slope > 0 | data)  e.g. 0.98
quantile(draws$b_age, c(0.025, 0.975))   # 95% credible interval

mean(draws$b_age > 0) is just the fraction of posterior draws with a positive slope — a genuine probability that the gene’s expression increases with age.
No null hypothesis, no p-value: a probability you can report and act on.
Want the chance the effect exceeds a biologically meaningful size? mean(draws$b_age > 0.01).

This is the payoff: coefficients you can reason about probabilistically.


Show how trivially the posterior answers real questions: a probability is just a proportion of draws. P(slope > 0) is the fraction of the MCMC table with positive slope - report it directly as the probability the gene goes up with age. Contrast with the frequentist detour through a null hypothesis and p-value. Emphasise the flexibility: you can ask about any threshold, including a minimum biologically relevant effect size (a ROPE-style question), which a p-value cannot address. This is the slide that makes Bayesian regression feel useful rather than philosophical.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
text:
Prediction with uncertainty: two questions
For a new donor aged 70, “predict the expression” is really two questions:

Where is the average line? Uncertainty in \(a\) and \(b\) only → a credible interval for the mean expression at age 70. Narrow.
Where will one new donor land? Adds the noise \(\sigma\) on top → a wider prediction interval for a single observation.

newdata <- data.frame(age = 70)

# uncertainty in the regression line (mean response)
fitted(fit, newdata = newdata)          # estimate + 95% credible interval

# uncertainty for a brand-new individual (adds sigma)
predict(fit, newdata = newdata)         # estimate + 95% prediction interval
Confusing these two is a classic error: the second band is always wider because it includes donor-to-donor scatter, not just uncertainty about the line.


This is the single most useful practical distinction and a frequent exam-style trap. Two sources of uncertainty: (1) we do not know the true line (parameter uncertainty in a and b), giving a credible band for the mean; (2) even if we knew the line exactly, a new donor scatters around it by sigma, giving a wider prediction band for an individual. fitted() gives the first, predict() gives the second. Draw both bands: the mean band hugs the line, the prediction band is fatter and roughly parallel. Stress that reporting the narrow band when you meant an individual prediction badly understates uncertainty.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
section: Prediction bands over the whole range
text:
Prediction bands over the whole range
conditional_effects draws the fitted line with its uncertainty across all ages at once:
conditional_effects(fit)                          # mean line + 95% credible band

# to show the wider band for individual new donors:
conditional_effects(fit, method = "posterior_predict")

The shaded band is narrowest near the mean age (where the data are densest) and flares out at the extremes — we extrapolate with less confidence.
Every point on the band is a summary of the posterior-predictive draws at that age.



Reinforce visually: the uncertainty band is not constant width. It pinches near the centre of the data and flares at the ends, which is the honest statement that extrapolation beyond your donors’ ages is uncertain. Distinguish again the mean band (default) from the wider posterior-predictive band for individuals. Everything shown is derived by pushing every posterior draw through the model at each age and summarising - the same draw-counting logic as the coefficient slide, just done pointwise. This picture is the emotional payoff of the whole lecture: a fit that shows its own uncertainty.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
section: Bayesian vs least squares, side by side
text:
Bayesian vs least squares, side by side








Aspect
Least squares (lm)
Bayesian (brms)




Output per coefficient
one number + CI
full posterior distribution


Slope reading
estimate + p-value
\(P(b>0\mid\text{data})\) directly


Interval meaning
long-run procedure
probability about this parameter


Prior knowledge
hard to include
built in as the prior


Small samples
can look over-precise
prior regularises honestly


Prediction
interval formulae
posterior-predictive draws


Cost / speed
instant
MCMC, slower; needs diagnostics


When the priors are flat
—
posterior peak = least-squares fit



Same line, same likelihood — Bayes keeps the whole distribution where least squares keeps only its peak.

The consolidation slide. Walk each row as a contrast, but keep returning to the unifying fact in the last row: with flat priors the posterior mode is exactly the least-squares estimate, so Bayes is a strict generalisation, not a competitor. The costs are real and worth stating honestly - MCMC is slower and demands convergence checks, so for a quick look lm is fine; you reach for brms when uncertainty, priors, or principled prediction bands matter. Encourage students to see the two as the same regression with different amounts of information retained.

title: Fitting equations (regression)
text:
Summary







Idea
Key fact




Model
\(y = a + b\,x + \varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\) — same as ordinary regression


Bayesian shift
parameters \(a,b,\sigma\) get distributions, not single numbers


Bayes’ theorem
posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior


Prior
weakly-informative; slope centred at 0 = sceptical, regularising


Likelihood
Gaussian; maximised alone → least-squares line


Posterior
sampled by MCMC; draws = a cloud of plausible \((a,b,\sigma)\)


Coefficient reading
\(P(b>0\mid\text{data})\) = fraction of draws with \(b>0\)


Credible interval
direct probability the parameter lies in the range


Prediction
mean band (narrow) vs individual band (wider, adds \(\sigma\))


Diagnostics
check Rhat \(\approx 1\) and trace plots before interpreting



Builds on: least-squares fitting and the normal equations (linear algebra block); prior / likelihood / posterior (Bayes’ theorem). Generalises to: swapping family = gaussian() for a count family, linking to the Poisson / negative-binomial models in the distributions block.

The summary is the revision sheet. Drill the through-line one more time: identical model, priors turn parameters into distributions, Bayes combines prior and likelihood, MCMC samples the posterior, and every question - is the slope positive, predict a new donor - is answered by summarising draws. Remind them least squares is the flat-prior peak, so nothing they learned earlier is discarded. Point forward: the same brms machinery with a different family handles the overdispersed count data from the distributions block, which is the natural next step for omics. And repeat: diagnostics before interpretation, always.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
About this lecture
Every earlier unit in this block built one piece of a Bayesian model. Today we assemble all of them on a single, realistic biological dataset and take it end to end.

Turn a biological question into a generative model: error model + covariates + hierarchy + priors.
Recognise why count data across patients and treatments needs a negative-binomial error model, not a Gaussian.
Read a fitted posterior: point estimate, credible interval, and a direct probability statement about a treatment effect.
Check the model with posterior predictive checks — the Bayesian version of “does my model actually reproduce my data?”
See the whole workflow as STATIC R code (via brms, which compiles to Stan). Nothing is executed here — this is the map, not the drive.







Warning


Provisional block. The Bayesian statistics block may move to a later statistics / machine-learning course. Treat it as a coherent capstone of the ideas you have met, not as examined by-hand material in its current form.




This is a consolidation lecture: no single new technique, but the integration of everything from the block — Bayes’ theorem, the Poisson/negative-binomial error models, covariates, hierarchy, and priors — into one workflow on one dataset. Emphasise the shift in mindset: we write down a story for how the data were generated, put that story into a model, fit it, and then interrogate the posterior and check the fit. Keep reminding students the code will not run at render time; it is here to be read and recognised, and they will run analogous code in the exercise. Flag the provisional status honestly up front.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
The biological question
A small immunology trial. For each blood sample we count activated T cells (a discrete count) by flow cytometry or from single-cell data.

12 patients, each sampled under placebo and under drug (paired design).
Question: does the drug change the number of activated T cells, and by how much?
Nuisance structure we must respect: patients differ in baseline immune activity (age matters), samples differ in how many total cells were assayed (exposure), and repeated samples from one patient are not independent.

A naive t.test(count ~ treatment) ignores all three. We will build a model that handles them together.


Ground the whole lecture in one concrete question with a real answer we want: the size and direction of a treatment effect on a count. Name the three complications now because each maps onto one building block later: exposure -> offset in the error model; age -> a covariate; repeated samples per patient -> hierarchy. The paired design is deliberately simple so students can hold the whole dataset in their heads. Stress that the frequentist one-liner throws away the pairing, the exposure, and the count nature of the data all at once.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
What the data look like
One row per sample. Counts are small, integer, and right-skewed — the hallmark of biological count data.
head(dat)
#>   patient treatment   age  count  n_cells   log_exp
#> 1     P01   placebo    34     18    50218    10.824
#> 2     P01      drug    34     41    48903    10.797
#> 3     P02   placebo    51      7    39044    10.572
#> 4     P02      drug    51     12    52771    10.874
#> 5     P03   placebo    29     55    61233    11.022
#> 6     P03      drug    29     96    60918    11.017

str(dat)
#> 'data.frame': 24 obs. of 6 variables:
#>  $ patient  : Factor w/ 12 levels "P01",...
#>  $ treatment: Factor w/ 2 levels "placebo","drug"
#>  $ age      : num  34 51 29 ...
#>  $ count    : int  18 41 7 12 55 96 ...
#>  $ n_cells  : int  50218 48903 ...
#>  $ log_exp  : num  10.82 10.80 ...   # = log(n_cells), the exposure offset

Walk the columns: count is the response; treatment and age are the effects we care about and want to adjust for; patient labels the grouping for the hierarchy; n_cells is how many cells were assayed, and log_exp is its log, which becomes the offset. Point out that the raw counts are not comparable across samples until we account for n_cells — 41 out of 49k cells is very different from 41 out of 5k. This is exactly the library-size problem they met with RNA-seq counts. Twenty-four rows, twelve patients, two treatments each.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
section: Why not a Gaussian linear model?
text:
Why not a Gaussian linear model?
A lm(count ~ treatment) assumes the response is continuous, symmetric, and constant-variance. Counts violate all three:

counts are non-negative integers — a Gaussian puts probability on \(-3.7\) cells;
their spread grows with the mean — big-count samples are noisier in absolute terms;
they are often overdispersed: variance \(>\) mean, more than Poisson allows.

We met these facts in the count-distributions unit (Poisson and the negative binomial). The fix is to choose an error model that generates counts, and let the mean depend on covariates through a log link.


This slide reactivates the count-distributions unit and motivates the whole modelling choice. The three bullets are the standard case against a linear model for counts. The log link is the bridge: it keeps the mean positive and turns multiplicative biological effects (fold changes) into additive terms we can reason about. Do not re-derive the negative binomial here; just recall that it is the Poisson with an extra dispersion knob, and that biological count data almost always needs that knob.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
Building block 1 — the error model
Model each count with a negative binomial, the overdispersed cousin of the Poisson:
\[y_i \sim \text{NegBinomial}(\mu_i, \phi), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(y_i) = \mu_i + \frac{\mu_i^2}{\phi}.\]

\(\mu_i\) is the expected count; \(\phi\) (the shape / dispersion) controls the extra spread.
As \(\phi \to \infty\) the extra term vanishes and we recover the Poisson (\(\operatorname{Var}=\mu\)).
Small \(\phi\) = strong overdispersion: biological heterogeneity between samples beyond pure counting noise.

Letting the data estimate \(\phi\) means we test whether Poisson would have been enough, rather than assuming it.


This is the NB2 parameterisation used by brms and most count-modelling tools: mean mu, variance mu + mu^2/phi. The key teaching point is that phi is not a nuisance to be hidden — it is a biologically meaningful quantity measuring sample-to-sample heterogeneity, and by putting a prior on it and estimating it we let the data tell us how far from Poisson we are. Reassure students that if the data really were Poisson, phi would be estimated large and the model would reduce to Poisson automatically. Overdispersion in immune counts is the rule, not the exception.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
Building block 2 — covariates and exposure
Let the log of the mean be a linear predictor — the same additive structure as a linear model, on the log scale:
\[\log \mu_i = \underbrace{\log(\text{n\_cells}_i)}_{\text{offset (exposure)}} + \alpha + \beta_{\text{drug}}\,x_i + \beta_{\text{age}}\,(\text{age}_i - \overline{\text{age}})\]

The offset (coefficient fixed at 1) turns counts into rates per cell assayed — the standard fix for library size / sequencing depth.
\(x_i = 1\) for drug, \(0\) for placebo, so \(\beta_{\text{drug}}\) is the drug effect on the log scale.
\(e^{\beta_{\text{drug}}}\) is a rate ratio: a multiplicative fold-change in activated T cells. Centring age makes \(\alpha\) interpretable at the mean age.



Everything here reuses the linear-model machinery students already have, but with two twists: the log link (so coefficients are multiplicative, i.e. fold changes) and the offset (so we model a rate, not a raw count). The offset is the same idea as dividing by library size in RNA-seq, done properly inside the model rather than as a pre-normalisation. Drill the interpretation of exp(beta) as a rate ratio because that is what a biologist actually reports: “the drug multiplies activated T-cell abundance by 1.6.” Centring covariates is a small but real habit that keeps the intercept meaningful and helps sampling.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
Building block 3 — hierarchy
Two samples from the same patient share that patient’s biology. Give each patient a random intercept:
\[\log \mu_i = \dots + u_{\text{patient}[i]}, \qquad u_p \sim \text{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_{\text{patient}}).\]

\(u_p\) shifts a patient up or down; \(\sigma_{\text{patient}}\) is the between-patient spread (the biological replicate variance).
The remaining scatter within a patient is technical / residual — captured by \(\phi\).
Hierarchy gives partial pooling: noisy patients are shrunk toward the group, borrowing strength across the cohort.

This is the hierarchical-models unit (biological vs technical replicates) applied to our cohort.


The hierarchy is what makes this a proper analysis of a repeated-measures design rather than a pile of pseudo-replicated points. Split the variance conceptually: sigma_patient is variation between individuals (biological replicates), phi absorbs the leftover within-patient counting noise (closer to technical replication). Partial pooling / shrinkage is the payoff — a patient with only extreme samples is not trusted at face value; the model pulls it toward the cohort in proportion to how noisy it is. Connect explicitly to the replicates discussion from the hierarchical unit: ignoring the grouping inflates false positives.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
Try it: shrinking the patients
A Gaussian sketch on the log scale: a patient with \(c\) activated cells counted has a raw log-rate with noise variance \(\approx 1/c\), so its weight is \(w_p = c/(c + 1/\sigma_{\text{patient}}^2)\).




This is the normal–normal version of partial pooling from the hierarchical unit, transplanted onto our twelve patients. It is a sketch, not the brms fit: on the log scale a Poisson count of c cells has a raw log-rate with variance about 1/c, so the number of cells counted plays the role of n_i/sigma^2. Rows are patients sorted by how many activated cells they contributed; the slider is sigma_patient^2, the between-patient variance; the green tick is the simulated true patient effect. At the true value, low-count patients (8–20 cells) are pulled strongly toward the cohort mean, high-count patients barely move. Slide to 0 (every patient identical: complete pooling) and to infinity (every patient on its own: no pooling), and point at the error box: the middle is usually best. In the real model sigma_patient is estimated, so the data choose the amount of shrinkage.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
Building block 4 — priors
Bayesian fitting needs a prior on every parameter. We use weakly informative priors on the log scale:
priors <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 2),   class = "Intercept"),  # baseline log-rate, broad
  prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b"),           # each effect: fold-changes mostly within ~e^2
  prior(exponential(1), class = "sd"),          # between-patient SD, positive, modest
  prior(gamma(0.01, 0.01), class = "shape")     # NB dispersion phi, very diffuse
)

normal(0, 1) on a log-scale coefficient says: effects near zero are most plausible, but a rate ratio of \(e^{\pm 2}\approx 0.14\)–\(7.4\) is easily allowed. Sceptical, not restrictive.
Priors here play the role that regularisation will play in the penalized-models block: they tame the fit without dictating the answer.



Priors are where students new to Bayes get nervous, so make the point that weakly informative priors encode common sense (a treatment is unlikely to change abundance a thousand-fold) without forcing a conclusion — the likelihood dominates once there is real data. Explain each: broad Normal on the intercept because we do not know the baseline rate; Normal(0,1) on effects because they live on the log scale where 1 is already a big fold change; a positive-only prior (exponential) on the standard deviation because SDs cannot be negative; a diffuse prior on the dispersion. Plant the forward link to penalized models: an L2 penalty is exactly a Gaussian prior on coefficients. This is the “explore similarity to Bayesian models” connection.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
section: The full model on one slide
text:
The full model on one slide
The generative story, read top to bottom — how a count is born:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_i &\sim \text{NegBinomial}(\mu_i,\ \phi) &&\text{(error model)}\\
\log \mu_i &= \log(\text{n\_cells}_i) + \alpha + \beta_{\text{drug}} x_i + \beta_{\text{age}}\,\widetilde{\text{age}}_i + u_{\text{patient}[i]} &&\text{(covariates + hierarchy)}\\
u_p &\sim \text{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_{\text{patient}}) &&\text{(between-patient)}\\
\alpha \sim \text{N}(0,2),\ \ \beta &\sim \text{N}(0,1),\ \ \sigma_{\text{patient}} \sim \text{Exp}(1),\ \ \phi \sim \text{Gamma}(0.01,0.01) &&\text{(priors)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Bayes’ theorem ties it together: \(\;p(\text{parameters}\mid\text{data}) \propto \underbrace{p(\text{data}\mid\text{parameters})}_{\text{likelihood (NB)}}\;\underbrace{p(\text{parameters})}_{\text{priors}}.\)


This is the whole model in one place: read it as a recipe that manufactures a count. Every line is a building block from earlier slides. The final proportionality is Bayes’ theorem from the opening unit of the block — posterior proportional to likelihood times prior — now instantiated with a negative-binomial likelihood and the priors we just chose. Emphasise that “fitting” means characterising that posterior distribution over alpha, the betas, sigma_patient, phi, and the twelve u_p, not finding a single best value. This slide is the one to photograph.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
Fitting it in R
One brms call expresses the entire model; it writes and compiles a Stan program under the hood (the R-STAN unit).
library(brms)

# Centre age before using it in the formula; this makes the intercept the
# baseline log-rate at the average age.
dat$age_c <- dat$age - mean(dat$age)

fit <- brm(
  count ~ treatment + age_c + offset(log_exp) + (1 | patient),
  data    = dat,
  family  = negbinomial(),        # log link + dispersion phi
  prior   = priors,               # from the previous slide
  chains  = 4, iter = 2000, warmup = 1000,
  cores   = 4, seed = 1
)

treatment + age_c are the fixed effects; offset(log_exp) is the exposure term.
(1 | patient) is the per-patient random intercept — the hierarchy.
4 chains of MCMC explore the posterior; warmup samples are discarded.


The formula is the model: response on the left, fixed effects and offset in the middle, the (1 | patient) grouping on the right giving the random intercept. family = negbinomial() supplies the log link and the dispersion parameter. Point out that brms is a friendly front end that generates Stan code and runs Hamiltonian Monte Carlo — the same R-STAN engine from the fitting unit, without hand-writing the Stan blocks. Four chains started from different points let us check they agree. Nothing here executes at render time; in the exercise students run an analogous fit on a provided dataset.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
Did the sampler work?
Before interpreting anything, check that the MCMC actually converged. Diagnostics come before conclusions.
summary(fit)
#> Group-Level Effects (patient):  sd(Intercept)  ...
#> Population-Level Effects:
#>                 Estimate  Est.Error  l-95% CI  u-95% CI  Rhat  Bulk_ESS  Tail_ESS
#> Intercept        -7.31      0.14      -7.59     -7.04    1.00     2600      2900
#> treatmentdrug     0.47      0.09       0.29      0.65    1.00     4100      3200
#> age_c            -0.012     0.010     -0.031     0.008   1.00     3500      3000

Rhat \(\approx 1.00\) (want \(< 1.01\)): the chains agree — they mixed.
ESS in the thousands: enough effectively-independent draws to trust the summaries.
Also check 0 divergent transitions (a Stan-specific warning); divergences mean the geometry was too hard and the fit is untrustworthy.



Hammer the discipline: convergence diagnostics are a gate, not an afterthought. Rhat compares within-chain and between-chain variance; values above ~1.01 mean the chains disagree and the posterior summaries are meaningless. Effective sample size accounts for autocorrelation in MCMC — a few thousand is plenty for stable 95% intervals. Divergent transitions are Stan’s honest signal that Hamiltonian dynamics broke down, often fixed by reparameterising or raising adapt_delta. Only once these pass do we read the estimates. This mirrors checking residuals before trusting an lm.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
Reading the posterior
The treatment coefficient lives on the log scale; exponentiate for the biological quantity — a rate ratio.
post <- as_draws_df(fit)

# Rate ratio for the drug: multiplicative fold-change in activated T cells
exp(quantile(post$b_treatmentdrug, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)))
#>     2.5%      50%    97.5%
#>    1.34     1.60     1.92

# Direct probability the drug increases the count
mean(post$b_treatmentdrug > 0)
#> [1] 0.9998

Point estimate: the drug multiplies activated T cells by \(\approx 1.6\).
95% credible interval \([1.34,\ 1.92]\): a plausible range for the true effect — a statement about the parameter, unlike a confidence interval.
\(P(\beta_{\text{drug}} > 0 \mid \text{data}) \approx 0.9998\): an answer to the actual question, no null hypothesis needed.



This is the Bayesian payoff and the place to contrast framings explicitly. The credible interval is a direct probability statement about the parameter: given the data and model, there is 95% posterior probability the rate ratio lies in [1.34, 1.92]. That is what people wrongly wish a confidence interval meant. The probability of direction, P(effect > 0), answers the biologist’s question directly without a p-value or a null. Keep the interpretation multiplicative because of the log link: 1.6-fold more activated T cells on the drug. Age’s interval straddles zero, so the data are inconclusive about age here.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
Model checking — the idea
A converged sampler only means we fitted the model we wrote. Is that model any good? Posterior predictive checking asks: if the model is right, would it generate data that look like ours?
\[y^{\text{rep}} \sim p(y^{\text{rep}} \mid \text{data}) = \int p(y^{\text{rep}}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta\mid\text{data})\,d\theta\]

Draw parameters from the posterior, then simulate new datasets \(y^{\text{rep}}\) from the error model.
Compare those simulated datasets to the real data. Systematic mismatch = the model is missing something.

This is the Bayesian analogue of residual plots — but it checks the whole generative story, counts and all.


Make the logic crisp: we already have a posterior over parameters; for each posterior draw we can generate a fake dataset from the negative-binomial error model. If the model captures the data-generating process, these fake datasets should be statistically indistinguishable from the real one. Where they differ systematically, that difference names the model’s flaw — too few zeros, wrong tail, missed skew. Contrast with a converged-but-wrong model: MCMC can perfectly sample a bad model. Posterior predictive checks are how we catch that, and they are far more informative than a single goodness-of-fit number.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
Model checking — what to plot
# Overlay: distribution of observed counts vs many simulated datasets
pp_check(fit, ndraws = 100)

# Targeted checks on summary statistics the model must reproduce
pp_check(fit, type = "stat", stat = "mean")
pp_check(fit, type = "stat", stat = "max")                 # is the tail right?
pp_check(fit, type = "stat", stat = function(y) mean(y == 0))  # zero-inflation?

Density overlay: the observed count histogram should sit inside the cloud of simulated ones.
Test statistics: if the observed max or proportion of zeros falls in the tail of the simulated distribution, the error model is wrong — e.g. real data are more overdispersed or zero-inflated than a negative binomial allows.
A failed check sends you back to the model (a different error model, an extra covariate), not to the data.



Give students a concrete menu. The density overlay is the first look: observed distribution as a dark line, simulated datasets as a light band; the dark line should be unremarkable within the band. Then targeted statistics catch specific failures the overlay can blur: the max tests the tail (is dispersion adequate?), the proportion of zeros tests for zero-inflation common in single-cell data. The crucial habit: a failing check is diagnostic feedback about the model, so you iterate on the model — maybe a zero-inflated negative binomial, maybe a missing covariate — never by deleting inconvenient data points.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
section: Frequentist vs Bayesian, on this case
text:
Frequentist vs Bayesian, on this case
Same data, two philosophies — and this block chose the Bayesian one for concrete reasons.








Question
Frequentist tool
Bayesian answer here




Effect size
coefficient \(\pm\) SE from a GLM
full posterior for \(\beta_{\text{drug}}\)


Uncertainty
95% confidence interval
95% credible interval (a real probability)


“Is there an effect?”
p-value vs a null
\(P(\beta_{\text{drug}}>0\mid\text{data})\) directly


Patient structure
random effects via glmer
hierarchy with partial pooling


Prior knowledge
none (or ad-hoc)
encoded, and dominated by data when data are plentiful


Model check
residual diagnostics
posterior predictive checks



Neither is “correct”; the Bayesian workflow makes the uncertainty and the assumptions explicit, which suits small, structured biological datasets.

Return to the Bayesian-vs-frequentist distinction from the opening of the block, now grounded in a worked case. A frequentist GLMM (glmer with a negative-binomial family) would give broadly similar point estimates here — the point is not that one is right, but that the Bayesian version answers the biologist’s question in its native language (probabilities about effects), handles small hierarchical datasets gracefully through partial pooling, and forces the assumptions (priors, error model) into the open where they can be criticised and checked. With large data the prior washes out and the two largely agree.

title: A worked Bayesian case study
text:
Summary







Step
What we did




Question
drug effect on activated T-cell counts, paired across 12 patients


Error model
negative binomial — counts, mean-variance link, overdispersion \(\phi\)


Covariates
log link; offset for exposure; \(e^{\beta}\) = rate ratio


Hierarchy
per-patient random intercept → partial pooling of replicates


Priors
weakly informative on the log scale (regularisation, not dictation)


Fit
one brms formula → Stan → MCMC (the R-STAN engine)


Trust it
Rhat, ESS, divergences before interpreting


Read it
posterior, credible interval, \(P(\text{effect}>0\mid\text{data})\)


Check it
posterior predictive checks on distribution, max, zeros



You now have the full arc: question → generative model → fit → posterior → check. That arc, not any one formula, is the deliverable of this block.

The summary is the workflow, and the workflow is the exam of this unit conceptually even if the block is provisional. Recite the arc once more: write a generative story combining an error model, covariates, hierarchy and priors; fit it with Stan via brms; gate on convergence diagnostics; read the posterior as direct probability statements; and check the model against its own predictions, iterating on the model when checks fail. Point forward: the penalized-models block reframes priors as regularisation, and the single-cell block reuses count models at scale. The exercise walks a smaller version of this exact pipeline by hand and in static R.

title: Exercise: a worked Bayesian case
text:
Background
We reuse the case from the lecture: for sample \(i\) we count activated T cells, with a per-patient random intercept and an exposure offset.
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_i &\sim \text{NegBinomial}(\mu_i,\ \phi), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(y_i)=\mu_i+\tfrac{\mu_i^2}{\phi}\\
\log \mu_i &= \log(\text{n\_cells}_i) + \alpha + \beta_{\text{drug}}\,x_i + \beta_{\text{age}}\,\widetilde{\text{age}}_i + u_{\text{patient}[i]}\\
u_p &\sim \text{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_{\text{patient}})
\end{aligned}
\]
Two facts you will use repeatedly:

Log link ⇒ multiplicative effects. A coefficient \(\beta\) on the log scale means the mean is multiplied by \(e^{\beta}\) (a rate ratio) when that predictor increases by one unit.
Conjugacy gives a posterior by hand. For a Poisson likelihood with a Gamma\((a,b)\) prior on the rate \(\lambda\) (shape \(a\), rate \(b\), so prior mean \(a/b\)), observing counts \(y_1,\dots,y_n\) with total \(S=\sum y_i\) gives a Gamma posterior: \[\lambda \mid \text{data} \sim \text{Gamma}\big(a + S,\ \ b + n\big), \qquad \text{posterior mean } = \frac{a+S}{b+n}.\] This is Bayes’ theorem (posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior) in a case where the algebra closes in one line — the same logic the sampler does numerically for the full model.

title: Exercise: a worked Bayesian case
text:
By hand
B1. In the model above, match each symbol to its role: \(\phi\), the \(\log(\text{n\_cells}_i)\) term, \(\beta_{\text{drug}}\), \(\sigma_{\text{patient}}\). Which one measures between-patient (biological replicate) variation, and which absorbs leftover within-patient noise?
B2. The fitted drug coefficient is \(\beta_{\text{drug}} = 0.47\) on the log scale. Convert it to a rate ratio and state, in one biological sentence, what the drug does to the activated-T-cell count. (Use \(e^{0.47}\approx 1.60\).)
B3. The 95% credible interval for \(\beta_{\text{drug}}\) is \([0.29,\ 0.65]\). Convert both ends to the rate-ratio scale, and write the correct one-sentence interpretation of the resulting interval. How does that interpretation differ from a frequentist confidence interval?
B4. (overdispersion). Across placebo samples the activated-T-cell count has sample mean \(\approx 24\) and sample variance \(\approx 210\). Would a Poisson error model be adequate? Justify using the Poisson mean–variance relationship, and say what the negative-binomial dispersion \(\phi\) is there to fix.
B5. (conjugate posterior — the core by-hand skill). Forget covariates for a moment: model the placebo counts of a single patient as Poisson with rate \(\lambda\). You place a Gamma\((a=2,\ b=0.1)\) prior on \(\lambda\) (prior mean \(a/b = 20\) cells). You then observe \(n=3\) samples from this patient with counts \(18,\ 26,\ 22\). (a) Write the posterior distribution of \(\lambda\). (b) Compute the posterior mean. (c) The prior mean was 20 and the data mean is 22. Explain, in one sentence, why the posterior mean lands where it does relative to those two numbers.
B6. (log-link prediction). Using \(\alpha = -7.31\), \(\beta_{\text{drug}} = 0.47\), \(\beta_{\text{age}} = -0.012\), ignore the patient term (\(u_p = 0\)), and take a drug sample from a patient of average age (\(\widetilde{\text{age}} = 0\)) assayed over \(\text{n\_cells} = 50000\) cells. Compute the expected count \(\mu\). (Recall \(\log \mu = \log(\text{n\_cells}) + \alpha + \beta_{\text{drug}}\cdot 1 + \beta_{\text{age}}\cdot 0\).)
B7. (posterior predictive reasoning). You run a posterior predictive check and find the observed proportion of zero counts sits far in the upper tail of the simulated datasets (the model predicts fewer zeros than you see). What does this tell you about the model, and what is a reasonable next modelling step? Why is deleting the zero-count samples the wrong response?

title: Exercise: a worked Bayesian case
text:
Explore
Do B4 by hand first. The demo draws 1000 counts from a negative binomial in the convention of this unit (and of brms), \(\operatorname{Var}(y) = \mu + \mu^2/\phi\), where \(\phi\) is the shape: a large \(\phi\) means close to Poisson and \(\phi = \infty\) is exactly Poisson. The bars are the simulated counts, the red dots the NB probabilities, and the dashed blue outline the Poisson with the same mean.



E1. The demo starts at the placebo numbers of B4: \(\mu = 24\), \(\phi = 3\). Compare the theoretical variance with the observed \(\approx 210\). Then click Poisson: what variance would a Poisson model assume, and how does the histogram change?
E2. Back at \(\phi = 3\), click draw again a few times. Does the sample variance stay near theory? Could Poisson counts with mean 24 ever give a sample variance near 210?
E3. Click strong (many zeros). How many samples have zero activated cells, compared with the Poisson? Then tick mean–variance plot and move \(\mu\) from 5 to 500: how does var/mean change, and in which direction does the NB curve move when you increase \(\phi\)?






Solutions





E1. \(24 + 24^2/3 = 216\), close to the observed 210 (B4 estimated \(\phi \approx 3.1\)). A Poisson assumes variance \(= 24\), about 9 times too small; at \(\phi = \infty\) the histogram narrows onto the dashed Poisson outline and var/mean \(= 1\).
E2. Yes: the first draw gives a sample variance of about 205 against the theoretical 216, and further draws stay in the same range. A Poisson with mean 24 has variance 24; with 1000 counts its sample variance stays within a few units of 24, nowhere near 210.
E3. With \(\phi = 0.5\) and \(\mu = 24\) theory gives \((1 + \mu/\phi)^{-\phi} \approx 14\%\) zeros (the first draw shows 128 of 1000), while the Poisson predicts essentially none (\(1000\,e^{-24} \approx 0\)). var/mean \(= 1 + \mu/\phi\) grows with \(\mu\), so overdispersion matters most for large counts. Increasing \(\phi\) moves the NB curve down toward the Poisson line var \(= \mu\); at \(\phi = \infty\) they coincide.

title: Exercise: a worked Bayesian case
text:
In R
The code below is static — read it and predict each result; you will run analogous code in a live session. It confirms the by-hand answers.

Confirm the conjugate update (B5)
a <- 2; b <- 0.1                 # Gamma(shape, rate) prior, mean a/b = 20
y <- c(18, 26, 22)               # this patient's placebo counts
n <- length(y); S <- sum(y)      # n = 3, S = 66

a_post <- a + S                  # 68
b_post <- b + n                  # 3.1
a_post / b_post                  # posterior mean = 68 / 3.1 = 21.94...

# a Gamma prior with Poisson data stays Gamma: draw from the posterior to see it
lambda_draws <- rgamma(1e5, shape = a_post, rate = b_post)
mean(lambda_draws)               # ~ 21.9, matches a_post / b_post
quantile(lambda_draws, c(0.025, 0.975))   # a 95% credible interval for lambda


Rate ratio and credible interval (B2, B3)
beta_drug <- 0.47
exp(beta_drug)                   # 1.60  -> drug multiplies the count by ~1.6

ci_log <- c(0.29, 0.65)          # 95% credible interval on the log scale
exp(ci_log)                      # 1.34  1.92  -> rate-ratio scale


The full model as a brms formula (do not run at render time)
library(brms)

# Centre age before using it in the formula; this makes the intercept the
# baseline log-rate at the average age.
dat$age_c <- dat$age - mean(dat$age)

fit <- brm(
  count ~ treatment + age_c + offset(log_exp) + (1 | patient),
  data   = dat,
  family = negbinomial(),
  prior  = c(prior(normal(0, 2),    class = "Intercept"),
             prior(normal(0, 1),    class = "b"),
             prior(exponential(1),  class = "sd"),
             prior(gamma(0.01,0.01),class = "shape")),
  chains = 4, iter = 2000, cores = 4, seed = 1
)

summary(fit)                     # check Rhat ~ 1.00 and ESS before reading estimates
pp_check(fit, ndraws = 100)      # density overlay: observed among simulated
pp_check(fit, type = "stat",
         stat = function(y) mean(y == 0))   # the zero-count check from B7


Tasks
R1. Reproduce B5 in R using the conjugate block above: confirm a_post, b_post, and the posterior mean, then report a 95% credible interval for \(\lambda\) from quantile(lambda_draws, ...).
R2. Change the prior in R1 to Gamma(a = 20, b = 1) (same prior mean 20, but far more concentrated). Recompute the posterior mean. Does the posterior move closer to the prior mean or closer to the data mean than before, and why?
R3. Using the rate-ratio block, confirm the drug rate ratio and its 95% interval. Then compute mean(post$b_treatmentdrug > 0) conceptually: what quantity is this, and why can a frequentist analysis not report exactly this number?

title: Exercise: a worked Bayesian case
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — which term is which (B1)





Map each symbol to a lecture building block. The offset \(\log(\text{n\_cells}_i)\) turns a count into a rate; \(\beta_{\text{drug}}\) is a fixed effect (a fold change on the log scale); \(\sigma_{\text{patient}}\) is the standard deviation of the per-patient intercepts \(u_p\) — variation between patients; \(\phi\) (the negative-binomial dispersion) soaks up the extra scatter within a patient beyond Poisson counting noise.









Hint 2 — rate ratios from log coefficients (B2, B3)





A log link means effects are multiplicative: increasing a predictor by one unit multiplies the mean by \(e^{\beta}\). So exponentiate. For an interval, exponentiate both endpoints — the transform is monotonic, so the order is preserved. In R this is exp(beta).









Hint 3 — credible vs confidence interval (B3)





A credible interval is a direct probability statement about the parameter: given the data and model, there is 95% posterior probability that \(\beta_{\text{drug}}\) lies in the interval. A confidence interval instead describes the long-run coverage of the procedure across hypothetical repeated experiments, not the probability that this particular interval contains the value. Say the credible-interval version in plain words.









Hint 4 — is it overdispersed? (B4)





For a Poisson, the variance equals the mean. Compare the sample variance (210) to the sample mean (24): if variance \(\gg\) mean, the data are overdispersed and Poisson will understate the noise. The negative-binomial variance is \(\mu + \mu^2/\phi\); the extra \(\mu^2/\phi\) term is exactly what accommodates the excess.









Hint 5 — the conjugate posterior (B5)





With a Gamma\((a,b)\) prior (shape \(a\), rate \(b\)) and Poisson data, the posterior is Gamma\((a + S,\ b + n)\) where \(S = \sum y_i\) and \(n\) is the number of observations. Here \(S = 18+26+22 = 66\) and \(n = 3\), so the posterior is Gamma\((2+66,\ 0.1+3)=\) Gamma\((68,\ 3.1)\) with mean \(68/3.1\). The posterior mean is a data-weighted blend of the prior mean and the sample mean.









Hint 6 — log-link prediction (B6)





Add the terms on the log scale, then exponentiate once at the end. \(\log \mu = \log(50000) + (-7.31) + 0.47 = 10.820 - 7.31 + 0.47\). Compute that sum, then \(\mu = e^{\text{sum}}\) with exp. Sanity check: the answer should be a plausible small count (tens of cells), not thousands.









Hint 7 — reading a failed posterior predictive check (B7)





A posterior predictive check compares a statistic of the real data (here the proportion of zeros) to the same statistic computed on many datasets simulated from the fitted model. If the observed value sits in the extreme tail of the simulated distribution, the model cannot generate data like yours in that respect. Too many observed zeros points to zero-inflation; a zero-inflated negative binomial (or a missing covariate) is the fix. See pp_check.

title: Exercise: a worked Bayesian case
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. \(\log(\text{n\_cells}_i)\) is the offset / exposure (fixed coefficient 1), converting counts to a per-cell rate. \(\beta_{\text{drug}}\) is a fixed effect, the log-scale drug effect. \(\sigma_{\text{patient}}\) is the between-patient standard deviation — the biological-replicate variation among the \(u_p\). \(\phi\) is the negative-binomial dispersion, absorbing leftover within-patient (nearer technical) scatter beyond Poisson noise. So: \(\sigma_{\text{patient}}\) = between-patient; \(\phi\) = within-patient.
B2. Rate ratio \(= e^{0.47} \approx 1.60\). Biological reading: on the drug, the expected number of activated T cells is about 1.6 times that on placebo (a 60% increase), holding age, exposure and patient fixed.
B3. Exponentiate the endpoints: \(e^{0.29} \approx 1.34\) and \(e^{0.65} \approx 1.92\), giving a rate-ratio interval \([1.34,\ 1.92]\). Interpretation: given the data and model, there is 95% posterior probability that the drug’s rate ratio lies between 1.34 and 1.92. A frequentist confidence interval cannot be read this way — it describes the long-run coverage of the interval-making procedure over hypothetical repeated experiments, not the probability that this particular interval holds the true value. The credible interval is a statement about the parameter; the confidence interval is a statement about the procedure.
B4. For a Poisson the variance equals the mean, so we would expect variance \(\approx 24\). The observed variance is \(\approx 210\), roughly 9× the mean — strong overdispersion. A Poisson model would badly understate the noise, producing over-confident intervals and inflated significance. The negative binomial adds a \(\mu^2/\phi\) term to the variance (\(\operatorname{Var}=\mu+\mu^2/\phi\)); a moderate, estimated \(\phi\) lets the model match the excess spread. (Here \(210 \approx 24 + 24^2/\phi \Rightarrow \phi \approx 24^2/186 \approx 3.1\) — a small \(\phi\), i.e. clearly non-Poisson.)
B5. (a) \(S = 18+26+22 = 66\), \(n = 3\). Posterior \(\lambda \mid \text{data} \sim \text{Gamma}(a+S,\ b+n) = \text{Gamma}(2+66,\ 0.1+3) = \text{Gamma}(68,\ 3.1)\). (b) Posterior mean \(= \dfrac{a+S}{b+n} = \dfrac{68}{3.1} \approx 21.9\) cells. (c) The posterior mean (21.9) sits between the prior mean (20) and the data mean (22), but very close to the data: with three observations the likelihood already carries far more weight than the weak prior (prior “rate” \(b=0.1\) acts like a tenth of one prior observation), so the data dominate and pull the estimate almost all the way to 22.
B6. \(\log \mu = \log(50000) + \alpha + \beta_{\text{drug}}\cdot 1 + \beta_{\text{age}}\cdot 0 = 10.8198 - 7.31 + 0.47 + 0 = 3.9798\). Then \(\mu = e^{3.9798} \approx 53.5\) activated T cells. A plausible small count, as expected.
B7. The check says the model, as written, generates too few zeros — its error model cannot reproduce a feature of the real data (excess zeros). This is a signal that the model is misspecified, most likely zero-inflation (a separate process producing structural zeros, common in single-cell counts) or a missing covariate that explains the zero samples. A reasonable next step is a zero-inflated negative binomial, or adding the relevant covariate, then re-running the same posterior predictive check. Deleting the zero-count samples is wrong because it discards real data to make a flawed model look adequate — it hides the misspecification rather than fixing it, and biases every downstream estimate. Posterior predictive failures are feedback about the model, not about the data.
R1. The static block gives a_post = 68, b_post = 3.1, posterior mean 68/3.1 ≈ 21.94. A 95% credible interval from quantile(lambda_draws, c(0.025, 0.975)) will be roughly \([17,\ 27]\) (Monte-Carlo estimate; exact via qgamma(c(0.025, 0.975), 68, 3.1)). It matches the analytic Gamma\((68, 3.1)\).
R2. With Gamma(a = 20, b = 1) the posterior is Gamma\((20+66,\ 1+3) = \text{Gamma}(86,\ 4)\), mean \(86/4 = 21.5\). This prior is much more concentrated (it acts like one prior observation’s worth of rate, \(b=1\), with a large shape), so it pulls the posterior mean closer to the prior mean (20) than the weak prior did — 21.5 versus 21.9. A stronger prior resists the data more; the posterior is always a precision-weighted blend of prior and likelihood.
R3. exp(0.47) ≈ 1.60 with interval exp(c(0.29, 0.65)) = c(1.34, 1.92), matching B2–B3. mean(post$b_treatmentdrug > 0) is the posterior probability that the drug effect is positive — the fraction of posterior draws above zero (the probability of direction). A frequentist analysis cannot report this because, in that framework, the parameter is a fixed unknown constant, not a random quantity — there is no probability distribution over \(\beta_{\text{drug}}\) to integrate, only statements about data given a hypothesis (p-values). Assigning a probability to the parameter itself requires the Bayesian posterior.

title: Exercise: a worked Bayesian case
text:
Where this leads

Penalized linear models (next block): the weakly informative priors you placed on the coefficients are exactly regularisation — an L2 (ridge) penalty is a Gaussian prior, an L1 (lasso) penalty a Laplace prior. The same model, read through a different lens.
Single-cell analysis: the negative-binomial count model with an exposure offset scales up to thousands of genes; the zero-inflation you reasoned about in B7 is a central issue there.
Model comparison: posterior predictive checking is qualitative; formal Bayesian model comparison (information criteria, cross-validation such as loo) puts a number on which of two competing generative models predicts held-out data better.
