title: Exercise: fitting equations the Bayesian way (regression)
text:
Background
The model is the ordinary regression line with Gaussian scatter:
\[y_i = a + b\,x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).\]
Least squares (from the linear algebra block) picks the single \(a,b\) minimising the sum of squared residuals \(\sum_i (y_i - a - b x_i)^2\); via the normal equations \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf y\).
Bayesian regression instead reports a distribution for each parameter. By Bayes’ theorem (prior / likelihood / posterior unit),
\[\underbrace{p(a,b,\sigma \mid \text{data})}_{\text{posterior}} \ \propto\ \underbrace{p(\text{data}\mid a,b,\sigma)}_{\text{likelihood}}\ \times\ \underbrace{p(a)\,p(b)\,p(\sigma)}_{\text{prior}}.\]
Two facts we use repeatedly:

The Gaussian likelihood of one point is \(p(y_i\mid a,b,\sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{(y_i - a - b x_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\big)\). For a fixed \(\sigma\), the likelihood is largest when the squared residual is smallest — so maximising the likelihood is least squares.
To turn unnormalised numbers (prior \(\times\) likelihood) into a posterior, divide each by their total so they sum to 1. Any constant common to all candidates (like \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\)) cancels in this division.

Everything Bayesian below is computed by summarising draws: a probability is a fraction of draws, a credible interval is a pair of quantiles of the draws.

title: Exercise: fitting equations the Bayesian way (regression)
text:
By hand
B1. Least squares on three points. A tiny experiment measures a response \(y\) at three doses \(x\):



\(x\)
0
1
2




\(y\)
1
2
2



Fit \(y = a + b x\) by least squares. (Hint: with \(\bar x, \bar y\) the means, \(\hat b = \dfrac{\sum (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2}\) and \(\hat a = \bar y - \hat b\,\bar x\).) Report \(\hat a\) and \(\hat b\).
B2. Residuals and which line the data prefer. For the same data, compare two candidate lines: line P is \(y = 1 + 0.5x\); line Q is \(y = 1 + x\). For each, write the three residuals \(y_i - a - b x_i\) and compute the sum of squared residuals (SSR). Which line has the higher likelihood, and why does “smaller SSR” mean “more likely”?
B3. A toy posterior over the slope (uniform prior). Simplify to a through-the-origin model \(y_i = b\,x_i + \varepsilon_i\) with known \(\sigma = 1\), and only two data points \((x_1,y_1) = (1,1)\) and \((x_2,y_2) = (2,2)\). Consider just three candidate slopes \(b \in \{0, 1, 2\}\), each with prior probability \(\tfrac13\).

For each candidate \(b\), compute the SSR \(= \sum_i (y_i - b x_i)^2\).
The (unnormalised) likelihood is \(\propto \exp(-\tfrac12\,\text{SSR})\) since \(\sigma=1\). Compute it for each \(b\) (use \(\exp(-2.5)\approx 0.082\)).
Multiply by the prior \(\tfrac13\), then normalise so the three posterior probabilities sum to 1.
What is the posterior probability that the slope is positive, \(P(b>0)\)?

B4. The prior matters (but the data speak). Repeat B3 with a sceptical prior that favours a flat line: \(P(b{=}0)=0.5\), \(P(b{=}1)=0.3\), \(P(b{=}2)=0.2\). Recompute the normalised posterior. Did the sceptical prior change the conclusion (which slope is most probable)? By how much did \(P(b{=}1)\) move?
B5. Reading a coefficient from draws. An MCMC fit returns these 10 posterior draws of a slope \(b\) (already sorted, units = change per year):
\[-0.002,\ 0.004,\ 0.006,\ 0.009,\ 0.011,\ 0.014,\ 0.016,\ 0.019,\ 0.023,\ 0.028\]

Estimate \(P(b > 0)\) from the draws.
Give an approximate 80% credible interval by trimming the lowest and highest 10% (i.e. drop one draw at each end).
In one sentence, state what the interval means, and contrast it with how a frequentist confidence interval is interpreted.

B6. Two kinds of prediction band. For a new donor at a given age, you can report (i) a credible interval for the mean expression at that age, or (ii) a prediction interval for one new donor’s expression. Which is wider, and which extra source of uncertainty does it include? Which would you quote when asked “what expression should I expect if I measure one new 70-year-old?”

title: Exercise: fitting equations the Bayesian way (regression)
text:
In R
Use R to confirm the by-hand answers, then fit the full model.

Least squares (B1), the familiar way
dat <- data.frame(x = c(0, 1, 2),
                  y = c(1, 2, 2))
fit_ls <- lm(y ~ x, data = dat)
coef(fit_ls)        # (Intercept) and slope -> compare with your B1


The toy posterior (B3/B4) as a grid
x <- c(1, 2); y <- c(1, 2)          # through-origin data
b_grid <- c(0, 1, 2)                # candidate slopes

ssr  <- sapply(b_grid, function(b) sum((y - b * x)^2))
lik  <- exp(-0.5 * ssr)             # sigma = 1, constants cancel

prior_flat <- c(1, 1, 1) / 3
post_flat  <- prior_flat * lik
post_flat  <- post_flat / sum(post_flat)   # normalise
round(post_flat, 3)                 # posterior for b = 0, 1, 2

prior_skept <- c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)     # B4: sceptical prior
post_skept  <- prior_skept * lik
post_skept  <- post_skept / sum(post_skept)
round(post_skept, 3)

sum(post_flat[b_grid > 0])          # P(b > 0) under the flat prior


Summarising draws (B5)
b_draws <- c(-0.002, 0.004, 0.006, 0.009, 0.011,
              0.014, 0.016, 0.019, 0.023, 0.028)

mean(b_draws > 0)                          # P(b > 0)
quantile(b_draws, c(0.10, 0.90))           # ~80% credible interval


The full Bayesian fit with brms
library(brms)

fit <- brm(
  expr ~ age,                       # same formula as lm()
  data   = donors,
  family = gaussian(),
  prior  = c(
    prior(normal(0, 5),   class = "Intercept"),
    prior(normal(0, 0.1), class = "b"),         # slope
    prior(exponential(1), class = "sigma")      # noise scale
  ),
  chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 1
)

summary(fit)                        # check Rhat ~ 1 and ESS before reading estimates
plot(fit)                           # trace plots: overlapping "fuzzy caterpillars"


Reading coefficients and predicting
posterior_summary(fit)              # mean + 95% credible interval per parameter

draws <- as_draws_df(fit)
mean(draws$b_age > 0)               # P(slope > 0 | data)

newdata <- data.frame(age = 70)
fitted (fit, newdata = newdata)     # credible interval for the MEAN line
predict(fit, newdata = newdata)     # wider PREDICTION interval for one new donor

conditional_effects(fit)            # fitted line + uncertainty band across ages


Tasks
R1. Run the least-squares block and confirm coef(fit_ls) matches your B1 \(\hat a, \hat b\).
R2. Run the grid block and check post_flat against your B3 posterior and post_skept against your B4 posterior. Confirm sum(post_flat[b_grid > 0]) equals your hand value of \(P(b>0)\).
R3. Run the draws block and confirm mean(b_draws > 0) and the quantile(...) interval match your B5 answers (the quantile interval will be close to, but not exactly, your trim-by-hand interval — quantile interpolates).
R4. In the brms block, identify where each of the three priors from the lecture appears, and state which line you would check first to decide whether the estimates are trustworthy.

title: Exercise: fitting equations the Bayesian way (regression)
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — least-squares formulas (B1)





Compute the means first: \(\bar x = (0+1+2)/3 = 1\), \(\bar y = (1+2+2)/3 = 5/3\). Then \(\hat b = \dfrac{\sum (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2}\) and \(\hat a = \bar y - \hat b\bar x\). In R this is lm(y ~ x).









Hint 2 — residuals and likelihood (B2)





A residual is (observed \(-\) predicted): \(r_i = y_i - (a + b x_i)\). The SSR is \(\sum_i r_i^2\). Under Gaussian noise the likelihood is \(\propto \exp(-\text{SSR}/2\sigma^2)\), which is a decreasing function of SSR — so the smaller the SSR, the larger the likelihood. Least squares and maximum likelihood pick the same line.









Hint 3 — the grid posterior recipe (B3)





For each candidate \(b\): (1) SSR \(=\sum_i (y_i - b x_i)^2\); (2) likelihood \(\propto \exp(-\tfrac12\text{SSR})\) because \(\sigma=1\); (3) multiply by the prior; (4) divide every number by the total of the three so they sum to 1. The \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\) constant is the same for all three candidates and cancels at step 4.









Hint 4 — arithmetic for B3





\(b=0\): predictions \(0,0\), residuals \(1,2\), SSR \(=1+4=5\). \(b=1\): predictions \(1,2\), residuals \(0,0\), SSR \(=0\). \(b=2\): predictions \(2,4\), residuals \(-1,-2\), SSR \(=1+4=5\). So the likelihoods are \(\exp(-2.5),\ \exp(0)=1,\ \exp(-2.5)\) with \(\exp(-2.5)\approx0.082\).









Hint 5 — did the prior flip the answer? (B4)





Re-use the same three likelihoods \(0.082,\ 1,\ 0.082\); only the prior weights change. Multiply, sum, divide. Compare which \(b\) has the largest posterior before and after. A weakly-informative prior nudges the numbers but rarely overturns a clear likelihood.









Hint 6 — probabilities and intervals from draws (B5)





\(P(b>0)\) is just (count of positive draws) / (total draws) — see mean applied to a logical. For an 80% interval from 10 sorted draws, trimming 10% at each end drops the 1st and 10th values, leaving the 2nd and 9th as the interval endpoints. In R, quantile(b_draws, c(0.1, 0.9)) does the interpolated version.









Hint 7 — which band is wider? (B6)





The mean-line band uses only uncertainty in \(a\) and \(b\). A single new donor also scatters around the line by \(\sigma\), so its prediction band adds that noise on top and is always wider. For “one new 70-year-old” you want the wider band (predict-style / posterior-predictive), not the mean band.

title: Exercise: fitting equations the Bayesian way (regression)
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. Means: \(\bar x = 1\), \(\bar y = 5/3 \approx 1.667\). Deviations \(x_i-\bar x\): \(-1, 0, 1\). Deviations \(y_i-\bar y\): \(-2/3, 1/3, 1/3\). Numerator \(\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y) = (-1)(-2/3) + 0(1/3) + (1)(1/3) = 2/3 + 1/3 = 1\). Denominator \(\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2 = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2\). So \(\hat b = 1/2 = 0.5\), and \(\hat a = \bar y - \hat b \bar x = 5/3 - 0.5\cdot1 = 5/3 - 1/2 = 7/6 \approx 1.167\). The least-squares line is \(\hat y = 1.167 + 0.5\,x\). lm(y ~ x) returns the same.
B2. Predictions and residuals (data \(y = 1,2,2\) at \(x=0,1,2\)):

Line P, \(y = 1 + 0.5x\): predictions \(1, 1.5, 2\); residuals \(0, 0.5, 0\); SSR \(= 0 + 0.25 + 0 = 0.25\).
Line Q, \(y = 1 + x\): predictions \(1, 2, 3\); residuals \(0, 0, -1\); SSR \(= 0 + 0 + 1 = 1\).

Line P has the smaller SSR (0.25 vs 1), so line P has the higher likelihood. Because the Gaussian likelihood is \(\propto \exp(-\text{SSR}/2\sigma^2)\), a smaller SSR gives a larger exponent (closer to 0, less negative) and hence a larger likelihood — maximising likelihood is minimising SSR. (Note line P here is close to, but not exactly, the B1 least-squares line \(1.167 + 0.5x\), which is the true SSR minimiser.)
B3. Through-origin model, \(\sigma=1\), data \((1,1),(2,2)\). (a) SSR: \(b=0 \to (1-0)^2+(2-0)^2 = 1+4 = 5\); \(b=1 \to (1-1)^2+(2-2)^2 = 0\); \(b=2 \to (1-2)^2+(2-4)^2 = 1+4 = 5\). (b) Likelihoods \(\propto \exp(-\tfrac12\text{SSR})\): \(b=0 \to \exp(-2.5)\approx 0.082\); \(b=1 \to \exp(0)=1\); \(b=2 \to \exp(-2.5)\approx 0.082\). (c) Times prior \(\tfrac13\): \(0.0274,\ 0.333,\ 0.0274\). Total \(= 0.388\). Normalise: \[P(b{=}0) = 0.0274/0.388 \approx 0.070,\quad P(b{=}1) \approx 0.859,\quad P(b{=}2) \approx 0.070.\] (d) \(P(b>0) = P(b{=}1) + P(b{=}2) \approx 0.859 + 0.070 = 0.930\).
B4. Same likelihoods \(0.082,\ 1,\ 0.082\), sceptical prior \(0.5, 0.3, 0.2\). Prior \(\times\) likelihood: \(0.5(0.082)=0.041\), \(0.3(1)=0.300\), \(0.2(0.082)=0.0164\). Total \(=0.3574\). Normalise: \(P(b{=}0)\approx 0.115\), \(P(b{=}1)\approx 0.839\), \(P(b{=}2)\approx 0.046\). The conclusion is unchanged: \(b=1\) is still by far the most probable slope. The sceptical prior only moved \(P(b{=}1)\) from \(\approx0.859\) down to \(\approx0.839\) (about two percentage points) — the data (a perfect fit at \(b=1\)) dominate the weak prior.
B5. (a) Nine of the ten draws are positive (only \(-0.002\) is negative), so \(P(b>0) \approx 9/10 = 0.90\). (b) Trimming 10% at each end drops the 1st (\(-0.002\)) and 10th (\(0.028\)) draws; the interval runs from the 2nd to the 9th draw: \([0.004,\ 0.023]\) per year. (R’s interpolating quantile(b_draws, c(0.1,0.9)) gives a very close \([0.0044,\ 0.0235]\).) (c) The 80% credible interval means: given the data and priors, there is an 80% probability the true per-year slope lies in \([0.004, 0.023]\) — a direct probability statement about the parameter. A frequentist confidence interval cannot be read that way: its 95% (or 80%) refers to the long-run coverage of the procedure across hypothetical repeated experiments, not the probability for this particular interval.
B6. The prediction interval for one new donor is wider. The mean-line (credible) band reflects only uncertainty in the regression line itself (\(a\) and \(b\)). A single new donor additionally scatters around that line by the noise \(\sigma\), so its prediction band adds \(\sigma\) on top of the line uncertainty and is always wider. For “what expression should I expect from one new 70-year-old?” you quote the wider prediction interval (posterior-predictive / predict-style), because it includes donor-to-donor variability, not just uncertainty about the average trend.
R1–R4.
# R1
dat <- data.frame(x = c(0,1,2), y = c(1,2,2))
coef(lm(y ~ x, data = dat))     # (Intercept) 1.1667  x 0.5  -> matches B1

# R2
x <- c(1,2); y <- c(1,2); b_grid <- c(0,1,2)
lik <- exp(-0.5 * sapply(b_grid, function(b) sum((y - b*x)^2)))
post_flat  <- (c(1,1,1)/3 * lik);      post_flat  <- post_flat / sum(post_flat)
post_skept <- (c(0.5,0.3,0.2) * lik);  post_skept <- post_skept / sum(post_skept)
round(post_flat,  3)            # 0.070 0.859 0.070  -> matches B3
round(post_skept, 3)            # 0.115 0.839 0.046  -> matches B4
sum(post_flat[b_grid > 0])      # 0.930                -> matches B3(d)

# R3
b_draws <- c(-0.002,0.004,0.006,0.009,0.011,0.014,0.016,0.019,0.023,0.028)
mean(b_draws > 0)               # 0.9
quantile(b_draws, c(0.1, 0.9))  # ~0.0044 .. 0.0235   -> close to B5(b) [0.004, 0.023]
R4. In the brm() call, prior(normal(0,5), class="Intercept") is the prior on \(a\), prior(normal(0,0.1), class="b") is the prior on the slope \(b\), and prior(exponential(1), class="sigma") is the prior on the noise scale \(\sigma\). Before reading any estimate, check the summary(fit) output first — specifically that every Rhat is \(\approx 1.00\) (and ESS is large); if the chains have not converged, the coefficient numbers are not trustworthy no matter how reasonable they look.

title: Exercise: fitting equations the Bayesian way (regression)
text:
Where this leads

Count models (distributions block): swapping family = gaussian() for family = poisson() or negbinomial() turns this same brms workflow into a regression for sequencing count data — the honest model for overdispersed omics counts, instead of forcing a Gaussian.
Prior / likelihood / posterior: the grid computation in B3–B4 is Bayes’ theorem in miniature; MCMC (used by brms) does the same prior \(\times\) likelihood combination when the parameter space is too large to grid.
Markov chains: the “MC” in MCMC is a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior — the sampler walks parameter space and its long-run visiting frequencies are the posterior draws you summarise here.
Least squares (linear algebra block): with flat priors, the peak of the posterior coincides exactly with the least-squares line — the Bayesian fit is a strict generalisation of the fit you already know.

title: Exercise: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Background
Two views of probability. A frequentist treats a parameter \(p\) as a fixed unknown and probability as a long-run frequency; results are point estimates, confidence intervals, and p-values. A Bayesian treats \(p\) as uncertain and describes it with a probability distribution, updated by data.
Bayes’ rule. For a hypothesis \(H\) (a value of \(p\)) and observed data \(D\),
\[P(H \mid D) = \frac{P(D \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(D)} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \underbrace{P(H\mid D)}_{\text{posterior}} \;\propto\; \underbrace{P(D\mid H)}_{\text{likelihood}}\;\underbrace{P(H)}_{\text{prior}}.\]
The denominator \(P(D)\) does not depend on \(H\), so it is just a normaliser; the shape of the posterior is prior \(\times\) likelihood.
The conjugate Beta–binomial (memorise this). To estimate a proportion \(p\) from \(k\) successes in \(n\) trials:

Likelihood (binomial): \(P(k\mid p) \propto p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}\).
Prior (Beta): \(p \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\), with \(P(p) \propto p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}\). Read \(\alpha,\beta\) as prior pseudo-counts of successes and failures. \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\) is uniform (“no opinion”).
Posterior — multiply and add the exponents: \[p \mid \text{data} \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha + k,\ \beta + n - k).\] The update is pure arithmetic: add your successes to \(\alpha\) and your failures to \(\beta\).
Summaries. Posterior mean \(= \dfrac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\) (using the posterior \(\alpha,\beta\)). A 95% credible interval holds 95% of the posterior probability; you may say “there is a 95% probability that \(p\) lies inside.”

Interpretation traps. A frequentist confidence interval is a statement about the long-run procedure, not a probability about the parameter. A p-value is \(P(\text{data this extreme}\mid H_0)\), not \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\).

title: Exercise: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
By hand
Throughout, the running example is counting marker-positive cells: \(k\) positive out of \(n\) examined.
B1. In one sentence each, contrast the frequentist and Bayesian meaning of the word “probability.” Then say which of the two is willing to write \(P(p = 0.3)\), and why.
B2. Label the three pieces of \(\text{posterior} \propto \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior}\) for the cell-counting problem: which is the binomial term, which is the Beta term, and which is what you report at the end?
B3. You examine \(n = 20\) cells and find \(k = 6\) positive. Using a uniform prior \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\): (a) write the posterior distribution; (b) compute the posterior mean; (c) compare it to the frequentist estimate \(\hat p = k/n\). Why are they close but not identical?
B4. Repeat B3 with an informative prior \(\text{Beta}(2,8)\) (three earlier experiments suggested about 20% positive). Write the posterior and its mean. Does the estimate move up or down relative to B3, and why?
B5. Now suppose you had examined ten times as many cells, \(n = 200\) with \(k = 60\) (same fraction \(0.30\)). Redo the posterior mean under both priors \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\) and \(\text{Beta}(2,8)\). What happens to the gap between the two answers, and what general principle does this illustrate?
B6. A colleague reports a 95% confidence interval of \([0.14,\ 0.52]\) and says “so there’s a 95% probability the true fraction is between 0.14 and 0.52.” Is that interpretation correct for a confidence interval? State the correct meaning, and say under which framework the quoted sentence would be legitimate.
B7. You test whether the positive fraction exceeds 25%. A frequentist reports \(p\text{-value} = 0.08\) for \(H_0: p = 0.25\). A student concludes “there’s only an 8% chance the true fraction is 0.25 or below.” Explain what the p-value actually says, and what Bayesian quantity the student is really reaching for.
B8. (pseudo-counts) Explain why \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\) barely moves the estimate while \(\text{Beta}(20,80)\) (same 20% centre) would move it a lot, even though both are “centred at 0.2.” Relate your answer to the idea of prior pseudo-counts.

title: Exercise: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Explore
Do B3–B5 by hand first, then use the demo to check your numbers and to see the curves. The sliders set the prior Beta(\(\alpha,\beta\)) and the data (\(k\) positive of \(n\) cells); the presets load the lecture’s cases. The solid red curve is the posterior, with its 95% credible interval shaded; below the plot the Bayesian interval is drawn next to the frequentist \(k/n\) with its usual 95% confidence interval \(\hat p \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}\).



E1. Load “6/20 flat” and then “6/20 Beta(2,8)”. Check the posterior parameters and means against your B3 and B4 answers. Which of the two intervals below the plot moves when you change the prior, and which does not? Why?
E2. Load “6/20 wrong prior” (Beta(40,10), centred at 0.8). Where does the posterior end up? Now load “60/200 wrong prior”. Has the data “won” yet? Use the readout line prior share of counts to explain.
E3. Keep the prior at Beta(2,8) and \(k/n = 6/20\), but raise \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) to Beta(20,80) (same centre 0.2). What happens to the posterior mean and the width of the credible interval? Relate this to B8.
E4. Set a flat prior, press “no data”, then “+1 negative” five times (\(k = 0\), \(n = 5\)). Compare the frequentist interval with the Bayesian credible interval. Which one gives a sensible statement of uncertainty, and why does the other one fail?






Solutions





E1. Flat prior: posterior Beta(7, 15), mean 0.318, 95% credible interval about [0.146, 0.522]. With Beta(2,8): posterior Beta(8, 22), mean 0.267, interval about [0.127, 0.435]. Only the Bayesian interval moves. The frequentist estimate \(k/n = 0.30\) and its confidence interval [0.10, 0.50] use the data alone, so the prior has no way to enter them.
E2. With 6/20 the posterior is Beta(46, 24), mean 0.657 — much closer to the prior’s 0.8 than to the data’s 0.3, and its credible interval [0.54, 0.76] does not even contain 0.3. The prior carries 50 pseudo-counts against 20 real cells (prior share 71%). With 60/200 the posterior is Beta(100, 150), mean 0.40: better, but still well above 0.30, since the prior still makes up 20% of the counts. A confident prior in the wrong place needs a lot of data to overcome, which is why priors have to be defended and checked (sensitivity analysis).
E3. Beta(20,80) + 6/20 gives Beta(26, 94), mean 0.217 (versus 0.267 with Beta(2,8)), and a narrower interval, about [0.15, 0.29] instead of [0.13, 0.44]. Both priors are centred at 0.2, but Beta(20,80) is worth 100 pseudo-cells, five times the data, so it pulls the estimate almost all the way to 0.2. The strength \(\alpha+\beta\), not only the centre, decides how much a prior matters (B8).
E4. The frequentist estimate is \(0/5 = 0\) and the formula gives SE \(= 0\), so the “95% interval” collapses to the single point [0, 0] — it claims certainty from five cells. The flat-prior posterior is Beta(1, 6), mean 0.143, with credible interval about [0.004, 0.46]: small fractions are most plausible, but values up to almost one half are not ruled out. The simple \(\pm 1.96\,\text{SE}\) interval is an approximation that breaks down for small \(n\) or when \(k\) is 0 or \(n\) (better frequentist intervals exist, e.g. binom.test in R); the Bayesian posterior handles these cases without a special rule.

title: Exercise: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
In R
Use R only to confirm your by-hand answers. Everything here is base R — no package needed.

The Beta–binomial update
k <- 6; n <- 20

# frequentist point estimate
p_hat <- k / n                       # 0.30

# Bayesian update, uniform prior Beta(1, 1)
a0 <- 1; b0 <- 1
a  <- a0 + k                         # posterior alpha = 7
b  <- b0 + (n - k)                   # posterior beta  = 15

a / (a + b)                          # posterior mean          -> 0.318


Credible interval and a tail probability
# 95% credible interval = 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the posterior
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b)         # ~ 0.14 .. 0.52

# posterior probability that p exceeds 0.25
1 - pbeta(0.25, a, b)                # ~ 0.75


Swapping in an informative prior
a0 <- 2; b0 <- 8                     # centred near 0.2, weak
a  <- a0 + k                         # 8
b  <- b0 + (n - k)                   # 22
a / (a + b)                          # posterior mean          -> 0.267
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b)         # narrower, shifted down


Tasks
R1. Reproduce your B3 posterior mean and add a 95% credible interval with qbeta. Confirm the mean matches \(\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)\).
R2. Reproduce your B4 informative-prior mean, and compute 1 - pbeta(0.25, a, b) under both priors. Which prior makes you more confident that \(p > 0.25\), and does that match your intuition?
R3. Reproduce B5 in R: set n <- 200; k <- 60 and recompute the posterior mean under both priors. Verify numerically that the two answers are much closer than in the \(n = 20\) case.
R4. (Seeing the shift.) Evaluate the two posterior densities on a grid and eyeball where they peak:
p <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 501)
plot(p, dbeta(p, 7, 15),  type = "l",              # uniform-prior posterior
     xlab = "p", ylab = "posterior density")
lines(p, dbeta(p, 8, 22), lty = 2)                 # informative-prior posterior
abline(v = 6/20, col = "grey")                     # frequentist estimate 0.30
Which curve sits a little to the left, and why?

title: Exercise: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — the two meanings of probability





Frequentist probability is a long-run frequency of repeatable events, so a fixed parameter has no distribution — a frequentist will not write \(P(p = 0.3)\). Bayesian probability is a degree of belief, so it can describe uncertainty about a fixed-but-unknown parameter. See the Wikipedia summary of the two interpretations.









Hint 2 — the conjugate update





Counting \(k\) positives out of \(n\) is binomial; the matching prior for the proportion is the Beta distribution. Multiplying \(p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}\) by \(p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}\) just adds the exponents, giving \(\text{Beta}(\alpha+k,\ \beta+n-k)\). So: add successes to \(\alpha\), failures to \(\beta\).









Hint 3 — posterior mean





The mean of \(\text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\) is \(\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)\). Use the posterior parameters (after adding the data), not the prior ones.









Hint 4 — why prior vs data pull against each other





Think of \(\alpha,\beta\) as pretend prior counts. The total “evidence” is \(\alpha+\beta+n\); the prior’s share is \((\alpha+\beta)/(\alpha+\beta+n)\). When \(n\) is small the prior is a big share (it moves the answer); when \(n\) is large the data dominates and the prior fades.









Hint 5 — confidence vs credible





A credible interval is a probability statement about the parameter (“95% probability \(p\) is inside”). A confidence interval is a statement about the procedure: repeat the experiment many times and 95% of the intervals you build would contain the true fixed \(p\). A single realised interval either contains \(p\) or not — no probability attached. See confidence interval vs credible interval.









Hint 6 — what a p-value is





A p-value is \(P(\text{data at least this extreme}\mid H_0)\) — the probability of the data assuming the null is true. It is not \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\). The quantity the student wants (the probability the hypothesis is true given the data) is a posterior probability, obtainable with pbeta on the posterior.









Hint 7 — the R functions





Build the posterior parameters by adding counts, then use dbeta (density), qbeta (quantiles → credible interval), and pbeta (cumulative → tail probabilities). qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b) gives a 95% credible interval; 1 - pbeta(x, a, b) gives \(P(p > x \mid \text{data})\).

title: Exercise: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. Frequentist: probability is the long-run relative frequency of an outcome over many repetitions of an experiment. Bayesian: probability is a degree of belief about a proposition, given what you know. Only the Bayesian will write \(P(p = 0.3)\), because Bayesian probability may describe uncertainty about a fixed-but-unknown parameter; for a frequentist the parameter is fixed (not random), so it has no probability distribution.
B2. The binomial term \(p^{6}(1-p)^{14}\) is the likelihood (how probable the observed 6-of-20 is for each value of \(p\)). The Beta term \(p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}\) is the prior (belief about \(p\) before the data). What you report is the posterior, \(\text{Beta}(\alpha+6,\ \beta+14)\), obtained by multiplying the two and renormalising.
B3. (a) Add successes to \(\alpha\) and failures to \(\beta\): \(\text{Beta}(1+6,\ 1+14) = \text{Beta}(7,\ 15)\). (b) Posterior mean \(= \dfrac{7}{7+15} = \dfrac{7}{22} \approx 0.318\). (c) The frequentist estimate is \(\hat p = 6/20 = 0.30\). They are close because the uniform prior carries almost no information (just one pseudo-success and one pseudo-failure). They are not identical because those pseudo-counts nudge the estimate very slightly toward \(0.5\) (the centre of the uniform prior).
B4. \(\text{Beta}(2+6,\ 8+14) = \text{Beta}(8,\ 22)\), mean \(= \dfrac{8}{30} \approx 0.267\). The estimate moves down relative to B3 (0.318 → 0.267) because the informative prior \(\text{Beta}(2,8)\) is centred near \(0.2\) (its mean is \(2/10 = 0.2\)) and pulls the posterior toward the earlier experiments. With only \(n = 20\) cells that pull is noticeable.
B5. With \(n = 200\), \(k = 60\), failures \(= 140\):

Uniform \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\): posterior \(\text{Beta}(61,\ 141)\), mean \(= 61/202 \approx 0.302\).
Informative \(\text{Beta}(2,8)\): posterior \(\text{Beta}(62,\ 148)\), mean \(= 62/210 \approx 0.295\).

The gap shrinks from \(0.318\) vs \(0.267\) (a difference of \(0.051\) at \(n=20\)) to \(0.302\) vs \(0.295\) (a difference of \(0.007\) at \(n=200\)). Principle: as data accumulates, the likelihood dominates and the choice of prior matters less — the two posteriors converge on the data estimate \(0.30\). Priors matter most when data is scarce.
B6. The interpretation is not correct for a confidence interval. Correct meaning: the interval was produced by a procedure that, over many repeated experiments, yields intervals containing the true fixed \(p\) 95% of the time. For this one realised interval \([0.14, 0.52]\), \(p\) is either inside it or not — there is no 95% probability attached. The quoted sentence would be legitimate for a credible interval (a Bayesian interval), because there \(p\) has a probability distribution.
B7. The p-value \(0.08\) is \(P(\text{data at least this extreme}\mid H_0: p = 0.25)\) — the probability of seeing data this far from the null if the null were exactly true. It says nothing directly about how probable \(H_0\) itself is. The student is reaching for a posterior probability, \(P(p \le 0.25 \mid \text{data})\), which is a Bayesian quantity: you get it from the posterior with pbeta(0.25, a, b). Confusing \(P(\text{data}\mid H_0)\) with \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\) is the classic p-value misreading.
B8. Both \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\) and \(\text{Beta}(20,80)\) (and \(\text{Beta}(2,8)\)) can share the centre \(0.2\)-ish, but they carry very different amounts of prior information, measured by \(\alpha+\beta\). \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\) has \(\alpha+\beta = 2\) pseudo-counts, tiny next to \(n = 20\) real observations, so the data dominates. \(\text{Beta}(20,80)\) has \(\alpha+\beta = 100\) pseudo-counts, five times the data, so it dominates and drags the estimate strongly toward \(0.2\). The width/strength of a prior, not just its centre, controls how much it moves the answer — the concentration \(\alpha+\beta\) is an effective prior sample size.
R1.
k <- 6; n <- 20
a <- 1 + k; b <- 1 + (n - k)         # Beta(7, 15)
a / (a + b)                          # 0.3181818  -> matches 7/22
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b)         # ~ 0.1459 .. 0.5218
The mean equals \(\alpha/(\alpha+\beta) = 7/22\); the 95% credible interval is roughly \([0.14, 0.52]\).
R2.
k <- 6; n <- 20

# uniform prior
a <- 1 + k; b <- 1 + (n - k)         # Beta(7, 15)
1 - pbeta(0.25, a, b)                # ~ 0.75

# informative prior Beta(2,8)
a <- 2 + k; b <- 8 + (n - k)         # Beta(8, 22)
a / (a + b)                          # 0.2667
1 - pbeta(0.25, a, b)                # ~ 0.55
The uniform prior gives a higher \(P(p > 0.25)\) (~0.75) than the informative prior (~0.55). That matches intuition: the informative prior is centred at \(0.2\), so it pulls belief below \(0.25\) and makes you less sure the fraction exceeds a quarter.
R3.
n <- 200; k <- 60

a <- 1 + k; b <- 1 + (n - k)         # Beta(61, 141)
a / (a + b)                          # 0.3020

a <- 2 + k; b <- 8 + (n - k)         # Beta(62, 148)
a / (a + b)                          # 0.2952
The two means (0.302 and 0.295) differ by under \(0.01\), far less than the \(n = 20\) gap (0.318 vs 0.267). With ten times the data the prior barely matters.
R4. The dashed curve, the \(\text{Beta}(8,22)\) posterior from the informative prior, sits slightly to the left of the solid \(\text{Beta}(7,15)\) curve, because the informative prior is centred near \(0.2\) and pulls the posterior toward smaller \(p\). The flat-prior posterior Beta(7,15) peaks exactly on the grey line at \(0.30\) (its mode \((7-1)/(7+15-2) = 6/20\) is the data estimate); the informative-prior posterior Beta(8,22) peaks below it, at \(7/28 = 0.25\), pulled toward the prior’s \(0.2\). With more data both curves would narrow and slide onto \(0.30\).

title: Exercise: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Where this leads

Bayesian inference in R (if this block stays): for non-conjugate models there is no closed-form posterior, and we sample it with MCMC (e.g. Stan / rstan, brms). The Beta–binomial here is the rare case that needs only qbeta/pbeta.
Hierarchical / empirical-Bayes shrinkage: the per-gene estimates in differential-expression tools (limma, DESeq2) borrow strength across genes exactly in the spirit of a prior — a hierarchical Bayesian idea, even when the software calls it something else.
Count distributions: the Poisson and negative binomial distributions (introduced with overdispersion in the count-data material) are the likelihoods you would pair with priors when modelling sequencing counts the Bayesian way.

title: Quiz: Bayesian vs frequentist
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of Bayesian thinking and how it contrasts with the frequentist statistics you met earlier. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Several are written in the style of the on-campus exam (no computer). The running example is estimating a proportion \(p\) from \(k\) successes in \(n\) trials — e.g. marker-positive cells.

Q1. In one sentence each, state what “probability” means to a frequentist and to a Bayesian. Which of the two is willing to write \(P(p = 0.3)\) for a fixed unknown parameter \(p\)?






Hint





One meaning is a long-run frequency of repeatable events; the other is a degree of belief. Only one allows a distribution over a fixed parameter.









Answer





Frequentist: probability is the long-run frequency of an outcome over many repetitions. Bayesian: probability is a degree of belief about a proposition given what you know. The Bayesian is willing to write \(P(p=0.3)\), because Bayesian probability can describe uncertainty about a fixed-but-unknown parameter; the frequentist treats \(p\) as fixed (not random), so it has no distribution.




Q2. Write Bayes’ rule and name the four pieces. Which piece is “what you believed before the data,” and which is “what you believe after”?






Hint





\(P(H\mid D) = P(D\mid H)P(H)/P(D)\). Before = prior; after = posterior.









Answer





\(P(H\mid D) = \dfrac{P(D\mid H)\,P(H)}{P(D)}\). Pieces: \(P(H)\) = prior (belief before data), \(P(D\mid H)\) = likelihood (how probable the data is under \(H\)), \(P(H\mid D)\) = posterior (belief after data), \(P(D)\) = evidence (normalising constant). Prior = before, posterior = after.




Q3. Explain the working shorthand \(\text{posterior} \propto \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior}\). Why are we allowed to drop the denominator \(P(D)\)?






Hint





Does \(P(D)\) depend on the hypothesis \(H\)?









Answer





\(P(D)\) is the same number for every hypothesis \(H\) — it does not depend on \(H\) — so it only rescales the posterior to sum to 1 without changing its shape. We can therefore compute prior \(\times\) likelihood and fix the constant at the end. In words: posterior belief = prior belief reweighted by how well each hypothesis explains the data.




Q4. You examine \(n = 20\) cells and find \(k = 6\) positive. Starting from a uniform prior \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\), write the posterior distribution and its mean.






Hint





Conjugate update: add successes to \(\alpha\), failures to \(\beta\). Mean of \(\text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\) is \(\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)\).









Answer





Successes \(k = 6\), failures \(n-k = 14\). Posterior \(= \text{Beta}(1+6,\ 1+14) = \text{Beta}(7,\ 15)\). Mean \(= \dfrac{7}{7+15} = \dfrac{7}{22} \approx 0.318\) — just above the frequentist estimate \(6/20 = 0.30\).




Q5. Same data (\(k=6\), \(n=20\)), but now an informative prior \(\text{Beta}(2,8)\) from earlier experiments. Give the posterior and its mean, and say which way it moves relative to Q4.






Hint





\(\text{Beta}(2,8)\) is centred at \(2/10 = 0.2\). Add the same counts.









Answer





Posterior \(= \text{Beta}(2+6,\ 8+14) = \text{Beta}(8,\ 22)\), mean \(= \dfrac{8}{30} \approx 0.267\). It moves down from \(0.318\) toward the prior’s centre of \(0.2\), because with only 20 cells the informative prior still carries real weight.




Q6. A 95% confidence interval comes back as \([0.14, 0.52]\). Is it correct to say “there is a 95% probability that \(p\) is between 0.14 and 0.52”? Give the correct interpretation, and say for which kind of interval the quoted sentence is legitimate.






Hint





A confidence interval is a statement about the long-run procedure, not about this one interval.









Answer





No. Correct meaning: if the experiment were repeated many times, 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true fixed \(p\); this particular interval either contains \(p\) or it does not, with no probability attached. The “95% probability \(p\) is inside” statement is legitimate only for a Bayesian credible interval, where \(p\) has a probability distribution.




Q7. For \(H_0: p = 0.25\) a test gives \(p\text{-value} = 0.08\). A student says “so there’s an 8% chance the true fraction is 0.25 or less.” What does the p-value actually mean, and what quantity does the student really want?






Hint





\(P(\text{data}\mid H_0)\) is not the same as \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\).









Answer





The p-value is \(P(\text{data at least this extreme}\mid H_0)\) — the probability of the observed (or more extreme) data assuming the null is true. It is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true. The student wants a posterior probability such as \(P(p \le 0.25 \mid \text{data})\), a Bayesian quantity you read from the posterior (pbeta(0.25, a, b)).




Q8. True or false: with a very large, clean dataset, the Bayesian posterior and the frequentist estimate usually agree, so the choice of a reasonable prior barely matters. Explain.






Hint





Think of \(\alpha,\beta\) as pseudo-counts competing against \(n\) real observations.









Answer





True. The prior contributes a fixed number of pseudo-counts (\(\alpha+\beta\)); as the real sample size \(n\) grows, the likelihood dominates and swamps the prior, so the posterior concentrates on the data estimate. Priors matter most when data is scarce (small \(n\)) or when the prior is very strong (large \(\alpha+\beta\)); with abundant clean data a reasonable prior barely changes the answer.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
About this lecture
A spectrum is a curve: how much light a sample absorbs at each wavelength. Today we treat that curve as what it really is — a vector of numbers — and everything from the linear-algebra block suddenly applies to real chemistry.

What a spectrum is, and why “intensity vs wavelength” is just a high-dimensional vector.
The Beer–Lambert law: absorbance is proportional to concentration — the reason linear models are the natural language of spectroscopy.
Why raw spectra are messy, and the standard preprocessing toolkit: baseline correction, smoothing, normalization, derivatives.
Multivariate calibration: predicting a concentration from a whole spectrum, and why ordinary regression breaks — leading to PLS.

This is an Applications unit: it reuses dot products, linear models, and principal component analysis on data biologists and chemists actually collect.

The single mental shift for today: a spectrum looks like a picture (a wiggly curve), but to a computer it is a list of a few hundred to a few thousand numbers — a point in a high-dimensional space. Once students accept that, every tool from the linear-algebra and stats blocks transfers. Beer–Lambert is the physical reason the maths is linear; preprocessing is the practical reality of real instruments; PLS is the destination. Keep an R session mental-model only — no packages render here, so all code is illustrative. This is “Chemometrics I”; a second unit will go deeper into the multivariate models.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
A biology picture first
You have a bioreactor of cells and you want to know the glucose concentration in the medium — continuously, without pipetting out samples and running an assay every hour.

Shine near-infrared (NIR) light through the medium and record how much is absorbed at each wavelength.
Glucose, lactate, protein, water each absorb light in their own characteristic pattern.
The measured spectrum is a mixture of all of these, weighted by how much of each is present.

The task: read the concentration off the spectrum. Cheap, fast, non-destructive, and it works on living cultures, food, tissue, blood, soil.


Anchor the abstraction in a concrete measurement problem before any maths. Spectroscopy is attractive to biologists precisely because it is fast and non-destructive: you can monitor a fermentation, grade fruit ripeness, or screen blood without consuming the sample. The catch is that the signal is a superposition of every absorbing species, so you cannot just “read off” glucose — you need to model the mixture. That modelling problem is what makes this a linear-algebra topic. Emphasise the words mixture and weighted by concentration; those two ideas become Beer–Lambert and linear calibration.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
What is a spectrum?
Pass light of many wavelengths through a sample and, for each wavelength \(\lambda\), measure how much is absorbed.

Transmittance \(T = I / I_0\): fraction of light that gets through.
Absorbance \(A = -\log_{10}(T) = \log_{10}(I_0 / I)\): the quantity chemists model, because it behaves linearly (next slides).

A spectrum is the function \(A(\lambda)\) — absorbance at each wavelength.



Technique
Probes
Typical use




UV–Vis
electronic transitions
DNA/protein quantification


IR / NIR
molecular vibrations
composition, moisture, sugars


Raman
vibrational (scattering)
aqueous samples, live cells





Define the measurement cleanly. Transmittance is the raw fraction of light through; absorbance is its negative log, and the log is not cosmetic — it is exactly what makes the signal proportional to concentration (Beer–Lambert, next slide). Give students the landscape of techniques without going deep: UV–Vis for the nucleic-acid/protein quantification they already do on a NanoDrop, IR/NIR for bulk composition, Raman for watery and living samples. The common structure is identical: a number at each wavelength. That shared structure is why one set of maths serves them all.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
A spectrum is a vector
The instrument does not record a smooth curve — it records absorbance at a discrete grid of wavelengths \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_p\).
\[\mathbf{x} = (A(\lambda_1),\ A(\lambda_2),\ \dots,\ A(\lambda_p)) \in \mathbb{R}^p\]

Each wavelength is a coordinate; a spectrum is one point in a \(p\)-dimensional space.
\(p\) is large — often several hundred to a few thousand wavelengths.
Two similar samples give two nearby points; the distance between spectra is an ordinary vector distance.

Everything from Vectors and dot products applies: length, distance, angle, projection — now on chemical data.


This is the conceptual keystone of the unit. The curve the software draws is just a connect-the-dots of a numeric vector. Re-frame the plot: the horizontal axis (wavelength) indexes the vector’s entries, the vertical axis is the entry’s value. So a spectrum with 1000 wavelengths is a single point in 1000-dimensional space. This is exactly the high-dimensional setting where geometric intuition helps and where naive methods struggle. Point back to the dot-product unit: cosine similarity between spectra, Euclidean distance for “how different are these two samples” — the machinery is already in their hands.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
The data matrix
Measure \(n\) samples, each on the same grid of \(p\) wavelengths. Stack the spectra as rows:
\[X = \begin{pmatrix} \text{— spectrum}_1 \text{ —} \\ \text{— spectrum}_2 \text{ —} \\ \vdots \\ \text{— spectrum}_n \text{ —} \end{pmatrix} \quad (n \times p)\]

Rows = samples, columns = wavelengths. Same layout as an expression matrix (samples × features).
Usually wide: far more wavelengths than samples, \(p \gg n\).

# X: 50 samples (rows) measured at 700 wavelengths (columns)
dim(X)              # 50 700
X[1, ]              # the first spectrum, as a length-700 vector
matplot(t(X), type = "l")   # overlay all spectra: wavelength on x, absorbance on y


Promote the single spectrum to a dataset. The samples-as-rows, features-as-columns convention is identical to the gene-expression tables they already know, which lowers the barrier. Stress \(p \gg n\): this “short and wide” shape is the defining difficulty of chemometrics and the reason ordinary regression fails later. The matplot idiom (transpose so each spectrum is a line) is the standard first look at spectral data; note we transpose because matplot draws columns as lines. Keep the code illustrative — nothing runs at render time.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
Beer–Lambert law
For a single absorbing substance, absorbance is proportional to concentration:
\[A = \varepsilon\, \ell\, c\]

\(c\) — concentration of the substance,
\(\ell\) — path length the light travels through the sample,
\(\varepsilon\) — molar absorptivity, a constant of the substance at that wavelength.

Double the concentration → double the absorbance. This is the linear relationship at the heart of quantitative spectroscopy.
At a fixed path length, at one wavelength, \(A\) is just a straight line through the origin in \(c\): \(A = (\varepsilon\ell)\,c\).


This is the physical law that licenses everything linear we do. State it plainly: absorbance = molar absorptivity × path length × concentration. The proportionality to concentration is the crucial part — it means a calibration line (absorbance against known concentration) is straight, and its slope lets you invert an unknown absorbance back to a concentration. Mention the limits honestly but briefly: Beer–Lambert holds for dilute, non-scattering samples; at high concentration or with scattering it bends. That caveat motivates preprocessing later. Do not derive it from first principles; take it as the empirical law it is used as.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
Mixtures add up
Real samples contain many absorbing species. At each wavelength, their absorbances simply add:
\[A(\lambda) = \varepsilon_1(\lambda)\,\ell\,c_1 + \varepsilon_2(\lambda)\,\ell\,c_2 + \dots + \varepsilon_k(\lambda)\,\ell\,c_k\]
Writing the whole spectrum at once, with \(\mathbf{s}_i\) the pure-component spectrum of substance \(i\):
\[\mathbf{x} = c_1\mathbf{s}_1 + c_2\mathbf{s}_2 + \dots + c_k\mathbf{s}_k\]
A measured spectrum is a linear combination of pure-component spectra, weighted by concentrations.

This is exactly a linear model — the same object as in Linear models, now with spectra as the vectors.
Recovering the \(c_i\) from \(\mathbf{x}\) is the calibration problem.



This slide is the bridge from physics to linear algebra. Because absorbances are additive, a mixture spectrum is a weighted sum of the pure spectra — a linear combination, the central operation of the whole linear-algebra block. Read the vector equation aloud: the observed spectrum lives in the span of the pure-component spectra, and the concentrations are the coefficients. If you knew all pure spectra you could in principle solve for concentrations directly (a linear system). In practice you rarely know them all, which is why data-driven calibration (fit coefficients from samples with known concentrations) wins. This additivity is why linear methods dominate chemometrics.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
section: Why raw spectra can’t be used directly
text:
Why raw spectra can’t be used directly
Beer–Lambert is clean; real instruments and samples are not. Raw spectra carry artefacts unrelated to chemistry:

Baseline drift / offset — the whole curve floats up or down (light scattering, instrument warm-up).
Multiplicative scaling — path length and particle size scale the whole spectrum up or down.
Random noise — detector noise wiggles on top of the signal.
Overlapping peaks — chemically distinct bands blur into one broad hump.

If we feed these straight into a model, it will happily fit the artefacts instead of the chemistry.


Set up the need for preprocessing by being honest about real data. The same physical sample, measured twice, gives two visibly different curves: a vertical offset from scattering, an overall scaling from path-length differences, a fuzz of noise, and broad overlapping bands. None of that variation is the analyte of interest. A model that has not been told to ignore it will attribute variation to the wrong source. Preprocessing is the disciplined removal of these known nuisance effects so that what remains varies mainly with composition. The next four slides each target one artefact. Emphasise: preprocessing choices matter as much as the model, and are usually validated, not guessed.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
Preprocessing 1 — baseline correction
An additive baseline shifts the whole spectrum: \(A_\text{measured}(\lambda) = A_\text{true}(\lambda) + b(\lambda)\).

Simplest case: a constant offset \(b\) — subtract the minimum, or the value at a signal-free wavelength.
General case: a slowly varying curved baseline — fit a smooth curve (polynomial, asymmetric least squares) and subtract it.

# constant-offset removal: subtract each spectrum's own minimum
X_bc <- X - apply(X, 1, min)      # per-row (per-sample) baseline

# a signal-free anchor wavelength (say column 1) set to zero
X_bc <- X - X[, 1]
Goal: two samples with the same chemistry but different baselines should end up on top of each other.


Baseline correction removes additive, chemistry-free trends. Start with the trivial constant offset — subtract the minimum or the reading at a wavelength where nothing absorbs — because it makes the idea concrete. Then generalise to a curved baseline that drifts across the spectrum, handled by fitting a smooth function and subtracting it (asymmetric least squares is the workhorse but do not detail it). The R shown is base-R illustration of the constant case; note the per-row apply so each sample gets its own correction. The success criterion is invariance: same chemistry, same corrected spectrum, regardless of baseline.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
Preprocessing 2 — smoothing
High-frequency noise rides on top of the real, smooth bands. Averaging neighbouring wavelengths suppresses it.

Moving average: replace each point with the mean of a small window — simple, but blunts peaks.
Savitzky–Golay: fit a low-order polynomial in a sliding window and take its value at the centre — smooths while preserving peak shape. The standard choice.

# crude moving-average smoother (window of 5), illustrative only
smooth5 <- function(v) stats::filter(v, rep(1/5, 5))
X_sm <- t(apply(X, 1, smooth5))
Trade-off: too little smoothing leaves noise; too much erases real narrow peaks. Choose the window deliberately.


Smoothing trades variance for a little bias. A moving average is the intuition — local averaging cancels zero-mean noise — but it flattens sharp peaks. Savitzky–Golay is the field standard because the local polynomial fit follows curvature, so peaks survive. Do not derive SG; name it and say why it is preferred. The key teaching point is the trade-off: the window width is a knob, and both extremes are harmful, so it is tuned, often by cross-validation together with the model. The R is a deliberately crude illustration; real work uses a package (prospectr, signal). Nothing runs here.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
Preprocessing 3 — normalization
Multiplicative effects (path length, particle size, sample density) scale the whole spectrum by an unknown factor. Normalization removes that scale.

Vector normalization: divide each spectrum by its own length \(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\) → all spectra have length 1.
Standard Normal Variate (SNV): per spectrum, subtract its mean and divide by its standard deviation (centre + scale each row).

# vector (L2) normalization: each spectrum scaled to unit length
X_vn <- X / sqrt(rowSums(X^2))

# SNV: centre and scale each spectrum (row) on its own statistics
X_snv <- t(scale(t(X)))     # scale() works on columns, so transpose in/out
Now differences between spectra reflect shape (composition), not overall intensity.


Normalization targets multiplicative nuisance, the counterpart to baseline correction’s additive nuisance. Physically, a longer light path or denser packing multiplies every absorbance by a common factor; that factor carries no compositional information, so we divide it out. Vector normalization (unit length) connects directly to the norm from the vectors unit — the same \(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\). SNV is the spectroscopist’s default: row-centre and row-scale. Note the transpose trick because R’s scale() operates on columns while we need per-row (per-spectrum) statistics. The payoff: after normalization, two spectra differ because their chemistry differs, not because one sample was thicker.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
Preprocessing 4 — derivatives
Taking the derivative of the spectrum with respect to wavelength is a preprocessing step in its own right.

First derivative removes a constant baseline offset (the derivative of a constant is zero).
Second derivative removes a linear (sloping) baseline, and sharpens overlapping peaks into resolvable dips.

In practice the derivative is computed and smoothed together, usually by Savitzky–Golay (fit a polynomial, differentiate it).
# crude first difference along wavelength: approximates the derivative
X_d1 <- t(apply(X, 1, diff))      # one column shorter than X
Cost: differentiation amplifies noise, which is why it is paired with smoothing.


Derivatives are a clever two-for-one: they attack baselines and resolve overlap at once. The differentiation logic is worth stating explicitly — d/dλ of a constant offset is zero, so a first derivative is blind to constant baselines; a second derivative additionally kills any linear slope. And because a broad hump made of two overlapping bands has structure in its curvature, the second derivative separates them into distinct features. The catch is noise amplification: differencing noisy data makes it noisier, so derivatives are always computed with a smoothing polynomial (Savitzky–Golay), never as a raw difference in serious work. The diff() line is the toy version. Emphasise: derivative order and smoothing window are joint choices.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
The calibration problem
We have \(n\) calibration samples with spectra (matrix \(X\), \(n \times p\)) and known reference concentrations (vector \(\mathbf{y}\), measured by a slow gold-standard assay).
Goal: learn a rule that turns a new spectrum into a predicted concentration — so future samples skip the slow assay.
A linear predictor (the natural choice, from Beer–Lambert) is a weighted sum of the absorbances:
\[\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + b_p x_p = b_0 + \mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{x}\]

The weights \(\mathbf{b} = (b_1,\dots,b_p)\) are a vector, one weight per wavelength.
Predicting is a single dot product between the coefficient vector and the spectrum.



Frame the supervised problem cleanly. You pay once for a set of samples measured both ways — fast spectrum and slow reference assay — and use them to learn a predictor, after which only the cheap spectrum is needed. Because Beer–Lambert makes concentration linear in absorbance, a linear predictor is principled, not just convenient. Highlight that the model is entirely a coefficient vector b plus an intercept, and that prediction is the dot product from the vectors unit. This connects the whole preprocessing pipeline to a familiar regression target. The next slide explains why we cannot just call lm() on this.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
Why ordinary regression breaks
Ordinary least squares needs to invert \(X^\top X\) (a \(p\times p\) matrix). On spectra it fails on two counts:

\(p \gg n\): with more wavelengths than samples, \(X^\top X\) is singular — no unique solution. Infinitely many coefficient vectors fit the calibration data perfectly and predict garbage on new samples (overfitting).
Collinearity: adjacent wavelengths are almost identical (spectra are smooth), so columns of \(X\) are highly correlated — even when \(n > p\), \(X^\top X\) is near-singular and the coefficients are wildly unstable.

We need a method that works when predictors are many and correlated. The idea: compress the spectrum into a few good directions first.


Explain the failure concretely so PLS feels necessary, not arbitrary. Two distinct problems: dimensionality (more wavelengths than samples makes the normal equations singular — recall singular matrices from the linear-systems unit) and collinearity (neighbouring wavelengths carry nearly the same information, so the design matrix is ill-conditioned). Both make plain OLS coefficients meaningless — huge, unstable, over-fitted. The resolution is dimension reduction: instead of one weight per wavelength, first find a handful of informative combinations of wavelengths, then regress on those. This is exactly the principal-component idea, and it sets up PLS on the next slide.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
section: From spectra to a few components
text:
From spectra to a few components
Reduce the \(p\) correlated wavelengths to a few latent variables — weighted combinations of wavelengths — then regress on those.

Principal Component Regression (PCR): run principal component analysis on \(X\) (from the PCA unit), keep the top few components, regress \(\mathbf{y}\) on their scores. Components are chosen to capture variance in \(X\) — but the biggest variance might be nuisance, not analyte.
Partial Least Squares (PLS): choose components that capture variance in \(X\) and correlate with \(\mathbf{y}\). It uses the response while building the components.

PLS is the workhorse of chemometric calibration because it aims its components at the quantity you want to predict.


Position both dimension-reduction regressions side by side. PCR is the honest first idea: compress with PCA, regress on the scores — it fixes the singularity and collinearity problems in one move. Its weakness is that PCA looks only at X, so its leading components maximise total spectral variance, which may be dominated by water or scattering rather than the analyte. PLS repairs this by letting the response y steer the components: each latent variable is chosen to have high covariance with y, not just high variance in X. That is the one-sentence distinction to drill. Reference the PCA unit explicitly since students meet PCA there; PLS is PCA’s supervised cousin.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
Partial Least Squares, in words
PLS builds a small number of latent variables (components), one at a time:

Find the direction in wavelength space \(\mathbf{w}_1\) along which the spectra vary and that variation tracks \(\mathbf{y}\) (maximal covariance with \(\mathbf{y}\)).
Project every spectrum onto it → a score \(t_1\) (one number per sample).
Use \(t_1\) to predict \(\mathbf{y}\); remove what it explained from both \(X\) and \(\mathbf{y}\).
Repeat on the remainder for \(\mathbf{w}_2, \mathbf{w}_3, \dots\)


Each component is a linear combination of wavelengths — a direction (a vector) in spectral space.
The number of components is the one dial to tune — chosen by cross-validation.



Give the mechanism at an intuitive level without the NIPALS algebra. The core is covariance-maximising directions: unlike PCA’s variance-only directions, each PLS weight vector is tilted toward the response. Walk the loop — find a direction, project to get scores, regress, deflate (subtract what has been explained), repeat — so students see it as greedy, one component at a time. Two anchors to prior units: each component is a direction/vector in the p-dimensional spectral space (vectors unit), and the whole thing collapses to a final coefficient vector b so prediction stays a dot product. The single hyperparameter is the number of components; too few underfits, too many refits noise, so it is set by cross-validation — the same validation logic used for smoothing windows.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
PLS in R
The pls package fits PLS with built-in cross-validation. Illustrative workflow (not run here):
library(pls)

# df has a response column `conc` and a spectral matrix column `X`
fit <- plsr(conc ~ X, data = df, ncomp = 10, validation = "CV")

# how many components? look for where CV error stops improving
validationplot(fit, val.type = "RMSEP")

# predict a new spectrum using, say, 4 components
predict(fit, newdata = new_df, ncomp = 4)

validation = "CV" cross-validates over component counts.
RMSEP (root-mean-square error of prediction) tells you the expected error on new samples — pick the smallest sensible ncomp.



Show the standard tooling so students know the real workflow exists, while keeping every line illustrative. The pls package’s plsr() with validation = “CV” does the heavy lifting; validationplot with RMSEP is the canonical way to choose the number of components — you look for the elbow where adding components stops lowering cross-validated error and resist going further to avoid overfitting. Reinforce that preprocessing (the four earlier steps) happens before this and is itself part of what you validate. The biological payoff: once fit, predict() turns a two-second spectrum into a concentration, replacing a slow wet assay. Chemometrics II will treat the model and validation more carefully.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
section: It was linear algebra all along
text:
It was linear algebra all along







Chemometrics idea
Course concept




Spectrum = intensity vs wavelength
a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^p\)


Distance / similarity of spectra
norm, dot product, angle


Mixture spectrum
linear combination of pure spectra


Predict concentration
linear model, \(\hat y = b_0 + \mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{x}\)


Compress correlated wavelengths
principal component analysis


Supervised compression
PLS (PCA’s response-aware cousin)



Beer–Lambert makes the chemistry linear; the linear-algebra block is precisely the toolkit for linear things.

Zoom out and make the unifying claim explicit: nothing in this lecture is new machinery, only new data. Each chemometric step maps onto something already taught — spectra are vectors, similarity is dot products, mixtures are linear combinations, calibration is a linear model, and dimension reduction is PCA (supervised, in PLS). The reason it all lines up is physical: Beer–Lambert’s proportionality is what makes concentration a linear function of absorbance, so the linear-algebra toolkit is the right one rather than a convenient approximation. This table is the slide to leave up while summarising.

title: Chemometrics I: spectra as data
text:
Summary

A spectrum is a high-dimensional vector: absorbance at each wavelength. A dataset is a wide matrix, samples × wavelengths, usually \(p \gg n\).
Beer–Lambert (\(A = \varepsilon\ell c\)) makes absorbance proportional to concentration, and mixture spectra are linear combinations of pure-component spectra — so linear models are the natural fit.
Raw spectra need preprocessing: baseline correction (additive), normalization (multiplicative), smoothing (noise), derivatives (baseline + overlap). These are validated, not guessed.
Multivariate calibration predicts concentration from a spectrum. Ordinary regression fails (\(p\gg n\), collinearity); PLS compresses wavelengths into a few response-aware components, tuned by cross-validation.

Next (Chemometrics II): classification of spectra, model validation, and interpreting which wavelengths drive a prediction.

The summary is the take-home. Drill the through-line one more time: spectrum → vector, Beer–Lambert → linear, artefacts → preprocessing, calibration → PLS. Stress that preprocessing and component count are choices validated on held-out data, not aesthetic decisions — this is the single most common beginner mistake. Remind students that everything rested on prior units (vectors, linear models, PCA), which is the point of the Applications block: the abstract machinery pays off on real chemical and biological measurements. Preview Chemometrics II: turning spectra into classes, honest validation, and reading the model to learn which wavelengths — and thus which chemistry — carry the signal.

title: Exercise: chemometrics II — applications & validation
text:
Draft skeleton — pending expert review



This exercise is a provisional draft written to accompany the Chemometrics II skeleton lecture while a subject-matter contributor is recruited. The concepts drilled here (task framing, validation, RMSEP) are standard and safe, but the exercise has not yet been reviewed by a chemometrics expert and contains no real dataset. Numbers in the worked problems are small illustrative toys, not measured data.

title: Exercise: chemometrics II — applications & validation
text:
Goal
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

decide whether a spectroscopy problem is a classification or a regression / calibration task,
explain why ordinary least squares (lm) is the wrong tool for wide, collinear spectral data,
distinguish RMSEC (training), RMSECV (cross-validated), and RMSEP (independent test), and say which one to trust,
compute RMSEP by hand from a small table of predictions,
read a components-vs-error curve and choose the number of latent components,
spot data leakage — the ways a reported error is made falsely optimistic.

This is a concepts and judgement day. The by-hand skill practised is the error calculation and the reasoning about validation, not any spectral algorithm.

title: Exercise: chemometrics II — applications & validation
text:
Background
A spectrum is a vector of many correlated measurements (absorbance at many wavelengths). Stack \(n\) samples into a wide matrix \(X\) (\(n \times p\), often \(p \gg n\)) and let \(\mathbf{y}\) be the property or class we want to predict.
Two tasks. Regression / calibration predicts a continuous \(y\) (a concentration); classification predicts a category (a group label).
Why not lm. With \(p \gg n\) and highly collinear columns, \(X^\top X\) is not invertible and an OLS fit is unstable. Chemometrics instead projects \(X\) onto a few latent components first (PCR, PLS) and models in that low-dimensional space — the machinery from PCA and The OPLS model.
Validation vocabulary. The root-mean-square error of prediction is
\[\mathrm{RMSEP} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\hat{y}_i - y_i\right)^2},\]
in the same units as \(y\). The same formula gives different names depending on which samples it is computed on:

RMSEC — on the training samples (used to fit). Optimistic.
RMSECV — on cross-validated held-out predictions (used to tune, e.g. choose the number of components).
RMSEP — on an independent test set, touched once. The number you report.

Bias is the mean signed error \(\frac{1}{n}\sum(\hat{y}_i - y_i)\): a systematic offset, ideally near zero.
The cardinal rule. Anything fit on the data — preprocessing, scaling, component count, variable selection — must be decided without the test set, or the reported error is too rosy.

title: Exercise: chemometrics II — applications & validation
text:
By hand
B1. For each scenario, say whether it is regression (calibration) or classification, and name the target \(y\): (a) predict the protein percentage of a grain sample from its NIR spectrum; (b) decide whether a Raman spectrum comes from a tumour or from healthy tissue; (c) estimate the glucose concentration of a fermentation broth from IR; (d) identify which of four bacterial species an isolate is, from its spectrum.
B2. Explain in one or two sentences why you cannot simply fit lm(y ~ .) on a matrix of 200 wavelengths measured on 30 samples. What quantity fails to exist, and what do PCR / PLS do instead?
B3. A calibration model predicts analyte concentration (units: mg/mL) on a held-out test set of five samples:

Since this is the independent test set, which of RMSEC / RMSECV / RMSEP does your number deserve to be called?

B4. The same model was also evaluated on the training samples and gave an error of \(0.2\) mg/mL, whereas your test-set error in B3 is larger. Which number should be reported to a collaborator, and why is the training number smaller?
