B6. (leakage hunt). For each workflow, say whether the reported test error is trustworthy or optimistically biased, and why: (a) mean-centre and scale using the mean/SD of the whole dataset, then split into train/test; (b) choose the number of components by picking whichever gives the lowest error on the test set; (c) select the 20 “best” wavelengths using all samples, then run cross-validation on just those 20; (d) fit preprocessing and model on the training set, then apply them unchanged to a test set held out from the start.
B7. (classification metric). A spectral classifier is tested on 100 samples: 90 controls and 10 cases. It labels everything “control”. What is its overall accuracy, and why is that number misleading here? What would you report instead?

title: Exercise: chemometrics II — applications & validation
text:
In R
Static illustrations only. No packages are installed at render time, so nothing below is executed — read it as a template.

RMSEP from a vector of predictions
y_meas <- c(10.0, 12.0,  8.0, 14.0, 11.0)   # measured
y_pred <- c(10.5, 11.0,  8.0, 15.0, 10.5)   # model predictions

resid <- y_pred - y_meas
rmsep <- sqrt(mean(resid^2))                # same units as y
bias  <- mean(resid)

rmsep   # root-mean-square error of prediction
bias    # systematic offset


Choosing components from a cross-validation curve
ncomp  <- 1:7
rmsecv <- c(3.1, 1.8, 1.0, 0.9, 0.92, 1.4, 2.6)

best <- which.min(rmsecv)   # index of the minimum
best                        # -> 4  (fewest error)
plot(ncomp, rmsecv, type = "b",
     xlab = "number of components", ylab = "RMSECV")


A PLS calibration with built-in cross-validation (sketch)
# Illustrative only: the `pls` package provides plsr().
library(pls)

fit <- plsr(y ~ ., data = train, ncomp = 10, validation = "CV")
validationplot(fit, val.type = "RMSEP")   # inspect the curve
summary(fit)

# predict the untouched test set with the chosen number of components
yhat  <- predict(fit, newdata = test, ncomp = 4)
rmsep <- sqrt(mean((yhat - test$y)^2))
rmsep


Tasks
R1. Reproduce B3 with the RMSEP block above. Confirm your hand-computed RMSEP and bias match the R output.
R2. Enter the B5 table into the components block. Confirm which.min(rmsecv) gives the component count you chose by hand, and describe the shape of the plotted curve in one sentence.
R3. Write two lines of R that compute RMSEP for a second candidate model whose predictions are y_pred2 <- c(9.5, 12.5, 8.5, 13.5, 11.5) against the same y_meas. Which of the two models has the lower RMSEP?

title: Exercise: chemometrics II — applications & validation
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — regression vs classification





Ask: is the answer a number on a continuous scale (a concentration, a percentage) or a label from a fixed set of groups (tumour/healthy, one of four species)? A number → regression/calibration; a label → classification.









Hint 2 — why lm fails on wide data





OLS needs to invert \(X^\top X\). With more predictors than samples (\(p > n\)) and collinear columns, that matrix is singular — no unique inverse, so no stable coefficient vector (recall the “no unique solution” case from the Linear systems unit). PCR/PLS sidestep it by regressing on a few latent components instead of the raw wavelengths.









Hint 3 — computing RMSEP by hand





Work column by column: (1) residual \(\hat y_i - y_i\) for each sample; (2) square each residual; (3) average the squares (divide by \(n\), here 5); (4) take the square root. Keep units of \(y\) throughout. See sqrt and mean for the R version: sqrt(mean((y_pred - y_meas)^2)).









Hint 4 — bias vs RMSEP





Bias is the signed average error mean(y_pred - y_meas) — positive means predictions run high. RMSEP squares first, so it measures magnitude regardless of sign. A model can have near-zero bias but a large RMSEP (errors cancel in the mean but not in the squares).









Hint 5 — reading the components curve





Training error falls forever as you add components; cross-validated error falls, bottoms out, then rises as the model starts fitting noise. Choose the component count at (or just before) the minimum of the cross-validated curve — not the training curve. When two nearby counts are within noise of each other, prefer the simpler (fewer-component) model. which.min finds the minimum’s index.









Hint 6 — spotting leakage





Ask of every step: did this use any information from the test set? Preprocessing statistics, component count, and variable selection are all fitted quantities. If any of them saw the test samples (or the whole dataset before splitting), the test error is optimistic. Only a set held out before any fitting, and touched once, gives an honest number.









Hint 7 — accuracy with imbalanced classes





If 90 of 100 samples are controls, always guessing “control” scores 90% accuracy while catching zero cases. With imbalanced groups, report sensitivity and specificity (or a confusion matrix) rather than overall accuracy.

title: Exercise: chemometrics II — applications & validation
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. (a) Regression / calibration — \(y\) = protein percentage (continuous). (b) Classification — \(y\) = tumour vs healthy (two groups). (c) Regression / calibration — \(y\) = glucose concentration (continuous). (d) Classification — \(y\) = species identity (one of four groups).
B2. OLS requires inverting \(X^\top X\). With 200 wavelengths and only 30 samples (\(p \gg n\)) and strongly correlated columns, that matrix is singular / non-invertible, so there is no unique, stable coefficient vector — the fit is undetermined and wildly sensitive to noise. PCR and PLS instead compress \(X\) into a few latent components (linear combinations of wavelengths) and regress \(y\) on those, which is well-posed. PLS chooses components that are relevant to \(y\); PCR uses the largest-variance components of \(X\) regardless of \(y\).
B3. (a) Residuals \(\hat y_i - y_i\): \(10.5-10.0 = +0.5\); \(11.0-12.0 = -1.0\); \(8.0-8.0 = 0.0\); \(15.0-14.0 = +1.0\); \(10.5-11.0 = -0.5\). (b) Square them: \(0.25,\ 1.00,\ 0.00,\ 1.00,\ 0.25\). Sum \(= 2.50\). Mean \(= 2.50/5 = 0.50\). RMSEP \(= \sqrt{0.50} \approx \mathbf{0.71}\) mg/mL. (c) Bias \(= \frac{1}{5}(0.5 - 1.0 + 0.0 + 1.0 - 0.5) = \frac{0}{5} = \mathbf{0}\) mg/mL — no systematic offset (the errors happen to cancel; note RMSEP is still \(0.71\)). (d) It is computed on the independent test set, so it is honestly called RMSEP.
B4. Report the test-set number (\(\approx 0.71\) mg/mL, the RMSEP). The training error (\(0.2\)) is smaller because the model was fit to those very samples — it has partly memorised them, so its error on them is optimistic and does not reflect performance on new samples. Only the independent test set estimates future performance.
B5. (a) Choose 4 components (or arguably 3): RMSECV is minimised at 4 (\(0.9\)), and 3 (\(1.0\)) is nearly as good — if you favour simplicity, 3 is defensible, but 4 is the strict minimum. (b) At 6–7 components the cross-validated error rises sharply (\(1.4\), then \(2.6\)): the model is overfitting, fitting noise in the training spectra that does not generalise. (c) No. A lower training error (RMSEC) at 7 components just confirms the model is fitting the training data more closely, including its noise. The cross-validated error, which reflects new samples, is worse at 7 than at 4. Trust the cross-validated curve, not the training curve.
B6. (a) Optimistically biased. The centering/scaling statistics were computed using the test samples, leaking information from test into the fitted preprocessing. (b) Optimistically biased. Tuning the component count on the test set makes the test set part of model selection — it is no longer independent. Choose components by cross-validation within the training data. (c) Optimistically biased. Selecting wavelengths using all samples (including those later used to estimate error) lets the selection peek at the validation data; selection must happen inside the cross-validation loop. (d) Trustworthy. Preprocessing and model were fit on the training set only and applied unchanged to a test set held out from the start — no leakage.
B7. Accuracy \(= 90/100 = \mathbf{90\%}\), but it is misleading because the classifier catches none of the 10 cases (sensitivity \(= 0\)) — the high number comes entirely from the majority class. Report sensitivity and specificity (or the full confusion matrix); with imbalanced groups, overall accuracy hides total failure on the minority class.
R1.
y_meas <- c(10.0, 12.0,  8.0, 14.0, 11.0)
y_pred <- c(10.5, 11.0,  8.0, 15.0, 10.5)
sqrt(mean((y_pred - y_meas)^2))   # 0.7071068  -> matches ~0.71
mean(y_pred - y_meas)             # 0          -> bias is zero
Matches the hand answers: RMSEP \(\approx 0.71\), bias \(= 0\).
R2.
ncomp  <- 1:7
rmsecv <- c(3.1, 1.8, 1.0, 0.9, 0.92, 1.4, 2.6)
which.min(rmsecv)    # 4  -> minimum at 4 components
which.min returns 4, matching the by-hand choice. The curve falls steeply from 1 to 3–4, flattens at its minimum, then rises from 5 onward — the classic underfit-then-overfit U-shape.
R3.
y_meas  <- c(10.0, 12.0,  8.0, 14.0, 11.0)
y_pred2 <- c( 9.5, 12.5,  8.5, 13.5, 11.5)
sqrt(mean((y_pred2 - y_meas)^2))   # 0.5  -> lower than 0.71
The residuals are all \(\pm 0.5\), so RMSEP \(= \sqrt{\text{mean}(0.25)} = 0.5\) mg/mL — lower than the first model’s \(0.71\), so the second model predicts this test set more accurately.

title: Exercise: chemometrics II — applications & validation
text:
Where this leads

PCA and The OPLS model supply the latent-variable machinery (scores, components) that every method here builds on; this unit is about applying and validating them.
Chemometrics I covers the spectra themselves and preprocessing in more detail; revisit it for the signal-processing steps named only briefly here.
The validation discipline — hold out an independent test set, tune by cross-validation, report error in interpretable units — is not specific to spectra. It carries into every later data-analysis unit, including the single-cell applications.







Warning



Reminder: this is a draft skeleton. A chemometrics expert should replace the toy tables with a real spectral dataset and add a hands-on PLS calibration once the unit is staffed.

text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

title: Exercise: compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

title: Exercise: compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Background
In a flow cytometer each detector collects one band of colours, but a dye’s light also reaches the other detectors (spillover). With two dyes, FITC and PE, and two detectors:
\[\begin{pmatrix} \text{FITC detector} \\ \text{PE detector} \end{pmatrix} = S \begin{pmatrix} \text{FITC} \\ \text{PE} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & s_{12} \\ s_{21} & 1 \end{pmatrix}\]
Column \(j\) of \(S\) is where one unit of dye \(j\)’s light lands: \(s_{21}\) is the fraction of FITC light seen by the PE detector, \(s_{12}\) the fraction of PE light seen by the FITC detector. Compensation recovers the dye amounts with the inverse: true \(= S^{-1}\) measured. For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix,
\[\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}.\]
The number \(ad - bc\) is the determinant \(\det S\): near 0 means the columns are nearly parallel and the inverse has large entries. Bonus material: you do not need to memorise determinants for the exam.
Spectral unmixing is the same equation, with \(S\) built from each dye’s measured reference spectrum (one column per dye, one row per detector).

title: Exercise: compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
By hand
Use \(S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) in B1–B3.
B1. What do the detectors measure for a cell with (FITC, PE) \(= (2000, 0)\)? For \((0, 1000)\)? For \((2000, 1000)\)? Which column of \(S\) did you use for the first two?
B2. Compute \(\det S\) and \(S^{-1}\). Check that \(S^{-1}S = I\).
B3. A cell is measured as \((2100, 1400)\). Compensate it by hand: how much FITC and PE does it carry? Is it double positive?
B4. Two dyes with similar spectra give \(S_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.9 \\ 0.9 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). Compute \(\det S_2\) and \(S_2^{-1}\). A cell measured as \((1000, 900)\) compensates to \((1000, 0)\). Now the PE detector reads 10 units too high, \((1000, 910)\): compensate again. How large is the error in each dye? Compare with the same 10-unit error under the \(S\) of B1–B3.

title: Exercise: compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Explore
The demo below simulates a new sample with the same four populations but an unknown spillover. Left: what the detectors measure. Right: the cells after compensation with your guess, \(S^{-1} \times\) measured, where \(S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & s_{12} \\ s_{21} & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) is set with the sliders. The thick lines are least-squares lines through the FITC+ cells (green) and the PE+ cells (orange); the dashed lines are the medians of the unstained cells.



E1. Click No compensation. Which population is tilted the most, and in which direction? Read off the slope of the green line: what does it tell you about \(S\)?
E2. Find \(s_{21}\) and \(s_{12}\) by making both single-positive populations lie flat, at the same level as the unstained cells. Then click Reveal true S to check.
E3. Set \(s_{21} = 0.20\), then \(0.45\) (keep your \(s_{12}\)). Describe the FITC+ population each time. Which of the two produces cells with negative PE, and why is that a sign of a mistake?
E4. With your answer from E2, multiply the \(S^{-1}\) shown in the readout by \(S\) (first row only, by hand). Do you get the first row of the identity?






Solutions





E1. The FITC+ population (green) tilts upwards: the brighter its FITC, the more false PE. Its slope is about \(0.32\): without compensation the slope of a FITC-only population estimates \(s_{21}\), as with the single-stained control in the lecture. The PE+ population (orange) leans slightly to the right, with slope about \(0.08\): that estimates \(s_{12}\).
E2. \(s_{21} = 0.32\) and \(s_{12} = 0.08\). At these values both lines are flat (slopes within about \(\pm 0.01\) of 0), the FITC+ cells have median PE about 100, like the unstained cells, and the PE+ cells have median FITC about 100. One step (0.01) away the slope hardly changes, but the median moves by about 30, so the median is a sensitive check too.
E3. With \(0.20\) (under-compensated) too little FITC light is subtracted from the PE detector: the FITC+ cells still tilt up, median PE about 480. With \(0.45\) (over-compensated) too much is subtracted: they tilt down, median PE about −300, and almost all of them have negative PE. A cell cannot emit negative light, so a population pushed clearly below the unstained cells means the spillover was set too high.
E4. The readout shows \(S^{-1} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 1.026 & -0.082 \\ -0.328 & 1.026 \end{pmatrix}\). First row times the columns of \(S\): \(1.026 \cdot 1 + (-0.082) \cdot 0.32 = 1.026 - 0.026 = 1.000\) and \(1.026 \cdot 0.08 + (-0.082) \cdot 1 = 0.082 - 0.082 = 0\). So \((1, 0)\), the first row of \(I\) (up to rounding).

title: Exercise: compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
In R
All data are simulated: four populations of cells, with one cell per column (as the pixels in Transforming images with matrices).
set.seed(1)
make_pop <- function(n, fitc, pe) {               # true dye amounts, one cell per COLUMN
  rbind(FITC = rlnorm(n, log(fitc), 0.3), PE = rlnorm(n, log(pe), 0.3))
}
true <- cbind(make_pop(600,  100,  100),          # unstained
              make_pop(400, 3000,  100),          # FITC+
              make_pop(400,  100, 2000),          # PE+
              make_pop(200, 3000, 2000))          # FITC+ PE+
group <- rep(c("unstained", "FITC+", "PE+", "FITC+ PE+"), c(600, 400, 400, 200))

S <- matrix(c(1,    0.02,                         # rows = detectors, columns = dyes
              0.25, 1   ), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
            dimnames = list(c("FITC det", "PE det"), c("FITC", "PE")))
noise <- function(n) matrix(rnorm(2 * n, 0, 30), nrow = 2)   # detector noise
measured <- S %*% true + noise(ncol(true))

cols <- c("unstained" = "grey55", "FITC+" = "#009E73", "PE+" = "#D55E00", "FITC+ PE+" = "#7B3294")
plot(t(measured), col = cols[group], pch = 16, cex = 0.4, asp = 1)
Run the tasks in order: each uses random numbers, so the numbers in the solutions match only if you do.
R1. Plot true and measured side by side, coloured by group. Which population moves most, and in which direction? Compute the median of each detector per population with apply(measured, 1, function(v) tapply(v, group, median)). How much PE signal does the FITC+ population seem to have?
R2. In practice \(S\) is unknown. Simulate two single-stained controls and estimate it:
ctrl_fitc <- S %*% rbind(FITC = rlnorm(500, log(3000), 0.5), PE = 0) + noise(500)
ctrl_pe   <- S %*% rbind(FITC = 0, PE = rlnorm(500, log(2000), 0.5)) + noise(500)
Use lm to estimate \(s_{21}\) (PE detector against FITC detector in the FITC-only control) and \(s_{12}\) (the other way round in the PE-only control). Build S_hat and compare it with S.
R3. Compensate with comp <- solve(S_hat) %*% measured. Plot before and after. Compute the population medians again: does the FITC+ population now have the same PE level as the unstained cells? Check that solve(S_hat) %*% S_hat is the identity.
R4. Compensate with a wrong spillover: \(s_{21} = 0.15\) (too small), then \(0.35\) (too large), keeping \(s_{12}\) from R2. Plot both. What does the FITC+ population look like in each case, and how could you spot the mistake in real data, where you do not know the truth?
R5. Similar dyes. Simulate with \(S_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.9 \\ 0.9 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\): measured2 <- S2 %*% true + noise(ncol(true)), compensate with solve(S2), and plot. Compare the standard deviation of the unstained cells in true, in comp (R3) and in comp2. Relate the result to det(S2) and to your answer in B4.
R6. Spectral unmixing with four detectors. Each dye’s reference spectrum is a column of the \(4 \times 2\) matrix
S4 <- cbind(FITC = c(1,    0.45, 0.10, 0.02),
            PE   = c(0.02, 0.30, 1,    0.40))
measured4 <- S4 %*% true + matrix(rnorm(4 * ncol(true), 0, 30), nrow = 4)
Why does solve(S4) fail? Unmix all cells at once with qr.solve(S4, measured4) (least squares) and compare the population medians with the truth.

title: Exercise: compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — estimating a spillover coefficient





In the FITC-only control, every signal in the PE detector comes from FITC, so PE detector \(\approx s_{21} \times\) FITC detector. lm(ctrl_fitc[2, ] ~ ctrl_fitc[1, ]) fits that straight line; coef(...)[2] is the slope, i.e. \(s_{21}\). Row 1 of a detector matrix is the FITC detector, row 2 the PE detector.









Hint 2 — spotting wrong compensation





Compare the PE level of the FITC+ cells with that of the unstained cells after compensation. If FITC carries no PE, the two should be the same, and the FITC+ population should lie flat (no tilt) however bright the FITC is.









Hint 3 — more detectors than dyes





solve() needs a square matrix: as many equations as unknowns. With 4 detectors and 2 dyes there are 4 equations for 2 unknowns per cell, and with noise they cannot all hold exactly. qr.solve(A, B) finds, for every column of B, the dye amounts whose predicted spectrum is closest to the measured one (least squares).

title: Exercise: compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. \(S\binom{2000}{0} = \binom{2000}{400}\) (column 1 times 2000), \(S\binom{0}{1000} = \binom{100}{1000}\) (column 2 times 1000), and \(S\binom{2000}{1000} = \binom{2000 + 100}{400 + 1000} = \binom{2100}{1400}\), the sum of the two.
B2. \(\det S = 1 \cdot 1 - 0.1 \cdot 0.2 = 0.98\) and \[S^{-1} = \frac{1}{0.98}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -0.1 \\ -0.2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 1.020 & -0.102 \\ -0.204 & 1.020 \end{pmatrix}.\] Check, first entry: \(\frac{1}{0.98}(1 \cdot 1 + (-0.1)(0.2)) = \frac{0.98}{0.98} = 1\); the others work the same way.
B3. \(S^{-1}\binom{2100}{1400} = \frac{1}{0.98}\binom{2100 - 140}{-420 + 1400} = \frac{1}{0.98}\binom{1960}{980} = \binom{2000}{1000}\). The cell carries FITC 2000 and PE 1000: yes, double positive (it is the third cell of B1).
B4. \(\det S_2 = 1 - 0.81 = 0.19\), \(S_2^{-1} = \frac{1}{0.19}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -0.9 \\ -0.9 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 5.26 & -4.74 \\ -4.74 & 5.26 \end{pmatrix}\). \(S_2^{-1}\binom{1000}{910} = \frac{1}{0.19}\binom{1000 - 819}{-900 + 910} \approx \binom{953}{53}\). A 10-unit error in one detector became errors of about 47 and 53 in the dyes: the 10 is multiplied by the large entries of \(S_2^{-1}\). Under the \(S\) of B1–B3, \(S^{-1}\binom{0}{10} = \frac{1}{0.98}\binom{-1}{10} \approx \binom{-1}{10.2}\): the error stays about 10. Similar spectra mean nearly parallel columns, a small determinant, and a large inverse that amplifies noise.
R1.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(t(true),     col = cols[group], pch = 16, cex = 0.4, asp = 1, main = "true")
plot(t(measured), col = cols[group], pch = 16, cex = 0.4, asp = 1, main = "measured")
round(apply(measured, 1, function(v) tapply(v, group, median)))
#           FITC det PE det
# FITC+         3007    850
# FITC+ PE+     3174   2901
# PE+            142   2014
# unstained      104    127





The FITC+ population moves most: it is tilted upwards along the direction of column 1, \((1, 0.25)\), so the brighter a cell’s FITC, the more false PE it shows. It seems to have a median PE of 850, although its true PE is about 100, like unstained cells. The PE+ population barely moves (2 % spillover back). The double-positive cells move up too.
R2.
s21 <- coef(lm(ctrl_fitc[2, ] ~ ctrl_fitc[1, ]))[2]
s12 <- coef(lm(ctrl_pe[1, ] ~ ctrl_pe[2, ]))[2]
S_hat <- matrix(c(1,   s12,
                  s21, 1  ), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
round(S_hat, 3)               # [1, 0.021; 0.249, 1]





The estimates, 0.249 and 0.021, are close to the true 0.25 and 0.02. They are not exact because of the detector noise in the controls.
R3.
comp <- solve(S_hat) %*% measured
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(t(measured), col = cols[group], pch = 16, cex = 0.4, asp = 1, main = "before")
plot(t(comp),     col = cols[group], pch = 16, cex = 0.4, asp = 1, main = "after")
round(apply(comp, 1, function(v) tapply(v, group, median)))
#           FITC   PE
# FITC+     3005  105
# FITC+ PE+ 3122 2063
# PE+         97 1989
# unstained  102  103
round(solve(S_hat) %*% S_hat, 10)     # the 2 x 2 identity





After compensation the FITC+ population lies flat, with a median PE of 105, the same as the unstained cells (103). All four populations are aligned with the axes again.
R4.
for (k in c(0.15, 0.35)) {
  Sk <- matrix(c(1, s12,
                 k, 1  ), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
  ck <- solve(Sk) %*% measured
  plot(t(ck), col = cols[group], pch = 16, cex = 0.4, asp = 1, main = paste("s21 =", k))
  print(round(tapply(ck[2, ], group, median)))
}





With 0.15 (under-compensated) too little is subtracted: the FITC+ population still tilts up, with a median PE of 407. With 0.35 (over-compensated) too much is subtracted: it tilts down, to a median PE of −194, below the unstained cells (negative light is impossible). Without knowing the truth, the tell-tale sign is a tilt: a single-positive population should be flat, at the same PE level as the unstained cells, whatever its FITC brightness. A population that rises or falls along FITC means the spillover is wrong.
R5.
S2 <- matrix(c(1,   0.9,
               0.9, 1  ), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
measured2 <- S2 %*% true + noise(ncol(true))
comp2 <- solve(S2) %*% measured2
plot(t(comp2), col = cols[group], pch = 16, cex = 0.4, asp = 1)
sd_un <- function(m) round(apply(m[, group == "unstained"], 1, sd))
sd_un(true); sd_un(comp); sd_un(comp2)   # 33 33; 45 45; 206 208
det(S2)                                  # 0.19





The true spread of the unstained cells is 33; with well-separated dyes it is 45 after compensation (the detector noise of 30 adds to it). With similar dyes it is about 207: the populations smear out, and the unstained cells form a diagonal streak. The medians are still about right, but individual cells are not. As in B4, \(\det(S_2) = 0.19\) makes the inverse large (entries around 5), and the inverse multiplies the detector noise as well as the signal.
R6. solve(S4) fails because S4 is \(4 \times 2\), not square: it has no inverse.
unmixed <- qr.solve(S4, measured4)       # 2 x 1600: one column per cell
round(apply(unmixed, 1, function(v) tapply(v, group, median)))
#           FITC   PE
# FITC+     3009  100
# FITC+ PE+ 3113 2071
# PE+        104 1996
# unstained   99   99
The medians match the true populations (FITC about 3000 or 100, PE about 2000 or 100). Each cell’s four detector values are explained as well as possible by a mix of the two reference spectra. Using four detectors instead of two also averages out some of the noise.

title: Exercise: compensation & spectral unmixing
text:
Where this leads

Linear systems: compensation is solving \(S\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) for every cell; a singular \(S\) (identical spectra) has no unique solution.
Least squares and regression: R6 is the same least squares used to fit regression models later in the course; with many detectors, spectral cytometers unmix 20 or more dyes this way.
Eigenvalues & eigenvectors: how much a matrix can stretch noise is measured more precisely by its eigenvalues (for symmetric \(S_2\): 1.9 and 0.1; the inverse stretches by \(1/0.1 = 10\)).
Real data: the Bioconductor package flowCore reads cytometry files (read.FCS), estimates spillover (spillover) and compensates (compensate); data(GvHD) is an example data set shipped with it.

title: Exercise: handling covariates
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

write a model formula for a research question and say what each term does,
turn a formula into a design matrix \(X\) by hand, for both continuous and categorical predictors,
read off what each coefficient means, including the crucial “holding the other predictors constant,”
explain confounding and why adjusting for a covariate can change — even reverse — an apparent effect,
interpret an interaction term (\(a * b\)) and compute a subgroup-specific effect,
recognise the common pitfalls (wrong reference level, collinearity, over-adjustment).

By-hand design-matrix and coefficient interpretation are the examined skills; the R section only confirms your answers.

title: Exercise: handling covariates
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

write a model formula for a research question and say what each term does,
turn a formula into a design matrix \(X\) by hand, for both continuous and categorical predictors,
read off what each coefficient means, including the crucial “holding the other predictors constant,”
explain confounding and why adjusting for a covariate can change — even reverse — an apparent effect,
interpret an interaction term (\(a * b\)) and compute a subgroup-specific effect,
recognise the common pitfalls (wrong reference level, collinearity, over-adjustment).

By-hand design-matrix and coefficient interpretation are the examined skills; the R section only confirms your answers.

title: Exercise: handling covariates
text:
Background
A model formula is a recipe for a design matrix. The model is
\[
\mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}, \qquad
\hat y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \dots
\]
Building the columns of \(X\):

Intercept — a column of all 1’s (present by default). Its coefficient \(\beta_0\) is the predicted outcome when every other predictor is 0 (for factors: at the reference level).
Continuous predictor (age, BMI) — the raw numbers, one column. Coefficient = change in \(\hat y\) per unit.
Categorical predictor (a factor with \(k\) levels) — \(k-1\) dummy (0/1) columns under the default treatment contrasts. The omitted level is the reference, folded into the intercept; each dummy’s coefficient = that level minus the reference.

Adjustment. Adding + z gives \(z\) its own column, so the other coefficients are now interpreted holding \(z\) constant. A confounder (a common cause of the predictor of interest and the outcome) must be adjusted for, or the effect you report is biased.
Interaction. a * b expands to a + b + a:b. The product term a:b lets the effect of a depend on the level of b. Under treatment contrasts, the main effect of a is the effect of a at the reference level of b, and the interaction is the extra effect at the other level.
Reference levels. R orders factor levels alphabetically by default, so the alphabetically-first level is the reference. Change it with relevel or factor(x, levels = ...).

title: Exercise: handling covariates
text:
By hand
B1. Write model formulas (in y ~ ... form) for each question: (a) does expression depend on treatment alone? (b) does expression depend on treatment, adjusting for age? (c) does expression depend on treatment and sex, allowing the treatment effect to differ between the sexes?
B2. You have 4 samples:



sample
treatment
age




1
ctrl
10


2
treat
40


3
ctrl
22


4
treat
35



Write out the design matrix \(X\) for the formula expr ~ treatment + age by hand (treatment coding, ctrl as reference). Label the columns.
B3. For the fitted model expr ~ treatment + age you obtain \(\beta_0 = 5\), \(\beta_1 = 3\) (treatmenttreat), \(\beta_2 = 0.1\) (age). In words: (a) what is the predicted expression for a treated animal aged 30? (b) what is the treatment effect, and what does “holding age constant” add to that statement? (c) what does \(\beta_0 = 5\) correspond to, and why is it not very meaningful here?
B4. (categorical with three levels) A factor tissue has levels brain, gut, liver. For expr ~ tissue: (a) how many dummy columns does \(X\) have (besides the intercept)? (b) which level is the reference under the default coding? (c) if the intercept is 2 and the coefficient tissuegut is 4, what is the predicted mean expression in gut? In brain?
B5. (confounding) In a study, treated animals were mostly old and controls mostly young, and expression rises with age. The unadjusted model expr ~ treatment gives a large positive treatmenttreat. After fitting expr ~ treatment + age, the treatmenttreat coefficient shrinks toward 0. (a) explain, in terms of confounding, why it shrank; (b) which of the two estimates is the honest treatment effect, and why?
B6. (interaction) For expr ~ treatment * sex with references ctrl and F, you fit: \[\beta_0 = 5,\quad \beta_1\,(\text{treat}) = 2,\quad \beta_2\,(\text{M}) = 1,\quad \beta_3\,(\text{treat:M}) = 3.\] (a) what is the treatment effect in females? (b) what is the treatment effect in males? (c) what does \(\beta_3 = 3\) mean in words? What would \(\beta_3 = 0\) imply?
B7. (reference level) Your treatment factor has levels drug and placebo. You fit expr ~ treatment and get a coefficient named treatmentplacebo. (a) which level did R choose as the reference, and why? (b) the coefficient treatmentplacebo is \(-4\). Interpret it. Is the drug raising or lowering expression relative to placebo? (c) how would you make placebo the reference so the coefficient reads as the drug effect?

title: Exercise: handling covariates
text:
In R
Use R to confirm the by-hand answers. The models below are illustrative; the same formulas work in a Bayesian fit (rstanarm::stan_glm, brms::brm) with priors added.

See the design matrix a formula builds
treatment <- factor(c("ctrl","treat","ctrl","treat"))
age       <- c(10, 40, 22, 35)

model.matrix(~ treatment + age)
#   (Intercept) treatmenttreat age
# 1           1              0  10
# 2           1              1  40
# 3           1              0  22
# 4           1              1  35


Check the reference level of a factor
levels(treatment)                 # "ctrl" "treat"  -> ctrl is the reference
contrasts(treatment)              # shows the 0/1 coding

# force a different reference:
treatment2 <- relevel(treatment, ref = "treat")
levels(treatment2)                # "treat" "ctrl"


A factor with three levels
tissue <- factor(c("brain","gut","liver","gut"))
model.matrix(~ tissue)
#   (Intercept) tissuegut tissueliver
# 1           1         0           0     # brain = reference (all dummies 0)
# 2           1         1           0
# 3           1         0           1
# 4           1         1           0


An interaction expands into three terms
sex <- factor(c("F","M","F","M"))
colnames(model.matrix(~ treatment * sex))
# "(Intercept)" "treatmenttreat" "sexM" "treatmenttreat:sexM"


Tasks
R1. Reproduce the design matrix from B2 with model.matrix(~ treatment + age) and confirm it matches your hand answer column-for-column.
R2. For B4, build tissue <- factor(c("brain","gut","liver")) and run model.matrix(~ tissue). Confirm the number of dummy columns and which level is the reference.
R3. For B7, build treatment <- factor(c("drug","placebo","drug","placebo")), check levels(), then relevel() to make placebo the reference and re-check levels().
R4. Confirm the interaction expansion from B6: colnames(model.matrix(~ treatment * sex)) should list treatmenttreat, sexM, and the product treatmenttreat:sexM.

title: Exercise: handling covariates
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — reading a formula





+ means “also include this term as a predictor” (not arithmetic). y ~ a + b fits an additive model; y ~ a * b adds the interaction a:b on top of the two main effects. There is always an intercept unless you write y ~ 0 + ... or y ~ ... - 1.









Hint 2 — building the design matrix





Start with a column of 1’s (the intercept). Continuous predictors go in as their raw numbers. For a factor under the default treatment contrasts, add one 0/1 column per non-reference level: 1 when the sample is that level, 0 otherwise. Use model.matrix to check.









Hint 3 — what a coefficient means





Every coefficient is read “holding the other predictors constant.” For a continuous predictor it is the change in \(\hat y\) per unit. For a factor dummy it is the difference between that level and the reference. The intercept is \(\hat y\) when all predictors are 0 / at their reference levels.









Hint 4 — predicting from coefficients (B3)





Plug the sample’s values into \(\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1\cdot\text{treat} + \beta_2\cdot\text{age}\). A treated animal has treat = 1; a control has treat = 0. So a treated animal aged 30 gives \(\hat y = 5 + 3(1) + 0.1(30)\).









Hint 5 — confounding (B5)





A confounder is associated with both the group and the outcome. The unadjusted treatment coefficient captures the real treatment effect plus the age difference between groups. Adding age to the model lets the age effect be estimated separately, so the treatment coefficient keeps only what is left over — the effect “at the same age.”









Hint 6 — interaction coefficients (B6)





Under treatment coding the main effect \(\beta_1\) is the treatment effect in the reference sex (F). The interaction \(\beta_3\) is the extra treatment effect in males, so the male treatment effect is \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\). If \(\beta_3 = 0\) the effect is identical in both sexes (no interaction).









Hint 7 — reference levels (B7)





R orders factor levels alphabetically, so drug (before placebo) becomes the reference and the reported coefficient is treatmentplacebo = placebo − drug. To read it as the drug effect instead, make placebo the reference with relevel(treatment, ref = "placebo").

title: Exercise: handling covariates
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. (a) expr ~ treatment (b) expr ~ treatment + age (c) expr ~ treatment * sex (equivalently expr ~ treatment + sex + treatment:sex). The * allows the treatment effect to differ between sexes via the interaction term.
B2. Intercept column of 1’s; a single treatment dummy (treatmenttreat = 1 for treated, 0 for control, since ctrl is the reference); and the raw age column.
\[
X = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 10 \\
1 & 1 & 40 \\
1 & 0 & 22 \\
1 & 1 & 35
\end{pmatrix}
\quad
\begin{array}{l}
\text{col 1: (Intercept)} \\
\text{col 2: treatmenttreat} \\
\text{col 3: age}
\end{array}
\]
B3. (a) \(\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1\cdot 1 + \beta_2\cdot 30 = 5 + 3 + 0.1\times30 = 5 + 3 + 3 = 11\). (b) The treatment effect is \(\beta_1 = 3\): treated animals have expression 3 units higher than controls of the same age. “Holding age constant” makes clear this is not contaminated by any age imbalance between the groups — it is the treatment effect after age has been accounted for. (c) \(\beta_0 = 5\) is the predicted expression for a control animal of age 0. Age 0 is outside any real data (and biologically a newborn / extrapolation), so the raw intercept is not scientifically meaningful. Centring age (I(age - mean(age))) would move the intercept to the mean age and make it interpretable.
B4. (a) Three levels → \(3 - 1 = 2\) dummy columns (tissuegut, tissueliver), plus the intercept. (b) brain — it is alphabetically first, so it is the reference (all its dummies are 0). (c) Gut mean \(=\) intercept \(+\) tissuegut \(= 2 + 4 = 6\). Brain mean \(=\) intercept \(= 2\) (brain is the reference, so both dummies are 0).
B5. (a) Age is a confounder: it differs between the groups (treated older, controls younger) and affects the outcome (expression rises with age). In expr ~ treatment the treatment coefficient absorbs the treatment effect plus the age-driven difference between the groups, inflating it. Adding + age gives age its own coefficient, so the age contribution is removed from the treatment coefficient, and it shrinks toward the true value. (b) The adjusted estimate (expr ~ treatment + age) is the honest one: it estimates the treatment effect among animals of the same age, disentangling it from the age imbalance. The unadjusted estimate conflates the two.
B6. (a) Treatment effect in females (the reference sex): \(\beta_1 = 2\). (b) Treatment effect in males: \(\beta_1 + \beta_3 = 2 + 3 = 5\). (c) \(\beta_3 = 3\) is the extra treatment effect in males compared with females — the treatment raises expression 3 units more in males than in females (a difference of treatment effects). \(\beta_3 = 0\) would mean the treatment acts equally in both sexes, i.e. no interaction, and the additive model expr ~ treatment + sex would suffice.
B7. (a) drug — factor levels are ordered alphabetically, and drug comes before placebo, so drug is the reference; the non-reference dummy is treatmentplacebo. (b) treatmentplacebo \(= -4\) means placebo expression is 4 units lower than drug. Equivalently, the drug raises expression by 4 units relative to placebo. (The sign is about placebo-minus-drug because drug is the reference.) (c) treatment <- relevel(treatment, ref = "placebo") (or factor(treatment, levels = c("placebo","drug"))). Then the coefficient becomes treatmentdrug \(= +4\), directly the drug effect.
R1–R4. These confirm the hand answers.
treatment <- factor(c("ctrl","treat","ctrl","treat"))
age       <- c(10, 40, 22, 35)
model.matrix(~ treatment + age)     # R1: matches the X in B2

tissue <- factor(c("brain","gut","liver"))
model.matrix(~ tissue)              # R2: 2 dummies; brain is reference

treatment <- factor(c("drug","placebo","drug","placebo"))
levels(treatment)                   # R3: "drug" "placebo" -> drug is reference
treatment <- relevel(treatment, ref = "placebo")
levels(treatment)                   # "placebo" "drug"  -> placebo now reference

sex <- factor(c("F","M","F","M"))
colnames(model.matrix(~ treatment * sex))   # R4: main effects + product term

title: Exercise: handling covariates
text:
Where this leads

Error models (Poisson / negative binomial): for count outcomes (RNA-seq), the covariates still enter through the design matrix \(X\boldsymbol\beta\), but inside a log link (\(\log \mu = X\boldsymbol\beta\)) with a count likelihood instead of a Gaussian one.
Hierarchical models: when samples share structure (several technical replicates per animal, several animals per group), covariate effects can be allowed to vary across replicates — the distinction between biological and technical replicates becomes a modelling choice.
Penalized linear models: when you have many covariates or collinear ones, plain fitting becomes unstable (an identifiability problem); L1/L2 penalties shrink the coefficients to tame it.
Design and contrast matrices recur in every differential-expression tool (limma, DESeq2, edgeR): the model.matrix() you built here is exactly the design = argument those tools expect.

title: Exercise: cross-validation & model selection
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain why training error is optimistic and what overfitting looks like,
lay out the folds of a k-fold cross-validation and say what each is for,
compute a held-out MSE by hand from a few predictions,
read a CV error curve and pick both lambda.min and lambda.1se,
spot information leakage in a described workflow and fix it,
run cv.glmnet and read lambda.min, lambda.1se, and the selected coefficients.

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

read a CV error curve and pick both lambda.min and lambda.1se,

title: Exercise: cross-validation & model selection
text:
Background
Why hold data out. Error measured on the data you fitted is an optimistic estimate: a flexible model can memorise noise. To estimate performance on future samples, score the model on samples it never saw during fitting.
k-fold cross-validation. Split the \(n\) samples into \(k\) equal folds. For each fold \(f = 1,\dots,k\): hold out fold \(f\), fit on the other \(k-1\) folds, and record the error on fold \(f\). Average the \(k\) errors: \[\text{CV error} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{f=1}^{k}\text{error on fold } f.\] Every sample is held out exactly once. Special case \(k=n\): leave-one-out CV (LOOCV).
Held-out MSE. For held-out points with true values \(y_i\) and predictions \(\hat y_i\), \[\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}(y_i - \hat y_i)^2, \qquad \text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{MSE}}.\]
Choosing \(\lambda\). Run CV at each candidate \(\lambda\) and plot CV error vs \(\lambda\).

lambda.min — the \(\lambda\) with the lowest CV error.
lambda.1se — the largest \(\lambda\) (simplest model) whose CV error is within one standard error of the minimum. Rule: let \(m\) be the smallest mean CV error and \(s\) its standard error; lambda.1se is the largest \(\lambda\) with mean CV error \(\le m + s\).

The leakage rule. Any step that uses the outcome \(y\) — supervised gene filtering, choosing a threshold, scaling using \(y\) — is part of fitting and must happen inside each CV fold, on the training portion only. Otherwise the held-out data has already influenced the model and can no longer test it.

title: Exercise: cross-validation & model selection
text:
Explore: leakage on pure noise
The demo runs the B5 blunder on data that contain no signal at all: \(n\) samples × \(p\) genes of random noise, with random disease labels (half cases, half controls). A simple classifier (nearest centroid: a held-out sample is assigned to the class whose average profile over the \(k\) selected genes is closest) is scored by 5-fold CV in two ways:

Leaky: the \(k\) genes with the largest \(|t|\)-statistic between the two classes are chosen once, using all samples; then CV is run on those genes.
Honest: the split comes first; inside each fold the \(k\) genes are re-chosen on the training part only.

Since the labels are random, no method can truly predict them: an honest estimate should sit around 50% (chance). Each dot under the accuracy is one held-out sample (filled = classified right).



E1. With the default \(n = 40\), \(p = 2000\), \(k = 20\), press Repeat 50×. Where does each histogram sit relative to the chance line? Which of the two numbers would you report for new patients?
E2. Keep \(n = 40\), \(k = 20\) and try \(p = 100\), \(p = 500\) and \(p = 5000\) (press Repeat 50× after each change). How does the leaky accuracy change with \(p\)? Why do more noise genes make the leak worse?
E3. Set \(p = 2000\), \(k = 20\) and compare \(n = 20\) with \(n = 100\). What happens to the leaky accuracy? Does the centre of the honest histogram move? Does its width change?
E4. In the honest panel, single datasets sometimes reach 65–75%. Why is that not evidence of a real signal, and what does it say about trusting one CV run on a small study?






Solutions





E1. The leaky histogram piles up near the top (mean about 95–97%, almost every dataset above 90%); the honest one is centred on 50% with a spread of roughly ±10 percentage points. Only the honest number estimates performance on new patients: on new samples the labels are still random, so the true accuracy is 50%. The leaky 97% is pure leakage.
E2. The leaky accuracy rises with \(p\): roughly 82% at \(p = 100\), 92% at \(p = 500\) and 98% at \(p = 5000\). With more genes there are more chances for some gene to separate these particular 40 labels by luck, and the filter on all samples finds exactly those lucky genes, including their luck on the samples later held out. The honest estimate stays at about 50% for every \(p\).
E3. The leaky accuracy falls as \(n\) grows (about 99% at \(n = 20\), about 87% at \(n = 100\)): with more samples a noise gene is less likely to line up with the labels by chance, so the leak is smaller, but it is still far above 50%. The honest histogram stays centred at 50%; it gets narrower with larger \(n\) (spread roughly ±15 points at \(n = 20\), ±6 at \(n = 100\)), because the accuracy is then averaged over more held-out samples.
E4. The honest estimate is unbiased but noisy: with 40 held-out predictions, chance alone moves the accuracy by about ±10 points, so 65–75% turns up now and then even though there is nothing to find. One CV run on a small study is one draw from that histogram. Before believing a modest accuracy, look at its uncertainty (for example the standard error across folds) and compare it with the chance level.

title: Exercise: cross-validation & model selection
text:
In R
Use R to confirm the reasoning above. Nothing here needs a large dataset; the point is to read the outputs, not to build a real classifier (that comes in the elastic-net and chemometrics units).

Fit a cross-validated lasso
library(glmnet)

# x: samples x genes matrix ; y: 0/1 disease label
x <- as.matrix(expr)
y <- pheno$disease

set.seed(1)                      # folds are random -> seed for reproducibility
cvfit <- cv.glmnet(x, y,
                   family       = "binomial",
                   alpha        = 1,          # lasso
                   nfolds       = 10,
                   type.measure = "auc")

cvfit$lambda.min                 # best-CV lambda
cvfit$lambda.1se                 # simplest within 1 SE of the best
plot(cvfit)                      # CV curve with error bars + two dashed lines


Read the chosen model
coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.1se")    # sparse coefficients; non-zeros are the signature
sum(coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.1se") != 0) - 1   # number of selected genes (minus intercept)


MSE by hand, then check it
y_true <- c(3, 5, 2, 6)
y_hat  <- c(2, 5, 4, 5)
mse  <- mean((y_true - y_hat)^2)
rmse <- sqrt(mse)
mse; rmse


Tasks
R1. Reproduce B3 with the mse/rmse block above and confirm your hand answer.
R2. Explain in one sentence why running the cv.glmnet block a second time without set.seed(1) can give a slightly different lambda.min.
R3. Given the honest fold loop below, state exactly which line makes it leakage-free (contrast with a version that filters before the loop):
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(x)))
for (f in 1:10) {
  tr <- folds != f; te <- folds == f
  gc   <- abs(cor(x[tr, ], y[tr]))            # <-- filter on TRAIN rows only
  keep <- order(gc, decreasing = TRUE)[1:50]
  fit  <- glmnet(x[tr, keep], y[tr], family = "binomial")
  # predict x[te, keep], score against y[te]
}

title: Exercise: cross-validation & model selection
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — counting folds (B1, B2)





In \(k\)-fold CV each of the \(n\) samples sits in exactly one fold. Fold size is \(n/k\). A model trains on the other \(k-1\) folds, so on \(n - n/k\) samples. Each sample is validated once (its own fold) and trained on in the other \(k-1\) folds. You fit one model per fold. LOOCV is just \(k = n\); see cv.glmnet’s nfolds.









Hint 2 — MSE by hand (B3)





Subtract each prediction from its truth, square each residual, add them up, divide by the number of points. RMSE is the square root of that. In R: mean((y_true - y_hat)^2) and sqrt().









Hint 3 — the one-standard-error rule (B4)





Find the row with the smallest mean CV error; call it \(m\) and read its standard error \(s\). Compute the threshold \(m + s\). Now scan from the largest \(\lambda\) downward and take the first (largest) \(\lambda\) whose mean CV error is \(\le m + s\). That is lambda.1se. Larger \(\lambda\) = more shrinkage = fewer non-zero genes.









Hint 4 — spotting leakage (B5)





Ask: did any step look at the outcome \(y\) before the data was split into folds? Correlating genes with disease status uses \(y\). If that happened on all patients, the “held-out” fold already helped choose the genes. The fix is to move the gene filter inside the fold loop and compute it on the training rows only. See the wrong-vs-right slide.









Hint 5 — overfitting signature (B6)





Overfitting = tiny training error but much larger CV error (a big gap). The model to trust on new data is the one with the best CV error, not the best training error. To shrink the gap, increase \(\lambda\) (regularise harder).









Hint 6 — matching a metric (B7)





Continuous outcome → squared-error metrics (MSE/RMSE, \(R^2\)). Count outcome → deviance under a Poisson/negative-binomial model. Binary with rare positives → prefer AUC (ranking, threshold-free, robust to imbalance) over plain accuracy, which a “predict the majority” model can game.

title: Exercise: cross-validation & model selection
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. \(n = 20\), \(k = 5\). (a) Fold size \(= n/k = 20/5 = \mathbf{4}\) samples per fold. (b) Each model trains on the other \(k-1 = 4\) folds \(= 20 - 4 = \mathbf{16}\) samples. (c) Each sample is in its own fold once, so it is used for validation once and for training in the other 4 folds (\(k-1 = 4\) times). (d) One model per fold \(\Rightarrow \mathbf{5}\) models.
B2. LOOCV on \(n = 20\). (a) \(k = n = \mathbf{20}\). (b) Fold size \(= 1\) sample. (c) \(\mathbf{20}\) models (one per left-out sample). (d) Drawbacks: it is expensive (20 fits vs 5), and the LOOCV estimate has high variance because the 20 training sets are nearly identical (they overlap in 19 of 20 samples), so the fold errors are highly correlated. 5- or 10-fold is the usual compromise.
B3. Residuals \(y - \hat y = (3-2,\ 5-5,\ 2-4,\ 6-5) = (1,\ 0,\ -2,\ 1)\). Squares: \((1,\ 0,\ 4,\ 1)\); sum \(= 6\); there are \(4\) points. \[\text{MSE} = 6/4 = \mathbf{1.5}, \qquad \text{RMSE} = \sqrt{1.5} \approx \mathbf{1.22}.\]
B4. (a) The smallest mean CV MSE is \(0.24\) at \(\lambda = 0.10\), so lambda.min \(= \mathbf{0.10}\). (b) Standard error at the minimum is \(s = 0.03\), so the threshold is \(m + s = 0.24 + 0.03 = 0.27\). Scanning from the largest \(\lambda\) down: \(\lambda = 0.50\) has \(0.40 > 0.27\) (no); \(\lambda = 0.20\) has \(0.27 \le 0.27\) (yes). So lambda.1se \(= \mathbf{0.20}\). (c) lambda.1se \(= 0.20 > 0.10\), so it shrinks harder and yields a simpler model with fewer genes. For a biomarker paper this is often preferable: it is within statistical noise of the best CV error yet gives a shorter, more reproducible gene list.
B5. (a) Leakage: the genes were selected by correlating with disease status across all 100 patients before forming the folds. The filter used the outcome of the very patients later “held out.” (b) Because the held-out fold already helped choose the 100 genes, it is no longer naive test data — the model has indirectly seen it. So the 94% measures how well the genes fit these patients, not how well the model predicts new ones. The estimate is optimistically biased (can be dramatically so when \(p \gg n\)). (c) Honest workflow: split into folds first, then inside each fold recompute the gene filter on the training rows only, fit the lasso on those genes, and score the held-out fold. Average the fold scores. Concretely, wrap filter + fit in the fold loop (see R3), or hold out a final test set that no filtering step ever touched.
B6. (a) Model A is overfitting: near-zero training error (\(0.02\)) but much worse CV error (\(0.31\)) — a large train–CV gap. Model B’s errors are close (\(0.19\) vs \(0.22\)). (b) Deploy Model B: it has the better CV error (\(0.22 < 0.31\)), which is the honest estimate of performance on new patients. (c) Increase \(\lambda\) (more shrinkage) to reduce overfitting — exactly the move from A to B.
B7. (a) Age is continuous → MSE / RMSE (or \(R^2\)); squared error is the natural loss and RMSE is in years. (b) Read counts are counts → Poisson (or negative-binomial) deviance; it is the loss the count error model actually optimises, and squared error would mis-weight the mean–variance relationship. (c) 8% tumours is imbalanced → AUC; it scores the ranking and is threshold-free, so a lazy “always predict normal” model (92% accurate!) does not look good. Plain accuracy would be misleading.
R1.
y_true <- c(3, 5, 2, 6)
y_hat  <- c(2, 5, 4, 5)
mse  <- mean((y_true - y_hat)^2)   # 1.5
rmse <- sqrt(mse)                  # 1.2247...
mse; rmse
Matches the hand answer: MSE \(= 1.5\), RMSE \(\approx 1.22\).
R2. cv.glmnet assigns samples to folds at random; without set.seed the fold assignment differs between runs, so the CV error curve (and thus lambda.min/lambda.1se) can shift slightly. Setting the seed fixes the fold assignment and makes the result reproducible.
R3. The line gc <- abs(cor(x[tr, ], y[tr])) computes the gene filter on the training rows tr only — the held-out rows te never enter the correlation, so they stay naive test data. (A leaking version would compute cor(x, y) on all rows once, before the loop, letting each held-out fold influence which genes are kept.)

title: Exercise: cross-validation & model selection
text:
Where this leads

L1, L2 and elastic-net penalties: the same CV folds let you compare lasso vs ridge vs elastic net and tune both \(\lambda\) and the mixing \(\alpha\) on one honest scale.
Chemometrics (PLS / OPLS): latent-variable models are validated by cross-validation too — the number of components is chosen exactly the way we chose \(\lambda\) here.
Single-cell analysis: grouped/stratified folds matter when many cells come from one patient — splitting them across folds leaks and inflates performance.

title: Quiz: cross-validation & model selection
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of cross-validation and honest model selection. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Several are in the style of the on-campus exam (no computer).

Q1. In one sentence, why is the error measured on your training data a poor estimate of how the model will do on new patients?






Hint





What can a flexible model do to the data it was fitted on, especially when there are far more genes than samples?









Answer





A flexible model can fit the noise of the training samples, so its training error is optimistically low; the honest test is data the model never saw during fitting. The bias is worst when \(p \gg n\) (many genes, few patients).




Q2. You run 10-fold CV on 90 samples. How large is each fold, how many samples does each model train on, and how many models are fitted?






Hint





Fold size is \(n/k\); each model trains on the other \(k-1\) folds; one model per fold.









Answer





Fold size \(= 90/10 = 9\) samples. Each model trains on the other \(9\) folds \(= 90 - 9 = 81\) samples. 10 models are fitted (one per held-out fold), and every sample is validated exactly once.




Q3. What are the two distinct jobs cross-validation does in a penalized-regression workflow?






Hint





One job is about choosing a knob; the other is about reporting a number.









Answer






Tuning — choosing the penalty strength \(\lambda\) (the value that minimises CV error), and (2) estimation — giving an honest estimate of predictive performance. If the same CV both chose \(\lambda\) and reports the number, the number is mildly optimistic, which is why a separate held-out test set (or nested CV) is needed for the final estimate.





Q4. In cv.glmnet, what is the difference between lambda.min and lambda.1se, and why might you prefer lambda.1se?






Hint





One is the outright minimum; the other applies a “within one standard error” rule and gives a simpler model.









Answer





lambda.min is the \(\lambda\) with the lowest CV error. lambda.1se is the largest \(\lambda\) (most shrinkage, fewest genes) whose CV error is still within one standard error of that minimum. Since the two are statistically indistinguishable, lambda.1se gives a simpler, more reproducible signature — usually the better scientific choice for a biomarker list.




Q5. A student filters 20,000 genes down to the 200 most correlated with disease using all samples, then cross-validates a lasso on those 200 genes and reports 95% accuracy. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?






Hint





Did the gene filter look at the outcome of the samples that later become “held out”?









Answer





This is information leakage: the gene filter used the outcome \(y\) of every sample, including those later held out, so the folds are no longer naive and 95% is optimistically biased. Fix: move the gene selection inside each CV fold and compute it on the training rows only (or hold out a test set that no filtering step ever touches). Any step that uses \(y\) is part of fitting.




Q6. True or false: the test set may be used to decide which of several models to keep. Explain.






Hint





How many times may a genuine test set be used, and for what?









Answer





False. The moment you use the test set to choose something, it has influenced the model and is no longer an unbiased test — it has become a validation set. A genuine test set is locked away and opened once, only to report the final performance. Model selection belongs to the validation (CV) stage.




Q7. You are classifying a disease where only 6% of samples are cases. Why is plain accuracy a bad CV metric here, and what is a better one?






Hint





What accuracy does a model that always predicts “healthy” achieve?









Answer





A trivial model that always predicts “healthy” is 94% accurate, so accuracy rewards ignoring the cases entirely. AUC is better: it scores whether the model ranks cases above controls, is threshold-free, and is robust to class imbalance. (Deviance / log-loss is another honest choice.)




Q8. Training error is \(0.03\) and 10-fold CV error is \(0.28\). What does the gap tell you, and which way should you move \(\lambda\)?






Hint





A large gap between memorising the training data and doing well in CV is the fingerprint of one specific problem.









Answer





The large train–CV gap is the signature of overfitting: the model nearly memorises the training data but generalises poorly. Increase \(\lambda\) (shrink harder) to reduce flexibility and close the gap; trust the CV error (\(0.28\)), not the training error, as the estimate of real performance.




Q9. You have single-cell data with thousands of cells from each of 12 patients, and you want to predict a patient-level phenotype. Why is a plain random split of cells into folds misleading, and what should you do instead?






Hint





Are cells from the same patient independent? What happens if the same patient appears in both training and validation?









Answer





Cells from one patient are not independent, so a random cell-level split puts the same patient in both training and validation — the model can recognise the patient rather than the phenotype, leaking information and inflating performance. Use grouped CV: keep all cells from a patient together in one fold, so folds split at the patient level.

title: Exercise: eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Background
For a square matrix \(A\), eigen(A) returns a list:

$values — the eigenvalues. For a symmetric matrix they come largest-first.
$vectors — a matrix whose columns are the (unit-length) eigenvectors; column \(k\) pairs with $values[k].

Eigenvectors are unique only up to scale and sign, so R’s unit-length vector may be the negative of your hand answer — same direction, still correct.
Reconstruction. With \(V\) = eigenvectors (columns) and \(\Lambda = \text{diag}(\text{eigenvalues})\): \[A = V\,\Lambda\,V^{-1}, \qquad\text{and for symmetric } A:\quad A = V\,\Lambda\,V^\top .\]
Biology. The covariance matrix cov(X) (with samples in rows, features in columns) is symmetric. Its leading eigenvector is the direction of greatest variation — the engine of PCA.

title: Exercise: eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
By hand
Just a couple, to keep your Eigenvalues & eigenvectors fluency warm and to predict what R will print.
B1. For \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) you found \(\lambda = 3, 1\) with eigenvectors \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\). R returns unit-length vectors — what numbers should appear in eigen(A)$vectors? (Divide each by its length.)
B2. A covariance matrix \(C = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\). Predict its two eigenvalues by hand, and say which eigenvector is the leading one (the main axis of variation).

title: Exercise: eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
In R
Work through every block in order. Re-run with your own numbers to build intuition.

1. Decompose and read the output
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
e <- eigen(A)
e$values            # 3 1   (largest first)
e$vectors           # eigenvectors in COLUMNS, each length 1

e$values[1]         # 3
e$vectors[, 1]      # eigenvector paired with lambda = 3
e$vectors[, 2]      # eigenvector paired with lambda = 1


2. Verify the eigen relation
lambda <- e$values[1]
v      <- e$vectors[, 1]

A %*% v             # should equal lambda * v
lambda * v

# == is unsafe for floats; use all.equal
all.equal(as.vector(A %*% v), lambda * v)   # TRUE


3. Reconstruct the matrix
V      <- e$vectors
Lambda <- diag(e$values)

# general formula
V %*% Lambda %*% solve(V)      # rebuilds A

# symmetric shortcut (A is symmetric here)
isSymmetric(A)                 # TRUE
V %*% Lambda %*% t(V)          # also rebuilds A, no inverse needed
crossprod(V)                   # V^T V = identity -> columns orthonormal


4. Biology: covariance and the main axis of variation
set.seed(1)
n  <- 200
g1 <- rnorm(n)
g2 <- 0.8 * g1 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.4)   # gene 2 tracks gene 1 + noise
X  <- cbind(g1, g2)                   # rows = cells, cols = genes

C  <- cov(X)                          # symmetric 2x2 covariance
ec <- eigen(C)
ec$values                             # variance along each eigen-axis
pc1 <- ec$vectors[, 1]                # leading eigenvector

plot(X, asp = 1, pch = 19, col = "grey40",
     xlab = "gene 1", ylab = "gene 2")
m <- colMeans(X)
arrows(m[1], m[2], m[1] + 2*pc1[1], m[2] + 2*pc1[2],
       col = "red", lwd = 3)
# red arrow lies along the long axis of the cloud


Tasks
R1. Run block 1 and confirm eigen(A)$vectors[, 1] matches your B1 prediction (up to sign).
R2. In block 2, replace e$vectors[, 1] with e$vectors[, 2] and e$values[1] with e$values[2], and re-verify \(A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}\) for the second eigenpair.
R3. Make A non-symmetric, e.g. A <- matrix(c(2, 1, 0, 3), 2, byrow = TRUE). Run eigen(A). Do the eigenvectors come out orthogonal? Check with crossprod(eigen(A)$vectors) — is it the identity? Why or why not?
R4. For block 4, compute the fraction of total variance captured by the leading axis: ec$values[1] / sum(ec$values). (This number is what PCA calls “proportion of variance explained by PC1”.)
R5. Increase the noise: set sd = 1.5 when making g2, rebuild X, C, and ec. How does the leading eigenvalue’s share of the variance change, and what does the cloud look like? Explain in one sentence.
R6. Confirm the symmetric reconstruction numerically: with C and its ec from block 4, check all.equal(unname(C), unname(ec$vectors %*% diag(ec$values) %*% t(ec$vectors))) returns TRUE. unname() ignores the feature labels, which eigen() does not retain on the reconstructed matrix.
R7. (complex eigenvalues) Run eigen(matrix(c(0, -1, 1, 0), 2, byrow = TRUE)). What kind of numbers are the eigenvalues, and how does that match the fact that a \(90^\circ\) rotation has no real eigen-direction (Eigenvalues & eigenvectors)?

title: Exercise: eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — eigenvectors are columns





eigen(A)$vectors[, k] is the \(k\)-th eigenvector and pairs with eigen(A)$values[k]. Grabbing a row by mistake gives the wrong vector. See eigen.









Hint 2 — compare floats with all.equal, not ==





A %*% v and lambda * v agree only to ~15 digits because of floating point. Use all.equal(as.vector(A %*% v), lambda * v), which returns TRUE when they match within tolerance. (A %*% v is a column matrix, hence as.vector.)









Hint 3 — building V and Lambda





V <- e$vectors already has eigenvectors in columns. diag(e$values) turns the eigenvalue vector into the diagonal matrix \(\Lambda\). The inverse is solve(V); the transpose is t(V).









Hint 4 — symmetric vs general





For symmetric \(A\), eigenvectors are orthonormal, so \(V^{-1} = V^\top\) and crossprod(V) (which is \(V^\top V\), see crossprod) is the identity. For a non-symmetric \(A\) this fails — the eigenvectors are generally not orthogonal.









Hint 5 — covariance orientation





cov(X) expects samples in rows and features in columns. Build X <- cbind(g1, g2). The result is symmetric: variances on the diagonal, covariance off-diagonal.









Hint 6 — proportion of variance





Total variance = sum(ec$values). The share along the leading axis is ec$values[1] / sum(ec$values). More noise makes the cloud rounder, so this share drops toward 0.5.

title: Exercise: eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. R returns unit-length eigenvectors, so divide each hand vector by its length. Each has length \(\lVert(1,\pm1)\rVert = \sqrt{1^2+1^2} = \sqrt2\). For \(\lambda=3\): \((1,1)/\sqrt2 = (1/\sqrt2,\ 1/\sqrt2) \approx (0.707,\ 0.707)\). For \(\lambda=1\): \((1,-1)/\sqrt2 = (1/\sqrt2,\ -1/\sqrt2) \approx (0.707,\ -0.707)\). So eigen(A)$vectors should print roughly these columns. R may flip the sign of either whole column (an eigenvector is only defined up to sign and scale) — same direction, still correct.
B2. \(C\) has the symmetric pattern \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}\) with \(a = 4\), \(b = 2\), so the eigenvectors are \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\): \(C(1,1) = (4+2,\ 2+4) = (6,6) = 6\,(1,1)\), so \(\lambda = 6\); and \(C(1,-1) = (4-2,\ 2-4) = (2,-2) = 2\,(1,-1)\), so \(\lambda = 2\). The leading eigenvector (largest eigenvalue, \(\lambda=6\)) is \(\mathbf v=(1,1)\) — the main axis of variation. Check: trace \(4+4 = 8 = 6+2\) ✓. (Bonus, not for exam: the characteristic equation \((4-\lambda)^2 - 4 = 0\) gives the same \(\lambda = 6, 2\).)
R1. Run block 1 and read off the first eigenvector column.
A <- matrix(c(2, 1, 1, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
eigen(A)$vectors[, 1]   # 0.7071068 0.7071068   (or its negative)
This matches the B1 prediction \((1,1)/\sqrt2 \approx (0.707, 0.707)\), up to an overall sign.
R2. Repeat the verification for the second eigenpair (index 2).
e <- eigen(A)
lambda <- e$values[2]    # 1
v      <- e$vectors[, 2] # eigenvector for lambda = 1, e.g. (0.707, -0.707)

A %*% v                  # equals lambda * v
lambda * v               # same numbers
all.equal(as.vector(A %*% v), lambda * v)   # TRUE
Both A %*% v and lambda * v give the same vector (\(1\cdot v = v\) here), and all.equal returns TRUE, confirming \(A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v\) for the second pair too.
R3. Build the non-symmetric matrix and test orthogonality with crossprod (\(V^\top V\)).
A <- matrix(c(2, 1, 0, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)   # not symmetric
crossprod(eigen(A)$vectors)
#       [,1]  [,2]
# [1,] 1.000 0.707
# [2,] 0.707 1.000
The off-diagonal entries are not 0, so the result is not the identity — the eigenvectors are not orthogonal. The orthogonality guarantee comes from the spectral theorem, which applies only to symmetric matrices; this \(A\) is not symmetric, so it does not hold.
R4. Compute the share of total variance carried by the leading axis.
ec$values[1] / sum(ec$values)   # ~ 0.939
About 94% of the variance lies along the leading axis, because the two genes are strongly correlated, producing a thin, elongated cloud. This is exactly what PCA reports as “proportion of variance explained by PC1”.
R5. Rebuild the cloud with more noise on gene 2 and recompute the share.
set.seed(1)
n  <- 200
g1 <- rnorm(n)
g2 <- 0.8 * g1 + rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)   # noisier than before
X  <- cbind(g1, g2)
C  <- cov(X)
ec <- eigen(C)
ec$values[1] / sum(ec$values)         # ~ 0.82  (was ~0.94)
With sd = 1.5, gene 2 is noisier and less tied to gene 1, so the cloud becomes rounder and the leading eigenvalue’s share of total variance drops from about 0.94 to about 0.82 — the two genes share less common variation, so the single leading axis no longer dominates as strongly. (Push the noise much higher and the noisy gene’s own variance eventually dominates instead — try sd = 4 and watch the leading axis swing toward the gene-2 direction.)
R6. Reconstruct the symmetric covariance matrix from its eigen-decomposition and compare.
all.equal(unname(C), unname(ec$vectors %*% diag(ec$values) %*% t(ec$vectors)))   # TRUE
It returns TRUE: the symmetric reconstruction \(V\Lambda V^\top\) rebuilds the covariance matrix exactly (within floating-point tolerance). Because \(C\) is symmetric its eigenvectors are orthonormal, so \(V^{-1}=V^\top\) and the transpose form works — no solve() needed.
R7. Decompose the \(90^\circ\) rotation and inspect the eigenvalues.
eigen(matrix(c(0, -1, 1, 0), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE))$values
# [1] 0+1i 0-1i
The eigenvalues are complex (\(0+1i\) and \(0-1i\)), not real. A \(90^\circ\) rotation moves every real direction, so it has no real eigenvector — the same conclusion as B6 in Eigenvalues & eigenvectors. (Bonus, not for exam: the characteristic equation \(\lambda^2 + 1 = 0\), i.e. \(\lambda = \pm i\), predicts exactly these imaginary values.)

title: Exercise: eigenvalues in R with eigen()
text:
Where this leads

PCA (Week 2): today’s eigen(cov(X)) is the heart of PCA. PCA adds mean-centring, projecting samples onto the eigenvectors to get scores, and ordering components by variance explained (your R4 number). It scales to thousands of genes at once.
Markov chains: you will apply a transition matrix repeatedly; the stationary distribution is the eigenvector with eigenvalue \(\lambda = 1\), found with the same eigen() you used today.
Numerical habit: comparing floats with all.equal and remembering eigenvectors are sign/scale-free will save you throughout the course.

title: Exercise: eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain what makes an eigenvector special (\(A\) only scales it, never rotates it),
write and read the eigen relation \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\),
test whether a given vector is an eigenvector by multiplying, and read off its eigenvalue,
read the eigenvalues of diagonal and triangular matrices, and use the symmetric \(2\times2\) pattern,
find the eigenvector for a known eigenvalue from \((A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\), and verify it,
find eigenvectors from the geometry of a transformation (projection, mirror, shear, rotation),
use the trace check to catch arithmetic slips,
explain why a symmetric matrix (such as a covariance matrix) has real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.

This is a concept day and the by-hand skills are examined directly. None of them needs a determinant. Spend most of your time on the pen-and-paper problems; the R section is only to confirm your hand answers (full R fluency comes in Eigenvalues in R).
