title: Exercise: eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Background
A nonzero vector \(\mathbf{v}\) is an eigenvector of \(A\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) when
\[A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}.\]
The matrix acts on that one direction like a plain number \(\lambda\): it stretches (\(|\lambda|>1\)), shrinks (\(|\lambda|<1\)), or flips (\(\lambda<0\)) the vector, but never knocks it off its line.
The by-hand toolbox:

Test a candidate. Compute \(A\mathbf{v}\). If it equals \(\lambda\mathbf{v}\) for one number \(\lambda\) (the same ratio in every entry), \(\mathbf{v}\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(\lambda\).
Diagonal and triangular matrices. The eigenvalues are the diagonal entries. For a diagonal matrix the axes are the eigenvectors.
The symmetric pattern. \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}\) has eigenvectors \((1,1)\) with \(\lambda = a+b\) and \((1,-1)\) with \(\lambda = a-b\).
Eigenvector for a known \(\lambda\). Subtract \(\lambda\) from each diagonal entry to get \(A-\lambda I\), then solve \((A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\): one row gives the relation between \(v_1\) and \(v_2\); pick the simplest integers.
Geometry. Directions that a transformation leaves on their own line are eigenvectors (a projection keeps its line, a mirror keeps its mirror line, a rotation keeps nothing).
Check. The eigenvalues add up to the trace (sum of the diagonal). Always verify \(A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}\) by multiplying.

For any other matrix, use eigen() in R (Eigenvalues in R).
Symmetric matrices (\(A = A^\top\), e.g. any covariance matrix) always have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.

title: Exercise: eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
By hand
B1. For \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\), find the eigenvalues by inspection (it is diagonal). What are the eigenvectors? What does \(A\) do geometrically?
B2. For the triangular matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\): (a) read off the eigenvalues; (b) show that \((1,0)\) is an eigenvector, and for which eigenvalue; (c) find the eigenvector for the other eigenvalue from \((A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\), and verify it; (d) check the trace.
B3. For the symmetric matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\): (a) find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors with the symmetric pattern; (b) verify both by multiplying; (c) verify the two eigenvectors are orthogonal (dot product 0); (d) check the trace.
B4. Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) and of \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & -2 \\ -2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\). Which eigenvalue is the largest in each case?
B5. Show that \(\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}\) is an eigenvector of \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) by computing \(A\mathbf{v}\) and reading off \(\lambda\). Then test \(\mathbf{w} = (1, 1)\) and \(\mathbf{u} = (1, 0)\). Use the trace to check that you have found both eigenvalues.
B6. The rotation matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) (rotate \(90^\circ\)). Compute \(A(1,0)\), \(A(0,1)\) and \(A(1,1)\). Explain, from what the matrix does geometrically, why it has no real eigenvector.
B7. (covariance flavour) A small dataset has covariance matrix \(C = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\). Find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors by hand. Which eigenvector points along the direction of greatest variation, and what is the variance along it?
B8. (geometry first) For each matrix, say what it does, predict the eigenvectors and eigenvalues without calculating, then verify by multiplying: (a) \(P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\); (b) \(F = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\); (c) \(S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\); (d) \(H = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) (is \((1,1)\) an eigenvector?).
B9. (bonus, not for exam) The characteristic equation \(\det(A-\lambda I) = (a-\lambda)(d-\lambda) - bc = 0\) finds the eigenvalues of any \(2\times2\) (see the bonus slides at the end of the lecture). (a) Use it on \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) and compare with B3. (b) Use it on \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\), which fits none of the patterns; the quadratic needs the quadratic formula. (c) Use it on the rotation from B6, and connect “no real root” to the geometry. Bonus material: you do not need to memorise determinants for the exam.

title: Exercise: eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Explore
Turn the unit vector \(\mathbf{v}\) (black handle, or the “direction of v” slider) and watch \(A\mathbf{v}\) (orange). When \(A\mathbf{v}\) lands on the dotted line through \(\mathbf{v}\), it turns green and the demo shows \(\lambda\). “Sweep v around” turns \(\mathbf{v}\) once round and marks every direction it finds. Set \(A\) with the sliders or the presets.



E1. With the Symmetric preset (the matrix of B3), find both eigen-directions by turning \(\mathbf{v}\). Do the directions and \(\lambda\) values match your answer to B3? (The demo uses unit vectors: \((0.71, 0.71)\) is the same direction as \((1, 1)\).)
E2. Use the sliders to set the matrix of B5, \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\), and sweep. Which directions does it find, and do they match \((1, 2)\) and \((1, 1)\)?
E3. Set the first matrix of B4, \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). Find the direction with a negative \(\lambda\). What does \(A\mathbf{v}\) look like there?
E4. Before sweeping, predict how many eigen-directions each preset has: Shear, Rotate 90°, Projection, Scale ×2. Then sweep and compare with B6 and B8.






Solutions





E1. \(\lambda = 3\) along \((0.71, 0.71)\), the direction of \((1, 1)\); \(\lambda = 1\) along \((0.71, -0.71)\), the direction of \((1, -1)\). Same as B3: the unit vectors are just \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\) shrunk to length 1.
E2. \(\lambda = 2\) along \((0.45, 0.89)\) and \(\lambda = 1\) along \((0.71, 0.71)\). Since \(0.89 / 0.45 = 2\), the first is the direction of \((1, 2)\); the second is the direction of \((1, 1)\). Trace check: \(2 + 1 = 3 = 0 + 3\).
E3. Along \((0.71, -0.71)\), i.e. \((1, -1)\): \(A\mathbf{v}\) points the opposite way, still on the dotted line, so \(A\mathbf{v} = -1\cdot\mathbf{v}\) and \(\lambda = -1\). (The other direction is \((1, 1)\) with \(\lambda = 3\).)
E4. Shear: one direction, the x-axis, \(\lambda = 1\). Rotate 90°: none, every \(A\mathbf{v}\) is turned by \(90^\circ\) (B6). Projection: two, \((1, 0)\) with \(\lambda = 1\) and \((0, 1)\) with \(\lambda = 0\) (there \(A\mathbf{v}\) shrinks to nothing). Scale ×2: every direction, \(\lambda = 2\), so \(A\mathbf{v}\) is always on the line.

title: Exercise: eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
In R
Use R only to confirm the hand answers above. (In Eigenvalues in R we use eigen() in earnest; today we lean on simple checks.)

Verify an eigen relation directly
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
v <- c(1, 1)          # claimed eigenvector
A %*% v               # 3 3  -> equals 3 * v, so lambda = 3
3 * v                 # 3 3  -> matches
# B5: is (1,2) an eigenvector of this A?
A <- matrix(c(0, 1,
             -2, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
v <- c(1, 2)
A %*% v               # 2 4 = 2 * (1,2) -> yes, lambda = 2


Check eigenvalues with the trace
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
sum(diag(A))          # trace = 4  -> should equal lambda1 + lambda2
# your hand answers were 3 and 1:  3 + 1 = 4  ->  checks out


Confirm two eigenvectors are orthogonal
v1 <- c(1,  1)        # for lambda = 3
v2 <- c(1, -1)        # for lambda = 1
sum(v1 * v2)          # 0  -> orthogonal (as expected for symmetric A)


Tasks
R1. Verify both eigenpairs from B3 with A %*% v and the trace block (you should already know the eigenvalues are 3 and 1).
R2. For B7, build C <- matrix(c(5,4,4,5), 2, byrow = TRUE), then verify your hand eigenvalues with sum(diag(C)), and confirm both eigenvectors satisfy C %*% v == lambda * v.
R3. Take the rotation matrix from B6, A <- matrix(c(0,-1,1,0), 2, byrow = TRUE). Pick any nonzero vector and compute A %*% v for a few different v. Convince yourself no nonzero real vector comes back as a multiple of itself (every vector is rotated).

title: Exercise: eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — testing a candidate eigenvector





Compute \(A\mathbf v\). If the result is a scalar multiple of \(\mathbf v\) — i.e. \(A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v\) for one single number \(\lambda\) — then \(\mathbf v\) is an eigenvector and that \(\lambda\) is its eigenvalue. Read \(\lambda\) off by dividing entry by entry; both ratios must agree. (If an entry of \(\mathbf v\) is 0, the matching entry of \(A\mathbf v\) must be 0 too.)









Hint 2 — diagonal and triangular matrices





The eigenvalues are on the diagonal. For an upper-triangular \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & d \end{pmatrix}\), the x-axis \((1,0)\) is always an eigenvector, with eigenvalue \(a\): \(A(1,0)\) is the first column, \((a, 0)\).









Hint 3 — the symmetric pattern





For \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}\) (equal diagonal entries, equal off-diagonal entries), multiply by \((1,1)\) and by \((1,-1)\): you get \((a+b)(1,1)\) and \((a-b)(1,-1)\). Watch the signs when \(b\) is negative.









Hint 4 — the eigenvector for a known eigenvalue





Subtract \(\lambda\) from only the diagonal entries; the off-diagonals are unchanged. Write out the two equations \((A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\). They say the same thing (or one is \(0 = 0\)) — use one row to get \(v_2\) in terms of \(v_1\), then pick \(v_1 = 1\) (or whatever gives nice integers).









Hint 5 — the trace check





Sum of eigenvalues = trace (sum of diagonal) = sum(diag(A)). If your two eigenvalues do not add up to the trace, one of them is wrong. If you know one eigenvalue, the trace gives you the other.









Hint 6 — no real eigenvalue (B6)





A rotation has no direction it leaves on its own line: every output points in a new direction, so no output is a multiple of its input. Compare the direction of \(A\mathbf v\) with that of \(\mathbf v\) for each test vector.









Hint 7 — verifying in R





Build matrices with matrix(..., byrow = TRUE), multiply with %*%, and compare A %*% v against lambda * v. The dot product sum(v1 * v2) should be 0 for orthogonal eigenvectors. Check the eigenvalues with sum(diag(A)) (trace).

title: Exercise: eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. A diagonal matrix acts like a number on each axis, so the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: \(\lambda_1 = 4\) with \(\mathbf v_1 = (1,0)\) and \(\lambda_2 = 2\) with \(\mathbf v_2 = (0,1)\). Verify: \(A(1,0)=(4,0)=4(1,0)\) ✓ and \(A(0,1)=(0,2)=2(0,1)\) ✓. Trace \(4+2=6=\lambda_1+\lambda_2\) ✓. Geometrically \(A\) stretches the x-axis by 4 and the y-axis by 2.
B2. (a) Triangular, so the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: \(\lambda = 3\) and \(\lambda = 2\). (b) \(A(1,0) = (3, 0) = 3(1,0)\), so \((1,0)\) is an eigenvector with \(\lambda = 3\). (c) For \(\lambda=2\): \(A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\). Row 1: \(v_1+v_2=0\), so \(v_2 = -v_1\) and \(\mathbf v=(1,-1)\). Verify: \(A(1,-1) = (3-1,\ 0-2) = (2,-2) = 2(1,-1)\) ✓. (d) Trace \(3+2=5=3+2\) ✓.
B3. (a) Pattern with \(a = 2\), \(b = 1\): \((1,1)\) with \(\lambda = a+b = 3\), and \((1,-1)\) with \(\lambda = a-b = 1\). (b) \(A(1,1) = (2+1,\ 1+2) = (3,3) = 3(1,1)\) ✓; \(A(1,-1) = (2-1,\ 1-2) = (1,-1) = 1\cdot(1,-1)\) ✓. (c) Orthogonality: \((1)(1) + (1)(-1) = 0\) → orthogonal ✓ (expected, since \(A\) is symmetric). (d) Trace \(= 2+2 = 4 = 3+1\) ✓.
B4. First matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\): pattern with \(a=1\), \(b=2\). \((1,1)\): \(\lambda = 3\); \((1,-1)\): \(\lambda = 1-2 = -1\). Verify: \(A(1,-1) = (1-2,\ 2-1) = (-1, 1) = -1\cdot(1,-1)\) ✓. Trace \(2 = 3 + (-1)\) ✓. Largest: \(3\), along \((1,1)\). The negative eigenvalue means \(A\) flips the \((1,-1)\) direction.
Second matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}5&-2\\-2&5\end{pmatrix}\): pattern with \(a=5\), \(b=-2\). \((1,1)\): \(\lambda = 5 + (-2) = 3\); \((1,-1)\): \(\lambda = 5 - (-2) = 7\). Verify: \(A(1,-1) = (5+2,\ -2-5) = (7,-7) = 7(1,-1)\) ✓. Trace \(10 = 3+7\) ✓. Largest: \(7\), along \((1,-1)\): with a negative off-diagonal, the long axis is the other diagonal.
B5. \[A\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0+2\\ -2+6\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\4\end{pmatrix} = 2\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}.\] So \(\mathbf v=(1,2)\) is an eigenvector with \(\lambda = 2\). \(A\mathbf w = (0+1,\ -2+3) = (1, 1) = 1\cdot\mathbf w\): also an eigenvector, with \(\lambda = 1\). \(A\mathbf u = (0, -2)\), not a multiple of \((1,0)\) (the second entry would have to be 0): not an eigenvector. Trace \(0 + 3 = 3 = 2 + 1\) ✓, so \(2\) and \(1\) are both eigenvalues of this \(2\times2\) matrix.
B6. \(A(1,0) = (0,1)\), \(A(0,1) = (-1,0)\), \(A(1,1) = (-1,1)\). Each output is the input turned by \(90^\circ\); none lies on the input’s own line, so none is a multiple of its input. \(A\) rotates every direction by \(90^\circ\), so there is no special unrotated direction and hence no real eigenvector (and no real eigenvalue).
B7. Pattern with \(a = 5\), \(b = 4\): \((1,1)\) with \(\lambda = 9\) and \((1,-1)\) with \(\lambda = 1\). Verify: \(C(1,1) = (9,9) = 9(1,1)\) ✓; \(C(1,-1) = (1,-1)\) ✓. The direction of greatest variation is the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue, \(\mathbf v_1=(1,1)\); the variance along that axis is \(9\). Checks: trace \(=5+5=10=9+1\) ✓; orthogonal: \((1)(1)+(1)(-1)=0\) ✓.
B8. (a) \(P\) projects onto the y-axis: it keeps \((0,1)\) (\(\lambda = 1\)) and squashes \((1,0)\) to zero (\(\lambda = 0\)). Verify: \(P(0,1) = (0,1)\), \(P(1,0) = (0,0) = 0\cdot(1,0)\) ✓. Trace \(1 = 1 + 0\) ✓. (b) \(F\) mirrors in the y-axis: the mirror line \((0,1)\) stays (\(\lambda = 1\)), the perpendicular \((1,0)\) is flipped (\(\lambda = -1\)). Verify: \(F(1,0) = (-1,0)\) ✓. Trace \(0 = 1 + (-1)\) ✓. (c) \(S\) scales everything by 2: every nonzero vector is an eigenvector, with \(\lambda = 2\) (twice). Trace \(4 = 2+2\) ✓. (d) \(H\) is a shear (triangular): eigenvalue \(1\) twice, and the x-axis stays put: \(H(1,0) = (1,0)\) ✓. \(H(1,1) = (3,1)\), not a multiple of \((1,1)\), so no. A shear has only one eigen-direction.
B9. (bonus, not for exam) (a) \(\det(A-\lambda I) = (2-\lambda)^2 - 1 = \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 = (\lambda-3)(\lambda-1) = 0\), so \(\lambda = 3, 1\), as in B3. Product check: \(3\cdot1 = 3 = \det A = 4 - 1\) ✓. (b) \((2-\lambda)(-\lambda) - 1 = \lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 1 = 0\). The quadratic formula gives \(\lambda = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 4}}{2} = 1 \pm \sqrt2 \approx 2.414,\ -0.414\). Trace check: \((1+\sqrt2) + (1-\sqrt2) = 2\) ✓. (c) \((-\lambda)^2 - (-1)(1) = \lambda^2 + 1 = 0\), so \(\lambda^2 = -1\): no real solution. The algebra (“no real root”) matches the geometry (“every direction is turned”).
R1.
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
A %*% c(1, 1)   # 3 3   = 3 * (1, 1)
A %*% c(1, -1)  # 1 -1  = 1 * (1, -1)
sum(diag(A))    # 4   -> equals lambda1 + lambda2 = 3 + 1
Both eigenpairs check out, and the eigenvalues add up to the trace.
R2.
C <- matrix(c(5, 4,
              4, 5), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
sum(diag(C))        # 10  -> = 9 + 1

v      <- c(1, 1)   # leading eigenvector from B7
lambda <- 9
C %*% v             # 9 9
lambda * v          # 9 9   -> identical, so C v = 9 v
C %*% c(1, -1)      # 1 -1  -> = 1 * (1, -1)
The trace (10) matches \(9+1\), and \(C\mathbf v = 9\mathbf v\) and \(C(1,-1) = 1\cdot(1,-1)\) confirm both eigenpairs.
R3. Multiply the rotation by several vectors and look at where each lands.
A <- matrix(c(0, -1,
              1,  0), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
A %*% c(1, 0)   #  0 1   -> x-axis swings to the y-axis
A %*% c(2, 1)   # -1 2   -> not a multiple of (2,1)
A %*% c(3, 3)   # -3 3   -> not a multiple of (3,3)
Each output is the input rotated \(90^\circ\); none lands on the same line as its input (no scalar \(\lambda\) makes \(A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v\) for real \(\mathbf v\)), confirming there is no real eigenvector — exactly the B6 conclusion.

title: Exercise: eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Where this leads

Eigenvalues in R: eigen(A) returns all eigenvalues and (unit-length) eigenvectors at once. You will read its $values and $vectors, sort them, verify \(A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}\), and reconstruct \(A = V\Lambda V^{-1}\).
Covariance & PCA (Applications block): the leading eigenvector of a covariance matrix (largest eigenvalue) is the first principal component — the main axis of variation in your data. B7 was a miniature PCA computation.
Markov chains & Markov chains in R: the stationary distribution of a Markov chain is the eigenvector with eigenvalue \(\lambda = 1\) of its transition matrix.

title: Quiz: eigenvalues & eigenvectors
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Most are in the style of the on-campus exam (no computer).

Q1. In one sentence: what makes a vector \(\mathbf{v}\) an eigenvector of a matrix \(A\)?






Hint





Think about how the direction of \(\mathbf{v}\) changes (or doesn’t) when you apply \(A\).









Answer





\(A\) only scales \(\mathbf{v}\) — it stays on the same line through the origin — instead of rotating it onto a new direction. Formally \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\) for some scalar \(\lambda\) (with \(\mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}\)).




Q2. \(A\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}\). Is \(\mathbf{v}\) an eigenvector? If so, what is \(\lambda\)?






Hint





Is the output a scalar multiple of \(\mathbf{v}\)?









Answer





\((6,9) = 3(2,3)\), so yes — \(\mathbf{v}\) is an eigenvector with \(\lambda = 3\).




Q3. What are the eigenvalues of the triangular matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\)? Show that \((1, 0)\) is an eigenvector.






Hint





For a triangular matrix the eigenvalues sit on the diagonal. For the eigenvector, multiply.









Answer





\(\lambda = 5\) and \(\lambda = 4\), the diagonal entries. \(A(1,0) = (5, 0) = 5\,(1,0)\), so \((1,0)\) is an eigenvector with \(\lambda = 5\).




Q4. Without calculating: what are the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of \(P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\), which projects every vector onto the x-axis?






Hint





Which direction does a projection leave alone, and which does it squash?









Answer





The x-axis \((1,0)\) is kept as it is: \(\lambda = 1\). The y-axis \((0,1)\) is squashed to zero: \(P(0,1) = (0,0) = 0\cdot(0,1)\), so \(\lambda = 0\). (Trace check: \(1 + 0 = 1\).)




Q5. Find the eigenvalues of \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{pmatrix}\) by inspection.






Hint





For a diagonal matrix the eigenvalues are sitting right there.









Answer





\(\lambda = 2\) and \(\lambda = 7\) — the diagonal entries. (Eigenvectors are the axes \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\).)




Q6. Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\).






Hint





It has the symmetric pattern \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}\). Try \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\).









Answer





\(A(1,1) = (5,5) = 5\,(1,1)\) and \(A(1,-1) = (1,-1)\). So \(\lambda = 5\) for \((1,1)\) and \(\lambda = 1\) for \((1,-1)\). (Check: trace \(6 = 5+1\).)




Q7. Your \(2\times2\) matrix has trace 7. One eigenvalue is 3. What is the other?






Hint





The eigenvalues add up to the trace.









Answer





The other is \(7 - 3 = 4\). Eigenvalues 3 and 4.




Q8. For \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) (eigenvalue \(\lambda = 4\), repeated), find an eigenvector.






Hint





Solve \((A - 4I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\). What does the top row force?









Answer





\(A - 4I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\). Row 1 says \(v_2 = 0\), with \(v_1\) free, so \(\mathbf{v} = (1, 0)\). (Note: even though \(\lambda=4\) is repeated, this matrix has only one eigen-direction — it is not symmetric.)




Q9. Why is a symmetric matrix nice? Give the two guarantees.






Hint





Spectral theorem — think about realness and angles.









Answer






All eigenvalues are real (never complex). (2) Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal. This is why covariance matrices give clean perpendicular axes of variation.





Q10. A pure rotation \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) has no real eigenvector. Explain why, geometrically.






Hint





What does a \(90^\circ\) rotation do to every direction?









Answer





A \(90^\circ\) rotation moves every vector onto a new direction, so no nonzero real vector comes back as a multiple of itself. (Bonus, not for exam: the characteristic equation \(\lambda^2 + 1 = 0\) has no real root, confirming this.)




Q11. A covariance matrix has eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = 12\) (eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}_1\)) and \(\lambda_2 = 2\) (eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}_2\)). Along which direction does the data vary most, and how much variance is there along the perpendicular direction?






Hint





The eigenvalue measures the variance captured along its eigenvector.









Answer





The data vary most along \(\mathbf{v}_1\) (largest eigenvalue, 12) — the long axis of the cloud. Along the perpendicular direction \(\mathbf{v}_2\) the variance is 2. (This is exactly the idea behind the first principal component.)




Q12. True or false: if \(\mathbf{v}\) is an eigenvector of \(A\), then so is \(-5\mathbf{v}\), with the same eigenvalue.






Hint





\(A(-5\mathbf{v}) = -5(A\mathbf{v})\).









Answer





True. \(A(-5\mathbf{v}) = -5(A\mathbf{v}) = -5(\lambda\mathbf{v}) = \lambda(-5\mathbf{v})\). Any nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector with the same eigenvalue — an eigenvector really specifies a whole line (a direction).

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
About this lecture
Every statistical analysis makes an assumption about how the data scatter around the truth — the error model, or likelihood. Choosing it well is most of the battle in genomics.

What an error model is: the probability distribution you assume generated your data.
Gaussian for continuous measurements; Poisson for counts; exponential for waiting times; negative binomial for overdispersed counts.
The signature of Poisson counts: mean = variance.
Why real RNA-seq counts break Poisson (overdispersion) and need the negative binomial.
Why the wrong error model misleads — the practical cost is false discoveries.








Provisional block


This block (“Bayesian statistics”) is provisional and may move to a later statistics / machine-learning course. Treat the placement as a working draft, not a contract.





The one idea for today: before you fit anything, you commit to a story about how noise entered your data, and that story is a probability distribution. Pick the wrong one and every downstream number — p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes — is quietly wrong. This is a concept day: no heavy algebra, just building the reflex “what kind of data is this, and which distribution matches it?” We will lean on distributions students have used before (Gaussian, Poisson) but re-derive why each fits a data type. The likelihood introduced here is the same likelihood that plugs into Bayes’ theorem in the prior, likelihood and posterior unit — flag that connection but do not teach Bayes today.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
A biology picture first
You sequence RNA from two groups of cells and, for one gene, count how many reads map to it in each sample:

Group A: 12, 9, 15, 11, 8
Group B: 41, 38, 52, 44, 47

You want to know if the gene is differentially expressed. A first instinct from earlier stats courses: run a t-test, which assumes the data are Gaussian with constant variance.
But look: group B has a much larger spread than group A. That is not sloppy data — it is what counts do. A t-test’s constant-variance assumption is already wrong here.


Anchor everything in a concrete count table before any distribution theory. The key observation students should feel: the group with the higher mean also has the higher spread. For counts this is not a nuisance to be scrubbed away — it is a law (Poisson: variance equals mean). So the standard t-test / Gaussian assumption of one common variance is violated from the start. This motivates the whole lecture: count data has its own error model. Do not resolve the example yet; the payoff (Poisson, then negative binomial, then why it matters for the test) comes over the next slides.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
What is an error model?
A measurement is signal + noise. The error model is the probability distribution you assume for the noise — equivalently, the distribution the data are drawn from given the underlying truth.
\[\text{data} \sim \text{Distribution}(\text{parameters})\]

It answers: “If the true value were \(\mu\), how likely is the number I actually observed?”
That “how likely” is the likelihood — the same likelihood that feeds into Bayes’ theorem in the prior, likelihood and posterior unit.
Fitting a model (a t-test, a linear model with lm, a genomics tool) always assumes some error model, whether or not you named it.

Choosing the error model = choosing the distribution that matches your data type.


Make the abstraction explicit: whenever you compute a p-value or fit a curve, a distribution is assumed in the background. lm assumes Gaussian residuals; a Poisson GLM assumes Poisson counts. The likelihood is just this distribution read as a function of the parameters for fixed data — the bridge to the Bayesian unit, where likelihood times prior gives the posterior. Today we stay frequentist-flavoured and focus only on picking the distribution. The recurring question for the rest of the lecture: what does my data type look like — continuous? counts? waiting times? — and which named distribution has that shape?

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Gaussian: continuous measurements
The Gaussian (normal) distribution fits measurements that are continuous and scatter symmetrically around a mean.
\[X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\, e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\]

Two separate parameters: mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) (spread is independent of the mean).
Good for: protein concentration, cell diameter, \(\log\)-transformed intensities, height, temperature.
The default assumption behind the t-test, linear regression, and lm.

It can take any real value — including negatives — which is exactly why it is wrong for counts.


Gaussian is the students’ familiar ground, so use it to set up the contrast. Two independent knobs: you can have a large mean with a small variance or vice versa — nothing ties them together. That is fine for genuinely continuous quantities. The tell-tale weakness for count data is on the last line: a Gaussian puts probability on negative numbers and on fractional values, but you can never observe -3 reads or 4.5 reads. Log-transforming counts is a common patch that partly Gaussian-ises them, but for low counts it distorts things; the honest fix is a count distribution, which is where we go next.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Counts are not Gaussian
Sequencing gives counts: reads per gene, molecules per cell, variants per kilobase, colonies per plate. Counts have structure a Gaussian ignores:

Non-negative integers — you cannot observe \(-2\) or \(3.7\) reads.
Discrete, especially near zero (many genes have 0, 1, 2 reads).
Spread grows with the mean — highly expressed genes vary more, in absolute terms, than lowly expressed ones (we saw this in the two groups).

A distribution built for counts should be discrete, non-negative, and let variance depend on the mean. That distribution is the Poisson.


List the three ways count data violates Gaussian assumptions so students can recognise count data in the wild. The third point is the deepest and the one earlier stats courses rarely stress: for counts the variance is not a free parameter, it is welded to the mean. This is why you cannot just pool a single variance across genes of very different expression, and why naive constant-variance methods misbehave. The next slide introduces the distribution that has exactly these properties baked in.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Poisson: the count distribution
The Poisson distribution models the number of independent events in a fixed interval (of time, space, or sequencing depth), occurring at constant average rate.
\[X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda), \qquad P(X = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}, \quad k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\]

One parameter \(\lambda > 0\) — the average count (the rate).
Discrete and non-negative by construction.
Defining property: \(\;\mathbb{E}[X] = \lambda \;\) and \(\; \text{Var}(X) = \lambda\).

\[\boxed{\text{mean} = \text{variance} = \lambda}\]


Introduce Poisson as the natural law for “count of rare-ish independent events in a fixed window.” Reads mapping to a gene fit this picture: each of millions of reads independently has a small probability of landing on this gene. The headline, worth repeating aloud, is mean equals variance — a single parameter controls both. This is a strong, testable claim about data: if counts are truly Poisson, their sample variance should roughly equal their sample mean. Keep the factorial formula on screen but do not dwell on it; the conceptual content is the mean = variance identity and the “events in a window” picture.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Poisson: a small example
A gene receives on average \(\lambda = 3\) reads per sample. Then:
\[P(0) = \frac{3^0 e^{-3}}{0!} = e^{-3} \approx 0.050, \quad P(3) = \frac{3^3 e^{-3}}{3!} = \frac{27 e^{-3}}{6} \approx 0.224\]
The distribution is right-skewed for small \(\lambda\) and piles up near zero; as \(\lambda\) grows it becomes more symmetric.
# probabilities for counts 0..8 when lambda = 3
lambda <- 3
k <- 0:8
dpois(k, lambda)         # P(X = k)

mean_sim <- mean(rpois(1e5, lambda))   # ~ 3
var_sim  <- var(rpois(1e5, lambda))    # ~ 3  -> mean = variance


Do the two hand calculations so the formula is not abstract: P(0) is just e^-lambda, P(3) plugs in and simplifies. Point out the shape: for small lambda the mass sits near zero and the tail stretches right — nothing like a symmetric bell. The static R shows the two functions they will use, dpois for exact probabilities and rpois to simulate; the simulated mean and variance both land near 3, confirming mean = variance empirically. Remind them these chunks are illustrative and not executed at render time. This mean = variance check is exactly the diagnostic they will apply to real data to decide whether Poisson is adequate.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
section: Where Poisson comes from: rare events
text:
Where Poisson comes from: rare events
Poisson is the limit of many independent trials, each with tiny success probability.

\(n\) reads in a library, each landing on our gene with small probability \(p\).
Total on-gene reads is \(\text{Binomial}(n, p)\); as \(n \to \infty\), \(p \to 0\) with \(np = \lambda\) fixed, this becomes \(\text{Poisson}(\lambda)\).

That is precisely the sequencing picture: millions of reads, each with a tiny chance of hitting any one gene. So idealised counts of independent molecules are Poisson.
This same “stream of random events” also has a waiting-time description — which is where the exponential enters.


Give the mechanistic justification so Poisson is not a distribution pulled from a hat. The binomial-to-Poisson limit is the law of rare events: huge number of chances, each unlikely, expected count fixed. Sequencing is the textbook instance — n in the millions, p per gene minuscule. Under idealised independence, counts are therefore Poisson; the fact that real data exceeds Poisson variance (overdispersion) is a signal that some assumption — usually independence / identical rate across samples — is violated, which we reach shortly. End by teeing up the dual view: the same event stream, described by the gaps between events instead of the count, gives the exponential distribution.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Exponential: waiting times
The exponential distribution models the waiting time until the next event in a stream of random events occurring at rate \(\lambda\).
\[T \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda), \qquad f(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}, \quad t \ge 0\]

Continuous and non-negative (a time, a distance, a length).
\(\mathbb{E}[T] = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}, \qquad \text{Var}(T) = \dfrac{1}{\lambda^2}\).
Memoryless: the chance of waiting another \(s\) seconds does not depend on how long you have already waited.

Biology: time between action-potential spikes, intervals between mutations along a genome, survival/dwell times, gaps between binding events.


Exponential is the continuous partner to Poisson: Poisson counts events, exponential times the gaps between them. Stress it is continuous and non-negative — a duration or a distance, never a count. The memoryless property is the striking feature: an exponential process has no aging, the wait resets at every instant. Biological examples worth naming: inter-spike intervals in neurons, spacing of mutations along a chromosome (events per base), dwell times of a molecule bound to DNA. The rate lambda is the same lambda as in Poisson when both describe one underlying process — the next slide makes that link explicit.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Exponential: a small example
Mutations fall along a genome at rate \(\lambda = 2\) per megabase. The waiting distance to the next mutation is \(\text{Exp}(2)\) (in Mb):
\[\mathbb{E}[T] = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5 \text{ Mb}, \qquad P(T > 1) = e^{-\lambda \cdot 1} = e^{-2} \approx 0.135\]
So there is a ~13.5% chance of a gap longer than 1 Mb.
lambda <- 2
pexp(1, rate = lambda, lower.tail = FALSE) # P(T > 1) = e^{-2} ~ 0.135
mean(rexp(1e5, rate = lambda)) # ~ 0.5  = 1/lambda

# count of events in a 1-Mb window is Poisson(lambda) -- same process
mean(rpois(1e5, lambda))       # ~ 2


Concrete numbers again. The mean gap is 1/lambda = 0.5 Mb, and the survival probability P(T > 1) is just e^{-lambda} — a clean hand calculation. The R uses lower.tail = FALSE to request the exponential tail probability and rexp to simulate gaps averaging 0.5. The final rpois line quietly makes the punchline of the next slide: the same rate lambda describes both the gaps (exponential, mean 1/lambda) and the count per window (Poisson, mean lambda). Keep it light; the goal is that students see waiting-time data and reach for exponential, and count-per-window data and reach for Poisson.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Two views of one process
The Poisson process is a single model of random events at rate \(\lambda\), seen two ways:








Question
Distribution
Parameter meaning




How many events in a fixed window?
\(\text{Poisson}(\lambda)\)
mean count \(= \lambda\)


How long until the next event?
\(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\)
mean wait \(= 1/\lambda\)




Counts in a window \(\to\) Poisson.
Gaps between events \(\to\) exponential.

Same underlying randomness, different question. Which one you use is set by what you measured, not by the biology alone.


This is the unifying slide. One process, two questions. If you tallied events per fixed interval you have counts and use Poisson; if you recorded the time or distance between consecutive events you have waiting times and use exponential. The distinction is about the measurement, not the phenomenon — the same neuron gives Poisson spike counts per second or exponential inter-spike intervals depending on what you logged. Getting students to ask “did I measure a count or a gap?” is the transferable skill. Next we return to counts and confront the fact that real genomics counts are wilder than Poisson allows.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Real counts are overdispersed
Poisson makes a strict promise: variance = mean. Real RNA-seq counts break it — their variance is larger than the mean. This excess is called overdispersion.
Why? Poisson assumes every sample has the identical underlying rate. But biological replicates differ:

genetically and environmentally variable individuals,
cell-state and batch differences,
the true rate \(\lambda\) itself varies from sample to sample.

Extra variation in \(\lambda\) adds variance on top of the Poisson counting noise. Technical replicates can look Poisson; biological replicates almost never do.


This is the single most important practical fact for genomics count analysis. Poisson is the floor of variability — pure counting noise assuming a fixed rate. Real biological replicates carry additional variation because the rate itself fluctuates between samples (genetics, environment, cell state, batch). By the law of total variance, letting lambda vary inflates the variance above the mean. The classic distinction: technical replicates (same sample resequenced) can be near-Poisson; biological replicates (different organisms/cultures) are overdispersed. Any method that assumes Poisson for biological replicates will understate the true variability — the consequence, quantified two slides on, is too many false positives.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Negative binomial: overdispersed counts
The negative binomial (NB) is a count distribution with a separate dispersion knob, letting variance exceed the mean.
\[X \sim \text{NB}(\mu, \phi), \qquad \text{Var}(X) = \mu + \phi\,\mu^2\]

\(\mu\) = mean; \(\phi \ge 0\) = dispersion.
\(\phi = 0\) recovers Poisson (variance \(= \mu\)); larger \(\phi\) = more overdispersion.
The extra \(\phi\mu^2\) term is why highly expressed genes vary disproportionately more.

It arises naturally as a Poisson whose rate \(\lambda\) is itself Gamma-distributed — exactly the “rate varies between samples” story.
The workhorse error model of DESeq2 and edgeR for RNA-seq differential expression.


NB is the fix for overdispersion: it is Poisson plus a dispersion parameter phi that decouples variance from mean. Variance = mu + phi*mu^2, so at phi = 0 it collapses back to Poisson, and the quadratic term means the variance gap widens for high-expression genes. Mechanistically it is a Gamma-Poisson mixture: draw a per-sample rate from a Gamma, then a Poisson count given that rate — precisely the “lambda varies between biological replicates” model from the previous slide. Name-drop DESeq2 and edgeR as the Bioconductor tools students will actually use; both are NB GLMs with clever dispersion estimation. Different sources parameterise phi differently (size = 1/phi in R’s dnbinom) — mention only if asked. This connects forward to the Poisson and negative binomial distributions unit if listed separately.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
section: Try it: Poisson vs negative binomial
text:
Try it: Poisson vs negative binomial




The histogram is 1000 simulated counts (think: reads of one gene in 1000 cells) from a negative binomial with mean mu and dispersion phi, in this lecture’s convention Var = mu + phi mu^2; the red dots are the NB probabilities, the dashed blue outline the Poisson with the same mean. Start at mu = 50, phi = 0.5 (exercise B5): the counts spread from near 0 to several hundred while the Poisson is a narrow bump around 50; the table shows theory and sample side by side, variance 1300, var/mean 26. Click “Poisson”: phi = 0, histogram and dashed outline coincide, var/mean = 1. Then “mild” and “strong (many zeros)”: the histogram flattens, piles up at zero (watch the zero count in the corner; the Poisson would give none) and grows a long right tail, while the mean stays at 50. “Low mean” with strong overdispersion shows the zero spike most clearly. “Draw again” shows that the sample variance jumps around much more than the sample mean. If time allows, tick the mean–variance plot: the Poisson line var = mu and the NB curve bending away above it — overdispersion grows with the mean.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Why the wrong model misleads
Using an error model whose variance is too small makes you overconfident — you declare differences “significant” that are just noise.

Gaussian / t-test on counts: assumes one shared variance and allows negative values; mis-estimates spread, especially for low counts and near zero.
Poisson on overdispersed RNA-seq: variance assumed \(= \mu\), but true variance is \(\mu + \phi\mu^2\) (larger). The test understates noise \(\Rightarrow\) p-values too small \(\Rightarrow\) inflated false positives.

# same mean (mu = 50), very different spread
mean(rpois(1e5, 50)); var(rpois(1e5, 50))          # ~50, ~50
mu <- 50; size <- 2                                 # NB: size = 1/phi
mean(rnbinom(1e5, mu = mu, size = size))            # ~50
var(rnbinom(1e5, mu = mu, size = size))             # >> 50 (overdispersed)
Right shape, right conclusions. The error model is not a technicality — it sets your false-discovery rate.


This is the “so what”. The direction of the error matters: assuming too little variance makes you anti-conservative — p-values shrink, and you call noise as signal. Poisson-on-biological-replicates is the canonical mistake, and it is why the field moved to negative binomial methods. The R makes it visceral: Poisson(50) has variance ~50; NB with the same mean but size = 2 has variance far above 50 (Var = mu + mu^2/size = 50 + 1250). A Poisson test on the NB data would treat that huge spread as if it were only 50, and every borderline gene becomes a false positive. Emphasise size = 1/phi in R’s parameterisation so the code matches the earlier formula. Land the closing line: choosing the error model directly controls how many false discoveries you make.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Choosing the error model
Match the data type to the distribution:








Your data
Distribution
Key feature




Continuous, symmetric spread
Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\)
mean and variance independent


Counts, idealised / technical
Poisson\((\lambda)\)
variance = mean


Counts, biological replicates
Negative binomial\((\mu,\phi)\)
variance = \(\mu + \phi\mu^2\)


Waiting times / gaps (continuous, \(\ge 0\))
Exponential\((\lambda)\)
memoryless, mean \(1/\lambda\)



Diagnostic: for counts, compare the sample variance to the sample mean. Variance \(\approx\) mean \(\to\) Poisson may do; variance \(\gg\) mean \(\to\) overdispersed, use NB.

The decision table is the take-home cheat-sheet. Walk each row: what does the data look like, and what is the one feature that picks the distribution. The practical diagnostic is the mean-variance comparison for counts — cheap and decisive. If variance tracks the mean, Poisson is defensible (often only for technical replicates); if variance blows past the mean, you have overdispersion and need the negative binomial. Note that exponential is the odd one out here — continuous waiting times, not counts — included because it is the same Poisson process seen the other way. Students should leave able to look at a column of numbers and name the right error model.

title: Error models: exponential & Poisson
text:
Summary







Idea
Key fact




Error model
the distribution you assume generated the data (the likelihood)


Gaussian
continuous, symmetric; mean and variance independent


Poisson
counts; variance = mean = \(\lambda\); limit of many rare events


Exponential
waiting times/gaps; memoryless; mean \(1/\lambda\)


Poisson process
one process: counts \(\to\) Poisson, gaps \(\to\) exponential


Overdispersion
real biological counts have variance > mean


Negative binomial
counts with dispersion; \(\text{Var} = \mu + \phi\mu^2\); RNA-seq (DESeq2, edgeR)


Wrong model
too-small variance \(\to\) overconfidence \(\to\) false positives



Connects to: the prior, likelihood and posterior unit (this likelihood plugs into Bayes’ theorem); the Poisson and negative binomial distributions for count data.

Recap as an exam cheat-sheet. Drill the reflex: name the data type, name the distribution, name its defining feature. The three claims most worth memorising: Poisson has variance = mean, real biological counts are overdispersed so need the negative binomial, and assuming too little variance inflates false positives. Close by pointing forward — the likelihood defined today is exactly what multiplies the prior in the Bayesian unit, and the negative binomial gets fuller treatment alongside the Poisson for count data. Keep the provisional-block caveat in mind: this material may relocate to a later stats/ML course.

title: Exercise: Fourier transform & basis functions
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

describe a sinusoid by its frequency, amplitude, and phase, and read those off a picture,
explain in your own words why the Fourier transform is a change of basis, and why it is reversible,
explain why sinusoids of different frequencies form an orthogonal basis, and how that lets each amplitude be read off as a projection,
contrast the fixed Fourier basis with the data-driven PCA basis, and say when each is appropriate,
reason about what a spectrum shows, and how low-pass / high-pass / notch filtering and compression act on it,
read a small fft() output in R and interpret the magnitude spectrum.

This is an Applications-block appreciation exercise. It builds conceptual fluency and light intuition — there is no by-hand transform to grind through. Do the reasoning parts on paper first, then use the short R section to confirm the picture.

title: Exercise: Fourier transform & basis functions
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:
