Which model is clearly overfit? Which look trustworthy? What single feature of the numbers gives the overfit one away?
B8. (permutation reasoning). You run 200 label-permutations of an OPLS-DA model and record \(Q^2\) each time; the shuffled \(Q^2\) values pile up around \(0\) and never exceed \(0.25\). Your real model has \(Q^2 = 0.62\). What do you conclude? Separately: a different study’s real model has \(Q^2 = 0.20\), while its permuted values reach up to \(0.30\) — what do you conclude there?

title: Exercise: the OPLS model
text:
In R
Nothing here needs to run for the exercise; read the code as a template. In R you would compute the toy quantities and then fit a real model with ropls.

The toy dataset: variance vs covariance-with-Y
A <- c(10, 12, 4, 6)
B <- c(20, 10, 20, 10)
y <- c(1, 1, -1, -1)      # case = +1, control = -1  (mean 0)

var(A)                    # variance of feature A
var(B)                    # variance of feature B  -> larger
cov(A, y)                 # covariance of A with the label
cov(B, y)                 # covariance of B with the label -> 0
The point: var(B) > var(A) (so PCA leans toward B), yet cov(A, y) is the non-zero one (so a supervised component leans toward A).


Fitting OPLS-DA with ropls (sketch)
library(ropls)

# X: samples x features matrix;  cls: factor with two levels (case/control)
model <- opls(X, cls,
              predI  = 1,     # one predictive component (single response)
              orthoI = NA,    # cross-validation chooses the orthogonal count
              permI  = 200)   # 200-permutation validation test

model                        # prints R2X, R2Y, Q2 and permutation p-values
getScoreMN(model)            # predictive & orthogonal scores (score plot)
getLoadingMN(model)          # feature loadings (which metabolites)


Why \(p \gg n\) is dangerous (a thought experiment in code)
set.seed(1)
n <- 20; p <- 2000                 # 20 samples, 2000 features
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)    # pure noise, no signal at all
cls <- factor(rep(c("case","ctrl"), each = 10))  # arbitrary labels

# An OPLS-DA on this CAN still look like it separates the groups on the
# training data. Only Q2 and the permutation test reveal there is nothing:
# a high R2Y with Q2 near or below 0 is the fingerprint of fitting noise.


Tasks
R1. Reproduce B2/B3 in R: build A, B, y as above and print var(A), var(B), cov(A, y), cov(B, y). Confirm the feature with the larger variance is not the feature that covaries with the label.
R2. Explain, in a comment, what each argument of opls(...) does: predI = 1, orthoI = NA, permI = 200. Which of the three is your main guard against overfitting?
R3. In the \(p \gg n\) thought experiment, the data are pure noise. Write one sentence saying what you would expect the permutation test to show if the model is honest — i.e. how the real \(Q^2\) should compare with the permuted \(Q^2\) values when there is genuinely no signal.

title: Exercise: the OPLS model
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — the two objectives





PCA maximises var(Xw) — spread in \(X\) only. PLS maximises cov(Xw, Y) — spread that also tracks \(Y\). Covariance factors as \(\operatorname{sd}(Xw)\cdot\operatorname{cor}(Xw,Y)\cdot\operatorname{sd}(Y)\), so a PLS direction must both vary and correlate with \(Y\).









Hint 2 — centring and variance by hand





Centre a feature by subtracting its mean. Sample variance \(= \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2\). For \(A\): mean \(= 8\), centred \((2, 4, -4, -2)\). For \(B\): mean \(= 15\), centred \((5, -5, 5, -5)\). Use var to check.









Hint 3 — covariance with the label





\(\operatorname{cov}(x, y) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)\). Here \(\bar y = 0\), so just multiply each centred feature value by the matching \(y\), add up, divide by \(3\). A feature that is high for cases and low for controls gives a positive sum; a feature that ignores the class gives \(0\).









Hint 4 — predictive vs orthogonal vs residual





Predictive = correlated with \(Y\). Orthogonal = structured (systematic) but uncorrelated with \(Y\) — batch, age, sex, diet. Residual = unstructured random noise. Ask of each source: does it track the disease (predictive), is it systematic but off-topic (orthogonal), or is it just noise (residual)?









Hint 5 — reading the OPLS-DA plot





By construction the predictive axis \(t_p\) (horizontal) is the one that carries the group difference; the orthogonal axis \(t_o\) (vertical) holds systematic variation that does not separate the classes. So horizontal = disease signal, vertical = quarantined nuisance.









Hint 6 — R2 vs Q2





\(R^2Y\) is in-sample fit (optimistic; only ever rises as you add components). \(Q^2\) is the cross-validated predicted variance — the honest one. A big gap, especially \(R^2Y\) high while \(Q^2\) is near \(0\) or negative, means the model fits the training data but does not generalise: overfitting.









Hint 7 — the permutation test





Shuffling \(Y\) destroys any real \(X\)–\(Y\) link but keeps the matrix shapes, so the permuted \(Q^2\) values show what this method achieves on chance alone for data of this size. Your real \(Q^2\) must sit clearly in the tail, well above the permuted values, to be believable.

title: Exercise: the OPLS model
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. PCA maximises the variance captured by each component (\(\max \operatorname{var}(Xw)\)) — the spread in \(X\) alone. PLS maximises the covariance of a component with the response (\(\max \operatorname{cov}(Xw, Y)\)) — spread that also tracks \(Y\). A supervised objective can find disease signal PCA misses because it deliberately favours directions that correlate with the outcome, even when they are not the directions of largest overall variance (which may be batch or physiology).
B2. Centre each feature.

\(A\): mean \(= (10+12+4+6)/4 = 8\); centred \((2, 4, -4, -2)\). Variance \(= \frac{1}{3}(2^2 + 4^2 + (-4)^2 + (-2)^2) = \frac{1}{3}(4+16+16+4) = \frac{40}{3} \approx 13.3\).
\(B\): mean \(= (20+10+20+10)/4 = 15\); centred \((5, -5, 5, -5)\). Variance \(= \frac{1}{3}(25+25+25+25) = \frac{100}{3} \approx 33.3\).

\(B\) has the larger variance (\(33.3 > 13.3\)), so PCA’s first component would lean toward \(B\).
B3. Covariance with \(y = (1,1,-1,-1)\) (and \(\bar y = 0\)), dividing by \(3\):

\(\operatorname{cov}(A, y) = \frac{1}{3}\big[(2)(1) + (4)(1) + (-4)(-1) + (-2)(-1)\big] = \frac{1}{3}(2+4+4+2) = \frac{12}{3} = 4.\)
\(\operatorname{cov}(B, y) = \frac{1}{3}\big[(5)(1) + (-5)(1) + (5)(-1) + (-5)(-1)\big] = \frac{1}{3}(5-5-5+5) = 0.\)

\(A\) covaries with the class label; \(B\) does not. So a PLS/OPLS predictive component leans toward \(A\) — the opposite of PCA.
B4. \(A\) is the predictive feature (it tracks the disease), \(B\) is orthogonal (large, structured, but uncorrelated with the class — note both cases and controls take \(B \in \{20,10\}\), so it separates nothing). A PCA loading plot, ranking features by variance, would put \(B\) first and could lead you to nominate \(B\) as a “biomarker” — but \(B\) carries no disease information. This is exactly the failure OPLS avoids by separating predictive from orthogonal variation.
B5. (a) predictive — genuinely tied to the disease, i.e. correlated with \(Y\). (b) orthogonal — a real, systematic batch effect, but it is confounded structure, not the biology of interest (and here it is partly aliased with the label because of poor run design — a reason to randomise run order; still, as a source, it is nuisance structure, not the causal disease signal). (c) orthogonal — age is systematic but not the disease outcome. (d) residual — unstructured random noise, goes into \(E\).
(Note on (b): if batch is perfectly confounded with class it becomes indistinguishable from signal — which is why run order should be randomised. This is a study-design warning, discussed further in the Chemometrics and Cross-validation units.)
B6. The horizontal separation on the predictive axis \(t_p\) is the disease signal: cases and controls occupy different positions along the one axis OPLS built to carry \(Y\)-related variation. The vertical spread on the orthogonal axis \(t_o\) is systematic variation within the data (batch, individual physiology) that OPLS has deliberately set aside; because it is orthogonal to \(Y\), it does not distinguish the groups — both classes spread up and down similarly.
B7. M2 is clearly overfit: \(R^2Y = 0.97\) (excellent in-sample fit) but \(Q^2 = -0.05\) (worse than predicting the mean under cross-validation). The tell-tale is the large gap between a high \(R^2Y\) and a near-zero/negative \(Q^2\). M1 (\(0.88\) vs \(0.80\)) and M3 (\(0.70\) vs \(0.55\)) both have \(Q^2\) comfortably positive and reasonably close to \(R^2Y\), so they look trustworthy.
B8. First study: the real \(Q^2 = 0.62\) sits far above the permuted values (which top out at \(0.25\)), so the model performs much better than chance for data of this size — the separation is likely real. Second study: the real \(Q^2 = 0.20\) is within the range the permuted (label-shuffled) models reach (\(\le 0.30\)), so it is not distinguishable from noise — the apparent separation is not trustworthy, despite \(Q^2\) being positive. A positive \(Q^2\) alone is not enough; it must beat the permutation null.
R1.
A <- c(10, 12, 4, 6)
B <- c(20, 10, 20, 10)
y <- c(1, 1, -1, -1)

var(A)      # 13.333...
var(B)      # 33.333...   -> larger variance
cov(A, y)   # 4           -> covaries with the label
cov(B, y)   # 0           -> no relation to the label
The larger-variance feature (B) is not the one that covaries with y (A) — PCA and a supervised component point at different features.
R2.
opls(X, cls,
     predI  = 1,    # one PREDICTIVE component: a single response has one Y-axis
     orthoI = NA,   # let cross-validation choose how many ORTHOGONAL comps to keep
     permI  = 200)  # run a 200-label-permutation validation test
permI (the permutation test) is the main guard against being fooled by a chance separation; orthoI = NA also protects you by not letting you bolt on arbitrarily many orthogonal components (which would inflate \(R^2\) without helping \(Q^2\)).
R3. If the model is honest and the data are pure noise, the real \(Q^2\) should be no better than the permuted \(Q^2\) values — it should sit right in the middle of the permutation null (around \(0\)), not out in the tail. Seeing that is the correct, reassuring outcome: it tells you there is nothing to find, exactly as designed.

title: Exercise: the OPLS model
text:
Where this leads

Chemometrics: OPLS and its relatives are workhorses for spectral data (NMR, LC–MS, IR); you will apply them to real chemometric datasets and biomarker discovery, including the S-plot for shortlisting features.
Multiome data integration: the same latent-variable thinking extends to relating two data blocks (e.g. RNA-seq vs proteomics), where components summarise shared structure across omics layers.
Cross-validation: the \(Q^2\) and permutation machinery you used here as a black box is built up properly — how to split data, what leakage is, and how to choose the number of components without fooling yourself.

title: Quiz: the OPLS model
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of supervised latent-variable modelling with PLS and OPLS. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. These are conceptual: they ask you to reason about when and why, not to run the algorithm by hand.

Q1. In one sentence each, what does PCA maximise and what does PLS maximise?






Hint





One objective looks only at \(X\); the other brings in the response \(Y\).









Answer





PCA maximises the variance captured in \(X\) (\(\max \operatorname{var}(Xw)\)), ignoring any outcome. PLS maximises the covariance of a component with the response (\(\max \operatorname{cov}(Xw, Y)\)) — variation in \(X\) that also tracks \(Y\).




Q2. Your top principal component of a serum metabolomics dataset separates samples by run day, not by disease. Is your data useless? What kind of method should you reach for instead?






Hint





PCA ranks directions by size of variance, not by relevance to your question.









Answer





No — it just means the loudest variation is a batch effect, not the biology. PCA optimises for variance, not relevance, so a real but smaller disease signal can hide in later components. Reach for a supervised latent-variable method (PLS / OPLS) that uses the case/control label \(Y\) to find the disease-related direction. (Better run-order randomisation would also help.)




Q3. What are the three kinds of variation OPLS distinguishes, and which one is used to predict \(Y\)?






Hint





Correlated with \(Y\); structured but uncorrelated with \(Y\); unstructured noise.









Answer





Predictive (correlated with \(Y\)), orthogonal (structured but uncorrelated with \(Y\) — batch, age, physiology), and residual (unstructured noise). Only the predictive component — its scores \(t_p\) — is used to predict \(Y\); the orthogonal part is set aside.




Q4. For a single response, how many predictive components does OPLS have? Why is that convenient for interpretation?






Hint





Think about how many axes you need to read off “how case-like is this sample.”









Answer





Exactly one predictive component. That means the whole \(Y\)-related signal is summarised by a single score per sample (\(t_p\)), so the group difference lives on one interpretable axis of the score plot; any remaining systematic spread is quarantined in orthogonal components.




Q5. True or false: OPLS predicts the outcome more accurately than PLS. Explain.






Hint





OPLS is a re-parameterisation (a rotation) of the same information.









Answer





False. OPLS has essentially the same predictive performance as PLS — it is a rotation of the same solution. Its advantage is purely interpretational: it concentrates the \(Y\)-related variation into one predictive component and pushes nuisance structure into separate orthogonal components. Same prediction, cleaner picture.




Q6. You have 30 samples and 5000 metabolite features, and your OPLS-DA score plot cleanly separates cases from controls. Why is that plot, on its own, not evidence of a real effect?






Hint





What can a supervised method do when there are far more features than samples?









Answer





Because \(p \gg n\) (5000 features, 30 samples): with far more features than samples, some linear combination will separate any labelling — even a random one — by chance. Supervised fitting can therefore produce a beautiful separation from noise alone. The training-data score plot proves nothing until it is validated.




Q7. Which two numbers/checks tell you whether an OPLS-DA model actually generalises, and what does each add?






Hint





One is cross-validated; the other shuffles the labels.









Answer





\(Q^2\) — the cross-validated predicted variance (honest fit; \(R^2Y\) alone is optimistic and always rises with more components). And the permutation test — shuffle the labels many times to build a null distribution of \(Q^2\); the real model must sit clearly in its tail. Together: \(Q^2\) says how well it predicts held-out samples, permutation says whether that beats chance for data of this size.




Q8. A model reports \(R^2Y = 0.95\) but \(Q^2 = -0.08\). What is going on, and what is the general fingerprint of this problem?






Hint





Compare in-sample fit against cross-validated prediction.









Answer





The model fits the training data almost perfectly (\(R^2Y = 0.95\)) but predicts held-out samples worse than the mean (\(Q^2 < 0\)) — classic overfitting. The general fingerprint is a large gap between a high \(R^2Y\) and a near-zero or negative \(Q^2\).

title: PCA in R
text:
About this lecture
In Eigenvalues & eigenvectors you learned that the eigenvectors of a covariance matrix point along the axes of greatest variation in a dataset. Principal component analysis (PCA) is exactly that idea turned into a practical tool. Today we run it in R.

What PCA does: find new axes (principal components) that capture the most variation in a high-dimensional dataset, in order.
Run it with one function: prcomp, and inspect its three outputs — $sdev, $rotation, $x.
See that prcomp is just the eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix — the engine you already built.
Read variance explained from $sdev, plot scores ($x) to separate sample groups, and read loadings ($rotation) to find the genes that drive the separation.
Practical craft: samples as rows, why we center, and why scaling matters when features live on different scales.

This is a hands-on day. The exam may ask you to interpret PCA output and explain what each piece means.

The one-sentence takeaway: PCA re-expresses your data in a new coordinate system whose axes are ordered by how much variation they capture, and in R that is a single call to prcomp. Everything else today is reading the three outputs and knowing which knobs (center, scale) to turn. Lean hard on Eigenvalues & eigenvectors: students already proved that the leading eigenvector of a covariance matrix is the direction of greatest spread. PCA is that theorem made into a workflow. Keep this a code-and-interpretation day, not a derivation day, but do show the eigen equivalence once so the tool is not a black box. No package is installed at render time, so all R here is shown as static code with results in comments.

title: PCA in R
text:
The biology problem
You have an expression matrix: 20 samples (rows) measured over 10,000 genes (columns). Some samples are tumor, some are healthy.

You cannot plot 10,000 dimensions. You cannot eyeball 10,000 genes per sample.
But you suspect the samples fall into groups, and that a few underlying patterns (a proliferation program, an immune program) explain most of the differences.

The question: can we collapse 10,000 gene-columns into 2 or 3 informative axes that reveal the group structure — and then ask which genes define those axes?
That is precisely what PCA delivers. The first axis is the single direction along which the samples differ the most.


Ground the abstraction in a real omics shape before any math: a samples-by-genes matrix that is far too wide to visualise. The biological bet behind PCA is that the thousands of measured genes are not independent — they are driven by a handful of coordinated programs, so the true dimensionality is small. PCA finds those few dominant directions. Emphasise the two payoffs students will get today: (1) a 2D picture that separates sample groups, and (2) the loadings, which name the genes responsible. This dual payoff — a map plus its legend — is the whole reason PCA is the first thing biologists run on a new dataset.

title: PCA in R
section: What PCA is, in one picture
text:
What PCA is, in one picture
Think of the data cloud from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors: samples plotted in gene-space form a tilted, elongated blob.

PC1 is the direction along which the cloud is most stretched — the axis of greatest variance.
PC2 is the direction of next-greatest variance, perpendicular to PC1.
Each further PC is orthogonal to all the previous ones and captures the most remaining variance.

PCA rotates the coordinate system so the new axes line up with the natural axes of the cloud. The data does not change — only the description of it.
\[\text{principal components} = \text{eigenvectors of the covariance matrix}\]


Reuse the exact mental image from the eigen lecture — the tilted sausage-shaped cloud — because that is the bridge students already own. PCA just names the long axis PC1 and the perpendicular short axis PC2, and keeps going into higher dimensions. Stress two properties: the PCs are ordered by variance (PC1 captures the most), and they are mutually orthogonal (guaranteed because the covariance matrix is symmetric, per the spectral theorem from the eigen unit). Emphasise that PCA is a rotation, not a distortion: no information is lost if you keep all PCs; dimension reduction happens only when you choose to keep the first few.

title: PCA in R
section: The toy dataset we will use all lecture
text:
The toy dataset we will use all lecture
Four samples, three genes. Small enough to check every number by hand.
X <- matrix(c(
  # geneA geneB geneC
     2,    0,   1,     # sample1
     4,    1,   2,     # sample2
     6,    2,   2,     # sample3
     8,    3,   1      # sample4
  ), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(X) <- c("sample1", "sample2", "sample3", "sample4")
colnames(X) <- c("geneA", "geneB", "geneC")
X
#         geneA geneB geneC
# sample1     2     0     1
# sample2     4     1     2
# sample3     6     2     2
# sample4     8     3     1
Convention (memorise): samples are rows, features (genes) are columns. geneA and geneB rise together across samples (perfectly correlated); geneC just wobbles, independent of the trend.

A tiny matrix that students can hold in their head is worth more than a realistic one they cannot check. Point out the built-in structure: geneA and geneB increase steadily from sample1 to sample4 (in fact perfectly correlated), while geneC wobbles 1,2,2,1 with no relation to that trend. That planted structure is what PCA should recover: PC1 will be the geneA-geneB trend, and geneC will not contribute to PC1 at all. Hammer the orientation convention now — samples as rows — because getting it backwards is the single most common PCA mistake, and R’s prcomp assumes exactly this layout. We will feed this same X to prcomp and to eigen and show they agree.

title: PCA in R
text:
One call: prcomp
pca <- prcomp(X, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
Two arguments you should always think about explicitly:

center = TRUE — subtract each gene’s mean so the cloud is centered on the origin. PCA is about variation, so you must remove the mean first. (Default TRUE.)
scale. = TRUE — divide each gene by its standard deviation, putting all genes on a common scale. (Default FALSE — you usually want to set it.)

The result is a list with three pieces we will now open:

pca$sdev — standard deviation along each PC (→ variance explained),
pca$rotation — the loadings (how genes combine into PCs),
pca$x — the scores (coordinates of each sample on the PCs).


This is the whole tool in one line, but the two named arguments carry the practical wisdom. Centering is not optional in spirit: PCA measures spread around the mean, so if you do not center, PC1 will chase the distance from the origin rather than the direction of variation. prcomp centers by default; still say it out loud. Scaling is the real decision and gets its own slide later, so here just flag that the default is FALSE and biologists usually want TRUE. Note the dot in scale. — it is an unfortunate but real quirk of the function signature (scale is taken by another meaning), so students who type scale = TRUE get a surprise. Preview the three outputs as the map of the rest of the lecture.

title: PCA in R
text:
Output 1: pca$sdev and variance explained
$sdev holds the standard deviation of the data along each PC. Square it to get variance, then normalise:
pca$sdev
# [1] 1.4142 1.0000 0.0000

variances <- pca$sdev^2                 # variance captured by each PC
prop <- variances / sum(variances)      # proportion of total variance
round(prop, 3)
# [1] 0.667 0.333 0.000

cumsum(prop)
# [1] 0.667 1.000 1.000
PC1 alone explains ~67% of the variation; PC1 + PC2 explain 100%. The third PC is exactly zero — because geneA and geneB are perfectly correlated, the data truly lives in two dimensions.


This is the payoff of the whole eigenvalue story: variance along PC k equals the k-th eigenvalue of the (scaled) covariance matrix, and sdev is its square root. Walk the arithmetic: square sdev to get variances, divide by the total to get proportions, and cumsum to see how fast you accumulate the signal. Here PC1 grabs two thirds because geneA and geneB move together — one dominant program. The exactly-zero third value confirms the data really lives in two dimensions (perfect correlation collapses one dimension entirely). Introduce the word scree plot for the bar chart of these proportions; the elbow tells you how many PCs to keep. This is how biologists justify reducing thousands of genes to a handful of components.

title: PCA in R
text:
Output 2: pca$rotation (the loadings)
$rotation is the matrix of loadings: each column is a PC, each row a gene. It tells you how much each gene contributes to each PC.
pca$rotation
#          PC1  PC2     PC3
# geneA  0.707    0   0.707
# geneB  0.707    0  -0.707
# geneC  0.000   -1   0.000

The columns are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (unit length, mutually orthogonal).
PC1: geneA and geneB have equal loadings (0.707) and geneC is exactly 0 → PC1 is purely “geneA and geneB together”.
PC2: entirely geneC (loading −1) → PC2 is the geneC wobble, independent of the trend.

Reading loadings tells you the biological meaning of an axis: which genes define this direction?


Loadings are where PCA stops being a black box and starts naming biology. Each PC is a weighted combination of the original genes, and rotation holds those weights. Large-magnitude loadings (positive or negative) are the genes that define the axis; zero loadings are irrelevant to it. Here PC1 is an equal mix of the two co-varying genes with geneC exactly absent — the proliferation-program idea from the motivation — and PC2 isolates the independent geneC wobble. Remind students these columns are literally the eigenvectors from the eigen unit: unit length, orthogonal, sign-ambiguous. The sign point matters: R may flip a whole column, which flips the axis but changes no interpretation, just like eigenvector sign freedom.

title: PCA in R
text:
Output 3: pca$x (the scores)
$x gives the coordinates of each sample in the new PC space — one row per sample, one column per PC.
pca$x
#              PC1     PC2   PC3
# sample1  -1.643   0.866    ~0
# sample2  -0.548  -0.866    ~0
# sample3   0.548  -0.866    ~0
# sample4   1.643   0.866    ~0

The PC1 scores increase steadily sample1 → sample4: PCA recovered the geneA-geneB trend we planted.
These scores are what you plot to see sample structure.

Scores are the projections of each (centered, scaled) sample onto the PC directions: \[\text{scores} = X_{\text{centered, scaled}} \cdot \text{rotation}\]

Scores answer where does each sample land on the new axes. Each sample’s PC1 score is its position along the direction of greatest variation. Here the PC1 scores march monotonically from sample1 to sample4, recovering exactly the trend built into the toy data. Make the projection explicit: scores equal the preprocessed data matrix times the rotation matrix — a change of basis, the same matrix-times-vector operation from the linear algebra block. This is the object we visualise: a plot of PC1 vs PC2 scores is the map that separates sample groups. Rotation is the legend (genes), scores are the map (samples); students should keep the two straight.

title: PCA in R
section: The plot that starts every omics analysis
text:
The plot that starts every omics analysis
Plot PC1 score vs PC2 score, one point per sample. This 2D map often reveals the group structure hidden in thousands of genes.
plot(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2],
     xlab = "PC1 (67% of variance)",
     ylab = "PC2 (33% of variance)",
     pch = 19)
text(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], labels = rownames(X), pos = 3)
In a real study you would colour the points by a known label (tumor vs healthy, treated vs control) and look for separation:
group <- c("healthy", "healthy", "tumor", "tumor")
plot(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], col = factor(group), pch = 19)
If groups separate along PC1, then PC1’s loadings name the genes that distinguish them.


This slide is the practical climax. Every RNA-seq or single-cell analysis begins with a PC1-vs-PC2 scatter because it is the fastest sanity check and discovery tool at once. Axis labels should always carry the percent variance explained (from the sdev slide) so viewers know how much of the story each axis tells. The real move is colouring points by a known metadata label and asking: do my biological groups separate? If yes along PC1, you immediately jump to PC1’s loadings to get the gene list — closing the loop from map to mechanism. Also flag the diagnostic use: if samples separate by batch or by which day they were processed rather than by biology, PCA just caught a confounder. Keep the code base-R and simple.

title: PCA in R
section: The biplot: scores and loadings together
text:
The biplot: scores and loadings together
A biplot overlays the two things we have been reading — sample scores (points) and gene loadings (arrows) — on one PC1–PC2 picture.
biplot(pca)

Points are samples positioned by their scores.
Arrows are genes; an arrow points in the direction that gene increases.
A gene whose arrow points strongly along PC1 is a gene that drives PC1 — and thus separates samples along it.

One glance links which samples differ to which genes explain the difference.


The biplot is the one-figure summary of a PCA: it fuses the map (scores) and the legend (loadings) into a single view so you can read sample structure and its gene drivers simultaneously. Arrows pointing the same direction as a cluster of samples are the genes elevated in those samples. Here geneA and geneB arrows lie along PC1 (they drive the main separation) while geneC points along PC2. Caution students that biplots get crowded fast with thousands of genes, so in practice you subset to the top-loading genes; but conceptually it is the cleanest illustration of the scores-plus-loadings duality. Mention prcomp’s biplot works directly on the returned object.

title: PCA in R
section: PCA is eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix
text:
PCA is eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix
prcomp is not magic — it is the machinery from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors. On the scaled, centered data:
Xs <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)   # same preprocessing prcomp does
C  <- cov(Xs)                                 # 3x3 covariance (here = correlation) matrix
e  <- eigen(C)

e$values
# [1] 2 1 0                     # variance along each PC = eigenvalues

pca$sdev^2
# [1] 2 1 0                     # identical!

e$vectors        # eigenvectors == columns of pca$rotation (up to sign)
The eigenvalues are the per-PC variances; the eigenvectors are the loadings. PCA = eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix. You built this engine already.

This slide pays off the promise that PCA is not a new black box. Show the equivalence concretely: scale the data yourself, form the covariance matrix (which for scaled data equals the correlation matrix), and call eigen on it — the eigenvalues match pca\(sdev squared and the eigenvectors match pca\)rotation up to sign. Emphasise that scale() and cov() reproduce exactly prcomp’s internal preprocessing. Two honest footnotes for the curious: prcomp actually uses the SVD of the data matrix rather than forming the covariance explicitly (numerically better), but the result is identical; and the eigenvalues here match sdev^2 exactly because cov uses the n-1 denominator, the same convention prcomp uses. The point for students: everything they proved by hand about symmetric matrices governs PCA.

title: PCA in R
text:
Why centering is not optional
PCA finds directions of variation around the mean. If you skip centering, “variation” is measured from the origin instead — and PC1 will chase the mean position of the cloud, not its shape.

With genes on wildly different baseline levels (a housekeeping gene at 10,000 counts, a transcription factor at 5), the uncentered PC1 is dominated by the high-mean gene’s offset, telling you nothing.
prcomp centers by default (center = TRUE). Leave it on unless you have a specific reason.

\[\text{centered value} = x_{ij} - \overline{x_{\cdot j}}\quad(\text{subtract gene } j\text{'s mean})\]


Centering is conceptually mandatory because variance is defined as spread about the mean; measuring spread about the origin conflates the mean with the variation and PC1 ends up pointing at the centroid. The count-data example makes it vivid: a highly expressed housekeeping gene sits far from zero, so an uncentered analysis wastes PC1 on that constant offset. prcomp defaults center to TRUE, so students rarely need to change it, but they must understand why it is there. Contrast with scaling, the next slide, which is a genuine judgement call. Keep the formula trivial: subtract each column’s mean.

title: PCA in R
text:
Why scaling usually matters
scale. = TRUE divides each gene by its standard deviation, so every gene contributes on an equal footing.

Without scaling, a gene with large numerical variance (say raw counts in the thousands) dominates PC1 purely because its numbers are big — not because it is biologically important.
With scaling, PCA weighs the pattern of each gene equally, regardless of its units or magnitude.

When to scale:







Situation
Scale?




Features on different units/scales (gene counts, protein levels, pH)
Yes


Features already comparable (e.g. all log-transformed expression)
Often no



prcomp does not scale by default (scale. = FALSE) — decide deliberately.


Scaling is the one real decision in a basic PCA and a favourite exam question. The mechanism: variance has units, so a gene measured in large numbers has large variance for trivial reasons and hijacks PC1 if you do not scale. Scaling to unit variance puts every gene on equal footing so PCA responds to correlation patterns, not magnitudes. The nuance: if all features are already on a common, meaningful scale — for instance log-transformed expression where differences are comparable — scaling can throw away real information by inflating quiet, noisy genes. So it is genuinely situational. The safe default for heterogeneous features is scale = TRUE, but say the reasoning, do not memorise a rule. Note again that prcomp’s default is FALSE, the opposite of what beginners expect.

title: PCA in R
text:
Practical checklist
Before you trust a PCA plot, confirm:

Orientation: samples are rows, features are columns. (Transpose with t if your matrix is genes × samples — omics tables often are.)
Centering: on (default). PCA needs it.
Scaling: decided on purpose, based on whether features share a scale.
Missing values: prcomp cannot handle NA — impute or drop first.
Variance explained: report it on the axis labels; a PC1 with 8% is a very different story from one with 80%.
Sign/rotation: an axis may be flipped between runs or software; the interpretation is unchanged.


A pre-flight checklist consolidates the practical craft. Orientation is the number one bug: many omics matrices ship as genes-by-samples (the transpose of what prcomp wants), so a t() is often the first line of a real analysis; a PCA run on the wrong orientation silently gives you a PCA of genes instead of samples. NA handling trips people up because prcomp errors or misbehaves with missing data, so imputation or filtering must come first. Reporting variance explained on axes keeps the audience honest about how much structure PC1 actually holds. And remind them of sign freedom one more time so a flipped plot between sessions does not cause panic. This slide is the thing to photograph before doing PCA on real data.

title: PCA in R
text:
From toy to real data
The workflow is identical at scale — only the matrix is bigger.
# expr: a matrix with samples in rows, genes in columns
# (transpose first if yours is genes x samples)
pca <- prcomp(expr, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

# how many PCs carry real signal?
prop <- pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
round(prop[1:5], 3)

# the map: colour samples by a metadata label
plot(pca$x[, 1], pca$x[, 2], col = factor(metadata$condition), pch = 19)

# the drivers: top genes on PC1
sort(abs(pca$rotation[, 1]), decreasing = TRUE)[1:20]
For large genomics datasets you will later meet production tools (Bioconductor workflows, DESeq2’s plotPCA) that wrap these same steps with sensible defaults.

Close by showing that nothing changes going from four samples to four thousand: same prcomp call, same three outputs, same two questions (how many PCs, and what drives PC1). The only new habit is checking orientation and pulling the top-loading genes with sort(abs(…)) to get a ranked driver list you can hand to a biologist or feed to enrichment analysis. Name the production tools — Bioconductor, DESeq2::plotPCA — so students know the base-R version they learned today is the transparent core inside those wrappers, consistent with the course principle of teaching the honest engine first, then pointing at the optimised tool. Do not teach those wrappers now; just signpost them.

title: PCA in R
text:
Summary



Idea
In R




Run PCA (samples = rows)
prcomp(X, center=TRUE, scale.=TRUE)


Std dev per PC → variance
pca$sdev, then pca$sdev^2


Proportion of variance
pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)


Loadings (gene weights)
pca$rotation — the eigenvectors


Scores (sample coords)
pca$x — what you plot


The map
plot(pca$x[,1], pca$x[,2])


Map + legend in one
biplot(pca)


Same as
eigen(cov(scale(X)))



Core message: PCA is the eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix — it finds ordered, orthogonal axes of variation. Scores map your samples; loadings name the genes; sdev says how much each axis matters.
Builds on: Eigenvalues & eigenvectors. Leads to: clustering, and latent-variable methods in the Applications block.

The summary table is the exam cheat-sheet and the lab reference card. Drill the three outputs one more time by role: sdev tells you how much each axis matters, rotation (loadings) tells you which genes define each axis, and x (scores) tells you where each sample sits — plot the last one. Re-state the unifying fact: prcomp equals eigen of the covariance of the scaled data, so all the by-hand eigenvalue skills transfer directly. Point forward: PC scores are a natural input to clustering, and PCA is the gateway to the broader family of latent-variable and dimension-reduction methods in the Applications block. Remind students the two knobs, center and scale, are the only real decisions and they should be able to justify both.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
text:
About this lecture
In Computing PCA you learned to run a PCA and read its scores and loadings. PCA always hands you as many principal components as you have features — but only the first few carry signal. Today’s two questions: how many components do I keep, and how can PCA quietly mislead me?

Read the variance explained by each PC (an eigenvalue in disguise) and turn it into a proportion.
Choose a number of PCs with a scree plot / elbow, a cumulative-variance threshold, or simple rules of thumb.
Know the pitfalls: PCA is unsupervised, so the biggest-variance axis need not be the biologically interesting one; batch effects can hijack PC1; results shift with scaling and outliers; and PCA only sees linear structure.
A teaser of what lies beyond: ICA (independent, not merely uncorrelated) and non-linear maps like UMAP (seen in the single-cell block).

This is a judgement day: fewer formulas, more “what would a careful analyst do here.”

The students can already produce a PCA; the gap this lecture closes is interpretation and scepticism. Two threads run in parallel: a constructive one (how to pick the number of PCs) and a cautionary one (why the answer PCA gives can be biologically wrong). Emphasise that none of the “how many PCs” rules is a law — they are heuristics, and the honest analyst reports which one they used. Keep an R session mental-model handy but remember nothing executes at render time; all code here is for reading. Reference earlier units by name (Computing PCA, Eigenvalues & eigenvectors) rather than by day.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
section: The biology: you ran a PCA, now what?
text:
The biology: you ran a PCA, now what?
You have a gene-expression matrix: 60 tumour samples \(\times\) 20,000 genes. You run prcomp and get 60 principal components back.

Plotting PC1 vs PC2 shows two clean clusters. Great — but are two components enough?
Would PC3 split a cluster into two disease subtypes? Would PC4? Where do you stop?
And the clusters you see on PC1: are they biology (tumour subtype) or technology (two sequencing runs)?

Keeping too few PCs discards real signal; keeping too many re-imports noise. And a confident-looking plot can be showing you the wrong thing entirely.


Ground the whole lecture in a concrete, familiar object: an expression matrix with far more genes than samples, exactly the shape they meet in omics. The tension is real and practical — the number of PCs you retain is a modelling choice that changes every downstream step (clustering, distances, differential tests on scores). Plant both worries now: (1) how many to keep, (2) whether the leading axis is even biological. The batch-vs-subtype hook returns later as a full pitfall slide.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
section: Each PC carries a slice of variance
text:
Each PC carries a slice of variance
From Eigenvalues & eigenvectors: PCA diagonalises the (centred) data’s covariance matrix. Each PC is an eigenvector; its eigenvalue \(\lambda_k\) is the variance of the data along that PC.

PCs come sorted: \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_p \ge 0\). PC1 captures the most variance, PC2 the most of what remains, and so on.
The eigenvalues sum to the total variance in the data: $_k _k = $ total variance.
In R, prcomp reports the standard deviation of each PC in sdev, so the variance (the eigenvalue) is sdev^2.

“How many PCs to keep” is really: how many eigenvalues are big enough to matter?


Re-anchor to the eigen material so PCA does not feel like a new black box: principal components ARE the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and the eigenvalue is literally the variance along that direction. Two facts to nail: eigenvalues are non-negative and sorted descending, and they sum to the total variance. The prcomp detail (sdev is a standard deviation, so square it to get the eigenvalue/variance) is a recurring source of bugs — say it explicitly. Everything about “choosing components” is downstream of reading these eigenvalues.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
section: From eigenvalue to proportion of variance
text:
From eigenvalue to proportion of variance
Raw eigenvalues depend on units. Convert each to a proportion of variance explained (PVE):
\[\text{PVE}_k = \frac{\lambda_k}{\sum_{j=1}^{p} \lambda_j}\]

PVE\(_k\) is a number in \([0,1]\): the fraction of total variance living on PC \(k\).
The cumulative PVE, \(\sum_{j\le k}\text{PVE}_j\), is the fraction captured by the first \(k\) PCs together.
Example: if the first three PVEs are \(0.42, 0.18, 0.07\), then PC1–PC3 together explain \(0.42+0.18+0.07 = 0.67\), i.e. 67% of the variance.

This is the raw material for every rule that follows.


The move from eigenvalue to proportion is what makes the numbers comparable and interpretable — an eigenvalue of “8.3” means nothing on its own, but “42% of variance” does. Define both the per-PC proportion and the cumulative proportion, because the two rules that follow (elbow vs threshold) use them respectively. Walk the tiny arithmetic example so the cumulative idea is concrete before the plots.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
section: The scree plot and the elbow
text:
The scree plot and the elbow
Plot PVE (or the eigenvalue) against PC number. Typically it drops steeply then flattens into a shallow tail — the shape of a rubble slope, hence scree.

The elbow is where the steep drop gives way to the flat tail.
Heuristic (Cattell’s): keep the PCs before the elbow; treat the flat tail as noise.
The first few PCs are structure; the long flat tail is many tiny, roughly-equal eigenvalues — the fingerprint of noise.

Judgement call: the elbow is read by eye and is often ambiguous. Report how you chose it.


The scree plot is the single most common tool, so give it a clear mental image: a cliff then a rubble slope. The elbow separates the two. Be honest that “read the elbow by eye” is exactly as soft as it sounds — real scree plots frequently have no clean elbow, or two candidate elbows, and two analysts can disagree. That softness is the point: this is a heuristic, not a theorem. The noise intuition (a flat tail of many near-equal small eigenvalues) is worth stating because it also motivates the permutation/parallel-analysis idea later.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Cumulative-variance threshold
A more decisive rule: keep as many PCs as needed to reach a target cumulative PVE — commonly 80%, 90%, or 95%.

“Keep enough PCs to explain 90% of the variance” → find the smallest \(k\) with cumulative PVE \(\ge 0.90\).
Good when PCA is a compression / denoising step feeding a downstream model, and you want a guaranteed amount of signal retained.
The threshold is still a choice: 90% is a convention, not a fact. A flat scree tail means the last few percent cost many PCs.

Elbow and threshold often disagree — that disagreement is information about how structured your data is.


Contrast this with the elbow: the threshold rule is reproducible (no eyeballing) but the threshold itself is arbitrary, so you have simply moved the judgement from “where is the elbow” to “which percentage.” Tie it to purpose: for data reduction before clustering or regression you care about how much signal you keep, so a cumulative threshold is natural. Warn that in high-dimensional omics with a long flat tail, reaching 95% can demand a huge number of PCs — evidence that most of the variance is diffuse noise, not that you need 200 components. When elbow and threshold disagree, that is diagnostic, not a failure.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
section: Two more rules you will meet
text:
Two more rules you will meet

Kaiser criterion — on standardised data (correlation matrix), keep PCs with eigenvalue \(> 1\). Rationale: after standardising, each original variable contributes variance 1, so the average eigenvalue is 1; a PC “worth more than one variable” clears the bar. Known to over-retain; use with care.
Parallel analysis / permutation — compare your eigenvalues to those from randomised data (columns shuffled independently, so real correlations are destroyed). Keep only PCs whose eigenvalue exceeds what pure noise produces. More principled, needs a little computation.

No rule is authoritative. Sensible practice: look at the scree plot, sanity-check with a threshold, and if it matters, run a permutation check.


Round out the toolkit without overselling any tool. Kaiser is popular because it is a single clean number, but it is tied to the correlation-matrix setting (eigenvalues average to 1 only after standardising) and is notorious for keeping too many components — say both things. Parallel analysis / permutation is the most defensible because it builds an explicit noise baseline from the data itself, which connects back to the “flat tail = noise” intuition. The meta-message: triangulate across rules rather than trusting one, and always report which you used.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
section: In R: variance explained and a scree plot
text:
In R: variance explained and a scree plot
prcomp returns sdev; square it for the eigenvalues, then normalise.
pca <- prcomp(X, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)  # X: samples x genes

eig <- pca$sdev^2            # eigenvalues = variance per PC
pve <- eig / sum(eig)        # proportion of variance explained
cumsum(pve)                  # cumulative PVE: 0.42, 0.60, 0.67, ...

# scree plot: PVE vs PC index
plot(pve, type = "b", xlab = "PC", ylab = "Proportion of variance")

# smallest k reaching 90% cumulative variance
which(cumsum(pve) >= 0.90)[1]
summary(pca) prints the same PVE and cumulative rows directly. screeplot(pca) draws the eigenvalues, but a hand-rolled PVE plot is clearer.

Keep this purely illustrative — nothing runs at render. The load-bearing lines: sdev must be squared to become an eigenvalue/variance; dividing by the sum gives PVE; cumsum gives the cumulative curve; the which(…)[1] idiom finds the smallest k crossing a threshold. Mention summary(prcomp) because students will reach for it and it already tabulates PVE and cumulative proportion. Note scale. = TRUE here because the next pitfall block is exactly about that choice — flag that it is deliberate, not a default.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Pitfall 1: PCA is unsupervised
PCA maximises variance. It never sees your labels (tumour vs normal, treated vs control). So the largest-variance direction is not guaranteed to be the direction that separates your biological groups.

The interesting contrast might live on PC4, buried under three larger axes of nuisance variation.
Two samples far apart on PC1 need not differ in any way you care about.

If you have labels and want the axis that best separates them, that is a supervised question — the job of tools like the OPLS model (under Extra material) or LDA, not PCA.


This is the most important conceptual pitfall. Students internalise “PC1 = most important,” but “most variance” and “most biologically relevant” are different claims that happen to coincide only sometimes. The classic picture: two groups separated along a low-variance direction while the high-variance axis is some irrelevant gradient (library size, a continuous covariate). PCA will rank the irrelevant axis first. Name the fix without teaching it: if separation of known groups is the goal, use a supervised method (OPLS in this block, or LDA), because those methods do look at the labels.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
section: Pitfall 2: batch effects can dominate PC1
text:
Pitfall 2: batch effects can dominate PC1
A batch effect is unwanted technical variation — two sequencing runs, two reagent lots, two hospitals. It is often large, so PCA, chasing variance, can put it on PC1.

You interpret PC1 as “disease subtype”; it is really “sequencing run.” The clusters are machines, not biology.
Colour the PCA by known technical variables (batch, run date, library size) before interpreting anything. If a technical variable lines up with a PC, that PC is suspect.

Batch effects are addressed by experimental design (randomise samples across batches) and correction methods (later, in the single-cell block), not by staring harder at the plot.


This is the practical, career-saving warning. Batch effects are ubiquitous in omics and frequently larger than the biological signal, so an unsupervised variance-chaser will surface them first. The habit to drill: always colour the score plot by every technical covariate you have (batch, run, date, RIN, library size, sex) before believing any biological story. If batch aligns with a PC, stop and correct. Reference that correction/integration is taught later (single-cell block) so they know the fix exists without derailing today. The deeper lesson connects to Pitfall 1: PCA has no idea which variance is wanted.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Pitfall 3: sensitivity to scaling
PCA is driven by variance, and variance depends on units. A feature measured in large numbers can dominate purely because its numbers are big.

scale. = FALSE (covariance PCA, the default): high-variance / high-expression genes dominate. Sensible only when all features share units and their spread is meaningful.
scale. = TRUE (correlation PCA): every feature standardised to variance 1, so all contribute equally regardless of scale. Usual choice when features are heterogeneous.

The two can give different PCs and a different scree plot. Scaling is a real modelling decision — state which you used and why.
prcomp(X, scale. = FALSE)   # covariance PCA: big-variance features dominate
prcomp(X, scale. = TRUE)    # correlation PCA: all features weighted equally


Make scaling feel consequential, not cosmetic. Because PCA is literally an eigen-decomposition of either the covariance matrix (scale = FALSE) or the correlation matrix (scale = TRUE), the choice changes the matrix being decomposed and therefore the components and the whole scree plot. Rule of thumb: standardise when features are on different scales or units (mixed measurements, metabolomics with wildly different abundances); leave unscaled only when a common unit makes raw spread meaningful. Note this also interacts with the Kaiser rule, which assumes standardised data. The professional habit: report the choice explicitly.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Pitfall 4: sensitivity to outliers
Variance is dominated by large deviations, so a single aberrant sample can bend a whole principal component toward itself.

One mislabelled or degraded sample can define PC1 by itself: everyone else collapses to a blob while the outlier sits alone at the far end.
Symptom: one point far off, the rest bunched — a PC that “explains variance” but only that one point’s variance.

Look at the score plots, investigate extreme points (technical failure? contamination?), and decide deliberately whether to fix, exclude, or keep them. Robust PCA variants exist for heavily contaminated data.


Outliers exploit the same weakness as scaling and batch: PCA rewards large variance uncritically, and an outlier is maximal variance in one point. The tell-tale score plot is one lonely dot far out with everything else crushed into a corner — a red flag that PC1 is describing an artefact, not the population. The action is investigative, not automatic: find out WHY the point is extreme (failed library, swapped label, real biological extreme) before deciding to drop it. Mention robust PCA exists but do not teach it. This closes the trio of “variance is not automatically meaningful” pitfalls (2, 3, 4).

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
section: Try it: three ways PC1 can mislead
text:
Try it: three ways PC1 can mislead




One small 2D demo for pitfalls 3, 4 and 1, in that order. The red solid line is PC1, the dashed red line PC2; the two strips underneath show every sample’s score on PC1 and on PC2, drawn at the same scale as the scatter. Preset 1, Units: metabolite A has SD around 100, B around 1.6, so on equal axes the cloud is a flat line and PC1 is essentially “A” with 99.99% of the variance. Tick “Scale variables”: now both have SD 1, PC1 turns to 45 degrees and mixes A and B equally, explaining about 87%. Same samples, different PCs. Preset 2, Outlier: without the red sample PC1 runs along the cloud at about 18 degrees (grey dashed); with it PC1 swings to about 100 degrees and points at the one sample. Drag the red point in towards the cloud and watch PC1 snap back; drag it out and the PC1 strip shows the symptom from the last slide, one lonely point and a crushed bunch. Preset 3, Two groups: PC1 takes almost 90% of the variance yet the colours overlap completely on the PC1 strip; they separate only on PC2. PCA ranked the variance, not the labels, which is pitfall 1.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
section: Pitfall 5: PCA only sees linear structure
text:
Pitfall 5: PCA only sees linear structure
Every PC is a linear combination of the original features — a straight axis through the data. PCA can only find linear structure.

Data on a curved manifold (an S-curve, a spiral, a developmental trajectory) has no good straight axis; PCA flattens the curve and may need many PCs to describe something simple.
Nonlinear biological structure — a differentiation trajectory, a cyclic process — is exactly where PCA struggles to summarise cleanly.

This is a built-in limitation, not a bug, and it motivates the non-linear methods on the next slide.


The final pitfall is structural rather than a mistake you can avoid: linearity is baked into what a principal component IS (a linear combination = a straight direction). When the real structure is curved — a 1D trajectory bent through high-dimensional space, a cell-cycle loop — a straight axis cannot follow it, and PCA either misrepresents it or spreads it across many components. This is the natural bridge to nonlinear embeddings. Do not frame it as PCA being bad; frame it as PCA answering a linear question, and some biological questions being nonlinear.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Beyond PCA (1): ICA
PCA gives axes that are uncorrelated and orthogonal, ordered by variance. Sometimes you want axes that correspond to separate underlying sources instead.

Independent Component Analysis (ICA) seeks components that are statistically independent, not merely uncorrelated — a stronger condition.
Uncorrelated and independent are the same only for Gaussian data; for non-Gaussian signals, independence says much more.
Motivating picture (the “cocktail party”): unmix overlapping sources. In biology, ICA can separate mixed transcriptional programmes co-occurring in the same samples.
ICA components are not ordered by importance, and their sign/scale are arbitrary — so “how many components” is decided differently than for PCA.



Keep this a teaser, not a method lesson. The one crisp idea: PCA only removes correlation (a second-order, linear notion), while ICA targets full statistical independence (a stronger, higher-order notion), and the two coincide only in the Gaussian case. The cocktail-party framing lands well; the biological analogue is separating overlapping regulatory or transcriptional programmes that PCA would blend because it only decorrelates. Flag the practical differences (no natural ordering, arbitrary sign/scale) so they are not surprised. This directly answers the linearity limitation only partly — ICA is still linear — which is why the next slide moves to nonlinear maps.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Beyond PCA (2): non-linear maps
To capture curved structure, use methods that preserve local relationships rather than global straight axes.

UMAP (and t-SNE) build a low-dimensional map that keeps nearby points nearby — good for visualising clusters and trajectories PCA flattens. You will use UMAP in the single-cell block.
Caveats: these embeddings are non-linear and stochastic; distances between clusters are not meaningful, axes have no units, and results depend on tuning parameters and the random seed. Great for seeing structure, poor for measuring it.
Common pipeline: PCA first to denoise and reduce dimensions, then UMAP on the top PCs — so today’s “how many PCs” question feeds directly into it.



Close the constructive arc: nonlinear embeddings exist precisely for the curved structure PCA cannot follow, and UMAP is the one they will actually use in the single-cell block, so name it. The essential warnings: UMAP/t-SNE are for visualisation, not measurement — inter-cluster distances and axis directions are not interpretable, and different seeds/parameters give different-looking maps. Crucially, the standard pipeline runs PCA first (denoise, reduce to a few dozen PCs) and UMAP on those PCs, which means the “how many PCs to keep” decision from today is an input to that later workflow. That ties the whole lecture together.

title: Choosing components & pitfalls
text:
Summary







Question
Tool / idea




How much does PC \(k\) explain?
PVE\(_k = \lambda_k / \sum_j \lambda_j\) (in R: sdev^2, normalise)


How many PCs? (eyeball)
scree plot, keep PCs before the elbow


How many PCs? (reproducible)
cumulative-variance threshold (80/90/95%)


Other rules
Kaiser (\(\lambda>1\), standardised; over-retains), permutation / parallel analysis


Largest variance \(\ne\) interesting
PCA is unsupervised; use OPLS/LDA to separate known groups


PC1 looks like biology?
check it is not a batch effect — colour by technical variables


Same data, different PCs
sensitive to scaling (scale.) and outliers


Curved structure
PCA is linear; try ICA (independence) or UMAP (non-linear, single-cell)



Bottom line: every “how many PCs” rule is a heuristic — triangulate and report your choice; and always ask whether the variance PCA ranked highest is the variance you actually care about.

The summary doubles as the exam cheat-sheet and the analyst’s checklist. Drill two takeaways above all: (1) no component-count rule is authoritative, so look at the scree plot, cross-check with a threshold or permutation, and state what you did; (2) PCA is an unsupervised, linear, variance-maximising method, so its top axis can be a batch effect, an outlier, a scaling artefact, or simply the wrong (linear) answer to a nonlinear question. Point forward: OPLS (this block) for supervised separation, and UMAP (single-cell block) for nonlinear structure, with PCA feeding into it.

text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

title: Exercise: principal component analysis
text:
Background
PCA takes a data matrix (samples × variables) and finds a new set of orthogonal axes — the principal components (PCs) — ordered so that the first captures the most variance, the second the most of what remains, and so on.
The pipeline (memorise this):

Centre each column (subtract its mean). Optionally scale (divide by its standard deviation) if variables are on different units.
Form the covariance matrix \(C\) (symmetric, \(p\times p\)): \(C_{ii} = \text{var}(\text{var}_i)\) on the diagonal, \(C_{ij} = \text{cov}(\text{var}_i,\text{var}_j)\) off it. For \(n\) samples use the sample covariance with divisor \(n-1\).
Eigen-decompose \(C\). The eigenvectors are the PCs (orthogonal, because \(C\) is symmetric); the eigenvalues are the variances captured along each PC.
Scores = projections of centred samples onto a PC: \(\text{score} = \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{u}\) for centred sample \(\mathbf{x}\) and unit PC \(\mathbf{u}\). Scores describe samples.
Loadings = the entries of the eigenvector — the weight of each variable in that PC. Loadings describe variables (genes).
Variance explained by PC\(_k\) = \(\lambda_k / \sum_j \lambda_j\). The denominator equals the total variance (the trace of \(C\)).

Throughout we use a tiny dataset of 2 genes measured in 5 samples:

title: Exercise: principal component analysis
text:
By hand
B1. Compute the mean of each gene, then write out the centred data matrix (subtract each column’s mean). Check that each centred column sums to 0. Why do we centre before PCA — what goes wrong if we skip it?
B2. Using the centred data, compute \(\text{var}(A)\), \(\text{var}(B)\), and \(\text{cov}(A,B)\) with divisor \(n-1 = 4\). Assemble the covariance matrix \(C\). Confirm it is symmetric.
B3. Find the eigenvalues of \(C\) (it has the symmetric pattern from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors). Verify by multiplying, and check them with the trace.
B4. Find a unit eigenvector for each eigenvalue. These are PC1 (largest eigenvalue) and PC2. Confirm they are orthogonal. Which one points along the long axis of the data cloud?
B5. (scores) Project each centred sample onto PC1 (the unit eigenvector \(\mathbf{u}_1\)) to get its PC1 score, using \(\text{score} = \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{u}_1\). Which sample sits at each extreme of PC1?
B6. (loadings) Write down the loadings of PC1 (the entries of \(\mathbf{u}_1\)). Do the two genes contribute equally to PC1? What does that say biologically about how genes A and B behave?
B7. (variance explained) What fraction of the total variance does PC1 capture? PC2? Confirm the two fractions add to 1 and that the denominator equals the trace of \(C\).
B8. (concept) Suppose you had not centred, and instead ran the whole procedure on the raw numbers. In one or two sentences, explain why the leading direction would then mostly point from the origin toward the data’s centre, rather than along the direction of greatest spread.

title: Exercise: principal component analysis
text:
Explore
Do the by-hand part first; then use this demo to see the same numbers move. The green axis can be turned by dragging a white handle or with the slider; the dashed lines are the perpendicular projections, the orange dots the scores, and the percentage is the variance of the scores out of the total variance. The five samples are the ones above, already centred.



E1. Set the axis angle to \(0^\circ\) (along GENE_A) and then to \(90^\circ\) (along GENE_B). What percentage is captured each time? Which entries of \(C\) from B2 are these numbers?
E2. Turn the axis to make the percentage as large as possible. At what angle, and how much variance is captured? Then find the angle that makes it as small as possible. Compare with your eigenvalues (B3) and variance explained (B7), then tick “Show PC1 and PC2”.
E3. At \(45^\circ\), compare the scores in the readout with your PC1 scores from B5. Then turn the axis to any other angle: what do “along the axis” and “perpendicular” always add up to, and why?
E4. Press Reset, then drag s3 from the centre to roughly \((-2, 2)\) (up and to the left, across the long axis). Does PC1 turn? What happens to the percentage of variance PC1 explains?






Solutions





E1. Both give 50%: at \(0^\circ\) the scores are just the centred GENE_A values, so the variance captured is \(\text{var}(A) = C_{11} = 5\) out of \(10\); at \(90^\circ\) it is \(\text{var}(B) = C_{22} = 5\) out of \(10\).
E2. The maximum is at \(45^\circ\): variance \(9\), i.e. 90% — this is \(\lambda_1\) and the PC1 direction \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)\). The minimum is at \(135^\circ\): variance \(1\), 10% — this is \(\lambda_2\) along PC2, perpendicular to PC1. No other angle beats 90%, which is what “PC1 is the direction of greatest variance” means.
E3. At \(45^\circ\) the scores are \(-2.83, -2.83, 0, 1.41, 4.24\), the same as B5. “Along” plus “perpendicular” is always 10, the total variance (the trace of \(C\)). For each centred sample, its squared distance from the centre splits into (score along the axis)\(^2\) + (distance from the axis)\(^2\) (Pythagoras), so turning the axis only moves variance between the two directions.
E4. PC1 stays at \(45^\circ\): s3 was moved exactly along the PC2 direction, so the spread along PC1 is still \(9\). But the spread across the long axis grows (PC2 goes from \(1\) to about \(2.6\)), so the total rises to about \(11.6\) and PC1 explains only about \(9/11.6 \approx 78\%\). A sample off the main trend adds variance PCA cannot summarise with PC1 alone. (If you drop it somewhere else, PC1 will also turn a little.)

title: Exercise: principal component analysis
text:
In R
Use R only to confirm the hand answers. (In PCA in R we use prcomp; today we build each piece with base R so the mapping to the maths is explicit — no PCA function is called here.)

Centre the data and form the covariance matrix
X <- matrix(c(1, 5,
              3, 3,
              4, 6,
              5, 7,
              7, 9), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
colnames(X) <- c("GENE_A", "GENE_B")

colMeans(X)              # 4 6  -> the two gene means

Xc <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)   # centre only, no scaling
colMeans(Xc)             # ~0 0 -> columns now centred

C <- cov(Xc)             # 2x2 covariance matrix (divisor n-1 = 4)
C                        # [[5, 4], [4, 5]]


Eigen-decompose the covariance matrix (this is PCA, by hand)
E <- eigen(C)
E$values                 # 9 1   -> variances along PC1, PC2
E$vectors                # columns are the unit eigenvectors (PC1, PC2)


Scores: project centred samples onto the PCs
scores <- Xc %*% E$vectors   # each row: (PC1 score, PC2 score) for that sample
scores


Variance explained
E$values / sum(E$values)     # 0.9 0.1  -> PC1 90%, PC2 10%
sum(E$values)                # 10 = trace(C) = total variance
sum(diag(C))                 # 10  -> same total, from the trace directly


Tasks
R1. Reproduce your B2 covariance matrix with cov(Xc) and confirm it equals your hand answer.
R2. Run eigen(C) and match $values to your B3 eigenvalues and $vectors to your B4 eigenvectors. (Signs may be flipped — an eigenvector and its negative describe the same axis.)
R3. Compute scores <- Xc %*% E$vectors and check the first column against the B5 PC1 scores you found by hand.
R4. Confirm E$values / sum(E$values) gives the B7 variance-explained fractions, and that sum(E$values) equals sum(diag(C)).

title: Exercise: principal component analysis
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — centring





Subtract each column’s own mean from every entry in that column. The mean of GENE_A is \((1+3+4+5+7)/5\) and of GENE_B is \((5+3+6+7+9)/5\). After centring, each column must sum to exactly 0 — a quick self-check. In R, scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE) centres without scaling.









Hint 2 — sample covariance





With centred values, \(\text{cov}(A,B) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (A_i-\bar A)(B_i-\bar B)\) and \(\text{var}(A)=\text{cov}(A,A)\). Here \(n=5\) so the divisor is \(4\). This matches R’s cov and var, so your hand answer should equal cov(Xc).









Hint 3 — eigenvalues of a 2×2





\(C=\begin{pmatrix}5&4\\4&5\end{pmatrix}\) has the form \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&a\end{pmatrix}\), so try \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\): the eigenvalues are \(a+b\) and \(a-b\). Check: \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2\) should equal the trace \(5+5\). (Bonus, not for exam: the characteristic equation \((5-\lambda)^2-16=0\) gives the same.)









Hint 4 — eigenvectors and normalising





Plug each \(\lambda\) into \((C-\lambda I)\mathbf v=\mathbf 0\) and read \(v_2\) in terms of \(v_1\) from one row. To make it a unit vector, divide by its length \(\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2}\); e.g. \((1,1)\) has length \(\sqrt2\), so the unit version is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)\approx(0.707,0.707)\).









Hint 5 — scores are projections





A score is a dot product (the projection you met in vector geometry). For centred sample \(\mathbf x=(x_A,x_B)\) and unit PC \(\mathbf u=(u_A,u_B)\), the score is \(x_A u_A + x_B u_B\). In R, Xc %*% E$vectors does all samples and both PCs at once — column 1 is the PC1 scores.









Hint 6 — loadings vs scores





Loadings are the eigenvector entries (one weight per gene) — they describe how genes combine to build the PC. Scores are per-sample projections — where samples land. Same eigenvector, two readings: down the vector (loadings, genes) vs dotting a sample against it (scores, samples).









Hint 7 — variance explained





Divide each eigenvalue by the sum of all eigenvalues: \(\lambda_k/\sum_j\lambda_j\). The sum of eigenvalues equals the trace of \(C\) (sum of the diagonal, sum(diag(C))), which is the total variance — so the fractions are guaranteed to add to 1.

text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. Means: \(\bar A = (1+3+4+5+7)/5 = 20/5 = 4\) and \(\bar B = (5+3+6+7+9)/5 = 30/5 = 6\). Centred data (subtract the column mean):

Column sums: \(-3-1+0+1+3 = 0\) and \(-1-3+0+1+3 = 0\) ✓. We centre because PCA describes variation around the mean. If we skip it, the leading direction is pulled toward the data’s centroid (the mean vector) instead of lying along the direction of greatest spread — so PC1 would partly encode where the cloud sits, not how it is shaped (see B8).
B2. With divisor \(n-1 = 4\): \[\text{var}(A) = \tfrac14\big[(-3)^2+(-1)^2+0^2+1^2+3^2\big] = \tfrac14(9+1+0+1+9) = \tfrac{20}{4} = 5.\] \[\text{var}(B) = \tfrac14\big[(-1)^2+(-3)^2+0^2+1^2+3^2\big] = \tfrac14(1+9+0+1+9) = \tfrac{20}{4} = 5.\] \[\text{cov}(A,B) = \tfrac14\big[(-3)(-1)+(-1)(-3)+0+(1)(1)+(3)(3)\big] = \tfrac14(3+3+0+1+9) = \tfrac{16}{4} = 4.\] \[C = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}.\] Symmetric (\(C_{12}=C_{21}=4\)) ✓.
B3. \(C\) has the symmetric pattern with \(a=5\), \(b=4\): \(C(1,1) = (5+4,\ 4+5) = (9,9) = 9\,(1,1)\) and \(C(1,-1) = (5-4,\ 4-5) = (1,-1)\). Hence \(\lambda_1 = 9\) and \(\lambda_2 = 1\). Check: trace \(5+5 = 10 = 9+1\) ✓. (Bonus, not for exam: \(\det(C-\lambda I) = (5-\lambda)^2 - 16 = 0\) gives \(5-\lambda = \pm 4\), the same eigenvalues, and their product \(9 = \det C = 25-16\).)
B4. For \(\lambda_1 = 9\): \(C-9I = \begin{pmatrix}-4 & 4\\ 4 & -4\end{pmatrix}\); row 1 gives \(-4v_1+4v_2=0 \Rightarrow v_2=v_1\), so \((1,1)\). Unit version: \(\mathbf u_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1) \approx (0.707, 0.707)\). For \(\lambda_2 = 1\): \(C-I = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 4\\ 4 & 4\end{pmatrix}\); row 1 gives \(v_1+v_2=0 \Rightarrow v_2=-v_1\), so \((1,-1)\). Unit version: \(\mathbf u_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1) \approx (0.707,-0.707)\). Orthogonal: \(\mathbf u_1\cdot\mathbf u_2 = \tfrac12[(1)(1)+(1)(-1)] = 0\) ✓. \(\mathbf u_1\) (largest eigenvalue, \(\lambda=9\)) is PC1; it points along the \(45^\circ\) long axis of the cloud.
B5. PC1 score of a centred sample \(\mathbf x\) is \(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf u_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(x_A + x_B)\):









sample
centred \((x_A,x_B)\)
\(x_A+x_B\)
PC1 score \(=\frac{x_A+x_B}{\sqrt2}\)




s1
\((-3,-1)\)
\(-4\)
\(-2.83\)


s2
\((-1,-3)\)
\(-4\)
\(-2.83\)


s3
\((0,0)\)
\(0\)
\(0\)


s4
\((1,1)\)
\(2\)
\(1.41\)


s5
