\(6\)
\(4.24\)



Sample s5 sits at the high end of PC1; s1 and s2 are tied at the low end. So PC1 orders the samples from low overall A+B expression to high.
B6. PC1 loadings are the entries of \(\mathbf u_1 = (0.707, 0.707)\) — one weight per gene. Both genes have the same loading, so PC1 is (proportional to) \(A+B\): the two genes contribute equally. Biologically this reflects that A and B rise and fall together (strong positive covariance), so the main axis of variation is their shared programme, weighting both genes alike.
B7. Total variance \(= \lambda_1+\lambda_2 = 9+1 = 10\), which equals the trace \(5+5\). \[\text{PC1}: \frac{9}{10} = 0.9 = 90\%, \qquad \text{PC2}: \frac{1}{10} = 0.1 = 10\%.\] They sum to \(1\) ✓, and the denominator \(10\) is the trace of \(C\) ✓. PC1 alone captures 90% of the variation, so a one-number-per-sample (PC1 score) summary keeps most of the signal.
B8. Variance measures spread about the mean. If the data are not centred, the sum of squares is taken about the origin, not the centroid, so the direction that “explains the most” is dominated by the offset of the whole cloud from the origin — it points roughly from the origin to the mean of the data. Centring removes that offset so the leading direction reflects the shape of the cloud (how it is stretched) rather than its location.
R1–R4. The R blocks reproduce every hand result:
X <- matrix(c(1,5, 3,3, 4,6, 5,7, 7,9), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
Xc <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
C  <- cov(Xc)
C                            # matches B2:  [[5,4],[4,5]]

E <- eigen(C)
E$values                     # 9 1        -> matches B3
E$vectors                    # +/-(0.707,0.707), (0.707,-0.707)  -> matches B4 (up to sign)

scores <- Xc %*% E$vectors
scores[, 1]                  # PC1 scores -> matches B5 (up to overall sign)

E$values / sum(E$values)     # 0.9 0.1    -> matches B7
sum(E$values); sum(diag(C))  # 10 and 10  -> total variance = trace
If eigen reports the PC1 eigenvector as \((-0.707,-0.707)\), that is the same axis as \((0.707,0.707)\) with the sign flipped, and every PC1 score flips sign with it — the geometry (ordering, separation, variance explained) is unchanged.

title: Exercise: principal component analysis
text:
Where this leads

PCA in R: prcomp does the centring, optional scaling (scale. = TRUE), and eigen-decomposition in a single call, returning scores ($x), loadings ($rotation), and standard deviations ($sdev, whose squares are the eigenvalues). Everything you computed by hand here is one function call there.
Scaling and the correlation matrix: running PCA with scaling is the same as eigen-decomposing the correlation matrix instead of the covariance matrix — the right choice when variables are on different units.
Larger data: for wide \(p \gg n\) omics matrices, PCA is computed via the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the data matrix rather than by forming a huge \(p\times p\) covariance matrix — same principal components, a faster route.

title: Quiz: principal component analysis
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of the concept of PCA. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Several are written in the style of the on-campus exam (no computer). Throughout, PCA means the eigen-decomposition of the (centred) data’s covariance matrix.

Q1. In one sentence, what is a principal component, in terms of the covariance matrix?






Hint





Which matrix do we diagonalise, and what are its eigenvectors?









Answer





A principal component is an eigenvector of the covariance matrix — a direction in variable space. PC1 is the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue (the direction of greatest variance), and successive PCs are the next eigenvectors, orthogonal to the earlier ones.




Q2. Why are the principal components guaranteed to be orthogonal (perpendicular) to each other?






Hint





What special property does the covariance matrix have, and what did the eigen unit prove about such matrices?









Answer





The covariance matrix is symmetric (\(\text{cov}(g_i,g_j)=\text{cov}(g_j,g_i)\)). By the spectral theorem (from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors), a symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors — so the PCs are automatically perpendicular.




Q3. What does the eigenvalue of a principal component represent, biologically and numerically?






Hint





Think about spread along that direction.









Answer





The eigenvalue is the variance captured along that PC — how much the samples spread out in that direction. A large eigenvalue means the samples vary a lot along that axis; a small one means they barely move along it. Eigenvalues are non-negative because variances cannot be negative.




Q4. What is the difference between a score and a loading?






Hint





One is per sample, the other is per gene. Both come from the same eigenvector.









Answer





A score is a per-sample number: the projection (dot product) of a centred sample onto a PC — where that sample lands along the axis. A loading is a per-gene number: an entry of the eigenvector — how much that gene contributes to the PC. Scores describe samples; loadings describe genes.




Q5. A covariance matrix has eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = 12\), \(\lambda_2 = 6\), \(\lambda_3 = 2\). What fraction of the total variance does PC1 explain?






Hint





Variance explained by PC\(_k\) is \(\lambda_k\) divided by the sum of all eigenvalues.









Answer





Total variance \(= 12+6+2 = 20\). PC1 explains \(12/20 = 0.6 = \mathbf{60\%}\). (PC2: \(6/20=30\%\); PC3: \(2/20=10\%\); they sum to 100%.)




Q6. Why must you centre the data before running PCA? What tends to happen to PC1 if you forget?






Hint





Variance is spread about the mean. What is spread measured about if you don’t centre?









Answer





PCA describes variation about the mean, so we subtract each variable’s mean first. If you skip centring, spread is measured about the origin, and PC1 is pulled toward the direction from the origin to the data’s centroid — it encodes where the cloud sits rather than how it is shaped.




Q7. You have two variables: gene expression measured in the thousands, and a pH measured between 6 and 8. If you run PCA on the raw covariance matrix, which variable dominates PC1, and how do you fix an unwanted dominance?






Hint





Larger numeric range means larger variance. What does dividing each variable by its standard deviation do?









Answer





The gene (huge numeric range → huge variance) dominates PC1 purely because of its units, not its biology. Fix it by scaling: divide each variable by its standard deviation so every variable has variance 1 (equivalently, run PCA on the correlation matrix instead of the covariance matrix), giving each variable an equal say.




Q8. PCA is unsupervised. Give one consequence of that: what is not guaranteed about PC1?






Hint





PCA optimises variance and never sees the sample labels.









Answer





Because PCA maximises variance without using labels, PC1 is the direction of greatest variation, which is not guaranteed to be the biologically interesting axis. The largest source of variance might be a batch effect or a technical artefact. Always colour the PCA plot by known covariates (condition, batch) to interpret what each PC actually represents.




Q9. True or false: rotating the data onto the principal component axes throws away information. Explain.






Hint





Distinguish rotating the axes from keeping only the first few PCs.









Answer





False — the rotation itself is loss-less: keeping all the PCs is just the same points described in a new, rotated coordinate system. Information is only discarded when you truncate — keep the first few PCs and drop the rest — which is the (approximate) dimension-reduction step, separate from the (exact) rotation.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
text:
About this lecture
In Ridge, lasso & elastic net you learned what a penalty does, and in Cross-validation & model selection you learned how to tune it. Today we put a penalized model to work on a real biological question and, crucially, stare hard at how it can mislead us.

Identifiability: when predictors are correlated (as biological features almost always are), the lasso picks one member of a correlated group more or less arbitrarily — and the choice flips under tiny data changes.
Stability selection: a resampling idea that turns an unstable one-shot selection into a selection frequency you can trust.
Interpretation: a selected gene is a predictor, not proven causal. Coefficients are shrunk and biased; naive p-values after selection are invalid.
Reporting: what an honest methods paragraph must state so the analysis is reproducible.







Note


Provisional block. Penalized linear models may move to a later statistics / machine-learning course. Treat this unit as a first pass; the depth and placement are still being decided.




This is a judgement day, not a formula day. The students can already fit and tune a penalized model; the gap we close is scepticism about what the output means. Two threads run in parallel: a constructive one (stability selection to get a trustworthy variable list) and a cautionary one (why the single fitted model over-claims). Nothing executes at render time — all R here is for reading. Reference earlier units by name (Ridge, lasso & elastic net; Cross-validation & model selection; Penalties as Bayesian priors) rather than by day. Keep hammering the course principle: every method idea is tied to a concrete biological problem.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
section: The biology: predict drug response from expression
text:
The biology: predict drug response from expression
A pharmacogenomics study measures, for 80 cancer cell lines:

gene expression for ~18,000 genes (a samples × genes matrix), and
sensitivity to a drug, summarised as a continuous \(\log \text{IC}_{50}\) (lower = more sensitive).

The question: which genes predict drug response, and can we build a compact predictive signature?

Far more genes (\(p \approx 18{,}000\)) than samples (\(n = 80\)) — the classic \(p \gg n\) regime. Ordinary lm cannot even be fit uniquely.
A penalty makes the problem solvable and hands us a sparse shortlist. This is exactly the job the lasso was built for.



Ground the whole lecture in one concrete dataset and keep coming back to it. The \(p \gg n\) point is essential: with more genes than samples the design matrix has no unique least-squares solution, so a penalty is not a nicety, it is what makes the problem well-posed at all. This connects straight back to Why penalize: overfitting & identifiability. Frame the deliverable the biologists actually want: a short, interpretable gene signature — which is precisely where the pitfalls bite, because “short and interpretable” tempts over-interpretation.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
section: Recap: the model we are fitting
text:
Recap: the model we are fitting
We fit a penalized linear model. For the lasso (\(L_1\) penalty):
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - \beta_0 - \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta\big)^2}_{\text{fit to the data}} \;+\; \underbrace{\lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|}_{L_1\text{ penalty}}\]

\(\lambda\) (chosen by cross-validation) sets how hard we shrink; larger \(\lambda\) → more coefficients driven exactly to zero → sparser signature.
Predictors are standardized before fitting so the penalty treats every gene on the same scale (glmnet does this internally by default).

library(glmnet)
x <- as.matrix(expr)          # 80 samples x 18000 genes
y <- logIC50                  # length-80 response

fit <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1, standardize = TRUE, nfolds = 10)
coef(fit, s = "lambda.1se")   # sparse: most genes have coefficient 0


A one-slide refresher so the case is self-contained. Two things to stress. First, standardization: the \(L_1\) penalty is scale-dependent, so genes must be put on a common scale or the penalty silently favours high-variance genes; glmnet standardizes internally and reports coefficients back on the original scale. Second, alpha = 1 is the lasso; we will vary alpha shortly. lambda.1se (the largest lambda within one standard error of the CV minimum) gives a sparser, more stable model than lambda.min — a point from Cross-validation & model selection we will lean on again.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
section: The trap: biological predictors are correlated
text:
The trap: biological predictors are correlated
Genes do not vary independently. They travel in co-regulated groups:

genes in the same pathway or co-expression module rise and fall together,
members of a protein complex are transcriptionally coupled,
a cell-type proportion shift moves hundreds of marker genes in lockstep.

So the design matrix has whole blocks of highly correlated columns — often \(r > 0.9\).
This is not a data-quality problem to be cleaned away. Co-regulation is the biology. And it is precisely what makes variable selection unstable.


This slide reframes correlation from “nuisance” to “the signal”. Biologists intuitively know genes co-vary — that is the whole basis of pathways and modules — but they may not connect it to why a selection method misbehaves. Make the link explicit: co-expression means the columns of X are near-duplicates, and near-duplicate predictors are mathematically hard to tell apart. Everything on the next few slides follows from this one fact. Foreshadow: the lasso is forced to choose among interchangeable columns.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
section: Identifiability: why the lasso picks just one
text:
Identifiability: why the lasso picks just one
Suppose genes \(A\) and \(B\) are almost perfectly correlated and each truly relates to the response.

To the fit, \(\beta_A x_A + \beta_B x_B\) with \(x_A \approx x_B\) is almost the same as putting all the weight on \(A\), or all on \(B\), or splitting it.
The \(L_1\) penalty \(|\beta_A| + |\beta_B|\) is smallest when the weight sits on one predictor, not split — so the lasso concentrates on a single member and zeros the rest.
Which one? Whichever has a hair more correlation with \(y\) in this particular sample. That tie-break is essentially noise.

The model’s predictions are fine. The selected gene list is not identifiable: a different sample would pick \(B\) instead of \(A\).


This is the conceptual heart of the lecture. Walk the geometry verbally: with two collinear columns the loss surface has a long flat valley (many coefficient combinations fit equally well), and the L1 penalty’s diamond geometry snaps the solution to a corner — a single nonzero coefficient. The choice of corner is decided by a vanishingly small difference in sample correlation, i.e. by noise. The key distinction to leave them with: prediction is stable, selection is not. Students routinely conflate “the model predicts well” with “these are the important genes” — that conflation is the error this whole lecture attacks.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
section: Watch it happen: same data, tiny perturbation
text:
Watch it happen: same data, tiny perturbation
Fit the lasso, then refit after dropping a single cell line, and compare which genes survive:
sel <- function(cvfit) which(as.vector(coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.1se"))[-1] != 0)

set.seed(1)
fit_all  <- cv.glmnet(x,        y,        alpha = 1)
fit_drop <- cv.glmnet(x[-1, ],  y[-1],    alpha = 1)   # drop one sample

colnames(x)[sel(fit_all)]
#> [1] "MKI67"  "TYMS"   "ABCB1"   ...
colnames(x)[sel(fit_drop)]
#> [1] "PCNA"   "TYMS"   "ABCB1"   ...   # MKI67 out, PCNA in
MKI67 and PCNA are both proliferation markers — near-interchangeable columns. The lasso swapped one for the other on a one-sample change. Re-run with a different set.seed and the list shifts again.

Make the instability visceral. The output is illustrative (nothing runs), but it mirrors exactly what students see in the exercise: dropping one sample, or changing the CV seed, swaps members within a correlated module. The punchline biology: MKI67 and PCNA are both textbook proliferation markers, so swapping them changes nothing biologically — yet a naive reader of “the selected genes” would report a different signature each time. Warn them that this is not a bug in glmnet; it is the correct behaviour of L1 selection on correlated data. The fix is not a better single fit but a different question: how often is each gene selected?

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
section: Ridge and elastic net handle groups differently
text:
Ridge and elastic net handle groups differently
The three penalties treat a correlated group in three distinct ways:








Penalty
alpha
Correlated group behaviour




Ridge (\(L_2\))
0
keeps all members, shrinks them together, splits the weight


Lasso (\(L_1\))
1
keeps one, zeros the rest (unstable choice)


Elastic net
\(0<\alpha<1\)
grouping effect: correlated members tend to enter or leave together




Ridge never gives you a short list (nothing is exactly zero) but its coefficients are stable.
Elastic net is the usual compromise for omics: sparse and it keeps co-regulated genes as a group rather than picking a lone representative.

fit_enet <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0.5)   # a middle ground; tune alpha too


Position this as the menu of trade-offs, not a winner. Ridge: stable coefficients, no selection — good when you want a predictor and do not need a short list. Lasso: maximal sparsity, unstable membership. Elastic net (Zou & Hastie’s grouping effect): the practical default for correlated omics because it retains groups. Note honestly that alpha is a second tuning parameter — you cross-validate over it too, which costs you some of the tidiness. Tie back to Ridge, lasso & elastic net for the geometry; today we only care about the consequence for a correlated design.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
section: Try it: which gene does the lasso keep?
text:
Try it: which gene does the lasso keep?




Two co-expressed genes with correlation 0.9: the RSS contours are long thin ellipses lying along the valley where beta-1 + beta-2 is roughly constant, so many splits of the weight fit almost equally well. With the lasso at lambda = 2.5, the solution sits on the corner of the diamond: gene 1 is kept and gene 2 is exactly zero (red mark). Now drag the OLS point along the valley to about (0.5, 1.5): the choice flips to gene 2. Point out that with highly correlated genes the OLS point itself moves a lot along that valley from one sample to the next, so this drag is what dropping a single cell line can do; it is the MKI67/PCNA swap from the previous slides. Then click Ridge: both genes are kept with nearly equal, shrunk weights, and the drag barely changes them. Elastic net (alpha = 0.5) also keeps both, close to equal: the grouping effect. This sets up the question stability selection answers next: how often is each gene picked?

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
text:
Stability selection: the idea
If one fit is unstable, don’t trust one fit. Resample and count.

Draw many subsamples of the data (e.g. 100 random halves of the cell lines).
Refit the lasso on each subsample.
For each gene, record the fraction of subsamples in which it was selected — its selection frequency \(\pi_j \in [0,1]\).
Keep the genes whose frequency clears a threshold (e.g. \(\pi_j \ge 0.6\)).


A gene selected in 90 of 100 subsamples is a robust finding.
A gene selected in 8 of 100 was a coin-flip winner in one particular sample — discard it.

This converts a fragile yes/no into a graded, reproducible shortlist.


Give credit lightly: this is the stability-selection idea of Meinshausen and Bühlmann. The mental model is a democratic vote across resamples rather than a single verdict. The crucial reframing: we stop asking “which genes does the lasso select?” (unstable) and start asking “which genes does the lasso select reliably?” (stable). For a correlated module, expect the vote to spread across its members — that itself is informative: it tells you the module matters even when no single gene dominates. Threshold choice (0.6, 0.8) is a judgement call to be reported, echoing the “no rule is a law” theme from Choosing components & pitfalls.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
text:
Stability selection in R
set.seed(1)
B <- 100
n <- nrow(x); p <- ncol(x)
counts <- integer(p)

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  idx  <- sample(n, floor(n / 2))            # a random half of the samples
  fb   <- cv.glmnet(x[idx, ], y[idx], alpha = 1)
  beta <- as.vector(coef(fb, s = "lambda.1se"))[-1]   # drop intercept
  counts <- counts + as.integer(beta != 0)   # tally each gene's selection
}

freq        <- counts / B                     # selection frequency in [0, 1]
names(freq) <- colnames(x)
stable      <- sort(freq[freq >= 0.6], decreasing = TRUE)
stable
#>  TYMS  ABCB1   ...
#>  0.94   0.88   ...
TYMS and ABCB1 are robust; the proliferation markers PCNA/MKI67 each sit near 0.5 — split within one module, exactly as expected.

Read the loop aloud: subsample half the cell lines, refit lasso with its own inner cross-validation, mark which genes survived, tally. The result is a frequency per gene. This is a static illustration but structurally identical to what they build in the exercise; keep B small in class for speed and note that real use wants B in the hundreds. Point at the output interpretation: high-frequency genes are keepers; the proliferation pair splitting near 0.5 is the module-splitting phenomenon, not a failure. Mention set.seed for reproducibility — resampling methods must be seeded or results are not repeatable, which matters for the reporting slide.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
text:
Reading the selection-frequency plot
Plot every gene’s selection frequency, sorted:
barplot(sort(freq, decreasing = TRUE)[1:30],
        las = 2, ylab = "selection frequency")
abline(h = 0.6, col = "red", lty = 2)        # the reporting threshold
What to look for:

A clear gap between a handful of high-frequency genes and a long low-frequency tail → a defensible signature.
No gap, everything smeared around 0.3–0.5 → the data cannot support a stable signature; say so rather than forcing one.
Several correlated genes all at moderate frequency → report the module, not a single “top” gene.



Teach them to read the shape, the way the scree plot was read in Choosing components & pitfalls — look for an elbow / gap. A big gap licenses a confident shortlist; a smeared distribution is the data telling you it is underpowered for selection, and the honest move is to report that limitation, not to lower the threshold until you get a story. The “report the module” advice is the biologically literate response to the identifiability problem: if five complex members all sit at 0.5, the biology is “this complex matters”, not “gene X matters”. This is where quantitative humility and biological insight meet.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
text:
Selected does not mean causal
A gene in your signature earned its place by predicting \(y\). That is weaker than it sounds:

It may be a proxy — correlated with the true driver but not itself functional (the interchangeable-module problem again).
It may be a downstream consequence of the phenotype, not a cause (reverse direction).
It may be a confounder marker — e.g. it tracks tumour purity or a batch, and drug response also tracks that; the gene rides the confounder.

Prediction is about association in this data. Causation needs perturbation (knockdown/knockout, CRISPR screens) or a proper causal design. A penalized fit supplies hypotheses, not conclusions.


This is the interpretation slide that matters most for a biology audience, because the temptation to read a coefficient as a mechanism is enormous. Give the three failure modes concrete handles: proxy (correlated non-functional gene), reverse causation (the phenotype changes the transcriptome), and confounding (purity/batch drives both predictor and response). The constructive close: the right role of a penalized model is hypothesis generation; the shortlist is a ranked list of things to test at the bench. Never let a lasso coefficient stand in for a validation experiment.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
text:
The coefficients themselves are biased
Even for genes you keep, be careful reading the numbers:

Shrinkage pulls every coefficient toward zero on purpose. The magnitudes are biased low — they are not unbiased effect sizes, and comparing their sizes across genes is fraught.
The sign is usually trustworthy for strongly selected genes, but a small coefficient’s sign can flip between resamples.
Do not report naive lm-style p-values or confidence intervals for the selected coefficients. Selecting and then testing on the same data invalidates the standard errors (this is post-selection inference; it needs specialised methods, not summary(lm(...))).

Report: which genes are stably selected, their sign, and their predictive performance — not a table of “significant” effect sizes.


Two distinct cautions. First, shrinkage bias: the penalty deliberately trades bias for variance, so coefficients are systematically shrunk — they rank predictors but are not clean effect sizes, and glmnet coefficients should never be reported as if from an unbiased regression. Second, and more serious, is the double-use-of-data problem: choosing variables by lasso and then computing p-values for them on the same data gives anticonservative, meaningless p-values. Name post-selection / selective inference as the honest remedy but keep it out of scope. The practical instruction is concrete: report stable selection + sign + held-out predictive performance, not a significance table. This connects to the frequentist-vs-Bayesian and MAP framing from Penalties as Bayesian priors — the penalty is a prior, not a hypothesis test.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
text:
A checklist of quieter pitfalls

Data leakage. Any step that peeks at \(y\) — pre-filtering genes by correlation with the response, or standardizing using the whole dataset — must live inside the cross-validation loop, never before it. Leakage inflates performance.
lambda.min vs lambda.1se. lambda.min predicts marginally better; lambda.1se is sparser and more stable — usually the better choice when the goal is an interpretable signature.
Unscaled predictors. If you switch off standardization, the penalty favours high-variance genes for the wrong reason. Keep standardize = TRUE unless you have a specific reason.
Ignoring the CV seed. Cross-validation folds and subsampling are random; set and report a seed, and check the result is not knife-edge dependent on it.


A grab-bag of the mistakes that silently break a penalized analysis. Leakage is the biggest and most common: any supervised preprocessing (filtering genes by their correlation with y, or scaling with statistics computed on all the data) done outside the CV fold leaks label information and produces optimistic, irreproducible performance — this is the single error most likely to embarrass them in a paper. The lambda.min/lambda.1se point recurs from Cross-validation & model selection. The seed point ties back to stability selection: randomness that is not seeded is not reproducible. Keep this slide as a scannable checklist they can return to.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
text:
Putting it together: the mini-case
A defensible pharmacogenomics workflow for the drug-response question:

Assemble the standardized samples × genes matrix and the \(\log\text{IC}_{50}\) response; keep all preprocessing inside the CV.
Fit elastic net (cv.glmnet, tune both \(\alpha\) and \(\lambda\)) for prediction; report held-out performance honestly.
Run stability selection (subsample + refit) to get selection frequencies; report genes above a stated threshold, and report modules where a group splits.
Read the shortlist as hypotheses: cross-reference known pathways, then propose perturbation experiments to test causality.
Write a methods paragraph stating: standardization, \(\alpha\)/\(\lambda\) choice and rule (lambda.1se), CV scheme, resampling count \(B\), threshold, and seed.



This is the synthesis: the whole lecture assembled into a workflow the students could actually run. Emphasise the split of duties — elastic net for the predictor, stability selection for the interpretable gene list; these answer different questions and should not be conflated. Step 4 is where biology re-enters: the shortlist meets pathway knowledge and becomes an experimental plan. Step 5 is the reporting discipline that makes the analysis reproducible; walk through each item they must state. This mirrors the structure of the exercise, so it doubles as a preview.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
section: Reporting: what an honest methods paragraph states
text:
Reporting: what an honest methods paragraph states
Everything a reader needs to reproduce and trust the analysis:







Item
Example




Preprocessing
genes standardized inside CV; log-response


Model & tuning
elastic net; \(\alpha=0.5\); \(\lambda\) = lambda.1se by 10-fold CV


Selection method
stability selection, \(B=100\) half-subsamples, threshold \(\pi \ge 0.6\)


Performance
held-out \(R^2\) on an untouched test set (not the CV used for tuning)


Reproducibility
random seed, package versions, code available


Interpretation stance
signature = predictive hypotheses, not causal effects



The last row is not boilerplate — it is the sentence that stops a reader over-reading your coefficients.

Reporting is a first-class scientific skill, not an afterthought. The table is the deliverable students should be able to produce for their own analyses. Two things to underline: performance must be reported on data untouched by tuning (the CV used to pick lambda cannot also certify performance — that needs a held-out set or nested CV), and the interpretation-stance sentence explicitly caps what the reader may conclude. Tell them that reviewers increasingly demand exactly this level of detail, and that omitting the seed or the threshold makes an analysis unreproducible by definition. Good reporting is what separates a hypothesis-generating result from noise dressed as discovery.

title: Case analysis & pitfalls
text:
Summary







Idea
Take-home




Correlated predictors
biology is correlated (pathways, modules) — expect it


Identifiability
lasso picks one of a correlated group, near-arbitrarily


Ridge / elastic net
ridge keeps groups together but never sparse; elastic net = sparse + grouping


Stability selection
subsample + refit + count → a selection frequency you can trust


Selected ≠ causal
proxies, reverse causation, confounders — validate by perturbation


Coefficients
shrunk and biased; no naive post-selection p-values


Reporting
state standardization, \(\alpha/\lambda\) rule, CV, \(B\), threshold, seed



A penalized model is a superb hypothesis generator and a stable predictor. It is not, by itself, a discovery of the genes that matter — that claim needs stability, then the bench.

The summary is the exam-and-life cheat-sheet. Drill the one distinction that ties the whole lecture together: prediction is stable, single-shot selection is not, and stability selection is how you recover a trustworthy list. Reiterate that a selected gene is a hypothesis awaiting perturbation, that coefficients are biased and not testable naively, and that reproducible reporting is non-negotiable. Close by reminding them this block is provisional and may migrate to a later stats/ML course — but the scepticism it teaches (a model that fits well can still mislead about mechanism) generalises far beyond penalized regression.

title: Why penalize?
text:
About this lecture







Provisional block


This block is provisional. Depending on how the syllabus settles, “Penalized linear models” may move to a later statistics / machine-learning course. Treat it as a bridge from the linear-algebra block into modelling, not as a fixed exam topic.




In the linear-algebra block we learned how to solve a linear system and when a solution is unique. Today we ask a harder question: what do we do when the honest least-squares answer is either impossible to compute or untrustworthy?

Why fitting many genes from few samples (p ≫ n) breaks ordinary least squares.
The bias–variance tradeoff: why the “best fit to this data” is often a bad predictor.
The core idea of penalization — pay a price for large coefficients to buy stability.
This is a concept day: no formulas to grind, one idea to internalise.


This is the motivation lecture for the whole penalized-models block. The single message: ordinary least squares assumes you have more samples than parameters and that the parameters are well-determined. In genomics that assumption is routinely violated — thousands of genes, dozens of samples. When it breaks, we do not get a slightly worse answer, we get no unique answer at all, or a wildly overfit one. Penalization is the fix. Keep it conceptual today; the ridge and lasso mechanics come in later units. Flag the provisional status honestly so students know where this sits.

title: Why penalize?
text:
A biology picture first
A typical transcriptomics experiment: measure the expression of 20,000 genes across 30 patients, and predict a clinical outcome (say, drug response) from expression.

Each patient is one row; each gene is one column (a predictor).
You want a linear model: outcome \(\approx \beta_1 g_1 + \beta_2 g_2 + \dots + \beta_p g_p\).
You have 30 equations (patients) but 20,000 unknowns (the \(\beta\)’s).

There are vastly more predictors than samples. This is the defining shape of omics data, and ordinary regression was never designed for it.


Anchor the abstraction in the standard omics shape before any math: the data matrix is wide and short. In the statistics they have seen (the linear-models material with lm), n was always comfortably larger than the number of predictors. Here it inverts. Stress that this is not an exotic edge case — it is the normal situation in gene expression, methylation, proteomics. The whole block exists because classical regression assumes the opposite shape. Do not define p and n formally yet; just plant “more genes than patients.”

title: Why penalize?
text:
Recall: the linear model
A linear model predicts an outcome \(y\) from predictors as a weighted sum:
\[y \approx \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_p x_p\]
Stacked over all \(n\) samples, this is a matrix equation:
\[\mathbf{y} \approx X\boldsymbol{\beta}\]

\(\mathbf{y}\): the outcome, one number per sample (\(n\) long).
\(X\): the design matrix, \(n\) rows (samples) × \(p\) columns (predictors).
\(\boldsymbol{\beta}\): the coefficients we want to learn (\(p\) long).

You have used this as lm() in the statistics block. Today we look underneath it.


Reconnect to what they already know: lm() fits exactly this. The novelty is not the model but the linear-algebra view of it — y is approximately X times beta, a single matrix equation. This links straight back to the Linear systems units: fitting a linear model is solving (a best-fit version of) a linear system. Keep the notation light; the point is only to set up X, beta, y so the next slide can talk about what “solve” means here.

title: Why penalize?
text:
What least squares wants
We can’t hit \(\mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol{\beta}\) exactly (data is noisy), so ordinary least squares (OLS) picks the \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) that makes the total squared error smallest:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \ \|\mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2\]
Working this out gives the normal equations:
\[X^\top X\,\boldsymbol{\beta} = X^\top \mathbf{y} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}\]
Everything hinges on that inverse: we can only solve for \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) if \(X^\top X\) is invertible.


State the least-squares objective in words: find the coefficients that minimise the total squared gap between prediction and truth. Don’t derive the normal equations — just present them and point at the single load-bearing object, the matrix X-transpose-X (a p by p matrix), and its inverse. The entire rest of the lecture is about when that inverse fails to exist or is untrustworthy. Students met invertibility and singular matrices in the Linear systems units and eigenvalues; lean on that vocabulary: a matrix you cannot invert is singular.

title: Why penalize?
section: When p > n, the inverse does not exist
text:
When p > n, the inverse does not exist
\(X^\top X\) is a \(p \times p\) matrix, but it is built from only \(n\) samples. A basic fact of linear algebra:
\[\text{rank}(X^\top X) \le n\]
So when \(p > n\) (more genes than patients), \(X^\top X\) is a \(p\times p\) matrix of rank at most \(n < p\) — it is singular. It has no inverse.

There is no unique least-squares solution — infinitely many \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) fit the data equally (perfectly) well.
The model is unidentifiable: the data cannot pin down the coefficients.



This is the hard failure mode, and it is pure linear algebra. X-transpose-X is p by p but its rank cannot exceed n, the number of samples. When p exceeds n the matrix is rank-deficient, hence singular, hence not invertible — the normal equations have no unique solution. Give the intuition: with more unknowns than constraints, infinitely many coefficient vectors reproduce y perfectly. Connect to the Linear systems picture of “infinitely many solutions” when there are fewer independent equations than unknowns. This is not “OLS does badly” — it literally cannot return one answer.

title: Why penalize?
section: Even when it inverts, it can be bad
text:
Even when it inverts, it can be bad
Suppose \(p < n\), so \(X^\top X\) is invertible. You are still not safe if predictors are correlated — which genes always are (co-regulated pathways, batch structure).

Correlated columns make \(X^\top X\) nearly singular (an eigenvalue close to 0).
Inverting a nearly-singular matrix amplifies noise: tiny changes in the data cause huge swings in \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\).
The fitted coefficients become large, unstable, and hard to interpret — often big positive and negative values that cancel.

This is multicollinearity, and in genomics it is the rule, not the exception.


The second, softer failure mode. Even with more samples than predictors, biology gives you highly correlated predictors — genes in the same pathway move together. Correlated columns push X-transpose-X toward singularity: one of its eigenvalues gets close to zero. Recall from the eigenvalue unit that a near-zero eigenvalue means the inverse blows up along that direction. The practical symptom is coefficients that are enormous and unstable — refit on a slightly different sample and they lurch. This motivates wanting to control coefficient size, which is exactly what penalization does.

title: Why penalize?
section: The real goal: prediction, not perfect fit
text:
The real goal: prediction, not perfect fit
It is tempting to want the \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) that fits this dataset best. But we almost never care about this dataset — we care about the next patient.

A model with enough free parameters can fit the training data perfectly, noise and all.
That model has learned the noise, not the biology — it overfits.
On new patients it predicts badly, because the noise it memorised won’t repeat.

The best fit to the data at hand is often the worst predictor of new data.


Reframe the objective. Beginners equate “best model” with “smallest error on my data.” That is exactly wrong for prediction. With enough flexibility you interpolate the training data perfectly, but you have fit the noise, and noise does not generalise. The classic picture: a high-degree polynomial threading every point versus a smooth line — the smooth line is worse on training data but better on new data. This slide sets up the bias–variance tradeoff, which names the tension formally.

title: Why penalize?
text:
The bias–variance tradeoff
Prediction error decomposes into two competing parts:

Bias — error from the model being too rigid to capture the true pattern. (Underfitting.)
Variance — error from the model being so flexible it chases noise, changing wildly from sample to sample. (Overfitting.)

\[\text{expected prediction error} \;=\; \text{bias}^2 \;+\; \text{variance} \;+\; \text{irreducible noise}\]
OLS with many predictors is a low-bias, high-variance machine: flexible enough to fit anything, so unstable it generalises poorly. We can often lower total error by accepting a little bias to cut variance a lot.


This is the conceptual heart of the lecture. Two sources of error pull in opposite directions. A too-simple model misses the real signal (bias); a too-flexible model fits noise and swings around (variance). Total expected error is their sum plus irreducible noise. The key insight that justifies everything downstream: you can trade a small increase in bias for a large decrease in variance and come out ahead on total error. OLS in high dimensions sits at the high-variance extreme, so there is lots of variance to trade away. Penalization is the knob that makes the trade.

title: Why penalize?
text:
The idea: penalize large coefficients
Instead of minimising only the fit error, add a penalty that grows with the size of the coefficients:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \ \underbrace{\|\mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2}_{\text{fit the data}} \;+\; \lambda\underbrace{\,\text{(size of }\boldsymbol{\beta}\text{)}}_{\text{stay small}}\]

The first term still rewards fitting the data.
The second term punishes large coefficients. \(\lambda \ge 0\) sets how hard.
The fit now has to justify every unit of coefficient it uses against the penalty.

We deliberately move away from the perfect-fit solution to buy stability.

Here is the whole idea in one equation, stated conceptually so the specific penalty (sum of squares for ridge, sum of absolute values for lasso) can come later. We augment the objective with a term that charges for coefficient magnitude. Lambda is the price. With lambda = 0 we are back to OLS; as lambda grows, coefficients are pulled toward zero. The intuition to leave them with: the model can no longer spend coefficient magnitude freely — it must earn each unit by improving the fit more than the penalty costs. That is what stops it from chasing noise.

title: Why penalize?
text:
What the penalty buys, geometrically
Two ways to see why shrinking coefficients helps:
It fixes the inverse. The penalized normal equations replace \(X^\top X\) with
\[X^\top X + \lambda I\]
Adding \(\lambda\) to the diagonal lifts every eigenvalue by \(\lambda > 0\), so the matrix is always invertible — even when \(p > n\). The unidentifiable problem becomes solvable.
It calms the variance. Shrinking coefficients toward zero makes them less sensitive to noise in any one sample. Estimates stop swinging.


Two payoffs, one from each failure mode. First, the hard failure: the penalized solution uses X-transpose-X plus lambda times the identity. Recall from the eigenvalue unit that adding lambda*I shifts every eigenvalue up by lambda; a matrix with all-positive eigenvalues is invertible. So the singular p > n case becomes solvable, and there is again a unique answer. Second, the soft failure: shrinking coefficients directly reduces variance — smaller, steadier coefficients that do not lurch when you resample. This slide ties the abstract penalty back to concrete linear algebra they already own.

title: Why penalize?
text:
The trade, made honest
Penalization is not free. By pulling coefficients toward zero we introduce bias: the estimates are systematically shrunk, so they no longer match the true values on average.

Small \(\lambda\): close to OLS — low bias, high variance (overfits).
Large \(\lambda\): heavy shrinkage — high bias, low variance (underfits, coefficients near 0).
Somewhere in between minimises total prediction error.

\[\text{penalty strength } \lambda \;\longleftrightarrow\; \text{the bias–variance dial}\]
Choosing \(\lambda\) well (e.g. by cross-validation, in a later unit) is the whole game.


Be honest about the cost, per the course’s “honest about what we defer” principle. Shrinkage biases the estimates — that is the price. So lambda is literally the bias–variance dial: turn it up and you move from the overfit OLS end toward the oversmoothed end. The sweet spot in the middle minimises total error. How to find it — cross-validation — is deferred to a later unit; name it, don’t teach it today. The takeaway: penalization does not magically improve everything; it lets you choose a better point on the tradeoff than OLS forces on you.

title: Why penalize?
text:
Biological payoff
Why this matters for the wide, short omics matrix we started with:

Solvable at all. With \(p \gg n\), penalization is what makes a gene-expression predictor computable in the first place.
Stable signatures. Shrinkage gives coefficients that don’t flip sign when you swap a few patients — reproducible gene signatures.
Better prediction on held-out patients, which is what a clinical model is for.
Some penalties select genes. One flavour (coming in a later unit) drives most coefficients exactly to zero, yielding a short, interpretable gene list.


Close the loop back to the opening biology. The four payoffs map onto real genomics needs: you can actually fit a model when p >> n; the resulting signatures are reproducible rather than an artifact of which patients you happened to sample; predictions generalise to new patients; and one penalty variant (lasso, named but deferred) performs feature selection, handing biologists a short gene list instead of twenty thousand tiny coefficients. Don’t teach lasso here — just promise it. This slide answers “why should a biologist care,” which is the course’s core pairing principle.

title: Why penalize?
text:
A first look in R
You have used lm() for ordinary least squares. Penalized models use glmnet, which fits along a whole range of \(\lambda\) at once:
# ordinary least squares -- fails or overfits when p >> n
fit_ols <- lm(response ~ ., data = expr)

# penalized regression (ridge / lasso) with glmnet
library(glmnet)
x <- as.matrix(expr[, genes])   # n samples x p genes
y <- expr$response

fit_pen <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0)   # alpha = 0 is ridge; alpha = 1 is lasso
Don’t worry about the details yet — later units unpack alpha, the \(\lambda\) path, and choosing \(\lambda\) by cross-validation. Today only the idea matters.

Show the tool at the horizon so the code is not a surprise later, but keep it static and unrun — no package is installed at render time, and today is conceptual. The one thing to register: lm() gives OLS; glmnet adds the penalty and fits many lambdas at once. Mention that alpha picks the penalty flavour (0 = ridge, 1 = lasso) without explaining the difference — that is a later unit. Reassure them the details come later; do not let them get lost in glmnet arguments today.

title: Why penalize?
section: Link back to the linear-algebra block
text:
Link back to the linear-algebra block
Everything today rested on machinery you already built:







From the linear-algebra block
Used here




Solving \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\), unique vs. infinite solutions
when OLS has no unique \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\)


Rank and singular matrices
why \(p>n\) makes \(X^\top X\) non-invertible


Matrix inverse
the normal equations \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}\)


Eigenvalues near zero
why correlated genes make the inverse explode


Adding \(\lambda I\) shifts eigenvalues up
why the penalty restores invertibility



Penalized regression is applied linear algebra with a statistical purpose.

Make the continuity explicit — this block is the payoff for the linear-algebra grind. Each row of the table is a concept they already learned, now doing real work. Rank and singularity explain the p > n breakdown; the inverse is the normal-equations solution; near-zero eigenvalues explain multicollinearity blow-up; the lambda*I eigenvalue shift explains the fix. Emphasise that they are not learning new linear algebra today, they are seeing why it mattered. Reference units by topic name, never by day number.

title: Why penalize?
text:
Summary







Idea
Takeaway




p ≫ n biology
omics has many genes, few samples


OLS solution
\(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}\) — needs an invertible \(X^\top X\)


Hard failure
\(p>n\) ⇒ \(X^\top X\) singular ⇒ no unique solution


Soft failure
correlated genes ⇒ near-singular ⇒ unstable, huge coefficients


Real goal
predict new patients, not fit this data perfectly


Bias–variance
trade a little bias for a large cut in variance


Penalize
add \(\lambda\cdot(\text{coefficient size})\) to the objective


The fix
\(X^\top X + \lambda I\) is always invertible; coefficients shrink & stabilise


The cost
shrinkage adds bias; \(\lambda\) is the dial, tuned later



Next in this block: the specific penalties — ridge and lasso — and how to choose \(\lambda\).

The summary is the whole argument in one table. Drill the storyline verbally one more time: omics is wide and short; OLS needs an invertible X-transpose-X; p > n makes it singular (hard failure) and correlated genes make it nearly singular (soft failure); we actually care about predicting new data, not fitting this data; the bias–variance tradeoff says we can trade bias for variance; penalization does exactly that by charging for coefficient size, which also restores invertibility via lambda*I. The cost is bias, controlled by lambda. Next units make the penalty concrete (ridge, lasso) and teach choosing lambda. Remind them the block is provisional.

title: Exercise: penalties as priors
text:
Provisional unit



This bridge unit links the penalized-regression and Bayesian blocks and may later move to a dedicated statistics / machine-learning course. It assumes you have already met ridge and lasso as optimisation and Bayes’ theorem (prior / likelihood / posterior).

title: Exercise: penalties as priors
text:
Goal
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

state, in one sentence, why a penalty is the same thing as a prior,
turn maximise posterior into minimise (negative log-likelihood + negative log-prior) and read off the fit term and the penalty term,
match ridge ⇔ Gaussian prior and lasso ⇔ Laplace prior, and derive each penalty from the prior’s density,
explain the identity \(\lambda_{\text{ridge}} = \sigma^2/\tau^2\) and what it says about prior precision,
explain, from the shape at \(\beta = 0\), why lasso produces exact zeros but ridge does not,
translate a biological belief (polygenic vs sparse) into the matching prior/penalty.

This is a concept day. Spend most of your time on the by-hand reasoning; the R section only illustrates the ideas (a full glmnet treatment lives in Ridge and lasso regression).

title: Exercise: penalties as priors
text:
Background
The bridge in one move. The posterior peak (the MAP estimate) is
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ p(\boldsymbol\beta\mid\text{data}) = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \big[\underbrace{-\log p(\text{data}\mid\boldsymbol\beta)}_{\text{fit term}} \;+\; \underbrace{-\log p(\boldsymbol\beta)}_{\text{penalty term}}\big].\]
(We may take \(-\log\) because the logarithm is increasing, so it does not move the location of the peak; it turns the product prior \(\times\) likelihood into a sum.)
The fit term. With Gaussian noise, \(y_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta + \varepsilon_i\), \(\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\), the negative log-likelihood is \(\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\,\text{RSS} + \text{const}\). So the fit term is just the residual sum of squares.
The penalty term is the negative log of whatever prior you place on the coefficients:










Prior on each \(\beta_j\)
density \(\propto\)
\(-\log\) prior \(\propto\)
Penalty
Method




Gaussian \(\mathcal N(0,\tau^2)\)
\(e^{-\beta_j^2/2\tau^2}\)
\(\sum_j \beta_j^2\)
\(\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2\)
ridge


Laplace (scale \(b\))
\(e^{-|\beta_j|/b}\)
\(\sum_j |\beta_j|\)
\(\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1\)
lasso



Clearing the \(\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\) from the fit term gives \(\lambda_{\text{ridge}} = \sigma^2/\tau^2\) and \(\lambda_{\text{lasso}} = 2\sigma^2/b\). In words: a large penalty is a tight, confident prior that effects are near zero.

title: Exercise: penalties as priors
text:
By hand
B1. In one sentence each, translate between the two languages: (a) what does the penalty term correspond to on the Bayesian side? (b) what does the fit term (RSS) correspond to? (c) what point summary of the posterior does penalised regression compute — the mean, the mode/peak, or the median?
B2. Starting from the Gaussian prior density \(p(\beta_j) \propto \exp\!\big(-\beta_j^2/2\tau^2\big)\), take \(-\log\) and sum over \(j\) to show the penalty term is \(\tfrac{1}{2\tau^2}\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2\) (up to a constant). Which method does this give?
B3. Do the same for the Laplace prior \(p(\beta_j) \propto \exp\!\big(-|\beta_j|/b\big)\): take \(-\log\), sum over \(j\), and read off the penalty. Which method does this give?
B4. Combine B2 with the Gaussian-noise fit term and show that \[\arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\text{RSS} + \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2 \;=\; \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \text{RSS} + \lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2\] and give \(\lambda\) in terms of \(\sigma^2\) and \(\tau^2\). (Hint: multiply the whole objective by a constant that does not change the minimiser.)
B5. (prior precision) Using \(\lambda_{\text{ridge}} = \sigma^2/\tau^2\): (a) Fix \(\sigma^2 = 1\). Compute \(\lambda\) for a tight prior \(\tau^2 = 0.01\) and for a loose prior \(\tau^2 = 100\). Which gives stronger shrinkage? (b) What happens to \(\lambda\) as \(\tau^2 \to \infty\) (a “flat”, no-information prior), and what familiar estimator do you recover?
B6. (why lasso zeros out) Sketch (or describe) the Gaussian and Laplace densities on the same axes, both centred at \(0\). Focus on the behaviour right at \(\beta = 0\). Which one has a sharp cusp there, and why does that cusp let the corresponding method set coefficients exactly to zero while the other only shrinks them?
B7. (biology → prior) For each biological situation, state whether a Gaussian (ridge) or Laplace (lasso) prior better encodes the belief, and say why in one line: (a) A complex, polygenic trait where hundreds of variants each nudge the phenotype a little. (b) A drug whose response is thought to be driven by two or three key genes, the other 19 997 being irrelevant. (c) You want to hand a wet-lab colleague a short, testable list of candidate genes. (d) Predictors are strongly correlated co-expressed genes and you would rather shrink them together than arbitrarily drop all but one. (Hint: think about which prior, or blend of priors, keeps correlated coefficients similar.)

title: Exercise: penalties as priors
text:
Explore: prior, likelihood and posterior
The demo shows two coefficients \((\beta_1,\beta_2)\). Green shading is the prior (darker = more prior belief), grey ellipses are the likelihood (centred on the OLS = maximum-likelihood point, which you can drag), purple contours are the posterior, and the purple dot is the posterior peak, the MAP, which is the penalized estimate. The demo fixes \(\sigma^2 = 1\), so the Gaussian prior has \(\tau^2 = 1/\lambda\) and the Laplace prior has \(b = 2/\lambda\). The right panel shows the MAP coefficients against \(\lambda\).



E1. With the Gaussian prior, move \(\lambda\) from \(0.1\) to \(10\). What happens to \(\tau^2\), to the prior shading and to the MAP? Which estimator do you approach as \(\lambda \to 0\) (compare B5)?
E2. Switch to the Laplace prior at \(\lambda = 2\). Where is the MAP, and is any coefficient exactly zero? Now lower \(\lambda\) to \(1\): is it still zero? What does that say about how strong the prior must be before it sets a coefficient to zero?
E3. Still with the Laplace prior at \(\lambda = 2\), look at the purple posterior contours where they cross the \(\beta_1\) axis. Are they smooth there, as they are for the Gaussian prior? Connect what you see to B6.






Solutions





E1. \(\tau^2 = 1/\lambda\) falls from \(10\) to \(0.1\): the prior circles shrink tightly around \(0\) (a more confident prior that effects are small). The MAP moves from close to the OLS point, about \((1.81, 0.61)\) at \(\lambda = 0.1\), to about \((0.20, 0.12)\) at \(\lambda = 10\): shrunk, but never exactly zero. As \(\lambda \to 0\) the prior becomes flat and the MAP becomes the OLS / maximum-likelihood estimate, as in B5(b).
E2. At \(\lambda = 2\) the MAP is about \((1.24, 0)\): it sits on the \(\beta_1\) axis and \(\hat\beta_2\) is exactly \(0\). At \(\lambda = 1\) it moves off the axis to about \((1.64, 0.24)\). The Laplace prior sets a coefficient to zero only once it is strong enough compared with the evidence for that coefficient (here from \(\lambda \approx 1.7\) on); weak effects are zeroed first, strong ones need a stronger prior.
E3. No: the Laplace posterior contours have a crease (a kink) along the axis, because the prior’s cusp at \(\beta = 0\) is carried into the posterior. The peak can sit right in that crease, which is why the MAP lands on exactly \(\beta_2 = 0\). The Gaussian prior is smooth at \(0\), so its posterior contours are smooth ellipses and their peak is almost never exactly on an axis (B6).

title: Exercise: penalties as priors
text:
In R
The code below only illustrates today’s concepts — the shapes of the two priors and the reading of a fit as a MAP estimate. (Running glmnet in earnest is the job of Ridge and lasso regression; here we keep it to a static illustration since packages are not run at render time.)

The two prior shapes
# Gaussian vs Laplace densities, both centred at 0, matched to unit variance.
b_grid <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 400)

gauss   <- dnorm(b_grid, mean = 0, sd = 1)          # Gaussian  N(0, 1)
laplace <- (1 / (2 * (1/sqrt(2)))) *                # Laplace, scale b = 1/sqrt(2)
           exp(-abs(b_grid) / (1/sqrt(2)))          #   -> also variance 1

plot(b_grid, laplace, type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "beta", ylab = "prior density")
lines(b_grid, gauss, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Laplace (lasso)", "Gaussian (ridge)"),
       lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2))
# Note the sharp CUSP of the Laplace at beta = 0  -> exact zeros (variable selection)
# vs the rounded top of the Gaussian            -> shrink but never exactly zero


The penalties are the negative log-priors
# Up to constants, the penalty term IS the negative log-prior.
neg_log_gauss   <- function(b, tau2 = 1) b^2 / (2 * tau2)   # -> ridge:  sum(beta^2)
neg_log_laplace <- function(b, bscale = 1) abs(b) / bscale  # -> lasso:  sum(|beta|)

neg_log_gauss(c(-2, 0, 2))    # 2 0 2      quadratic in beta
neg_log_laplace(c(-2, 0, 2))  # 2 0 2      linear in |beta|
# same values here by coincidence of inputs; the SHAPE differs (quadratic vs V-shaped)


Reading a glmnet call as a prior (illustration only)
library(glmnet)

# alpha selects the PRIOR SHAPE; lambda sets the PRIOR STRENGTH (precision).
fit_ridge <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0)     # Gaussian prior
fit_lasso <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)     # Laplace  prior
fit_enet  <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0.5)   # blend    -> elastic net

# Cross-validating lambda = letting the DATA choose how confident a prior to hold.
cvfit  <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)
lambda <- cvfit$lambda.min               # small lambda = weak prior, large = strong


Tasks
R1. Run the “two prior shapes” block. Zoom the plot near \(\beta = 0\) (e.g. restrict b_grid to seq(-0.5, 0.5, length.out = 400)). Describe in words how the two curves differ at the origin, and connect that to B6.
R2. Evaluate neg_log_gauss and neg_log_laplace on a grid such as seq(-3, 3, 0.5) and plot each against beta. Confirm one is a parabola (\(\beta^2\)) and the other a V (\(|\beta|\)). Which corresponds to ridge and which to lasso?
R3. With \(\sigma^2 = 1\), compute lambda <- 1 / tau2 for tau2 <- c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100). Tabulate \(\tau^2\) against \(\lambda\) and state, in one sentence, the relationship between prior confidence and penalty strength (this is B5 in code).

title: Exercise: penalties as priors
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — the master equation





Everything follows from taking \(-\log\) of posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The \(-\log\) turns the product into a sum, and turns maximise into minimise: \(-\log(\text{likelihood}) + (-\log(\text{prior}))\). The first piece is the fit term, the second is the penalty term. See the summary table on the dnorm reference for the Gaussian density form.









Hint 2 — negative log of a Gaussian (B2, B4)





For \(p(\beta_j)\propto e^{-\beta_j^2/2\tau^2}\), \(-\log p(\beta_j) = \dfrac{\beta_j^2}{2\tau^2} + \text{const}\). Summing over \(j\) gives \(\dfrac{1}{2\tau^2}\sum_j\beta_j^2 = \dfrac{1}{2\tau^2}\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2\) — the ridge (\(\ell_2\)) penalty. To get a clean \(\lambda\), multiply the whole objective by \(2\sigma^2\): minimisers are unchanged by scaling by a positive constant.









Hint 3 — negative log of a Laplace (B3)





For \(p(\beta_j)\propto e^{-|\beta_j|/b}\), \(-\log p(\beta_j) = \dfrac{|\beta_j|}{b} + \text{const}\). The absolute value in the exponent becomes an absolute value in the penalty: \(\dfrac{1}{b}\sum_j|\beta_j| = \dfrac{1}{b}\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1\) — the lasso (\(\ell_1\)) penalty.









Hint 4 — prior precision (B5)





\(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2\), and precision is \(1/\tau^2\). A small \(\tau^2\) (tight prior, high precision) makes \(\lambda\) large → strong shrinkage. As \(\tau^2\to\infty\) the prior goes flat, \(\lambda\to 0\), and MAP collapses to maximum likelihood = ordinary least squares.









Hint 5 — the cusp (B6)





Compare the two densities at the origin. The Gaussian \(e^{-\beta^2}\) has a rounded top with zero slope at \(0\), so it never forces a coefficient to be exactly \(0\). The Laplace \(e^{-|\beta|}\) has a kink / cusp at \(0\) — that corner is what lets the lasso land on coefficients that are exactly zero, giving variable selection.









Hint 6 — biology to prior (B7)





Ask: do I believe many small effects, or a few large ones? Many small effects (polygenic) → dense, smooth shrinkage → Gaussian / ridge. A few drivers, most exactly zero → sparse → Laplace / lasso. If you need a short candidate list, you want the exact zeros of lasso. For correlated predictors you want a blend — the elastic net (mixed Gaussian + Laplace prior) shrinks correlated coefficients together instead of arbitrarily keeping one.









Hint 7 — the R illustration





Build the density grid with seq, the Gaussian with dnorm, and the Laplace by hand as \(\tfrac{1}{2b}e^{-|\beta|/b}\) using abs and exp. Plot with plot / lines. In glmnet, alpha mixes the two penalties (prior shapes) and lambda sets strength.

title: Exercise: penalties as priors
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. (a) The penalty term is the negative log-prior on the coefficients — a penalty is a prior belief that coefficients are small. (b) The fit term (RSS) is the negative log-likelihood under Gaussian noise (up to the \(\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\) factor and a constant). (c) Penalised regression finds the mode / peak of the posterior — the MAP estimate — not the posterior mean or median.
B2. Take the negative log of the Gaussian density: \[-\log p(\beta_j) = -\log\!\Big(c\,e^{-\beta_j^2/2\tau^2}\Big) = \frac{\beta_j^2}{2\tau^2} - \log c.\] The \(-\log c\) is a constant (no \(\boldsymbol\beta\)), so drop it. Summing over \(j\): \[-\log p(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\sum_{j}\beta_j^2 = \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2 + \text{const}.\] This is the sum-of-squares (\(\ell_2\)) penalty → ridge.
B3. Same steps with the Laplace density: \[-\log p(\beta_j) = -\log\!\Big(c\,e^{-|\beta_j|/b}\Big) = \frac{|\beta_j|}{b} - \log c.\] Drop the constant and sum: \[-\log p(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{b}\sum_j |\beta_j| = \frac{1}{b}\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1 + \text{const}.\] This is the sum-of-absolute-values (\(\ell_1\)) penalty → lasso.
B4. Add the Gaussian-noise fit term \(\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\text{RSS}\) to the B2 penalty: \[\arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\text{RSS} + \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2.\] Multiplying the whole objective by the positive constant \(2\sigma^2\) does not change where the minimum is: \[= \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \text{RSS} + \frac{2\sigma^2}{2\tau^2}\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2 = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \text{RSS} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2.\] So \(\lambda = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}\) — the ridge penalty strength is the noise variance over the prior variance.
B5. (a) With \(\sigma^2 = 1\): tight prior \(\tau^2 = 0.01 \Rightarrow \lambda = 1/0.01 = 100\); loose prior \(\tau^2 = 100 \Rightarrow \lambda = 1/100 = 0.01\). The tight prior (\(\tau^2 = 0.01\)) gives the far larger \(\lambda\) and hence much stronger shrinkage — as it should, since a tight prior insists the coefficients are near zero. (b) As \(\tau^2 \to \infty\), \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2 \to 0\). The prior becomes flat (no information), the penalty vanishes, and the MAP reduces to ordinary least squares (= maximum likelihood).
B6. Both densities are bell-ish and centred at \(0\), but they behave differently at the origin. The Gaussian \(e^{-\beta^2/2\tau^2}\) is smooth with zero slope at \(0\) — a rounded top — so shrinking a coefficient toward \(0\) is never quite “worth” driving it all the way; ridge shrinks but leaves every \(\beta_j \ne 0\). The Laplace \(e^{-|\beta|/b}\) has a sharp cusp (kink) at \(0\) because of the \(|\beta|\): the penalty has a corner there. That corner means the optimum frequently sits exactly at \(\beta_j = 0\), so the lasso performs variable selection (exact zeros), whereas ridge does not.
B7. (a) Gaussian / ridge — a polygenic trait is many small nonzero effects, which is exactly a dense Gaussian prior that shrinks all coefficients gently without zeroing them. (b) Laplace / lasso — “a few drivers, the rest exactly irrelevant” is a sparse belief; the Laplace prior’s cusp zeroes out the irrelevant genes. (c) Laplace / lasso — you want the exact zeros so that only a short set of genes has nonzero coefficients, i.e. a testable candidate list. (d) A blend (elastic net) — pure lasso tends to pick one gene from a correlated group and zero the rest arbitrarily; adding a Gaussian (ridge) component shrinks correlated coefficients together. The elastic net is the MAP under a mixed Gaussian + Laplace prior.
R1. Restricting the grid to \([-0.5, 0.5]\) shows the Laplace forming a sharp point (cusp) at \(\beta = 0\) while the Gaussian is rounded there. This is the visual form of B6: the cusp is what enables lasso’s exact zeros; the rounded top means ridge only shrinks.
b_grid  <- seq(-0.5, 0.5, length.out = 400)
gauss   <- dnorm(b_grid, 0, 1)
laplace <- (1 / (2 * (1/sqrt(2)))) * exp(-abs(b_grid) / (1/sqrt(2)))
plot(b_grid, laplace, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "beta", ylab = "density")
lines(b_grid, gauss, lwd = 2, lty = 2)   # Laplace has the pointed top; Gaussian is rounded
R2. The Gaussian negative-log is a parabola (\(\propto\beta^2\)) → ridge; the Laplace negative-log is a V (\(\propto|\beta|\)) → lasso.
beta <- seq(-3, 3, 0.5)
plot(beta, beta^2,  type = "b", ylab = "-log prior (up to const)")  # parabola -> ridge
plot(beta, abs(beta), type = "b", ylab = "-log prior (up to const)") # V-shape  -> lasso
R3. \(\lambda\) and \(\tau^2\) move in opposite directions: the more confident (smaller-variance, higher-precision) the prior, the larger the penalty.
tau2   <- c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100)
lambda <- 1 / tau2          # sigma^2 = 1, so lambda = sigma^2 / tau2
data.frame(tau2, precision = 1/tau2, lambda)
#   tau2 precision lambda
#  0.01     100.00 100.00   <- tight, confident prior -> strong penalty
#  0.10      10.00  10.00
#  1.00       1.00   1.00
# 10.00       0.10   0.10
# 100.00      0.01   0.01   <- loose prior            -> weak penalty
In one sentence: penalty strength is prior precision — a tighter (more confident) prior that effects are small corresponds to a larger \(\lambda\) and stronger shrinkage.

title: Exercise: penalties as priors
text:
Where this leads

Bayesian inference: here we found only the posterior peak (MAP). A full Bayesian treatment reports the whole posterior — the peak and its width — giving credible intervals on each coefficient that the MAP alone cannot.
Ridge and lasso regression: the penalties, the geometry of the \(\ell_1\)/\(\ell_2\) constraint, cross-validating \(\lambda\), and the elastic net in practice with glmnet.
Hierarchical / empirical-Bayes models: rather than fixing the prior variance \(\tau^2\) (or cross-validating \(\lambda\)), one can put a prior on it too and let the data estimate how strong the prior should be — the principled version of tuning \(\lambda\).

title: Exercise: polar coordinates — measuring a ring
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

convert between \((x, y)\) and polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) around a chosen centre, by hand and with sqrt and atan2,
explain why the change to polar coordinates is not a matrix transformation,
compute a radial profile of an image and find the edge of a ring in it,
unwrap an image around a centre and measure how round a zone is,
turn a distance in pixels into millimetres with an object of known size.

This builds on Transforming images with matrices; the image setup is the same. Polar coordinates are a very useful transformation, but a nonlinear one: no matrix can do it.

title: Exercise: polar coordinates — measuring a ring
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

convert between \((x, y)\) and polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) around a chosen centre, by hand and with sqrt and atan2,
explain why the change to polar coordinates is not a matrix transformation,
