title: Exercise: ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
Background
Ordinary least squares minimizes the residual sum of squares and has the closed form \[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{OLS}} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y},\] which needs \(X^\top X\) to be invertible. When \(p > n\) or predictors are collinear, \(X^\top X\) is singular (or nearly so) and OLS is unstable or undefined.
Penalized regression adds a competing goal — keep the coefficients small: \[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \lVert\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2 + \lambda\cdot\text{penalty}(\boldsymbol\beta), \qquad \lambda \ge 0.\]









Method
penalty
effect
closed form?




Ridge (L2)
\(\sum_j\beta_j^2\)
shrinks all; keeps all
yes: \((X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}\)


Lasso (L1)
\(\sum_j\lvert\beta_j\rvert\)
shrinks; sets some to 0
no (kink at 0)


Elastic net
\(\alpha\sum\lvert\beta_j\rvert+(1-\alpha)\sum\beta_j^2\)
grouped selection
no



Key facts to keep in hand:

Standardize predictors before penalizing (glmnet does this); never penalize the intercept.
\(\lambda=0\) → OLS; \(\lambda\to\infty\) → all coefficients \(\to 0\).
Choose \(\lambda\) by cross-validation — never by training error, which just falls as \(\lambda\to0\).

title: Exercise: ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
By hand
B1. Explain in one or two sentences why OLS has no unique solution when you have \(p = 3\) predictors but only \(n = 2\) samples. (Think about the number of unknowns versus equations, and about whether \(X^\top X\) can be inverted.)
B2. (ridge on a 1-D toy). Suppose after centring there is a single predictor and \(X^\top X = 4\), \(X^\top\mathbf{y} = 8\) (so the OLS slope is \(8/4 = 2\)). The 1-D ridge estimate is \[\hat\beta_{\text{ridge}}(\lambda) = \frac{X^\top\mathbf{y}}{X^\top X + \lambda} = \frac{8}{4+\lambda}.\] Compute \(\hat\beta_{\text{ridge}}\) for \(\lambda = 0,\ 4,\ 12,\ \text{and as }\lambda\to\infty\). What happens to the coefficient as \(\lambda\) grows?
B3. (ridge on a 2×2, by hand). Take the standardized design \[X^\top X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad X^\top\mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.\] (a) Find the OLS estimate \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{OLS}} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}\). (b) Find the ridge estimate at \(\lambda = 1\) using \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}\). (Note \(X^\top X + I = 2I\), easy to invert.) (c) By what factor was each coefficient shrunk? Did either become exactly zero?
B4. (collinearity and the diagonal). For a collinear design suppose \(X^\top X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). (a) Show it is singular (its columns are parallel; row-reduce \([\,X^\top X \mid I\,]\) and see what happens) — so OLS cannot invert it. (b) Form \(X^\top X + \lambda I\) with \(\lambda = 1\) and find its inverse by row-reducing \([\,X^\top X + I \mid I\,]\). Is it now invertible? (c) In one sentence, connect this to the eigenvalue fact that adding \(\lambda I\) shifts every eigenvalue up by \(\lambda\) (recall Eigenvalues & eigenvectors).
B5. (the geometry). Sketch, in the \((\beta_1,\beta_2)\) plane: (a) the ridge budget region \(\beta_1^2+\beta_2^2\le t\) and the lasso budget region \(\lvert\beta_1\rvert+\lvert\beta_2\rvert\le t\); (b) a set of elliptical RSS contours centred at an OLS solution like \((2, 0.3)\). Argue from the picture which method is likely to return a solution with \(\beta_2 = 0\) exactly, and why the shape of the region is responsible.
B6. (reading a path plot). A lasso plot(fit, xvar="lambda") shows coefficient paths against \(\log\lambda\). As \(\lambda\) increases (moving right), do the coefficients get larger or smaller? What does it mean when a path hits the horizontal axis and stays there? At the far right, how many predictors does the model use?
B7. (choosing among the three). For each scenario, say whether you would start with ridge, lasso, or elastic net, and why: (a) 15 000 genes, 30 samples, you want a short panel to validate in the lab; (b) a handful of highly co-regulated genes that you believe are all biologically relevant and want to keep; (c) 15 000 genes, 30 samples, many correlated pathway modules, you want selection but stable to resampling.

title: Exercise: ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
Explore: the geometry, live
The demo draws B5 for you. The grey ellipses are RSS contours around the OLS point (drag it); the green region is the penalty region \(\alpha(|\beta_1|+|\beta_2|) + (1-\alpha)(\beta_1^2+\beta_2^2) \le t\), drawn at the budget \(t\) that the current \(\lambda\) leads to; the purple ellipse is the smallest RSS contour that touches it, and the touching point is the penalized estimate \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\). The slider “corr” sets the correlation between the two (standardized) predictors, which tilts and stretches the ellipses. The right panel is the coefficient path: \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(\hat\beta_2\) against \(\lambda\), with the current \(\lambda\) dashed.



E1. Start from Reset (lasso, OLS \(= (2, 0.6)\), corr \(= 0.4\)). Move \(\lambda\) slowly up from \(0.01\). At roughly which \(\lambda\) does \(\hat\beta_2\) become exactly \(0\), and where on the diamond is \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) from then on? At which \(\lambda\) is \(\hat\beta_1\) also \(0\)?
E2. Click Ridge at \(\lambda = 2\). Is either coefficient exactly zero? Push \(\lambda\) to \(100\) and look at the path panel: do the ridge paths ever reach zero?
E3. Back to Lasso at \(\lambda = 2\). Drag the OLS point around the first quadrant. For which OLS points does the solution stay on the \(\beta_1\) axis (\(\hat\beta_2 = 0\))? Does the same happen for ridge?
E4. Click Elastic net (\(\alpha = 0.5\)) with the reset settings. Compare the shape of the region and the path with the lasso: does elastic net still produce exact zeros, and does \(\hat\beta_2\) drop out at a smaller or larger \(\lambda\) than with the lasso?






Solutions





E1. \(\hat\beta_2\) hits zero at \(\lambda \approx 1.7\). From then on \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) sits on the corner of the diamond on the \(\beta_1\) axis (the red mark), and the region shrinks along that axis as \(\lambda\) grows. \(\hat\beta_1\) reaches zero at \(\lambda \approx 4.5\); beyond that both coefficients are exactly \(0\) and the region has shrunk to the origin.
E2. No: at \(\lambda = 2\) ridge gives about \((0.70, 0.37)\), both nonzero, and the touching point is on the smooth circle, off the axes. At \(\lambda = 100\) both are tiny (about \(0.02\) and \(0.01\)) but still not zero; the ridge paths approach zero smoothly and never reach it.
E3. The solution stays on the \(\beta_1\) axis for a whole band of OLS points: roughly, whenever the OLS \(\beta_2\) is small compared with \(\beta_1\) (with \(\lambda = 2\), about \(\beta_2 < 0.7\) when \(\beta_1 = 2\)). Every ellipse centred in that band touches the diamond first at its corner. For ridge the touching point moves smoothly with the OLS point and lands exactly on an axis only if the OLS point itself is on that axis.
E4. The elastic-net region is a diamond with rounded sides, but it keeps its corners on the axes, so it still produces exact zeros. Its \(|\beta|\) part only has weight \(\alpha = 0.5\), so the pull towards exactly zero is weaker and \(\hat\beta_2\) drops out later: at \(\lambda \approx 5.2\) instead of \(\approx 1.7\), and \(\hat\beta_1\) at \(\lambda \approx 9\) instead of \(\approx 4.5\).

title: Exercise: ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
In R
We use glmnet. If needed, install it once with install.packages("glmnet"). The code below is illustrative — read it, then adapt it in the tasks.

Simulate a wide problem (\(p > n\))
library(glmnet)
set.seed(1)

n <- 40      # samples (patients)
p <- 200     # predictors (genes)  -> p > n
x <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
colnames(x) <- paste0("gene", seq_len(p))

# only 5 genes truly drive the phenotype; the rest are noise
beta_true      <- rep(0, p)
beta_true[1:5] <- c(3, -2, 2, -1.5, 1)
y <- as.numeric(x %*% beta_true + rnorm(n))   # continuous phenotype


Fit ridge, lasso, elastic net
fit_ridge <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0)      # ridge:   keeps all genes
fit_lasso <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1)      # lasso:   sparse
fit_enet  <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0.5)    # elastic net

plot(fit_lasso, xvar = "lambda")           # watch coefficients enter/leave
print(fit_lasso)                           # Df = number of nonzero coefficients


Choose lambda by cross-validation, then read off the genes
set.seed(1)
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)

plot(cv_lasso)                             # CV error vs log(lambda)
cv_lasso$lambda.min                        # minimum CV error
cv_lasso$lambda.1se                        # sparser model within 1 SE

beta <- coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.1se")   # sparse coefficient vector
selected <- rownames(beta)[which(beta != 0)]
selected                                   # includes "(Intercept)" + kept genes


Tasks
R1. Run the simulation block. Confirm the shape of x with dim(x) and check p > n.
R2. Fit fit_ridge and fit_lasso. Using predict(fit, type = "nonzero", s = 0.5) or the Df column of print(fit), compare how many genes each model keeps at a moderate \(\lambda\). Which one is sparse?
R3. Run cv.glmnet for lasso. Report lambda.min and lambda.1se, and extract the selected genes at lambda.1se. Did the model recover any of the 5 true genes (gene1…gene5)?
R4. Refit with alpha = 0 (ridge) via cv.glmnet, and coef(...) at lambda.1se. Confirm that essentially no coefficient is exactly zero (ridge keeps all predictors).
R5. Change the outcome to binary — y_bin <- as.integer(y > median(y)) — and fit cv.glmnet(x, y_bin, family = "binomial", alpha = 1). This is penalized logistic regression. Extract the selected genes the same way.

title: Exercise: ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — why OLS fails when p > n (B1)





OLS solves a system with one unknown per predictor. With more unknowns (\(p\)) than equations (\(n\)), the system is underdetermined — infinitely many \(\boldsymbol\beta\) fit perfectly. Equivalently, \(X^\top X\) is a \(p\times p\) matrix of rank at most \(n < p\), so it is singular and \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) does not exist. See the solution-space discussion in Linear systems by hand.









Hint 2 — the 1-D ridge formula (B2)





Just plug into \(\hat\beta(\lambda) = \dfrac{8}{4+\lambda}\). The denominator grows with \(\lambda\), so the estimate shrinks monotonically toward \(0\) but never quite reaches it for finite \(\lambda\). That “shrinks but does not zero” behaviour is the signature of the L2 penalty.









Hint 3 — inverting 2I (B3)





When \(X^\top X\) is the identity, \(X^\top X + \lambda I = (1+\lambda)I\), whose inverse is \(\frac{1}{1+\lambda}I\). So the ridge estimate is simply \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{ridge}} = \frac{1}{1+\lambda}\,X^\top\mathbf{y}\) — every OLS coefficient scaled by \(\frac{1}{1+\lambda}\). At \(\lambda=1\) that factor is \(\tfrac12\).









Hint 4 — a singular matrix and adding lambda*I (B4)





A matrix with parallel columns is singular (non-invertible): row reduction gives a row of zeros on the left. Adding \(\lambda I\) adds \(\lambda\) to each diagonal entry, which breaks the parallel columns. For the eigenvalues of \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), use the symmetric pattern from Eigenvalues & eigenvectors. A zero eigenvalue means some direction is squashed to zero (singular); adding \(\lambda I\) raises every eigenvalue by \(\lambda\), so it becomes \(\lambda > 0\) and the matrix becomes invertible.









Hint 5 — the geometry (B5)





The ridge region is a circle (round, no corners); the lasso region is a diamond with corners on the axes. The penalized estimate is where the smallest RSS ellipse first touches the region. A corner sticks out furthest, so the ellipse tends to hit it first — and a corner on an axis has one coordinate exactly \(0\).









Hint 6 — reading the glmnet path (B6)





On plot(fit, xvar="lambda") the x-axis is \(\log\lambda\) increasing to the right. More penalty (right) means smaller coefficients. A path that reaches \(0\) and stays there means that gene has been dropped. At the far right (very large \(\lambda\)) all coefficients are \(\approx 0\) and the model uses essentially no genes. See glmnet.









Hint 7 — running glmnet and cv.glmnet





glmnet(x, y, alpha = a) needs x as a matrix (use as.matrix); alpha is 1 lasso, 0 ridge, in between elastic net. cv.glmnet adds cross-validation and stores $lambda.min and $lambda.1se. Get coefficients with coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.1se"). Set a seed — the folds are random.

title: Exercise: ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. With \(p=3\) unknown coefficients but only \(n=2\) data points (equations), the linear system is underdetermined: there are infinitely many \(\boldsymbol\beta\) that fit the two points exactly. Concretely \(X^\top X\) is a \(3\times3\) matrix but has rank at most \(2\), so it is singular and \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) does not exist — OLS has no unique solution.
B2. \(\hat\beta(\lambda) = \dfrac{8}{4+\lambda}\):

\(\lambda=0\): \(8/4 = 2\) (the OLS value).
\(\lambda=4\): \(8/8 = 1\).
\(\lambda=12\): \(8/16 = 0.5\).
\(\lambda\to\infty\): \(\to 0\).

The coefficient shrinks monotonically toward \(0\) as \(\lambda\) grows, but stays strictly positive for any finite \(\lambda\) — ridge never sets it exactly to zero.
B3. (a) OLS: \((X^\top X)^{-1} = I^{-1} = I\), so \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{OLS}} = I\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\1\end{pmatrix}\). (b) Ridge at \(\lambda=1\): \(X^\top X + I = 2I\), so \((2I)^{-1} = \tfrac12 I\) and \[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{ridge}} = \tfrac12 I\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1.5\\0.5\end{pmatrix}.\] (c) Each coefficient was multiplied by \(\tfrac{1}{1+\lambda}=\tfrac12\) — shrunk to half. Neither became exactly zero; ridge shrinks proportionally but keeps both predictors.
B4. (a) The two columns are both \((1,1)\) — parallel. Row reduction: \(\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] \xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,\text{R1}\;} \left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 1 \end{array}\right]\): a zero row on the left → singular, so OLS cannot invert it. (b) \(X^\top X + I = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\). Row reduction: \[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,\frac12\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac32 & -\tfrac12 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\frac23\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -\tfrac13 & \tfrac23 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\frac12(\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2})\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & \tfrac23 & -\tfrac13 \\ 0 & 1 & -\tfrac13 & \tfrac23 \end{array}\right],
\] so it is now invertible, with inverse \(\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\). (c) By the symmetric pattern, \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) has eigenvalue \(2\) for \((1,1)\) and \(0\) for \((1,-1)\): the \((1,-1)\) direction is squashed to zero, which is why it is singular. Adding \(\lambda I\) shifts the eigenvalues to \(2+\lambda\) and \(\lambda\), so the previously-zero eigenvalue becomes \(\lambda>0\) and the matrix is no longer singular. (Bonus, not for exam: the determinant goes from \(1 - 1 = 0\) to \(4 - 1 = 3\); it is the product of the eigenvalues, \(3 \cdot 1\).)
B5. (a) The ridge region \(\beta_1^2+\beta_2^2\le t\) is a disk / circle; the lasso region \(\lvert\beta_1\rvert+\lvert\beta_2\rvert\le t\) is a diamond with corners on the axes at \((\pm t,0)\) and \((0,\pm t)\). (b) The RSS contours are ellipses centred on the OLS point \((2,0.3)\), growing outward. The lasso is the one likely to return \(\beta_2 = 0\) exactly: the diamond’s corner on the \(\beta_1\)-axis is the part sticking out toward the ellipses, so an expanding contour tends to first touch there — and that corner has \(\beta_2 = 0\). The circle has no corners, so the ridge touch point sits at a generic location with both coefficients nonzero. The shape (corners vs. smoothness) is what creates, or prevents, sparsity.
B6. As \(\lambda\) increases (moving right), the penalty is stronger, so coefficients get smaller. A path that reaches the horizontal axis and stays there means that predictor’s coefficient has been set to exactly zero — the gene is dropped from the model. At the far right (largest \(\lambda\)) essentially no predictors remain (the model collapses toward just the intercept, predicting \(\bar y\)).
B7. (a) Lasso (or elastic net): you explicitly want a short, interpretable panel, which requires setting most coefficients to zero — ridge would keep all 15 000 genes. (b) Ridge: you want to keep the co-regulated genes and let them share the weight; ridge shrinks them together without dropping any, whereas lasso would arbitrarily discard all but one. (c) Elastic net: you want selection (\(p\gg n\)) but stability across correlated modules — the L2 part makes correlated genes enter or leave together, giving a more reproducible list than pure lasso.
R1.
dim(x)      # 40 200  -> n = 40 rows, p = 200 columns
40 < 200    # TRUE: p > n
R2.
fit_ridge <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0)
fit_lasso <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1)

# number of nonzero coefficients at a moderate lambda = 0.5
length(predict(fit_lasso, type = "nonzero", s = 0.5)[[1]])  # small: a handful
length(predict(fit_ridge, type = "nonzero", s = 0.5)[[1]])  # all 200: ridge keeps everything
Lasso is sparse (few nonzero coefficients); ridge keeps essentially all 200 genes.
R3.
set.seed(1)
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
cv_lasso$lambda.min
cv_lasso$lambda.1se

beta <- coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.1se")
selected <- rownames(beta)[which(beta != 0)]
selected     # "(Intercept)" plus a short list; should include several of gene1..gene5
With a strong true signal the model typically recovers most of gene1…gene5, plus perhaps a few false positives. The exact set varies with the seed and CV split — an honest reminder that selection is not perfectly stable at small \(n\).
R4.
set.seed(1)
cv_ridge <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 0, nfolds = 10)
beta_r <- coef(cv_ridge, s = "lambda.1se")
sum(beta_r == 0)     # 0 (or nearly): ridge does not zero coefficients
Ridge shrinks every coefficient but leaves them nonzero — no feature selection.
R5.
y_bin <- as.integer(y > median(y))
set.seed(1)
cv_bin <- cv.glmnet(x, y_bin, family = "binomial", alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)

beta_b <- coef(cv_bin, s = "lambda.1se")
rownames(beta_b)[which(beta_b != 0)]   # selected genes for the binary phenotype
This is penalized logistic regression: same penalty machinery, a binary responder/non-responder outcome, still returning a sparse gene list.

title: Exercise: ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
Where this leads

Cross-validation and model selection are given a first look here; the full treatment (train/validation/test splits, nested CV, performance metrics) belongs to Statistics and machine learning in bioinformatics.
Predictive vs. causal: a selected gene is predictive, not proven causal — collinearity means a dropped gene may be equally relevant. Validation is experimental, not statistical.
Penalized generalized linear models: the same penalties extend to logistic and Poisson / negative-binomial outcomes — connecting to the count-distribution material (Poisson & negative binomial) for RNA-seq counts.
Relation to PCA: ridge and PCA both stabilise collinear predictors, but PCA (Applications block) builds new orthogonal directions, whereas ridge keeps the original genes — worth comparing once you have met both.

title: Quiz: ridge, lasso & elastic net
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of penalized linear models. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Several are written in the style of the on-campus exam (no computer).

Q1. Why does ordinary least squares fail (or become unstable) when you have 20 000 genes and 40 samples?






Hint





Count unknowns versus equations, and ask whether \(X^\top X\) can be inverted.









Answer





There are far more unknown coefficients (\(p = 20\,000\)) than samples (\(n = 40\)), so the system is underdetermined — infinitely many \(\boldsymbol\beta\) fit perfectly, and OLS picks unstable, noise-fitting coefficients. Equivalently \(X^\top X\) has rank at most \(n < p\), so it is singular and \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) does not exist. This is the \(p \gg n\) regime.




Q2. Write the general penalized objective, and state the penalty term for ridge and for lasso.






Hint





Fit term plus \(\lambda\) times a penalty. Squares vs. absolute values.









Answer





\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ \lVert\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2 + \lambda\cdot\text{penalty}(\boldsymbol\beta).\] Ridge (L2): penalty \(= \sum_j \beta_j^2\). Lasso (L1): penalty \(= \sum_j \lvert\beta_j\rvert\).




Q3. What is the single most important behavioural difference between ridge and lasso?






Hint





What happens to a coefficient that is not useful?









Answer





Lasso sets some coefficients exactly to zero (dropping those predictors — automatic feature selection, a sparse model). Ridge shrinks all coefficients toward zero but keeps them all nonzero. So lasso selects; ridge only shrinks.




Q4. In the constraint-geometry picture, the ridge budget region is a circle and the lasso region is a diamond. Why does that difference produce zero coefficients for lasso but not for ridge?






Hint





Where are the corners of the diamond, and what does the RSS ellipse tend to touch first?









Answer





The diamond has corners that lie on the axes, where one coordinate is exactly zero. The expanding RSS ellipse tends to first touch a pointy corner, so the lasso solution often lands with a coefficient exactly \(0\). The circle is smooth with no corners, so ridge’s touch point sits at a generic location with all coefficients nonzero.




Q5. What does the ridge closed form \((X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top\mathbf{y}\) show about how ridge handles collinearity or the \(p>n\) case?






Hint





What does adding \(\lambda I\) do to the eigenvalues of \(X^\top X\)?









Answer





Adding \(\lambda I\) raises every eigenvalue of \(X^\top X\) by \(\lambda\), so a zero (or near-zero) eigenvalue — which makes \(X^\top X\) singular / non-invertible — becomes \(\lambda > 0\). The matrix is then invertible and well-conditioned, giving stable coefficients even when predictors are collinear or \(p > n\).




Q6. What is the elastic net, and what practical problem with lasso does it fix in genomics?






Hint





It mixes two penalties with a parameter \(\alpha\). Think about a group of co-regulated genes.









Answer





Elastic net uses a mix of L1 and L2: penalty \(= \alpha\sum_j\lvert\beta_j\rvert + (1-\alpha)\sum_j\beta_j^2\), with \(\alpha=1\) pure lasso and \(\alpha=0\) pure ridge. It fixes lasso’s tendency to pick one gene arbitrarily from a group of correlated (co-regulated) genes and drop the rest: the L2 part encourages correlated genes to be selected or dropped together (the grouping effect), giving more stable, biologically sensible selection.




Q7. How should you choose \(\lambda\), and why can you not just pick the \(\lambda\) that minimizes the training error?






Hint





What happens to training error as \(\lambda \to 0\)? Which model does that favour?









Answer





Choose \(\lambda\) by cross-validation — estimate error on held-out folds and pick the \(\lambda\) with the lowest cross-validated error (lambda.min, or the sparser lambda.1se within one SE). You cannot use training error because it falls monotonically as \(\lambda \to 0\), so it would always select the overfit OLS model. Only out-of-sample error reveals the right amount of shrinkage.




Q8. You run cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1) and extract coefficients at lambda.1se. Most entries are zero; a few genes are nonzero. In biological terms, what is that short list, and what is one important caveat about it?






Hint





Selected genes are a signature. Does “selected” mean “causal”?









Answer





The nonzero genes are the model’s selected predictive signature — a short, testable panel that predicts the phenotype and could be turned into a targeted assay. Caveat: these genes are predictive, not proven causal. Because of collinearity a dropped gene may be just as relevant as the one kept, and the exact list can shift across CV splits at small \(n\). Interpret it as a hypothesis to validate experimentally, not as established biology.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
About this lecture
In the Bayesian inference units you learned the idea: combine a prior with a likelihood to get a posterior. Today we learn the tool that computes that posterior for real models — Stan, driven from R.

What Stan is, and why we need a computer once a model is bigger than a toy.
The anatomy of a Stan model: the data, parameters, and model blocks.
How to declare a prior and a likelihood in that language.
How to run the model from R with rstan, and the shortcut package brms.
The idea of MCMC: the fit is a big pile of draws from the posterior, not one number.
How to read the output: posterior means, credible intervals, Rhat, and effective sample size.








Provisional unit


This whole Bayesian statistics block is provisional and may move to a later statistics / machine-learning course. Treat today as a first look at the machinery, not an exam-critical by-hand skill.





Set expectations clearly. Earlier Bayesian units built the concept — prior, likelihood, posterior, and the Bayesian-vs-frequentist distinction. Those were done on toy problems where the posterior could be written down by hand (conjugate priors). Today is the jump to a general-purpose engine: Stan writes and samples the posterior for almost any model you can specify. Emphasise this is a mechanics-and-fluency lecture, not a derivation lecture, and flag the provisional status so students know the block may relocate. Keep an R session open conceptually but remember nothing here is executed at render time — all code is static.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
A biology problem first
You stain a tissue and score cells for a marker gene. Out of 20 cells, 13 express it. What fraction \(\theta\) of cells in this tissue express the marker?

The naive point estimate is \(13/20 = 0.65\). But with only 20 cells, how sure are we?
A frequentist gives a confidence interval. A Bayesian wants the whole posterior distribution of \(\theta\) — a probability curve over every value \(\theta\) could take.
We also have prior knowledge: this marker is usually expressed in roughly half the cells, rarely near 0 or 1.

The question is not “what is \(\theta\)?” but “what does the data plus prior tell us about the plausible values of \(\theta\)?” That is a posterior, and Stan will compute it.


Anchor the abstraction in a concrete count. Scoring 13 of 20 cells positive is exactly the kind of small-sample problem where uncertainty matters and a single ratio is misleading. Contrast the frequentist confidence interval (which students met in their prior stats course) with the Bayesian posterior: a full probability distribution over the unknown fraction. Plant the prior naturally — biological background says the marker sits around half — so priors feel like real information, not a philosophical imposition. This binomial-proportion problem is the running example for the whole lecture; keep coming back to it.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
Recap: prior, likelihood, posterior
Bayes’ theorem, in the form we actually use:
\[\underbrace{p(\theta \mid y)}_{\text{posterior}} \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(y \mid \theta)}_{\text{likelihood}} \times \underbrace{p(\theta)}_{\text{prior}}\]
For the marker example:

Parameter: \(\theta\), the fraction expressing (a number between 0 and 1).
Likelihood: the count \(y=13\) out of \(N=20\) is Binomial: \(y \sim \text{Binomial}(N, \theta)\).
Prior: “usually about half” — a Beta distribution, e.g. \(\theta \sim \text{Beta}(2,2)\), a gentle hump centred on \(0.5\).

The posterior is the prior reshaped by the data. Stan’s job is to produce that posterior for us.


Re-state Bayes in the proportional form, because the normalising constant is exactly what makes this hard by hand and what Stan sidesteps. Name each piece against the running example so the three abstract words become three concrete choices. The Binomial likelihood should feel familiar from the distributions block; the Beta prior is the natural companion on [0,1]. Beta(2,2) is a mild prior favouring the middle without excluding the extremes — contrast it mentally with Beta(1,1), the flat/uniform prior. Do not derive the Beta-Binomial conjugacy here; the point is that Stan does not need conjugacy at all.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
Why we need a computer
For this one example the posterior happens to have a clean formula (Beta prior + Binomial likelihood is conjugate). But that is a lucky special case.
\[p(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\,p(\theta)}{\displaystyle\int p(y \mid \theta)\,p(\theta)\,d\theta}\]

The denominator is an integral over all parameter values. For one parameter it is doable; for a realistic model with dozens or hundreds of parameters it is a hopeless high-dimensional integral.
Almost no real model is conjugate, so there is no formula for the posterior.
The escape: don’t compute the curve — draw samples from it. That is what MCMC does, and what Stan is built for.


This is the motivating “why”. Students may have solved conjugate posteriors by hand in the earlier units and could wonder why a whole software package is needed. The honest answer: conjugacy is rare, and the normalising integral in the denominator is intractable the moment the model has more than a couple of parameters — think of a regression with many coefficients, or a hierarchical model over many genes. The conceptual pivot is that we never need the normalised curve; a large sample of draws from the posterior lets us compute any summary we want. That reframing is the whole reason MCMC and Stan exist.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
What is Stan?
Stan is a probabilistic programming language: you describe a model, and Stan figures out how to sample from its posterior.

You write the model in Stan’s own small language (a .stan file or a string).
Stan compiles it to fast C++ and runs an MCMC sampler (a modern one called HMC / NUTS).
You drive it entirely from R. Two common front-ends:

rstan — you write the Stan model yourself. Maximum control; you see every block.
brms — you write a familiar R formula (y ~ x) and it generates the Stan model for you.


Today we write one model by hand with rstan to see the moving parts, then show the brms shortcut.


Define Stan plainly: a language for describing statistical models, plus an engine that samples their posteriors. Stress the division of labour — you specify the model, Stan works out the sampling. Mention that under the hood it compiles to C++ and uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (the No-U-Turn Sampler), but do not go into HMC mechanics; the name is enough. The two front-ends matter pedagogically: rstan exposes the anatomy (our teaching goal), while brms hides it behind lm-style formulas they already know. We deliberately do the hand-written version first so the formula shortcut later is demystified, not magic.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
section: The anatomy of a Stan model
text:
The anatomy of a Stan model
A Stan model is organised into named blocks. The three essential ones:








Block
What it declares
Analogy




data
the known inputs (counts, sample sizes, predictors)
what you pass in from R


parameters
the unknowns you want to learn
what the posterior is over


model
the priors and the likelihood
how data and parameters connect



Order matters: data, then parameters, then model. Every variable must be declared with a type before use (Stan is strict, like C++).


Give the mental scaffold before showing code. Three blocks, three roles: data is what you know, parameters are what you want to find out, model wires them together with priors and a likelihood. The R-to-Stan hand-off is that the data block names exactly the things you must supply from R as a list. Warn that Stan is statically typed and picky about declaration order and semicolons — this is the number-one source of beginner frustration, so naming it now saves pain. There are more blocks (transformed data, generated quantities) but three are enough for a first model.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
The data block
Declare everything you will pass in from R, with its type and any constraints.
data {
  int<lower=0> N;   // number of cells assayed
  int<lower=0> y;   // number of them expressing the marker
}

int = integer; real = continuous. Vectors and matrices have their own types.
<lower=0> is a constraint: a count cannot be negative. Constraints are checked — they catch bad input early.
The names here (N, y) are exactly the names R must supply.


Walk the block line by line. Types are mandatory: N and y are counts, so int. The <lower=0> bound documents and enforces that these are non-negative — Stan will error loudly if you pass a negative count, which is a feature. Emphasise the contract: the identifiers declared here (N, y) are the keys R will provide in a named list. Comments use // like C++. This is deliberately the simplest possible data block; a regression would add a vector of predictors and an int for the number of observations.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
The parameters block
Declare the unknowns — the quantities the posterior is a distribution over.
parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;   // fraction of cells expressing
}

theta is our unknown fraction. It is real (continuous).
<lower=0, upper=1> constrains it to a valid probability. Stan samples only inside this range.
This one line is why the whole model exists: the posterior we want is \(p(\theta \mid y)\).


The parameters block is short but conceptually central: it names what we are trying to learn and therefore what the posterior lives on. theta is a fraction, so it is continuous and bounded to [0,1] — the lower/upper constraints are not decoration, they tell Stan to only ever propose valid probabilities, which also makes the sampler behave. Contrast with the data block: data are fixed numbers you supply; parameters are never supplied, they are inferred. Everything the printout reports later will be about this theta.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
The model block: prior + likelihood
Two statements: the prior on the parameter, and the likelihood of the data.
model {
  theta ~ beta(2, 2);          // prior: gentle hump around 0.5
  y ~ binomial(N, theta);      // likelihood: 13 of 20 expressed
}

~ reads “is distributed as”. theta ~ beta(2,2) is the prior \(p(\theta)\).
y ~ binomial(N, theta) is the likelihood \(p(y \mid \theta)\) — it links the known counts to the unknown \(\theta\).
Stan multiplies these together (adds their logs) to get the posterior — you never write the normalising integral.


This block is where the Bayes’ theorem slide becomes code, almost line for line. The tilde is the key syntax: “distributed as”. The first tilde places the prior on theta; the second places the likelihood on the observed count y given N and theta. Point out that Stan works on the log scale internally and simply accumulates these contributions, which is exactly prior-times-likelihood — the intractable denominator never appears because sampling does not need it. If a student asks “where is the posterior written?”, the answer is: nowhere explicitly; it emerges from these two lines plus sampling.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
Introduction to R-STAN
section: Running it from R with rstan
text:
Running it from R with rstan
Pass the data as a named list whose names match the data block, then call stan().
library(rstan)

stan_data <- list(N = 20, y = 13)     # names match the data block

fit <- stan(
  file   = "gene_marker.stan",
  data   = stan_data,
  chains = 4,          # run 4 independent samplers
  iter   = 2000,       # 2000 iterations each (half are warmup)
  seed   = 1           # reproducibility
)

The list keys N and y are the same identifiers declared in the model’s data block.
stan() compiles the model (once) and runs the sampler. fit holds all the posterior draws.


This is the R-side mechanics. The single most important correspondence: the named list handed to data= must have exactly the identifiers declared in the Stan data block (N and y), or Stan complains. Explain the arguments plainly: chains launches several independent samplers (used later to check convergence), iter is the length of each, and seed makes the run reproducible — worth stressing because MCMC is stochastic and results vary run to run without a seed. Compilation to C++ happens on the first call and can take a minute; the returned fit object is the pile of draws we will summarise. Note this code is illustrative and not executed here.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
section: What comes back: draws from the posterior
text:
What comes back: draws from the posterior
MCMC does not return the value of \(\theta\). It returns thousands of samples of \(\theta\), drawn in proportion to the posterior.

After warmup, 4 chains \(\times\) 1000 kept iterations \(=\) 4000 draws of \(\theta\).
A histogram of those draws is the posterior distribution.
Any summary you want is just a summary of the draws:

posterior mean \(\approx\) mean(draws)
95% credible interval \(\approx\) the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the draws.


\[\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3, \dots, \theta_{4000} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{histogram} = \text{posterior}\]


This is the single most important conceptual slide and worth dwelling on. The output of Bayesian computation is not a point but a sample — a cloud of thousands of plausible theta values whose density reproduces the posterior. Everything downstream is descriptive statistics on that sample: the mean of the draws estimates the posterior mean, and the empirical 2.5%/97.5% quantiles give a 95% credible interval. Contrast a credible interval (“95% probability theta is in here”, a direct probability statement) with a frequentist confidence interval, which students learned has a more contorted interpretation — this directness is a selling point of the Bayesian approach. The more draws, the sharper these estimates.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
Chains, warmup, and convergence
Why four chains instead of one long run?

Each chain starts from a different random point and wanders the posterior.
The first half (warmup) is discarded — the sampler is still finding the high-probability region and tuning itself.
If all four chains, from different starts, end up exploring the same distribution, we trust the result. If they disagree, something is wrong.

Running several chains is a built-in sanity check, not just extra samples.


Motivate the multi-chain design. A single chain could get stuck in a bad region and you would never know. Four independent chains from different starting points give a cheap, powerful diagnostic: if they converge to the same distribution they agree on the answer; if they wander apart, the model or sampler has a problem. Warmup (Stan’s term; also called burn-in) is the initial phase where the sampler locates and adapts to the posterior — those iterations are tuning, not sampling, so they are thrown away. The next slide turns “do the chains agree” into a single number, Rhat.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
Try it: inside the sampler




A look inside the black box, on a 2D posterior: intercept a and slope b of a small regression of gene expression on age (the example of the Bayesian fitting lecture; noise fixed so there are only two parameters). The orange ellipses are the true posterior, which a real problem would not show us. The sampler here is the simplest MCMC, random-walk Metropolis: propose a random jump of about “step size”; always accept if the posterior is higher there, sometimes accept if lower; if rejected, stay and record the same point again. Stan uses a smarter sampler (HMC/NUTS), but the output is read the same way. Press Step a few times first: each chain moves or shows a red cross for a rejected jump. Then Run: four chains start in the corners, walk in (warm-up, shaded on the traces and drawn faint on the left), then wander around the ellipses; the histograms fill with post-warm-up draws and match the orange curves. Then the presets: “tiny steps” accepts almost everything but crawls, so the chains have not met even after warm-up and R-hat is far above 1; “huge steps” rejects almost every jump, the traces become flat staircases and R-hat is again poor; “good steps” gives about 30% acceptance, overlapping fuzzy-caterpillar traces and R-hat close to 1. Optionally drag a start point (big circle) far away to show warm-up doing its job. The run is seeded, so it replays identically.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
Reading the output: print(fit)
print(fit, pars = "theta")
        mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
theta   0.63    0.00 0.10  0.42  0.56  0.63  0.70  0.82  1580    1

mean \(0.63\) — the posterior mean of \(\theta\) (pulled slightly from \(13/20=0.65\) toward the prior’s \(0.5\)).
2.5% … 97.5% \(= [0.42,\ 0.82]\) — a 95% credible interval: there is a 95% posterior probability that \(\theta\) lies in this range.
n_eff and Rhat are diagnostics — the next slide.


Read the summary table like a lab result. The mean column is the posterior mean; note it sits a touch below the raw 0.65 because the Beta(2,2) prior gently pulls toward 0.5 — a concrete illustration of the prior “reshaping” the data, and of shrinkage with small samples. The 2.5% and 97.5% columns bracket the central 95% of the draws: the credible interval, stated as a direct probability about theta. The median (50%) is another point summary. Do not gloss over how wide the interval is — with only 20 cells the uncertainty is large, which is exactly the honesty the Bayesian posterior gives you. Then hand off to the diagnostics columns.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
section: Did it work? Rhat and n_eff
text:
Did it work? Rhat and n_eff
Two numbers tell you whether to trust the draws:

Rhat (\(\hat R\)): compares variation between chains to variation within chains.

\(\hat R \approx 1.00\) means the chains agree → converged. Want \(\hat R < 1.01\).
\(\hat R = 1.1\) or more → chains disagree → do not trust the result. Run longer or fix the model.

n_eff (effective sample size): MCMC draws are correlated, so 4000 draws are worth fewer independent ones. n_eff is that effective count.

Bigger is better; a few hundred is usually plenty. Very low n_eff → estimates are noisy.


Always check these before reading the means. A pretty posterior from an unconverged sampler is meaningless.


These are the go/no-go gauges and students must build the habit of reading them first. Rhat, the potential scale reduction factor, formalises the four-chains-agree check into one number: at convergence between-chain and within-chain variance match and Rhat is 1; values above ~1.01 signal the chains have not mixed and the summaries are untrustworthy. Effective sample size acknowledges that consecutive MCMC draws are autocorrelated, so the real information content is less than the raw draw count; low n_eff means your posterior summaries are themselves noisy and you should sample more. The discipline to state: check Rhat and n_eff before you ever quote a posterior mean. This mirrors checking model diagnostics before trusting an lm fit.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
The shortcut: brms
For standard models you rarely hand-write Stan. brms takes an lm-style formula and generates the Stan model for you.
Say each of many cells has a marker outcome (expressed = 0/1) and a treatment:
library(brms)

fit <- brm(
  expressed ~ treatment,          # familiar formula interface
  data   = cells,
  family = bernoulli(),           # 0/1 outcome -> logistic regression
  prior  = prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),   # prior on coefficients
  chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 1
)

summary(fit)                      # same Rhat / credible-interval output
Same engine, same diagnostics — you just didn’t write the blocks. Understanding the rstan version is what lets you read and trust what brms builds.

Show the payoff of understanding the anatomy. brms lets you specify a Bayesian regression with the exact formula syntax students already use for lm/glm, and it writes, compiles, and runs the underlying Stan code automatically — including sensible defaults you can override, like the normal(0,1) prior on the regression coefficients. The family argument picks the likelihood (bernoulli for a 0/1 outcome gives Bayesian logistic regression; you could use poisson or negative_binomial for counts). Crucially, the output is the same posterior-draws-plus-Rhat picture, so everything learned today transfers. The pedagogical point: brms is not magic once you have seen the three blocks by hand — you know what it generated and how to check it.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
Common pitfalls

Data names must match. The list passed from R must use the exact identifiers in the data block (N, y), or Stan errors.
Types and constraints are strict. A count is int; a probability is real<lower=0, upper=1>. Mismatches fail to compile.
Ignoring Rhat / n_eff. Never quote a posterior before checking convergence.
Too few iterations. If Rhat is high or n_eff low, increase iter (and warmup).
The prior is a choice. State it and, ideally, check whether the posterior is sensitive to it. A flat prior is still a prior.


A short troubleshooting tour so first errors are less baffling. The name-matching and type-strictness points cover the overwhelming majority of “it won’t compile” beginner failures — worth saying explicitly. The diagnostic points reinforce the previous two slides: a run can complete and still be untrustworthy, so Rhat and n_eff gate everything. The prior reminder is both practical and philosophical: choosing a prior is unavoidable (even “flat” is a decision), it should be reported alongside results, and a good habit is a sensitivity check — does the conclusion change under a reasonable alternative prior? This connects back to the Bayesian-vs-frequentist discussion from earlier units.

title: Introduction to R-STAN
text:
Summary







Idea
Takeaway




Goal
compute the posterior \(p(\theta\mid y)\) for real models


Stan
a language + engine that samples the posterior


data block
the knowns you pass in from R (typed, constrained)


parameters block
the unknowns the posterior is over


model block
~ statements: prior and likelihood


Run it
stan(file, data = list(...), chains, iter)


Output
thousands of draws; summarise them


Posterior mean
mean of the draws


Credible interval
2.5% / 97.5% quantiles of the draws


Rhat
\(\approx 1\) = chains agree = trust it (\(<1.01\))


n_eff
effective (independent) sample size — bigger is better


brms
writes the Stan model from an lm-style formula



The mantra: describe the model, sample the posterior, check Rhat, then read the draws.

The summary is the working checklist. Drill the pipeline verbally one more time: pick a likelihood and priors, write the three blocks, hand R a matching data list, call stan, and — before anything else — check Rhat and n_eff; only then read the posterior mean and credible interval off the draws. Reiterate the one-sentence mantra. Remind them brms automates the writing but not the understanding or the checking. Close by re-flagging that the block is provisional and may move, so this is groundwork rather than exam material, and point them to the exercise, which walks through a Poisson count model in the same three-block pattern.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
About this lecture
In UMAPs and clustering you turned a single-cell dataset into clusters — groups of cells that look alike. But a cluster is just a number (“cluster 3”). The biology question is: cluster 3 is which cell type?

A cluster is a cloud of cells in gene space; annotation asks what that cloud is.
Marker genes: the genes a cluster switches on that the others do not — found by differential expression (DE) of each cluster against the rest.
Two routes to a label: manual (match markers to known cell-type signatures) and reference-based (let a labelled dataset vote).
The honest caveats: ambiguous clusters, doublets, and continuous states that resist discrete labels.
The maths underneath is the same as before: cells are vectors, a cluster mean is a centroid, and a marker is a coordinate where two groups of vectors differ.


The one sentence for today: clustering groups cells, annotation names the groups. Everything else — marker genes, differential expression, reference mapping — is machinery for attaching a biological label to an otherwise anonymous cluster. Stress that this is where the linear-algebra and statistics of the whole course pay off in a real workflow: each cell is a vector of gene counts, a cluster is a cloud of those vectors, and finding markers is comparing coordinates between clouds. Keep an R session narrative going but remind them nothing here runs live; the point is to read the output of a FindMarkers-style table, not to memorise a package API.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
A biology picture first
You dissociate a piece of tissue — say a tumour biopsy — into single cells, sequence them, and cluster. The UMAP shows a dozen blobs.

One blob is probably T cells, another macrophages, another tumour epithelium — but the algorithm does not know that. It only knows “these cells are similar.”
To use the experiment — “how many T cells infiltrated the tumour?”, “which cluster is proliferating?” — every blob needs a name.
Immunologists already know that T cells express CD3D, B cells express MS4A1 (CD20), macrophages express CD68. That prior knowledge is what we exploit.

Annotation is the bridge from clusters the computer found to cell types the biologist recognises.


Ground the abstraction in a concrete experiment before any method. A tumour biopsy is ideal because the audience already has the intuition that tissue is a mixture of cell types, and the whole point of single-cell is to pull that mixture apart. Emphasise that the clustering step is unsupervised and therefore label-free: the algorithm returns “cluster 0..11”, not “T cell”. The biological knowledge that CD3D marks T cells etc. lives in the literature and in the biologist’s head; annotation is the disciplined way of injecting it. Do not yet say how we find that CD3D is high in a cluster — that is the DE step, coming up.

title: Cell-type annotation
section: What a cluster is, in vector terms
text:
What a cluster is, in vector terms
From PCA and clustering: each cell is a vector of measured genes,
\[\mathbf{x}_{\text{cell}} = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_G), \qquad x_g = \text{(normalised) expression of gene } g.\]

A cluster is a set of these vectors that sit close together — a cloud in \(G\)-dimensional gene space.
Its mean vector (the average over cells in the cluster) is the cluster centroid — the “typical expression profile” of that cell type.
Annotation compares centroids: which genes is this cluster’s centroid high in, relative to the others?

So the question “what is cluster 3?” becomes “on which gene coordinates does cluster 3’s centroid stick out?”


This slide explicitly reconnects to the vector and PCA language the students already own. A cell is a point/vector; a cluster is a cloud; the centroid is the mean vector, coordinate by coordinate. Framing annotation as comparing centroids coordinate-by-coordinate sets up differential expression as nothing exotic — it is per-gene comparison of group means, exactly the sort of two-group comparison they met in the statistics course. Resist introducing the test yet; just plant that a “marker” will be a coordinate where one centroid is far above the others.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
Marker genes: the core idea
A marker gene for a cluster is a gene that is expressed much more highly in that cluster than in the rest of the cells.

Markers are how we recognise a type: high CD3D → T cell, high MS4A1 → B cell, high HBB → red blood cell.
Good markers are specific (on in one cluster, off elsewhere) and sensitive (on in most cells of that cluster).
We do not pick markers by eye across thousands of genes — we rank genes by how strongly they separate the cluster from everything else.

That ranking is a differential expression problem: for each gene, compare its expression inside the cluster to outside.


Define a marker crisply: differentially high in one group. Two quality axes matter and map onto quantities we will see in the output table — specificity (expressed elsewhere or not, i.e. pct.2 low) and sensitivity (expressed in most of the cluster, i.e. pct.1 high). Make the point that with ~20000 genes you cannot eyeball this; you need a systematic score per gene. That score is a differential-expression statistic, which is the next block. Note that “marker” is relative — a gene is a marker with respect to a particular comparison (this cluster vs the rest).

title: Cell-type annotation
section: Differential expression: one cluster vs the rest
text:
Differential expression: one cluster vs the rest
To find markers for cluster \(k\), split the cells into two groups and test every gene:

Group 1: the cells in cluster \(k\).
Group 2: all other cells (the “rest”).

This is the one-vs-rest comparison. For each gene we ask: is its expression distribution different between the two groups, and by how much?
Two numbers summarise each gene:

a log fold change — how many-fold higher (or lower) the mean is in group 1 vs group 2, on a \(\log_2\) scale;
a p-value — is the difference bigger than we would expect by chance?

Repeat for every cluster and you have candidate markers for all of them.


One-vs-rest is the standard framing for marker discovery: cluster k against the pooled remainder. Contrast with a pairwise comparison (cluster k vs cluster j), which is also possible and sometimes needed to separate two similar types, but one-vs-rest is the default first pass. Emphasise the two outputs per gene: an effect size (log fold change, a difference of log means) and a significance (p-value). Both matter — a huge but noisy difference and a tiny but rock-solid difference are both misleading on their own. This is exactly the effect-size-plus-p-value thinking from their statistics course, now applied per gene across the transcriptome.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
The statistic under the hood
For a single gene, we are comparing two sets of numbers (its expression in group 1 vs group 2). The default test in single-cell tools is the Wilcoxon rank-sum test:

rank all the cells by that gene’s expression, then ask whether group-1 cells sit systematically higher in the ranking;
it is non-parametric — it does not assume the counts are Gaussian, which matters because single-cell counts are sparse and skewed (recall the negative-binomial / overdispersion story for count data).

The log fold change is the effect size:
\[\text{log}_2\text{FC} = \log_2\frac{\text{mean expression in group 1}}{\text{mean expression in group 2}}.\]
A large positive \(\log_2\)FC and a small p-value together flag a marker.


Name the default test honestly: Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney). Explain the intuition — rank cells by the gene, see if one group is shifted up — rather than the formula. Justify non-parametric by pointing back to the count-data thread of the course: expression counts are overdispersed and zero-inflated, not Gaussian, so a t-test’s assumptions are shaky; a rank test sidesteps the distributional assumption. Then define log fold change as a difference of log means (log of a ratio = difference of logs). Stress that neither number alone is a marker: you filter on both effect size and significance. Mention that other tests exist (t-test, negative-binomial-based, MAST) but Wilcoxon is the common default.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
Reading a marker table (FindMarkers-style)
In practice you run a one-vs-rest scan across all clusters. A typical call (Seurat):
# cells already clustered; identities set to cluster labels
markers <- FindAllMarkers(
  seurat_obj,
  only.pos       = TRUE,   # keep genes UP in each cluster (candidate markers)
  min.pct        = 0.25,   # gene must be detected in >=25% of one group
  logfc.threshold = 0.25   # require at least this log2 fold change
)
This returns one row per (gene, cluster) that passes the filters. The columns are the quantities from the last two slides.

Show the call as static code they read, not run. Walk the arguments: only.pos keeps upregulated genes because markers are things a type switches ON; min.pct is a detection filter (skip genes seen in almost no cells, which are unstable); logfc.threshold is a minimum effect size so you are not testing thousands of flat genes. FindAllMarkers loops the one-vs-rest test over every cluster and stacks the results. Emphasise that these thresholds are pragmatic speed/false-positive filters, not deep truths. Next slide dissects the output columns.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
What the columns mean
A few rows of the output for one cluster:
#        p_val avg_log2FC pct.1 pct.2 p_val_adj cluster   gene
#  0.000e+00       3.85   0.98  0.05  0.000e+00       3  CD3D
#  1.2e-270        3.10   0.95  0.11  4.1e-266        3  CD3E
#  8.7e-190        2.40   0.90  0.20  3.0e-186        3   IL7R

avg_log2FC — effect size: \(\log_2\) fold change, cluster vs rest. \(3.85\) means \(\approx 2^{3.85} \approx 14\times\) higher.
pct.1 — fraction of cluster cells expressing the gene (sensitivity). \(0.98\) = nearly all.
pct.2 — fraction of the rest expressing it (specificity). \(0.05\) = almost none elsewhere.
p_val_adj — p-value after multiple-testing correction (you tested ~20 000 genes).

CD3D: high fold change, on in 98% of the cluster, off (5%) elsewhere → a textbook T-cell marker.

This is the heart of the practical skill: read a marker table. Spell out each column and tie it to a concept. avg_log2FC is the difference of log means from the DE slide; convert 3.85 to ~14-fold so the log scale feels concrete. pct.1 and pct.2 are the sensitivity/specificity pair from the marker-quality slide — pct.1 high and pct.2 low is exactly what “specific and sensitive” looks like numerically. p_val_adj must be the adjusted p-value because we ran ~20000 tests per cluster; recall multiple-testing from statistics (Seurat uses Bonferroni by default here). Land the reading: CD3D scores well on all axes, so cluster 3 is T cells. Warn that a good p-value alone is not enough — with thousands of cells almost everything is “significant”; the fold change and the pct columns are what make it a marker.

title: Cell-type annotation
section: From markers to a label: the manual workflow
text:
From markers to a label: the manual workflow
The classic annotation loop, cluster by cluster:

Find markers — one-vs-rest DE for each cluster (previous slides).
Compare to known markers — look the top genes up against curated cell-type signatures (CellMarker, PanglaoDB, or the lab’s own list).
Label the cluster with the best-matching type; sanity-check on the UMAP.

top <- head(markers[markers$cluster == 3, ], 10)$gene
top   # "CD3D" "CD3E" "IL7R" "CD2" "CD3G" ...  -> T cells

seurat_obj <- RenameIdents(seurat_obj, `3` = "T cell")
Repeat for every cluster until the whole UMAP is named.


This is the workflow the prompt asks us to make explicit: find markers, compare to known signatures, label. Databases (CellMarker, PanglaoDB) or a curated in-house list turn a gene list into a cell-type guess. Stress that this is human-in-the-loop and iterative: you propose a label, then check it makes biological sense (do the neighbouring clusters make a coherent lineage? does the fraction match expectation?). RenameIdents just attaches the human-readable name. Warn that top-10 lists can be dominated by housekeeping or ribosomal genes if normalisation was sloppy — another reason a human eye is in the loop.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
Known cell-type signatures
A signature is a small set of genes expected to be high in a given type. Matching a cluster’s markers to signatures is the manual annotator’s dictionary.



Cell type
Canonical markers




T cell
CD3D, CD3E, CD2


B cell
MS4A1 (CD20), CD79A


Macrophage / monocyte
CD68, LYZ, CD14


NK cell
NKG7, GNLY


Endothelial
PECAM1 (CD31), VWF


Red blood cell
HBB, HBA1




Instead of eyeballing one gene, you can score each cell for a whole signature (mean expression of the set) and see which cluster lights up.
A signature is a direction in gene space; scoring a cell is essentially a dot product of its expression with the signature.



Give them a real, standard marker table — these are all textbook and safe. The move from single markers to signatures matters: one gene is noisy (dropout means a real T cell may show zero CD3D reads), but the average over several markers is robust. Introduce module/signature scoring (AddModuleScore in Seurat) as averaging a gene set per cell. The linear-algebra payoff: a signature is a weighted direction in gene space and scoring a cell is a dot product / projection onto that direction — a callback to vectors and projection. Keep it conceptual; no need for the exact scoring algorithm.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
Reference-based annotation
Instead of curating markers by hand, borrow labels from an already-annotated dataset (a reference atlas).

Each reference cell type has a known expression profile (a centroid, or many labelled cells).
For each query cell (yours), find which reference profile it most resembles, and copy that label.
“Resembles” is a similarity measure — typically correlation between the query cell’s expression vector and each reference profile.

Tools: SingleR (correlation to reference profiles), Azimuth (mapping onto a reference atlas), CellTypist (a trained classifier). All answer the same question: which reference does this cell look like?


Reference-based annotation automates the label transfer: given a trustworthy labelled dataset, assign each query cell the label of the reference it correlates with most. Frame the similarity as correlation between expression vectors — another vector-geometry callback (correlation is a centred, normalised dot product / cosine). Name the common tools truthfully and by what they do: SingleR correlates to reference profiles, Azimuth maps to a curated atlas, CellTypist is a logistic-regression classifier trained on labelled data. The key dependency to flag: the answer is only as good as the reference. A cell type absent from the reference cannot be labelled correctly — it will be forced onto the nearest wrong label.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
Manual vs reference-based









Manual (markers)
Reference-based




Input
curated marker lists
a labelled reference dataset


Granularity
your choice, cluster-level
as fine as the reference


Strength
transparent, uses expert knowledge
fast, consistent, per-cell


Weakness
slow, subjective, needs expertise
only as good as the reference; misses novel types


Best for
new/unusual tissue, discovery
well-studied tissue (blood, common atlases)



In practice you combine them: reference-based for a fast first pass, manual markers to confirm, refine, and catch anything the reference lacks.

A balanced comparison so students choose appropriately. Manual is transparent and encodes expert judgement but is slow and subjective, and it labels clusters (not cells). Reference-based is fast, reproducible, and per-cell, but inherits every gap and bias of the reference — crucially it cannot discover a cell type the reference never saw. Best practice is to combine: run a reference method for speed, then verify with a handful of canonical markers per cluster. Emphasise that neither is “automatic truth”; both need the human sanity check on the UMAP and against known biology.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
Caveat: ambiguous clusters
Not every cluster names cleanly.

No clear markers — a cluster’s top DE genes are weak or generic (ribosomal, mitochondrial). Often low-quality cells or a clustering artefact.
Mixed markers — one cluster shows both T-cell (CD3D) and myeloid (LYZ) markers. Real biology? A doublet cluster? Under-clustering?
Resolution — turning the clustering resolution up may split a vague blob into two clean types; too high and you over-split one type into noise.

Annotation and clustering are iterative: an unnameable cluster is a signal to re-cluster, adjust resolution, or check quality control.


Set expectations: real datasets always have a couple of clusters that resist a label. Enumerate the usual culprits — a cluster dominated by ribosomal/mito genes is usually dying or stressed cells (QC problem), not a cell type; a cluster with two lineages’ markers is either a doublet artefact or a signal that the resolution is wrong. The takeaway is that annotation feeds back into clustering: you rarely get the resolution right on the first try, and an ambiguous cluster is diagnostic. This reinforces that the UMAPs-and-clustering step and the annotation step are one loop, not a pipeline you run once.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
Caveat: doublets
A doublet is two cells captured in one droplet and sequenced as if they were one “cell.”

Its expression profile is a sum of two types → it shows both sets of markers (e.g. T-cell and B-cell genes).
Doublets can form their own small cluster that looks like a fake “hybrid” cell type — a classic annotation trap.
Detect them with dedicated tools (scDblFinder, DoubletFinder) that flag cells looking like blends of two profiles, then remove them before finalising annotation.

A “cell type” that co-expresses two lineages’ exclusive markers should raise a doublet suspicion first.


Doublets are the most common way annotation goes wrong for a beginner: a droplet catches two cells, the reads combine, and you get a profile that is literally the sum of two centroids. Because it carries both marker sets, an untrained eye may christen a new “T/B hybrid” cell type that does not exist. The linear-algebra intuition — the doublet vector is roughly the sum of two cell vectors — is worth stating. Practically: run a doublet detector, remove flagged cells, then annotate. Give the rule of thumb: exclusive markers of two distinct lineages appearing together is a doublet until proven otherwise.

title: Cell-type annotation
section: Caveat: continuous states vs discrete types
text:
Caveat: continuous states vs discrete types
We label clusters as if cell identity were discrete boxes. Biology is often a continuum.

Differentiation: stem → progenitor → mature is a smooth trajectory; any cut into “types” is partly arbitrary.
Activation states: a resting vs activated T cell is the same type in a different state, not two types.
Cell cycle: proliferating cells shift along a cycle axis — a continuous state that can even drive spurious clusters (revisited in Cell-cycle analysis).

Clustering discretises a continuum. Sometimes that is fine (blood has fairly distinct types); sometimes a trajectory / pseudotime view is truer than any set of labels.


The deepest caveat: the discrete-type model is a convenient fiction. Where cells sit on a smooth developmental or activation gradient, drawing cluster boundaries is a modelling choice, not a discovery of nature. Give the three canonical continua: differentiation trajectories, activation states (same type, different state), and the cell cycle (which is a continuous axis and can create artefactual clusters — a direct hook to the following Cell-cycle analysis unit). The honest message: match the representation to the biology. Discrete labels for discrete tissue; pseudotime/trajectory methods when the biology is a gradient. This is design principle 6 in action — be honest about what the simplification hides.

title: Cell-type annotation
section: Tying it back: DE is comparing groups of vectors
text:
Tying it back: DE is comparing groups of vectors
Everything today is the course’s linear-algebra and statistics, reused:

A cell is a vector of gene expression; a cluster is a cloud of such vectors (UMAPs and clustering, PCA).
A cluster centroid is the mean vector — the typical profile of a type.
A marker gene is a coordinate where one cluster’s centroid stands far from the rest.
Differential expression is a two-group comparison per coordinate — effect size (log fold change = difference of log means) plus significance (a rank test), with multiple-testing correction because there are ~20 000 coordinates.
A signature score is a dot product of a cell with a cell-type direction; reference mapping is correlation to reference profiles.

No new mathematics — a new application of vectors, means, and hypothesis tests.

Consolidation slide: make the students see that annotation invented nothing mathematically new. Cells-as-vectors and clusters-as-clouds come from PCA and clustering; centroids are means; a marker is a coordinate where centroids separate; DE is the two-group hypothesis test from statistics applied per gene with multiple-testing control; signature scoring and reference mapping are dot products and correlations from vector geometry. This is the payoff of the whole course architecture — the same small toolkit (vectors, means, tests) recombines into a real single-cell workflow. Send them into the exercise with this map in mind.

title: Cell-type annotation
text:
Summary







Idea
Key point




Clusters vs types
clustering groups cells; annotation names the groups


Marker gene
gene high in one cluster, low elsewhere (specific + sensitive)


Differential expression
one-vs-rest per gene: log fold change and adjusted p-value


Default test
Wilcoxon rank-sum (non-parametric — counts aren’t Gaussian)


Reading the table
avg_log2FC, pct.1, pct.2, p_val_adj


Manual workflow
find markers → match to known signatures → label → check


Reference-based
copy labels from a labelled atlas by similarity (correlation)


Caveats
ambiguous clusters, doublets, continuous states


Under the hood
cells = vectors, centroids = means, markers = separating coordinates



Next (Cell-cycle analysis): a continuous state that can dominate clustering — how to score it and, if needed, regress it out.

The summary is the take-home map. Drill the reading of a marker table one more time because it is the concrete exam-and-lab skill: fold change for effect size, pct.1/pct.2 for sensitivity/specificity, adjusted p-value for significance under massive multiple testing. Restate the two annotation routes and when to use each, and the three caveats that catch beginners. Close on the unifying idea — vectors, means, and two-group tests — and hand off to Cell-cycle analysis, where a continuous state (the cycle) is treated head-on.

title: Exercise: cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain why the cell cycle is a major axis of variation in single-cell data,
compute a module score for a gene set by hand (average expression, then a background-corrected version),
assign a cell-cycle phase (G1 / S / G2M) from two scores using the standard rule,
reason about why a cell-cycle program lands on a top principal component,
diagnose what a PC represents using loadings and correlation with a covariate,
decide when to regress the cell cycle out and when to keep it, and describe the per-gene lm that does the regression.

This is an applied concept day. The R below is shown for understanding and is not meant to be run (no single-cell object is provided); the by-hand parts are the ones to master.

title: Exercise: cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain why the cell cycle is a major axis of variation in single-cell data,
compute a module score for a gene set by hand (average expression, then a background-corrected version),
assign a cell-cycle phase (G1 / S / G2M) from two scores using the standard rule,
reason about why a cell-cycle program lands on a top principal component,
diagnose what a PC represents using loadings and correlation with a covariate,
decide when to regress the cell cycle out and when to keep it, and describe the per-gene lm that does the regression.

This is an applied concept day. The R below is shown for understanding and is not meant to be run (no single-cell object is provided); the by-hand parts are the ones to master.

title: Exercise: cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
Background
The cell cycle is a coordinated transcriptional program. As a cell moves toward division it turns on S-phase genes (DNA replication: PCNA, MCM family, TYMS) and then G2/M genes (mitosis: TOP2A, MKI67, CCNB1/2, CDK1). Because hundreds of genes move together, the cycle contributes a large amount of covariance — and PCA finds directions of large covariance. So a top principal component often is the cell cycle, and clustering (built on the PCA embedding) can end up grouping cells by how much they divide rather than what they are.
Scoring a phase. For a gene set \(\mathcal{S}\) and cell \(c\), the plain module score is the average expression of the set,
\[\text{Score}_{\mathcal{S}}(c) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{S}} x_{gc},\]
where \(x_{gc}\) is log-normalised expression. The background-corrected score (the AddModuleScore / CellCycleScoring idea) subtracts the average of a set of expression-matched control genes,
\[\text{Score}_{\mathcal{S}}(c) = \overline{x}_{\mathcal{S}}(c) - \overline{x}_{\text{ctrl}}(c),\]
so a score near 0 means “no more than background” and a clearly positive score means the program is on.
Assigning the phase. With \(\text{Score}_S\) and \(\text{Score}_{G2M}\): if both are low (near/below 0) call it G1; otherwise take the phase of the larger positive score.
Removing it. If the cycle is a nuisance, regress it out per gene before PCA: \[x_{gc} = \beta_{0g} + \beta_{1g}\,\text{Score}_S(c) + \beta_{2g}\,\text{Score}_{G2M}(c) + \varepsilon_{gc},\] and feed the residuals \(\varepsilon_{gc}\) to PCA. Only do this when proliferation is not part of the answer you want.

title: Exercise: cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
By hand
B1. In one sentence, explain why the cell cycle is a much bigger problem in single-cell RNA-seq than in bulk RNA-seq.
B2. A cell has log-normalised expression for four S-phase markers: PCNA \(=2.0\), MCM6 \(=1.6\), TYMS \(=2.4\), MCM2 \(=2.0\). Compute the plain (uncorrected) S-phase module score.
B3. For the same cell, the matched control gene set averages to \(\overline{x}_{\text{ctrl}} = 1.4\). Compute the background-corrected S-phase score. Is the S program on or off for this cell?
B4. Three cells have the following scores. Assign each a phase (G1 / S / G2M) using the standard rule.

B6. You cross-tabulate your clusters against the assigned phase and get the table below. Which cluster is a likely cell-cycle artefact, and why? What is one reason you should not immediately delete it?
