title: Exercise: cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
In R
The code below is illustrative (static — nothing to run here). It mirrors the standard Seurat workflow so you recognise it later.

Score the cell cycle
library(Seurat)

s.genes   <- cc.genes.updated.2019$s.genes     # curated S-phase markers
g2m.genes <- cc.genes.updated.2019$g2m.genes   # curated G2/M markers

# obj must already be normalised (LogNormalize) before scoring
obj <- CellCycleScoring(
  obj,
  s.features   = s.genes,
  g2m.features = g2m.genes,
  set.ident    = FALSE
)

head(obj[[]][, c("S.Score", "G2M.Score", "Phase")])


Diagnose whether a PC is the cell cycle
obj <- RunPCA(obj)

pc1 <- Embeddings(obj, "pca")[, 1]
cor(pc1, obj$S.Score)      # strong correlation => PC1 tracks the cycle
cor(pc1, obj$G2M.Score)

# and cross-tabulate clusters against phase
table(Cluster = Idents(obj), Phase = obj$Phase)


Regress it out (only if it is a nuisance) and re-check
obj <- ScaleData(obj, vars.to.regress = c("S.Score", "G2M.Score"),
                 features = rownames(obj))
obj <- RunPCA(obj)

pc1 <- Embeddings(obj, "pca")[, 1]
cor(pc1, obj$S.Score)      # should now be near 0 if the correction worked


A tiny by-hand version of the module score (base R)
This toy computes the plain module score for one gene set, to show there is no magic — it is a mean over chosen rows of the expression matrix.
# expr: genes (rows) x cells (columns), log-normalised
s.set <- c("PCNA", "MCM6", "TYMS", "MCM2")
score_S <- colMeans(expr[s.set, ])     # one number per cell
head(score_S)


Tasks
R1. In the toy base-R snippet, explain in words what colMeans(expr[s.set, ]) returns and why its length equals the number of cells.
R2. Sketch (in words or pseudocode) how you would turn the plain score_S into a background-corrected score using a control gene set ctrl.set, matching the formula in the Background.
R3. Given S.Score and G2M.Score columns, write a one-line rule (in words or R) that reproduces the phase-assignment logic from B4.

title: Exercise: cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — bulk vs single-cell (B1)





In bulk RNA-seq you average over millions of cells, so cells in different phases cancel out. In single-cell data each cell is captured at one definite phase, so the cell-to-cell differences survive and become a visible axis of variation.









Hint 2 — the plain module score (B2)





The plain score is just the mean of the listed values: add the four numbers and divide by four. This is the same average you would get from colMeans applied to those rows of the expression matrix.









Hint 3 — background correction (B3)





Subtract the control average from the marker average: \(\overline{x}_{\mathcal{S}} - \overline{x}_{\text{ctrl}}\). A positive result means the markers are above the background level the cell would show anyway, so the program is on.









Hint 4 — assigning a phase (B4)





Rule: if both scores are \(\le 0\) (or near 0), call it G1. Otherwise pick the phase whose score is the largest positive value. Compare the two scores per cell.









Hint 5 — what a PC means (B5)





The loadings are the eigenvector entries — how much each gene contributes to the axis (see Principal component analysis). If cell-cycle genes dominate the loadings, the PC is the cell cycle. Confirm by correlating that PC’s scores with S.Score / G2M.Score using cor.









Hint 6 — reading the cross-tab (B6)





A cluster that is almost entirely one phase is suspicious: it may be grouping cells by division state rather than identity. But some real cell types (transit-amplifying / progenitor cells) genuinely are highly proliferative — so treat it as a flag to investigate, not an automatic delete.









Hint 7 — regress or keep? (B7)





Ask: is proliferation part of the answer I want? If yes (development, tumour, activation, stem/progenitor comparisons), keep it — regressing it out could erase your result. If it merely hides the identities you are after, remove it. When you care that a cell cycles but not where in the cycle, regress the difference S.Score - G2M.Score.









Hint 8 — the check failed (B8)





If the correlation is still high after regressing out, the correction did not take. Check that scoring ran before ScaleData, that the score columns were actually passed to vars.to.regress, and that RunPCA used the scaled (residual) data. Always verify a correction rather than assuming it worked.

title: Exercise: cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. In bulk RNA-seq the signal is averaged over millions of cells so cell-cycle differences cancel; in single-cell data every cell has a definite phase, so cell-cycle variation is preserved and becomes one of the largest axes of variation.
B2. Plain S-phase score \(= \dfrac{2.0 + 1.6 + 2.4 + 2.0}{4} = \dfrac{8.0}{4} = 2.0\).
B3. Background-corrected score \(= \overline{x}_{\mathcal{S}} - \overline{x}_{\text{ctrl}} = 2.0 - 1.4 = 0.6\). This is clearly positive, so the S program is on in this cell.
B4. - Cell A: \(\text{Score}_S = 0.61\) (positive) beats \(\text{Score}_{G2M} = -0.10\) → S. - Cell B: \(\text{Score}_{G2M} = 0.55\) (positive) beats \(\text{Score}_S = -0.04\) → G2M. - Cell C: both scores negative → G1.
B5. PC1 most likely represents the cell cycle (specifically a G2/M-heavy division signature — MKI67, TOP2A, CCNB1, CDK1 are G2/M markers, PCNA is S-phase). To confirm, compute the correlation between each cell’s PC1 score and its G2M.Score (and S.Score); a high value confirms PC1 tracks the cycle.
B6. Cluster 1 is the likely artefact: it is almost entirely S + G2M cells (389 of 404), so it appears to be grouping cells by division state rather than by identity. You should not immediately delete it because some real cell types are genuinely highly proliferative (e.g. transit-amplifying or progenitor cells) — the one-phase cluster is a flag to investigate (check its marker genes, or re-cluster after regressing out the cycle), not a guaranteed technical artefact.
B7. (a) Regress out — here proliferation is not the question; the cycle just blurs the resting-T-cell subtypes you want to resolve. (b) Keep — proliferating vs. quiescent is the biology; regressing it out would erase the comparison. (c) Regress out the difference S.Score - G2M.Score: this removes the phase gradient among cycling cells but keeps the cycling-vs-non-cycling contrast you care about.
B8. A correlation of \(0.72\) means the cell cycle is still driving PC1, so the correction did not take effect. Check that (i) CellCycleScoring ran and produced the score columns before ScaleData; (ii) vars.to.regress = c("S.Score","G2M.Score") was actually passed; and (iii) RunPCA was run on the scaled/residual data (not a cached earlier PCA). Re-run in the correct order and re-check — the correlation should drop close to 0.
R1. expr[s.set, ] selects the rows of the expression matrix for the S-phase genes, giving a (genes-in-set × cells) submatrix. colMeans averages down each column, i.e. over the genes in the set, producing one score per cell — hence its length equals the number of cells (columns).
R2. Compute the marker average and a control average, then subtract:
score_S_raw  <- colMeans(expr[s.set, ])
score_S_ctrl <- colMeans(expr[ctrl.set, ])
score_S      <- score_S_raw - score_S_ctrl     # background-corrected
(The real AddModuleScore picks ctrl.set to have expression levels matched to the markers; the subtraction logic is identical.)
R3. One rule: for each cell, if S.Score <= 0 & G2M.Score <= 0 assign G1, else assign S if S.Score > G2M.Score and G2M otherwise. In R, for example:
phase <- ifelse(S.Score <= 0 & G2M.Score <= 0, "G1",
         ifelse(S.Score >  G2M.Score,          "S", "G2M"))

title: Exercise: cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
Where this leads

Multiome data integration and clustering workflows: the same “interpret your components” discipline applies to every latent space, not just PCA — always ask whether a shared axis is biology or a technical artefact.
Batch, depth, and stress as confounders: cell cycle is one example of a covariate that can seize a principal component. Sequencing depth (nCount_RNA), mitochondrial fraction (percent.mt), and batch/donor are diagnosed and, if needed, regressed out with exactly the same recipe.
Cell-type annotation: once nuisance axes are handled, the clusters you interpret and label reflect identity rather than division state.

title: Quiz: cell cycle & connection to PCA
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of cell-cycle scoring and its link to PCA. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Several are written in the style of the on-campus exam (no computer).

Q1. Why is the cell cycle a much larger problem in single-cell RNA-seq than in bulk RNA-seq?






Hint





What happens to phase differences when you average over millions of cells?









Answer





Bulk RNA-seq averages over millions of cells, so cells in different phases cancel and the cycle largely washes out. In single-cell data each cell is captured at one definite phase, so cell-cycle variation is preserved and becomes one of the largest axes of variation across cells.




Q2. A cell-cycle module score is computed from a set of marker genes rather than a single marker gene. Give one reason why.






Hint





Think about dropouts and noise in single-cell counts.









Answer





Single-cell counts are sparse and noisy (dropouts), so any one gene is unreliable. Averaging over a curated set of co-expressed phase markers gives a robust, stable estimate of whether the program is on.




Q3. In the background-corrected score \(\text{Score}_{\mathcal{S}}(c) = \overline{x}_{\mathcal{S}}(c) - \overline{x}_{\text{ctrl}}(c)\), what is the purpose of subtracting the control-gene average?






Hint





Some cells have more total counts / more genes detected than others.









Answer





It removes the background a cell would show anyway due to its overall expression level / sequencing depth. The expression-matched control set tracks that background, so subtracting it isolates the genuine cell-cycle signal. A score near 0 then means “no more than background”.




Q4. A cell has \(\text{Score}_S = -0.05\) and \(\text{Score}_{G2M} = 0.48\). Which phase is it assigned, and why?






Hint





If a program is on, its score is clearly positive; take the larger positive score.









Answer





G2M. The G2/M score is clearly positive and larger than the S score (which is around/below 0), so the G2/M program is the active one.




Q5. Why does the cell cycle so often show up as one of the top principal components?






Hint





What does PCA maximise, and how do co-expressed genes affect covariance?









Answer





PCA returns the directions of greatest variance (eigenvectors of the covariance matrix). Cell-cycle genes are strongly co-expressed, so they contribute a large block of shared variance/covariance. That coordinated variation forms a leading eigenvector, so a top PC frequently aligns with the cell-cycle axis.




Q6. You want to check whether PC1 represents the cell cycle. Name two things you could look at.






Hint





One uses the eigenvector entries; the other relates PC scores to a covariate you measured.









Answer






The loadings of PC1 — if the top-loading genes are cell-cycle markers (MKI67, TOP2A, PCNA, TYMS…), the PC is the cycle. (2) The correlation between each cell’s PC1 score and its S.Score / G2M.Score — a high correlation confirms PC1 tracks the cycle.





Q7. Regressing the cell cycle out is done with a per-gene linear model. Which part of the model do we keep and feed to PCA, and why?






Hint





Split each gene’s expression into a fitted part and what is left over.









Answer





We keep the residuals \(\varepsilon_{gc}\). For each gene we regress its expression on the cell-cycle scores; the fitted part is the variation explained by the cycle, and the residual is the expression with that part removed. Feeding residuals to PCA flattens the cell-cycle axis so it no longer claims a top PC.




Q8. True or false: you should always regress the cell cycle out before clustering. Explain.






Hint





Is proliferation ever the biology you actually want to study?









Answer





False. Regression removes real signal, so it is a judgement call. If proliferation is the biology (tumour, development, immune activation, stem/progenitor comparisons), removing the cycle can erase your result. Regress it out only when it is a nuisance hiding the cell identities you want — and consider regressing only S.Score - G2M.Score when you care that a cell divides but not where in the cycle it is.




Q9. State the general lesson this unit teaches about principal components (beyond the cell cycle specifically).






Hint





What else besides cell cycle can a top PC turn out to be — batch, depth, stress…?









Answer





A principal component is simply the direction of greatest variance, and that can be anything — cell cycle, sequencing depth, mitochondrial/stress, batch/donor, ambient RNA, or real cell identity. PCA is unsupervised: it hands you directions, not meanings. The analyst must interpret each component (biological signal vs. technical artefact), typically by reading loadings and correlating PC scores with known covariates.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
text:
About this lecture
Until now a gene-expression experiment gave you one number per gene per sample — a bulk average over millions of cells. Single-cell RNA-seq gives you one number per gene per cell, for thousands of cells at once. That changes both the biology we can ask and the data structure we handle.

The data object: a sparse cells × genes count matrix, mostly zeros.
Where the numbers come from: the droplet workflow, at a high level.
Why the counts are noisy and sparse, and what that forces us to do.
Quality control: removing low-quality cells, empty droplets, and doublets.
Preprocessing: normalization, log transform, and picking highly variable genes.

This is a concept + data-handling day. No new by-hand math; the log transform gets its own unit next (Log and pseudolog transforms), and the linear algebra payoff (PCA, UMAP) comes after that, in Dimensionality reduction & clustering.

Frame the whole unit as a shift in resolution: bulk RNA-seq averages over a tissue, single-cell resolves the individual cells that make it up. Everything today is about (1) understanding the data structure that comes out of the machine and (2) cleaning it so the downstream analysis is trustworthy. Emphasise that we deliberately stop before PCA/clustering — those need the cleaned matrix we build today. Keep it conceptual; the R shown is Seurat-style pseudocode to read, not to run in the lecture.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
text:
A biology picture first
A tumour biopsy is not one thing. It is tumour cells, immune cells (T cells, B cells, macrophages), fibroblasts, and endothelial cells — all mixed together.

Bulk RNA-seq measures the average expression across all of them. A gene that is high in a rare T-cell population but absent elsewhere looks like faint background.
Single-cell RNA-seq measures each cell separately, so you can ask: which cell types are present, in what proportions, and what is each one doing?

The biological question — what cell types make up this tissue, and how do they differ? — is only answerable if we can read out expression one cell at a time.


This is the motivating pairing for the whole unit. The killer application of single-cell is resolving cellular heterogeneity that bulk averages away — rare cell types, mixtures, cell states. Use the tumour microenvironment because students know it and it is a real, high-stakes use case. Plant the idea that “many cells, measured separately” is what makes the new data structure (a big matrix) and the new problems (noise, sparsity, doublets) unavoidable. Do not mention PCA/clustering yet; just motivate why we want per-cell data.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
section: The data: a cells × genes count matrix
text:
The data: a cells × genes count matrix
The output of a single-cell experiment is a table of counts:

rows = cells (often 1,000–50,000+),
columns = genes (often ~20,000 for human/mouse),
entry \(X_{cg}\) = the number of RNA molecules of gene \(g\) detected in cell \(c\) (a non-negative integer count).

\[X = \begin{pmatrix} X_{11} & X_{12} & \cdots & X_{1G} \\ X_{21} & X_{22} & \cdots & X_{2G} \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\ X_{C1} & X_{C2} & \cdots & X_{CG} \end{pmatrix}\]
Same sample × feature shape you met with bulk expression tables — just with cells as the samples, and a lot more rows.


Anchor on the object they will actually manipulate: a count matrix. Stress it is the same conceptual shape as any omics table (samples in rows, features in columns) so it is not alien — but the “samples” are now individual cells and there are thousands to tens of thousands of them. Some toolkits (Bioconductor’s SingleCellExperiment, and Seurat internally) store the transpose with genes in rows and cells in columns; mention this so a transposed matrix later does not confuse them, but keep the mental model as cells = observations. Counts are integers; that matters for the distribution discussion later.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
text:
It is mostly zeros: sparsity
Most entries in the matrix are exactly 0. Typically 90–95% of the matrix is zero.
Two reasons a zero appears:

Biological: the gene is genuinely not expressed in that cell.
Technical (“dropout”): the gene is expressed, but its few molecules were not captured or sequenced — a false zero from limited sensitivity.

We usually cannot tell the two apart from the count alone. Because so few molecules are sampled per cell, single-cell data is sparse and noisy by nature.
Practically, we store it as a sparse matrix (only the non-zero entries) — a dense \(20{,}000 \times 50{,}000\) table of doubles would be tens of gigabytes.


Two key ideas here. First, sparsity is real and large (order 90%+ zeros), which is why we store the data in a sparse format — record only non-zeros. This is a genuine memory necessity, not an optimisation. Second, a zero is ambiguous: it can be true absence or a technical dropout caused by capturing only a tiny fraction of each cell’s mRNA. Do not overclaim exact percentages of dropout; the honest statement is that low capture efficiency produces many false zeros and we generally cannot distinguish them per-entry. This ambiguity is why downstream methods are built to tolerate noise rather than trust individual counts.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
section: Where the counts come from: droplets
text:
Where the counts come from: droplets
The dominant technology (e.g. 10x Genomics) is droplet-based. High level:

A microfluidic chip pairs single cells with barcoded gel beads inside tiny oil droplets — ideally one cell per droplet.
The cell is lysed; each captured mRNA is tagged with that droplet’s cell barcode (which cell) and a UMI — unique molecular identifier (which original molecule).
All droplets are pooled, reverse-transcribed, amplified, and sequenced together.
Computationally, reads are sorted by cell barcode back into cells, and UMIs are counted to rebuild the count matrix.



Keep this high level — students need the concepts, not the wet-lab protocol. The three ideas that matter downstream: (1) the cell barcode is how reads get grouped back into cells; (2) the UMI lets us count original molecules rather than PCR duplicates, which is what makes the entries meaningful integer counts; (3) “ideally one cell per droplet” is an ideal that fails sometimes, which sets up empty droplets and doublets on the next slides. Everything is sequenced in one pool and de-multiplexed computationally by barcode.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
text:
Why UMIs matter
Sequencing involves a PCR amplification step that copies molecules unevenly. Without correction, a gene that happened to amplify well would look highly expressed.

A UMI is a short random barcode attached to each original mRNA molecule before amplification.
After sequencing, all reads sharing the same UMI (and cell barcode and gene) came from one original molecule — so we count them once.

Counting unique UMIs instead of raw reads removes most amplification bias, giving counts that better reflect the true number of molecules captured.


This slide justifies why the matrix entries are trustworthy-ish integer counts and not just read pileups. Amplification is exponential and noisy, so raw read counts are badly distorted. The UMI tags each starting molecule, so collapsing duplicate UMIs recovers a molecule count. This is why people say “UMI counts”. Note it removes amplification bias but does not fix capture efficiency — molecules never captured are still missing (the dropout story). Keep it short; the takeaway is UMI = de-duplicated molecule count.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
section: The count matrix is raw — it needs cleaning
text:
The count matrix is raw — it needs cleaning
The matrix that comes off the pipeline is not ready for analysis. Two big problems, both from the “one cell per droplet” ideal breaking down, plus general quality issues:

Empty droplets: a droplet with no cell still captures stray ambient RNA → a “cell” that is really background.
Doublets: two cells share one droplet → one barcode that mixes two cells’ expression.
Low-quality cells: dying or damaged cells (leaked cytoplasm, stressed).

If we skip QC, these masquerade as real cells and create fake cell types and fake intermediate states downstream. QC is not optional bookkeeping — it protects every conclusion that follows.


Set up the QC section by naming the three failure modes. The framing to drill: bad cells do not just add noise, they produce artefacts that look like biology — an empty droplet full of ambient RNA can cluster as a “cell type”; a doublet of a T cell and a B cell looks like a novel cell expressing both programs. This is why QC comes before any dimensionality reduction or clustering. The next slides give the concrete signatures we filter on.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
section: QC signature 1: counts and genes per cell
text:
QC signature 1: counts and genes per cell
For each cell we compute two simple numbers:

total counts (library size): \(n_c = \sum_g X_{cg}\) — total UMIs in the cell.
number of genes detected: \(\#\{g : X_{cg} > 0\}\) — how many distinct genes are non-zero.

Interpreting the extremes:

Very low on both → an empty droplet or a broken cell with little RNA. Filter out.
Very high on both → possibly a doublet (two cells’ worth of RNA). Flag / filter.

These are cheap, per-cell summaries — the first thing you look at.


These two per-cell QC metrics are the workhorses. Total counts (library size) and number of detected genes are strongly correlated and both track “how much real cell was in this droplet”. Very low = empty/broken; very high = suspiciously much RNA, a doublet flag. Emphasise that thresholds are dataset-dependent and chosen by looking at the distributions, not universal magic numbers. Mention the “knee plot” idea: ranked barcodes by total counts show a sharp drop separating real cells from empty droplets, which dedicated tools use to call cells.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
text:
QC signature 2: mitochondrial fraction
Compute the fraction of each cell’s counts coming from mitochondrial genes (in human, gene symbols starting MT-):
\[\text{pct.mt}_c = 100 \times \frac{\sum_{g \in \text{MT}} X_{cg}}{\sum_g X_{cg}}\]

When a cell’s membrane is compromised (dying/stressed), cytoplasmic mRNA leaks out, but mitochondrial mRNA stays trapped in mitochondria.
So a high mitochondrial fraction is a hallmark of a low-quality / dying cell. Filter cells above a threshold.

The threshold is dataset-dependent (a common starting point is ~5–20%), and some healthy tissues are genuinely mito-rich — so inspect, don’t blindly apply.


This is the classic third QC metric. Mechanism: membrane damage lets cytoplasmic RNA escape while mitochondrial RNA is retained inside mitochondria, so the proportion that is mitochondrial rises. High pct.mt therefore flags dying cells. Be honest that the cutoff varies — 5% is common for some cell lines, but cardiomyocytes and other metabolically active tissues legitimately have high mitochondrial content, so a fixed threshold can throw away good cells. The design principle: look at the distribution, pick a threshold for your data. Ribosomal fraction is sometimes used similarly; mention only if asked.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
section: Empty droplets and the ambient RNA problem
text:
Empty droplets and the ambient RNA problem
When cells are lysed during prep, some mRNA floats freely in the suspension — ambient RNA. Every droplet, even an empty one, captures a little.

A droplet with no cell yields a low-count profile that is just ambient background.
Ranking barcodes by total counts shows a sharp “knee”: real cells (high counts) drop off steeply to the empty-droplet background (low counts).

Simple low-count filtering removes the obvious empties; dedicated tools (e.g. EmptyDrops) model the ambient profile statistically to rescue small real cells and remove background.


Concept only. The ambient RNA pool is created by lysed cells before/during droplet formation and contaminates every droplet. Empty droplets contain only this background, so they sit at low total counts. The barcode-rank (“knee”) plot is the standard diagnostic: sort barcodes by total UMI descending, plot on log-log, and there is a visible knee separating true cells from empties. Name-drop EmptyDrops as the principled tool but do not teach its statistics — the point is that “call which barcodes are real cells” is its own step. Ambient contamination also motivates later correction tools (SoupX/DecontX), which you can mention as deferred.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
text:
Doublets
A doublet is one barcode that captured two cells. Its expression is a blend of two profiles.

Why it is dangerous: a doublet of a T cell and a B cell expresses both T-cell and B-cell markers — it can masquerade as a novel “hybrid” cell type or a fake transitional state.
Signatures: unusually high total counts / genes; co-expression of markers that should be mutually exclusive.
Detection: dedicated tools (e.g. DoubletFinder, scDblFinder) simulate artificial doublets by averaging random pairs of cells, then flag real cells that resemble those simulations.

Doublet rate scales with how many cells you load — more cells per run means more collisions.


Doublets are the second consequence of the one-cell-per-droplet ideal failing. The conceptual danger is the important bit: a doublet does not look like noise, it looks like a plausible new cell expressing two programs, which can lead to invented cell types. Detection tools work by simulating synthetic doublets (average pairs of real cells) and finding real barcodes that look like those synthetics. Also mention the practical trade-off: loading more cells increases throughput but raises the collision (doublet) rate — roughly linearly with the number of cells loaded for droplet platforms. Keep tool details out; the concept is what matters.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
text:
After filtering: normalization
Cells differ in total counts just from technical capture efficiency, not biology — one cell might have 2,000 UMIs and another 20,000. Comparing raw counts across cells is unfair.
Library-size normalization: divide each cell’s counts by its total, then rescale to a common size (a “scale factor”, e.g. 10,000):
\[\tilde{X}_{cg} = \frac{X_{cg}}{\sum_{g'} X_{cg'}} \times s\]
This makes cells comparable — it converts counts into relative expression per cell. It is the single-cell cousin of CPM/TPM from bulk RNA-seq.


Motivate normalization by the fact that library size (total UMIs per cell) varies a lot for purely technical reasons — differences in capture and sequencing depth — so raw counts across cells are not comparable. Library-size (a.k.a. total-count) normalization rescales each cell to a common total, turning counts into within-cell relative abundances. Connect to CPM/TPM which they may recall from bulk. Be honest that this simple normalization is a first-pass standard; more sophisticated approaches (scran pooling factors, SCTransform/Pearson residuals) exist and are deferred. Do not overstate that this fully removes technical effects.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
text:
Then the log transform
After scaling we apply \(\log(1+x)\) (often written log1p):
\[Y_{cg} = \log\!\big(1 + \tilde{X}_{cg}\big)\]
Why log?

Expression spans orders of magnitude; a few very-high-count genes would otherwise dominate every distance and variance calculation.
Log compresses the large values and stabilizes variance, so highly and lowly expressed genes contribute more comparably.
The \(+1\) keeps zeros as zeros (\(\log(1+0)=0\)) and avoids \(\log 0 = -\infty\).

The pair (library-size normalize, then log1p) is the standard baseline single-cell transform. More in the next unit, Log and pseudolog transforms.


The log serves two purposes: it tames the enormous dynamic range (a handful of housekeeping/ribosomal genes can be thousands of counts while most are single digits) so they do not swamp variance-based methods, and it roughly stabilises variance for count-like data. The +1 pseudocount is what lets zeros survive as zeros and avoids log(0). Emphasise this normalize-then-log pipeline is the default baseline that PCA/clustering assume downstream. Flag that Poisson/negative-binomial-aware alternatives exist (and that the count nature connects to the overdispersion topic from the distributions block) but are beyond today. Keep this slide short: the next unit, Log and pseudolog transforms, covers why the log, why it is nonlinear (average before you log), and how the pseudocount and the 10,000 scale factor change low counts.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
text:
Feature selection: highly variable genes
Of ~20,000 genes, most are uninformative for telling cell types apart — housekeeping genes are steadily on everywhere; many genes are just noise.
Highly variable genes (HVGs): keep the genes whose variation across cells is larger than expected for their mean expression level.

Genes with real biological signal (cell-type markers) vary more than technical noise predicts.
We rank genes by variability relative to a mean–variance trend and keep the top ~2,000.

Working with ~2,000 informative genes instead of 20,000 cuts noise and computation — and sets up the dimensionality reduction that comes next.


Feature selection is the last preprocessing step. The key subtlety: you cannot just pick the highest-variance genes, because in count data variance grows with the mean — highly expressed genes are variable simply because they are big. So HVG selection ranks genes by variance relative to what their mean predicts (variance above a fitted mean-variance trend). Keeping ~2,000 top HVGs is the common default. Motivate it as noise reduction and computational tractability, and as the natural hand-off to Dimensionality reduction & clustering, where PCA runs on these selected, scaled genes. This is where the eigen/PCA machinery from the linear algebra block finally gets used on real data.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
section: The standard pipeline in code (read, don’t run)
text:
The standard pipeline in code (read, don’t run)
Seurat-style pseudocode for the whole QC + preprocessing pass:
library(Seurat)

# 1. Load the raw counts (cells x genes) into an object
counts <- Read10X("filtered_feature_bc_matrix/")
obj    <- CreateSeuratObject(counts, min.cells = 3, min.features = 200)

# 2. Per-cell QC metrics
obj[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(obj, pattern = "^MT-")

# 3. Filter low-quality cells (thresholds are dataset-dependent!)
obj <- subset(obj,
              subset = nFeature_RNA > 200 &
                       nFeature_RNA < 6000 &
                       percent.mt   < 15)

# 4. Normalize + log, then select highly variable genes
obj <- NormalizeData(obj)                       # library-size + log1p
obj <- FindVariableFeatures(obj, nfeatures = 2000)
Doublet detection (e.g. scDblFinder) is a separate step, usually run before or alongside filtering.

Walk the pipeline top to bottom so the concepts map to real function names they will meet. Read10X loads the sparse matrix; CreateSeuratObject already does light gene/cell filtering (min.cells, min.features). PercentageFeatureSet computes pct.mt via the MT- pattern. subset() applies the QC thresholds — stress again these numbers are illustrative and must be chosen from the data. NormalizeData is the library-size + log1p we derived; FindVariableFeatures is HVG selection. Emphasise this is STATIC code to read — nothing is executed at render time and no packages are installed. The doublet step is separate. Dimensionality reduction & clustering picks up the obj and runs PCA/UMAP/clustering.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
text:
What we deliberately deferred
Today stopped at a clean, normalized, HVG-selected matrix. Not covered yet:

PCA / UMAP — reducing the ~2,000-gene matrix to a few dimensions you can plot and cluster. (Single-cell RNA-seq: dimensionality reduction.)
Clustering & cell-type annotation — grouping cells and naming the types.
Count-aware models — Poisson / negative-binomial treatments of the counts, connecting to the overdispersion ideas from the distributions block.
Ambient-RNA correction and advanced normalization (Pearson residuals / SCTransform).

The eigenvalue/eigenvector and PCA machinery you built earlier is exactly what Dimensionality reduction & clustering applies to this cleaned matrix.

Be explicit about the stepping stones, per the course’s “honest about what we defer” principle. The cleaned matrix is the deliverable; everything glamorous (dimensionality reduction, clustering, annotation) comes next and reuses the eigen/PCA foundation from the linear algebra block. Flag that the simple normalize+log baseline will be contrasted with count-aware models, tying back to Poisson/negative-binomial and overdispersion from the probability block. This slide is the map: students should see today as the data-cleaning foundation the rest of single-cell analysis stands on.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Data object
sparse cells × genes integer count matrix


Sparsity
~90%+ zeros; zeros can be real or technical dropout


Droplet workflow
cell + barcoded bead in oil; barcode = which cell, UMI = which molecule


Empty droplets
low counts = ambient background; seen as a knee in the barcode-rank plot


Doublets
two cells, one barcode → blended profile; fake “hybrid” cell types


QC metrics
total counts, genes detected, % mitochondrial


Normalization
library-size scale, then \(\log(1+x)\)


Feature selection
keep ~2,000 highly variable genes (variance above the mean trend)


Biology payoff
resolve cell-type heterogeneity a bulk average hides



Next (Log and pseudolog transforms): why we log, what the +1 changes; then PCA and UMAP on this cleaned matrix.

The summary is the revision sheet. Drill the pipeline as a story: counts come off the machine sparse and noisy → filter empties, doublets, and dying (high-mito) cells → normalize by library size and log → keep the highly variable genes → hand the clean matrix to PCA. Reconnect each technical step to its biological motivation (heterogeneity is the reason we do any of this). Preview what follows: a closer look at the log transform (next unit), then the eigen/PCA tools from the linear algebra block get applied to exactly this matrix to make the cell-type structure visible.

title: Exercise: log and pseudolog transforms
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute and read \(\log_2\) fold changes,
show with numbers that the log is not linear, and say what that means for averaging and pseudobulk,
apply the pseudolog \(\log(1 + x)\) (log1p) and a general pseudocount \(\log(x + c)\), and explain how the pseudocount changes low counts and fold changes,
find the pseudocount hidden in library-size normalization with a scale factor,
compare the mean–variance relation and a PCA before and after the transform,
plot data with zeros without losing them.

This builds on Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC (normalization, then log1p) and on PCA. The linearity test is the one from Polar coordinates.

title: Exercise: log and pseudolog transforms
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute and read \(\log_2\) fold changes,
show with numbers that the log is not linear, and say what that means for averaging and pseudobulk,
apply the pseudolog \(\log(1 + x)\) (log1p) and a general pseudocount \(\log(x + c)\), and explain how the pseudocount changes low counts and fold changes,
find the pseudocount hidden in library-size normalization with a scale factor,
compare the mean–variance relation and a PCA before and after the transform,
plot data with zeros without losing them.

This builds on Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC (normalization, then log1p) and on PCA. The linearity test is the one from Polar coordinates.

title: Exercise: log and pseudolog transforms
text:
Background
Log rules. \(\log(a b) = \log a + \log b\) and \(\log(a / b) = \log a - \log b\). A fold change \(b / a\) becomes the difference \(\log_2 b - \log_2 a\): \(\log_2\) FC \(= 1\) is a doubling, \(-1\) a halving. Changing the base only rescales: \(\log_2 x = \ln x / \ln 2\). In R, log() is the natural log; log2(), log10() and log(x, base) give the others.
Linear test. A function \(f\) is linear if \(f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b)\) and \(f(c\,a) = c\,f(a)\). Every matrix map passes; the log does not.
Pseudolog. Counts contain zeros and \(\log 0 = -\infty\). Adding a pseudocount \(c\) fixes that: \(\log(x + c)\). With \(c = 1\) we call it the pseudolog, \(\log(1 + x)\), in R log1p(x). It maps 0 to 0, is close to \(x\) for small \(x\) and close to \(\log x\) for large \(x\).
Library-size normalization with scale factor \(s\) (Seurat uses \(s = 10{,}000\)): \(\log\!\big(1 + \tfrac{x}{n} s\big)\) for a gene with \(x\) UMIs in a cell with \(n\) UMIs in total.

title: Exercise: log and pseudolog transforms
text:
By hand
A calculator is fine.
B1. A gene has 50 UMIs per cell on average in control cells and 200 after treatment. What is the fold change, and the \(\log_2\) fold change? Another gene goes from 40 to 10. A third has \(\log_2\) FC \(= 3\): by what factor did it change? And \(\log_2\) FC \(= -1\)?
B2. Check the linear test for \(f(x) = \log_{10} x\) with \(a = 10\), \(b = 1000\), \(c = 2\): compute \(f(a + b)\), \(f(a) + f(b)\), \(f(c\,a)\) and \(c\,f(a)\). Then: a cell captured twice as much RNA as another, so all its counts are doubled. What happens to its \(\log_2\) values?
B3. Three cells have 1, 10 and 100 normalized UMIs of a gene. Compute the log of the mean, \(\log_{10}(\text{mean})\), and the mean of the logs, the average of \(\log_{10}\) of each value. Which is smaller? Which value does the mean of the logs correspond to on the original scale?
B4. The \(\log_2\) fold change between two counts \(a \to b\) with pseudocount \(c\) is \(\log_2 \frac{b + c}{a + c}\). Fill in the table:



\(a \to b\)
\(c = 0.1\)
\(c = 1\)
\(c = 10\)




0 → 1





1 → 3





100 → 300






The last two rows have the same true fold change. Which pseudocount reports it best, and for which counts? Why is a large \(\log_2\) FC for 0 → 1 a problem?
B5. Compute \(\log(1 + x)\) (natural log) and \(\log x\) for \(x = 0\), \(0.01\), \(1\) and \(1000\). Where does the +1 matter, and where does it not?
B6. A cell has \(n = 5{,}000\) UMIs in total, of which \(x = 3\) are of gene G. Compute \(\log(1 + \tfrac{x}{n} \cdot 10{,}000)\). Show that it equals \(\log 2 + \log(x + 0.5)\). What is the pseudocount in raw counts? Do the same for the same 3 UMIs in a cell with \(n = 20{,}000\).
B7. (concept) Five B cells have normalized expression \(0, 0, 0, 2, 8\) for a T-cell marker. What is the median? You plot it with a log-scaled y axis, which drops the zeros: what median does the boxplot now show, and what would a reader conclude?

title: Exercise: log and pseudolog transforms
text:
Explore: choose the pseudocount
The demo uses a smaller simulation than the R part: 200 cells (100 T, 100 B) with total counts \(n\) from about 1,300 to 12,600 UMIs, 60 background genes, 4 very high genes and 10 cell-type markers. (a) is the curve \(\log(x + c)\) with the values for 0 and 1 UMI; (b) shows the transformed values of all cells for a low gene (orange) and a high gene (blue); (c) shows the variance after the transform for every gene, with a dashed line at the 10th largest: those 10 genes are what highly variable gene selection would pick.



E1. With raw counts (normalization off), base \(e\), set \(c = 0.01\), 1 and 100. For each, note the step from 0 to 1 UMI in (a) and the variance of the low gene in (b). Check the step for \(c = 0.01\) by hand.
E2. For the same three values of \(c\), how many of the 10 most variable genes in (c) are markers, and what kind of genes are the others? Explain both failures with the curve in (a).
E3. Switch the base from \(e\) to 2. What changes in the three panels, and what does not? By what factor do the variances change?
E4. Set \(c = 1\) and tick normalize first. Read off the step from 0 to 1 UMI in the deepest, the median and the shallowest cell. Relate it to the effective pseudocount \(c \cdot n / 10{,}000\) from B6. What happens to the variance of the high gene, and why?






Solutions





E1. The step is \(\log(1 + c) - \log c = \log\frac{1 + c}{c}\): 4.62 for \(c = 0.01\) (\(\log 101\)), 0.69 for \(c = 1\) (\(\log 2\)) and 0.01 for \(c = 100\). The low gene (mean 0.35, 73% zeros) has variance 4.62, 0.14 and 0.00. With a small \(c\) its zeros sit far below its ones and twos, so it looks very variable; with a large \(c\) all its values are squashed together.
E2. \(c = 0.01\): 5 of 10 are markers, the other 5 are background genes with many zeros, whose variance is mostly the 0-or-1 sampling noise blown up by the steep curve near 0. \(c = 1\): all 10 are markers. \(c = 100\): 2 markers, 4 very high genes and 4 high background genes. For counts well below \(c\) the curve is almost flat, so low and moderate genes, including most markers, lose their variance; only genes with counts comparable to \(c\) or larger still vary, and among them the biggest win, as on raw counts. Both ends of the slider hide the markers, for opposite reasons.
E3. The axes in (a) and (b) are relabelled (all values are multiplied by \(1 / \ln 2 = 1.44\)), and all variances are multiplied by \(1 / (\ln 2)^2 = 2.08\). The shape of every panel and the ranking of the genes do not change: the base is a choice of units.
E4. The normalized value of 1 UMI is \(10{,}000 / n\), so the step \(\log(1 + 10{,}000 / n)\) is about 0.6 in the deepest cell, 1.13 in the median cell and 2.2 in the shallowest. Equivalently, the pseudocount in raw counts is \(c \cdot n / 10{,}000\), from 0.13 to 1.26 here: a single UMI counts for more in a shallow cell. The variance of the high gene drops from 0.35 to 0.25, because on raw counts part of its spread is just sequencing depth (deep cells have more of everything); dividing by \(n\) removes that.

title: Exercise: log and pseudolog transforms
text:
In R
Base R is enough, except R5, which also uses ggplot2. The simulated data are the same as in the lecture: 400 cells (200 T cells, 200 B cells) and 300 genes, with negative-binomial counts.
set.seed(1)
type <- rep(c("T", "B"), each = 200)                 # 400 cells: 200 T, 200 B
lib  <- rlnorm(400, 0, 0.35)                         # capture efficiency per cell
gene_mean <- c(exp(seq(log(0.01), log(30), length.out = 280)),   # 280 background genes
               150, 200, 250, 300, 400)                           # 5 very high genes
marker <- rbind(matrix(rep(c(4, 0.3), c(8, 7)), 200, 15, byrow = TRUE),   # T cells
                matrix(rep(c(0.3, 4), c(8, 7)), 200, 15, byrow = TRUE))   # B cells
mu <- cbind(outer(lib, gene_mean), lib * marker)     # expected count, cells x genes
X  <- matrix(rnbinom(length(mu), mu = mu, size = 5), nrow = 400)   # negative binomial counts
colnames(X) <- c(paste0("bg", 1:280), paste0("hi", 1:5), paste0("mk", 1:15))
The background genes bg1…bg280 have the same mean in both cell types; hi1…hi5 are very highly expressed (like ribosomal genes); the markers mk1…mk8 are on in T cells and mk9…mk15 in B cells.
R1. What fraction of X is zero? Compute the library size n per cell, the normalized matrix N (scale factor 10,000) and L <- log1p(N). For every gene, compute the mean and variance of the raw counts X, and the variance of L. Plot variance against mean for X on log–log axes with the line variance = mean, and the variance of L against the mean. Which five genes have the largest variance before the log, and which after?
R2. Run prcomp on N and on L. Plot PC1 against PC2 for both, coloured by cell type. Which genes have the largest absolute loadings on PC1 in each case? What fraction of the total variance do the 5 hi genes make up in N and in L?
R3. For each gene, compute the mean normalized expression in T cells and in B cells (colMeans of N for each group). Then compute the \(\log_2\) fold change T vs B, \(\log_2 \frac{\bar x_T + c}{\bar x_B + c}\), for \(c = 0.01\), 0.1, 1 and 10. Report it for mk1 and hi1, and count how many background genes get \(|\log_2 \text{FC}| > 0.5\). Their true fold change is 1. What happens to the markers when \(c\) is large, and to the background genes when \(c\) is small?
R4. For mk1, compare the mean of the log, mean(L[type == "T", "mk1"]), with the log of the mean, log1p(mean(N[type == "T", "mk1"])), in each cell type. Then make a pseudobulk: pb <- rowsum(X, type) sums the raw counts per cell type. Compute the \(\log_2\) fold change of mk1 from the pseudobulk proportions, and compare it with the difference of mean log1p values (converted to \(\log_2\) units by dividing by log(2)). The simulation used means 4 and 0.3: which estimate is closer to \(\log_2(4 / 0.3)\)?
R5. Plot N[, "mk1"] for all cells with base R plot(..., log = "y") and read the warning. Then make a ggplot boxplot of mk1 by cell type three ways: linear axis, scale_y_log10(), and log1p values. What median does each show for B cells? Compare with median(N[type == "B", "mk1"]).
R6. The effective pseudocount in raw counts is \(n / 10{,}000\) per cell. Find its range across the 400 cells. What is the log1p-normalized value of a single UMI in the smallest and in the largest cell? What would the pseudocount be with CPM (scale factor \(10^6\)) for the median cell?

title: Exercise: log and pseudolog transforms
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — per-gene summaries





Cells are rows and genes are columns, so a per-gene summary works on columns: colMeans(X) and apply(X, 2, var). Library sizes are per cell: rowSums(X). X / n divides row \(i\) by n[i], because R recycles n down the columns, which is exactly what normalization needs.









Hint 2 — top genes and loadings





names(sort(v, decreasing = TRUE))[1:5] gives the names of the five largest values of a named vector v. For PCA, p$rotation[, 1] holds the PC1 loadings, one per gene; sort their absolute values. The variance share of the hi genes is sum(v[281:285]) / sum(v), with v the per-gene variances.









Hint 3 — fold changes for many genes at once





mT <- colMeans(N[type == "T", ]) and mB <- colMeans(N[type == "B", ]) are vectors with one entry per gene. Then log2((mT + c) / (mB + c)) gives all fold changes at once. Background genes are positions 1:280.









Hint 4 — boxplot medians and log axes





For R5, ggplot2::ggplot_build(p)$data[[1]] holds the computed boxplot statistics (column middle). On a scale_y_log10() plot they are in \(\log_{10}\) units, so take 10^middle.

title: Exercise: log and pseudolog transforms
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. \(200 / 50 = 4\), \(\log_2 4 = 2\). From 40 to 10: fold change \(0.25\), \(\log_2 0.25 = -2\). \(\log_2\) FC \(= 3\) means \(2^3 = 8\)-fold up; \(-1\) means halved. Up and down by the same factor give the same size with opposite signs.
B2. \(f(a + b) = \log_{10} 1010 = 3.004\) but \(f(a) + f(b) = 1 + 3 = 4\). \(f(2 \cdot 10) = \log_{10} 20 = 1.30\) but \(2 f(10) = 2\). Both parts of the test fail, so the log is not linear. Doubling all counts adds \(\log_2 2 = 1\) to every \(\log_2\) value: a multiplication becomes a shift. (With a pseudocount the shift is exact only for counts well above \(c\).)
B3. Mean \(= 111 / 3 = 37\), \(\log_{10} 37 = 1.57\). Logs: \(0, 1, 2\), mean \(= 1\). The mean of the logs is smaller; it is always \(\le\) the log of the mean. \(10^1 = 10\) is the geometric mean, which gives the large value less weight than the arithmetic mean (37).

At 1 count, \(c = 0.1\) is closest (1.49), \(c = 1\) gives 1.00 and \(c = 10\) shrinks it to 0.24. But a small \(c\) also turns 0 → 1, a difference of a single molecule that is mostly sampling noise, into a 3.46 \(\log_2\) FC (11-fold). The pseudocount sets the level below which differences are damped.

In general \(1 + 2x = 2(x + 0.5)\), so the pseudocount in raw counts is \(0.5 = n / 10{,}000\). For \(n = 20{,}000\): \(\log(1 + 1.5) = 0.916 = \log 0.5 + \log(3 + 2)\), pseudocount 2. The same 3 UMIs are damped more in a bigger cell.
B7. The median of \(0, 0, 0, 2, 8\) is 0: most B cells do not express the marker. Without the zeros the values are \(2, 8\), median 5. The plot suggests B cells express the T-cell marker at a moderate level, which is wrong.
R1.
mean(X == 0)                          # 0.50
n <- rowSums(X)
N <- X / n * 10000
L <- log1p(N)
median(n)                             # 2375

m  <- colMeans(X)
v  <- apply(X, 2, var)
vL <- apply(L, 2, var)
plot(m, v, log = "xy", xlab = "mean UMIs per cell", ylab = "variance")
abline(0, 1)                          # variance = mean (Poisson)
plot(colMeans(N), vL, log = "x", xlab = "mean (normalized)", ylab = "variance of log1p")
names(sort(v,  decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]    # "hi5" "hi4" "hi3" "hi2" "hi1"
names(sort(vL, decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]    # "mk2" "mk1" "mk7" "mk3" "mk6"





Half the matrix is zero (real data have more). Raw-count variances grow with the mean and lie above the Poisson line for higher means (negative-binomial overdispersion); the 5 hi genes top the list only because they are big. After log1p the top five are all markers: the genes that differ between cell types.
R2.
pN <- prcomp(N)
pL <- prcomp(L)
col <- ifelse(type == "T", "#0072B2", "#D55E00")
plot(pN$x[, 1:2], col = col, pch = 16, main = "normalized counts")
plot(pL$x[, 1:2], col = col, pch = 16, main = "log1p")
names(sort(abs(pN$rotation[, 1]), decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]   # "hi5" "hi4" "hi3" "hi2" "bg280"
names(sort(abs(pL$rotation[, 1]), decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]   # "mk2" "mk1" "mk6" "mk11" "mk7"
vN <- apply(N, 2, var)
sum(vN[281:285]) / sum(vN)            # 0.92
sum(vL[281:285]) / sum(vL)            # 0.005





On normalized counts, 92% of the total variance comes from the 5 hi genes, and PC1 (41% of the variance) is their noise: T and B cells overlap. On log1p data they contribute 0.5%; PC1 (11%) is built from markers and separates the two cell types completely.
R3.
mT <- colMeans(N[type == "T", ])
mB <- colMeans(N[type == "B", ])
for (c in c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10)) {
  lfc <- log2((mT + c) / (mB + c))
  cat("c =", c, " mk1:", round(lfc["mk1"], 2), " hi1:", round(lfc["hi1"], 2),
      " background |lfc| > 0.5:", sum(abs(lfc[1:280]) > 0.5), "\n")

The marker mk1 (means 17.2 in T, 0.88 in B) loses fold change as \(c\) grows: with \(c = 10\) a 20-fold difference looks like 2.5-fold. With \(c = 0.01\), 58 of 280 background genes, all with true fold change 1, get \(|\log_2 \text{FC}| > 0.5\). They are the rarely detected genes (means around 0.01–1), where a handful of UMIs in one group decides the ratio. The pseudocount trades false fold changes at low counts against shrinking real ones.

pb <- rowsum(X, type)                 # rows B and T; raw counts summed per cell type
