log2((pb["T", "mk1"] / sum(pb["T", ])) / (pb["B", "mk1"] / sum(pb["B", ])))   # 4.13
(mean(L[type == "T", "mk1"]) - mean(L[type == "B", "mk1"])) / log(2)          # 3.29
log2(4 / 0.3)                                                                 # 3.74
T cells: mean of log1p 2.60, log1p of mean 2.90. B cells: 0.32 and 0.63. The mean of the logs is smaller in both, as in B3. The pseudobulk \(\log_2\) FC is 4.13, the difference of mean log1p values 3.29; the simulation’s value is 3.74. The two estimates measure different things: the pseudobulk is a ratio of total expression, the mean-of-logs difference is a ratio of geometric means shrunk by the pseudocount. Neither is exactly 3.74 here because the B-cell pseudobulk has only 49 UMIs, so it is noisy. For a test between conditions with replicates, sum counts per sample and use a count-based bulk method.
R5.
plot(N[, "mk1"], log = "y")           # warning: 173 y values <= 0 omitted

library(ggplot2)
d  <- data.frame(type = factor(type, levels = c("T", "B")), expr = N[, "mk1"])
p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(type, expr)) + geom_boxplot()
p2 <- p1 + scale_y_log10()
p3 <- ggplot(d, aes(type, log1p(expr))) + geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = log1p(c(0, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100)), labels = c(0, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100))
ggplot_build(p1)$data[[1]]$middle[2]          # 0      (B cells)
10^ggplot_build(p2)$data[[1]]$middle[2]       # 3.82   (zeros dropped)
expm1(ggplot_build(p3)$data[[1]]$middle[2])   # 0
median(N[type == "B", "mk1"])                 # 0





173 of 400 values are 0 (161 of the 200 B cells). Base R omits them with a warning; ggplot2 warns that the log transformation “introduced infinite values” and computes the boxplot without them, so the B-cell median jumps from 0 to 3.82. The log1p plot keeps every cell and shows the right median. expm1() is the inverse of log1p().
R6.
range(n / 10000)                      # 0.084 to 0.672
log1p(1 / min(n) * 10000)             # 2.56  (cell with 841 UMIs)
log1p(1 / max(n) * 10000)             # 0.91  (cell with 6721 UMIs)
median(n) / 1e6                       # 0.0024 with CPM
The effective pseudocount varies 8-fold between cells, from 0.08 to 0.67 raw counts, so a single UMI becomes 2.56 in the smallest cell and 0.91 in the largest. With CPM the median cell would get a pseudocount of 0.0024: the gap between 0 and 1 UMI becomes \(\log(1 + 421) = 6.0\), larger than most real differences between cell types. Ahlmann-Eltze & Huber (2023, Nature Methods 20:665) relate the pseudocount to the overdispersion \(\alpha\) of the counts, \(c \approx 1 / (4\alpha)\), and recommend against CPM for single cells.

title: Exercise: log and pseudolog transforms
text:
Where this leads

Dimensionality reduction & clustering: PCA, the neighbour graph and UMAP all run on the log-normalized matrix from this exercise. R2 is the reason.
Highly variable genes: selecting genes by variance only works on a scale where variance is not decided by size (R1). Seurat’s default HVG method fits the mean–variance trend instead.
Count models: instead of transforming, model the counts directly (Poisson, negative binomial; Pearson residuals, SCTransform). These avoid choosing a pseudocount but make their own choices.
Differential expression: a reported log fold change depends on whether it is a ratio of means or a difference of mean logs, and on the pseudocount (R3, R4). Read the documentation of the tool.

title: Quiz: log and pseudolog transforms
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of log and pseudolog transforms of count data. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Give two reasons why single-cell counts are log-transformed before PCA.






Hint





Think about how far apart the gene means are, and about how the variance of a count depends on its mean.









Answer






Expression spans orders of magnitude: a few genes (ribosomal, mitochondrial) have hundreds of UMIs per cell, most fewer than one. Biological changes are multiplicative (fold changes), and the log puts a doubling at 1 UMI and at 200 UMIs on the same footing. (2) For counts the variance grows with the mean (Poisson: variance = mean; negative binomial: more). On raw or normalized counts the few highly expressed genes have by far the largest variance, so PCA, which looks for directions of largest variance, describes their noise instead of the cell types. After the log, genes that vary because of biology (markers) have the largest variance.





Q2. A gene has a \(\log_2\) fold change of \(-3\) between treated and control. What happened to its expression? What is the \(\log_2\) fold change of a gene that goes from 30 to 120?






Hint





\(\log_2\) FC \(= \log_2(\text{treated} / \text{control})\).









Answer





\(2^{-3} = 1/8\): expression dropped to one eighth (8-fold down). From 30 to 120 is a fold change of 4, so \(\log_2\) FC \(= 2\). On the log scale, 8-fold up and 8-fold down are \(+3\) and \(-3\): symmetric.




Q3. Is \(f(x) = \log x\) a linear function? Justify with the linear test and one numerical example.






Hint





Linear means \(f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b)\) and \(f(c\,a) = c\,f(a)\). Try \(a = 10\), \(b = 1000\) with \(\log_{10}\).









Answer





No. \(\log_{10}(10 + 1000) = 3.004\), but \(\log_{10} 10 + \log_{10} 1000 = 4\). Scaling fails too: \(\log_{10}(2 \cdot 10) = 1.30 \ne 2 \log_{10} 10 = 2\). The log turns products into sums (\(\log(ab) = \log a + \log b\)), not sums into sums, and scaling by \(c\) becomes adding \(\log c\). So no matrix can do it, and the order of operations matters.




Q4. You want the expression of a gene in a cluster of cells, to compare between patients. Colleague A averages the log1p-normalized values of the cells. Colleague B sums the raw counts of the cells (pseudobulk), then normalizes and logs. Why can they get different answers, and which one is the usual choice for comparing samples?






Hint





Is “the mean of the logs” the same as “the log of the mean”?









Answer





Because the log is not linear, the mean of logs is not the log of the mean; it is always smaller or equal (it is the log of a geometric mean, which gives large values less weight). For counts 0, 1, 3, 15: the mean of \(\log_2(1 + x)\) is 1.75, but \(\log_2(1 + 4.75) = 2.52\). Summing is linear, so it belongs on the count scale: pseudobulk (sum counts per sample, then normalize, log, or use a count-based bulk method) is the usual choice for comparing samples.




Q5. What is the pseudolog, what problem does it solve, and what happens to a zero?






Hint





What is \(\log 0\)? What is \(\log(1 + 0)\)?









Answer





The pseudolog is \(\log(1 + x)\), the log with a pseudocount of 1 (log1p(x) in R). Single-cell matrices are mostly zeros and \(\log 0 = -\infty\); adding 1 makes the log defined everywhere. A zero stays a zero (\(\log 1 = 0\)), so the matrix stays sparse. For large \(x\) it is almost \(\log x\); near 0 it is almost \(x\).




Q6. Two analysts compute a \(\log_2\) fold change for a lowly expressed gene with mean 1 UMI in group A and 3 in group B. One uses pseudocount \(c = 0.1\), the other \(c = 10\). What does each get, and what is the general lesson?






Hint





\(\log_2 \frac{3 + c}{1 + c}\).









Answer





\(c = 0.1\): \(\log_2(3.1 / 1.1) = 1.49\), close to the true \(\log_2 3 = 1.58\). \(c = 10\): \(\log_2(13 / 11) = 0.24\), almost no change. A large pseudocount squashes low counts and shrinks their fold changes towards 0; a small one keeps them but also blows up noise, e.g. 0 → 1 UMI becomes \(\log_2(1.1 / 0.1) = 3.46\). Counts well above \(c\) are hardly affected. The pseudocount is a choice that sets below which count level differences are damped.




Q7. Seurat’s NormalizeData computes \(\log(1 + \tfrac{x}{n} \cdot 10{,}000)\), with \(n\) the total UMIs of the cell. What is the pseudocount in raw counts for a cell with 5,000 UMIs, and for a cell with 20,000? Why does this matter?






Hint





Factor out \(\tfrac{10{,}000}{n}\): \(1 + \tfrac{10{,}000}{n} x = \tfrac{10{,}000}{n}\big(x + \tfrac{n}{10{,}000}\big)\).









Answer





The pseudocount in raw counts is \(n / 10{,}000\): 0.5 for the 5,000-UMI cell and 2 for the 20,000-UMI cell. So the pseudocount differs between cells, and changing the scale factor changes it for all cells: CPM (\(10^6\)) makes it about 100 times smaller, so the step from 0 to 1 UMI becomes huge. The scale factor is therefore not just a choice of units.




Q8. You plot the expression of a T-cell marker in B cells, where most cells have 0, using scale_y_log10(). The boxplot shows a B-cell median of about 4. What went wrong, and how do you fix it?






Hint





What is \(\log_{10} 0\)? What does ggplot2 do with values that become infinite?









Answer





\(\log_{10} 0 = -\infty\). A log axis transforms the values before the boxplot statistics are computed, so all zeros are removed (only a console warning says so), and the median is that of the few B cells that expressed the gene. The true median is 0. Fix: plot log1p(expr) (labels can still be in counts), so every cell is kept.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
About this lecture
In Single-cell RNA-seq: data & QC and Log and pseudolog transforms you turned raw droplets into a clean matrix: ~2000 genes × thousands of cells, QC-filtered, normalized and log-transformed. Today we turn that matrix into a map of cells — a picture you can actually look at, with cell groups marked on it.

Reduce & denoise first with PCA — reuse the machinery from Principal component analysis and PCA in R.
Build a k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) graph: who sits next to whom in gene-expression space.
Lay the graph out in 2D with UMAP — a non-linear map that preserves local neighbourhoods (contrast the linear PCA).
Find cell groups with graph-based clustering (Louvain / Leiden).
Caveats: UMAP axes and distances are not quantitative, the resolution parameter changes how many clusters you get, and none of this is ground truth.

This is an applied concept day. The pipeline is short; the discipline is in reading the output honestly.

The one-sentence framing: we are going from a matrix nobody can look at (thousands of genes, thousands of cells) to a two-dimensional map with coloured islands of cells. Emphasise that every step is something they have already met in pieces — PCA from the Applications block, distances and neighbours from vector geometry, graphs from the Markov-chain state diagrams. Today just assembles them into the standard single-cell workflow. Flag early and often that the payoff picture (the UMAP) is seductive and easy to over-read, and that half of today’s learning outcome is knowing what NOT to conclude from it.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
section: The biology: what is a cell type?
text:
The biology: what is a cell type?
A tissue is a mixture of cell types — neurons, T cells, macrophages, fibroblasts — each running its own programme of active genes.

Single-cell RNA-seq measures, for every cell, how much of each gene is expressed.
Cells of the same type express similar sets of genes → they sit close together in gene-expression space.
Cells of different types sit far apart.

The biological question is simple to state: how many cell populations are in this sample, and which cells belong to which?
We never told the computer the cell types. We want to discover them from the expression alone — this is unsupervised learning, exactly like PCA.


Ground the whole lecture in one biological question before any method: given a dissociated tissue, find the cell populations and assign every cell to one. Stress the geometric intuition that “same cell type = similar expression = nearby point”. This is the bridge between biology and the linear algebra: a cell is a point in a space whose axes are genes. Also plant the word unsupervised — we discover groups without labels, the same stance PCA took. Cell-type naming (matching clusters to known markers) is a separate later unit, cell-type annotation; today we only find the groups.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
section: Each cell is a point in gene space

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
The pipeline in one picture
\[
\underbrace{X}_{\text{cells × genes}}
\;\xrightarrow{\;\text{PCA}\;}\;
\underbrace{Z}_{\text{cells × }\sim 30\text{ PCs}}
\;\xrightarrow{\;\text{kNN}\;}\;
\underbrace{G}_{\text{neighbour graph}}
\;\xrightarrow{\;\begin{array}{c}\text{UMAP}\\\text{clustering}\end{array}\;}\;
\underbrace{\text{2D map + cluster labels}}_{\text{what you look at}}
\]








Step
What it does
Why




PCA
2000 genes → ~30 components
denoise, speed up, remove redundancy


kNN graph
connect each cell to its nearest neighbours
capture local structure


UMAP
graph → 2D coordinates
a picture you can plot


Clustering
cut the graph into communities
name the cell groups



Notice: UMAP and clustering both run on the same kNN graph. They are two views of one neighbourhood structure.


This is the roadmap slide — return to it between steps. The key conceptual point students miss: UMAP (the picture) and clustering (the groups) are computed independently from the same graph, so clusters are not “found in the UMAP” — both are downstream of the neighbour graph. That is why a cluster can occasionally look split or mixed in the UMAP: the 2D layout and the community detection are different algorithms fed the same input. Also note PCA does double duty: denoising AND making the downstream distance computations fast and meaningful (fewer, less noisy dimensions).

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
section: Step 1: PCA to denoise and reduce
text:
Step 1: PCA to denoise and reduce
Before anything else, run PCA on the (scaled) cell × gene matrix — the exact method from Principal component analysis and PCA in R.

The first ~30–50 principal components capture the coordinated variation across genes (real biology: shared expression programmes).
The discarded components are dominated by technical noise and gene-by-gene sampling scatter.
We keep the top PCs and work in that space from now on: cells × 30, not cells × 2000.

Why this matters for what follows:

Distances are more meaningful in ~30 denoised dimensions than in 2000 noisy ones.
Everything downstream (kNN, UMAP, clustering) is faster and more stable.

Choosing how many PCs is the elbow / scree decision from Choosing components & pitfalls.


Reassure students that Step 1 is not new — it is the PCA they already built from the eigen-decomposition of a covariance matrix, applied to cells × genes. The single new idea is the reason: PCA here is a denoising and compression pre-step, not the final visualization. Counts are noisy and high-dimensional; distances computed directly in 2000-gene space are swamped by noise (a mild “curse of dimensionality” point). Reducing to ~30 PCs concentrates the signal. The number of PCs is a real choice with the same scree/elbow tools from the pitfalls unit; 30 is a common default, not a law.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
section: Why PCA alone is not the picture
text:
Why PCA alone is not the picture
PCA already gives coordinates — why not just plot PC1 vs PC2?

PCA is linear: every PC is a straight-line (weighted-sum) combination of genes. PC1 vs PC2 shows only the two directions of greatest variance.
Real cell populations lie on curved, branched structures (differentiation trajectories, discrete islands). A linear projection flattens them — distinct types overlap.
The top 2 PCs capture a lot of variance but usually not the fine local separation between similar cell types.

We used ~30 PCs precisely because 2 are not enough. But we can only plot 2 dimensions.
Need: a map that uses all 30 PCs’ worth of neighbourhood information but draws it in 2D, and is allowed to bend. That is a non-linear embedding — UMAP.


This is the linear-vs-non-linear pivot, and it echoes the “PCA only sees linear structure” pitfall from Choosing components & pitfalls. Make the contrast sharp: PCA is a rigid rotation of the axes — a straight-line projection — so it can only show the two highest-variance directions and it cannot unfold a curved manifold. Cell states often sit on curved or branched manifolds, and similar-but-distinct types get smeared together in PC1/PC2. UMAP is permitted to distort distances non-linearly, which is exactly what lets it pull apart local neighbourhoods that PCA overlaps. Preview honestly: that same freedom to distort is why UMAP distances stop being quantitative.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
Step 2: the k-nearest-neighbour graph
Work in the ~30-PC space. For each cell, find its \(k\) nearest neighbours (typical \(k \approx 15\)) by Euclidean distance, and draw an edge to each.
\[
\text{dist}(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) = \lVert \mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j \rVert = \sqrt{\sum_{p=1}^{30} (x_{ip} - x_{jp})^2}
\]

The result is a graph \(G\): nodes = cells, edges = “is a near neighbour of”.
It records only local relationships — who is close to whom — and throws away exact long-range distances.
Densely connected clumps of cells = candidate cell populations.

This graph is the shared input to both UMAP and clustering.


Define the kNN graph concretely: pick k (default around 15), connect each cell to its k closest cells in PC space. The distance is the ordinary Euclidean norm from vector geometry, just in 30 dimensions. Two teaching points: (1) the graph keeps only local structure — it deliberately forgets that two far-apart clusters are “very” far vs “extremely” far, which is why global distances later become meaningless; (2) this is the same object as a Markov-chain state diagram — nodes and weighted edges — so the graph idea is not new. Cells in a dense region get a tightly interconnected subgraph, which is what clustering will later carve out.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
section: Step 3: UMAP lays the graph out in 2D
text:
Step 3: UMAP lays the graph out in 2D
UMAP = Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection. Input: the kNN graph. Output: an \((x, y)\) coordinate for every cell.
The idea (no formulas today):

Assume the cells lie on a smooth low-dimensional manifold curled up inside gene space.
Find 2D coordinates so that cells that are neighbours in the graph stay close in the plot, and non-neighbours are pushed apart.
It is non-linear: it may stretch and bend the space differently in different regions to make local neighbourhoods fit on a flat page.

The result: tight islands of similar cells, visibly separated — the canonical single-cell figure.
t-SNE is an older method with the same goal; UMAP is faster and is now the default. Neither is “more correct” — both are visualization tools.


Keep UMAP at the intuition level — the manifold assumption plus “preserve local neighbours, separate the rest.” Do not attempt the fuzzy-simplicial-set / cross-entropy math; it is beyond this course and not examined. The load-bearing word is non-linear: UMAP is allowed to warp the space region by region, unlike PCA’s single global rotation, and that warping is what produces clean separated islands. Mention t-SNE so students recognise it in papers, but frame both as visualization aids, not measurements. Set up the next slide: the price of that warping is that the axes and inter-island gaps carry no quantitative meaning.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
section: UMAP vs PCA: two different jobs
text:
UMAP vs PCA: two different jobs









PCA
UMAP




Mapping
linear (rotation / projection)
non-linear (bends locally)


Preserves
global variance directions
local neighbourhoods


Axes mean
variance (PC1 = most variance)
nothing interpretable


Distances
meaningful (in PC space)
not quantitative


Reversible
yes (loadings map back to genes)
no


Used here for
denoising / reduction
visualization only



They are complementary, not competitors: we run PCA then UMAP. PCA cleans and compresses; UMAP draws.

This table is the conceptual anchor of the lecture — worth pausing on. The single biggest misconception to kill: that UMAP “replaces” or “improves on” PCA. They do different jobs and we use both in sequence. PCA’s axes and distances are interpretable (a PC is a weighted sum of genes; distance in PC space is real); UMAP’s are not (the axes are unlabelled and the gaps between islands are not to scale). PCA is invertible via loadings back to genes; UMAP is a one-way picture. Have students copy this table — several exam-style conceptual questions come straight from it.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
Reading a UMAP honestly
What you may read off a UMAP:

Cells that fall in the same tight island are similar to each other. ✔
The presence of several distinct islands suggests several cell populations. ✔

What you may not read off a UMAP:

The distance between two islands is not how different those populations are. ✘
The size/spread of an island is not how variable or abundant that population is. ✘
The axes (UMAP-1, UMAP-2) mean nothing — do not report values. ✘
Rotations / flips are arbitrary; re-running with a new seed gives a different-looking (but equivalent) picture. ✘

Rule of thumb: local = trustworthy, global = decorative.


Devote real time here — this is the discipline half of the lecture. Walk each forbidden reading: inter-cluster gaps are meaningless (a huge gap can separate near-identical states and a small gap can separate very different ones), island area reflects the algorithm’s crowding control, not biological variance or cell count, and the axes are unnamed by construction. Stress reproducibility: UMAP depends on a random seed and on parameters, so the exact shape is not stable — only the local grouping is. Give them the mantra “local trustworthy, global decorative.” Tell them reviewers and examiners specifically look for over-read UMAPs.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
Step 4: graph-based clustering
To name the cell groups we cut the same kNN graph into communities — sets of cells more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Louvain and Leiden are community-detection algorithms: they group nodes to maximize a modularity-style score (more within-group edges than expected by chance).
Leiden is a refinement of Louvain that guarantees the communities are internally well-connected; it is now the default.
Each community becomes a cluster = a candidate cell population, given an arbitrary label (0, 1, 2, …).

Crucially: clustering runs on the graph, not on the UMAP coordinates. The UMAP is only how we display the clusters, by colouring each cell.


Define clustering as community detection on the neighbour graph: partition the nodes so edges fall mostly within groups. Modularity is the score being optimized — within-community edge density above a random baseline; no need to write the formula. Emphasise Leiden over Louvain (Leiden fixes a known Louvain flaw where communities could be internally disconnected). The recurring point, stated a third time deliberately: clusters come from the graph, the UMAP is only a canvas to paint them on. That decoupling is why you sometimes see one colour split across the UMAP or two colours touching — the layout and the partition are separate computations.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
The resolution parameter
Community detection has a knob: resolution. It sets how fine-grained the partition is.

Low resolution → fewer, larger clusters (lumps related types together).
High resolution → more, smaller clusters (splits fine subtypes — and eventually splits noise).

\[
\text{resolution} \uparrow \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{number of clusters} \uparrow
\]
There is no single correct value and no true number of clusters. The “right” resolution depends on the biological question — do you want T cells, or CD4 vs CD8 vs regulatory T cells?
Good practice: try a range of resolutions, and judge clusters by known marker genes, not by which value looks tidiest.


Resolution is the parameter students most need to respect. Make the monotone relationship explicit: turn it up, get more clusters; turn it down, get fewer. Then the hard truth — there is no ground-truth cluster count; the biologically correct granularity depends entirely on the question. Over-clustering manufactures “cell types” that are really noise; under-clustering merges real distinct populations. The disciplined workflow is to scan several resolutions and validate with known marker genes (previewing the cell-type annotation unit), rather than trusting the number that produces the prettiest picture. This is a favourite exam-discussion point.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
The whole workflow in R (Seurat)
Assume seu is the QC-ed, normalized object from the preprocessing unit.
library(Seurat)

# 1. Scale, then PCA (denoise + reduce): reuse the PCA machinery
seu <- ScaleData(seu)
seu <- RunPCA(seu, npcs = 50)
ElbowPlot(seu)                       # scree/elbow: how many PCs to keep?

# 2. kNN graph on the top 30 PCs (Euclidean distance in PC space)
seu <- FindNeighbors(seu, dims = 1:30, k.param = 15)

# 3. Graph-based clustering (Leiden/Louvain) at a chosen resolution
seu <- FindClusters(seu, resolution = 0.5)

# 4. UMAP layout from the SAME 30 PCs, for display only
seu <- RunUMAP(seu, dims = 1:30)

# 5. Plot: UMAP coloured by cluster label
DimPlot(seu, reduction = "umap", label = TRUE)
Five function calls map exactly onto the four pipeline steps. No package is installed here — read this as a recipe, not runnable code.

Walk the code as a one-to-one map onto the roadmap: ScaleData + RunPCA is Step 1, FindNeighbors is Step 2 (the kNN graph, note dims = 1:30 selects the top PCs and k.param sets k), FindClusters is Step 4 (resolution is the knob from the previous slide), RunUMAP is Step 3 for display. Point out the load-bearing detail that FindNeighbors and RunUMAP both take dims = 1:30 — same PC input, two outputs. FindClusters uses the graph FindNeighbors built, not the UMAP. This is static illustration code; nothing runs at render time. Mention scanpy’s sc.pp.neighbors / sc.tl.leiden / sc.tl.umap are the exact same steps for Python users.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
section: Peeking under the hood: kNN by hand in R
text:
Peeking under the hood: kNN by hand in R
The Seurat calls are black boxes. Here is the kNN step on a toy PC matrix, in base R, so you can see there is no magic.
# six cells, each already reduced to 2 PCs
Z <- rbind(
  A = c(0, 0), B = c(1, 0), C = c(0, 1),   # group 1 (near origin)
  D = c(5, 5), E = c(6, 5), F = c(5, 6))    # group 2 (near (5,5))

D2 <- as.matrix(dist(Z))     # all pairwise Euclidean distances
round(D2, 2)

# the 2 nearest neighbours of each cell (column 1 is the cell itself)
apply(D2, 1, function(col) names(sort(col))[2:3])
Each cell’s two nearest neighbours are the other two members of its own group — the graph splits cleanly into two communities. That is clustering in miniature.


Demystify the pipeline by doing the neighbour step with dist() and sort() on six points — no special package. Students see that “kNN graph” is literally: compute Euclidean distances, take the k smallest per row. The toy coordinates are chosen so the two groups are obvious, and each cell’s nearest neighbours are its own group-mates, so the resulting graph has two disconnected pieces = two clusters. This is exactly the by-hand exercise, so it doubles as a preview of the exercise sheet. Reinforce that the real pipeline does the same thing in 30 dimensions on thousands of cells, then lays it out with UMAP.

title: Dimensionality reduction & clustering
text:
Caveats: do not over-interpret
Everything today is exploratory. It generates hypotheses; it does not test them.

UMAP is a cartoon. Local grouping is meaningful; axes, gaps, and island sizes are not.
Clusters are not ground truth. They depend on: which genes you kept, how many PCs, \(k\), the resolution, and the random seed.
The number of clusters is a choice, not a discovery. Validate against known marker genes, not visual tidiness.
A cluster is not yet a cell type. Assigning identities comes next, in cell-type annotation.
Reproducibility: fix and report the seed and every parameter, or your figure cannot be reproduced.

Honest single-cell analysis = the pipeline plus the disclaimers.

Consolidate the warnings into one slide they can revisit. The meta-point: this is exploratory analysis — it proposes cell populations, it does not prove them. Every output is contingent on a stack of choices (highly variable genes, PC count, k, resolution, seed), so two competent analysts can get different-looking maps from the same data and both be defensible. The remedy is transparency (report every parameter and the seed) and biological validation (marker genes), which is the handoff to the cell-type annotation unit. End on the framing that the disclaimers are part of the analysis, not an afterthought.

PCA denoises; UMAP draws; clustering groups. UMAP and clustering share the kNN graph.

Resolution sets the cluster count — there is no true number of clusters.

Next (cell-type annotation): turn anonymous clusters 0, 1, 2 … into named cell types using marker genes. Later, cell-cycle analysis revisits PCA to remove an unwanted source of variation.

The summary table is the exam cheat-sheet. Drill the pipeline verbally one more time: PCA to ~30 denoised PCs, kNN graph in that space, UMAP for the picture, Leiden for the groups — with UMAP and clustering both fed by the same graph. Restate the three non-negotiable caveats: UMAP geometry is not quantitative, resolution controls cluster count, and clusters are candidates not truths. Preview cell-type annotation (naming clusters via markers) and cell-cycle analysis (using PCA to regress out a nuisance signal), so students see today as one link in the single-cell chain, not a standalone trick.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
text:
About this lecture
In Linear systems by hand we solved small systems \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) on paper. Today we hand the work to R — and discover that not every system has a tidy answer. You will be able to:

Build \(A\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) in R and solve with solve.
Recognise the three kinds of solution space: exactly one, none, or infinitely many.
Connect each kind to a deconvolution scenario: exactly-, over-, or under-determined.
Know what to reach for when \(A\) is singular or non-square: least squares, via lm (full treatment later).


Today is the R day. The key conceptual jump is that “solve a linear system” is not always a well-posed request — there may be no answer, or a whole family of answers. We tie that to whether a cell-type deconvolution problem has enough, too few, or conflicting measurements. Keep the code minimal and the intuition front and centre.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
text:
Recap: the deconvolution problem
A bulk expression sample is a mixture. Known per-cell-type signatures (matrix \(A\), one column per cell type) and the measured bulk profile (vector \(\mathbf{b}\)) give a system \[
A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},
\] whose solution \(\mathbf{x}\) is the fractions (or amounts) of each cell type. Today: what if the system cannot be solved exactly?


Recall the running example. The number of measured genes is the number of equations (rows of A); the number of cell types is the number of unknowns (columns of A). The relationship between those two counts is what drives everything today.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
text:
Building \(A\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) in R
# Two cell types, two marker genes
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(8, 9)

A
#      [,1] [,2]
# [1,]    2    1
# [2,]    1    3

matrix with byrow = TRUE fills row by row, so the code reads like the equations on paper.
nrow sets the number of rows; c(...) is just the entries.
Default byrow = FALSE fills column by column — a classic bug.



Spend a moment on byrow because it bites everyone once. The default fills down the first column, so a matrix typed left-to-right comes out transposed unless you set byrow = TRUE. Always print the matrix and eyeball it against your equations before trusting it.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
text:
Solving with solve()
x <- solve(A, b)
x
# [1] 3 2          # 3 units tumour, 2 units immune

# Always check: does A x reproduce b?
A %*% x
#      [,1]
# [1,]    8
# [2,]    9

solve(A, b) returns the \(\mathbf{x}\) with \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) — it runs Gaussian elimination, exactly what you did by hand in Linear systems by hand.
%*% is matrix multiplication. Use it to verify, just like substituting back on paper.


solve is the workhorse. Two arguments means “solve this system”. Note that it returns the same 3, 2 we found by hand in Linear systems by hand. The verification step with the matrix product is the R equivalent of plugging back into the original equations — make it a reflex.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
text:
solve(A) alone gives the inverse
Ainv <- solve(A)        # one argument: the inverse of A
Ainv %*% b
# [1] 3 2               # same answer, x = A^{-1} b

solve(A, b) is preferred over solve(A) %*% b: it is faster and more numerically accurate (it never forms the inverse explicitly).
The inverse \(A^{-1}\) only exists when \(A\) is square and non-singular — precisely the “exactly one solution” case below.


Worth showing so they recognise both forms in the wild, but steer them toward the two-argument solve. Forming the inverse is wasteful and less stable. Flag that the inverse existing is equivalent to the system having a unique solution — this links directly into the next slides.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
text:
Three kinds of solution space
For \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) there are exactly three possibilities:

Exactly one solution — the system is consistent and determined.
No solution — the equations contradict each other.
Infinitely many solutions — the equations are consistent but leave freedom.

The next slides take each in turn and pair it with a deconvolution scenario.


This trichotomy is a theorem: a linear system has zero, one, or infinitely many solutions — never, say, exactly two. Geometrically (Vectors, dot product & projection) each equation is a line or plane, and we are asking how they intersect. For now, anchor each case to the biology.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
text:
Case 1 — exactly one (well-determined)
As many independent measurements as unknowns. \(A\) is square and non-singular.
Biology: #genes measured = #cell types, and the signatures are genuinely different. The deconvolution has a single answer.
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
solve(A, c(8, 9))
# [1] 3 2          # the unique solution
This is the happy case from Linear systems by hand. solve() just returns the answer.


This is the case students already understand from Linear systems by hand. Stress the two conditions: square (equations equal unknowns) and non-singular (the equations are genuinely independent, not rephrasings of each other). When both hold, there is one and only one solution and solve returns it.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
text:
Case 2 — no solution (over-determined)
More equations than unknowns, and they conflict. Often \(A\) is non-square (more rows than columns).
Biology: we measured more genes than cell types. With real noisy data the equations rarely agree exactly, so no \(\mathbf{x}\) fits all of them.
A <- matrix(c(1, 0,
              0, 1,
              1, 1), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)   # 3 eqns, 2 unknowns
b <- c(2, 3, 6)                                # but 2 + 3 = 5, not 6
solve(A, b)
# Error in solve.default(A, b) : 'a' must be a square matrix
solve() refuses: it only handles square systems.


Over-determined means too many equations. With exact data they might still all agree, but with measurement noise they generally do not — there is no x that satisfies every equation at once. solve flatly errors on a non-square A. The fix, least squares, is two slides away. Note this is actually the realistic omics case: thousands of genes, a handful of cell types.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
text:
Case 3 — infinitely many (under-determined)
Fewer independent equations than unknowns. \(A\) is singular (or has fewer rows than columns).
Biology: we measured too few genes to distinguish the cell types — many fraction combinations explain the data equally well.
A <- matrix(c(1, 1,
              2, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)   # row 2 = 2 x row 1
b <- c(3, 6)
solve(A, b)
# Error in solve.default(...) : Lapack routine dgesv: system is exactly singular
Both equations say the same thing (\(x_1 + x_2 = 3\)), so any \(\mathbf{x}\) on that line works. solve() errors on the singular matrix.


Under-determined means too few independent equations. Here row two is just twice row one — no new information — so the matrix is singular and there is a whole line of solutions. solve detects the singularity and stops. The biology: not enough markers to resolve the cell types. Contrast the two error messages on this and the previous slide so they can diagnose which case they hit.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
section: Detecting which case you are in
text:
Detecting which case you are in
dim(A)                 # rows (equations) vs cols (unknowns)
qr(A)$rank             # number of independent equations

dim non-square \(\Rightarrow\) over- or under-determined by shape.
qr$rank < #unknowns \(\Rightarrow\) the equations do not pin down every unknown: a square \(A\) is singular (some columns are combinations of others) \(\Rightarrow\) not Case 1.

A square \(A\) with full rank is exactly Case 1. (Bonus, not for exam: det(A) \(\approx 0\) flags the same thing.)


Give them a diagnostic toolkit. dim tells you the shape. Rank counts the independent equations; it is the most robust single number. det near zero also flags a singular square matrix, but determinants are bonus material, and with floating point det is rarely exactly zero anyway. Rank is the one to remember: full rank equal to the number of unknowns is the unique-solution condition.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
section: When there is no exact answer: least squares
text:
When there is no exact answer: least squares
For over-determined systems (Case 2) we cannot satisfy every equation, so we find the \(\mathbf{x}\) that comes closest — minimising the total squared mismatch \(\lVert A\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\rVert^2\). This is least squares.
A <- matrix(c(1, 0,
              0, 1,
              1, 1), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(2, 3, 6)

qr.solve(A, b)            # least-squares solution
# [1] 2.333333 3.333333

coef(lm(b ~ A - 1))       # same thing, via linear regression
qr.solve and lm both give the best-fit \(\mathbf{x}\). We treat this properly later in the course.


This is the bridge to the rest of the course. When you cannot fit everything, fit as well as possible by minimising squared error — that is least squares, and it is what lm does under the hood. Mention it lightly here; the geometry (projection, Vectors, dot product & projection) and the full regression treatment come later. The takeaway: an over-determined deconvolution is solved by least squares, not solve.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
text:
A note for real deconvolution
Real cell-type fractions must be non-negative and usually sum to 1. Plain solve/lm know nothing about that and can return negative fractions.

Production tools (e.g. CIBERSORT, and Bioconductor packages) add these constraints (non-negative least squares, support-vector regression, etc.).
The linear-system core is the same — the constraints are extra structure on top.

We use the unconstrained version to learn the mechanics; the constrained version is the real tool.


Honesty about what we defer, per the course design principles. The bare linear algebra can hand you a negative fraction, which is biologically nonsense. Real deconvolution adds constraints. We deliberately strip those away to expose the linear-system skeleton students need to learn first. Name-drop the real tools so they know where to look.

title: Linear systems in R; solution spaces
text:
Summary

Build systems in R with matrix (byrow = TRUE!) and solve with solve(A, b); check with %*%.
A linear system has one, none, or infinitely many solutions — matching well-, over-, and under-determined deconvolution.
Diagnose with dim and qr$rank.
Over-determined \(\Rightarrow\) least squares (qr.solve, lm); full treatment later.

Next: Vectors, dot product & projection — the geometric picture: vectors, dot products, and projection (which is why least squares works).

Pull the threads together: the R mechanics, the three solution spaces tied to the biology, the diagnostics, and the least-squares escape hatch. Preview Vectors, dot product & projection, where the geometry explains the least-squares idea we waved at today. Point them to the exercise to practise all three cases in R.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
About this lecture
Today we start the linear-algebra block. By the end you will be able to:

Recognise when a biology problem is a system of linear equations.
Write such a system in the standard form \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\).
Solve small \(2\times 2\) and \(3\times 3\) systems by hand using substitution and Gaussian elimination.
Check a candidate solution by plugging it back in.

No prior linear algebra is assumed. We build the ideas from a concrete example and keep all numbers small enough to do with pen and paper.

Welcome to the linear-algebra block. This is the foundation for everything that follows — eigenvalues, Markov chains, PCA — so we go slowly. Today is deliberately by-hand and concept-heavy: the exam is written and on-campus, so you need to be able to solve a small system without a computer. In Linear systems in R we do the same thing at scale.

title: Solving linear equation systems
section: A biology problem: what is in the mixture?
text:
A biology problem: what is in the mixture?
A tumour biopsy is not one cell type. It is a mixture: some tumour cells, some immune cells, some healthy tissue. Suppose we already know two marker readouts per cell type (say, expression of gene G1 and gene G2), measured per “unit” of each cell type:




Tumour
Immune




Gene G1 signal
2
1


Gene G2 signal
1
3



We sequence a bulk sample and measure total signal: G1 \(= 8\), G2 \(= 9\).
Question: how many units of tumour (\(x_1\)) and immune (\(x_2\)) cells were in the sample?


This is the motivating pairing for this unit and Linear systems in R: cell-type deconvolution. A bulk measurement is a sum over the cell types present. If we know the per-cell-type signature, recovering the amounts is exactly solving a linear system. Keep the numbers tiny here on purpose — we will make them realistic in Linear systems in R.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
Turning the biology into equations
Each measured signal is the sum of contributions from each cell type:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{2x_1 + 1x_2}_{\text{total G1}} &= 8\\[2pt]
\underbrace{1x_1 + 3x_2}_{\text{total G2}} &= 9
\end{aligned}
\]
Two unknowns (\(x_1, x_2\)), two equations. This is a system of linear equations.
“Linear” means every unknown appears only to the first power — no \(x_1^2\), no \(x_1 x_2\), no \(\sin x_1\). Just numbers times unknowns, added up.


Stress what “linear” rules out: no squares, no products of unknowns, no nonlinear functions. Each equation is a weighted sum of the unknowns set equal to a number. Almost every method in this course reduces, at its core, to solving or approximately solving a system like this.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
The standard form \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\)
We separate the known coefficients from the unknowns and the measurements:
\[
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}}_{A}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{x}}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{b}}
\]

\(A\) — the coefficient matrix. Here, the cell-type signatures (one column per cell type, one row per gene).
\(\mathbf{x}\) — the unknowns we want (the cell-type amounts).
\(\mathbf{b}\) — the right-hand side, our measurements.

The first row of \(A\) times \(\mathbf{x}\) reproduces the first equation; the second row gives the second. This packaging is what lets us scale to hundreds of genes later.


Introduce the names carefully: coefficient matrix A, unknown vector x, right-hand side b. Notation conventions for the course: uppercase for matrices, bold lowercase for vectors. Walk through how “row of A times x” rebuilds each equation — this is the first glimpse of matrix-vector multiplication, which we formalise in Matrices as transformations.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
Strategy 1 — Substitution
Solve one equation for one unknown, then substitute into the other.
From equation 1: \(\;2x_1 + x_2 = 8 \;\Rightarrow\; x_2 = 8 - 2x_1\).
Put that into equation 2:
\[
x_1 + 3(8 - 2x_1) = 9 \;\Rightarrow\; x_1 + 24 - 6x_1 = 9 \;\Rightarrow\; -5x_1 = -15
\]
So \(x_1 = 3\), and then \(x_2 = 8 - 2(3) = 2\).
Answer: 3 units of tumour, 2 units of immune cells.

Substitution is the method most students already half-remember from school. Do it slowly. Isolate one variable, push it into the other equation, you now have one equation in one unknown. Solve, then back-substitute. The arithmetic is the only place to slip up, so go step by step on the board.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
Always check your answer
Plug \(x_1 = 3,\; x_2 = 2\) back into the original equations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2(3) + 1(2) &= 6 + 2 = 8 \quad\checkmark\\
1(3) + 3(2) &= 3 + 6 = 9 \quad\checkmark
\end{aligned}
\]
Both hold, so the solution is correct.
Checking costs seconds and catches almost every arithmetic mistake. On the exam, always do it.

Make checking a habit and say so explicitly. Substituting back into the original equations is independent of how you got the answer, so it catches sign errors and arithmetic slips. This is free marks on an exam and free peace of mind in real analysis.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
Strategy 2 — Gaussian elimination
Substitution gets messy with three or more unknowns. Gaussian elimination is the systematic method that scales (it is what R uses internally).
The idea: add multiples of one equation to another to eliminate a variable, until the system is easy to read off.
Two moves are allowed (they never change the solution):

Multiply an equation by a non-zero number.
Add a multiple of one equation to another.

(A third, swapping two equations, just reorders them.)

Frame Gaussian elimination as “substitution made systematic”. The allowed operations are the row operations; emphasise that each one preserves the solution set, which is why we are allowed to do them. This is the algorithm behind solve() in R, so understanding it by hand demystifies the computer.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
Gaussian elimination on our 2×2
Start:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2x_1 + 1x_2 &= 8 \quad(\text{R1})\\
1x_1 + 3x_2 &= 9 \quad(\text{R2})
\end{aligned}
\]
Eliminate \(x_1\) from R2. Replace R2 by \(\;\text{R2} - \tfrac{1}{2}\text{R1}\):
\[
\Big(1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2\Big)x_1 + \Big(3 - \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1\Big)x_2
= 9 - \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot 8
\;\Rightarrow\; 0\,x_1 + 2.5\,x_2 = 5
\]
Now R2 says \(2.5\,x_2 = 5 \Rightarrow x_2 = 2\). Back-substitute into R1: \(2x_1 + 2 = 8 \Rightarrow x_1 = 3\). Same answer as before. \(\checkmark\)

Show the multiplier choice: we want to kill x1 in R2, R2 has coefficient 1 and R1 has coefficient 2, so subtract half of R1. The x1 term vanishes by design. Then the last equation has a single unknown — solve it, then back-substitute upward. Reassure them it gives the same answer as substitution; it is the same maths, organised.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
The augmented matrix shorthand
We do not need to keep writing \(x_1, x_2\). Track only the numbers in an augmented matrix \([\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]\):
\[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 2 & 1 & 8 \\ 1 & 3 & 9 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,\frac12\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 2 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 2.5 & 5 \end{array}\right]
\]
The bottom row reads \(2.5\,x_2 = 5\). The goal is this upper-triangular (“staircase”) shape: zeros below the diagonal. Then solve bottom-up.


The augmented matrix is bookkeeping: a vertical bar separates A from b, and we apply the same row operations to the whole row including the b entry. Target shape is upper triangular — once you are there, the last row is one equation in one unknown and you climb back up. This notation is essential for the 3x3 case.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
Scaling up: a 3×3 system
Three cell types (tumour, immune, stroma), three marker genes. Signatures and measurements give:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1x_1 + 1x_2 + 1x_3 &= 6\\
0x_1 + 2x_2 + 1x_3 &= 7\\
2x_1 + 1x_2 + 1x_3 &= 8
\end{aligned}
\qquad
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6\\
0 & 2 & 1 & 7\\
2 & 1 & 1 & 8
\end{array}\right]
\]
We eliminate column by column, top-left to bottom-right.

Now the payoff for systematic elimination. With three unknowns substitution becomes error-prone, but elimination is just “clear column 1, then clear column 2”. The first equation conveniently already has a 1 in the top-left, our pivot. Walk through the plan before doing the arithmetic.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
3×3 elimination — clear column 1
Pivot is the \(1\) in the top-left. R2 already has a \(0\) there. Clear R3 with \(\;\text{R3} - 2\,\text{R1}\):
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6\\
0 & 2 & 1 & 7\\
2 & 1 & 1 & 8
\end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R3}-2\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6\\
0 & 2 & 1 & 7\\
0 & -1 & -1 & -4
\end{array}\right]
\]
Column 1 now has zeros below the pivot.

R3 minus two times R1: 2 minus 2 is 0, 1 minus 2 is minus 1, 1 minus 2 is minus 1, and 8 minus 12 is minus 4. Do each subtraction out loud. The point is that the first unknown is now confined to the first equation only.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
3×3 elimination — clear column 2
Pivot is now the \(2\) in R2. Clear R3 with \(\;\text{R3} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{R2}\):
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6\\
0 & 2 & 1 & 7\\
0 & -1 & -1 & -4
\end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R3}+\frac12\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6\\
0 & 2 & 1 & 7\\
0 & 0 & -0.5 & -0.5
\end{array}\right]
\]
Now upper-triangular. The bottom row reads \(-0.5\,x_3 = -0.5\).

R2 has minus 1 in column 2 below the pivot 2, so add half of R2 to R3 to kill it. Minus 1 plus 1 is 0; minus 1 plus a half is minus a half; minus 4 plus 3.5 is minus a half. We have reached the staircase shape. Now we read off and back- substitute.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
3×3 — back-substitution
From the bottom up:
\[
\begin{aligned}
-0.5\,x_3 &= -0.5 &&\Rightarrow\; x_3 = 1\\
2x_2 + x_3 &= 7 &&\Rightarrow\; 2x_2 + 1 = 7 \;\Rightarrow\; x_2 = 3\\
x_1 + x_2 + x_3 &= 6 &&\Rightarrow\; x_1 + 3 + 1 = 6 \;\Rightarrow\; x_1 = 2
\end{aligned}
\]
Solution: \(x_1 = 2,\; x_2 = 3,\; x_3 = 1\).
Check in the original: \(2+3+1=6\,\checkmark\), \(0+6+1=7\,\checkmark\), \(4+3+1=8\,\checkmark\).

Back-substitution always starts at the last row, which has one unknown. Solve it, carry that value up into the second-last row which now has one remaining unknown, and so on. Then check all three original equations. This is the full recipe they need for the exam.

title: Solving linear equation systems
section: The inverse: one matrix that undoes \(A\)
text:
The inverse: one matrix that undoes \(A\)
The inverse \(A^{-1}\) is the matrix with \(A^{-1}A = I\). Once you have it, every system with this \(A\) is one multiplication:
\[A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\]
Why bother? In deconvolution the signatures \(A\) stay the same and only the measurements \(\mathbf{b}\) change from sample to sample. Invert once, reuse for every sample.
How: put the identity on the right, \([\,A \mid I\,]\), and keep doing row operations until the left side is \(I\). Then the right side is \(A^{-1}\):
\[[\,A \mid I\,] \;\longrightarrow\; \cdots \;\longrightarrow\; [\,I \mid A^{-1}\,]\]

Same row operations as before, applied to the whole row.
New: after reaching the staircase, also eliminate upwards, then divide each row by its diagonal number. (This is called Gauss–Jordan elimination.)


The augmented matrix [A | b] solved for one right-hand side. [A | I] solves for the two columns of I at the same time: the first column of the result solves A x = (1, 0), the second solves A x = (0, 1), and together those columns are A^{-1}. So nothing new is being invented: it is elimination with two right-hand sides at once, carried all the way to I instead of stopping at the staircase. No determinants needed.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
Inverse by hand: our 2×2
\(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) from before. Clear below the diagonal, then above it, then scale:
\[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,\frac12\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2.5 & -0.5 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,\div\,2.5\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -0.2 & 0.4 \end{array}\right]
\]
\[
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 0 & 1.2 & -0.4 \\ 0 & 1 & -0.2 & 0.4 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,\div\,2\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 0.6 & -0.2 \\ 0 & 1 & -0.2 & 0.4 \end{array}\right]
\]
So \(A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & -0.2 \\ -0.2 & 0.4 \end{pmatrix}\). Check: \(A^{-1}\mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6\cdot 8 - 0.2\cdot 9 \\ -0.2\cdot 8 + 0.4\cdot 9 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}\), the same answer as before. \(\checkmark\)
No inverse? If elimination leaves a row of zeros on the left, you can never reach \(I\): the matrix is singular (its columns point along the same line) and has no inverse.

Walk the four steps slowly: the first is exactly the elimination step from before, the second makes the pivot 1, the third clears the entry above the pivot, the fourth scales row 1. Every operation is applied to all four numbers in the row. Two checks students can always do: multiply A^{-1} b and compare with the earlier answer, or multiply A %*% A^{-1} and get I. The singular case connects to Linear systems in R: a zero row on the left is the same situation as “no unique solution”. (The ad - bc formula for 2x2 inverses is a bonus shortcut, not needed for the exam.)

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
The same idea in R (preview)
In Linear systems in R we let the computer do the elimination. The code is short:
A <- matrix(c(1, 1, 1,
              0, 2, 1,
              2, 1, 1), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(6, 7, 8)
solve(A, b)
# [1] 2 3 1
solve(A)       # one argument: the inverse
solve() runs Gaussian elimination internally — exactly what you just did by hand, but on any size. With one argument it returns \(A^{-1}\).

A quick reassurance and a hook into Linear systems in R. We will not type matrices by hand forever; solve does the elimination for us. But knowing what it does is what lets you trust it, debug it, and answer exam questions where no computer is allowed. Note byrow = TRUE so the matrix reads like the page.

title: Solving linear equation systems
text:
Summary

A linear system = weighted sums of unknowns set equal to numbers.
Standard form: \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) (\(A\) coefficients, \(\mathbf{x}\) unknowns, \(\mathbf{b}\) measurements).
Substitution for tiny systems; Gaussian elimination (via the augmented matrix) for anything bigger — eliminate to upper-triangular, then back-substitute.
Inverse: row-reduce \([\,A \mid I\,]\) to \([\,I \mid A^{-1}\,]\); then \(\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\) for any \(\mathbf{b}\). A zero row on the left means no inverse.
Always check by substituting back into the original equations.
Biology hook: recovering cell-type amounts from bulk measurements.

Next: Linear systems in R — what happens when there is no solution or infinitely many.

Recap the four takeaways and the biology framing. Flag the open question for Linear systems in R: so far every system has had exactly one answer, but that is not guaranteed — sometimes there is none, sometimes infinitely many, and that maps directly onto whether a deconvolution problem is well posed. Point them to the exercise and quiz.

title: Exercise: vectors, dot product & projection
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to, by hand and in R:

add and scale vectors,
compute a vector’s length (norm),
compute a dot product and read off its meaning,
compute the angle / cosine similarity between two vectors,
decide whether two vectors are orthogonal,
project one vector onto another and find the orthogonal leftover.

The by-hand problems are the ones that matter most for the written exam — the on-campus exam has no computer. Do them with pen and paper first, then check with R.

title: Exercise: vectors, dot product & projection
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to, by hand and in R:

add and scale vectors,
compute a vector’s length (norm),
compute a dot product and read off its meaning,
compute the angle / cosine similarity between two vectors,
decide whether two vectors are orthogonal,
project one vector onto another and find the orthogonal leftover.

The by-hand problems are the ones that matter most for the written exam — the on-campus exam has no computer. Do them with pen and paper first, then check with R.

title: Exercise: vectors, dot product & projection
text:
Background
A vector is an ordered list of numbers \(\mathbf{v} = (v_1, \dots, v_n)\). For us, a vector is a sample: a gene-expression profile across \(n\) genes.







Operation
Definition




Addition
\(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = (u_1 + v_1,\ \dots,\ u_n + v_n)\)


Scaling
\(c\,\mathbf{v} = (c v_1,\ \dots,\ c v_n)\)


Norm (length)
\(\|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + \dots + v_n^2} = \sqrt{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}}\)


Dot product
\(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = u_1 v_1 + \dots + u_n v_n\)


Angle
\(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|}\)


Orthogonal
\(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\)


Projection of \(\mathbf{u}\) onto \(\mathbf{v}\)
\(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}}\,\mathbf{v}\)



The geometric identity that ties dot product to angle: \[\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta.\]

title: Exercise: vectors, dot product & projection
text:
By hand
Use these vectors throughout (think of them as 2-gene mini-profiles): \[\mathbf{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{c} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}\]
B1. Compute \(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{c}\) and \(2\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}\).
B2. Compute the lengths \(\|\mathbf{a}\|\) and \(\|\mathbf{b}\|\). (Both are nice round numbers.)
B3. Compute the dot products \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}\).
B4. Using B2 and B3, compute \(\cos\theta\) for the angle between \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\). What is \(\theta\) in degrees?
B5. Show that \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}\) are orthogonal. Then find a number \(k\) so that \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ k \end{pmatrix}\) is orthogonal to \(\mathbf{a}\).
B6. Compare \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{d}\): compute \(\cos\theta\) between them. What do you notice, and what does it say about the two “samples”? (Hint: look at \(\mathbf{d}\) versus \(\mathbf{a}\) componentwise.)
B7. Project \(\mathbf{a}\) onto \(\mathbf{b}\), i.e. compute \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{a}\). Then compute the leftover \(\mathbf{a} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{a}\) and verify it is orthogonal to \(\mathbf{b}\).

title: Exercise: vectors, dot product & projection
text:
Explore
Check your by-hand answers with the interactive picture below. Drag the tips of \(\mathbf{u}\) (blue) and \(\mathbf{v}\) (orange); the tips snap to a 0.5 grid. The green arrow is the projection \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}\) and the dashed line the perpendicular drop. The depth slider replaces \(\mathbf{v}\) by \(k\mathbf{v}\): the same cell sequenced \(k\) times as deep.



E1. The picture starts with \(\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{a} = (3,4)\) and \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{b} = (4,0)\). Compare the readout with your answers to B3, B4 and B7.
E2. Keep \(\mathbf{v} = (4,0)\) and drag \(\mathbf{u}\) around. Where must the tip of \(\mathbf{u}\) be for \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\)? Where does the shadow point when \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} < 0\)?
E3. Click parallel (\(\mathbf{u} = (3,4) = \mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{v} = (6,8) = \mathbf{d}\), as in B6). Move the depth slider from \(k = 1\) down to \(k = 0.5\). What happens to the distance \(\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\|\), and what happens to \(\cos\theta\)?
E4. Click lecture (\(\mathbf{u} = (3,2)\), \(\mathbf{v} = (1,4)\)) and move the depth slider to \(k = 2\). Which of \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\), \(\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\|\), \(\cos\theta\) and \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}\) change? Explain why the projection stays put.






Solutions





E1. \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 3\cdot4 + 4\cdot0 = 12\), \(\cos\theta = 0.6\), \(\theta \approx 53.1^\circ\), and the shadow is \(\tfrac{12}{16}(4,0) = (3,0)\), with leftover \((0,4)\) straight up: the same numbers as B3, B4 and B7.
E2. \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 4u_1\), so it is zero exactly when \(u_1 = 0\): the tip must be on the vertical gene-2 axis, at a right angle to \(\mathbf{v}\). When \(u_1 < 0\) the dot product is negative and the shadow points the other way from \(\mathbf{v}\), onto the negative gene-1 axis.
E3. At \(k = 0.5\), \(\mathbf{v}\) becomes \((3,4) = \mathbf{u}\), so the distance falls from \(5\) to \(0\). The cosine stays at \(1\) the whole time: scaling a profile does not change its direction.
E4. \(\mathbf{v}\) becomes \((2,8)\). The dot product doubles (\(11 \to 22\)) and the distance grows (\(\sqrt{8} \approx 2.83 \to \sqrt{37} \approx 6.08\)), but \(\cos\theta\) stays \(0.740\). The projection stays \((0.65, 2.59)\): the coefficient \(\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}}\) is halved (\(\tfrac{11}{17} \to \tfrac{22}{68}\)) while \(\mathbf{v}\) is doubled, so the shadow only depends on the direction of \(\mathbf{v}\).

title: Exercise: vectors, dot product & projection
text:
In R
Define the vectors and verify your by-hand answers, then scale up to a realistic-sized profile.
a <- c(3, 4)
b <- c(4, 0)
cc <- c(-2, 6)   # 'c' is a reserved function name in R, so use cc
d <- c(6, 8)

# B1 — addition and scaling
a + cc
2*b - a

# B2 — norms
sqrt(sum(a^2))   # = 5
sqrt(sum(b^2))   # = 4

# B3 — dot products
sum(a * b)
sum(a * cc)

# B4 — angle between a and b
cos_ab <- sum(a*b) / (sqrt(sum(a^2)) * sqrt(sum(b^2)))
cos_ab
acos(cos_ab) * 180/pi   # angle in degrees

# B5 — orthogonality check
sum(b * c(0, 5))        # should be 0

# B6 — a vs d
sum(a*d) / (sqrt(sum(a^2)) * sqrt(sum(d^2)))

# B7 — projection of a onto b, and the leftover
proj_ab <- (sum(a*b) / sum(b*b)) * b
proj_ab
leftover <- a - proj_ab
leftover
sum(leftover * b)       # should be 0 (orthogonal)

Scale up: comparing real-ish profiles
Reusable helper functions, then a small “expression matrix” of samples in columns:
norm_vec <- function(v) sqrt(sum(v^2))
cos_sim  <- function(u, v) sum(u*v) / (norm_vec(u) * norm_vec(v))

set.seed(1)
genes <- 200
# two samples of the same "cell type": s2 is s1 at double depth plus a little noise
s1 <- rpois(genes, lambda = 5)
s2 <- 2 * s1 + rpois(genes, lambda = 1)
# an unrelated sample
s3 <- rpois(genes, lambda = 5)

cos_sim(s1, s2)   # close to 1: same direction despite different depth
cos_sim(s1, s3)   # lower: unrelated profiles

# Compare with Euclidean distance, which IS fooled by depth:
norm_vec(s1 - s2)   # large, because s2 is ~twice as big
norm_vec(s1 - s3)   # smaller, even though s3 is unrelated!
R1. Run the block above. Explain in one sentence why cosine similarity ranks s1–s2 as most similar but Euclidean distance does not.
R2. Build a cosine-similarity matrix for all three samples. (Hint: stack them as columns of a matrix and use crossprod, or just call cos_sim on each pair.)

title: Exercise: vectors, dot product & projection
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — building and combining vectors





Use c to build a vector. Plain +, - and * between a scalar and a vector, or between two equal-length vectors, work elementwise — exactly matching the by-hand definitions of addition and scaling.









Hint 2 — norm and dot product





The norm is sqrt(sum(v^2)). The dot product of u and v is sum(u*v); equivalently u %*% v (see %*%), which returns a \(1\times1\) matrix. Note \(\|\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v} =\) sum(v*v).









Hint 3 — angles in R





R’s trig functions work in radians. Get the angle with acos and convert to degrees by multiplying by 180/pi. Clamp arguments that drift slightly outside \([-1,1]\) from rounding if needed.









Hint 4 — orthogonality





Two vectors are orthogonal iff their dot product is exactly 0. For B5, set \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(2, k) = 0\) and solve the resulting linear equation for \(k\).









Hint 5 — projection





First compute the scalar coefficient \(\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}}\) = sum(u*v)/sum(v*v), then multiply it by the vector v. The leftover u - proj should dot to 0 with v.









Hint 6 — cosine vs distance, and the similarity matrix (R1/R2)





For R1, recall that cosine similarity divides out each vector’s length, so it sees only direction; Euclidean distance [norm_vec(s1 - s2)] keeps the magnitude, so doubling depth inflates it. For R2, the slick route is to normalise every column to unit length with apply, then crossprod(U) computes all pairwise dot products at once — and a dot product of unit vectors is their cosine, so that matrix is the cosine-similarity matrix. Or simply call cos_sim on each of the three pairs.

title: Exercise: vectors, dot product & projection
text:
Solutions






Solution





B1. \(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{c} = (3+(-2),\ 4+6) = (1,\ 10)\). \(2\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a} = (8,0)-(3,4) = (5,\ -4)\).
B2. \(\|\mathbf{a}\| = \sqrt{3^2+4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5\). \(\|\mathbf{b}\| = \sqrt{4^2+0^2} = 4\).
B3. \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = 3\cdot4 + 4\cdot0 = 12\). \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c} = 3(-2) + 4\cdot6 = -6 + 24 = 18\).
B4. \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{12}{5\cdot4} = \dfrac{12}{20} = 0.6\). So \(\theta = \arccos(0.6) \approx 53.13^\circ\).
B5. \(\mathbf{b}\cdot(0,5) = 4\cdot0 + 0\cdot5 = 0\) → orthogonal. For \((2,k)\): \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(2,k) = 3\cdot2 + 4k = 6 + 4k = 0 \Rightarrow k = -\tfrac{3}{2}\).
B6. Note \(\mathbf{d} = (6,8) = 2\mathbf{a}\). So \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot 2\mathbf{a}}{\|\mathbf{a}\|\,\|2\mathbf{a}\|} = \dfrac{2\|\mathbf{a}\|^2}{2\|\mathbf{a}\|^2} = 1\), i.e. \(\theta = 0^\circ\). \(\mathbf{d}\) points in the same direction as \(\mathbf{a}\) — same “shape” of profile, just twice the magnitude (like the same cell type sequenced at double depth). Cosine similarity is blind to that scaling.
B7. Coefficient \(= \dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{b}} = \dfrac{12}{16} = \tfrac{3}{4}\). So \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{a} = \tfrac{3}{4}(4,0) = (3,\ 0)\). Leftover \(= \mathbf{a} - (3,0) = (0,\ 4)\). Check: \((0,4)\cdot(4,0) = 0\) ✓ (orthogonal, as expected — the projection drops a perpendicular onto the line through \(\mathbf{b}\), here the x-axis).
R answers (selected output):
a + cc            # 1 10
2*b - a           # 5 -4
sqrt(sum(a^2))    # 5
sum(a*b)          # 12
cos_ab            # 0.6
acos(0.6)*180/pi  # 53.13010
proj_ab           # 3 0
leftover          # 0 4
sum(leftover*b)   # 0
R1. s2 is essentially 2 * s1, i.e. the same direction in gene space; cosine similarity measures direction and so reports ~1, whereas Euclidean distance measures absolute separation and is inflated by the doubled magnitude. With set.seed(1) the block prints (your numbers match if you used the same seed):
cos_sim(s1, s2)     # 0.9956318   (near 1: same direction)
cos_sim(s1, s3)     # 0.8509409   (lower: unrelated)
norm_vec(s1 - s2)   # 91.50956    (large: s2 is ~twice as big)
norm_vec(s1 - s3)   # 42.95346    (smaller, yet s3 is the unrelated one!)
So cosine ranks s1–s2 as most similar (\(0.996 > 0.851\)), but Euclidean distance ranks them as least similar (\(91.5 > 43.0\)) — fooled by the depth difference.
R2. One compact way — normalise each sample column to unit length, then the matrix of pairwise cross products is exactly the cosine-similarity matrix (a unit-vector dot product is its cosine):
M <- cbind(s1, s2, s3)        # genes in rows, samples in columns
U <- apply(M, 2, function(v) v / norm_vec(v))   # each column now has norm 1
round(crossprod(U), 3)        # 3x3 cosine-similarity matrix
#       s1    s2    s3
# s1 1.000 0.996 0.851
# s2 0.996 1.000 0.857
# s3 0.851 0.857 1.000
The diagonal is 1 (each sample with itself), the s1–s2 entry is near 1, and every entry involving s3 is lower — matching the pairwise cos_sim calls.

title: Exercise: vectors, dot product & projection
text:
Where this leads

Matrices as transformations turns the dot product into a building block: every entry of a matrix–vector product is a dot product of a matrix row with the vector. A matrix becomes a machine that transforms whole vectors.
Cosine similarity is the standard way to compare cells/samples in single-cell analysis (Week 5).
Projection is the engine of PCA (Week 2): a PCA score is the coordinate of a sample projected onto a principal axis, and the orthogonal-leftover idea is how successive components are made independent.

title: Quiz: vectors, dot product & projection
text:
Short questions to test your geometric intuition. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Several are written in the style of the on-campus exam (no computer).

Q1. A gene-expression profile of 12 000 genes is a vector. In how many dimensions does it “live”?






Hint





The dimension equals the number of components (measurements).









Answer





12 000 dimensions — one axis per gene. We cannot draw it, but every rule from 2-D and 3-D still applies.




Q2. Compute \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} + 3\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}\).






Hint





Scale first, then add componentwise.









Answer





\(3(1,2) = (3,6)\), then \((2,-1)+(3,6) = (5,\ 5)\).




Q3. What is the length of \(\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}\)?






Hint





\(\|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2}\).









Answer





\(\sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10\).




Q4. Compute the dot product \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}\).






Hint





Multiply matching components and add.









Answer





\(1\cdot4 + 3\cdot0 + (-2)\cdot5 = 4 + 0 - 10 = -6\).




Q5. The dot product of two non-zero vectors is negative. What does that tell you about the angle between them?






Hint





Recall \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta\), and lengths are positive.









Answer





Since the lengths are positive, a negative dot product forces \(\cos\theta < 0\), so the angle is greater than \(90^\circ\) — the vectors point in broadly opposite directions.




Q6. Are \(\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}\) orthogonal?






Hint





Orthogonal iff the dot product is exactly 0.









Answer





\(3(-1) + 1\cdot3 = -3 + 3 = 0\) → yes, orthogonal (a right angle).




Q7. Two samples have profiles \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v} = 5\mathbf{u}\). What is their cosine similarity, and why is that biologically reassuring?






Hint





\(\mathbf{v}\) is just \(\mathbf{u}\) scaled. Does scaling change direction?









Answer





Cosine similarity = 1. Scaling does not change direction, so two profiles that differ only by overall magnitude (e.g. sequencing depth) are correctly judged identical in shape. Cosine similarity is depth-invariant.




Q8. True or false: the dot product of two vectors is itself a vector.






Hint





Count the numbers in the result.









Answer





False. The dot product is a single scalar (one number).




Q9. Project \(\mathbf{u} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}\) onto \(\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\).






Hint





\(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}}\,\mathbf{v}\). Here \(\mathbf{v}\) is the x-axis.









Answer





\(\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}} = \dfrac{5}{1} = 5\), so the projection is \(5(1,0) = (5,\ 0)\) — the shadow on the x-axis. (Makes sense: projecting onto the x-axis just keeps the x-component.)




Q10. After projecting \(\mathbf{u}\) onto \(\mathbf{v}\), what is special about the leftover \(\mathbf{u} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}\)?






Hint





Think about the right angle a shadow makes with the ground.









Answer





It is orthogonal to \(\mathbf{v}\) (dot product 0). The projection captures the part of \(\mathbf{u}\) along \(\mathbf{v}\); the leftover is the part with no overlap with \(\mathbf{v}\). This is the seed of PCA and least-squares regression.




Q11. Which R expression computes the dot product of vectors u and v? (a) u * v (b) sum(u * v) (c) u %o% v






Hint





A dot product returns a single number. * is elementwise; %o% is the outer product.









Answer






sum(u * v). Option (a) gives the elementwise products (a vector), and %o% gives an outer-product matrix. u %*% v also works, returning a \(1\times1\) matrix.





Q12. A sample \(\mathbf{u}\) has cosine similarity 0 with sample \(\mathbf{v}\). Interpret this.






Hint





\(\cos\theta = 0\) means what angle?









Answer





The profiles are orthogonal (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)): as different in direction as possible without pointing opposite. The two samples share no common expression pattern in this geometric sense.
