title: Drills: matrix times vector
text:
Multiply a matrix by a vector by hand, one row at a time.
See each result entry as a dot product of a matrix row with the vector.
Check the shape rule: the number of columns of \(A\) must equal the length of \(\mathbf{x}\).

No biology here. Just small whole numbers, with clean answers.

title: Drills: matrix times vector
text:
The rule
We want to compute \(A\mathbf{x}\), where \(A\) is a matrix and \(\mathbf{x}\) is a column vector.
Shape rule first. If \(A\) has size \(m \times n\), then \(\mathbf{x}\) must have length \(n\) (it must be \(n \times 1\)). The number of columns of \(A\) has to match the length of \(\mathbf{x}\). The answer is a column vector of length \(m\) (one number per row of \(A\)).
How to compute it. Each entry of the answer comes from one row of \(A\) combined with the vector \(\mathbf{x}\). You walk along the row and the vector together, multiply matching numbers, and add them up. This is called a dot product.
Here is a tiny worked example with a \(2 \times 2\) matrix: \[
A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}.
\]

Row 1 of \(A\) is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). Combine with \(\mathbf{x}\): \[
(1)(5) + (2)(6) = 5 + 12 = 17.
\]
Row 2 of \(A\) is \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\). Combine with \(\mathbf{x}\): \[
(3)(5) + (4)(6) = 15 + 24 = 39.
\]

Stack the two results into a column: \[
A\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix} (1)(5)+(2)(6) \\ (3)(5)+(4)(6) \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} 17 \\ 39 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
That is the whole idea: one row at a time, multiply across, add up.

title: Drills: matrix times vector
Drills: matrix times vector
text:
Check in R
In R, build \(A\) with matrix (use byrow = TRUE so it looks like the paper version), make \(\mathbf{x}\) with c, and multiply with the matrix-multiply operator %*%. A plain * would be wrong here (that multiplies element by element).
A <- matrix(c(1, 2,
              3, 4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
x <- c(5, 6)
A %*% x        # drill from "The rule"
#      [,1]
# [1,]   17
# [2,]   39

# Drill 5
matrix(c(2, 1, 0, 5), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE) %*% c(3, 2)
#      [,1]
# [1,]    8
# [2,]   10

# Drill 13: identity leaves the vector unchanged
diag(3) %*% c(4, 5, 6)
#      [,1]
# [1,]    4
# [2,]    5
# [3,]    6

title: Drills: matrix times vector
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — one row at a time





The answer has one entry per row of \(A\). Do row 1 to get the first answer entry, row 2 to get the second, and so on.









Hint 2 — multiply across, then add





For a row, multiply its first number by the vector’s first number, its second by the vector’s second, and so on, then add all those products together.









Hint 3 — check the shape before you start





Columns of \(A\) must equal the length of \(\mathbf{x}\). If a \(1\times 3\) row meets a length-2 vector, the count does not match, so the product does not exist.









Hint 4 — the identity does nothing





Multiplying by the identity matrix gives back the same vector. Multiplying by a diagonal matrix just scales each entry of the vector.

title: Drills: matrix times vector
text:
Step-by-step solutions






Solutions





1. Identity times the vector returns it unchanged. Row 1: \((1)(4)+(0)(7)=4\). Row 2: \((0)(4)+(1)(7)=7\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}\).
2. Row 1: \((2)(5)+(0)(1)=10\). Row 2: \((0)(5)+(3)(1)=3\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
3. Row 1: \((1)(2)+(1)(3)=5\). Row 2: \((1)(2)+(1)(3)=5\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\).
4. Row 1: \((1)(1)+(2)(1)=3\). Row 2: \((3)(1)+(4)(1)=7\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}\).
5. Row 1: \((2)(3)+(1)(2)=6+2=8\). Row 2: \((0)(3)+(5)(2)=0+10=10\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix}\).
6. Row 1: \((4)(2)+(1)(1)=8+1=9\). Row 2: \((2)(2)+(3)(1)=4+3=7\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}\).
7. Row 1: \((1)(3)+(2)(4)=3+8=11\). Row 2: \((2)(3)+(1)(4)=6+4=10\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 11 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix}\).
8. Row 1: \((5)(2)+(0)(6)=10+0=10\). Row 2: \((1)(2)+(2)(6)=2+12=14\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 14 \end{bmatrix}\).
9. Row 1: \((3)(0)+(2)(5)=0+10=10\). Row 2: \((1)(0)+(4)(5)=0+20=20\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 20 \end{bmatrix}\).
10. Row 1: \((2)(1)+(3)(2)=2+6=8\). Row 2: \((4)(1)+(1)(2)=4+2=6\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}\).
11. Shape check: the row \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) has \(3\) columns, but the vector has length \(2\). They do not match, so the product cannot be computed.
12. Shape check: the matrix has \(2\) columns, but the vector has length \(3\). They do not match, so the product cannot be computed.
13. Identity times the vector returns it unchanged. Row 1: \((1)(4)+(0)(5)+(0)(6)=4\). Row 2: \((0)(4)+(1)(5)+(0)(6)=5\). Row 3: \((0)(4)+(0)(5)+(1)(6)=6\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}\).
14. Every row is all ones, so each entry is just the sum \(2+3+1=6\). Row 1: \((1)(2)+(1)(3)+(1)(1)=6\). Same for rows 2 and 3. \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 6 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}\).
15. Row 1: \((1)(1)+(2)(2)+(0)(1)=1+4+0=5\). Row 2: \((0)(1)+(1)(2)+(3)(1)=0+2+3=5\). Row 3: \((1)(1)+(0)(2)+(1)(1)=1+0+1=2\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 5 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
16. Row 1: \((2)(1)+(0)(1)+(1)(2)=2+0+2=4\). Row 2: \((1)(1)+(3)(1)+(0)(2)=1+3+0=4\). Row 3: \((0)(1)+(1)(1)+(2)(2)=0+1+4=5\). \(\Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 4 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\).

title: Drills: transpose, identity, symmetry
text:
Write the transpose \(A^\top\) of a small matrix by flipping rows and columns.
Recognise the identity matrix \(I\) and see that \(IA = A\).

title: Drills: transpose, identity, symmetry
text:
Write the transpose \(A^\top\) of a small matrix by flipping rows and columns.
Recognise the identity matrix \(I\) and see that \(IA = A\).
Recognise when a matrix is symmetric (\(A = A^\top\)).

title: Drills: transpose, identity, symmetry
text:
The rule
Transpose. \(A^\top\) turns rows into columns. The entry in row \(i\), column \(j\) of \(A\) becomes row \(j\), column \(i\) of \(A^\top\). The diagonal stays put; everything else reflects across it.
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
A^\top=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Transposing twice gives back the original: \((A^\top)^\top = A\).
Identity. \(I\) has 1s on the diagonal and 0s everywhere else. Multiplying by it changes nothing: \(IA = A\) and \(AI = A\).
\[
I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Symmetric. A matrix is symmetric when it equals its own transpose: \(A = A^\top\). In picture form, it is a mirror image across the diagonal — the entry at row \(i\), col \(j\) equals the entry at row \(j\), col \(i\).
\[
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ 5 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\text{ is symmetric}, \qquad
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\text{ is not.}
\]

title: Drills: transpose, identity, symmetry
text:
Drills
Write the transpose:

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}^\top\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ 7 & 0 \end{bmatrix}^\top\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}^\top\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}^\top\) (a row becomes a column)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}^\top\) (a column becomes a row)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}^\top\)

Transpose twice (\((A^\top)^\top = A\)):

Take \(A=\begin{bmatrix} 8 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). Write \(A^\top\), then transpose that result. What do you get back?

Multiply by the identity:

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 7 \\ 8 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 6 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 9 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}\)
Without computing fully: what is \(I\,\mathbf{x}\) when \(\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(I\) is \(3\times 3\)?

Is this matrix symmetric? (yes/no, and say why):

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 6 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)

A little harder:

Fill in the missing entry so that \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 7 \\ \square & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) is symmetric.
Is the identity matrix \(I\) symmetric? Explain in one line.

title: Drills: transpose, identity, symmetry
text:
Check in R
Transpose is t. The identity is built with diag. To test symmetry, compare a matrix with its transpose using all and ==, or use isSymmetric.
A <- matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
t(A)
#      [,1] [,2]
# [1,]    1    3
# [2,]    2    4
diag(3)            # the 3x3 identity
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    1    0    0
# [2,]    0    1    0
# [3,]    0    0    1
S <- matrix(c(1, 2, 2, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
all(S == t(S))     # TRUE  -> symmetric
# [1] TRUE
isSymmetric(S)
# [1] TRUE

title: Drills: transpose, identity, symmetry
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — flip across the diagonal





To transpose, leave the diagonal entries alone and swap each off-diagonal pair: the entry at (row 1, col 2) trades places with (row 2, col 1).









Hint 2 — rows become columns





A \(1\times 3\) row turns into a \(3\times 1\) column, and vice versa. The numbers stay in the same order; only their orientation changes.









Hint 3 — the identity changes nothing





\(I A = A\) and \(A I = A\). You do not need to compute — the answer is just the other matrix, unchanged.









Hint 4 — symmetry test





Compare the entry at (row \(i\), col \(j\)) with the one at (row \(j\), col \(i\)). If every such pair is equal, the matrix is symmetric. A single mismatch means it is not.

title: Drills: transpose, identity, symmetry
text:
Step-by-step solutions






Solutions





Drill 1. Diagonal \(1,4\) stays; swap the off-diagonal \(2\) and \(3\). \[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}.\]
Drill 2. Diagonal \(0,0\) stays; swap \(5\) (row 1, col 2) and \(7\) (row 2, col 1). \[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 7 \\ 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.\]
Drill 3. Off-diagonal entries are both \(0\), so swapping changes nothing. \[\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}.\] (This is a diagonal matrix; diagonal matrices are their own transpose.)
Drill 4. A \(1\times 3\) row becomes a \(3\times 1\) column. \[\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.\]
Drill 5. A \(3\times 1\) column becomes a \(1\times 3\) row. \[\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}.\]
Drill 6. A \(2\times 3\) matrix becomes \(3\times 2\). Row 1 \((1,2,3)\) becomes column 1; row 2 \((4,5,6)\) becomes column 2. \[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}.\]
Drill 7. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}8&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\). First transpose: \(A^\top=\begin{bmatrix}8&0\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\). Transpose again: \((A^\top)^\top=\begin{bmatrix}8&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}=A\). You get the original matrix back, illustrating \((A^\top)^\top = A\).
Drill 8. Multiplying by the identity on the left does nothing: \[\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 7 \\ 8 & 9 \end{bmatrix}.\]
Drill 9. Multiplying by the identity on the right does nothing: \[\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 6 & 7 \end{bmatrix}.\]
Drill 10. The \(3\times 3\) identity times the column leaves it unchanged: \[\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 9 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}.\]
Drill 11. \(I\,\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}\), so the answer is \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\) — the identity leaves any vector unchanged.
Drill 12. Off-diagonal pair: (row 1, col 2) \(=2\) and (row 2, col 1) \(=2\). Equal, so yes, symmetric.
Drill 13. (row 1, col 2) \(=2\) but (row 2, col 1) \(=3\). Not equal, so no, not symmetric.
Drill 14. Off-diagonal entries are both \(0\). They match, so yes, symmetric (every diagonal matrix is symmetric).
Drill 15. Check the three off-diagonal pairs: \((1,2)\!=\!4=(2,1)\); \((1,3)\!=\!0=(3,1)\); \((2,3)\!=\!5=(3,2)\). All match, so yes, symmetric.
Drill 16. Check pairs: \((2,3)=5\) but \((3,2)=6\). They differ, so no, not symmetric.
Drill 17. For symmetry, (row 2, col 1) must equal (row 1, col 2) \(=7\). So \(\square = 7\): \[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 7 \\ 7 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.\]
Drill 18. Yes. \(I\) has all off-diagonal entries equal to \(0\), so flipping across the diagonal changes nothing: \(I^\top = I\).

title: Drills: solving 3×3 systems by elimination
text:
Solve three equations in three unknowns \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) using Gaussian elimination.
Practice writing the system as an augmented matrix and clearing it to upper-triangular form.
Finish every problem with back-substitution and a check. The written exam rewards showing each row operation.

title: Drills: solving 3×3 systems by elimination
text:
Solve three equations in three unknowns \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) using Gaussian elimination.
Practice writing the system as an augmented matrix and clearing it to upper-triangular form.
Finish every problem with back-substitution and a check. The written exam rewards showing each row operation.

title: Drills: solving 3×3 systems by elimination
text:
The method
A 3×3 system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{11}x + a_{12}y + a_{13}z &= b_1 \\
a_{21}x + a_{22}y + a_{23}z &= b_2 \\
a_{31}x + a_{32}y + a_{33}z &= b_3
\end{aligned}
\]
We pack the coefficients and the right-hand side into an augmented matrix:
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
a_{11} & a_{12} & a_{13} & b_1 \\
a_{21} & a_{22} & a_{23} & b_2 \\
a_{31} & a_{32} & a_{33} & b_3
\end{array}\right].
\]
Gaussian elimination uses row operations to create zeros below the diagonal:

Use row 1 to make the entries below \(a_{11}\) zero (operations like \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - kR_1\)).
Use row 2 to make the entry below \(a_{22}\) zero (\(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - kR_2\)).
You now have an upper-triangular matrix. The bottom row reads off \(z\) directly.
Back-substitute: get \(z\), then \(y\), then \(x\).
Check by plugging \(x,y,z\) into all three original equations.

A legal row operation is: replace a row by (that row) \(\pm\) (a multiple of another row). It does not change the solution.

Tiny worked example
\[
\begin{aligned}
x + y + z &= 6 \\
\phantom{x} + y + z &= 5 \\
\phantom{x + y} + z &= 3
\end{aligned}
\qquad
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 3
\end{array}\right]
\]
This is already upper-triangular. Back-substitute from the bottom:

Row 3: \(z = 3\).
Row 2: \(y + z = 5 \Rightarrow y + 3 = 5 \Rightarrow y = 2\).
Row 1: \(x + y + z = 6 \Rightarrow x + 2 + 3 = 6 \Rightarrow x = 1\).

So \(x = 1,\ y = 2,\ z = 3\). Check: \(1+2+3=6\) ✓, \(2+3=5\) ✓, \(z=3\) ✓.

title: Drills: solving 3×3 systems by elimination
text:
Drills
Write each system as an augmented matrix, eliminate to upper-triangular form showing each row operation, then back-substitute and check. Drills 1–3 are already triangular (back-substitution only). Drills 4–6 need one elimination step. The rest need two or more.
1. \[
\begin{aligned}
x + y + z &= 9 \\
y + z &= 7 \\
z &= 4
\end{aligned}
\]
2. \[
\begin{aligned}
x + 2y + z &= 10 \\
y - z &= 1 \\
z &= 2
\end{aligned}
\]
3. \[
\begin{aligned}
2x + y + z &= 11 \\
3y + z &= 8 \\
2z &= 6
\end{aligned}
\]
4. \[
\begin{aligned}
x + y + z &= 6 \\
2x + 3y + z &= 11 \\
z &= 3
\end{aligned}
\]
5. \[
\begin{aligned}
x + y + z &= 6 \\
x + 2y + z &= 8 \\
2y + 3z &= 13
\end{aligned}
\]
6. \[
\begin{aligned}
x - y + z &= 2 \\
2x + y + z &= 7 \\
y + 2z &= 5

\]
7. \[

x + 2y + 3z &= 14 \\
x + 4y + 9z &= 36
\end{aligned}
\]
8. \[

2x - y + z &= 3 \\
x + 2y - z &= 3
\end{aligned}
\]
9. \[

2x - y + z &= 7 \\
x + 2y + z &= 3
\end{aligned}
\]

x + 2y - z &= 2 \\
2x - y + z &= 3 \\
-x + y + 2z &= 6
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Drills: solving 3×3 systems by elimination
text:
Check in R
Verify any answer with solve. Build the coefficient matrix A row-by-row with byrow = TRUE, the right-hand side b, then call solve(A, b).
Drill 7:
A <- matrix(c(1, 1, 1,
              1, 2, 3,
              1, 4, 9), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(6, 14, 36)
solve(A, b)
#> [1] 1 2 3      # x = 1, y = 2, z = 3
Drill 9:
A <- matrix(c(1, 1, 1,
              2, -1, 1,
              1, 2, 1), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(4, 7, 3)
solve(A, b)
#> [1] 1 -1 4     # x = 1, y = -1, z = 4

title: Drills: solving 3×3 systems by elimination
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — drills 1–3 (already triangular)





No row operations needed. Read \(z\) from the bottom row, substitute up into the middle row to get \(y\), then into the top row to get \(x\). In drill 3 the bottom row is \(2z = 6\), so divide by 2 first.









Hint 2 — drills 4–6 (one elimination)





Only one entry below the diagonal is nonzero. In drill 4, use \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1\) to kill the \(2x\). In drill 5, use \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - R_1\). After that single step the matrix is triangular and you can back-substitute.









Hint 3 — drills 7–8





Two eliminations under column 1, then one under column 2. Keep the pivot (top-left \(1\)) and subtract the right multiple of \(R_1\) from \(R_2\) and \(R_3\) so both \(x\)-entries become 0. Then use the new \(R_2\) to clear the \(y\)-entry in \(R_3\).









Hint 4 — drills 9–10





The top-left pivot is already a \(1\). Clear column 1 with \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1\) and \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 \pm R_1\), then clear column 2 with a multiple of the new \(R_2\). The middle pivot may be negative (like \(-3\) in drill 9); that is fine — just keep track of signs. Drill 10 lands on simple fractions over \(14\), which is expected.

title: Drills: solving 3×3 systems by elimination
text:
Step-by-step solutions






Solutions






Drill 1
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 9 \\
0 & 1 & 1 & 7 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 4
\end{array}\right]
\] Already triangular. Back-substitute:

Row 3: \(z = 4\).
Row 2: \(y + z = 7 \Rightarrow y + 4 = 7 \Rightarrow y = 3\).
Row 1: \(x + y + z = 9 \Rightarrow x + 3 + 4 = 9 \Rightarrow x = 2\).

Answer: \(x = 2,\ y = 3,\ z = 4\). Check: \(2+3+4=9\) ✓, \(3+4=7\) ✓, \(z=4\) ✓.


Drill 2
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 2 & 1 & 10 \\
0 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 2
\end{array}\right]
\] Back-substitute:

Row 3: \(z = 2\).
Row 2: \(y - z = 1 \Rightarrow y - 2 = 1 \Rightarrow y = 3\).
Row 1: \(x + 2y + z = 10 \Rightarrow x + 6 + 2 = 10 \Rightarrow x = 2\).

Answer: \(x = 2,\ y = 3,\ z = 2\). Check: \(2 + 2(3) + 2 = 10\) ✓, \(3 - 2 = 1\) ✓, \(z=2\) ✓.


Drill 3
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
2 & 1 & 1 & 11 \\
0 & 3 & 1 & 8 \\
0 & 0 & 2 & 6
\end{array}\right]
\] Back-substitute:

Row 3: \(2z = 6 \Rightarrow z = 3\).
Row 2: \(3y + z = 8 \Rightarrow 3y + 3 = 8 \Rightarrow 3y = 5 \Rightarrow y = \tfrac{5}{3}\).
Row 1: \(2x + y + z = 11 \Rightarrow 2x + \tfrac{5}{3} + 3 = 11 \Rightarrow 2x = 11 - \tfrac{14}{3} = \tfrac{19}{3} \Rightarrow x = \tfrac{19}{6}\).

Answer: \(x = \tfrac{19}{6},\ y = \tfrac{5}{3},\ z = 3\). Check: \(2(\tfrac{19}{6}) + \tfrac{5}{3} + 3 = \tfrac{19}{3} + \tfrac{5}{3} + 3 = 8 + 3 = 11\) ✓, \(3(\tfrac{5}{3}) + 3 = 5 + 3 = 8\) ✓, \(2(3) = 6\) ✓.


Drill 4
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
2 & 3 & 1 & 11 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 3
\end{array}\right]
\] Eliminate the \(2\) in row 2, column 1: \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1\). \[
R_2:\ (2-2,\ 3-2,\ 1-2 \mid 11-12) = (0,\ 1,\ -1 \mid -1).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & -1 & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 3
\end{array}\right]
\] Back-substitute:

Row 3: \(z = 3\).
Row 2: \(y - z = -1 \Rightarrow y - 3 = -1 \Rightarrow y = 2\).
Row 1: \(x + y + z = 6 \Rightarrow x + 2 + 3 = 6 \Rightarrow x = 1\).

Answer: \(x = 1,\ y = 2,\ z = 3\). Check: \(1+2+3=6\) ✓, \(2(1)+3(2)+3 = 2+6+3 = 11\) ✓, \(z=3\) ✓.


Drill 5
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
1 & 2 & 1 & 8 \\
0 & 2 & 3 & 13
\end{array}\right]
\] Eliminate the \(1\) in row 2, column 1: \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - R_1\). \[
R_2:\ (1-1,\ 2-1,\ 1-1 \mid 8-6) = (0,\ 1,\ 0 \mid 2).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \\
0 & 2 & 3 & 13
\end{array}\right]
\] Now clear the \(2\) in row 3, column 2: \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 2R_2\). \[
R_3:\ (0,\ 2-2,\ 3-0 \mid 13-4) = (0,\ 0,\ 3 \mid 9).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \\
0 & 0 & 3 & 9
\end{array}\right]
\] Back-substitute:

Row 3: \(3z = 9 \Rightarrow z = 3\).
Row 2: \(y = 2\).
Row 1: \(x + y + z = 6 \Rightarrow x + 2 + 3 = 6 \Rightarrow x = 1\).

Answer: \(x = 1,\ y = 2,\ z = 3\). Check: \(1+2+3=6\) ✓, \(1+2(2)+3 = 1+4+3 = 8\) ✓, \(2(2)+3(3) = 4+9 = 13\) ✓.


Drill 6
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\
2 & 1 & 1 & 7 \\
0 & 1 & 2 & 5
\end{array}\right]
\] Eliminate the \(2\) in row 2, column 1: \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1\). \[
R_2:\ (2-2,\ 1-(-2),\ 1-2 \mid 7-4) = (0,\ 3,\ -1 \mid 3).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\
0 & 3 & -1 & 3 \\
0 & 1 & 2 & 5
\end{array}\right]
\] Clear the \(1\) in row 3, column 2: \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - \tfrac{1}{3}R_2\). \[
R_3:\ \left(0,\ 1-1,\ 2-(-\tfrac{1}{3}) \,\middle|\, 5-1\right) = \left(0,\ 0,\ \tfrac{7}{3} \,\middle|\, 4\right).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\
0 & 3 & -1 & 3 \\
0 & 0 & \tfrac{7}{3} & 4
\end{array}\right]
\] Back-substitute:

Row 3: \(\tfrac{7}{3}z = 4 \Rightarrow z = \tfrac{12}{7}\).
Row 2: \(3y - z = 3 \Rightarrow 3y = 3 + \tfrac{12}{7} = \tfrac{33}{7} \Rightarrow y = \tfrac{11}{7}\).
Row 1: \(x - y + z = 2 \Rightarrow x = 2 + y - z = 2 + \tfrac{11}{7} - \tfrac{12}{7} = 2 - \tfrac{1}{7} = \tfrac{13}{7}\).

Answer: \(x = \tfrac{13}{7},\ y = \tfrac{11}{7},\ z = \tfrac{12}{7}\). Check: \(\tfrac{13}{7} - \tfrac{11}{7} + \tfrac{12}{7} = \tfrac{14}{7} = 2\) ✓; \(2(\tfrac{13}{7}) + \tfrac{11}{7} + \tfrac{12}{7} = \tfrac{26+11+12}{7} = \tfrac{49}{7} = 7\) ✓; \(\tfrac{11}{7} + 2(\tfrac{12}{7}) = \tfrac{11+24}{7} = \tfrac{35}{7} = 5\) ✓.


Drill 7
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
1 & 2 & 3 & 14 \\
1 & 4 & 9 & 36
\end{array}\right]
\] Clear column 1: \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - R_1\) and \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_1\). \[
R_2:\ (0,\ 1,\ 2 \mid 8), \qquad R_3:\ (0,\ 3,\ 8 \mid 30).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 2 & 8 \\
0 & 3 & 8 & 30
\end{array}\right]
\] Clear column 2 below the pivot: \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 3R_2\). \[
R_3:\ (0,\ 3-3,\ 8-6 \mid 30-24) = (0,\ 0,\ 2 \mid 6).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 2 & 8 \\
0 & 0 & 2 & 6
\end{array}\right]
\] Back-substitute:

Row 3: \(2z = 6 \Rightarrow z = 3\).
Row 2: \(y + 2z = 8 \Rightarrow y + 6 = 8 \Rightarrow y = 2\).
Row 1: \(x + y + z = 6 \Rightarrow x + 2 + 3 = 6 \Rightarrow x = 1\).

Answer: \(x = 1,\ y = 2,\ z = 3\). Check: \(1+2+3=6\) ✓; \(1 + 2(2) + 3(3) = 1+4+9 = 14\) ✓; \(1 + 4(2) + 9(3) = 1+8+27 = 36\) ✓.


Drill 8
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
2 & -1 & 1 & 3 \\
1 & 2 & -1 & 3
\end{array}\right]
\] Clear column 1: \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1\) and \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_1\). \[
R_2:\ (0,\ -3,\ -1 \mid -9), \qquad R_3:\ (0,\ 1,\ -2 \mid -3).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
0 & -3 & -1 & -9 \\
0 & 1 & -2 & -3
\end{array}\right]
\] Clear column 2 below the pivot: \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 + \tfrac{1}{3}R_2\). \[
R_3:\ \left(0,\ 1 + \tfrac{1}{3}(-3),\ -2 + \tfrac{1}{3}(-1) \,\middle|\, -3 + \tfrac{1}{3}(-9)\right) = \left(0,\ 0,\ -\tfrac{7}{3} \,\middle|\, -6\right).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\
0 & -3 & -1 & -9 \\
0 & 0 & -\tfrac{7}{3} & -6
\end{array}\right]
\] Back-substitute:

Row 3: \(-\tfrac{7}{3}z = -6 \Rightarrow z = \tfrac{18}{7}\).
Row 2: \(-3y - z = -9 \Rightarrow -3y = -9 + \tfrac{18}{7} = -\tfrac{45}{7} \Rightarrow y = \tfrac{15}{7}\).
Row 1: \(x + y + z = 6 \Rightarrow x = 6 - \tfrac{15}{7} - \tfrac{18}{7} = 6 - \tfrac{33}{7} = \tfrac{9}{7}\).

Answer: \(x = \tfrac{9}{7},\ y = \tfrac{15}{7},\ z = \tfrac{18}{7}\). Check: \(\tfrac{9+15+18}{7} = \tfrac{42}{7} = 6\) ✓; \(2(\tfrac{9}{7}) - \tfrac{15}{7} + \tfrac{18}{7} = \tfrac{18-15+18}{7} = \tfrac{21}{7} = 3\) ✓; \(\tfrac{9}{7} + 2(\tfrac{15}{7}) - \tfrac{18}{7} = \tfrac{9+30-18}{7} = \tfrac{21}{7} = 3\) ✓.


Drill 9
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 4 \\
2 & -1 & 1 & 7 \\
1 & 2 & 1 & 3
\end{array}\right]
\] Clear column 1: \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1\) and \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_1\). \[
R_2:\ (2-2,\ -1-2,\ 1-2 \mid 7-8) = (0,\ -3,\ -1 \mid -1),
\] \[
R_3:\ (1-1,\ 2-1,\ 1-1 \mid 3-4) = (0,\ 1,\ 0 \mid -1).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 4 \\
0 & -3 & -1 & -1 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & -1
\end{array}\right]
\] Clear column 2 below the pivot: \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 + \tfrac{1}{3}R_2\). \[
R_3:\ \left(0,\ 1 + \tfrac{1}{3}(-3),\ 0 + \tfrac{1}{3}(-1) \,\middle|\, -1 + \tfrac{1}{3}(-1)\right) = \left(0,\ 0,\ -\tfrac{1}{3} \,\middle|\, -\tfrac{4}{3}\right).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 4 \\
0 & -3 & -1 & -1 \\
0 & 0 & -\tfrac{1}{3} & -\tfrac{4}{3}
\end{array}\right]
\] Back-substitute:

Row 3: \(-\tfrac{1}{3}z = -\tfrac{4}{3} \Rightarrow z = 4\).
Row 2: \(-3y - z = -1 \Rightarrow -3y - 4 = -1 \Rightarrow -3y = 3 \Rightarrow y = -1\).
Row 1: \(x + y + z = 4 \Rightarrow x - 1 + 4 = 4 \Rightarrow x = 1\).

Answer: \(x = 1,\ y = -1,\ z = 4\). Check: \(1 + (-1) + 4 = 4\) ✓; \(2(1) - (-1) + 4 = 2 + 1 + 4 = 7\) ✓; \(1 + 2(-1) + 4 = 1 - 2 + 4 = 3\) ✓.


Drill 10
\[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 2 & -1 & 2 \\
2 & -1 & 1 & 3 \\
-1 & 1 & 2 & 6
\end{array}\right]
\] Clear column 1: \(R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1\) and \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 + R_1\). \[
R_2:\ (0,\ -5,\ 3 \mid -1), \qquad R_3:\ (0,\ 3,\ 1 \mid 8).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 2 & -1 & 2 \\
0 & -5 & 3 & -1 \\
0 & 3 & 1 & 8
\end{array}\right]
\] Clear column 2 below the pivot: \(R_3 \leftarrow R_3 + \tfrac{3}{5}R_2\). \[
R_3:\ \left(0,\ 3 + \tfrac{3}{5}(-5),\ 1 + \tfrac{3}{5}(3) \,\middle|\, 8 + \tfrac{3}{5}(-1)\right) = \left(0,\ 0,\ \tfrac{14}{5} \,\middle|\, \tfrac{37}{5}\right).
\] \[
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 2 & -1 & 2 \\
0 & -5 & 3 & -1 \\
0 & 0 & \tfrac{14}{5} & \tfrac{37}{5}
\end{array}\right]
\] Back-substitute:

Row 3: \(\tfrac{14}{5}z = \tfrac{37}{5} \Rightarrow z = \tfrac{37}{14}\).
Row 2: \(-5y + 3z = -1 \Rightarrow -5y = -1 - 3(\tfrac{37}{14}) = -1 - \tfrac{111}{14} = -\tfrac{125}{14} \Rightarrow y = \tfrac{125}{70} = \tfrac{25}{14}\).
Row 1: \(x + 2y - z = 2 \Rightarrow x = 2 - 2(\tfrac{25}{14}) + \tfrac{37}{14} = 2 - \tfrac{50}{14} + \tfrac{37}{14} = 2 - \tfrac{13}{14} = \tfrac{15}{14}\).

Answer: \(x = \tfrac{15}{14},\ y = \tfrac{25}{14},\ z = \tfrac{37}{14}\). Check: (row 1) \(\tfrac{15}{14} + 2(\tfrac{25}{14}) - \tfrac{37}{14} = \tfrac{15 + 50 - 37}{14} = \tfrac{28}{14} = 2\) ✓; (row 2) \(2(\tfrac{15}{14}) - \tfrac{25}{14} + \tfrac{37}{14} = \tfrac{30 - 25 + 37}{14} = \tfrac{42}{14} = 3\) ✓; (row 3) \(-\tfrac{15}{14} + \tfrac{25}{14} + 2(\tfrac{37}{14}) = \tfrac{-15 + 25 + 74}{14} = \tfrac{84}{14} = 6\) ✓.

title: Drills: the 2×2 inverse
text:
Compute the inverse of a \(2\times2\) matrix by row reduction on the augmented matrix \([\,A \mid I\,]\).
Check your answer by confirming \(A A^{-1} = I\).
Solve a small system \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) using \(\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\).
Recognise a singular matrix that has no inverse: row reduction gives a row of zeros on the left.

title: Drills: the 2×2 inverse
text:
Compute the inverse of a \(2\times2\) matrix by row reduction on the augmented matrix \([\,A \mid I\,]\).
Check your answer by confirming \(A A^{-1} = I\).
Solve a small system \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) using \(\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\).
Recognise a singular matrix that has no inverse: row reduction gives a row of zeros on the left.

title: Drills: the 2×2 inverse
text:
The method
The identity matrix \(I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) is the “1” of matrices: \(A A^{-1} = I\) for any invertible \(A\).
To find \(A^{-1}\), write \(A\) and \(I\) side by side in one augmented matrix \([\,A \mid I\,]\), the same shorthand as \([\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]\) in Linear systems by hand, now with two columns on the right. Then use row operations until the left half is \(I\). The right half is then \(A^{-1}\):
\[
[\,A \mid I\,] \;\longrightarrow\; [\,I \mid A^{-1}\,].
\]
The allowed row operations are the ones you already know:

Add a multiple of one row to another row (e.g. R2 \(-\) 2R1).
Multiply a row by a nonzero number (e.g. \(\tfrac12\)R1).
Swap two rows (R1 \(\leftrightarrow\) R2).

A good order for a \(2\times2\): make a zero below the diagonal, then make the diagonal entries \(1\), then make a zero above the diagonal.
Every operation is done to the whole row, both halves. Why it works: each row operation is the same as multiplying from the left by some matrix. When the left half has turned from \(A\) into \(I\), the product of all those matrices is \(A^{-1}\), and the right half, which started as \(I\), has been multiplied by exactly that product.
Worked example. \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
\[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,\frac12\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac12 & -\tfrac12 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;2\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 2 \end{array}\right]
\]
\[
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 0 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 2 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\frac12\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 2 \end{array}\right]
\]
The left half is \(I\), so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
Check: \(A A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I.\) Correct.
No inverse (singular). If the columns of \(A\) are parallel (one row is a multiple of the other), row reduction produces a row of zeros on the left. A zero row can never become a row of \(I\), so there is no inverse. For example, \(\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,2\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 1 \end{array}\right]\): stop here. In R, solve() gives an error for such a matrix.






Bonus shortcut (not for exam)



For a \(2\times2\) there is also a formula, using the determinant \(ad - bc\): \[
A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}.
\] Swap \(a\) and \(d\), negate \(b\) and \(c\), divide every entry by \(ad - bc\). If \(ad - bc = 0\) the matrix is singular. For the worked example, \(ad - bc = 2 - 1 = 1\), giving the same inverse. Bonus material: you do not need to memorise determinants for the exam.

title: Drills: the 2×2 inverse
text:
Drills
Find the inverse by row-reducing \([\,A \mid I\,]\) (all come out with simple numbers).

title: Drills: the 2×2 inverse
text:
Check in R
The inverse is computed by solve with a single argument; the matrix product uses %*%. To solve \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) directly, pass both: solve(A, b).
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 1), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
solve(A)
#      [,1] [,2]
# [1,]    1   -1
# [2,]   -1    2

A %*% solve(A)
#      [,1] [,2]
# [1,]    1    0
# [2,]    0    1      (the identity I)

b <- c(3, 2)
solve(A, b)
# [1] 1 1            (so x1 = 1, x2 = 1)

S <- matrix(c(1, 2,
              2, 4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
solve(S)
# Error: Lapack routine dgesv: system is exactly singular   (parallel columns, no inverse)

title: Drills: the 2×2 inverse
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — the order of row operations





Start from \([\,A \mid I\,]\). (1) Make the entry below the diagonal zero (R2 minus a multiple of R1; swap rows first if the top-left entry is \(0\) or awkward). (2) Divide each row by its diagonal entry, so the diagonal is \(1\). (3) Make the entry above the diagonal zero (R1 minus a multiple of R2). Always apply each operation to all four entries of the row.









Hint 2 — diagonal matrices





For \(\begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & d \end{bmatrix}\) only step (2) is needed: multiply R1 by \(1/a\) and R2 by \(1/d\). The inverse is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1/a & 0 \\ 0 & 1/d \end{bmatrix}\); the off-diagonal zeros stay zero.









Hint 3 — spotting a singular matrix





If one row of \(A\) is a multiple of the other (equivalently, the columns are parallel), subtracting that multiple gives a row of zeros on the left. A zero row cannot be turned into a row of \(I\): stop, there is no inverse.









Hint 4 — verifying the inverse





Row \(i\) times column \(j\): multiply matching entries and add. The diagonal products should give \(1\) and the off-diagonal should give \(0\).









Hint 5 — solving with the inverse





\(\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}\) is a matrix-times-vector product. Top entry of \(\mathbf{x}\) = (first row of \(A^{-1}\)) \(\cdot \mathbf{b}\); bottom entry = (second row) \(\cdot \mathbf{b}\).

title: Drills: the 2×2 inverse
text:
Step-by-step solutions






Solutions





Drill 1. \([\,I \mid I\,]\) is already finished: the left half is \(I\), so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.\) The identity is its own inverse.
Drill 2. \[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\frac12\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \tfrac12 \end{array}\right],
\qquad
A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Drill 3. \[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\frac12\text{R1},\ \frac15\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & \tfrac12 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \tfrac15 \end{array}\right],
\qquad
A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{5} \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Drill 4. Already zero below the diagonal and \(1\)s on it; only the entry above remains. \[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,2\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right],
\qquad
A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Drill 5. A shortcut first: R1 \(-\) R2 gives a \(1\) in the top-left corner. \[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 3 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,2\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3 \end{array}\right],
\] so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}.\)
Drill 6. \[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 2 \end{array}\right],
\] so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.\)
Drill 7. Swap the rows first, so the top-left entry is \(1\). \[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 4 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,\leftrightarrow\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 1 & 0 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,4\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & -4 \end{array}\right]
\] \[
\xrightarrow{\;-\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 4 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 4 \end{array}\right],
\] so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}.\)
Drill 8. \[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 3 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,2\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & 3 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\frac12\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \tfrac32 \end{array}\right],
\] so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & \tfrac{3}{2} \end{bmatrix}.\)
Drill 9. \[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R2}\,-\,2\text{R1}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 1 \end{array}\right].
\] The left half has a row of zeros, which can never become \((0\ 1)\). No inverse: the matrix is singular (the second row is \(2\times\) the first; the columns \((1,2)\) and \((2,4)\) are parallel).
Drill 10. \[
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 3 & 6 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\;\text{R1}\,-\,3\text{R2}\;}
\left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 0 & 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right].
\] A zero row on the left again: no inverse (the first row is \(3\times\) the second).
Drill 11. Using \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\): \[
A A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
(3)(1)+(1)(-2) & (3)(-1)+(1)(3) \\
(2)(1)+(1)(-2) & (2)(-1)+(1)(3)
\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I. \checkmark
\]
Drill 12. Using \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\): \[
A A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}
(2)(2)+(1)(-3) & (2)(-1)+(1)(2) \\
(3)(2)+(2)(-3) & (3)(-1)+(2)(2)
\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I. \checkmark
\]
Drill 13. This \(A\) is the worked example, so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \[
\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} (1)(3)+(-1)(2) \\ (-1)(3)+(2)(2) \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
\] So \(x_1 = 1,\ x_2 = 1\).
Drill 14. This \(A\) is drill 4, so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \[
\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} (1)(5)+(-2)(2) \\ (0)(5)+(1)(2) \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.
\] So \(x_1 = 1,\ x_2 = 2\).
Drill 15. This \(A\) is drill 5, so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \[
\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} (1)(4)+(-1)(3) \\ (-2)(4)+(3)(3) \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
\] So \(x_1 = 1,\ x_2 = 1\). (You could also row-reduce \([\,A \mid \mathbf{b}\,]\) directly, as in Linear systems by hand; the answer is the same.)

title: Course syllabus — 3MB00A
text:
Summary of the official syllabus, which is the binding version: https://www.umu.se/en/education/syllabus/3mb00a/



English title: Quantitative Biology and Integrative Biology
Swedish title: Kvantitativ biologi och integrativ omik
Course code: 3MB00A
Credits: 7.5 ECTS
Education level: Second cycle
Main field of study: Bioinformatics (second cycle, entry-level requirements only)
Grading scale: Three-grade scale (U / G / VG)
Responsible department: Department of Molecular Biology
Established: 2026-01-21 by the education board of the Faculty of Medicine
Validity: 2026-03-09 and until further notice




The course covers basic mathematical and statistical methods that are widely used in modern bioinformatics.

Linear algebra: matrices, vectors and eigenvalues, applied to observable and hidden Markov chains.
Changing bases, with examples from image and signal analysis.
Coordinate transformations and dimensional reduction (PCA and OLS) for high-dimensional data.
Bayesian statistics, including fitting complex models with tools such as RSTAN.
Statistical models common in bioinformatics, in particular the Poisson and negative binomial distributions.
Multilinear and nonlinear latent space models, with applications in chemometrics and single-cell analysis.




Knowledge and understanding. Students should be able to:

explain where common statistical distributions come from
contrast Bayesian and frequentist statistics
describe the solution spaces of over- and underdetermined linear systems
explain memoryless processes
distinguish linear from nonlinear systems
define a latent space

Skills and abilities. Students should be able to:

solve systems of linear equations
model biological problems with Markov chains
analyse large-scale data in latent spaces, with linear and nonlinear methods
build hierarchical models with alternative distributions, in particular Poisson and negative binomial
apply chemometrics and single-cell methods to large datasets

Judgement and approach. Students should be able to:

assess how valid the course’s mathematical formulations are for describing biological systems




90 ECTS from completed courses in biology, biomedicine, molecular biology, molecular ecology, molecular evolution, genetics, or related subjects; 5 credits in programming in R or Python.



Campus-based, with lectures (pre-recorded or on site) and teacher-led sessions for guidance on the assignments. Taught in English (Swedish if no participant needs English). Students need their own computer.




An individual written on-campus exam, graded Fail (U), Pass (G) or Pass with distinction (VG). The exam grade is the course grade.
The course coordinator may award bonus points for optional activities, up to 10 % of the exam score. Which activities count, and how, is announced at the start of the course.
After two failed attempts, a student may request a new examiner from the Deputy Head of the Department of Molecular Biology.
The examiner may adapt the exam format to a student’s needs, within the learning outcomes. Requests must be made at least 10 working days before the exam.




If the syllabus expires or is substantially revised, students keep at least three exam opportunities under the original syllabus, for up to two years.



The reading list is not available online; contact the department.
